nodes.name: "Interest Expense" in the Management Income Statement
aliases: Interest Expense in Managerial Income Statement
nodes.definition: The interest expense in the management income statement is a composite metric calculated as the difference between interest on financial liabilities and income from financial assets. It is not an original accounting item and is used to reflect the net cost generated by a company's financial activities, serving as a key component in calculating pre-tax operating profit.

formulas.source_formula: "Interest Expense" in the Management Income Statement = Interest on Financial Liabilities - Income from Financial Assets

nodes.name: 1%/10 Net 30
nodes.definition: 1%/10 net 30 are trade credit terms indicating the buyer may take a 1% cash discount if payment is made within 10 days; otherwise, the net (full) invoice amount is due within 30 days. These terms affect cash discounts recognition, accounts payable management, the cost of trade credit, and working capital efficiency.

nodes.name: 10-Year Treasury Yield
nodes.definition: The 10-year Treasury yield refers to the annualized return investors can obtain by holding a 10-year Treasury bond until maturity, commonly regarded as a key benchmark for the risk-free rate and a barometer for long-term market interest rates.

nodes.name: 12-Period Exponential Moving Average of Closing Prices
nodes.definition: The 12-period exponential moving average of closing prices is a technical analysis indicator calculated by applying a weighted average to the closing prices of the most recent twelve trading periods, where more recent prices are assigned higher weights, thereby more sensitively reflecting the latest trend in stock price movements.

nodes.name: 125% Loan
nodes.definition: A 125% loan is a high loan-to-value (LTV) financing product that allows a borrower to obtain a loan amount up to 125% of a property's appraised value. The loan amount is determined by multiplying the property's appraised value by the LTV ratio (expressed as a decimal, e.g., 1.25 for 125%), and is commonly used in mortgage or refinancing scenarios; such loans entail elevated credit risk and require robust underwriting.

nodes.name: 183-Day Rule
nodes.definition: The 183-Day Rule, under the IRS Substantial Presence Test, determines U.S. tax residency for noncitizens by evaluating physical presence over a three-year period. An individual is considered a U.S. tax resident if they are present at least 31 days in the current year and their weighted presence equals or exceeds 183 days, calculated as all days in the current year plus one-third of the days in the preceding year and one-sixth of the days in the year before that.

nodes.name: 2-1 Buydown
nodes.definition: A 2-1 buydown is a temporary interest rate reduction structure on a fixed-rate mortgage where the interest rate is reduced by 2 percentage points in the first year and by 1 percentage point in the second year before reverting to the note rate for the remainder of the term. It lowers initial monthly payments and is typically funded through prepaid buydown contributions by the borrower, seller, or builder.

nodes.name: 25% Rule
nodes.definition: The 25% rule is an intellectual property royalty guideline where the royalty amount payable to the licensor is calculated as a fixed percentage—typically 25%—of the licensee’s gross profit from sales of the protected product or service. In practice, parties may agree on different percentages depending on negotiations and industry norms.

nodes.name: 3-2-1 Buydown Savings
aliases: 抵押贷款利率买断节省
nodes.definition: 3-2-1 buydown savings represent the total interest cost avoided during the initial three years of a mortgage with a 3-2-1 rate buydown. Under a typical 3-2-1 structure, the interest rate is reduced by 3 percentage points in year 1, 2 percentage points in year 2, and 1 percentage point in year 3, usually funded by a seller or lender subsidy. When approximated using interest-only payments, the total savings equal the loan principal multiplied by the sum of the annual rate reductions over the buydown period.

nodes.name: 3/27 Adjustable-Rate Mortgage (ARM)
nodes.definition: A 3/27 Adjustable-Rate Mortgage (ARM) is a hybrid mortgage with an initial fixed interest rate period of 3 years followed by 27 years of variable-rate adjustments tied to a market index plus a lender margin. The monthly payment during the fixed period is determined by an amortizing loan payment formula, and after the reset, the payment is recalculated using the adjusted rate (index rate + margin). These calculations exclude taxes, insurance, and fees and assume level payments over the remaining term.

nodes.name: 360-Day Interest Convention
nodes.definition: The 360-day interest convention is a widely used day-count basis in the financial industry. It assumes a year has 360 days and a month has 30 days to simplify interest calculations, commonly applied to interest accruals for bank loans, bonds, commercial paper, and other financial instruments.

nodes.name: 360-Degree Assessment Score
nodes.definition: The 360-degree assessment score is a comprehensive performance evaluation result. It is a final calculated score obtained by collecting quantitative ratings on an individual's work capabilities, attitudes, and performance across multiple dimensions from various stakeholders closely related to the individual's work (such as supervisors, peers, subordinates, clients, etc.).

nodes.name: 3P Oil Reserves
nodes.definition: 3P oil reserves represent the total estimated quantity of hydrocarbons recoverable from known accumulations under existing economic and operating conditions, aggregating Proven (≈90% confidence), Probable (≈50% confidence), and Possible (≈10% confidence) reserves. This metric is used in upstream oil and gas reporting, valuation, and resource planning to indicate the full spectrum of reserve certainty.

formulas.source_formula: 3P Oil Reserves = Proven Reserves + Probable Reserves + Possible Reserves

nodes.name: 5-6 Hybrid Adjustable-Rate Mortgage (5-6 Hybrid ARM)
aliases: 5-6 混合型可调整利率抵押贷款
混合型可调利率抵押贷款
nodes.definition: A 5-6 Hybrid Adjustable-Rate Mortgage (5-6 Hybrid ARM) features an initial fixed interest rate period of five years, followed by rate adjustments every six months based on a designated index plus a margin (the fully indexed rate). After the fixed period, monthly payments are recalculated using the fully indexed rate and the remaining term, following the standard amortizing loan payment formula with monthly compounding.

nodes.name: 52-Week High/Low
nodes.definition: The 52-week high/low represents the highest and lowest closing prices a security has reached over the past 52 weeks (approximately one year). It is widely used in technical analysis to identify resistance and support levels, gauge momentum, and contextualize current price relative to its recent historical extremes.

formulas.source_formula: 52-Week Low = min(Daily Closing Prices (Past 52 Weeks))

nodes.name: 52-Week Range
nodes.definition: The 52-week range represents the highest and lowest trading prices of a security over the past 52 weeks. Investors assess a security's current position within this range using Percentage Below 52-Week High and Percentage Above 52-Week Low, which quantify how far the current price is from the 52-week high and low, respectively. These metrics support market context, momentum assessment, and risk awareness, assuming the 52-week high and low are positive and measured for the same security.

nodes.name: 80-10-10 Mortgage
nodes.definition: An 80-10-10 mortgage is a piggyback structure where a borrower finances 80% of the home value with a first mortgage, 10% with a second mortgage, and makes a 10% down payment. Monthly payments for each loan are determined using the standard amortizing loan formula based on the loan amount, interest rate, and term.

nodes.name: 90/10 Strategy
nodes.definition: The 90/10 strategy is an asset allocation approach that invests approximately 90% of a portfolio in equities and 10% in bonds. The portfolio's expected return is computed as the weighted average of the constituent asset class returns, where weights represent the allocation proportions. This framework assumes allocations sum to 100% and returns are expressed as decimals.

nodes.name: A-Share Price
nodes.definition: A-Share price refers to the transaction price of A-shares listed and traded on the secondary markets of the Shanghai Stock Exchange and Shenzhen Stock Exchange in mainland China. It is directly determined by market supply and demand and serves as fundamental data reflecting the real-time value of a stock.

formulas.source_formula: ARIMA Model = AR(p) + I(d) + MA(q)
AUM Fee = Assets Under Management × AUM Fee Percentage

nodes.name: Abnormal Return
nodes.definition: Abnormal return is the difference between an investment's realized (actual) return and its expected return based on a benchmark or asset pricing model (e.g., CAPM). It is used to assess performance relative to expectations, commonly in event studies and risk-adjusted performance evaluation.

formulas.source_formula: Abnormal Return = Realized Return - Expected Return
supporting_source_formulas: Abnormal Return = Actual Return - Expected Return
Abnormal Return = Realized Return - Expected Return

nodes.name: Abscissa
nodes.definition: The abscissa is the numerical value in a Cartesian coordinate system that represents the horizontal position of a point. It is typically used together with the ordinate (Y-axis) to precisely determine the location of a point on a plane. In charts, the abscissa is often used to represent time, progress, or independent variables.

nodes.name: Absolute Present Value of Negative Cash Flows
Absolute Return
nodes.definition: Absolute return is the unbenchmarked percentage change in the value of an investment over a period, calculated solely from its initial and final values, without reference to a benchmark or the length of the holding period.

formulas.source_formula: Absolute Return (%) = (Final Value - Initial Value) ÷ Initial Value × 100%

nodes.name: Absorption Cost per Unit
nodes.definition: Absorption cost per unit is the product cost calculated under absorption costing, which assigns all manufacturing costs—direct materials, direct labor, variable manufacturing overhead, and fixed manufacturing overhead—to units produced. It is computed as total manufacturing costs divided by units produced and is used for inventory valuation and cost of goods under GAAP/IFRS.

formulas.source_formula: Absorption Cost per Unit = (Direct Labor + Direct Materials + Variable Manufacturing Overhead + Fixed Manufacturing Overhead) ÷ Units Produced

nodes.name: Absorption Rate
nodes.definition: Absorption rate measures the speed at which available real estate inventory is sold over a specified period, indicating market demand and liquidity. It is commonly expressed as a percentage of homes sold relative to homes available and helps assess whether the market favors sellers or buyers.

formulas.source_formula: Absorption Rate = (Homes Sold ÷ Homes Available) × 100

nodes.name: Accelerated Depreciation
nodes.definition: Accelerated depreciation allocates a higher portion of an asset's cost to earlier periods to reflect faster consumption of economic benefits. Under the Double-Declining Balance (DDB) method, the depreciation rate equals twice the straight-line rate and is applied to the beginning book value each year. This approach results in higher depreciation expense in early years and lower expense later. The referenced function assumes no salvage value and applies a full year's depreciation in the first year.

nodes.name: Acceptable Margin of Error
nodes.definition: Acceptable margin of error refers to a predetermined error threshold established based on the cost-benefit principle, the importance of the application scenario, and professional judgment in activities such as statistical analysis, audit sampling, quality control, and market research. Errors within this threshold are considered tolerable or acceptable and will not significantly impact the reliability of decisions or conclusions.

nodes.name: Accident Severity
nodes.definition: Accident severity refers to the degree of seriousness of the consequences caused by an accident, typically measured by personnel casualties (e.g., fatalities, serious injuries), economic losses (direct and indirect), or specific severity indices. It is a key indicator for assessing risk levels and accident impact.

nodes.name: Account Balance
nodes.definition: Account balance refers to the remaining amount in the ledger of a specific accounting account (such as cash, bank deposits, accounts receivable, etc.) at a particular point in time (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It directly reflects the final result of the account after a series of transaction increases and decreases, serving as fundamental data for preparing financial statements.

nodes.name: Accounting Equation
nodes.definition: The accounting equation states that total assets equal total liabilities plus shareholders' equity. This function applies a rearranged form of the equation to compute shareholders' equity as the residual interest in the assets of the entity after deducting liabilities.

nodes.name: Accounting Expenses
nodes.definition: Accounting expenses typically refer to various expense items incurred by an enterprise in its daily business operations due to accounting, bookkeeping, financial reporting, and related financial transactions (such as interest payments, handling fees, exchange gains/losses, etc.).

nodes.name: Accounting Period
nodes.definition: The accounting period is a fundamental accounting assumption that artificially divides a company's continuous business operations into successive, equal-length time intervals (such as a year, a quarter, or a month). This division facilitates the periodic (rather than waiting until the ultimate cessation of operations) settlement of accounts, calculation of profit or loss, and preparation of financial statements, thereby timely reflecting the company's financial position and operating results.

nodes.name: Accounting Profit
nodes.definition: Accounting profit refers to the operating results calculated according to accounting standards by matching revenues earned during a specific period with the expenses and losses incurred to generate those revenues. It serves as the basis for calculating taxable income and income tax expense.

formulas.source_formula: Accounting Profit = Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses

Accounting Profit = Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Business Taxes and Surcharges - Selling Expenses - Administrative Expenses - Financial Expenses - R&D Expenses - Asset Impairment Losses - Credit Impairment Losses + Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Investment Income + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses

nodes.name: Accounting Rate of Return
nodes.definition: Accounting Rate of Return is a financial metric used in investment decision-making to evaluate project profitability. It is typically expressed as a percentage of net profit to average capital employed, or average annual net income to original investment, reflecting the accounting-level performance of investment returns.

formulas.source_formula: Accounting Rate of Return = Average Annual Profit ÷ Initial Investment

nodes.name: Accounting Standards Codification
nodes.definition: Accounting Standards Codification is a systematic, codified collection of accounting rules and standards used to guide and regulate how enterprises prepare and present their financial statements, ensuring comparability, reliability, and transparency of financial information. It is not a calculated metric itself, but rather an authoritative framework defining fundamental tasks such as accounting items, recognition, measurement, recording, and disclosure.

nodes.name: Accounting Subsidy Treatment
nodes.definition: Accounting subsidy treatment refers to the specific accounting process in accounting practice for recognizing, measuring, and recording various subsidy payments received by an enterprise (such as government grants, position subsidies, etc.). It involves allocating the subsidy amount to the correct accounting accounts (such as non-operating income, deferred income, administrative expenses, etc.) based on its nature and purpose, and completing the corresponding accounting entries.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable
nodes.definition: Accounts Payable (AP) refers to the amount a company owes to suppliers for goods or services received, recorded as a current liability on the balance sheet. It represents short-term obligations typically due within one year, distinct from formal debt instruments such as notes payable.

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Payable (Ending) = Accounts Payable (Beginning) - Payment on Account

nodes.name: Accounts Payable - Prior Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Payable - Prior Period refers to the outstanding balance owed to suppliers at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) for business activities including the purchase of materials, goods, or receipt of services.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts payable balance refers to the total amount owed by a company to its suppliers or creditors at a specific point in time (typically at the end of an accounting period) for the purchase of goods, receipt of services, or other operational activities, representing a current liability of the enterprise.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Beginning Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts Payable Beginning Balance refers to the total amount of unpaid invoices or service fees owed to suppliers or creditors at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the short-term payment obligations assumed by the enterprise at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts Payable Ending Balance refers to the total amount owed to suppliers or service providers for the purchase of materials, goods, or services received but not yet paid by the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end).

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Opening Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts Payable Opening Balance refers to the total book value of debts, such as unpaid amounts for goods purchased or services received from suppliers or creditors, that a company has not yet paid as of the first day of a fiscal year (or reporting period). It reflects the payment obligations assumed by the company at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Subsidiary Ledger Ending Debit Balance
aliases: AP Detail Debit Balance at Period End
Accounts Payable Subsidiary Ledger Debit Ending Balance
应付账款借方明细余额

nodes.definition: The accounts payable subsidiary ledger ending debit balance refers to the aggregate amount of debit balances across all subsidiary accounts in the accounts payable subsidiary ledger at the end of an accounting period. It typically indicates that prepayments made to suppliers exceed the actual amounts payable for goods or services. When preparing the balance sheet, this amount must be reclassified to the 'Prepaid Expenses' asset account.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Turnover
aliases: 应付账款周转天数倒数
nodes.definition: Accounts Payable Turnover is a financial metric that measures the efficiency with which a company pays its suppliers. It indicates the average number of times accounts payable are converted into cash within a given period (typically one year). A higher turnover generally indicates that the company pays its suppliers more quickly or utilizes supplier credit terms more effectively.

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Turnover Period
nodes.definition: The Accounts Payable Turnover Period, also known as Days Payable Outstanding (DPO) or Average Payment Period, measures how long a company takes to pay its suppliers. It falls under the analysis of operational efficiency and is used in working capital management.

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Payable Turnover Period = Average Accounts Payable × 360 ÷ Cost of Sales
Accounts Payable Turnover Period = Annual Average Accounts Payable × 365 ÷ Annual Cost of Sales

nodes.name: Accounts Payable Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: The Accounts Payable Turnover Ratio is a financial ratio that measures the turnover speed of accounts payable within a specific period, reflecting a company's ability to pay supplier invoices and the efficiency of fund utilization. It is commonly used to evaluate the management level of accounts payable in business operations and short-term solvency.

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Payable Turnover Ratio = Net Cost of Main Business ÷ Average Accounts Payable Balance × 100%
Accounts Payable Turnover Ratio = Cost of Main Business ÷ Average Accounts Payable Balance × 100%
Accounts Payable Turnover Ratio = (Cost of Main Business + Ending Inventory Cost - Beginning Inventory Cost) ÷ Average Accounts Payable × 100%

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Accounts receivable refers to the amounts owed to a company by its customers for goods sold or services rendered in the normal course of business. It is typically classified as a current asset and represents the amount customers owe the company due to credit transactions.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable - Prior Period
aliases: Accounts Receivable at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable - Prior Period refers to the total amount of outstanding customer debts carried forward from the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) at the beginning of the current accounting period. It is a fundamental item on the balance sheet, directly derived from the ending balance of the prior period.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Accrued Interest
aliases: 应收账款占用资金利息
nodes.definition: Accounts receivable accrued interest refers to the potential interest income that a company forgoes when funds are tied up in accounts receivable due to credit sales (sales on account), as these funds cannot be immediately collected and used for other investments (such as bank deposits or wealth management products), or the cost the company incurs to raise these funds to maintain operations. It measures the cost of capital tied up due to credit policies.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Aging
nodes.definition: Accounts receivable aging is an analytical method that categorizes outstanding accounts receivable by the length of time they have been unpaid (age buckets) to assess credit risk and estimate the allowance for doubtful accounts. Using historical non-collection rates for each age bucket, the estimated uncollectible receivables are computed as the sum of each bucket's balance multiplied by its corresponding uncollectible rate.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts receivable balance refers to the net amount of accounts receivable that a company has not yet collected at a specific point in time (typically at period-end), reflecting the scale of the company's receivables assets. In financial statements, it is usually calculated based on the opening balance, transaction amounts during the period, or detailed account balances and allowance for doubtful accounts, and is presented as the net amount after deducting the allowance for doubtful accounts.

operands.metric: Debit Balance of Accounts Receivable Detailed Accounts
Debit Balance of Advance Receipts Detailed Accounts
Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Receivable Balance = Debit Balance of Accounts Receivable Detailed Accounts + Debit Balance of Advance Receipts Detailed Accounts - Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

operands.metric: Accounts Receivable at Previous Period End

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Receivable Balance = Opening Accounts Receivable Balance + Debit Transactions During the Period - Credit Transactions During the Period

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Balance at Previous Period End
aliases: Accounts Receivable Balance of Prior Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Balance at Previous Period End refers to the total book value of customer credit sales that remain uncollected at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It serves as the starting point for calculating changes in accounts receivable and analyzing collection efficiency in the current period.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Balance for the Current Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Balance for the Current Period refers to the original book value of customer credit sales that have not yet been collected, directly derived from the accounting records at the end of the current accounting period (e.g., month, quarter, or year). It reflects the company's right to collect payments from customers at the end of the reporting period.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Beginning Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Beginning Balance refers to the total book value of receivables from customers for goods sold or services rendered that have not yet been collected at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as the basis for calculating changes in accounts receivable during the period and the ending balance.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Collection Amount
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Collection Amount refers to the actual amount of accounts receivable collected by an enterprise during a specific accounting period (usually one year), typically based on the credit side turnover of the accounts receivable account, net of written-off bad debt losses.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Collection Amount from Previous Period
aliases: Accounts Receivable Collected in Previous Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Collection Amount from Previous Period refers to the actual amount of accounts receivable collected by an enterprise during the last accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It reflects the enterprise's ability to successfully convert credit sales-generated receivables into cash in the preceding timeframe and is an important indicator for assessing the efficiency of accounts receivable management and the status of cash flow.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Collections
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Collections refer to the total amount of accounts receivable recovered by a company during a specific accounting period (typically one fiscal year) through actual cash payments received from customers. It reflects the cash recovery situation of the company's accounts receivable and is a key component in calculating financial metrics such as the accounts receivable collection rate.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Ending Balance refers to the book value of receivables arising from the sale of goods or provision of services that have not yet been collected from customers at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It reflects the amount of the company's claims against customers at the reporting date.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Ending Debit Balance
aliases: 期末应收账款借方余额
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Ending Debit Balance refers to the debit balance shown in the general ledger or subsidiary ledger under the 'Accounts Receivable' account at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It represents the total amount of funds from sales of goods or services rendered that the enterprise is entitled to collect from customers but has not yet received as of that specific point in time.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The Accounts Receivable Growth Rate is a financial metric that measures the change in accounts receivable balance over a specific period, used to evaluate a company's credit policy, sales collection efficiency, and potential bad debt risk.

operands.metric: Ending Accounts Receivable for Current Period
Ending Accounts Receivable for Previous Period

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Receivable Growth Rate = (Ending Accounts Receivable for Current Period - Ending Accounts Receivable for Previous Period) ÷ Ending Accounts Receivable for Previous Period × 100%

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Occupancy and Occurrence Amount
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Occupancy and Occurrence Amount refers to the amount of funds occupied by customers due to credit sales after a company sells goods or provides services, and its total occurrence within a specific period (e.g., one year). It reflects the scale of funds advanced by the enterprise due to credit sales and serves as the basis for calculating the opportunity cost (fund occupancy cost) of accounts receivable.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Occupied and Incurred Amount
Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger Debit Balance
aliases: 客户欠款明细借方余额
应收客户款明细借方余额

nodes.definition: The accounts receivable subsidiary ledger debit balance refers to the amount in the debit balance direction of individual subsidiary ledger accounts established separately for each specific customer or debtor in the enterprise's accounting books. It directly records the original amount receivable from specific customers but not yet collected due to business operations such as sales of goods and provision of services, serving as the fundamental data for calculating the general ledger balance of accounts receivable when preparing financial statements.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Turnover
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable Turnover reflects the frequency at which accounts receivable are converted into cash within a given period, measuring the efficiency of a company's collection process.

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Receivable Turnover = Total Credit Sales ÷ Average Accounts Receivable
Accounts Receivable Turnover = Credit Sales ÷ Average Accounts Receivable

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: The accounts receivable turnover ratio is a financial metric that measures the speed and efficiency of a company's collection of receivables. It indicates the average number of times accounts receivable are converted into cash within a specific period (typically one year), and is used to assess the liquidity and management efficiency of a company's receivables.

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio = Net Credit Sales ÷ Average Accounts Receivable
Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio = Net Credit Sales / Average Net Accounts Receivable

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable at End of Current Period
Accounts Receivable at End of Previous Period
Accounts Receivable at Period End
aliases: Closing Accounts Receivable for the Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable at Period End refers to the total amount of credit sales for goods or services provided that has not yet been collected from customers as of the end of the current accounting period (e.g., month, quarter, or year). It represents the company's outstanding receivables at a specific point in time and is an important current asset on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable at Previous Period End
aliases: Accounts Receivable at the End of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Accounts Receivable at Previous Period End refers to the total amount of funds generated from the sale of goods or provision of services that had not yet been collected from customers by the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It serves as the base data for calculating changes and growth rates in accounts receivable for the current period.

nodes.name: Accounts Receivable to Revenue Ratio
nodes.definition: The Accounts Receivable to Revenue Ratio reflects the proportion of accounts receivable to sales revenue, measuring the relationship between a company's credit sales scale and its revenue.

formulas.source_formula: Accounts Receivable to Revenue Ratio = Accounts Receivable ÷ Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Accredited Investor
nodes.definition: An accredited investor is an individual or entity that meets financial sophistication and wealth or income thresholds defined by securities regulators (e.g., the U.S. SEC), allowing participation in certain private offerings exempt from registration. One common criterion is the net worth test, which is calculated as total assets minus total liabilities, excluding the value of the primary residence.

nodes.name: Accredited Investor (Individual Qualification)
nodes.definition: An accredited investor (individual) is a natural person who meets specific financial thresholds under U.S. SEC regulations—namely, having a net worth exceeding $1,000,000 excluding the value of the primary residence, and meeting an income test of over $200,000 individually or over $300,000 jointly with a spouse for each of the past two years with a reasonable expectation of the same in the current year—thereby qualifying to participate in certain private securities offerings exempt from registration.

nodes.name: Accretion
nodes.definition: Accretion in mergers and acquisitions refers to a transaction outcome where post-acquisition earnings per share (EPS) exceed pre-transaction EPS. Accretion/dilution analysis assesses whether adding the target’s earnings and issuing new shares increases or decreases EPS. The formula below computes post-acquisition EPS for such analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Accretion Amount = Purchase Basis × (Yield to Maturity ÷ Accrual Periods per Year) - Coupon Interest

nodes.name: Accretion Rate
nodes.definition: Accretion is the systematic recognition of a bond discount as interest income over time. Under the straight-line method, the accretion rate represents the annual amount of discount recognized, calculated by dividing the total bond discount by the years to maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Accretion Rate = Bond Discount ÷ Term to Maturity
Accretion Rate = Discount ÷ Term (Years)

nodes.name: Accretion of Discount
nodes.definition: Accretion of discount is the periodic increase in the carrying amount of a bond purchased below par, measured under the effective interest (constant yield) method. For each accrual period, the accretion amount equals the purchase basis multiplied by the periodic effective yield, minus the coupon interest for the period, thereby moving the bond’s amortized cost toward its face value by maturity.

nodes.name: Accretive Deal EPS Increase
nodes.definition: Accretive Deal EPS Increase measures the percentage change in earnings per share (EPS) resulting from a transaction that is accretive to the acquirer. A positive value indicates that the transaction increases EPS, reflecting value creation for shareholders.

formulas.source_formula: Accretive Deal EPS Increase (%) = ((EPS After - EPS Before) ÷ EPS Before) × 100

nodes.name: Accrual Period
nodes.definition: Accrual period refers to the specific time interval used as the basis for calculating interest, typically determined by a start date and an end date, serving as the fundamental time parameter for computing financial metrics such as accrued interest.

nodes.name: Accrual Period Length
nodes.definition: Accrual period length is the time duration used for calculating interest, typically measured in days. It is derived according to different day count conventions (such as Actual/Actual, 30/360, Actual/360) and is a key parameter in pricing financial derivatives such as the present value of the floating leg.

formulas.source_formula: Accrual Period Length = Interest End Date - Interest Start Date
Accrual Period Length = Interest End Date - Interest Start Date + 1
Accrual Period Length = Whole Years × 360 + Whole Months × 30 + Remaining Actual Days

nodes.name: Accrued Employee Benefits
nodes.definition: Accrued employee benefits refer to welfare expenses that an enterprise has accrued according to regulations or that have been incurred but not yet paid to employees, such as medical expenses, hardship allowances, and canteen subsidies. These are recorded as a liability on the balance sheet prior to payment.

nodes.name: Accrued Employee Compensation Payable from Previous Period
aliases: Accrued Payroll at Beginning of Period
Beginning Balance of Employee Compensation Payable
应付职工薪酬期初余额
nodes.definition: Accrued employee compensation payable from the previous period refers to the total amount of various forms of remuneration that a company has accrued but not yet actually paid to its employees at the end of the last accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter), in accordance with the accrual accounting principle. It represents the company's liability to employees at the end of the previous period and is reflected as part of the cash paid to employees in the current period's cash flow statement.

nodes.name: Accrued Expenses
nodes.definition: Accrued expenses refer to liability items where a company, under the accrual basis accounting principle, estimates and records expenses that have been incurred but not yet actually paid into the current period's costs or expenses. This ensures that expenses are matched with related revenues in the correct accounting period, commonly seen in periodic payment items such as rent, interest, and insurance.

nodes.name: Accrued Interest
nodes.definition: Accrued interest refers to the amount of interest that has been earned or incurred but not yet paid or received, calculated based on principal, interest rate, and time from the last interest payment date to the settlement date. It is commonly seen in the interest accrual of financial instruments such as bonds and loans.

operands.metric: Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities

formulas.source_formula: Accrued Interest (Pro Rata) = Face Value × (Annual Coupon Rate ÷ Periods per Year) × (Days Lapsed ÷ Days in Period)

nodes.name: Accrued Interest Days
nodes.definition: Accrued interest days refer to the actual number of days from the interest accrual start date to the interest accrual end date (inclusive of both dates), which serves as the fundamental variable for calculating accrued interest on financial assets and liabilities.

formulas.source_formula: Accrued Interest Days = (Interest Accrual End Date - Interest Accrual Start Date) + 1

nodes.name: Accrued Wages Ending Balance
aliases: 应付职工薪酬期末余额
nodes.definition: Accrued wages ending balance refers to the total amount of various forms of compensation that have been incurred but not yet actually paid to employees by the enterprise at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end), in accordance with labor contracts and national regulations.

nodes.name: Accumulated Amortization
nodes.definition: Accumulated amortization is the cumulative amount of long-term assets such as intangible assets and long-term prepaid expenses that are systematically and rationally amortized into expenses over their estimated useful lives. It is a contra-asset account and is presented as a deduction from the related assets on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Accumulated Amortization = (Original Asset Cost - Estimated Residual Value) ÷ Estimated Useful Life × Number of Periods Amortized

nodes.name: Accumulated Benefit Obligation
nodes.definition: Accumulated Benefit Obligation refers to the present value of pension benefits that an enterprise is obligated to pay to employees in the future, based on their years of service up to the current date and their current salary levels. It represents the pension liability assumed by the enterprise due to past services rendered.

nodes.name: Accumulated Depreciation
nodes.definition: Accumulated depreciation refers to the total amount of depreciation expense that has been allocated to a tangible asset since it was put into use. It is a contra-asset account used to reduce the asset's carrying value on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Accumulated Depreciation = Annual Depreciation × Years Elapsed
Accumulated Depreciation = Initial Cost × Depreciation Rate × Useful Life (Years)

nodes.name: Accumulated Depreciation and Amortization
nodes.definition: Accumulated depreciation and amortization refers to the total sum of depreciation expenses and amortization expenses accrued by an enterprise since the commissioning of its fixed assets and intangible assets, calculated according to prescribed methods. It reflects the portion of value consumed by these long-term assets due to usage, passage of time, or technological obsolescence, and serves as a contra account to the original value of the assets.

nodes.name: Accumulated Depreciation on Disposed Fixed Assets
aliases: 固定资产清理累计折旧
nodes.definition: Refers to the total depreciation amount that has been accrued and accumulated for a fixed asset from its commissioning date to its disposal date (e.g., sale, scrapping, damage), calculated according to a specific method (e.g., straight-line method, accelerated depreciation method). In the accounting treatment for asset disposal, this amount needs to be removed from the 'Accumulated Depreciation' account to calculate the net gain or loss from the disposal.

nodes.name: Accumulated Months
nodes.definition: Accumulated months refer to the total number of months elapsed from a specific starting point (such as project commencement, beginning of the year, or a benchmark date) to the current or specified end date. It is commonly used in financial analysis, project management, and performance evaluation to calculate time-weighted metrics or measure cumulative effects over a period.

nodes.name: Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income
nodes.definition: Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) is a sub-item within the equity section of the balance sheet, used to aggregate all past and current Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) items. These items refer to gains and losses that are not recognized in the income statement but affect shareholders' equity, including unrealized gains/losses on available-for-sale financial assets, cash flow hedge adjustments, foreign currency translation adjustments, actuarial gains/losses on defined benefit plans, and revaluation surplus.

nodes.name: Accumulated Principal and Interest of Loans at Beginning of Year
aliases: Accumulated Loan Principal and Interest at Year Start
Beginning-of-Year Loan Principal and Interest Accumulated
nodes.definition: Accumulated principal and interest of loans at the beginning of the year refers to the total sum of the outstanding loan principal and the accumulated interest generated thereon at the start of a financial year. It reflects the total interest-bearing debt burden of the enterprise at the beginning of the year and serves as the basis for calculating interest for the new year.

nodes.name: Accumulation/Distribution Indicator (A/D)
nodes.definition: The Accumulation/Distribution (A/D) indicator is a price-volume technical measure that estimates buying (accumulation) and selling (distribution) pressure. It is computed by cumulatively summing Money Flow Volume (MFV), where MFV equals the Money Flow Multiplier (MFM) times trading volume. MFM positions the closing price within the period's high-low range to gauge directional pressure, and the resulting A/D line helps confirm trends and potential divergences between price and volume.

formulas.source_formula: Accumulation/Distribution Line = Previous Accumulation/Distribution Line + Current Money Flow Volume

nodes.name: Acid-Test Ratio
nodes.definition: The acid-test ratio, also known as the quick ratio, measures a company's ability to meet short-term obligations using its most liquid assets—cash, marketable securities, and accounts receivable—excluding inventory and prepaid expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Acid-Test Ratio = (Cash + Marketable Securities + Accounts Receivable) ÷ Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Acquisition Cost
nodes.definition: Acquisition cost refers to the purchase amount paid by an enterprise for acquiring inventory, which equals the annual requirement multiplied by the unit purchase price.

formulas.source_formula: Acquisition Cost = Annual Requirement × Unit Price
Acquisition Cost = Ordering Cost + Purchase Cost
Acquisition Cost = Fixed Ordering Cost + Variable Ordering Cost + Purchase Cost

nodes.name: Acquisition Premium
nodes.definition: Acquisition premium is the excess of the purchase price paid over the target company’s estimated fair (real) value in a merger or acquisition, reflecting expected synergies, control benefits, and strategic considerations.

formulas.source_formula: Acquisition Premium = Price Paid - Real Value
Acquisition Premium (%) = (Price Paid - Fair Value) ÷ Fair Value × 100
Acquisition Premium (%) = (Offered Price per Share ÷ Current Share Price - 1) × 100

nodes.name: Active Market
nodes.definition: Active market is a fundamental concept in accounting standards, specifically referring to a market in which assets or liabilities are traded with sufficient volume and frequency to continuously and reliably provide pricing information, thereby serving as a basis for fair value measurement.

nodes.name: Activity Consumption of the Product
nodes.definition: In Activity-Based Costing, this refers to the actual quantity of activities consumed in producing or providing a specific product or service. These are fundamental operational data points, such as the number of orders processed, times of material handling, machine running hours, or duration of customer service. They are typically sourced directly from production records, business systems, or statistical reports and serve as the primary raw data for calculating activity costs.

nodes.name: Activity Consumption per Unit
nodes.definition: Activity Consumption per Unit refers to the quantity of a specific activity consumed in producing one unit of product under Activity-Based Costing, such as the number of equipment setups or quality inspection time required per product unit. It serves as the key foundational data for allocating resource costs to specific products.

nodes.name: Activity Cost Adjustment
nodes.definition: Activity Cost Adjustment is the difference between the actual cost incurred in the current period and the allocated cost, used to dethe allocated cost to more accurately reflect the actual cost.

operands.metric: Actual Cost Incurred for the Activity in Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Activity Cost Adjustment = Actual Cost Incurred for the Activity in Current Period - Allocated Cost in Current Period

nodes.name: Activity Cost Adjustment Amount
nodes.definition: The Activity Cost Adjustment Amount is an adjustment item in Activity-Based Costing (ABC) used to reflect the variance between the actual cost incurred for a specific activity and its standard (or budgeted) cost. It is a composite metric whose calculation relies on fundamental data such as actual activity volume and cost driver rates, and is ultimately used to adjust and derive the actual activity cost of a product.

formulas.source_formula: Activity Cost Adjustment Amount = Actual Activity Cost - Budgeted Activity Cost
Activity Cost Adjustment Amount = Actual Activity Cost - Standard Activity Cost
Activity Cost Adjustment Amount = (Actual Activity Volume × Actual Cost Driver Rate) - (Standard Activity Volume × Standard Cost Driver Rate)

nodes.name: Activity Cost Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The activity cost allocation rate is the proportion used to allocate the total cost of a cost pool based on activity output (e.g., hours), measuring the cost borne per unit of activity output.

formulas.source_formula: Activity Cost Allocation Rate = Total Activity Cost ÷ Activity Output

nodes.name: Activity Cost Consumed by a Product
nodes.definition: Activity cost consumed by a product refers to the sum of all activity costs incurred during its production process, reflecting its actual consumption of resources.

nodes.name: Activity Cost Driver
nodes.definition: An activity cost driver is a measurable factor that causes an activity to consume resources and incur costs. In activity-based costing (ABC), costs are allocated to products or services based on the cost driver rate and the quantity of driver units. The total cost allocated from a driver is computed by multiplying the cost per unit (driver rate) by the number of units (driver units) associated with the activity.

nodes.name: Activity Cost Pool
nodes.definition: An activity cost pool is a core concept in activity-based costing, referring to a cost collection formed by aggregating resources consumed in the production process into various activity centers according to the principle of homogeneity (i.e., cost variations can be explained by a common cost driver). It serves as an intermediate cost accumulation point for allocating manufacturing overhead to final products or services.

nodes.name: Activity Cost Variance
nodes.definition: Activity cost variance is the difference between the actual activity costs incurred and the allocated costs calculated using the budgeted activity cost allocation rate and actual output, used to analyze cost control effectiveness.

nodes.name: Activity Level
nodes.definition: Activity level refers to the quantitative measure of the volume or scale of activities performed within a specific period to accomplish a task, produce a product, or provide a service. In Activity-Based Costing, it is commonly used as a cost driver to allocate resource costs to cost objects (such as products or services).

nodes.name: Activity Output
nodes.definition: Activity output refers to a quantitative measure used in Activity-Based Costing (ABC) to gauge the volume of specific activities performed. It typically manifests as concrete activity volumes such as labor hours, frequency, or production quantity, and serves as the key denominator for calculating the actual activity cost allocation rate. It is a calculable or statistical metric, not an original account in financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Activity Output = Output per Shift (Month) ÷ Number of Machines

nodes.name: Activity Quantity Consumed by the Product
Activity-Based Budgeting (ABB)
nodes.definition: Activity-Based Budgeting (ABB) is a budgeting methodology that estimates resource requirements and costs based on expected activity levels and their cost drivers. Under ABB, the budget for an activity is calculated as the anticipated number of activity units multiplied by the cost per unit, supporting more accurate planning, cost control, and performance management.

formulas.source_formula: Activity-Based Budget = Activity Units × Cost per Unit

nodes.name: Activity-Based Overhead Allocation
nodes.definition: Activity-based overhead allocation assigns indirect costs to activities based on their consumption of cost drivers. The overhead allocated to a specific activity equals the cost driver rate multiplied by the number of cost drivers related to that activity, providing a more accurate reflection of resource usage under activity-based costing.

formulas.source_formula: Activity-Based Overhead Allocation = Cost Driver Rate × Number of Cost Drivers

nodes.name: Actual Achievement
nodes.definition: Actual achievement refers to the specific numerical value or result ultimately attained for a given indicator, task, or objective within a specified period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It serves as key data for measuring plan execution and performance.

nodes.name: Actual Activity Cost
nodes.definition: Actual Activity Cost refers to the total cost actually incurred and recorded for completing specific activities or operations within a given accounting period under Activity-Based Costing. It is typically used to calculate the actual activity cost allocation rate for more accurate cost assignment to products or services.

nodes.name: Actual Activity Cost Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The actual activity cost allocation rate is a distribution ratio calculated based on the actual activity costs incurred in the current period and the actual activity output, reflecting the actual cost allocation situation.

nodes.name: Actual Activity Cost of Product
nodes.definition: Actual activity cost of product refers to the activity cost actually borne by the product during the production process, including allocated costs and adjustments, reflecting the true cost level.

nodes.name: Actual Activity Costs Incurred in the Current Period
aliases: Actual Activity Cost Incurred in Current Period
Actual Activity-Based Cost for the Period
Actual Cost of Activities for the Period
nodes.definition: Actual activity costs incurred in the current period refer to the total sum of resource costs, under Activity-Based Costing, that are actually consumed and allocated to various activity cost pools for performing specific activities (such as order processing, equipment setup, quality inspection, etc.) during the current accounting period. These costs originate directly from actual resource consumption, such as labor wages, power expenses, equipment depreciation, etc., and serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating activity cost allocation rates.

nodes.name: Actual Activity Driver Quantity
nodes.definition: Actual Activity Driver Quantity refers to the actual number of drivers consumed or utilized by various activities during a specific accounting period to produce actual output of products or services in Activity-Based Costing. It serves as the fundamental basis for allocating costs from activity cost pools to specific cost objects (such as products or services).

nodes.name: Actual Activity Level
nodes.definition: Actual Activity Level refers to the specific quantity of labor hours, resources consumed, or output produced to complete a specific activity or production operation within a given period. It serves as fundamental data for measuring activity execution efficiency, cost accounting, and budgetary control.

nodes.name: Actual Activity Output for the Current Period
Actual Activity Output for the Period
nodes.definition: Actual Activity Output for the Period refers to the actual quantity or volume of activities consumed by an enterprise during the current accounting period to complete products or services under Activity-Based Costing. It serves as fundamental raw data, typically measured in specific units such as machine hours, production batches, inspection counts, or order processing quantities, and is used to allocate activity costs to specific cost objects (e.g., products or services).

nodes.name: Actual Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The actual allocation rate is a ratio calculated based on the total actual amount to be allocated and the total actual allocation base. It is used to allocate indirect costs (such as manufacturing overhead) or specific resources (such as imported materials in processing trade) to various cost objects or business segments. It is a key calculation metric in cost accounting and tax verification.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Allocation Rate = Total Amount to be Allocated ÷ Total Allocation Base

nodes.name: Actual Annual Cost of Funds
nodes.definition: Actual Annual Cost of Funds refers to the total expenses actually paid by a company to its fund providers within a fiscal year for utilizing externally raised capital (such as loans, bonds, equity financing, etc.), primarily including interest, dividends, and similar payments. These expenses, typically obtainable directly from loan agreements, payment vouchers, or financial statements, serve as fundamental raw data for calculating metrics like the cost of capital and effective annual interest rate.

nodes.name: Actual Asset Utilization Time
nodes.definition: Actual Asset Utilization Time refers to the duration during which an asset is actually used for production, operations, or service provision within a specific period (such as an accounting period or production cycle), and serves as the key numerator in calculating asset utilization rates.

nodes.name: Actual Available Loan Amount
nodes.definition: The actual available loan amount refers to the net funds that a company can actually utilize after deducting various fees or restrictions such as handling charges and compensating balances when borrowing from banks or other financial institutions. It is a key foundational data point for calculating financing cost metrics such as the effective annual interest rate.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Available Loan Amount = Loan Principal - Handling Charges - Compensating Balance

nodes.name: Actual Consumption Volume
nodes.definition: Actual consumption volume refers to the total quantity or total value of resources such as raw materials, energy, and labor actually consumed by an enterprise for producing goods or providing services during a specific accounting period or production cycle. It serves as fundamental data for calculating wastage rates, cost analysis, and efficiency evaluation.

nodes.name: Actual Contribution Percentage Test (ACP)
aliases: 匹配供款非歧视性测试
nodes.definition: The Actual Contribution Percentage (ACP) test is a 401(k) nondiscrimination test that compares the average matching and after-tax contribution percentages of Highly Compensated Employees (HCEs) to those of Non-Highly Compensated Employees (NHCEs). A plan passes the ACP test if the average contribution percentage of HCEs does not exceed the NHCE average by more than two percentage points and is not more than twice the NHCE average.

nodes.name: Actual Cost
nodes.definition: Actual cost refers to the cost actually incurred and paid for acquiring or manufacturing an asset or completing an activity. It is typically calculated based on direct materials consumed, direct labor, and allocated manufacturing overhead during the production process, or derived by adjusting planned cost with cost variances.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Cost = Planned Cost × (1 + Cost Variance Rate)
Actual Cost = Acquisition Cost + Carrying Cost

nodes.name: Actual Cost Driver Rate
nodes.definition: Actual Cost Driver Rate refers to the unit cost allocation rate per driver calculated in Activity-Based Costing based on the actual incurred activity costs and the actual consumed quantity of activity drivers. It reflects the proportional relationship between the actual cost of performing an activity and the actual volume of activity drivers that cause that cost during a specific period, and is used to allocate actual activity costs more accurately to products or services.

nodes.name: Actual Cost Incurred for the Activity in Current Period
Actual Cost Incurred for the Activity in the Current Period
aliases: Actual Activity Cost Incurred in Current Period
Actual Cost of Activity for the Period
当期实际发生的作业成本
nodes.definition: In Activity-Based Costing (ABC), the actual cost incurred for an activity in the current period refers to the total sum of all resource costs actually consumed and accumulated by a specific activity center during the current accounting period. It serves as the basis for calculating the actual activity cost allocation rate. It is typically derived by allocating fundamental cost data, such as direct materials, direct labor, and various manufacturing overheads, to each activity center based on resource drivers.

operands.metric: Actual Activity Output for the Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Actual Cost Incurred for the Activity in the Current Period = Actual Activity Cost Allocation Rate × Actual Activity Output for the Current Period

nodes.name: Actual Cost at Actual Output
nodes.definition: Actual cost at actual output refers to the total sum of all costs actually incurred and recorded during a specific period for producing the actual quantity of output. It reflects the value of resources consumed in the real production process and serves as a crucial basis for cost control and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Actual Cost of Beginning Inventory
aliases: 月初结存存货实际成本
nodes.definition: The actual cost of beginning inventory refers to the historical purchase or production cost corresponding to the inventory already present in the warehouse at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., beginning of the month or year). It is directly derived from the book records carried forward from the previous accounting period or the results of a physical count, and serves as the base data for calculating the cost of goods issued during the current period (e.g., under the weighted average method).

nodes.name: Actual Cost of Current Period Cost Pool
aliases: Actual Cost of Current Cost Pool
nodes.definition: Actual cost of current period cost pool refers to the total costs actually incurred and allocated to a specific cost pool (such as a product, activity, or department) for producing goods or providing services during a specific accounting period. It is typically aggregated from fundamental cost items such as direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead, and serves as the basis for cost calculation, variance analysis, and performance evaluation.

operands.metric: Planned Cost of Current Period Cost Pool
Cost Variance Rate of Current Period Cost Pool

formulas.source_formula: Actual Cost of Current Period Cost Pool = Planned Cost of Current Period Cost Pool × (1 + Cost Variance Rate of Current Period Cost Pool)

operands.metric: Beginning Work-in-Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost
Production Expenses Incurred in Current Period
Ending Work in Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost

formulas.source_formula: Actual Cost of Current Period Cost Pool = Beginning Work-in-Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost + Production Expenses Incurred in Current Period - Ending Work-in-Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost

nodes.name: Actual Cost of Current Purchase
nodes.definition: The actual cost of the current purchase refers to the total sum of all reasonable and necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire inventory and bring it to its intended usable or salable condition, serving as the core basis for the initial measurement of inventory. Under the actual cost method of inventory accounting, this cost is used to record the value of inventory receipts, issues, and balances.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Cost of Current Purchase = Tax-inclusive Purchase Cost - Export Tax Rebate Amount

nodes.name: Actual Cost of Existing Inventory on Hand
Actual Cost of Multimodal Transport
nodes.definition: Actual cost of multimodal transport refers to the total sum of all direct and indirect expenses actually incurred by an enterprise in organizing multimodal transport operations to complete the entire transportation of goods from origin to destination. These expenses typically include freight charges for different transport segments, cargo handling and transshipment fees, insurance premiums, warehousing costs, and related management and coordination expenses, which are directly collected from actual business documents or reasonably allocated.

nodes.name: Actual Costs and Expenses Incurred in the Current Year
aliases: Actual Cost Incurred in Current Year
Actual Costs and Expenses for the Year
Current Year Actual Costs and Expenses
nodes.definition: Actual costs and expenses incurred in the current year refer to the total sum of various costs and expenses directly recorded and aggregated by an enterprise within the current fiscal year based on source documents (such as invoices, material requisition slips, payrolls, etc.) generated from genuine business activities. It reflects the actual consumption of resources by the enterprise during the year, serves as fundamental data for preparing financial statements, and cannot be derived indirectly through other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Actual Days of Dilutive Effect of Potential Common Shares in the Reporting Period
aliases: Actual Days with Dilutive Effect of the Potential Common Share in the Reporting Period
Days Outstanding of Dilutive Potential Common Shares
潜在普通股稀释期天数
稀释性潜在普通股当期存在天数
nodes.definition: Refers to the calendar days corresponding to potential common shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, stock options, etc.) that actually exist and have a dilutive effect during the reporting period, which need to be considered when calculating diluted earnings per share. These days are used to calculate the weighted average number of additional shares after the conversion of such potential common shares into common shares.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Decrease Percentage = (Current Rate - Future Rate Estimate) ÷ Current Rate × 100

nodes.name: Actual Deferral Percentage (ADP) Test
nodes.definition: The Actual Deferral Percentage (ADP) Test is a nondiscrimination test for 401(k) plans that compares the average salary deferral rates of highly compensated employees (HCEs) to those of non-highly compensated employees (NHCEs). A plan passes the ADP test when the average HCE deferral percentage does not exceed the NHCE average by more than two percentage points and is not more than twice the NHCE average, ensuring compliance with ERISA and Internal Revenue Code requirements.

nodes.name: Actual Exercise Quantity
nodes.definition: Actual exercise quantity refers to the specific number of underlying assets that holders of financial derivatives such as stock options or warrants actually choose to purchase or sell by exercising their rights. It reflects the volume scale at which options or warrants are converted from potential rights into actual transactions.

nodes.name: Actual Fixed Manufacturing Overhead
aliases: 固定制造费用实际发生额
实际固定制造费用总额
nodes.definition: Actual Fixed Manufacturing Overhead refers to the total amount of fixed indirect production costs actually incurred and recorded in the accounting books during a specific accounting period to support production activities. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting, reflects actual resource consumption, and is the starting point for cost variance analysis.

nodes.name: Actual Hours Worked
nodes.definition: Actual hours worked refers to the total duration an employee actually devotes to work during a specific period (such as a day, week, or month). It is typically captured directly by attendance systems, timesheets, or project management systems and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating compensation, analyzing labor costs, and evaluating production efficiency.

nodes.name: Actual Hours for Various Products
nodes.definition: Actual hours for various products refer to the effective working time actually consumed by different products during the production process, typically measured in hours. It includes hours directly spent on production, debugging, inspection, and other related activities, but excludes non-productive time such as downtime and rework. This data serves as the foundation for cost accounting and production management.

nodes.name: Actual Hours for the Product
aliases: Actual Hours Worked for the Product
nodes.definition: Actual hours for the product refer to the effective working time actually spent in the production process of a specific product, typically measured in hours. It includes direct product processing, necessary auxiliary operations, and reasonable rest intervals, serving as fundamental data for measuring production efficiency and calculating product costs.

nodes.name: Actual Income Tax Paid in that Country (Region)
Actual Incurred Input VAT
aliases: 购进货物实际负担的增值税
nodes.definition: Actual incurred input VAT refers to the value-added tax amount actually paid or borne by an enterprise during a specific period due to the purchase of goods, receipt of taxable services, or services. It reflects the actual VAT cost incurred by the enterprise during that period, which can be used to offset output VAT.

nodes.name: Actual Indicator
nodes.definition: Actual indicators refer to the financial or operational performance values calculated by an enterprise based on actual business data after a specific accounting period or operating cycle. They reflect the true operating results and financial condition of the enterprise during that period and serve as the foundational data for budget comparison, performance evaluation, and factor analysis.

nodes.name: Actual Labor Cost
nodes.definition: Actual labor cost refers to the total sum of labor expenditures actually incurred and recorded during a specific accounting period for the completion of products or services. It typically includes the base wages, bonuses, benefits, taxes, and other related expenses for personnel directly involved in production or service provision, and constitutes a significant component of the actual cost of products.

nodes.name: Actual Loss
nodes.definition: Actual loss refers to the reduction in property value that has actually occurred or been accounted for due to a specific event (such as default, accident, or risk event). In risk management and contract disputes, its calculation is typically based on contractual agreements, laws and regulations, or statistical standards, and is derived from components such as direct loss and indirect loss.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Loss = Direct Loss + Indirect Loss
Actual Loss = Building Loss Value + Structure Loss Value + Equipment Loss Value + Other Property Loss Value

nodes.name: Actual Material Consumption
nodes.definition: Actual material consumption refers to the quantity of materials actually requisitioned and consumed for product manufacturing during a specific production period. It is directly derived from original production records (such as material requisition forms and inventory count records) and serves as the fundamental data for calculating direct material costs and conducting cost variance analysis.

nodes.name: Actual Material Consumption Quantity
nodes.definition: Actual material consumption quantity refers to the physical amount of raw materials, auxiliary materials, and other supplies actually consumed for producing goods or providing services during a specific production cycle or cost accounting period. It serves as fundamental data for cost calculation and variance analysis, used to compare with standard or planned consumption quantities to evaluate material usage efficiency.

nodes.name: Actual Material Cost Incurred in Current Month
nodes.definition: Actual material cost incurred in the current month refers to the cost of various raw materials, auxiliary materials, and other supplies actually consumed or input by an enterprise for production or operational activities during the current accounting month. Its amount is the total actual expenditure directly aggregated and measured based on original documents such as purchase invoices, warehouse receipts, freight documents, and sorting/processing fees, serving as the fundamental raw data for cost accounting.

nodes.name: Actual Material Cost of Beginning Work-in-Process
Actual Material Cost of Work in Process at Beginning of Month
aliases: Actual Material Cost of Opening WIP
Beginning Work in Process Actual Material Cost
月初在制品实际材料成本
期初在制品实际材料成本
nodes.definition: Actual Material Cost of Work in Process at Beginning of Month refers to the cost value of direct materials actually consumed by all products that are in the production process but not yet completed (i.e., work in process) at the start of each accounting period (typically monthly). This data is usually obtained directly through physical inventory counts or cost records, and serves as the foundational starting point for accumulating and allocating production costs for the current month, as well as for cost allocation between completed products and work in process.

nodes.name: Actual Material Usage
nodes.definition: Actual material usage refers to the quantity or weight of raw materials actually consumed for product manufacturing during a specific production cycle or cost accounting period. It serves as fundamental data for cost calculation, efficiency analysis (e.g., material utilization rate), and variance assessment (e.g., quantity variance).

nodes.name: Actual Number of Days the Potential Common Stock Had a Dilutive Effect in the Reporting Period
Actual Operating Time
nodes.definition: Actual operating time refers to the time actually consumed to complete a specific task or operation, determined through actual observation, measurement, or recording. In the field of finance and accounting, it is commonly used for cost accounting, labor hour management, and efficiency analysis, serving as essential baseline data for calculating setup time, evaluating production efficiency, and formulating budgets.

nodes.name: Actual Output
nodes.definition: Actual output refers to the quantity of products or services actually completed and recorded through the production or harvesting process by an enterprise within a specific accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It is a fundamental production data point, typically entered directly based on production cost ledgers, production records, or product cost summaries, rather than being calculated from other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Actual Output in the First Period
Actual Output of Current Period Activities
aliases: Actual Activity Output for the Period
Actual Cost Driver Quantity at Standard Rate
实际作业成本分配基础
nodes.definition: Actual Output of Current Period Activities is a computational metric under Activity-Based Costing, referring to the cost allocation base or output quantity calculated based on the actual activity driver volume and the standard (or budgeted) activity allocation rate during a specific period. It serves as an intermediate calculation value for cost allocation and variance analysis, rather than being a fundamental data point directly sourced from original vouchers or financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Output of Current Period Activities = Actual Activity Driver Volume × Budgeted Activity Allocation Rate

nodes.name: Actual Physical Output
nodes.definition: Actual physical output refers to the quantity of products actually produced or completed by a production unit (such as an enterprise, project, or industry) within a specific period, measured in natural physical units (e.g., tons, cubic meters, units, square meters). It reflects the actual scale of production achievements and serves as important foundational data for calculating gross output value and evaluating plan fulfillment.

nodes.name: Actual Price
nodes.definition: Actual price refers to the final determined or calculated price or cost level in a specific financial or business context, after comprehensively considering factors such as cost, profit, taxes, and discounts. It is a composite concept that can be calculated using different formulas depending on the analytical purpose (e.g., cost accounting, break-even analysis, international trade pricing).

formulas.source_formula: Actual Price = Direct Material Cost + Direct Labor Cost + Manufacturing Overhead Allocation
Actual Price = Sales Revenue × Sales Price Ratio
Actual Price = Purchase Cost + Domestic Expenses + Net Profit
Actual Price = (Total Fixed Costs + Total Expected Profit) ÷ Break-even Point Sales Quantity + Unit Variable Cost

nodes.name: Actual Price per Unit of Material
Actual Price-to-Book Ratio
nodes.definition: The Actual Price-to-Book Ratio is a composite financial metric calculated by dividing the stock price by the net asset value per share. It measures the ratio of a stock's market price relative to the company's net asset value, reflecting the market's assessment of the company's asset quality. A lower ratio may indicate the stock is undervalued, while a higher ratio may suggest overvaluation. However, comprehensive analysis requires consideration of industry characteristics, profitability, growth potential, and other factors.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Price-to-Book Ratio = Total Market Capitalization ÷ Net Assets

nodes.name: Actual Production Time
nodes.definition: Actual production time refers to the direct labor hours or machine operating hours actually consumed during the production process to complete a specific quantity of products. It serves as fundamental raw data in cost accounting, used for allocating manufacturing overhead, calculating production efficiency, and conducting cost variance analysis.

nodes.name: Actual Purchase Volume
nodes.definition: Actual purchase volume refers to the quantity of goods or services that consumers or enterprises ultimately complete transactions and make payments for, after considering factors such as discounts, promotions, and returns. It reflects genuine consumption or procurement behavior, rather than planned or nominal purchase intentions.

nodes.name: Actual Quantity
nodes.definition: Actual quantity refers to the specific, real number of units that occur or exist in an economic activity or transaction within the financial and accounting domain, such as the exact number of inventory items, the actual tons of materials consumed in production, or the actual number of shares traded in a securities transaction. It serves as the fundamental physical unit for business records and typically must be combined with a unit price to calculate the corresponding monetary amount.

formulas.source_formula: Actual Quantity = Amount ÷ Unit Price

nodes.name: Actual Quantity of Direct Materials
nodes.definition: Actual quantity of direct materials refers to the amount of principal materials, purchased semi-finished goods, and auxiliary materials that constitute the physical product and are actually consumed during a specific production cycle for manufacturing products or providing services.

nodes.name: Actual Rate of Return on Securities
nodes.definition: The actual rate of return on securities refers to the ratio of the actual return (profit or loss) obtained by an investor after holding a security or investment instrument, when gains or losses have already been realized, to the initial investment amount. It reflects the actual outcome of the investment, rather than the expected outcome.

nodes.name: Actual Sales Amount
nodes.definition: Actual sales amount refers to the final amount actually received from customers after the sale of goods or provision of services. It is typically the net amount after deducting factors such as discounts, allowances, or returns granted to customers from the total sales price.

nodes.name: Actual Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Actual sales revenue refers to the net amount received by an enterprise after deducting price concessions such as sales discounts and allowances from the total price and extra-charges (excluding output VAT) collected from buyers following the sale of goods or provision of services. It reflects the enterprise's true sales performance.

nodes.name: Actual Service Life
nodes.definition: Actual service life refers to the actual length of time an asset has been in use from the date it was put into service until the valuation date. It reflects the actual wear and tear of the asset and is a key parameter for calculating physical deterioration and obsolescence in asset valuation.

nodes.name: Actual Tax Payable
nodes.definition: Actual tax payable refers to the amount of tax that a taxpayer is required to pay to the tax authority during a specific tax period, calculated based on the tax base and applicable tax rate in accordance with tax laws and regulations. It is a composite indicator typically derived from fundamental data (such as turnover, tax rate, output VAT, input VAT, taxable income, etc.) through specific formulas.
