nodes.definition: Annual Aggregate Income refers to the total annual income of an individual within a tax year, calculated by combining income from four categories: wages and salaries, remuneration for labor services, author's remuneration, and royalties, before deducting related expenses, special deductions, and special additional deductions. It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating individual income tax liability.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Amortization Expense (Straight-Line) = (Acquisition Cost - Residual Value) ÷ Useful Life

nodes.name: Annual Average Accounts Payable
nodes.definition: Annual Average Accounts Payable refers to the average balance of accounts payable during a specific accounting period (typically one year). It is a key metric for measuring the average level of funds a company utilizes from suppliers and evaluating the efficiency of working capital management, commonly used in calculating financial ratios such as the Accounts Payable Turnover Period.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Average Accounts Payable = Cost of Sales ÷ Accounts Payable Turnover
Annual Average Accounts Payable = (Beginning Accounts Payable Balance + Ending Accounts Payable Balance) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Annual Bad Debt Amount
nodes.definition: Annual bad debt amount refers to the total amount of accounts receivable that a company ultimately confirms as losses within a fiscal year due to customers' inability to repay. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as the bad debt ratio.

nodes.name: Annual Bond Interest Income
nodes.definition: Annual bond interest income refers to the fixed interest income received by bondholders each year, calculated based on the bond's face value and coupon rate. It is the most fundamental cash flow in bond investment and is typically determined at the time of bond issuance.

nodes.name: Annual Capital Charge
nodes.definition: Annual capital charge refers to the cost or expense that a company incurs within one year for using and occupying capital (including equity capital and debt capital). It reflects the opportunity cost of capital and serves as a crucial factor in measuring capital utilization efficiency and making investment decisions.

nodes.name: Annual Cash Inflow
nodes.definition: Annual cash inflow refers to the total amount of cash and cash equivalents actually received by an enterprise within one year through all channels, including operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities. It is an important indicator for measuring an enterprise's annual cash acquisition capability.

nodes.name: Annual Cash Outflow
nodes.definition: Annual cash outflow refers to the total amount of cash actually paid by an enterprise during a fiscal year due to operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities. It reflects the decrease in cash during the year and is an important component in calculating annual net cash flow.

nodes.name: Annual Cash Requirement
nodes.definition: Annual cash requirement refers to the total amount of cash needed by an enterprise during a complete future fiscal year to meet normal operating activities, investment activities, and financing activities. It is a forecast-based management metric, typically calculated through cash budgeting or financial models (such as inventory models), rather than directly derived from historical financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Cash Requirement = Total Cash Inflows - Total Cash Outflows

operands.metric: Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities
Transaction Cost per Sale of Marketable Securities to Replenish Cash

formulas.source_formula: Annual Cash Requirement = (Optimal Cash Balance ^ 2 × Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities) ÷ (2 × Transaction Cost per Conversion)
Annual Compound Rate of Return (%) = 72 ÷ Years to Double

nodes.name: Annual Compounded Stock Return
nodes.definition: Annual compounded stock return refers to the conversion of the total return on a stock investment over multiple periods into an annualized compound growth rate, typically accounting for the reinvestment effect of dividends.

nodes.name: Annual Comprehensive Income Amount
aliases: Total Annual Income from Comprehensive Sources
nodes.definition: Annual Comprehensive Income Amount refers to the total income earned by a resident individual within a tax year, derived from the comprehensive income categories specified in the Individual Income Tax Law. This typically includes four types of income: wages and salaries, remuneration for labor services, author's remuneration, and royalties. It serves as the gross income base before deducting various allowances when calculating the taxable income for individual income tax purposes.

nodes.name: Annual Cost of Capital Employed
nodes.definition: Annual cost of capital employed refers to the expense or cost that an enterprise or individual needs to pay or bear for utilizing others' funds (such as bank loans, accounts payable, shareholders' invested capital, etc.) over a one-year period. It reflects the annual cost of using funds, typically related to the amount of funds employed, the duration of use, and the agreed interest rate or cost of capital.

nodes.name: Annual Cost of Funds
nodes.definition: Annual cost of funds refers to the various expenses a company needs to pay within one year for raising and using capital, primarily including interest expenses, dividends, rents, etc., and is a key component in calculating the cost of capital.

nodes.name: Annual Cost of Funds Rate
nodes.definition: The Annual Cost of Funds Rate is the ratio of various expenses (such as interest, fees, etc.) that a company needs to pay within one year for raising and using funds to the total or net amount of funds raised, usually expressed as an annualized percentage, used to measure the cost of a company's use of funds.

nodes.name: Annual Cost of Goods Sold
nodes.definition: Annual Cost of Goods Sold refers to the total direct costs incurred by an enterprise within one year for selling goods or providing services, primarily including direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. It reflects the direct consumption of the enterprise's core business operations and is a key item on the income statement.

nodes.name: Annual Costs and Expenses
nodes.definition: Annual costs and expenses refer to the total sum of all expenditures incurred by an enterprise within one year for conducting business operations, maintaining operations, and raising funds, among other activities. It typically includes major categories such as cost of main operations, operating expenses, administrative expenses, and financial expenses. It serves as a key foundational data point for measuring the enterprise's annual resource consumption and calculating annual earnings (profit).

nodes.name: Annual Coupon Frequency
nodes.definition: Annual coupon frequency refers to the number of times within a complete calendar year that a bond or other fixed-income security pays interest to its holders. For example, annual payments correspond to a frequency of 1, semi-annual payments to 2, and quarterly payments to 4.

nodes.name: Annual Coupon Interest
nodes.definition: Annual coupon interest refers to the annual interest amount payable to the holder of a financial instrument such as a bond or note, calculated based on its face value and coupon rate. It represents the fixed interest payment promised by the issuer, irrespective of market interest rate fluctuations or the actual purchase price of the bond.

nodes.name: Annual Coupon Payment
nodes.definition: Annual coupon payment refers to the actual cash interest amount paid by the bond issuer to bondholders each year according to the terms agreed upon at the time of bond issuance. It is a fundamental payment obligation in the bond contract, directly reflecting the fixed interest income obtainable annually from holding the bond.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Coupon Payment = Par Value × Coupon Rate
Annual Coupon Payment = Face Value × Coupon Rate

nodes.name: Annual Credit Sales
nodes.definition: Annual credit sales refer to the total net sales revenue earned by a company through the sale of goods or provision of services on credit during a fiscal year, after deducting sales returns, sales allowances, and cash discounts. It reflects the actual revenue level achieved by the company through credit sales.

nodes.name: Annual Credit Sales for the Current Period
aliases: Net Credit Sales for the Period
nodes.definition: Annual credit sales for the current period refer to the total sales of goods or services realized through credit sales (i.e., allowing customers deferred payment) within the current fiscal year, typically representing the net amount after deducting sales returns, allowances, and discounts. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as accounts receivable turnover and pre-credit-cost income.

nodes.name: Annual Debt Service
nodes.definition: Annual Debt Service refers to the total amount of debt principal and interest that a company needs to repay within a fiscal year. It is a key composite financial metric for assessing a company's debt repayment capacity and financial risk. It is typically calculated using formulas based on fundamental data such as debt principal, interest, and cash flow, rather than existing as a direct fundamental data point. It is commonly used in the analysis and evaluation of fixed-income securities such as revenue bonds.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Debt Service = Total Debt × [Debt Interest Rate × (1 + Debt Interest Rate) ^ Debt Term] ÷ [(1 + Debt Interest Rate) ^ Debt Term - 1]

nodes.name: Annual Deductible Remaining
nodes.definition: Annual deductible remaining is the portion of the insurance deductible that has not yet been satisfied by the policyholder’s out-of-pocket spending during the policy year. It is calculated as the deductible limit minus cumulative qualifying out-of-pocket expenses paid toward the deductible, floored at zero.

nodes.name: Annual Demand
nodes.definition: Annual demand refers to the total amount of funds required by an enterprise to maintain normal operating activities over a specific period (typically one year). It can be calculated using financial indicators such as sales revenue, sales profit margin, and operating efficiency, and is commonly used for fund forecasting and inventory management.

nodes.name: Annual Demand for Goods
nodes.definition: Annual demand for goods refers to the total quantity of a specific product that consumers or the market are willing and able to purchase within one year under given conditions. It serves as a fundamental input for inventory management, production planning, and financial forecasting (such as calculating the Economic Order Quantity).

formulas.source_formula: Annual Depreciation = Total Depreciable Amount ÷ Useful Life (Years)

nodes.name: Annual Depreciation Expense
nodes.definition: Annual depreciation expense refers to the amount systematically allocated each year over the estimated useful life of a fixed asset according to a determined depreciation method, reflecting the gradual loss in value of the asset due to usage.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Depreciation Expense = Asset Cost ÷ Asset Lifetime
Straight-Line Depreciation = Asset Cost ÷ Useful Life
Annual Depreciation Expense = Asset Cost ÷ Useful Life (Years)
Annual Depreciation Expense = (Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life
supporting_source_formulas: Annual Depreciation Expense = (Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life

formulas.source_formula: Annual Depreciation = (Historical Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life
Annual Depreciation Expense = (Asset Original Cost - Estimated Net Residual Value) × (Remaining Useful Life ÷ Sum of the Years' Digits)

nodes.name: Annual Depreciation Expense (Straight-Line)
nodes.definition: Annual depreciation expense under the straight-line method allocates an asset’s depreciable amount evenly across its useful life. It is calculated by dividing the total depreciation (typically cost minus salvage value) by the asset’s useful life in years.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Depreciation Expense (Straight-Line) = Total Depreciation ÷ Useful Life

nodes.name: Annual Depreciation Rate
nodes.definition: The annual depreciation rate refers to the percentage of an asset's annual depreciation amount relative to its original cost (historical cost), used to measure the rate of asset value depletion within one year. It is a key ratio for calculating annual depreciation expense, with its specific value depending on the depreciation method adopted by the enterprise (such as straight-line method, sum-of-the-years'-digits method, double-declining balance method, etc.).

nodes.name: Annual Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The annual discount rate is the benchmark ratio used to discount expected returns or cash flows from the next year or a finite period to their present value. It reflects the time value of money, risk level, and opportunity cost, and is a key parameter for evaluating the value of investment projects, bonds, and other financial assets.

nodes.name: Annual Dividend Per Share
nodes.definition: Annual Dividend Per Share refers to the total cash dividends paid by a company to each common shareholder over one year. It reflects the level of direct cash return the company provides to its shareholders.

nodes.name: Annual EBIT
aliases: Annual Earnings Before Interest and Taxes
nodes.definition: Annual EBIT refers to a company's total profit before deducting interest expenses and income taxes within one year. It reflects the profitability of the company's core operating activities and is unaffected by capital structure and tax policies.

nodes.name: Annual Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Annual Earnings Per Share refers to the ratio of net profit attributable to common shareholders to the weighted average number of common shares outstanding during an accounting year. It is a key financial metric for measuring a company's profitability and evaluating stock value.

operands.metric: Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding

formulas.source_formula: Annual Earnings Per Share = Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Annual Equivalent Rate
nodes.definition: Annual Equivalent Rate (AER) is the effective annual interest rate that reflects the impact of compounding within a year, allowing consistent comparison of returns or borrowing costs across products with different compounding frequencies.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Equivalent Rate = (1 + (Nominal Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Periods per Year)) ^ Compounding Periods per Year - 1

nodes.name: Annual Expense Ratio
nodes.definition: The annual expense ratio refers to the percentage of total annual expenses relative to the relevant principal or total assets. It is a key metric for measuring investment costs, financing costs, or operating costs, widely used especially in fund management and financial services.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Expense Ratio = (Total Annual Expenses ÷ Relevant Principal or Total Assets) × 100%

nodes.name: Annual Fixed Dividend
nodes.definition: Annual fixed dividend refers to the cash dividend amount paid by a company to its shareholders each year under a fixed dividend payout ratio policy, calculated by multiplying the current year's net profit by the fixed dividend payout ratio.

nodes.name: Annual Gross Income
nodes.definition: Annual gross income refers to the total sum of all revenue earned by an individual or business within a complete fiscal year from all operating activities and sources, such as sales of goods, provision of services, investments, etc.

nodes.name: Annual Growth Rate of Common Dividends
nodes.definition: The annual growth rate of common dividends is a parameter used in calculating the cost of common equity (e.g., in the dividend growth model). It is typically derived from historical dividend data, management forecasts, or estimated using models such as the sustainable growth rate, making it a composite indicator that can be deduced or estimated.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Growth Rate of Common Dividends = Retention Ratio × Return on Equity

nodes.name: Annual Growth Rate of Common Stock
Annual Growth Rate of Common Stock Dividends
nodes.definition: The annual growth rate of common stock dividends refers to the expected or historical average growth rate of cash dividends paid by a company to its common shareholders over a one-year period. It is a key parameter for assessing a company's future profitability and the intrinsic value of its stock, commonly used in the dividend growth model to calculate the cost of equity capital.

nodes.name: Annual Holding Cost per Unit
aliases: Carrying Cost per Unit per Year
nodes.definition: Annual holding cost per unit refers to the average cost incurred by an enterprise to store and maintain one unit of goods (or inventory) for one year. It is typically a given, aggregated or estimated unit cost parameter derived from various operational costs such as warehousing fees, insurance, capital carrying cost, spoilage, and obsolescence, commonly used in calculations for inventory management models like the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ).

nodes.name: Annual Inflation Rate
nodes.definition: The annual inflation rate is an indicator measuring the rate at which a country's currency purchasing power declines over one year. It is typically calculated as the annual growth rate of price indices such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI) or Producer Price Index (PPI). It is not a primary accounting line item but a composite metric used for economic analysis, financial forecasting, and investment decision-making. It is often employed as a key parameter for determining nominal interest rates, adjusting real returns, and constructing benchmark return series.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Inflation Rate = (Current Price Level - Base Period Price Level) ÷ Base Period Price Level × 100%
Annual Inflation Rate = (Current Period Price Index - Base Period Price Index) ÷ Base Period Price Index × 100%

nodes.name: Annual Interest
nodes.definition: Annual interest refers to the amount of interest generated over a one-year period based on the principal of a loan or deposit and the agreed annual interest rate. It serves as fundamental data for calculating borrowing costs or investment returns.

nodes.name: Annual Interest Amount
nodes.definition: Annual interest amount refers to the total interest generated over a one-year period based on the principal amount borrowed and the agreed annual interest rate. It is the most fundamental data in interest calculation, typically derived directly through the simple multiplication of 'principal × annual interest rate', and serves as a basic input value for more complex financial calculations (such as interest coverage ratio).

nodes.name: Annual Interest Expense
nodes.definition: Annual interest expense refers to the total interest costs actually paid or accrued by a company within one year due to the use of external borrowings (such as bank loans, bond issuances, etc.), and is a significant cost item on the income statement.

nodes.name: Annual Interest Expense on Debt
nodes.definition: Annual interest expense on debt refers to the interest cost that a company is obligated to pay to creditors within a complete fiscal year due to its debt obligations. It is a key component in calculating financial expenses, net income after tax, and the cost of debt capital. Its core calculation is based on the debt principal and the agreed annual interest rate.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Interest Expense on Debt = Debt Principal × Annual Interest Rate
Annual Interest Expense on Debt = (Debt Principal × Annual Interest Rate) × (1 - Applicable Income Tax Rate)

operands.metric: Number of Days in Interest Period

formulas.source_formula: Annual Interest Expense on Debt = Debt Principal × Annual Interest Rate × Number of Days in Interest Period ÷ 365

nodes.name: Annual Interest Income
nodes.definition: Annual interest income refers to the total interest return received by an individual or enterprise within a complete fiscal year from interest-bearing assets such as deposits, bonds, and loans, based on the contractually agreed interest rate and period.

nodes.name: Annual Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Annual interest rate refers to the deposit or loan interest rate for one year, which is the ratio of the interest amount to the deposit principal or loan principal over a specific period, usually expressed as a percentage. It is a core indicator in the financial field for measuring the cost of capital or the rate of return.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Interest Rate = Daily Interest Rate × 360

nodes.name: Annual Interest Rate (Simple Interest)
nodes.definition: The Annual Interest Rate (Simple Interest) is the base rate specified in a loan or investment contract, used to calculate interest under the simple interest method. It is applied directly to the principal amount, without considering the reinvestment of interest or compounding effects, serving as the original parameter for interest calculation.

nodes.name: Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities
nodes.definition: The annual interest rate of marketable securities refers to the interest rate, calculated on an annual basis, that is either explicitly stipulated in the contract for securities such as bonds and notes or implied by their market price. It represents the ratio between the annual interest income obtainable from holding the security and the security's face value or investment principal, serving as a key known parameter for calculating interest income.

nodes.name: Annual Interest Rate on Marketable Securities
aliases: Annual Interest Rate of Marketable Securities
nodes.definition: The annual interest rate on marketable securities refers to the percentage of interest income, expected or actually earned within one year, relative to the security's principal (face value or purchase cost) when an investor holds securities such as bonds or notes. It is a key metric for measuring the fixed-income level of a security.

formulas.source_formula: Annual MIP = Base Loan Amount × Annual MIP Rate

nodes.name: Annual Management Fee
nodes.definition: Annual management fee typically refers to the ongoing fee paid to the management party over a one-year period for managing a specific asset, fund, investment portfolio, or service, usually calculated as a certain percentage (annual fee rate) of the total asset value.

nodes.name: Annual Mortgage Payment
nodes.definition: Annual mortgage payment is the fixed yearly installment required to fully amortize a loan over its term at a given annual interest rate. It applies to both traditional fixed-rate mortgages and the reset periods of hybrid adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs), assuming equal annual payments and full amortization.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Mortgage Payment = Principal × Annual Interest Rate ÷ (1 - (1 + Annual Interest Rate) ^ -Number of Years)

nodes.name: Annual Net Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Annual net cash flow refers to the difference between cash inflows and cash outflows of an investment project or enterprise in a specific year, reflecting the actual cash activities during that period based on the cash basis principle. It is a key indicator for assessing project feasibility and corporate financial condition.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Net Cash Flow = Net Profit + Depreciation
Annual Net Cash Flow = Operating Revenue - Cash Costs - Income Tax
Annual Net Cash Flow = Operating Revenue × (1 - Income Tax Rate) - Cash Costs × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation × Income Tax Rate

nodes.name: Annual Net Cash Inflow
nodes.definition: Annual net cash inflow refers to the difference between cash inflows and cash outflows generated by an investment project or enterprise within one year through operating, investing, and financing activities. It is a composite indicator derived from other financial data, commonly used in financial analyses such as payback period and net present value.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Net Cash Inflow = Net Profit + Non-cash Costs
Annual Net Cash Inflow = Cash Inflows - Cash Outflows
Annual Net Cash Inflow = Operating Revenue - Cash Costs - Income Tax

nodes.name: Annual Net Credit Sales
nodes.definition: Annual Net Credit Sales refers to the total sales revenue realized through credit sales within a specific fiscal year, net of sales returns, sales allowances, and cash discounts. It serves as a key foundational data point for calculating operational efficiency metrics such as accounts receivable turnover.

nodes.name: Annual Net Excess Operating Cost of the Appraised Asset
nodes.definition: Annual Net Excess Operating Cost of the Appraised Asset refers to the net additional cost incurred annually during the operation of the appraised asset compared to more advanced and efficient assets (or reference assets) available in the market, as assessed in asset valuation. This typically results from factors such as technological obsolescence, low efficiency, or high maintenance expenses of the asset. This cost is a key factor in calculating functional obsolescence depreciation and is used to measure the value loss of an asset due to functional inadequacy.

nodes.name: Annual Net Income
nodes.definition: Annual net income refers to the final operating results attributable to shareholders in a specific fiscal year, derived from total profit after deducting current income tax expense. It is a key indicator for measuring a company's annual profitability.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Net Income = Operating Revenue - Operating Cost - Taxes and Surcharges - Period Expenses + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses - Income Tax Expense
Annual Net Income = Total Profit for the Year × (1 - Income Tax Rate)
Annual Net Income = Total Profit for the Year - Current Income Tax Expense
Annual Net Income = Total Revenue - Total Cost - Total Expenses

nodes.name: Annual Net Profit
nodes.definition: Annual net profit refers to the total profit attributable to shareholders after deducting all costs, expenses, taxes, dividends, and other expenditures throughout an entire fiscal year, serving as a key indicator for measuring a company's annual profitability.

nodes.name: Annual Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Annual operating revenue refers to the total income generated by an enterprise within one year (typically one fiscal year) from its principal business activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, as well as other business operations.

nodes.name: Annual Order Frequency
nodes.definition: Annual order frequency refers to the total number of inventory orders placed by a company within one year, typically calculated by dividing the annual demand by the order quantity per order (such as the economic order quantity). It is a composite indicator in inventory management used to optimize ordering strategies and cost control, and is related to stockout costs.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Order Frequency = Annual Demand ÷ Economic Order Quantity
Annual Ordinary Income = (Monthly Income × 12) + Additional Income

nodes.name: Annual Pay
nodes.definition: Annual pay represents the total yearly compensation an employee receives, encompassing base salary plus all supplementary forms of remuneration such as bonuses, overtime, and the monetary value of benefits.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Pay = Base Pay + Bonuses + Overtime Pay + Benefits Value

nodes.name: Annual Payment Frequency
nodes.definition: Annual payment frequency refers to the number of times a borrower is required to make payments to a lender within one year in financial activities such as loans or installment payments. It is a crucial parameter for calculating financial metrics such as periodic payment amounts and total interest.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Payout = Account Balance × Payout Rate

nodes.name: Annual Percentage Rate (APR)
nodes.definition: The Annual Percentage Rate (APR) for a payday loan is the annualized borrowing cost expressed as a percentage. It is calculated by dividing the flat fee by the loan amount, scaling the result to a 365-day year based on the loan term in days, and converting to a percentage. This measure reflects the effective cost of short-term credit without compounding.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Percentage Rate (APR) = Money Factor × 2400
APR (%) = Flat Fee ÷ Loan Amount × 365 ÷ Loan Term (Days) × 100
Annual Percentage Rate (APR) = ((Total Fees + Total Interest) ÷ Principal ÷ Days in Loan Term) × 365 × 100

nodes.name: Annual Percentage Yield (APY)
nodes.definition: Annual Percentage Yield (APY) is the effective annual rate of return that incorporates the impact of compounding interest within the year. It converts a periodic interest rate and the number of compounding periods per year into an annualized percentage, enabling consistent comparison of investment and deposit returns when interest is compounded more frequently than annually.

formulas.source_formula: APY = (1 + Nominal Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Periods) ^ Compounding Periods - 1
Annual Percentage Yield (APY) = ((1 + Periodic Interest Rate) ^ Compounding Periods per Year - 1) × 100
Annual Pre-Tax Cash Flow = Gross Scheduled Rent + Other Income - Vacancy - Operating Expenses - Annual Mortgage Payments

nodes.name: Annual Preferred Stock Dividend
nodes.definition: Annual preferred stock dividend refers to the compensation paid by a company to its preferred shareholders each year, based on the fixed dividend rate or amount stipulated in the preferred stock issuance terms. Its calculation is typically based on the par value of the preferred stock and the fixed dividend rate.

nodes.name: Annual Product Output
nodes.definition: Annual product output refers to the total quantity of a specific product produced by an enterprise or production unit within one year (typically a fiscal year). It serves as a crucial fundamental metric for measuring production capacity, formulating production plans, and conducting financial forecasts (such as cost, revenue, and profit analysis).

nodes.name: Annual Requirement
nodes.definition: Annual requirement refers to the total amount of funds that an enterprise needs to invest in or occupy within the coming year to maintain normal production and operational activities or support expected sales growth. It is a composite financial metric calculated based on historical data and future forecasts (such as sales revenue, sales profit margin, turnover efficiency, etc.), commonly used in areas such as capital budgeting, financing planning, and inventory management.

operands.metric: Forecast Period Fund Turnover Speed Growth Rate

formulas.source_formula: Annual Requirement = (Base Period Average Fund Occupancy - Unreasonable Fund Occupancy) × (1 + Forecast Period Sales Growth Rate) × (1 - Forecast Period Fund Turnover Speed Growth Rate)
Annual Retirement Benefit = Years of Service × Salary Percentage × Career Average Salary

nodes.name: Annual Return
nodes.definition: Annual return is a financial metric that measures the return on an investment over a one-year period, typically expressed as a percentage, reflecting the efficiency of capital appreciation within a year. It is a composite indicator that can be calculated based on the relationship between investment returns and the principal amount.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Return = Annual Total Revenue - Annual Costs and Expenses
Annual Return = (Investment Return ÷ Investment Principal) × 100%
Annual Return = (Investment Internal Return ÷ Investment Principal) ÷ Investment Days × 365 × 100%

nodes.name: Annual Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The annual risk-adjusted discount rate, also known as the risk-adjusted discount rate, is a discount rate adjusted based on the risk level of a project or asset, building upon the risk-free discount rate. It is used to discount risky cash flows. Its core calculation formula is K = i + bQ, where i is the risk-free discount rate, b is the risk premium slope, and Q is the risk level.

nodes.name: Annual SEPP Withdrawal (Amortization Method)
aliases: 实质性相等定期付款（摊销法）年提取额
等额定期付款（摊销法）年提取额
nodes.definition: The annual SEPP withdrawal (amortization method) is the fixed annual payment from a qualified retirement account calculated by amortizing the account balance over the taxpayer’s life expectancy using a chosen interest rate, subject to IRS Rule 72(t) and the constraint that the interest rate not exceed 120% of the federal mid-term rate.

formulas.source_formula: Annual SEPP Withdrawal (Amortization Method) = (Account Balance × Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 ÷ (1 + Interest Rate) ^ Life Expectancy))
Annual SEPP Withdrawal (RMD Method) = Account Balance ÷ Life Expectancy

nodes.name: Annual Sales Revenue Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The annual sales revenue growth rate is a financial metric that measures the growth of a company's current period sales revenue relative to the previous period. It is used to assess the company's market expansion capability and growth potential, serving as an important basis for forecasting future cash flows and managing working capital.

nodes.name: Annual Sinking Fund
nodes.definition: Annual sinking fund refers to the equal amount that must be deposited at the end of each period, given a specified interest rate and number of periods, in order to accumulate a predetermined sum of money (future value) at a future point in time.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Sinking Fund = Target Future Value × Sinking Fund Factor
Annual Sinking Fund = Debt Future Value ÷ Ordinary Annuity Future Value Factor
Annual Sinking Fund Payment = Total Debt ÷ Years
Annual Straight-Line Depreciation = (Purchase Price - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life (Years)
Annual Swap Gain/Loss = Notional Principal × ((SOFR Change + Basis Points) - Fixed Rate)

nodes.name: Annual Total Credit Sales
aliases: Total Credit Sales for the Year
nodes.definition: Annual Total Credit Sales refers to the total sales revenue generated by a company within a fiscal year through credit sales (i.e., allowing customers deferred payment) for goods sold or services provided, representing the gross figure before any deductions for returns, allowances, or discounts.

nodes.name: Annual Total Dividend
nodes.definition: Annual Total Dividend refers to the sum of all cash dividends actually received by an investor within one year from a single stock held or from the entire investment portfolio. It reflects the total cash return distributed by the company to shareholders during that fiscal year.

nodes.name: Annual Total Expenses
nodes.definition: Annual total expenses refer to the aggregate sum of all costs and expenses incurred by an enterprise or project within one year to maintain operations, production, or service provision. It typically includes major categories such as cost of main operations, operating expenses, administrative expenses, and financial expenses, serving as a key metric for measuring annual expenditure levels and conducting budget management.

nodes.name: Annual Total Funding Requirement
nodes.definition: Annual Total Funding Requirement refers to the total amount of funds a company needs within a year to meet its operating and investment activities. It is typically calculated based on the increase in net operating assets or working capital requirements, and is used for financing planning and financial management.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Total Funding Requirement = Projected Net Operating Assets - Base Period Net Operating Assets
Annual Total Funding Requirement = (Projected Operating Assets - Projected Operating Liabilities) - (Base Period Operating Assets - Base Period Operating Liabilities)

nodes.name: Annual Total Investment
nodes.definition: Annual Total Investment refers to the sum of the future value of an investment at the end of a specific investment period (typically one year), or the total capital required to achieve a specific annual output target. It reflects the terminal value of the investment considering the time value of money, or the total funding scale required to launch a project.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Total Investment = Initial Investment Amount × (1 + Annualized Investment Return Rate) ^ Investment Period
Annual Total Investment = (Annual Product Output × Product Unit Price) ÷ Capital Turnover Ratio

nodes.name: Annual Total Profit
nodes.definition: Annual total profit refers to the final total profit achieved by an enterprise through all operating and non-operating activities within a complete fiscal year, serving as a crucial fundamental indicator for calculating corporate income tax and assessing corporate profitability.

nodes.name: Annual Turnover
nodes.definition: Annual turnover (portfolio turnover ratio) measures how actively an investment fund replaces its holdings over a year. It is calculated by dividing the greater of total fund purchases or total fund sales by the fund's average assets for the period, indicating the fund's trading activity intensity.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Turnover = Monthly Turnover Rate × Periods per Year
Annual Withdrawal = Initial Balance × Withdrawal Rate
Annual Withdrawal = Investment × Age-Based Withdrawal Rate

nodes.name: Annual Withdrawal Amount
nodes.definition: Annual withdrawal amount is the fixed sum that can be withdrawn each year from a retirement portfolio, computed as the product of the portfolio balance and the chosen withdrawal rate.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Withdrawal Amount = Portfolio Balance × Withdrawal Rate

nodes.name: Annualization Factor
nodes.definition: The annualization factor is an intermediate conversion factor used to convert a statistic (such as volatility or return) from an observation period to an annualized statistic, typically calculated by dividing the total number of periods in a year by the number of observation periods.

formulas.source_formula: Annualization Factor = Total Periods in a Year ÷ Number of Observation Periods
Annualized Forward Premium = ((Forward Rate - Spot Rate) ÷ Spot Rate) × (360 ÷ Period Days) × 100

nodes.name: Annualized Income
nodes.definition: Annualized income estimates a full-year income by projecting partial-period earned income to twelve months at the same rate, commonly used in budgeting, forecasting, and tax planning to standardize income over a calendar year.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Income = Earned Income × (12 ÷ Months of Data)

nodes.name: Annualized Income Installment Method
nodes.definition: The Annualized Income Installment Method allocates a taxpayer's estimated annual tax liability to each installment period based on the cumulative share of income earned by that date. This aligns estimated tax payments with uneven cash flows to reduce underpayment penalties and improve liquidity planning.

nodes.name: Annualized Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Annualized interest rate refers to the conversion of interest rates from different periods (such as daily or monthly) into a one-year period using specific calculation formulas. It is used to uniformly compare the yield or borrowing costs of different financial products, reflecting the true cost or return level of funds over one year.

nodes.name: Annualized Investment Return Rate
nodes.definition: The annualized investment return rate is a metric that converts investment returns from different time periods into a standardized one-year rate, used to uniformly measure and compare the profitability of different investment projects.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Yield = (YTD Growth Factor ^ (12 ÷ Months Passed) - 1) × 100

nodes.name: Annualized Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The annualized rate of return, commonly expressed as the compound annual growth rate (CAGR), represents the constant annual growth rate that equates the beginning and ending values of an investment over a specified holding period, assuming reinvestment and no interim cash flows.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Rate of Return = ( (End Value - Contributions) ÷ Start Value )^(1 ÷ Years) - 1
Annualized Rate of Return (CAGR) = (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1 ÷ Years) - 1

nodes.name: Annualized Return
nodes.definition: Annualized return converts a periodic return into an annual rate under a linear scaling assumption, enabling comparability across investments with different holding periods. When derived from a single quarter, it is computed by multiplying the quarterly return by the number of quarters in a year, assuming constant returns across quarters.

nodes.name: Annualized Return (Zero-Coupon Bond)
nodes.definition: Annualized return (simple) for a zero-coupon bond measures the average annual rate of return, calculated as the price appreciation from purchase price to face value divided by the purchase price, spread evenly over the years to maturity, and expressed as a percentage. It assumes holding to maturity and excludes compounding.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Return (%) = ((Face Value - Purchase Price) ÷ Purchase Price) ÷ Years to Maturity × 100

nodes.name: Annualized Return on Investment (ROI)
nodes.definition: Annualized return on investment (ROI) measures the average yearly return by dividing the total ROI by the number of years the investment was held. It enables comparison across investments with different holding periods and assumes a linear distribution of returns without compounding effects.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Return on Investment = Total ROI ÷ Years Held

nodes.name: Annualized Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Annualized standard deviation scales the daily standard deviation by the square root of the number of trading days in a year to express volatility on an annual basis. It is commonly used to compare and evaluate risk across assets or portfolios over a yearly horizon under the square-root-of-time assumption.

nodes.name: Annualized Total Return
nodes.definition: Annualized total return is the geometric average compound rate of return per year (or per specified period) derived from a sequence of periodic returns. It reflects the constant rate at which an investment grows over time, accounting for compounding, and is expressed as a decimal. It does not incorporate the effects of inflation, taxes, fees, or volatility.

formulas.source_formula: Annualized Total Return = (1 + Cumulative Return)^(365 ÷ Days Held) - 1

nodes.name: Annualized Volatility
nodes.definition: Annualized volatility is the standard deviation of returns scaled to an annual horizon by multiplying the periodic standard deviation by the square root of the number of periods per year, serving as a key measure of investment risk.

nodes.name: Annuitization
nodes.definition: Annuitization is the process of converting a lump-sum balance into a stream of periodic payments over a specified term. The periodic annuity payment is determined by the present value of the annuity, the periodic interest rate, and the number of payment periods, assuming a constant rate and fixed term.

nodes.name: Annuity
nodes.definition: An annuity refers to a series of equal cash flows occurring at regular intervals (such as annually, semi-annually, or monthly) over a specified period. It is a key concept in financial management and investment decision-making used to evaluate the present or future value of a series of fixed future payments or receipts.

nodes.name: Annuity Due
nodes.definition: An annuity due is a series of equal payments made at the beginning of each period. Its future value equals the present stream of payments compounded forward, with an additional compounding for the earlier payment timing relative to an ordinary annuity. The standard formula multiplies the ordinary annuity future value factor by (1 + interest rate) to reflect beginning-of-period payments.

formulas.source_formula: Annuity Factor = (1 - (1 + Discount Rate)^(-Lifespan Years)) ÷ Discount Rate
Annuity Payout = Principal ÷ Periods
Annuity Payout = Principal × [Interest Rate × (1 + Interest Rate)^Periods] ÷ [(1 + Interest Rate)^Periods - 1]

nodes.name: Anti-Dilution Provision
nodes.definition: An anti-dilution provision protects investors in convertible securities from value dilution when new shares are issued at a lower price. Under the weighted average method, the conversion price is adjusted based on the relative magnitude of the new issuance and the consideration received, yielding a balanced adjustment to the conversion terms.

nodes.name: Applicable Income Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The applicable income tax rate refers to the statutory taxation percentage directly applied to the taxable income of an enterprise or individual as stipulated by national tax laws. It is a parameter predetermined by law, typically determined based on different income brackets (such as progressive tax rates) or taxpayer types (such as general taxpayers), rather than being calculated from other financial data.

nodes.name: Applicable Tax Rate
nodes.definition: Applicable tax rate refers to the percentage or fixed amount, as stipulated by tax laws, that is directly used to calculate the tax payable for specific taxpayers, taxable items, or income brackets. It is typically explicitly defined by law and is not derived from the calculation of other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Applicable Unit Standard Property Price
nodes.definition: Applicable Unit Standard Property Price refers to the benchmark price standard set for a specific type or unit of property, used for calculating taxes or sale prices in contexts such as specific real estate tax policies or the sale of public housing. It is typically established by the government or relevant authorities based on factors such as cost, location, and construction standards, serving as the basis for tax assessment or pricing.

nodes.name: Applicable Unit Standard Rent Price
nodes.definition: Applicable Unit Standard Rent Price refers to the standard monthly rental price for leased properties, calculated by real estate management departments according to unified regulations, applicable to specific units (e.g., per square meter of usable area). It serves as a fundamental rental reference value used in related fields such as real estate tax for assessment or calculation purposes.

formulas.source_formula: Applied Capital Loss = min(Net Capital Loss, Maximum Offset against Ordinary Income)

nodes.name: Appreciation Rate
nodes.definition: Appreciation rate measures the compounded rate at which an asset's value increases over a specified number of periods, commonly expressed as the compound annual growth rate (CAGR). It is calculated by taking the ratio of future value to initial value, raising it to the power of one divided by the number of periods, and subtracting one. The metric assumes a constant growth path and is used in investment performance analysis, valuation, and financial planning.

formulas.source_formula: Appreciation Rate = (Future Value ÷ Initial Value)^(1 ÷ Periods) - 1

nodes.name: Appropriation for Employee Bonuses and Welfare, etc.
Appropriation of Discretionary Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Appropriation of discretionary surplus reserve refers to the appropriation of a specific portion of after-tax net profit, for designated purposes, into retained earnings after the appropriation of the statutory surplus reserve, based on the company's articles of association or resolutions of the shareholders' meeting or board of directors. The appropriation ratio and usage are determined by the company itself, primarily for purposes such as covering losses, expanding production and operations, or converting into capital.

nodes.name: Appropriation of Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Appropriation of surplus reserve refers to the allocation of a certain proportion of after-tax net profit, as required by law or determined by the company's own decisions, to be retained within the enterprise for specific purposes. It mainly includes statutory surplus reserve and discretionary surplus reserve.

formulas.source_formula: Appropriation of Surplus Reserve = Current Year Net Profit × Appropriation Rate
Appropriation of Surplus Reserve = (Current Year Net Profit + Beginning Retained Earnings - Beginning Uncovered Loss) × Appropriation Rate

nodes.name: Appropriation to Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund
Approved Credit Line
nodes.definition: Approved credit line refers to the maximum loan or credit limit formally granted to a borrower by a financial institution (such as a bank) after review. Within this limit, the borrower may draw funds in multiple installments or as a lump sum according to agreed conditions and purposes.

formulas.source_formula: Arbitrage Profit = Futures Price - Spot Price - Transaction Cost
Arbitrage Profit = Principal × (Foreign Interest Rate - Domestic Interest Rate)

nodes.name: Arbitrage Profit in Contango
nodes.definition: Arbitrage profit in a contango market represents the net gain achieved by simultaneously buying the underlying asset at the spot price and selling the corresponding futures contract when the futures price exceeds the spot price, after deducting all associated transaction costs.

nodes.name: Arc Elasticity of Demand
nodes.definition: Arc elasticity of demand measures the responsiveness of quantity demanded to a change in price between two discrete points. It is computed as the ratio of the percentage change in quantity demanded to the percentage change in price. This formulation uses the initial values as the base for percentage changes and is typically interpreted in absolute value.

formulas.source_formula: Arc Elasticity of Demand = [(Final Quantity - Initial Quantity) × 2 ÷ (Initial Quantity + Final Quantity)] ÷ [(Final Price - Initial Price) × 2 ÷ (Initial Price + Final Price)]
Arc Elasticity of Demand = ((Final Quantity - Initial Quantity) ÷ Initial Quantity) ÷ ((Final Price - Initial Price) ÷ Initial Price)

nodes.name: Arithmetic Mean
nodes.definition: The arithmetic mean is the sum of a set of values divided by the number of values in the set, and is the most commonly used and fundamental statistical measure for describing central tendency in data.

formulas.source_formula: Arithmetic Mean = Sum of Data Points ÷ Number of Data Points
Arithmetic Mean = Sum of Values ÷ Number of Observations

nodes.name: Arms Index
nodes.definition: The Arms Index, also known as the Trading Index (TRIN), is a breadth indicator that compares the ratio of advancing to declining stocks with the ratio of advancing to declining volume to assess overall market sentiment.

nodes.name: Arms Index (TRIN)
nodes.definition: The Arms Index (TRIN) is a market breadth technical indicator that measures short-term market sentiment by comparing the ratio of advancing to declining issues with the ratio of advancing to declining volume. Values below 1.0 typically indicate bullish conditions (relatively more volume in advancing issues), while values above 1.0 indicate bearish conditions (relatively more volume in declining issues).

formulas.source_formula: Arms Index (TRIN) = (Advancing Issues ÷ Declining Issues) ÷ (Advancing Volume ÷ Declining Volume)

nodes.name: Aroon Down
nodes.definition: Aroon Down is a technical analysis indicator that measures the time elapsed since the most recent low over a specified lookback period. Expressed on a 0–100 scale, higher values indicate that a recent low occurred more recently within the lookback window, helping assess the presence and strength of a downtrend.

formulas.source_formula: Aroon Down = (1 - Periods Since Most Recent Low ÷ Total Periods) × 100

nodes.name: Aroon Oscillator
nodes.definition: The Aroon Oscillator is a technical analysis indicator that measures the strength and timing of trends by evaluating the time elapsed since the most recent high and low. The Aroon Down component quantifies downtrend strength on a 0–100 scale based on how long it has been since the last low within a specified lookback period.

formulas.source_formula: Aroon Oscillator = Aroon Up - Aroon Down
Aroon Down = 100 × (Total Periods - Periods Since Low) ÷ Total Periods

nodes.name: Aroon Up
nodes.definition: Aroon Up is a technical analysis indicator that measures how recently a high price occurred within a specified look-back period, indicating the strength and timeliness of an uptrend. Values range from 0 to 100, with higher readings signaling more recent highs and stronger upward momentum.

formulas.source_formula: Aroon Up = 100 × (Total Periods - Periods Since High) ÷ Total Periods
Aroon Up = ((Total Periods - Periods Since High) ÷ Total Periods) × 100

nodes.name: Ascending Triangle Profit Target
nodes.definition: An ascending triangle profit target is a price objective derived from the measured height of an ascending triangle pattern added to or subtracted from the breakout price. Traders estimate the target by measuring the triangle’s maximum vertical height and applying it to the breakout point, using addition for upside breakouts and subtraction for downside breakouts.

nodes.name: Ask Price
nodes.definition: The ask price refers to the price at which a seller is willing to sell a specific asset (such as stocks, foreign exchange, commodities, etc.) and at which a transaction is ultimately executed. It is fundamental market transaction data that directly reflects the immediate liquidation value of the asset.

nodes.name: Assessed Value
nodes.definition: Assessed value is the taxable valuation of a property determined by applying an assessment rate to its fair market value. It serves as the base for calculating property taxes and may differ from market value due to statutory ratios, exemptions, and equalization adjustments.

formulas.source_formula: Assessed Value = Fair Market Value × Assessment Rate
supporting_source_formulas: Assessed Value = Fair Market Value × Assessment Rate

nodes.name: Asset A Average Return Rate
nodes.definition: Asset A Average Return Rate is an indicator that measures the average profitability of a specific Asset A over a period, typically calculated as the ratio of the net profit generated by the asset to its average total assets, reflecting the utilization efficiency and average return level of Asset A.

nodes.name: Asset A Periodic Return Rate
nodes.definition: Asset A Periodic Return Rate refers to the ratio of the return earned by Asset A over a specific period (such as a year, quarter, or month) to its value at the beginning of the period. It is typically composed of two parts: interest or dividend income during the period and capital gains resulting from changes in the asset's price.

nodes.name: Asset Acquisition Cost
nodes.definition: Asset acquisition cost refers to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire an asset and bring it to its intended usable condition, typically including purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, loading and unloading fees, installation and commissioning fees, and other direct expenses. It forms the basis for the initial recorded value of the asset.

nodes.name: Asset Acquisition Price
nodes.definition: Asset acquisition price refers to the consideration amount directly paid to the seller to obtain ownership of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, equipment, etc.) at the time of purchase. It is typically determined based on transaction contracts or documentation and serves as the fundamental original data for subsequent accounting treatment and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Asset Allocation
nodes.definition: Asset allocation is the implementation of an investment strategy aimed at achieving a balance between risk and return by adjusting the proportion of various asset classes in a portfolio according to the investor's risk tolerance, investment objectives, and investment horizon. Its focus lies in the characteristics of the overall investment portfolio.

nodes.name: Asset B Expected Average Rate of Return
aliases: Asset B's Expected Rate of Return
Mean Expected Return of Asset B
nodes.definition: Asset B Expected Average Rate of Return refers to the estimated average rate of return that Asset B is likely to achieve in the future, based on historical data, probability distributions, or model predictions under uncertain market conditions. It serves as a fundamental metric for evaluating the investment attractiveness of Asset B and conducting risk-return analysis.

nodes.name: Asset B Historical Average Return Rate
aliases: Historical Average Return of Asset B
Mean Historical Return of Asset B
nodes.definition: Asset B Historical Average Return Rate refers to the arithmetic mean calculated based on the actual return data of Asset B over a past period (such as several years or periods), used to measure the average profitability level of the asset during the historical period.

nodes.name: Asset B Weight
nodes.definition: In the context of banking regulation, the Asset B Weight specifically refers to the fixed risk weight percentage (e.g., 0%, 20%, 50%, etc.) assigned to different categories of on-balance-sheet assets (such as cash, corporate loans, residential mortgages, etc.) in the 'G4B-1 On-balance-sheet Credit Risk-Weighted Assets Calculation Table (Standardized Approach)'. This weight is directly prescribed by the regulatory authority (e.g., the China Banking and Insurance Regulatory Commission) based on the risk characteristics of the asset. It is used to calculate credit risk-weighted assets and serves as fundamental data for regulatory capital requirements, rather than being derived from financial formulas.

nodes.name: Asset Beta
nodes.definition: Asset Beta is the unlevered beta, which is a systematic risk measure that reflects only the business risk of a company after removing the effects of its capital structure.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Beta = Equity Beta ÷ [1 + (1 - Tax Rate) × (Debt ÷ Equity)]

nodes.name: Asset Class Adjustment Factor
aliases: 资产类别权重调整因子
nodes.definition: The Asset Class Adjustment Factor is a parameter used to modify or adjust the weight or value of a specific asset class in overall evaluation, risk measurement, or portfolio construction. It is typically calculated based on the specific risk, liquidity, market conditions, or other relevant characteristics of the asset class to more accurately reflect its true contribution or impact.

nodes.name: Asset Conversion to Renminbi
nodes.definition: Asset conversion to Renminbi refers to the process of translating foreign currency-denominated asset items into Renminbi amounts using a specific exchange rate (such as the spot rate on the balance sheet date or the historical rate). This is a key step in foreign currency financial statement translation, aimed at preparing consolidated statements or meeting other reporting requirements.

nodes.name: Asset Coverage Ratio
nodes.definition: Asset Coverage Ratio measures a company's ability to repay its debt obligations using its tangible assets after deducting short-term liabilities, indicating long-term solvency and financial stability.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Coverage Ratio = (Total Assets - Short-term Liabilities) ÷ Total Debt
Asset Coverage Ratio = ((Total Assets - Intangible Assets) - (Current Liabilities - Short-term Debt)) ÷ Total Debt
Asset Coverage Ratio = (Book Value of Total Assets - Intangible Assets - Current Liabilities + Short-term Debt Obligations) ÷ Total Debt Outstanding

nodes.name: Asset Depreciation or Amortization
nodes.definition: Asset depreciation or amortization is the process by which a company systematically allocates the cost of fixed assets (such as equipment, buildings) or intangible assets (such as patents, goodwill) as an expense over their estimated useful lives or periods of economic benefit generation. This reflects the consumption of asset value due to usage, passage of time, or technological obsolescence.

nodes.name: Asset Impairment Loss
nodes.definition: Asset impairment loss refers to the loss recognized in financial statements when the carrying value of an asset (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc.) exceeds its recoverable amount. This reflects a decline in the asset's value and directly impacts the company's current-period profit.

nodes.name: Asset Impairment Loss Adjustment
nodes.definition: Asset impairment loss adjustment refers to the process of recognizing and measuring the difference between the carrying amount of an asset and its recoverable amount in accordance with accounting standards, which will affect the total adjusted assets.

operands.metric: Recoverable Amount of Asset in Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Asset Impairment Loss Adjustment = Carrying Amount of Asset - Recoverable Amount of Asset
Asset Impairment Loss Adjustment = Original Value of Asset - Estimated Value of Impaired Asset

nodes.name: Asset Impairment Loss of Previous Period
Asset Impairment Provision
nodes.definition: Asset impairment provision refers to the reserve set aside when the carrying value of an enterprise's asset exceeds its recoverable amount, in order to reflect the decline in the asset's value. This typically occurs due to factors such as a sustained decline in the asset's market price, technological obsolescence, damage, or prolonged idleness, resulting in its future economic benefits being lower than its carrying value. The purpose of recognizing an impairment provision is to present the asset at a more true and fair value in the financial statements.

nodes.name: Asset Impairment Provision for Next Period
aliases: Next Period Impairment Provision for Assets
未来期间资产减值准备
nodes.definition: Asset impairment provision for the next period refers to the amount of asset impairment loss that an enterprise expects to recognize in the next accounting period when, at the balance sheet date, there are indications of asset impairment and its recoverable amount is lower than its carrying amount. This metric is an important adjustment item for calculating the net cash flow from operating activities in the next period.

operands.metric: Carrying Amount of Assets in Next Period
Recoverable Amount of Assets in Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Asset Impairment Provision for Next Period = Carrying Amount of Assets in Next Period - Recoverable Amount of Assets in Next Period
Asset Investment Amount = Total Investment × Allocation Proportion

nodes.name: Asset Management Fee
nodes.definition: Asset management fee refers to the compensation paid by asset owners (such as fund investors) to professional managers (such as fund management companies) for the investment operation and management of assets. This fee is typically accrued periodically as a certain percentage of the assets under management, serving as one of the primary revenue sources for the manager and is recorded as an expense in the income statement.

nodes.name: Asset Price Series
nodes.definition: An asset price series refers to a data sequence formed by recording and arranging the market transaction prices of a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) at different consecutive time points (e.g., per minute, daily, weekly) in financial markets. It is the most fundamental raw observational data in financial analysis and serves as the basis for calculating derived metrics such as asset returns and volatility.

nodes.name: Asset Replacement Cost
nodes.definition: Asset replacement cost refers to the total cost required to repurchase or reconstruct an asset that is identical or equivalent in function, condition, and utility to the original asset under current market conditions. It reflects the current acquisition cost of the asset and is a commonly used value measurement standard in asset valuation and financial accounting.

nodes.name: Asset Retirement Obligation
nodes.definition: An asset retirement obligation (ARO) is a legal obligation associated with the retirement, decommissioning, or restoration of a long-lived asset. In financial accounting (e.g., under ASC 410 and IAS 37), entities estimate the expected costs of dismantling and remediation, recognize a liability at the present value of those costs, and subsequently record accretion expense. The provided formula estimates the future nominal cost by compounding the current cost at an assumed annual inflation rate over a specified time horizon for planning and forecasting purposes.

nodes.name: Asset Return Series
nodes.definition: An asset return series is a time series formed by the returns of an asset at consecutive time points, typically calculated from asset price series or other underlying data. It is used to measure the volatility, risk, and correlation with other assets of asset returns, serving as fundamental data for portfolio analysis, risk management, and investment decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Return Series = Net Profit Margin Series × Asset Turnover Series
Asset Return Series = Risk-free Rate Series + Beta Coefficient × (Market Return Series - Risk-free Rate Series)

nodes.name: Asset Risk Exposure
nodes.definition: Asset risk exposure refers to the amount or value of assets that financial institutions or enterprises may face potential losses under specific risks (such as credit risk, market risk) without taking any hedging or protective measures. It measures the maximum loss exposure that may be incurred when a risk event occurs.

nodes.name: Asset Selling Price
nodes.definition: Asset selling price refers to the actual transfer amount of an asset agreed upon by both buyers and sellers in a specific transaction, which is the actual transaction price determined upon completion of the transaction.

formulas.source_formula: Sale Proceeds = Number of Shares × Final Share Price

nodes.name: Asset Swap Spread
nodes.definition: Asset swap spread is the yield differential between a fixed-rate bond and the fixed leg of an interest rate swap, adjusted for any price premium or discount paid over the life of the swap. It represents the bond's relative value versus the swap curve and is typically quoted in percentage points or basis points.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Swap Spread = Bond Yield - Swap Rate - Price Premium

nodes.name: Asset Turnover
nodes.definition: Asset turnover measures how efficiently a company uses its total assets to generate sales revenue over a period, calculated as sales divided by average total assets.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Total Assets
Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Total Assets
supporting_source_formulas: Asset Turnover = Revenue ÷ Average Total Assets

formulas.source_formula: Asset Turnover = Total Sales ÷ ((Beginning Total Assets + Ending Total Assets) ÷ 2)

nodes.name: Asset Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: The Asset Turnover Ratio is a core metric measuring the overall operating efficiency and utilization efficiency of a company's assets, indicating the sales revenue generated per unit of assets. A higher ratio suggests faster asset turnover and higher asset utilization efficiency, making it a key component for evaluating operating capability and conducting DuPont analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Turnover Ratio = Sustainable Growth Rate ÷ (Net Profit Margin × Retention Ratio × Equity Multiplier)
Asset Turnover Ratio = Sales Revenue ÷ Average Total Assets
Asset Turnover Ratio = Net Sales ÷ Total Assets
Asset Turnover Ratio = Net Operating Revenue ÷ Average Total Assets
Asset Turnover Ratio = Net Revenue from Principal Business ÷ Average Total Assets
Asset Turnover Ratio = Net Sales Revenue ÷ Average Total Assets
Asset Turnover Ratio = Net Turnover ÷ Average Total Assets

nodes.name: Asset Turnover Series
nodes.definition: The Asset Turnover Series is a set of metrics that measure a company's efficiency in using its total assets to generate sales revenue. The core metric is the Total Asset Turnover, which reflects the overall efficiency of a company's asset operations and serves as a key link connecting asset management and profitability in the DuPont Analysis System.

formulas.source_formula: Asset Turnover Series = Net Operating Revenue ÷ Average Total Assets

nodes.name: Asset Valuation
nodes.definition: Asset valuation is the process of estimating the economic value of a company's assets or equity. Common approaches include balance-sheet-based measures such as Net Asset Value (which may be adjusted to exclude intangible assets for a tangible measure) and income-based measures such as Discounted Dividend Value, which estimates the present value of expected future dividends discounted at an appropriate rate.

nodes.name: Asset Value
nodes.definition: Asset value refers to the economic value of an asset at a specific point in time, typically based on the future economic benefits it can generate. It is calculated through valuation models such as the income capitalization approach and discounted future cash flow method, serving as a crucial composite indicator for enterprise valuation, investment decision-making, and financial reporting.

nodes.name: Asset Weight
nodes.definition: Asset weight refers to the proportion of the value of a specific asset relative to the total value of the entire investment portfolio or asset base in portfolio management or financial analysis. It is used to measure the relative importance and influence of that asset within the whole, serving as a key parameter for calculating portfolio returns, risk (such as variance or standard deviation), and making asset allocation decisions.

nodes.name: Asset Weight in Portfolio
nodes.definition: Asset weight in portfolio refers to the proportion of each asset's value (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) to the total value of the constructed investment portfolio. It reflects the importance and influence of that asset on the overall portfolio and serves as key foundational data for asset allocation and risk management.

nodes.name: Asset Weights
nodes.definition: Asset weights refer to the proportion of each asset's market value relative to the total market value of the investment portfolio, used to calculate the expected return of a risky portfolio. It is a key derived metric in portfolio risk management and analysis.

nodes.name: Asset-Based Value
nodes.definition: Asset-based value is the net asset value of a company computed as total assets minus total liabilities. It is used in the asset-based valuation approach to estimate the value attributable to owners based on the balance sheet, typically requiring assets and liabilities to be measured at fair value and adjusted for intangible assets, non-operating items, and off-balance-sheet obligations.

formulas.source_formula: Asset-Based Value = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Asset-to-Sales Percentage
nodes.definition: Asset-to-Sales Percentage (also known as Operating Asset-to-Sales Percentage) refers to the ratio of a company's operating assets to its sales revenue. It is used to measure the efficiency of a company in generating sales revenue from its operating assets and serves as a key indicator in the Percentage of Sales Method for forecasting funding requirements.

formulas.source_formula: Asset-to-Sales Percentage = (Total Assets - Financial Assets) ÷ Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Assets
nodes.definition: Assets refer to resources arising from past transactions or events, owned or controlled by an enterprise, which are expected to generate economic benefits for the enterprise. On the balance sheet, total assets equal the sum of current assets and non-current assets.

nodes.name: Assets Under Management
nodes.definition: In the financial sector, Assets Under Management (AUM) refers to the total market value of all financial assets that a financial institution (such as a mutual fund, venture capital firm, or depository institution) or a decentralized network protocol manages and invests on behalf of its clients.

nodes.name: Assets/Equity
nodes.definition: Assets/Equity is a financial ratio calculated by dividing total assets by total owners' equity. It is a composite indicator that reflects the multiple relationship between a company's assets and shareholders' equity, commonly used to measure the degree of financial leverage and referenced in analyses such as sustainable growth rate.

nodes.name: Assets/Sales
nodes.definition: Assets/Sales is a financial ratio that represents the ratio of total assets to sales revenue, used to measure the level of asset investment required per unit of sales revenue. This ratio is the reciprocal of the total asset turnover ratio and serves as an important indicator in corporate financial analysis, asset efficiency evaluation, and sustainable growth rate calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Assets/Sales = 1 ÷ Total Asset Turnover
Assets/Sales = Total Assets ÷ Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Assigned Activity Cost for a Specific Item
nodes.definition: Assigned activity cost for a specific item refers to the portion of indirect costs that, under activity-based costing, are first accumulated for various activities and then allocated to a specific cost object (such as a product, service, or customer) based on activity drivers. It represents the value of activity resources actually consumed by that cost object.

operands.metric: Activity Quantity Consumed by the Product

formulas.source_formula: Assigned Activity Cost for a Specific Item = Activity Cost Allocation Rate × Activity Quantity Consumed by the Product

nodes.name: Assumed Average Misstatement Rate
nodes.definition: The assumed average misstatement rate is a concept in audit sampling, referring to the auditor's preliminary estimate or assumption made during the planning stage regarding the likely misstatement rate (i.e., the proportion of misstated items in the population) in the population, based on their understanding of the audited entity, prior years' audit experience, or industry data. This assumption is commonly used to determine sample size or assess sampling risk, particularly when combined with concepts such as tolerable misstatement.

nodes.name: At The Money
nodes.definition: At The Money (ATM) refers to an option whose strike price is equal to or very close to the current market price of the underlying asset. ATM options have zero intrinsic value; their premium consists entirely of time (extrinsic) value. Intrinsic value, computed as max(0, Market Price − Strike Price) for calls and max(0, Strike Price − Market Price) for puts, is the basis for determining whether an option is In-The-Money (ITM), At-The-Money (ATM), or Out-Of-The-Money (OTM).

nodes.name: Attributable Profit
nodes.definition: Attributable profit refers to the portion of net profit in consolidated financial statements that belongs to the owners of the parent company (i.e., the parent entity). It is typically derived by deducting the profit or loss attributable to non-controlling interests from the consolidated net profit. It is a key component in calculating the entity free cash flow for the final period of the forecast horizon.

nodes.name: Attribution Analysis
nodes.definition: Returns-based style analysis is a form of attribution analysis that evaluates how closely a fund's returns align with a benchmark by measuring the correlation between the fund and benchmark return series. The correlation coefficient indicates the strength and direction of the relationship, helping to assess investment style conformity and benchmark tracking characteristics.

nodes.name: Attribution Ratio
nodes.definition: Attribution ratio is a fundamental concept describing ownership, equity, or profit distribution relationships, used to define the share or percentage of specific interests (such as net profit, assets, cash flow, etc.) ultimately attributable to which entity (e.g., parent company shareholders, minority shareholders, etc.). It is not a financial ratio calculated by formula per se, but rather the core concept for understanding the meaning of 'attribution' in composite indicators such as 'attributable net profit'.

nodes.name: Attrition
nodes.definition: Attrition, often reported as the attrition rate, measures the percentage of employees who leave an organization during a specific period relative to the average number of employees. It is used to assess workforce stability, turnover dynamics, and the effectiveness of retention strategies.

formulas.source_formula: Attrition Rate = Departures ÷ Average Employees × 100

nodes.name: Autocorrelation
nodes.definition: Autocorrelation is a statistical measure that quantifies the linear relationship between a time series and its own lagged values. In finance, it is used to detect momentum, mean reversion, seasonality, and non-independence in asset returns or other financial time series, informing model selection, risk assessment, and trading strategy design.

formulas.source_formula: Autocorrelation Coefficient (Lag) = Autocovariance (Lag) ÷ Variance

nodes.name: Autonomous Consumption
nodes.definition: Autonomous consumption refers to the essential consumption expenditures required to maintain basic living standards, which are independent of an individual's or household's current income level. This portion of consumption is typically considered fixed; even when income is zero, people will maintain this consumption by drawing on savings or borrowing.

nodes.name: Autoregressive Integrated Moving Average (ARIMA)
aliases: 自回归差分移动平均模型
自回归综合移动平均模型
nodes.definition: An ARIMA model is a time series forecasting approach that combines autoregressive (AR) terms, differencing (I) to achieve stationarity, and moving average (MA) terms to capture residual autocorrelation. It is widely used in financial forecasting to model and predict short-term movements in non-stationary financial series, with model selection often guided by information criteria such as AIC and BIC.

nodes.name: Autoregressive Prediction
nodes.definition: An autoregressive (AR) prediction estimates the next value of a time series as a linear combination of its recent lagged observations weighted by AR coefficients, commonly used in financial time series forecasting under stationarity assumptions.

nodes.name: Auxiliary Materials Cost
nodes.definition: Auxiliary materials cost refers to the cost of various supplementary materials consumed by an enterprise in the production process for manufacturing products or providing services, which do not constitute the main substance of the product. These materials are typically used to support the production process, such as maintenance, cleaning, catalysis, or assisting product formation, but do not directly become part of the final product. Its cost calculation is usually based on the consumption quantity of materials and the weighted average unit price.

nodes.name: Auxiliary Production Unit Cost
aliases: 辅助生产费用单位成本
辅助生产车间单位成本
nodes.definition: Auxiliary production unit cost is a composite indicator calculated by dividing the total auxiliary production expenses by the total output or service volume. It is used to allocate auxiliary production expenses and is a core concept in auxiliary production cost accounting within cost accounting, conforming to the definition of a non-leaf node.

nodes.name: Auxiliary Time
nodes.definition: Auxiliary time refers to the time consumed by various supporting operations necessary for completing the basic process or core task during production or service delivery. It does not directly create core value but is essential for the execution of the basic process.
