For example, in machining, time spent measuring workpieces, changing tools, and adjusting equipment all fall under auxiliary time.

nodes.name: Available Assets
nodes.definition: Available assets refer to the portion of assets that an enterprise or individual can freely dispose of, use for payments, investments, or to meet financial needs at a specific point in time or over a period. It typically denotes the part of total assets, after deducting liabilities or specific restricted assets, that can be quickly liquidated or directly utilized, reflecting financial flexibility and payment capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Available Credit Line = Credit Line - Outstanding Balance

nodes.name: Available Financial Assets
nodes.definition: Available financial assets refer to financial assets that can be liquidated at a reasonable price to meet financing needs when a company requires funds. They are typically calculated by comparing the financial asset levels of the base period and the projected period, and their amount can be used to offset external financing requirements.

formulas.source_formula: Available Financial Assets = Reducible Financial Assets
Available Financial Assets = Base Period Financial Assets - Projected Financial Assets

nodes.name: Available Funds
nodes.definition: Available funds refer to the total amount of cash or cash equivalents that an enterprise or individual can freely allocate for payments, investments, or other financial needs within a specific period. It is typically composed of the beginning cash balance plus cash inflows during the period, reflecting immediate payment capacity and financial flexibility.

nodes.name: Available-for-Sale Financial Assets
nodes.definition: Available-for-sale financial assets refer to non-derivative financial assets designated as available for sale upon initial recognition, which are neither held for trading in the short term nor intended to be held to maturity as long-term investments. Such assets typically include stocks, bonds, and funds purchased by enterprises from secondary markets, with changes in their fair value recognized in other comprehensive income prior to disposal.

nodes.name: Available-for-Sale Security
nodes.definition: An available-for-sale security is a financial asset measured at fair value with unrealized gains and losses generally recognized in other comprehensive income (OCI) until realized. For balance sheet presentation, management classifies AFS securities as current or long-term based on the expected holding period: securities expected to be converted into cash within one year are reported as current assets; those expected to be held for more than one year are reported as long-term assets. Note: Under IFRS 9, the AFS category was superseded, while under US GAAP it remains applicable primarily to debt securities.

nodes.name: Available-for-sale Financial Assets and Other Non-current Assets
nodes.definition: Available-for-sale financial assets are non-derivative financial assets that are designated as available for sale at initial recognition and held by an enterprise on the balance sheet date, primarily including equity investments and debt investments classified as available for sale. They belong to non-current assets, representing financial assets held by an enterprise for the long term rather than for short-term trading or held to maturity.

nodes.name: Average
nodes.definition: The average is the sum of all values in a dataset divided by the number of data points, used to represent the central tendency or general level of the dataset.

nodes.name: Average Accounts Payable
nodes.definition: Average Accounts Payable is a derived metric calculated from the beginning and ending accounts payable balances, reflecting the average level of accounts payable during a specific period. It serves as the basis for calculating financial ratios such as Days Payable Outstanding.

formulas.source_formula: Average Accounts Payable = (Beginning Accounts Payable + Ending Accounts Payable) ÷ 2
Average Accounts Payable = (Beginning Accounts Payable Balance + Ending Accounts Payable Balance) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Accounts Payable Balance
nodes.definition: Average accounts payable balance refers to the average level of accounts payable during a specific period (typically an accounting period), calculated from the beginning and ending balances. It is used to measure the average scale of funds a company utilizes from its suppliers and serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as accounts payable turnover ratio.

nodes.name: Average Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Average accounts receivable refers to the average balance of funds and commercial bills receivable from buyers or service recipients due to business activities such as sales of goods, products, and provision of services during a specific period (typically an accounting period). It serves as fundamental data for evaluating accounts receivable management efficiency and calculating related turnover ratios.

formulas.source_formula: Average Accounts Receivable = (Beginning Accounts Receivable + Ending Accounts Receivable) ÷ 2
supporting_source_formulas: Average Accounts Receivable = (Beginning Accounts Receivable + Ending Accounts Receivable) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Accounts Receivable Balance
nodes.definition: Average accounts receivable balance refers to the average amount of funds that a company is entitled to collect from customers for goods sold or services rendered during a specific period (typically an accounting period). It is an important composite metric for evaluating a company's accounts receivable management efficiency and working capital effectiveness.

formulas.source_formula: Average Accounts Receivable Balance = Daily Sales × Average Collection Period
Average Accounts Receivable Balance = (Beginning Accounts Receivable Balance + Ending Accounts Receivable Balance) ÷ 2
Average Accounts Receivable Balance = Annual Net Credit Sales ÷ 360 × Average Accounts Receivable Turnover Days

nodes.name: Average Accounts Receivable Balance of Previous Period
aliases: Average Accounts Receivable Balance of Prior Period
前期应收账款平均余额
nodes.definition: Average accounts receivable balance of the previous period refers to the average outstanding level of accounts receivable generated by a company through the sale of goods or provision of services during the last accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). It is commonly used to calculate financial metrics like the accounts receivable turnover ratio for the previous period, in order to assess the efficiency of the company's accounts receivable management during that timeframe.

formulas.source_formula: Average Adjustment = Total Adjustments ÷ Number of Comparables

nodes.name: Average Age of Inventory
nodes.definition: Average Age of Inventory measures the average number of days inventory is held before being sold. It is derived from average inventory valued at cost relative to cost of goods sold, scaled to a 365-day year. Lower values indicate faster inventory turnover and more efficient inventory management.

formulas.source_formula: Average Age of Inventory (Days) = (Average Inventory ÷ Cost of Goods Sold) × 365

nodes.name: Average Annual Cost
nodes.definition: Average annual cost refers to the sum of the annual allocated investment cost, operating cost, and salvage value amortization of a fixed asset over its useful life, used to evaluate the asset's economic efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Average Annual Cost = Investment Amortization + Operating Cost - Salvage Value Amortization

nodes.name: Average Annual EBIT
aliases: Annual Average Earnings Before Interest and Taxes
nodes.definition: Average Annual EBIT refers to the average value of a company's Earnings Before Interest and Taxes over multiple fiscal years (typically the evaluation period). EBIT represents the company's profit before deducting interest expenses and income taxes, reflecting the profitability of its core business operations. Calculating the annual average helps smooth out fluctuations in individual years, providing a more stable assessment of the company's long-term operating performance.

nodes.name: Average Annual Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Average Annual Growth Rate (AAGR) is the arithmetic mean of a series of periodic growth rates over equal-length periods. It summarizes the average rate of change per period and is expressed as a decimal or percentage. Unlike compound growth measures, AAGR does not account for compounding effects.

formulas.source_formula: Average Annual Growth Rate (AAGR) = Sum of Periodic Growth Rates ÷ Number of Periods
Average Annual Growth Rate = (Q1 Growth Rate + Q2 Growth Rate + Q3 Growth Rate + Q4 Growth Rate) ÷ 4

nodes.name: Average Annual Net Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Average Annual Net Cash Flow refers to the equivalent annual net cash flow of an investment project over its lifespan, discounted to account for the time value of money. It is the result of distributing the total present value of net cash flows occurring at different points in time evenly across each year using the annuity present value factor, and is used to evaluate the average annual return level of an investment project.

formulas.source_formula: Average Annual Net Cash Flow = Net Profit + Depreciation

operands.metric: Total Present Value of Net Cash Flows

formulas.source_formula: Average Annual Net Cash Flow = Total Present Value of Net Cash Flows ÷ Annuity Present Value Factor
Average Annual Net Cash Flow = Operating Revenue - Cash Operating Costs - Income Tax
Average Annual Net Cash Flow = Operating Revenue × (1 - Income Tax Rate) - Cash Operating Costs × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation × Income Tax Rate

nodes.name: Average Annual Net Income
nodes.definition: Average Annual Net Income is a composite metric, typically calculated by dividing the total net income over multiple years by the number of years. It is used to measure the average annual net income level of a business and is often cited in metrics such as the Accounting Rate of Return.

operands.metric: Total Net Income Over Multiple Years

formulas.source_formula: Average Annual Net Income = Total Net Income Over Multiple Years ÷ Number of Years
Average Annual Net Income = Accounting Rate of Return × Original Investment Amount ÷ 100%

nodes.name: Average Annual Net Income of Investment Project
nodes.definition: Average Annual Net Income of an Investment Project refers to the average amount of net income generated annually over the entire life cycle of an investment project. It is commonly used to evaluate the profitability and investment recovery of a project, serving as the basis for calculating metrics such as the average rate of return.

nodes.name: Average Annual Return (AAR)
nodes.definition: Average Annual Return (AAR) is the arithmetic mean of a series of yearly investment returns, expressing the average percentage return per year over the evaluation period. It is useful for summarizing historical performance but does not account for compounding effects like the geometric mean.

formulas.source_formula: Average Annual Return (%) = (Sum of Annual Returns ÷ Number of Years) × 100

nodes.name: Average Annual Total Profit
nodes.definition: Average Annual Total Profit refers to the average value of a company's total profit over multiple fiscal years. Total profit represents the final financial result obtained from production and operating activities within a specific period (usually one year), serving as crucial underlying data for calculating indicators such as return on investment and average return rate.

nodes.name: Average Asset Scale Over the Past Three Years
aliases: Average Asset Size Over the Past Three Years
nodes.definition: Average Asset Scale Over the Past Three Years is a financial metric that measures the average level of a company's assets over a specific period (typically the most recent three complete fiscal years). It is calculated by averaging the total assets at the end of each of the last three years (or the average of beginning and year-end assets), and is commonly used to assess a company's average operating scale, asset utilization efficiency, or as a basis for calculating certain investment thresholds (such as qualified investment amounts).

nodes.name: Average Assets
nodes.definition: Average assets refer to the average level of a company's assets over a specific accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual). It is typically calculated as the average of the total assets at the beginning and end of the period, used to measure the average scale of assets occupied by the company during that period, and serves as an important basis for calculating financial metrics such as return on assets.

nodes.name: Average Balance of Interest-Earning Assets
nodes.definition: Average balance of interest-earning assets refers to the average amount of assets held by financial institutions (such as banks) over a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or a year) that are capable of generating interest income. It serves as a crucial foundational data point for calculating key profitability metrics such as net interest margin.

nodes.name: Average Balance of Total Interest-Earning Assets
nodes.definition: Average balance of total interest-earning assets refers to the average book value of assets that can generate interest income for a bank or other financial institution over a specific period (such as a quarter or a year). These assets include loans, bond investments, due from banks, etc. It is commonly used to calculate key financial metrics such as net interest margin to measure the institution's profitability.

nodes.name: Average Benchmark Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The average benchmark rate of return is a benchmark metric for measuring the expected return on an investment or project. It is typically calculated using the arithmetic average method based on historical returns, or determined comprehensively by considering factors such as the industry average return, cost of capital, investment risk, and inflation.

formulas.source_formula: Average Benchmark Rate of Return = Industry Average Return + Cost of Capital Adjustment + Risk Premium + Inflation Adjustment

nodes.name: Average Capital
nodes.definition: Average capital typically refers to the average level of total capital employed by a company over a specific period (e.g., an accounting period). It can be simply understood as total capital divided by the number of relevant entities or units, used to measure the average scale of a company's capital investment. In more specialized financial analysis, this concept is often associated with the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), which is used to evaluate the comprehensive cost of a company's financing.

nodes.name: Average Capital Employed
nodes.definition: Average Capital Employed refers to the average book value of all capital invested in the business by all investors, including debt capital and equity capital. It is a key denominator used for calculating profitability metrics such as Accounting Rate of Return. Debt capital primarily refers to various interest-bearing liabilities, excluding non-interest-bearing current liabilities arising from operating activities.

formulas.source_formula: Average Capital Employed = Average Total Assets - Average Non-interest-bearing Current Liabilities
Average Capital Employed = Debt Capital + Equity Capital
Average Capital Employed = (Beginning Capital Employed + Ending Capital Employed) ÷ 2
Average Capital Employed = Total Assets - Non-interest-bearing Current Liabilities
Average Capital Employed = Average Total Assets - Average Current Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Average Capital Employed = Average Total Assets - Average Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Average Cash Balance
nodes.definition: Average cash balance refers to the average amount of cash and cash equivalents held by a company over a specific period (e.g., one year) to meet daily operational and precautionary needs. In financial management, it is often associated with optimal cash balance models (such as the inventory model) to balance the opportunity cost of holding cash against the transaction costs of cash shortages or converting marketable securities.

nodes.name: Average Collection Period
nodes.definition: Average Collection Period is an indicator measuring the average time required for a company to convert sales into accounts receivable and then collect cash. It reflects the collection speed and management efficiency of accounts receivable and is a key composite metric in working capital management and financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Average Collection Period = Accounts Receivable Balance ÷ Average Daily Credit Sales
Average Collection Period = (Accounts Receivable Turnover Days + Inventory Turnover Days) ÷ 2
Average Collection Period = Days in Year ÷ Accounts Receivable Turnover
Average Collection Period = (Accounts Receivable Balance ÷ Total Sales) × 365
Average Collection Period = (Accounts Receivable × Days in Year) ÷ Annual Credit Sales
Average Collection Period = Days in Period ÷ Accounts Receivable Turnover

operands.metric: Number of Days in Calculation Period

formulas.source_formula: Average Collection Period = Number of Days in Calculation Period ÷ Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio

nodes.name: Average Collection Period (Previous Period)
nodes.definition: The Average Collection Period (Previous Period), also known as the Average Collection Period or Days Sales Outstanding (DSO), is a financial metric that measures the average number of days required for a company to convert its credit sales into cash. It reflects the efficiency of a company's accounts receivable management and the effectiveness of its credit policy execution.

formulas.source_formula: Average Collection Period (Previous Period) = (Accounts Receivable × Days in Year) ÷ Annual Credit Sales

nodes.name: Average Common Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Average Common Shareholders' Equity is a composite metric used to calculate financial ratios such as Return on Common Equity (ROCE), reflecting the average level of common shareholders' equity during the calculation period. It is typically calculated as the arithmetic mean of the beginning and ending common shareholders' equity, rather than being directly sourced from underlying data, thus constituting a non-leaf node in financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Average Common Shareholders' Equity = (Beginning Common Shareholders' Equity + Ending Common Shareholders' Equity) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Construction in Progress
nodes.definition: Average Construction in Progress refers to the average book value of fixed assets that are under construction or installation and have not yet reached their intended usable state during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It is commonly used in financial analysis to more accurately reflect the level of capital actually employed by the enterprise for long-term asset construction during the reporting period.

nodes.name: Average Cost Basis
nodes.definition: Average cost basis is a method of calculating the cost per unit of an investment by dividing the total amount invested by the total number of shares or units held, commonly used for mutual funds and stock portfolios to simplify capital gains reporting.

formulas.source_formula: Average Cost Basis = Total Investment ÷ Total Shares
Average Cost Basis = Total Cost ÷ Total Shares

nodes.name: Average Cost Method
nodes.definition: The Average Cost Method is an inventory valuation approach that assigns a uniform cost to each unit by dividing the total cost of goods purchased or produced during a period by the total number of units. It is used to value ending inventory and determine cost of goods sold (COGS), particularly for businesses with large volumes of similar items.

operands.metric: Total Cost of Goods Purchased or Produced
Total Number of Items Purchased or Produced

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Unit Cost = Total Cost of Goods Purchased or Produced ÷ Total Number of Items Purchased or Produced
Average Cost per Share = Total Investment ÷ Total Shares

nodes.name: Average Cost per Share (Dollar-Cost Averaging)
aliases: Average Cost per Share under SIP
Dollar-Cost Averaging Average Cost per Share
定期定额平均每股成本
美元成本平均法平均每股成本
nodes.definition: Average Cost per Share under Dollar-Cost Averaging represents the total capital invested across a sequence of regular, fixed-amount purchases divided by the total shares accumulated, indicating the effective purchase price per share achieved via a Systematic Investment Plan.

formulas.source_formula: DCA Average Cost per Share = Total Amount Invested ÷ Total Shares Purchased

nodes.name: Average Current Assets
nodes.definition: Average current assets is the mean value calculated from the beginning and ending balances of current assets, used to measure the scale and utilization efficiency of a company's current assets over a specific period. It is a composite metric in financial analysis, not an original line item in financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Average Current Assets = (Beginning Balance of Current Assets + Ending Balance of Current Assets) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Average current liabilities is the mean value calculated from the beginning and ending current liabilities, reflecting the average level of current liabilities over a specific period. It is a derived concept used to measure the average scale of a company's short-term debt and is commonly employed in calculating financial metrics such as average working capital.

formulas.source_formula: Average Current Liabilities = (Beginning Current Liabilities + Ending Current Liabilities) ÷ 2
Average Current Liabilities = (Current Liabilities at Beginning + Current Liabilities at End) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Customer Utilization Over the Past Six Months
aliases: Average Credit Utilization Over the Past Six Months
近六个月平均使用额度
nodes.definition: Average Customer Utilization Over the Past Six Months refers to a metric used in personal credit reporting or bank credit management to measure a customer's average usage of their credit facilities, such as credit cards or loans, over the past six months (180 days). It reflects the average level of credit resource occupation by the customer over a period and is one of the key indicators for assessing customer credit behavior and repayment capacity.

nodes.name: Average Daily Balance Method
nodes.definition: The Average Daily Balance Method is a credit card and consumer lending calculation approach that determines finance charges by averaging the daily outstanding balance over a billing cycle. It is computed by summing each day's balance in the cycle and dividing by the number of days in the billing period, providing a fair measure of typical borrowing during the cycle.

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Balance = Sum of Daily Balances ÷ Billing Cycle Days

nodes.name: Average Daily Credit Sales
nodes.definition: Average Daily Credit Sales refers to the average daily credit sales amount obtained by dividing the total annual credit sales by the number of days in a year (typically 365 or 360 days). It is an important composite metric used for calculating financial indicators such as Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) and opportunity cost.

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Credit Sales = Annual Credit Sales ÷ 365
Average Daily Credit Sales = Annual Credit Sales ÷ 360

nodes.name: Average Daily Demand
nodes.definition: Average Daily Demand refers to the average daily quantity required over a specific period, calculated by dividing the total demand by the total number of days in that period. It is a calculated composite metric (non-leaf node) rather than directly observed base data, primarily used in inventory management, safety stock, and reorder point calculations. It is an important concept in working capital management and financial forecasting.

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Demand = Annual Total Demand ÷ Annual Total Days

nodes.name: Average Daily Float
nodes.definition: Average daily float is the weighted average value of outstanding checks or deposits in transit over a specified period, calculated as the sum of each float amount multiplied by its outstanding days divided by the total days in the period.

nodes.name: Average Daily Net Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Average Daily Net Cash Flow is the daily average of net cash flow, calculated by dividing net cash flow by the number of days in the period. It is a composite indicator in cash management and liquidity analysis, commonly used to assess the volatility of expected daily cash balance changes.

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Net Cash Flow = (Cash Flow from Operating Activities + Cash Flow from Investing Activities + Cash Flow from Financing Activities) ÷ Number of Days in Period

nodes.name: Average Daily Rate (ADR)
nodes.definition: Average Daily Rate (ADR) measures the average room revenue earned per occupied (sold) room during a specific period, indicating pricing effectiveness and revenue performance in lodging operations. Complimentary or non-revenue rooms are excluded.

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Rate = Room Revenue ÷ Rooms Sold

nodes.name: Average Daily Requirement
nodes.definition: Average Daily Requirement refers to the average daily quantity of a specific material, capital, or other resource that an enterprise needs to consume or utilize over a given period (typically one year). It is a fundamental metric calculated by dividing the total requirement by the total number of days in the period (e.g., 360 or 365 days).

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Requirement = Total Requirement ÷ Period Days

nodes.name: Average Daily Sales
nodes.definition: Average Daily Sales refers to the average daily sales amount calculated by dividing the total sales revenue of an enterprise over a specific period (typically a month, quarter, or year) by the total number of days in that period. It is a fundamental metric commonly used to gauge daily sales levels, assess sales trends, and conduct financial ratio analysis (such as calculating Days Sales Outstanding).

nodes.name: Average Daily Trading Volume
nodes.definition: Average Daily Trading Volume (ADTV) is the mean number of shares or units of a security traded per trading day over a specified period. It serves as a proxy for market liquidity and investor interest, informing execution strategies, bid-ask spread expectations, and the potential market impact of trades.

formulas.source_formula: Average Daily Trading Volume (ADTV) = Sum of Daily Trading Volumes ÷ Number of Trading Days

nodes.name: Average Days Sales Outstanding
nodes.definition: Average Days Sales Outstanding refers to the average number of days required for a company to convert its accounts receivable into cash, from obtaining the right to collect receivables to actual cash receipt. It is a key metric for measuring the turnover speed and management efficiency of accounts receivable.

nodes.name: Average Delivery Time
nodes.definition: Average Delivery Time is a metric calculated from historical delivery data, measuring the average duration from order confirmation to goods delivery to the customer by a supplier or production system. It is a key performance indicator in supply chain management and inventory control (e.g., for calculating safety stock and reorder points).

formulas.source_formula: Average Delivery Time = Total Process Time ÷ Workload
Average Delivery Time = Total Delivery Time ÷ Number of Deliveries

nodes.name: Average Demand
nodes.definition: Average demand refers to the mean value of the market's demand for a specific product or service over a defined period (such as a year, quarter, or month). It serves as a crucial foundational data point for forecasting future demand, formulating production plans, and managing inventory.

nodes.name: Average Demand During Lead Time
aliases: 交货间隔期平均需求量
订交货间隔期内平均需求
nodes.definition: Average demand during lead time refers to the average quantity of materials or products that a company expects to consume per day or per cycle during the period from placing an order to receiving the goods (i.e., the lead time). It serves as a crucial foundational data point for calculating inventory management metrics such as safety stock.

nodes.name: Average Directional Index (ADX)
nodes.definition: The Average Directional Index (ADX), developed by J. Welles Wilder, quantifies the strength of a market trend regardless of its direction. ADX is derived from the Positive Directional Indicator (+DI) and Negative Directional Indicator (-DI), which are computed from Directional Movement (+DM, -DM) and the Average True Range (ATR) using Wilder’s smoothing method. Higher ADX values indicate stronger trends; ADX does not indicate whether the trend is upward or downward.

formulas.source_formula: Average Employees = (Beginning Employees + Ending Employees) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Equity
nodes.definition: Average equity refers to the average level of a company's equity over a specific period (typically an accounting period, such as a year). It reflects the average share of the company's net assets attributable to owners during that period and is commonly used in calculating financial metrics such as return on equity.

formulas.source_formula: Average Equity = (Initial Equity + Final Equity)/2

nodes.name: Average Equity Multiplier
nodes.definition: The Average Equity Multiplier is the arithmetic mean of the equity multiplier at the beginning and end of a period, used to smooth out periodical fluctuations in the equity multiplier and reflect the average level of financial leverage of a company. The equity multiplier equals total assets divided by total shareholders' equity and is a key metric in the DuPont analysis system for measuring the degree of financial leverage.

formulas.source_formula: Average Equity Multiplier = (Beginning Equity Multiplier + Ending Equity Multiplier) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Exchange Rate
nodes.definition: The average exchange rate refers to a representative rate calculated for a specific accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual) for financial reporting or foreign currency translation purposes. It is derived by applying methods like arithmetic average or weighted average to exchange rates at different points within the period. It is commonly used to translate foreign currency transactions or foreign currency financial statements into the reporting currency.

nodes.name: Average Expected Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The Average Expected Growth Rate is a composite metric calculated or estimated from historical growth rates, industry data, or forecast data, used to reflect the average growth level of a company's future earnings or cash flows. It is commonly used in the Modified Average Price-to-Earnings Ratio method in business valuation.

nodes.name: Average Expected Growth Rate of Comparable Companies
Average Expected Return on Equity of Comparable Companies
aliases: 可比公司平均预期股东权益净利率
nodes.definition: The Average Expected Return on Equity of Comparable Companies is the arithmetic mean of the expected return on equity for multiple comparable companies. It is a composite metric commonly used in relative valuation models, such as the adjusted average price-to-book ratio, as a benchmark for assessing enterprise value.

formulas.source_formula: Average Fixed Assets = (Beginning Fixed Assets + Ending Fixed Assets) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Fixed Cost
nodes.definition: Average fixed cost refers to the fixed cost allocated to each unit of product. It is calculated as Average Fixed Cost = Fixed Cost ÷ Output. As output increases, the average fixed cost continuously decreases, forming a rectangular hyperbola curve. It is a key metric in cost accounting and management accounting used for cost analysis and decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: Average Fixed Cost = Fixed Cost ÷ Output
Average Gain_t = (Average Gain_{t-1} × (Period - 1) + Gain_t) ÷ Period
Average HCE Deferral Rate = Sum of HCE Deferral Rates ÷ Number of HCEs

nodes.name: Average Historical Return
nodes.definition: Average Historical Return refers to an indicator that reflects the average profitability level of an asset or investment portfolio over historical periods, calculated by computing the returns over multiple past periods (such as years or quarters) and taking their arithmetic mean. It is commonly used to evaluate past performance.

nodes.name: Average Income Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The average income tax rate is the ratio of corporate income tax expense to total revenue (including revenue from main operations, other operations, and non-operating activities), reflecting the actual income tax burden level of an enterprise. It is commonly used in financial analysis, such as calculating after-tax operating profit.

formulas.source_formula: Average Income Tax Rate = Income Tax Expense ÷ (Revenue from Main Operations + Revenue from Other Operations + Non-operating Revenue) × 100%

nodes.name: Average Interest-Earning Assets
nodes.definition: Average interest-earning assets refer to the average balance of assets held by banks or other financial institutions during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) that generate interest income (e.g., loans, bond investments, interbank placements). It is commonly used to calculate key financial metrics such as net interest margin.

nodes.name: Average Interest-bearing Debt
nodes.definition: Average interest-bearing debt refers to the average balance of debt on which a company must pay interest during a specific accounting period (typically one year). It reflects the average level of debt, which incurs costs, that a company utilizes to maintain operations and investments, and serves as an important indicator for calculating financial costs and analyzing capital structure.

nodes.name: Average Inventory
nodes.definition: Average inventory refers to the average level of a company's inventory over a period of time, typically used to calculate holding costs.

formulas.source_formula: Average Inventory = 1/2 × (Maximum Inventory)
Average Inventory = (Beginning Inventory + Ending Inventory) ÷ 2
Average Inventory = 1/2 × (Order Quantity per Batch - (Order Quantity per Batch ÷ Daily Delivery Quantity) × Daily Consumption)

nodes.name: Average Inventory Balance
nodes.definition: Average inventory balance refers to the average level of inventory held by a company during a specific accounting period, commonly used to calculate financial metrics such as inventory turnover ratio and inventory turnover period to measure inventory management efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Average Inventory Balance = (Beginning Inventory Balance + Ending Inventory Balance) ÷ 2

operands.metric: Inventory Balance at Start of Year
Inventory Balance at End of Year

formulas.source_formula: Average Inventory Balance = (Inventory Balance at Start of Year + Inventory Balance at End of Year) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Liabilities
nodes.definition: Average liabilities refer to the average level of a company's total liabilities over a specific accounting period (typically a reporting period, such as one year). It is commonly calculated by adding the total liabilities at the beginning of the period to the total liabilities at the end of the period and dividing by two, which smooths out fluctuations in data at a single point in time. It serves as a fundamental metric for calculating other financial ratios, such as the average debt-to-assets ratio.

nodes.name: Average Life
nodes.definition: Average Life (Weighted Average Life, WAL) is the weighted average time it takes for the principal of an amortizing debt instrument to be repaid, computed by weighting each payment time by its principal amount and dividing by the total principal. It is used to assess the timing of principal cash flows and the risk profile of bonds, loans, and mortgage-backed securities, typically excluding interest payments and prepayments.

formulas.source_formula: Average Loss_t = (Average Loss_{t-1} × (Period - 1) + Loss_t) ÷ Period

nodes.name: Average Market Price of Common Shares during the Period
Average Market Price of Common Stock for the Period
aliases: Average Market Price of Common Stock
nodes.definition: The average market price of common stock for the period refers to the ratio of the total transaction value to the total number of shares traded in the public market for a company's common stock during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year), reflecting the average price level of common stock transactions during that period.

nodes.name: Average Market Return
nodes.definition: Average market return refers to the average level of return for all investment vehicles or market portfolios within a specific time period. It serves as a key benchmark indicator for measuring overall market performance and is typically calculated using arithmetic mean, weighted average, or geometric mean methods.

nodes.name: Average Multiple
nodes.definition: Average multiple is the arithmetic mean of a set of valuation multiples (e.g., Price-to-Earnings, EV/EBITDA) across comparable companies or periods. It is commonly used in the multiples approach to derive a benchmark multiple for valuing a target firm by smoothing idiosyncratic variations among peers.

formulas.source_formula: Average Multiple = Sum of Multiples ÷ Number of Multiples

nodes.name: Average Net Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Average Net Accounts Receivable is a composite metric used in calculating financial indicators such as accounts receivable turnover ratio. It is derived from the average of beginning and ending net accounts receivable, reflecting the average level of a company's accounts receivable over a specific period. It is utilized to assess liquidity, cash collection efficiency, and credit management effectiveness.

formulas.source_formula: Average Net Accounts Receivable = (Beginning Net Accounts Receivable + Ending Net Accounts Receivable) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Net Assets
nodes.definition: Average net assets refer to the average value of a company's net assets over a specific period (typically one fiscal year), used to smooth out fluctuations between the beginning and end of the period. It serves as a key foundational data point for calculating profitability metrics such as Return on Equity (ROE).

nodes.name: Average Net Assets Per Share
nodes.definition: Average Net Assets Per Share refers to the average net asset value corresponding to each average ordinary share during an accounting period (typically one year). It reflects the average book value of the company's net assets owned per share held by shareholders.

nodes.name: Average Net Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Average Net Operating Assets is the average value of net operating assets over a specific period (typically one fiscal year), calculated by dividing the sum of beginning and ending net operating assets by 2. This metric is primarily used to calculate key financial ratios that measure a company's operating efficiency and profitability, such as Return on Net Operating Assets (RNOA) and Net Operating Asset Turnover.

formulas.source_formula: Average Net Operating Assets = (Beginning Net Operating Assets + Ending Net Operating Assets) ÷ 2
Average Non-HCE Deferral Rate = Sum of Non-HCE Deferral Rates ÷ Number of Non-HCEs

nodes.name: Average Non-Interest-Bearing Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Average non-interest-bearing current liabilities refer to the average value of short-term debts held by an enterprise during a specific period (typically an accounting period, such as one year) that do not require interest payments. It is an important concept used in calculating metrics such as average capital employed and adjusted invested capital, serving to measure the actual short-term funding sources occupied by the enterprise that carry no cost of capital.

nodes.name: Average Outstanding Balance
nodes.definition: Average outstanding balance is the mean of daily outstanding balances over a specified period. It is widely used by credit card issuers and other revolving credit products to compute interest and finance charges based on the average daily balance method. The metric reflects typical utilization and repayment behavior across the period.

formulas.source_formula: Average Outstanding Balance = Total Outstanding Balance ÷ Number of Days
Average Outstanding Balance = (Beginning Balance + Ending Balance) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average P/B Ratio of Comparable Companies
Average P/E Ratio of Comparable Companies
Average P/S Ratio of Comparable Companies
Average Population
nodes.definition: Average population refers to the mean number of people in a specific region or group over a defined period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the typical population size during that period and serves as the base data for calculating per capita indicators (e.g., per capita consumption).

nodes.name: Average Prepaid Account Balance
nodes.definition: Average prepaid account balance refers to the average level of funds advanced to suppliers or service providers by an enterprise over a specific period (typically an accounting period, such as a year or a quarter). It reflects the scale of funds prepaid by the enterprise to secure future goods or services, and serves as one of the indicators for measuring the efficiency of the enterprise's fund utilization and supplier relationship management.

nodes.name: Average Price
nodes.definition: Average price (arithmetic mean) is the sum of a set of prices divided by the number of observations. It represents the central tendency of a price series and is widely used in financial time series analysis, portfolio monitoring, and as a baseline reference in mean reversion strategies.

formulas.source_formula: Average Price = Sum of Prices ÷ Number of Observations
Average Price Level = Money Supply × Velocity of Money ÷ Transactions

nodes.name: Average Price per Square Foot
nodes.definition: Average price per square foot is the mean value of property prices divided by their respective square footages, used in comparative market analysis to estimate the market price of similar properties.

nodes.name: Average Price-to-Book Ratio of Comparable Companies
nodes.definition: The average price-to-book ratio of comparable companies is an indicator obtained by selecting a group of comparable companies with similar business models, industries, and scales, and calculating the arithmetic mean of their price-to-book ratios. It is used to estimate the equity value of the target company in relative valuation methods.

nodes.name: Average Price-to-Sales Ratio of Comparable Companies
nodes.definition: The Average Price-to-Sales Ratio of Comparable Companies is a composite metric obtained by collecting the price-to-sales ratios (the ratio of total market capitalization to core operating revenue) of multiple comparable companies and calculating their arithmetic mean. It is commonly used in relative valuation methods to assess the value of a target company.

nodes.name: Average Project Investment Amount
nodes.definition: Average project investment amount refers to the value obtained by averaging the total investment amounts of multiple investment projects or a single project across different stages over a specific period, used to measure the average scale or level of project investment.

nodes.name: Average Propensity to Consume
nodes.definition: Average propensity to consume (APC) is the ratio of total consumption expenditure to total income, indicating the share of income spent on goods and services rather than saved. It is used in micro- and macroeconomic analysis to assess consumption behavior and income allocation.

formulas.source_formula: Average Propensity to Consume = Consumption ÷ Income

nodes.name: Average Propensity to Save
nodes.definition: Average propensity to save (APS) is the ratio of total savings to total income, indicating the proportion of income that is saved rather than consumed. It is used to assess saving behavior at individual, household, and aggregate economic levels.

formulas.source_formula: Average Propensity to Save = Savings ÷ Income

nodes.name: Average Rate of Profit
nodes.definition: The average rate of profit, also known as the general rate of profit, refers to the ratio between the total surplus value produced by the entire society or the capitalist class over a given period (usually one year) and the total advanced capital of the whole society. It reflects the result of the equalization of surplus value distribution among different capitals and serves as a key indicator for measuring the overall profitability of social capital.

nodes.name: Average Rate of Return
nodes.definition: Average Rate of Return is an indicator measuring the level of investment return, typically referring to the ratio of the average annual net income of an investment project to its average investment amount, or the arithmetic mean of periodic returns, used to evaluate the average profitability of an investment.

formulas.source_formula: Average Rate of Return = Income Amount ÷ Investment Amount

operands.metric: Average Annual Net Income of Investment Project

formulas.source_formula: Average Rate of Return = (Average Annual Net Income of Investment Project ÷ Average Investment Amount of Project) × 100%

nodes.name: Average Return
nodes.definition: Average return is the arithmetic mean of periodic investment returns, calculated as the sum of returns divided by the number of periods. It equally weights each period and does not account for compounding, so it may differ from the geometric average and may not reflect the true growth rate over time.

formulas.source_formula: Average Return = (Ending Value - Beginning Value) ÷ Beginning Value
Average Return = Sum of Returns ÷ Number of Periods

nodes.name: Average Return on Equity
nodes.definition: Average Return on Equity is a financial metric that measures the average level of return generated for shareholders over a specific period (such as multiple fiscal years), typically calculated as the average of the Return on Equity figures for each period within that timeframe. It reflects the average earnings level on shareholders' equity.

nodes.name: Average Return on Equity Capital of Comparable Companies

nodes.definition: The Average Return on Equity of Comparable Companies is the arithmetic mean of the return on equity of multiple comparable companies, used as a benchmark indicator in relative valuation. It is a composite metric derived by calculating the return on equity (net profit divided by average shareholders' equity) of each comparable company and then averaging the results. It is commonly referenced in valuation models such as the adjusted average price-to-book ratio.

nodes.name: Average Revenue per Unit (ARPU)
nodes.definition: Average Revenue per Unit (ARPU) measures the revenue generated per unit (e.g., user, subscriber, or revenue-generating unit) over a period. It is calculated by dividing total revenue by the average number of units during the period, providing insight into monetization efficiency and pricing effectiveness for businesses with recurring revenue and changing user bases.

formulas.source_formula: Average Revenue per Unit (ARPU) = Total Revenue ÷ ((Start Units + End Units) ÷ 2)

nodes.name: Average Selling Price
nodes.definition: Average Selling Price refers to the ratio of total revenue from goods sold or services provided to the corresponding total sales volume over a specific period, serving as a key financial metric for measuring the average revenue per unit of product.

nodes.name: Average Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Average Shareholders' Equity is a composite metric calculated as the average of beginning and ending shareholders' equity, used in financial ratio analysis to smooth fluctuations in shareholders' equity and more accurately reflect the level of shareholders' equity during the period. It is commonly used in the calculation of metrics such as Return on Equity (ROE) and Return on Net Assets (RONA).

formulas.source_formula: Average Shareholders' Equity = (Beginning Shareholders' Equity + Ending Shareholders' Equity) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Shares Held per Shareholder
aliases: Average Number of Shares per Shareholder
nodes.definition: Average shares held per shareholder is a composite metric calculated by dividing total share capital by the total number of shareholders. It measures the average shareholding level of shareholders, reflects the distribution of equity ownership, and is used in financial management and corporate governance to assess the concentration of shareholder equity.

nodes.name: Average Shares Outstanding
aliases: Weighted Average Number of Shares Outstanding
流通在外普通股加权平均数
nodes.definition: Average shares outstanding typically refers to the weighted average number of common shares outstanding during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It accounts for changes in the number of shares due to events such as new issuances, share repurchases, stock dividends, and stock splits during the period, and serves as a crucial underlying data point for calculating key financial metrics such as Earnings Per Share (EPS).

nodes.name: Average Stock Return
aliases: Average Rate of Return on Stocks
nodes.definition: Average stock return is a composite indicator derived through mathematical operations (such as simple arithmetic averaging) on stock returns over multiple periods. It is used to measure the average profitability of a stock over a period and serves as the basis for calculating risk metrics such as the standard deviation of stock returns.

nodes.name: Average Stockout Quantity
nodes.definition: Average stockout quantity refers to the average number of products or materials that cannot meet demand due to insufficient inventory within a given time period. It is commonly used in inventory management and supply chain analysis to assess the severity and frequency of stockouts, serving as an important basis for calculating stockout costs and determining safety stock levels.

nodes.name: Average Tax per Return
nodes.definition: Average Tax per Return is a composite metric that represents the total tax amount for all returns in a specific period divided by the number of returns, used to measure the average tax burden level. This metric is commonly used by tax authorities such as the Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and involves calculations for various taxes including Value-Added Tax and Income Tax.

operands.metric: Tax Payable Calculated under Simplified Tax Method
Tax Deficiency from Audit Calculated under Simplified Tax Method

formulas.source_formula: Average Tax per Return = [Output VAT - (Input VAT - Input VAT Transferred Out - Exempt, Credit, Refundable Tax Amount) + Tax Payable Calculated under Simplified Tax Method + Tax Deficiency from Audit Calculated under Simplified Tax Method - Tax Reduction Amount - Additional Deductible Amount] ÷ Number of Returns

nodes.name: Average Total Assets
aliases: 资产合计平均占用余额
nodes.definition: Average Total Assets refers to the average value of a company's total assets over a specific period (e.g., a fiscal year), used to measure the average scale of the company's assets. It is typically calculated as the average of the beginning and ending total assets and serves as a fundamental composite indicator for calculating financial metrics such as Total Asset Turnover and Return on Total Assets.

formulas.source_formula: Average Total Assets = (Beginning Total Assets + Ending Total Assets) ÷ 2
supporting_source_formulas: Average Total Assets = (Beginning Total Assets + Ending Total Assets) ÷ 2

Average Total Assets = (Total Assets at Beginning + Total Assets at End) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Total Assets for Second Quarter
Average Total Assets for the Second Quarter
aliases: 第二季度平均资产总额
nodes.definition: Average Total Assets for the Second Quarter refers to the average value of the total assets owned or controlled by an enterprise during the second quarter (typically from April 1 to June 30) that are expected to generate economic benefits. It serves as a key foundational data point for calculating financial metrics such as quarterly asset turnover ratio and return on total assets.

operands.metric: Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter
Total Assets at End of Q2

formulas.source_formula: Average Total Assets for the Second Quarter = (Total Assets at the Beginning of Q2 + Total Assets at the End of Q2) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Total Cost
nodes.definition: Average Total Cost refers to the total cost incurred by a company to produce each unit of product, calculated by dividing the total production cost by the total output. It reflects the average cost level per unit of product.

nodes.name: Average Total Liabilities
nodes.definition: Average Total Liabilities refers to the average value of a company's total liabilities over a specific accounting period (typically one fiscal year). It is usually calculated by adding the beginning total liabilities and the ending total liabilities, then dividing by two. This metric is used to more smoothly reflect the company's average liability level throughout the period and serves as important foundational data for calculating financial indicators such as average capital employed and adjusted invested capital.

nodes.name: Average Total Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Average Total Shareholders' Equity refers to the arithmetic mean of the total shareholders' equity at the beginning of a period and the total shareholders' equity at the end of the period, used to smooth out period fluctuations and serves as a key denominator for calculating profitability metrics such as Return on Equity.

formulas.source_formula: Average Total Shareholders' Equity = (Beginning Total Shareholders' Equity + Ending Total Shareholders' Equity) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Average Transaction Value
nodes.definition: Average Transaction Value refers to the average amount spent per unit of consumption, typically calculated by dividing total consumption expenditure by the number of consumption units. It is a derived metric in financial analysis, commonly used to assess consumption levels or analyze consumption trends.

nodes.name: Average True Range (ATR)
nodes.definition: Average True Range (ATR) is a technical analysis volatility indicator that measures the average magnitude of price movement by averaging True Range values over a specified number of periods. ATR is direction-neutral and is commonly used for position sizing, stop-loss placement, and risk management.

nodes.name: Average Working Capital
nodes.definition: Average working capital is the average value of working capital over a specific period, typically calculated as the arithmetic mean of beginning and ending working capital. It is used to measure the average level of a company's operating funds and often serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as working capital turnover ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Average Working Capital = Average Current Assets − Average Current Liabilities
Average Working Capital = (Beginning Working Capital + Ending Working Capital) ÷ 2
Average Working Capital = ( (Beginning Current Assets − Beginning Current Liabilities) + (Ending Current Assets − Ending Current Liabilities) ) ÷ 2

nodes.name: B Share Count
nodes.definition: B Share Count refers to the total number of shares issued by a company on the B-share market, which is fundamental data in the company's capital structure and is typically sourced directly from the company's share register or notes to the financial statements.

nodes.name: B-Share Price
nodes.definition: B-share price refers to the real-time transaction price of B-shares in the secondary market. B-shares are listed on mainland China stock exchanges, denominated in Renminbi but subscribed and traded in foreign currencies (such as US dollars or Hong Kong dollars). It is fundamental data directly generated from market transactions, reflecting investors' valuation of a specific B-share at a given moment.

formulas.source_formula: BOE from Gas = Natural Gas Production (Mcf) ÷ 6

nodes.name: Back-End Debt-to-Income Ratio
nodes.definition: Back-End Debt-to-Income Ratio measures the percentage of gross monthly income that goes toward paying all monthly debt obligations, including housing expenses and other debts such as credit cards, car loans, and student loans.

formulas.source_formula: Back-End DTI = (Total Debt Payments ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100
Back-end Debt-to-Income Ratio (%) = (Total Monthly Debt Payments ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100

nodes.name: Back-End Ratio
nodes.definition: Back-End Ratio is a personal finance metric that measures the percentage of a borrower's gross monthly income that is used to repay all monthly debt obligations, including mortgage payments, credit card debts, and other loans. It is a key criterion lenders use to evaluate mortgage eligibility and credit risk.

formulas.source_formula: Back-End Ratio = (Total Monthly Debt ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100
Back-End Ratio = (Total Monthly Debts ÷ Monthly Income) × 100

nodes.name: Backtesting
nodes.definition: Backtesting is the process of evaluating a trading strategy by applying it to historical price data to assess its performance, including total returns, number of trades, and net returns after accounting for trading costs.

nodes.name: Bad Debt
nodes.definition: Bad debt refers to the portion of accounts receivable that is estimated to be uncollectible, representing credit losses that reduce net income and are recognized under the allowance method.

nodes.name: Bad Debt Expense
nodes.definition: Bad debt expense represents the estimated portion of accounts receivable that is expected to be uncollectible, calculated using the aging of receivables method by applying different uncollectible percentages to receivables based on their age.

formulas.source_formula: Bad Debt Expense = Net Sales × Percentage of Sales
Bad Debt Expense = (Accounts Receivable < 30 Days × Uncollectible Percentage < 30 Days) + (Accounts Receivable > 30 Days × Uncollectible Percentage > 30 Days)

nodes.name: Bad Debt Loss Ratio
nodes.definition: The bad debt loss ratio refers to the percentage of bad debt losses to total credit sales over a specific period (usually one year). It is used to measure credit risk levels, assess the efficiency of accounts receivable management, and serves as a crucial monitoring indicator in financial management.

formulas.source_formula: Bad Debt Loss Ratio = Annual Bad Debt Amount ÷ Total Annual Credit Sales × 100%

nodes.name: Bad Debt Provision (Aging Method)
nodes.definition: The estimated amount of accounts receivable that will not be collected, calculated by applying specific uncollectible percentages to each age category of outstanding receivables.

nodes.name: Bad Debt Provision Balance at Prior Year-end
Bad Debt Provision Rate
aliases: 应收账款坏账计提比例
nodes.definition: The bad debt provision rate is a predetermined percentage set by an enterprise in accordance with accounting standards and its own operational risks, used to estimate the portion of assets such as accounts receivable that may be uncollectible, and to accordingly provide for bad debts. This rate is typically determined based on factors such as historical experience, customer credit status, and industry practices.

nodes.name: Balance Sheet
nodes.definition: In financial accounting, a balance sheet is a summary of the financial position of an individual or organization as of a specific date, listing assets, liabilities, and owner's equity. It provides a 'snapshot of a company's financial condition' and is the only one of the four basic financial statements that reflects the financial position at a specific point in time.

nodes.name: Balance of Additional Deduction Amount at End of Prior Period
Balance of Additional Deduction Amount at the End of the Previous Period
aliases: Balance of Additional Deduction at the End of Previous Period
nodes.definition: The balance of additional deduction amount at the end of the previous period refers to the amount of additional deduction calculated under the VAT additional deduction policy but not yet fully utilized by the enterprise at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous month or quarter), which is carried forward to the beginning of the current accounting period. It serves as one of the base data for calculating the actual amount available to offset the VAT payable in the current period.

nodes.name: Balance of Payments
nodes.definition: Balance of Payments is a comprehensive accounting record of all monetary transactions between a country and the rest of the world during a specific time period, theoretically summing to zero when all components are included.

formulas.source_formula: Balance of Payments = Current Account + Capital Account + Financial Account + Balancing Item

nodes.name: Balance of Trade
nodes.definition: Balance of Trade (BOT) is the difference between the monetary value of a country's exports and imports of goods and services over a certain period. A positive BOT indicates a trade surplus, while a negative BOT indicates a trade deficit.

operands.metric: Total Imports of Goods and Services

formulas.source_formula: Balance of Trade = Exports - Imports

nodes.name: Balloon Payment
nodes.definition: Balloon payment is the lump-sum principal balance that remains outstanding at the end of a balloon loan term, after a series of smaller periodic payments have been made.

formulas.source_formula: Balloon Payment = Principal

nodes.name: Balloon Payment (Open-End Lease)
aliases: 开放式租赁期末补缴款
nodes.definition: In an open-end lease, the balloon payment is the end-of-term settlement amount the lessee must pay if the asset's fair market value is less than the contractual residual value; it equals the non-negative difference between the residual value and the fair market value, and is zero when no deficiency exists.

nodes.name: Bank Bill Swap Rate
nodes.definition: Bank Bill Swap Rate (BBSW) is the average interest rate at which Australian banks are willing to exchange bank bills, used as a benchmark rate for AUD-denominated derivatives and securities, incorporating a market-derived risk premium.

nodes.name: Bank Deposit Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Bank deposit interest rate refers to the ratio at which financial institutions such as banks pay interest to depositors. It is typically set and announced by central banks or commercial banks based on market conditions and policies. It represents the proportion of interest that deposit principal can generate over a specific period (e.g., one year, one month, or one day) and serves as the basis for calculating deposit interest.

nodes.name: Bank Deposits
nodes.definition: Bank deposits refer to monetary funds held by enterprises or individuals in banks or other financial institutions, representing one of the most liquid components of corporate assets and constituting the primary component of monetary funds.

nodes.name: Bank Discount Yield
nodes.definition: Bank discount yield is the annualized yield on a pure discount instrument calculated using the discount from par value, expressed as a percentage of par and annualized on a 360-day basis, commonly used for Treasury bills and other short-term money-market instruments.

formulas.source_formula: Bank Discount Yield = (Face Value - Purchase Price) ÷ Face Value × 360 ÷ Time to Maturity
Bank Discount Yield = (Par Value - Purchase Price) ÷ Par Value × (360 ÷ Days to Maturity)

nodes.name: Bank Guarantee Amount
nodes.definition: Bank Guarantee Amount refers to the maximum financial liability or compensation limit that a bank, acting as a guarantor, commits to undertake on behalf of the guaranteed party (typically its client) to the beneficiary (such as a counterparty, creditor, or regulatory authority). It represents the maximum sum of funds that the bank is obligated to pay on behalf of the guaranteed party if the latter fails to fulfill its obligations under a specific contract or transaction.

nodes.name: Bank Reconciliation
nodes.definition: Bank reconciliation is the process of comparing and adjusting the company’s book balance with the bank statement balance by accounting for outstanding checks, deposits in transit, bank fees, and interest earned to ensure both balances agree.

nodes.name: Bank's Required After-tax Rate of Return
aliases: Bank's Required After-Tax Cost of Debt
Bank's Required After-Tax Rate of Return
银行要求的税后债务成本
银行要求的税后资本成本
nodes.definition: The bank's required after-tax rate of return refers to the minimum return rate demanded by a bank on the loans it provides, after considering the impact of corporate income tax. It reflects the cost of capital the bank expects to earn on an after-tax basis after bearing credit risk, typically calculated based on the risk-free rate, the bank's risk premium, and the corporate income tax rate of the borrowing company.

operands.metric: Bank's Required Pre-tax Rate of Return

formulas.source_formula: Bank's Required After-tax Rate of Return = Bank's Required Pre-tax Rate of Return × (1 - Corporate Income Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Bank's Required Pre-tax Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The bank's required pre-tax rate of return refers to the minimum yield or return rate that a bank demands on its loans or investments before considering the impact of income tax. It reflects the basic level of return the bank expects to earn on the use of its funds before deducting taxes.

nodes.name: Banker's Acceptance
nodes.definition: A banker's acceptance is a commercial bill issued by an enterprise, reviewed and accepted by a bank, which promises to pay a specified amount to the payee or holder unconditionally on a designated date. It is essentially a short-term payment instrument backed by a bank's credit guarantee, serving both payment and settlement functions as well as short-term financing.

nodes.name: Bargain Element
nodes.definition: The bargain element is the immediate gain or intrinsic value realized when exercising an Incentive Stock Option (ISO), calculated as the difference between the current market price of the stock and the option's strike price.

formulas.source_formula: Bargain Element = Market Price - Strike Price
Bargain Element = (Market Price - Exercise Price) × Number of Shares

nodes.name: Barrel Of Oil Equivalent
nodes.definition: Barrel Of Oil Equivalent (BOE) is a unit of energy that represents the amount of energy released by burning one barrel of crude oil, used to standardize different forms of energy resources for comparison and aggregation purposes.

formulas.source_formula: BOE = Natural Gas Volume (Mcf) ÷ 6

nodes.name: Barrels of Oil Equivalent Per Day
nodes.definition: Barrels of Oil Equivalent per Day (BOE/D) is a unit of measurement that converts natural gas production into its energy-equivalent volume of oil, allowing for standardized reporting and comparison of combined oil and gas production on a daily basis.

nodes.name: Base Amount
nodes.definition: Base amount refers to the original data or initial amount used as a benchmark for calculating percentage changes or conducting financial comparative analysis. It serves as the starting point for measuring the magnitude of subsequent value changes.

formulas.source_formula: Base Housing Amount = Daily Base Amount × Qualifying Days

nodes.name: Base Line
nodes.definition: The Base Line (Kijun Sen) is a key component of the Ichimoku Cloud indicator, calculated as the average of the highest high and the lowest low over a specified period (typically 26 periods). It serves as a dynamic support/resistance level and helps identify medium-term trend direction in technical analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Base Line = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Base Number
nodes.definition: The base number refers to the initial value used as a benchmark for comparison when calculating percentage changes, growth rates, or comparative analysis. It represents the original state or starting point before any change occurs.

nodes.name: Base Period
nodes.definition: The base period is the period or value used as a benchmark for comparison, typically employed in calculating growth rates, price indices, and other dynamic analysis indicators. The base period amount is not raw data directly obtained from financial statements, but rather a dynamic comparative indicator derived by calculating the current period amount and the growth rate (or growth amount).

formulas.source_formula: Base Period = Current Period ÷ (1 + Growth Rate)
Base Period = Current Period - Growth Amount

nodes.name: Base Period Actual Revenue
nodes.definition: Base period actual revenue refers to the actual operating revenue or sales achieved by a company during a specific benchmark period (the base period). It is a composite metric calculated from the current period value and the growth rate, used for trend comparison in financial analysis and forecasting.

nodes.name: Base Period Amount
nodes.definition: Base Period Amount refers to the indicator value of a specific historical period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark in statistical analysis or financial analysis. It serves as the fundamental reference value for calculating dynamic analysis indicators such as growth rates and changes.

nodes.name: Base Period Average Fund Occupancy
aliases: Average Fund Occupancy in Base Period
基期流动资金平均占用额
nodes.definition: Base Period Average Fund Occupancy refers to the average level of fund (typically working capital) utilization by an enterprise during a specific reference period (base period). It reflects the average scale of fund usage during the base period and serves as essential baseline data for calculating fund utilization efficiency, turnover rates, and other related metrics.

nodes.name: Base Period Basket Cost
aliases: Cost of Basket in Base Period
nodes.definition: Base period basket cost refers to the total expenditure required to purchase a fixed, representative set of goods and services (i.e., the 'basket') in a selected reference period (the base period) when calculating price indices such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). This cost serves as the starting point and benchmark for subsequent calculations of price changes and inflation rates.

nodes.name: Base Period Bookkeeping Subsidy
nodes.definition: Base period bookkeeping subsidy refers to the amount initially recognized and recorded for government grants received during a specific accounting period (typically the starting period used as a comparative benchmark). It reflects the original book value or balance of the grant in the base period and serves as fundamental data for subsequent accounting treatment and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Base Period Commodity Price
nodes.definition: Base period commodity price refers to the original market price of goods or services during a specific historical period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison when calculating economic indicators such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It is a fundamental observed value used directly in subsequent calculations, rather than a result derived from other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Base Period Constituent Stock Prices
nodes.definition: Base period constituent stock prices refer to the closing market prices of each individual stock that constitutes an index on the selected reference date (i.e., the base period) when calculating a stock index. These prices serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating the initial value of the index or for subsequent comparisons.

nodes.name: Base Period Consumer Price Index
aliases: 参考期消费者物价指数
nodes.definition: The Base Period Consumer Price Index is the price level at a reference point in time set for calculating the Consumer Price Index (CPI), typically assigned an index value of 100. The CPI for subsequent periods measures the degree of inflation or deflation by comparing it to this base period price level.

nodes.name: Base Period Consumption Quantity
nodes.definition: Base period consumption quantity refers to the consumption quantity in the base period used as a reference standard, typically employed for calculating dynamic indicators such as indices or changes. It is a composite indicator derived from metrics like current period consumption quantity and growth rate, commonly used in consumption economics and data analysis, and referenced in calculations such as current period basket cost.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Consumption Quantity = Current Period Consumption Quantity ÷ (1 + Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Contribution Margin
nodes.definition: Base period contribution margin refers to the balance of base period sales revenue minus base period variable costs. It reflects the contribution made by base period sales to covering fixed costs and generating profit, and is a key foundational metric for calculating the degree of operating leverage.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Contribution Margin = Base Period Sales Revenue - Base Period Variable Costs

nodes.name: Base Period Current Assets
nodes.definition: Base period current assets refer to the total assets owned by a company at the end of a specified period (typically the starting period or the previous period) that are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, serving as a comparative benchmark in financial analysis or forecasting. It serves as the foundational data for calculating metrics such as changes in working capital.

nodes.name: Base Period Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Base period current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that a company is obligated to repay within a normal operating cycle (typically one year or one operating cycle longer than a year) at the end of the period used as a comparative benchmark (usually the previous period or a specific period) in financial analysis.

nodes.name: Base Period Disposable Income
nodes.definition: Base period disposable income refers to the total amount available to residents in the base period for final consumption expenditure and savings. It is calculated based on various incomes and expenditures in the base period and is commonly used in financial and macroeconomic indicator assessments such as disposable income change analysis.

operands.metric: Base Period Social Security Contributions Paid by Individuals

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Disposable Income = Base Period Total Household Income - Base Period Income Tax Paid - Base Period Social Security Contributions Paid by Individuals

operands.metric: Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Disposable Income = Base Period Actual Income - Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure - Base Period Bookkeeping Subsidy - Base Period Personal Income Tax
Base Period Disposable Income = Base Period Wage Income + Base Period Net Operating Income + Base Period Net Property Income + Base Period Net Transfer Income

nodes.name: Base Period Dividend
nodes.definition: Base period dividend refers to the actual amount of dividends paid to shareholders by a company during a specific historical period (typically the starting point or benchmark period used for calculations). It is a historical figure, not a forecast derived from formulas, and is often used as a foundational input for calculating future expected dividends or the cost of capital.

nodes.name: Base Period Dividend Per Share
nodes.definition: Base Period Dividend Per Share refers to the amount of cash dividend paid per common share by a company during a specific period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison. It serves as important fundamental data for calculating indicators such as expected dividend growth rate.

nodes.name: Base Period Expenditure Amount
nodes.definition: The base period expenditure amount refers to the cost or expense amount set for a benchmark period used to calculate weighted averages (such as the weighted average of market basket base period prices). It is a derived metric calculated from the current period expenditure amount and the growth rate, used to measure and analyze the historical benchmark level of costs or expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Expenditure Amount = Current Period Expenditure Amount ÷ (1 + Expenditure Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Expenditure Share
nodes.definition: Base period expenditure share is the ratio of a specific expenditure component to the total expenditure in the base period, reflecting the distribution of the expenditure structure during the benchmark period. It is commonly used in market basket weighted average calculations and financial time series analysis, and is derived using current period data and growth rates.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Expenditure Share = Base Period Component Expenditure ÷ Base Period Total Expenditure
Base Period Expenditure Share = (Current Period Component Quantity ÷ Current Period Total Quantity) × (1 + Total Growth Rate) ÷ (1 + Component Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Financial Assets
nodes.definition: Base period financial assets refer to the total amount or book value of financial assets held during a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis or indicator calculation. It is typically used to compute dynamic indicators such as growth rates and change rates, in order to assess changes in the scale or value of financial assets in subsequent periods.

nodes.name: Base Period GDP Index
aliases: 基期国内生产总值指数
nodes.definition: The Base Period GDP Index is a statistical indicator used to measure and compare the total volume of economic activity across different periods. It uses the GDP level of a specific year (the base period) as a benchmark (typically set at 100). By calculating the ratio of GDP in other periods relative to the base period level, it reflects the actual economic growth or contraction, eliminating the impact of price changes.

nodes.name: Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure
nodes.definition: Base Period Household Sideline Production Expenditure refers to the total sum of direct, original costs incurred by a household during a specific reference period (the base period) for engaging in sideline production activities such as agriculture, handicrafts, and small-scale commerce, which are not the primary occupation. These expenditures represent essential foundational cash or resource consumption necessary for sideline production, typically not derivable from other financial metrics and must be recorded directly upon occurrence.

nodes.name: Base Period Income Tax Expense
aliases: Income Tax Expense for Base Period
nodes.definition: Base period income tax expense refers to the income tax expense that an enterprise should calculate and recognize for a specific period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark, based on its operating profit. It is a deduction item when calculating base period net operating income, reflecting the income tax burden the enterprise should bear during the base period.

nodes.name: Base Period Income Tax Payable
aliases: Income Tax Payable for the Period
