nodes.definition: Base Period Income Tax Payable refers to the amount of income tax that an enterprise calculates and is required to pay to the tax authority for a specific base period (usually the current period) in accordance with tax laws, based on its taxable income. The calculation is based on the product of taxable income and the applicable tax rate. Taxable income is derived from total revenue after deducting non-taxable revenue, tax-exempt revenue, various deductions, and allowable prior-year losses.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Income Tax Payable = Taxable Income × Applicable Tax Rate
Base Period Income Tax Payable = (Total Revenue - Non-taxable Revenue - Tax-exempt Revenue - Various Deductions - Allowable Prior-year Losses) × Applicable Tax Rate

nodes.name: Base Period Index
nodes.definition: The Base Period Index is a composite indicator in stock index calculation. It measures the proportional change of subsequent periods relative to a base period by setting the stock price or market capitalization of the base period to a specific value (typically 100). It is used to gauge the long-term performance trend of a market or asset portfolio and belongs to trend analysis tools.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Index = Reporting Period Total Market Capitalization ÷ Base Period Total Market Capitalization × Base Period Set Index Value
Base Period Index = Reporting Period Item Amount ÷ Base Period Item Amount × 100

nodes.name: Base Period Index Value
nodes.definition: The Base Period Index Value refers to a fixed initial numerical value, such as 100 points or 1000 points, artificially assigned to a selected reference date (base period) when compiling various indices like stock indices and price indices. It serves as the absolute reference starting point for calculating and comparing all subsequent period indices. It is a directly set original datum and cannot be derived from other financial indicators or formulas.

nodes.name: Base Period Individual Income Tax
nodes.definition: Base Period Individual Income Tax refers to the tax payable calculated for a specific base period, where an individual's taxable income is computed according to applicable tax rates and quick deduction amounts as stipulated by tax laws. It serves as a fundamental composite indicator for calculating base period disposable income.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Individual Income Tax = Taxable Income × Applicable Tax Rate - Quick Deduction
Base Period Individual Income Tax = (Base Period Income - Tax Threshold - Special Deductions - Special Additional Deductions - Other Deductions) × Applicable Tax Rate - Quick Deduction

nodes.name: Base Period Individual Medical Insurance Contribution Base
aliases: Medical Insurance Contribution Base for Individuals
个人医保缴费计算基数
nodes.definition: The base period individual medical insurance contribution base refers to the amount of wage income used as the calculation benchmark for determining the individual's payable medical insurance premiums. It is typically determined based on the individual's average monthly wage during the base period (e.g., the previous year), subject to upper and lower limits defined by the local average social wage.

nodes.name: Base Period Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Base
aliases: Pension Insurance Contribution Base for Individuals
个人养老保险缴费基数
养老保险个人缴费基数
nodes.definition: The Base Period Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Base refers to the wage-based income amount used as the calculation benchmark for determining an individual's required pension insurance premium contributions. It is typically based on the insured individual's average monthly wage from the previous year, assessed within the upper and lower limits for the contribution base stipulated by local policies, and serves as the fundamental data for calculating the individual's actual monthly contribution amount (contribution base multiplied by the individual contribution rate).

nodes.name: Base Period Individual Social Security Contributions
aliases: Base Period Personal Social Security Expenditure
nodes.definition: Base period individual social security contributions refer to the total amount paid by an individual into the social security system (such as basic pension insurance, basic medical insurance, unemployment insurance, etc.) during a specific period used as a comparative benchmark, based on statutory contribution bases and contribution rates. It is a key deduction item in calculating an individual's disposable income.

operands.metric: Base Period Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Base
Base Period Individual Medical Insurance Contribution Base
Base Period Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Individual Social Security Contributions = Base Period Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Base × Individual Pension Insurance Contribution Rate + Base Period Individual Medical Insurance Contribution Base × Individual Medical Insurance Contribution Rate + Base Period Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base × Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Rate

nodes.name: Base Period Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base
aliases: Base Period Individual UI Contribution Base
个人失业保险缴费基数
失业保险个人缴费基数
nodes.definition: The Base Period Individual Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base refers to the calculation basis used to determine the amount of individual unemployment insurance premiums payable during a specific period (the base period) that serves as the calculation benchmark. It is typically based on the individual's wage income during the base period and is subject to the upper and lower limits of the contribution base stipulated by local policies.

nodes.name: Base Period Item Amount
nodes.definition: The Base Period Item Amount refers to the base period value derived by reverse calculation from the current period amount and the growth rate. It is a composite metric commonly used in financial analysis, investment evaluation, and time value calculations, and serves as the foundation for indicators such as the base period index.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Item Amount = Current Period Amount ÷ (1 + Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Item Quantity
nodes.definition: Base period item quantity refers to the benchmark value of the number of items in a specific, representative period (known as the base period) selected for trend comparison or index calculation in financial and accounting analysis. The item can be a financial metric such as revenue or cost, or operational data such as product quantity or number of customers. It serves as a fixed reference point for comparison and calculation in subsequent periods.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Item Quantity = Current Period Item Quantity ÷ (1 + Item Quantity Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Level
nodes.definition: Base period level refers to the numerical value of a specific period selected as the reference standard in statistical analysis or financial comparison. It serves as the foundation and starting point for calculating dynamic indicators such as growth rates and growth amounts, and is used to measure changes in subsequent periods (current periods). For example, when comparing a company's profits in 2024 with those in 2023, the 2023 profit data is the base period level.

nodes.name: Base Period Market Basket Total Expenditure
nodes.definition: Base Period Market Basket Total Expenditure refers to the sum of the products of the prices and quantities of all goods and services in the market basket during the base period. It is a foundational composite indicator for calculating price indices (such as the Consumer Price Index) and is used to measure the total expenditure level of the market basket in the base period.

nodes.name: Base Period Net Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Base period net operating assets refers to the net amount of assets used for business operations at a specific benchmark point in time (the base period). It is calculated by subtracting base period operating liabilities from base period operating assets. It is a key metric for measuring the capital scale required for a company's core business operations and serves as the foundation for calculating subsequent indicators such as total demand.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Net Operating Assets = Base Period Operating Assets - Base Period Operating Liabilities

nodes.name: Base Period Net Profit
nodes.definition: Base period net profit refers to the net profit achieved in a specific accounting period (usually the previous fiscal year or reporting period) selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis. It serves as the denominator reference value when calculating growth rates, trend analysis, and other dynamic indicators.

nodes.name: Base Period Net Transfer Income
nodes.definition: Base period net transfer income refers to the difference between transfer income received and transfer payments made by economic entities (such as households, enterprises, or governments) during a specific base period, serving as a crucial intermediate indicator for calculating base period disposable income.

nodes.name: Base Period Nominal Value
nodes.definition: Base period nominal value refers to the nominal value of the reporting period (current period) adjusted back to the base period level by removing growth factors during the period. It serves as the basis for calculating indicators such as nominal growth rates.

nodes.name: Base Period Non-operating Net Profit
aliases: 基期非经常性损益净利润
nodes.definition: Base period non-operating net profit refers to the net profit generated by a company from non-recurring, non-core business activities during a specific period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison. It typically represents profit after deducting gains and losses not directly related to daily operations (such as gains from asset disposals, government grants, investment gains and losses, etc.), used to more accurately reflect the profitability of the company's core business.

nodes.name: Base Period Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Base Period Operating Assets (or Base Period Net Operating Assets) refers to the net amount of a company's operating assets minus operating liabilities during the base period (typically the previous reporting period or the starting point for forecasts). It reflects the net capital employed in the company's core operating activities and serves as the foundation for calculating predictive financial metrics such as external financing needs.

nodes.name: Base Period Operating Assets to Sales Percentage
aliases: Base Period Operating Assets Sales Percentage
nodes.definition: The Base Period Operating Assets to Sales Percentage refers to the ratio of total operating assets to total sales revenue in a specific base period (typically the previous year or period) used as the calculation benchmark in the percentage of sales method for financial forecasting. It reflects how much operating assets are required to generate one unit of sales revenue in the base period and serves as a key parameter for forecasting future operating asset requirements.

nodes.name: Base Period Operating Costs
nodes.definition: Base period operating costs refer to the total direct costs incurred by an enterprise during a specific period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark for daily business operations such as selling goods and providing services. They typically include main business costs and other business costs. This serves as a crucial reference benchmark for financial analysis, budget preparation, and trend comparison.

nodes.name: Base Period Operating Expenses
aliases: Base Period Selling, General and Administrative Expenses (SG&A)
nodes.definition: Base period operating expenses refer to the various expenses incurred by an enterprise to maintain daily business operations during a specific period selected as the benchmark for comparison (i.e., the base period) in financial forecasting, budgeting, or trend analysis. These expenses typically include selling expenses, administrative expenses, etc., and exclude cost of sales, taxes, and surcharges.

nodes.name: Base Period Operating Liabilities
nodes.definition: Base period operating liabilities refer to the total amount of liabilities directly related to daily business operations held by an enterprise at the end of a specific period (the base period) used as a comparative benchmark in financial forecasting or analysis. It typically includes items such as accounts payable, advance receipts, employee compensation payable, and taxes payable, and serves as a fundamental data point on the balance sheet that can be directly obtained from the base period's financial statements.

nodes.name: Base Period Operating Net Income
nodes.definition: Base Period Operating Net Income refers to the net earnings generated by a company from its core operating activities during the base period (the period used as a benchmark for comparison). It serves as the foundation for calculating indicators such as Base Period Disposable Income and reflects the profitability and operational efficiency of the company's main business.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Operating Net Income = Base Period Net Profit - Base Period Non-operating Net Profit
Base Period Operating Net Income = Base Period Operating Revenue - Base Period Cost of Sales - Base Period Operating Expenses - Base Period Taxes and Surcharges - Base Period Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Base Period Partial Expenditure Amount
nodes.definition: The Base Period Partial Expenditure Amount refers to the value obtained by adjusting a specific expenditure item from the reporting period (current period) back to the base period level according to its growth rate. It serves as the foundation for calculating composite indicators such as the base period expenditure share, reflecting the actual scale of that expenditure item in the base period after removing growth factors.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Partial Expenditure Amount = Current Period Partial Expenditure Amount ÷ (1 + Partial Expenditure Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Price
nodes.definition: Base period price refers to the price level of a specific period used as a benchmark for comparison. It is derived from the current price and the price growth rate or price increment, serving as a derived indicator in economic metrics such as real GDP and market basket weighted averages, rather than an original accounting line item.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Price = Current Price - Price Increment
Base Period Price = Current Price ÷ (1 + Price Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Base Period Price Index
nodes.definition: The base period price index is the price index of a selected period used as a benchmark for measuring changes in price levels. Its value is typically set at 100 or 1 to calculate the magnitude of price changes in subsequent reporting periods relative to this base period, serving as the foundation for computing indicators such as the inflation rate.

nodes.name: Base Period Price Level
nodes.definition: The base period price level refers to the average price level of a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for comparison when calculating price indices or measuring inflation. It serves as the starting point and reference standard for measuring the magnitude of price changes in subsequent reporting periods.

nodes.name: Base Period Price by Industry
nodes.definition: Base period price by industry refers to the market price of representative products or services in each industry during a specific period (the base period) selected for measuring price changes when compiling a price index. It serves as the original benchmark data for calculating price indices in subsequent periods and is typically obtained through direct market surveys or statistical collection.

nodes.name: Base Period Price of Goods
nodes.definition: The base period price of goods refers to the price of goods in a specific period (known as the base period) selected as a benchmark in statistical or financial analysis to eliminate the effects of price changes. This price remains constant during subsequent analysis periods and is used to calculate real value changes, thereby more accurately reflecting changes in quantity or real value.

nodes.name: Base Period Price of Goods and Services
nodes.definition: The base period price of goods and services refers to the average price level of a representative basket of goods and services in a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for comparison when calculating price indices (such as the Goods and Services Price Deflator). It serves as the reference point for measuring price changes in subsequent periods.

nodes.name: Base Period Producer Price Index
aliases: 工业品出厂价格指数基期
nodes.definition: The Base Period Producer Price Index serves as a benchmark point for measuring changes in the Producer Price Index (PPI). It typically designates a specific period (e.g., a particular year) as the base period, setting the producer price level of that period to 100 or 1. This is used to calculate and compare the magnitude of changes in producer prices in subsequent periods relative to the base period. It is one of the fundamental datasets for analyzing inflation trends.

nodes.name: Base Period Production and Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Base period production and sales volume refers to the quantity of products produced or sold by an enterprise during the selected benchmark period (base period) in financial or economic analysis. It serves as the fundamental reference value for calculating indicators such as change rates and growth rates.

nodes.name: Base Period Profit
nodes.definition: Base period profit refers to the profit amount from the previous accounting period (typically the previous year or quarter) used as a comparative benchmark. It is a raw data point directly obtained from historical financial statements, employed to calculate financial metrics such as growth rates and operating leverage coefficients, in order to assess changes in current performance relative to the historical benchmark.

nodes.name: Base Period Property Net Income
aliases: Net Property Income in Base Period
nodes.definition: Base period property net income refers to the net income earned by an individual or household from owned properties (such as deposits, stocks, bonds, real estate, etc.) during a specific reference period (the base period). It typically equals total property income minus related costs and expenses such as taxes, interest, and maintenance. It is an important component in calculating base period disposable income.

nodes.name: Base Period Quantity by Industry Product
nodes.definition: Base period quantity by industry product refers to the actual quantity of various products produced by each industry during a specific reference period (base period) when compiling economic indices such as price indices and output indices. These data are typically sourced directly from statistical surveys or original production records and serve as the fundamental raw data for index calculation.

nodes.name: Base Period Quantity of Goods
nodes.definition: Base period quantity of goods refers to the sales or consumption quantity of a specific commodity during the period (base period) used as a comparative benchmark in statistical or financial analysis. It is a fundamental historical data point, typically derived directly from past sales records or statistical reports, and is used for comparison with data from subsequent periods (reporting period or current period) to measure changes.

nodes.name: Base Period Real Gross Domestic Product
aliases: Real Gross Domestic Product at Base Period Prices
nodes.definition: Base period real gross domestic product is a composite indicator calculated by multiplying the output quantity of the reporting period by the base period prices, used to measure the real economic output level after removing the effects of price changes, and serves as the basis for calculating GDP growth rates.

nodes.name: Base Period Revenue
nodes.definition: Base period revenue refers to the total operating revenue from a specific historical accounting period selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis. It is an original financial figure, typically taken directly from the income statement of that historical period, and is used to compare with the operating revenue of subsequent periods (such as the current period or planning period) to analyze growth or changes.

nodes.name: Base Period Sales
nodes.definition: Base period sales refers to the actual sales revenue of a specific period (typically the previous period or a historical period) selected as the comparative benchmark in financial analysis or forecasting. It serves as the foundational historical data for calculating sales growth rates, conducting sales percentage method forecasting, and other financial analyses.

nodes.name: Base Period Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Base period sales revenue refers to the total sales revenue from a specific historical period (such as the previous fiscal year or a specific quarter) selected by a company as a benchmark for comparison. It is typically obtained directly from the financial statements or business records of that period and serves as fundamental data for calculating sales growth rates, conducting financial forecasting, and preparing budgets.

nodes.name: Base Period Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Base period sales volume refers to the quantity of products or services sold during a specific period (such as the previous fiscal year, previous quarter, or a particular historical period) selected as the benchmark for comparison in financial analysis or forecasting. It serves as a crucial reference data point for calculating sales growth rates, conducting trend analysis, and performing financial projections.

nodes.name: Base Period Social Security Contributions Paid by Individuals
Base Period Stock Price
nodes.definition: Base period stock price refers to the market price of a stock on a specific benchmark date (base period) selected for calculating stock indices, conducting financial analysis, or valuation. It is a fundamental data point directly obtained from market transactions, typically serving as the starting point for comparing and calculating subsequent stock price movements or changes in market capitalization.

nodes.name: Base Period Taxes and Surcharges
aliases: Taxes and Surcharges in Base Period
基期主营业务税金及附加
nodes.definition: Base Period Taxes and Surcharges refer to the total sum of various taxes and fees incurred by an enterprise due to its operating activities, which are recognized in the profit or loss of the current period, during a specific benchmark period (base period) used for comparative purposes in financial analysis. It typically includes consumption tax, urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge, resource tax, property tax, urban land use tax, vehicle and vessel tax, stamp duty, etc.

nodes.name: Base Period Total Expenditure
nodes.definition: Base Period Total Expenditure refers to the aggregate sum of all costs and expenses actually incurred by an enterprise or project during a historical period designated as the benchmark for comparison (i.e., the base period). It is typically derived directly from the summarized data in historical financial statements (such as cost and expense budget reports) and serves as the foundational raw data for subsequent financial analysis and budget preparation.

nodes.name: Base Period Total Household Income
nodes.definition: Base Period Total Household Income refers to the sum of all income received by all family members living together during a specific period (the base period) that serves as the benchmark for comparison in household income surveys. It is typically derived by directly aggregating wage income, business income, property income, and transfer income, and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating derived indicators such as base period disposable income.

nodes.name: Base Period Total Market Capitalization
nodes.definition: Base period total market capitalization refers to the total market value of all issued shares calculated by multiplying the base period total shares outstanding by the base period stock price at a specific base period point in time. It is a composite indicator rather than raw data, commonly used in the base period calculation of financial indices such as market capitalization-weighted indices, to reflect the overall market or company size at the base period.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Total Market Capitalization = Base Period Total Shares Outstanding × Base Period Stock Price

nodes.name: Base Period Total Shares Outstanding
nodes.definition: Base Period Total Shares Outstanding refers to the total number of all shares issued and outstanding by a company on a specific benchmark date selected for calculating or comparing financial metrics. This data is typically sourced directly from the company's share capital structure announcements or business registration information, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating indicators such as base period total market capitalization.

nodes.name: Base Period Transfer Expenditure
nodes.definition: Base period transfer expenditure refers to the expenditure during a specific period used as a comparative benchmark (base period) in which the government or an institution unilaterally and gratuitously transfers funds or resources to other governments, institutions, enterprises, or individuals. Such expenditures do not directly exchange for goods or services and are primarily used for purposes such as social security, fiscal subsidies, debt interest payments, and donations.

nodes.name: Base Period Transfer Income
nodes.definition: Base period transfer income refers to the various regular income transfers received gratuitously by households or units from the state, social organizations, other units, or other households during a specific period (the base period) used as a benchmark for comparison. It is an important component in calculating net transfer income for the base period.

nodes.name: Base Period Unit Price
nodes.definition: Base period unit price refers to the average or standard unit price of a specific good or service during the base period, which serves as the benchmark for comparison when calculating dynamic indicators such as price growth rates. It is the foundational value for measuring price changes.

nodes.name: Base Period Urban Household Total Income
aliases: 城镇居民家庭总收入（基期）
nodes.definition: Base Period Urban Household Total Income refers to the sum of all income received by members living together in an urban household during a specific reference period (base period) used as a benchmark in statistical surveys. It is directly calculated by aggregating four components: wage income, business income, property income, and transfer income, serving as the fundamental raw data for deriving indicators such as disposable income.

nodes.name: Base Period Value
nodes.definition: Base period value refers to the value or amount in the starting period used as a comparative benchmark in financial forecasting or trend analysis. It is typically combined with the current period value to calculate growth rates or forecast future values, serving as a fundamental concept in financial modeling and valuation analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Value = Current Period Value ÷ (1 + Growth Rate)
supporting_source_formulas: Base Period Value = Current Period Value ÷ (1 + Growth Rate)

formulas.source_formula: Base Period Value = Current Period Value - Increment

nodes.name: Base Period Variable Costs
nodes.definition: Base period variable costs refer to the total costs in a specific period (the base period) selected as the benchmark for cost analysis or budgeting, which change in direct proportion to changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume). It serves as the foundational data for calculating indicators such as the base period contribution margin.

nodes.name: Base Period Wage Income
nodes.definition: Base period wage income refers to the aggregate original data of all wage income earned by individuals or groups during the period selected as the benchmark (base period) in statistical analysis or financial comparison. It typically includes time wages, piece-rate wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies, serving as the foundational input data for calculating derived indicators such as average wages and wage growth rates.

nodes.name: Base Period Working Capital
nodes.definition: Base period working capital refers to the working capital amount in the starting period (typically the previous period or a specific period) used as a comparative benchmark in financial analysis or forecasting. It equals current assets minus current liabilities for that benchmark period, reflecting the enterprise's short-term financial health and the level of operating funds employed at the benchmark point in time.

nodes.name: Base Rate
nodes.definition: The base rate refers to the fee ratio or unit price used as the calculation basis or reference standard in specific economic activities or services. It typically excludes any surcharges, discounts, or adjustments under special circumstances, serving as the core benchmark for cost calculation.

nodes.name: Base Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The base rate of return typically refers to the rate of return used as a benchmark or minimum acceptable standard in investment decision-making. It represents the minimum level of return required by investors or a company for an investment, used to evaluate the feasibility of investment projects. In capital budgeting, if a project's expected rate of return is lower than the base rate of return, the project may be rejected.

nodes.name: Base Rent
nodes.definition: Base rent is the minimum rent stipulated in a lease agreement, excluding variable factors such as sales percentage rent, typically used to guarantee the lessor's basic income. Its calculation can be based on the cost-plus method or financial function method.

formulas.source_formula: Base Rent = Depreciation Fund + Major Repair Fund + Reasonable Profit + Business Tax

nodes.name: Base Sales
nodes.definition: Base sales refers to the sales data used as a calculation basis or comparative standard in financial accounting or human resource management (e.g., labor cost accounting). It is typically determined based on historical actual sales data (such as sales from previous years) or set target values, serving as the original input value or reference benchmark for subsequent calculations (e.g., target labor costs).

nodes.name: Base Year GDP Deflator
aliases: 基期国内生产总值平减指数
nodes.definition: The Base Year GDP Deflator is an index used to measure the price level of a specific benchmark year (base year), typically set at 100 or 1. It is a key tool for calculating real GDP. By dividing nominal GDP by this index, the effects of price changes are eliminated, thereby reflecting the real quantitative changes in economic output.

nodes.name: Base Year Index
nodes.definition: Base Year Index is a statistical measure that expresses each period's value as a percentage of a selected base year's value, with the base year typically set to 100, facilitating comparison of relative changes over time.

nodes.name: Base Year Nominal GDP
aliases: 基期名义国内生产总值
nodes.definition: Base year nominal GDP refers to the nominal gross domestic product of a specific year (i.e., the base year) selected as the price benchmark when calculating real GDP. It reflects the total market value of all final goods and services produced by a country or region in that base year, measured at the price level of the base year. In the base year, since the price benchmark is itself, the nominal GDP of the base year is numerically equal to the real GDP of that base year.

nodes.name: Base-period Operating Assets as a Percentage of Sales
Baseline Sales Level
nodes.definition: Baseline sales level refers to a referential, fundamental sales volume or standard used as a basis for comparison, evaluation, or setting new targets. It is typically employed to measure sales performance, calculate achievement rates, or serve as a starting point for performance assessment.

nodes.name: Basic Contingency Rate
nodes.definition: The Basic Contingency Rate is a percentage coefficient used to calculate the basic contingency reserve. The basic contingency reserve, also known as the unforeseen expenses reserve, is a pre-allocated fund in project investment estimates or budgetary estimates to cover potential expenditures during project implementation that are difficult to foresee during budget preparation (such as design changes, general natural disaster handling, concealed work acceptance, etc.). This rate is typically determined based on factors such as project characteristics, complexity, and risk level.

nodes.name: Basic Contingency Reserve
nodes.definition: Basic contingency reserve refers to a pre-allocated sum of money in the investment estimate or budget estimate of an engineering project, intended to cover unforeseen expenditures that may arise during project implementation and are difficult to predict during budget preparation. It is primarily used to address additional costs resulting from design changes, potential increases in construction expenses, natural disasters, and other unforeseeable factors.

nodes.name: Basic Credit Line
nodes.definition: Basic credit line refers to a fundamental credit loan or overdraft limit preliminarily approved by a financial institution (e.g., a bank) based on an initial credit assessment of a client (individual or corporate), taking into account factors such as their basic financial condition, repayment capacity, and credit history. It serves as the foundation and starting point for subsequent adjustments or the granting of a final credit limit.

nodes.name: Basic Deduction
nodes.definition: The Basic Deduction is a fixed deduction standard stipulated in China's Individual Income Tax Law. It is used to deduct a fixed amount from an individual's comprehensive income, such as wages and salaries, when calculating taxable income, in order to safeguard taxpayers' basic living needs. The current standard is RMB 5,000 per month, totaling RMB 60,000 annually.

nodes.name: Basic Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Basic Earnings Per Share (EPS) refers to the amount of earnings attributable to each issued common share during a specific period, calculated by subtracting preferred stock dividends from net profit and then dividing by the weighted average number of common shares outstanding.

operands.metric: Expected Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding

formulas.source_formula: Basic EPS = Earnings Available to Common ÷ Average Common Shares Outstanding

operands.metric: Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding

formulas.source_formula: Basic Earnings Per Share = Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding

operands.metric: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares

formulas.source_formula: Basic Earnings Per Share = (Net Profit - Preferred Stock Dividends) ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares

nodes.name: Basic Earnings Per Share (Pre-change)
aliases: Basic Earnings Per Share before Changes
nodes.definition: Basic Earnings Per Share (Pre-change) refers to the ratio of the current net profit attributable to the company's ordinary shareholders to the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding, calculated before considering the impact of potentially dilutive securities or specific capital changes. It is a fundamental indicator measuring the profitability per ordinary share and is commonly used in calculating derivative metrics such as the financial leverage coefficient.

operands.metric: Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders (Pre-change)
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding (Pre-change)

formulas.source_formula: Basic Earnings Per Share (Pre-change) = Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders (Pre-change) ÷ Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding (Pre-change)

nodes.name: Basic Earnings Per Share (Previous Period)
aliases: Basic Earnings Per Share for Prior Period
nodes.definition: Basic Earnings Per Share (Previous Period) is the prior period value of basic earnings per share, calculated by dividing the net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders in the previous period by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding in the previous period. It is a composite indicator used to measure the company's profitability per ordinary share in the prior period.

operands.metric: Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders (Previous Period)
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding (Previous Period)

formulas.source_formula: Basic Earnings Per Share (Previous Period) = Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders (Previous Period) ÷ Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding (Previous Period)

nodes.name: Basic Earnings Per Share for the Current Period
nodes.definition: Basic Earnings Per Share for the current period is a core financial metric measuring the profitability per ordinary share during the reporting period. It is calculated by dividing the net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders for the current period by the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period, reflecting the portion of net profit attributable to each ordinary share held by shareholders.

nodes.name: Basic Freight
nodes.definition: Basic freight refers to the core transportation cost calculated by the carrier based on fundamental billing units such as transportation distance, cargo weight, or volume, without considering any additional charges (e.g., bunker adjustment factor, port congestion surcharge). It constitutes the foundational component of the total freight cost.

nodes.name: Basic Freight Rate
nodes.definition: The Basic Freight Rate refers to the benchmark freight price charged by the carrier (such as a shipping company or freight conference) per unit of cargo (e.g., per ton or per cubic meter) according to its established tariff schedule. It serves as the fundamental unit price for calculating total ocean freight costs.

nodes.name: Basic Medical Insurance Premium
nodes.definition: Basic Medical Insurance Premium refers to the contributions jointly paid by employers and employees according to national regulations, used to establish the basic medical insurance fund. The individual contribution portion is typically calculated based on the employee's own wage at the locally prescribed rate and is deductible when calculating the taxable income for Individual Income Tax.

nodes.name: Basic Net Profit
nodes.definition: Basic net profit refers to the final residual profit obtained by an enterprise from its operating activities within a specific accounting period, after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes. It is a key indicator for measuring the core operating efficiency and profitability of an enterprise.

nodes.name: Basic Pension Insurance Premium
nodes.definition: The Basic Pension Insurance Premium refers to the contribution mandated by the national pension insurance system, jointly paid by employers and employees, to fund the basic pension insurance fund. The employer's contribution portion enters the social pooling account, primarily used to pay basic pensions; the employee's individual contribution portion enters the personal account, accumulating for individual retirement benefits.

nodes.name: Basic Safety Factor
nodes.definition: The Basic Safety Factor is a fundamental metric that measures the safety margin of a system, structure, or process under normal or expected conditions. It reflects the basic proportional relationship between the system's capacity to withstand loads or risks and its design or allowable limits, serving as the starting point for more complex safety assessments.

nodes.name: Basic Share Capital
nodes.definition: Basic share capital refers to the total par value or stated value of ordinary shares actually issued by a company and for which shareholder contributions have been received. It constitutes the most fundamental part of a company's shareholders' equity and directly reflects the initial capital scale of the company.

nodes.name: Basic Time
nodes.definition: Basic Time refers to the direct, effective operating time required to complete a specific task or produce a unit of product within a standard time system, excluding non-productive time such as setup, rest, and waiting. It is a core component of standard time calculation, typically derived from fundamental indicators such as number of workers, work efficiency, and daily working hours.

formulas.source_formula: Basic Time = Number of Workers × Work Efficiency ÷ Daily Working Hours
Basic Time = Standard Time - Setup Time - Rest Time - Lost Time

nodes.name: Basis
nodes.definition: Basis is the difference between the spot (cash) price of a commodity and the price of its corresponding futures contract, serving as a key indicator in hedging and arbitrage strategies.

formulas.source_formula: Basis = Spot Price - Futures Price
supporting_source_formulas: Basis = Spot Price - Futures Price

nodes.name: Basis Point
nodes.definition: A basis point is one hundredth of one percentage point, equivalent to 0.01%, 1/10,000, or 0.0001. In finance, it is commonly used to describe minute changes in interest rates, yields, or spreads.

formulas.source_formula: Basis Point = Percentage Change × 10000

nodes.name: Basis Risk
nodes.definition: Basis risk is the financial risk that the difference between the current market price of an asset being hedged and the price of the futures contract used for hedging will change unfavorably, leading to imperfect hedging outcomes.

nodes.name: Basis Trend
nodes.definition: Basis trend describes whether the basis (cash price minus futures price) is strengthening or weakening over time. A strengthening basis means the basis value increases (becomes less negative or more positive), indicating cash prices are rising relative to futures. A weakening basis means the basis value decreases (becomes more negative or less positive), indicating cash prices are falling relative to futures.

nodes.name: Basis of Assessment
nodes.definition: Basis of Assessment refers to a specific monetary amount, quantity, or value standard used as the foundation for calculating indirect costs or overhead expenses. It serves as the starting point and benchmark for allocating or computing related expenses.

nodes.name: Basket of Goods Weighted Index
aliases: Weighted Index for Basket of Goods
nodes.definition: A weighted index calculated for a basket of goods by multiplying each item's current price by its corresponding weight and summing the results, commonly used in constructing consumer price indices to measure inflation.

nodes.name: Batch-Related Total Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Batch-related total inventory cost refers to the sum of ordering and holding costs excluding fixed procurement costs, which varies with the order quantity.

formulas.source_formula: Batch-Related Total Inventory Cost = (Annual Demand × Ordering Cost per Order) ÷ Economic Order Quantity + (Economic Order Quantity ÷ 2) × Holding Cost per Unit

nodes.name: Bayes' Theorem
nodes.definition: Bayes' Theorem is a mathematical theorem based on conditional probability, used to calculate the posterior probability of an event occurring given the known probabilities of related events. Its core idea is to update the belief in the probability of an event using prior probability and new evidence (likelihood).

formulas.source_formula: Bayes' Theorem = (Likelihood × Prior Probability) ÷ Marginal Probability

nodes.name: Bear Call Spread
nodes.definition: A bear call spread is a vertical options strategy that involves selling a call option at a lower strike price and simultaneously buying a call option at a higher strike price, both with the same expiration. It is used when a moderate bearish outlook is expected, generating limited profit from the net premium received while capping maximum loss.

formulas.source_formula: Bear Call Spread Breakeven = Lower Strike Price + Net Credit

nodes.name: Bear Call Spread Maximum Loss
aliases: Maximum Loss on Bear Call Spread
熊市看涨价差最大亏损
nodes.definition: The maximum loss of a bear call spread options strategy, which is the difference between the strike prices minus the net credit received when initiating the spread.

nodes.name: Bear Put Spread
nodes.definition: A bear put spread is an options strategy that involves buying a put option with a higher strike price and simultaneously selling a put option with a lower strike price, both with the same expiration date. It is used when a moderate decline in the price of the underlying asset is expected.

nodes.name: Bear Put Spread Break-even Price
aliases: 熊市看跌价差盈亏平衡点
nodes.definition: The break-even price for a bear put spread strategy is the underlying asset price at expiration where the strategy neither gains nor loses money, calculated as the higher strike price minus the net debit paid to establish the position.

formulas.source_formula: Bear Put Spread Breakeven = Higher Strike Price - Net Debit

nodes.name: Bear Put Spread Maximum Profit
aliases: Maximum Profit of Bear Put Spread
熊市看跌价差最大收益
nodes.definition: The maximum profit of a bear put spread is the highest possible gain achievable from this options strategy, calculated as the difference between the higher and lower strike prices minus the net cost of establishing the spread.

nodes.name: Bear Spread Breakeven
nodes.definition: The breakeven point of a bear spread options strategy is the underlying asset price at which the strategy neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss at expiration.

nodes.name: Beginning Accounts Payable Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning accounts payable balance refers to the total amount owed by a company to suppliers or creditors for goods purchased or services received in business operations that remains unpaid at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental item on the balance sheet, carried forward directly from the ending accounts payable balance of the previous period.

nodes.name: Beginning Accounts Receivable Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning accounts receivable balance refers to the total book value of funds that a company is entitled to collect from customers for goods sold or services rendered but not yet received at the start of a financial reporting period (e.g., month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental item on the balance sheet, directly carried over from the ending balance of the previous reporting period, serving as the starting point for calculating changes in accounts receivable and the ending balance for the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Accumulated Depreciation
aliases: Accumulated Depreciation at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Beginning accumulated depreciation refers to the total amount of depreciation expenses that have been accrued for all fixed assets of an enterprise since their acquisition or commissioning, calculated according to established depreciation methods, at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the cumulative value impairment of fixed assets at the beginning of the period and is a crucial component in calculating the carrying value of fixed assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Accumulated Depreciation/Amortization
aliases: Accumulated Depreciation and Amortization at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Beginning accumulated depreciation/amortization refers to the total sum of depreciation and amortization expenses already recorded for all fixed assets and intangible assets of an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the cumulative reduction in asset value due to usage, wear and tear, or technological obsolescence from the acquisition date up to that beginning point, representing a historical cumulative book balance.

nodes.name: Beginning Actual Cost
nodes.definition: Beginning actual cost refers to the accumulated actual cost of work-in-process (or the production cost account) carried forward from the previous accounting period at the start of a new accounting period. It serves as the starting point data for cost calculation and allocation in the current period, typically derived from the cost accounting results of the prior period, representing the accumulation of historical expenses.

nodes.name: Beginning Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
aliases: Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
Opening Balance of Bad Debt Provision
nodes.definition: Beginning Allowance for Doubtful Accounts refers to the account balance of the 'Allowance for Doubtful Accounts' at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a contra-asset account on the balance sheet, reflecting the company's prior estimate and provision for the portion of beginning accounts receivable that may be uncollectible based on past experience. This balance is typically carried forward from the previous period-end and serves as the starting point for accounting calculations, rather than being derived from current-period computations.

nodes.name: Beginning Asset Value
nodes.definition: Beginning asset value refers to the total book value of all asset accounts at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is directly derived from the ending balance of the previous accounting period or the opening accounting ledger records, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating current-period financial changes and financial ratios (such as holding period return).

nodes.name: Beginning Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning balance refers to the carryover amount in a specific accounting account (such as cash, bank deposits, inventory, accounts receivable, etc.) at the start of a particular accounting period (e.g., a month, quarter, or year). It is directly carried forward from the ending balance of the previous accounting period, reflecting the financial position as of the beginning of the current period, and serves as the starting point for the current period's accounting.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Balance = Loan Amount
Beginning Balance (Next Period) = Ending Balance (Prior Period)

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Accrued Employee Benefits
aliases: Beginning Balance of Accrued Welfare Expenses
Opening Balance of Employee Welfare Payable
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of accrued employee benefits refers to the carryover amount in the accrued employee benefits account at the start of an accounting period (typically a fiscal year). It represents employee benefit expenses carried forward from the previous accounting period that have not yet been paid or utilized. Under the new accounting standards, this balance is generally transferred to the 'Accrued Employee Compensation' account and is prioritized for offset against actual benefit expenditures when they occur subsequently.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Allowance Accounts
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of allowance accounts refers to the book balance carried forward from the previous accounting period for various allowance accounts (such as allowance for doubtful accounts, accumulated depreciation, inventory write-down allowance, etc.) at the start of an accounting period. It reflects the cumulative amount of provisions made by the enterprise for asset impairment or value depletion up to the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
aliases: Opening Balance of Bad Debt Provision
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of allowance for doubtful accounts refers to the book value of the reserve provisionally set aside at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month) to cover potential non-collection risks of accounts receivable and similar items. It reflects the carryover balance of this reserve account from the end of the previous accounting period and serves as the basis for calculating changes in the current period's allowance and the ending balance.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Bonds Payable
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of bonds payable refers to the total carrying value of bonds payable that have not been repaid at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the amount of long-term liabilities assumed by the enterprise through bond issuance at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: 期初现金及现金等价物余额
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of cash and cash equivalents refers to the balance of cash and cash equivalents at the beginning of an accounting period, typically taken from the balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period, serving as a fundamental indicator for calculating changes in cash flows during the current period.

operands.metric: Ending Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents
Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents = Ending Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents - Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Construction in Progress
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of construction in progress refers to the cumulative book value of all actual expenditures incurred for capital construction projects, installation projects, technical renovation projects, etc., that are not yet completed or have not reached their intended usable state at the beginning of a specific accounting period (usually a fiscal year). It reflects the investment progress and incomplete status of these long-term assets at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Construction in Progress - Employee Compensation Payable
aliases: Beginning Balance of Construction in Progress Payroll Payable
Opening Balance of Employee Compensation for Construction in Progress
在建工程薪酬年初余额
工程人员薪酬期初余额
应付在建工程工资年初数
nodes.definition: Beginning Balance of Construction in Progress - Employee Compensation Payable refers to the cumulative amount of wages, bonuses, allowances, and other compensation payable but not yet paid to relevant construction personnel for construction-in-progress projects at the beginning of an accounting year. It reflects the initial status of the enterprise's labor cost liabilities for construction in progress.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Current Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of current assets refers to the total book value of all current asset items at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is directly taken from the ending balance of the previous accounting period's balance sheet and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as average current assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of current liabilities refers to the total book value of all debts that need to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle longer than one year at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is the opening figure of the current liabilities account on the balance sheet, typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous period's balance sheet, and serves as the fundamental baseline data for calculating changes in current liabilities during the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Deferred Tax Assets
aliases: 递延所得税资产年初余额
递延所得税资产期初值
递延所得税资产期初数
nodes.definition: The beginning balance of deferred tax assets refers to the book value of the 'Deferred Tax Assets' account on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It represents the asset value derived from deductible temporary differences carried forward from the prior period-end, which is expected to reduce taxable income and consequently decrease future income tax payments in subsequent periods.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Deferred Tax Liabilities
Beginning Balance of Deferred Tax Liability
aliases: Opening Balance of Deferred Tax Liability
递延所得税负债年初余额
递延所得税负债期初数
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of deferred tax liability refers to the amount recorded in the deferred tax liability account at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It represents the estimated additional income tax payable to tax authorities in future periods, based on taxable temporary differences existing at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Employee Compensation Payable
aliases: 应付职工薪酬期初余额
nodes.definition: Beginning Balance of Employee Compensation Payable refers to the book value of various forms of remuneration owed to employees but not yet paid at the start of the current fiscal year (i.e., January 1). It represents the total liability of the company for historical salary arrears, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, welfare benefits, and other employee-related obligations at the beginning of the year.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Fixed Asset Impairment Provision
aliases: Beginning Impairment Allowance for Fixed Assets
Opening Balance of Fixed Asset Impairment Provision
nodes.definition: Beginning Balance of Fixed Asset Impairment Provision refers to the cumulative balance of impairment provisions already accrued for fixed assets at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the portion of the carrying amount of fixed assets that may not be fully recoverable through use or disposal at the beginning of the period, and is an item to be deducted when calculating the beginning carrying value of fixed assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Monetary Funds
aliases: Beginning Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of monetary funds refers to the book balance of the 'Monetary Funds' account in the balance sheet at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the total amount of cash, bank deposits, and other monetary funds held by the enterprise at the beginning of the period, representing the base data carried forward directly from the previous period's financial statements or accounting records.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Net Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of net operating assets refers to the difference between operating assets and operating liabilities at the start of an accounting period, reflecting the net capital invested in operations at the beginning. It is typically carried forward from the ending balance of the previous period and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as net investment for the current year.

operands.metric: Ending Balance of Net Operating Assets from Previous Period

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Balance of Net Operating Assets = Ending Balance of Net Operating Assets from Previous Period
Beginning Balance of Net Operating Assets = Beginning Balance of Operating Assets - Beginning Balance of Operating Liabilities

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Notes Receivable
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of notes receivable refers to the total book value of commercial drafts (including bank acceptance drafts and trade acceptance drafts) that have not yet matured or been collected at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the entity's right to collect payment on drafts from customers or other parties held at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of operating assets refers to the total book value of all assets used for daily production and business operations at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year). It reflects the scale of assets invested in operations at the beginning of the period and serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as net operating assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Operating Current Assets
aliases: Opening Balance of Working Capital Assets
经营性流动资产期初数
营运流动资产期初余额
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of operating current assets refers to the total book value of assets at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter) that are used for daily business operations and are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle. It typically includes the initial book values of current assets directly related to core business activities, such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, and inventory.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Operating Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of operating liabilities refers to the total book value of all liabilities directly related to daily business operations that are due for repayment within one year or one operating cycle, at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the level of short-term debt undertaken by the enterprise at the beginning of the period to support its core business operations.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Owner's Equity
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of owner's equity refers to the total amount of owner's equity at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1), reflecting the net asset position of the enterprise at the beginning of the year.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Paid-in Capital
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and received by investors at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It serves as the starting point for accounting records, typically carried forward from the ending balance of the previous period or determined directly based on actual business transactions.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Retained Earnings
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of retained earnings refers to the balance in the retained earnings account at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year). It represents the portion of net profit accumulated from past business activities that has not yet been distributed to shareholders, serving as the basis for calculating changes in retained earnings during the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Surplus Reserve
aliases: 年初留存收益（盈余公积部分）
nodes.definition: Beginning balance of surplus reserve refers to the cumulative balance of surplus reserve carried forward from the previous year's balance sheet at the start of each accounting year. It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the portion of retained earnings, earmarked for specific purposes, that the enterprise has accumulated through profit appropriations from prior years up to the beginning of the year. It is a fundamental financial datum and cannot be derived from the current period's profits.

nodes.name: Beginning Balance of Wages Payable
aliases: Beginning Balance of Accrued Salaries and Wages
nodes.definition: Beginning Balance of Wages Payable refers to the total liability for wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies owed to employees but not yet paid at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the company's obligation to compensate employees at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Book Value
nodes.definition: Beginning book value refers to the net carrying amount of an asset, liability, or equity item at the start of a specific accounting period. For assets, the beginning book value typically equals the beginning carrying amount (or original cost) of the asset minus the corresponding balances of accumulated depreciation (or amortization), impairment provisions, and other contra accounts.

operands.metric: Prior Period Ending Contra Account Balance

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Book Value = Prior Period Ending Carrying Amount - Prior Period Ending Contra Account Balance

nodes.name: Beginning Capital
nodes.definition: Beginning capital refers to the total capital or book value of owners' equity that a company possesses at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous accounting period and serves as the starting point data for calculating current-period financial performance (such as economic profit, average cost of capital) and conducting financial analysis.

nodes.name: Beginning Capital Employed
nodes.definition: Beginning capital employed refers to the total amount of capital invested and occupied by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), typically including working capital used for operations and non-current capital occupied by long-term assets. It reflects the actual scale of capital locked in by the enterprise at the beginning of the period to maintain and conduct business activities.

nodes.name: Beginning Capital Reserve
nodes.definition: Beginning capital reserve refers to the book balance of the 'capital reserve' account on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It reflects the cumulative balance at the beginning of the period, including the portion of investor contributions exceeding their share in registered capital or share capital, as well as gains and losses directly recognized in owners' equity.

nodes.name: Beginning Cash Balance
aliases: 期初现金及现金等价物
nodes.definition: Beginning cash balance refers to the total book value of cash and cash equivalents held by a company at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It typically equals the ending cash balance from the conclusion of the previous accounting period.

nodes.name: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: Opening Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents
期初现金及现金等价物余额
nodes.definition: Beginning cash and cash equivalents refer to the balance of cash and cash equivalents carried forward from the end of the previous period in the balance sheet, reflecting the level of cash and cash equivalents at the start of an accounting period, and constitute a key component of the cash flow statement.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents = Beginning Monetary Funds + Cash Equivalents - Restricted Monetary Funds

nodes.name: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning cash and cash equivalents balance refers to the total amount of cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise at the start of the current accounting period (i.e., at the end of the previous accounting period). It is directly taken from the ending balance of the 'Cash and Cash Equivalents' item on the previous period's balance sheet and serves as the starting point data for preparing the statement of cash flows.

nodes.name: Beginning Common Shareholders' Equity
aliases: 期初所有者权益（普通股）
nodes.definition: Beginning Common Shareholders' Equity refers to the total amount of owners' equity attributable to common shareholders at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the net asset value at that specific point in time, comprising capital contributed by common shareholders and accumulated retained earnings not yet distributed to shareholders.

nodes.name: Beginning Current Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning current assets refer to the total value of all current assets owned by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). These assets are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle longer than a year. It is a critical point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, directly derived from the account balances in the accounting books or financial statements.

nodes.name: Beginning Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that a company is obligated to repay within one year or one normal operating cycle (whichever is longer) at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). This figure is typically derived directly from the balance sheet data at the end of the previous accounting period.

nodes.name: Beginning Debt Book Value
nodes.definition: Beginning debt book value refers to the recorded value on the books, in accordance with accounting standards, of the debt obligations (such as short-term borrowings, long-term borrowings, bonds payable, etc.) undertaken by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or a quarter). It typically includes the face value of the debt, any premium or discount arising from issuance, and related issuance costs, and serves as the basis for calculating current period interest expense and debt amortization.

nodes.name: Beginning Equity Multiplier
nodes.definition: The Beginning Equity Multiplier is the ratio of total assets at the beginning of the period to total owners' equity at the beginning of the period. It reflects the multiple relationship between assets and shareholders' invested capital at the beginning point, serving as a key indicator for measuring the degree of financial leverage at the start of the period. It is commonly used in the DuPont analysis system for decomposing the beginning return on equity.

nodes.name: Beginning Equity to Total Assets Multiplier
aliases: Beginning Equity to Ending Total Assets Multiplier
nodes.definition: The Beginning Equity to Total Assets Multiplier is a financial ratio that expresses the multiple relationship between total assets at the end of the period and shareholders' equity at the beginning of the period. It is used to measure the amplification effect of asset scale relative to beginning shareholders' equity and is a key composite indicator for calculating the sustainable growth rate.

nodes.name: Beginning Financial Current Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning financial current assets refer to the liquid assets held by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter) that can be quickly converted into cash and are primarily used for financial activities, mainly including cash, bank deposits, trading financial assets, etc. It is a fundamental point-in-time data item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Beginning Fixed Assets
aliases: 固定资产期初账面价值
期初固定资产账面价值
nodes.definition: Beginning fixed assets refer to the carrying value of tangible assets (such as plants, machinery, vehicles) owned by an enterprise at the start of each accounting period (e.g., a month or a year), which are used for production and operation and have an expected useful life exceeding one year. This figure is carried forward directly from the data at the end of the previous accounting period.

nodes.name: Beginning Fixed Assets Book Value
aliases: Beginning Book Value of Fixed Assets
Beginning Carrying Value of Fixed Assets
固定资产期初账面价值
nodes.definition: Beginning fixed assets book value refers to the book value of fixed assets at the start of an accounting period, reflecting the remaining value of fixed assets after deducting accumulated depreciation and impairment provisions. It serves as the basis for calculating current period depreciation expense and is an important indicator for analyzing a company's asset status and capital structure.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Fixed Assets Book Value = Beginning Fixed Assets Original Cost - Beginning Accumulated Depreciation - Beginning Fixed Assets Impairment Provision

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory refers to the book value of inventory at the start of an accounting period, which equals the ending inventory balance of the immediately preceding period and is a key component in calculating the cost of goods sold.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Inventory = Prior Period Ending Inventory

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory balance refers to the book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at the start of a fiscal year (i.e., the beginning of the year or the end of the previous fiscal year). It serves as the base data for calculating financial metrics such as average inventory balance and inventory turnover ratio.

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory cost refers to the total book value of all goods, materials, or raw materials available for sale or use in a company's warehouse at the start of a new accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is typically the ending inventory cost carried forward from the previous accounting period and serves as the foundational data for calculating financial metrics such as the cost of goods sold and ending inventory cost for the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory Markup
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory markup refers to the difference between the total value of inventory goods calculated at selling price and the total value calculated at purchase price (or cost) at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a month or a quarter). It represents the unrealized gross profit portion of the beginning inventory.

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory Quantity
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory quantity refers to the actual quantity of inventory held in a company's warehouse at the start of the current accounting period. It is typically determined through a physical count at the end of the previous accounting period and serves as fundamental data for calculating current period inventory costs, inventory management, and cost accounting.

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory Value
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory value refers to the book value of all inventory (including raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods) held by a company and available for use or sale at the start of a new accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is directly equal to the ending inventory balance from the previous accounting period and serves as the base data for calculating inventory changes and costs during the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Inventory of Materials
nodes.definition: Beginning inventory of materials refers to the actual quantity of raw materials, supplies, and other inventory items available for production or sale in a company's warehouse at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as a critical baseline data point for preparing procurement budgets and production plans.

nodes.name: Beginning Invested Capital
nodes.definition: Beginning invested capital refers to the total capital invested in a business at the start of a specific period, including debt capital and equity capital. It is typically calculated based on liability and owners' equity items on the balance sheet, or measured from an operational perspective as net operating assets. It is used for financial decisions such as business valuation and economic profit analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Invested Capital = Operating Working Capital + Net Operating Long-term Assets
Beginning Invested Capital = Fixed Capital Investment + Working Capital Investment

nodes.name: Beginning Long-term Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning long-term assets refer to the total carrying value of assets owned by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter), which are expected to have a useful life exceeding one accounting period (typically more than one year or one operating cycle). These assets generally include fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc., and form the foundation for the enterprise's long-term operations and value creation.

nodes.name: Beginning Long-term Capital
nodes.definition: Beginning long-term capital refers to the total amount of capital with long-term characteristics that an enterprise possesses at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically used to measure the capital base available for long-term investment and operations at the beginning of the period and serves as a crucial starting point for calculating financial metrics such as return on capital.

nodes.name: Beginning Long-term Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning long-term liabilities refer to the book value of debts with a repayment period exceeding one year that an enterprise bears at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the enterprise's long-term financial leverage level at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Beginning Net Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Beginning net accounts receivable refers to the net value of a company's total accounts receivable at the start of an accounting period after deducting the corresponding allowance for doubtful accounts, reflecting the estimated collectible amount of receivables. This metric serves as the basis for calculating financial ratios such as average net accounts receivable and is a composite concept that can be disaggregated into other financial indicators.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Net Accounts Receivable = Beginning Total Accounts Receivable - Beginning Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

nodes.name: Beginning Net Asset Value
nodes.definition: Beginning Net Asset Value refers to the book value of the total equity owned by the enterprise's owners (shareholders) at the start of an accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It is directly derived from the balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period and serves as the base data for calculating financial metrics such as average net assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Net Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning net assets refer to the net amount of a company's total assets minus total liabilities at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), which is the total owner's equity at the beginning of that accounting period.

nodes.name: Beginning Net Book Value
aliases: Carrying Value at the Beginning of the Year
nodes.definition: Beginning net book value refers to the book value of an asset on the first day of a fiscal year, which equals the historical cost of the asset minus the accumulated depreciation or amortization up to the end of the previous year. This figure is typically obtained directly from the balance sheet of the prior year.

nodes.name: Beginning Net Book Value of Assets
aliases: Beginning Net Book Value of Asset
nodes.definition: Beginning net book value of assets refers to the book value of assets at the start of an accounting period, calculated by subtracting accumulated depreciation or amortization from the original cost of assets. It is a decomposable composite metric commonly used in financial analysis such as investment amortization.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Net Book Value of Assets = Beginning Original Cost of Assets - Beginning Accumulated Depreciation/Amortization

nodes.name: Beginning Net Book Value of Fixed Assets
