aliases: Initial Net Carrying Amount of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning net book value of fixed assets refers to the remaining book value of an enterprise's fixed assets after deducting accumulated depreciation at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the depreciated value of fixed assets at the beginning of the period and serves as one of the bases for calculating current period depreciation.

nodes.name: Beginning Net Debt
nodes.definition: Beginning net debt is a composite indicator representing a company's net debt position at the start of an accounting period. It is calculated by subtracting beginning cash and cash equivalents from beginning total liabilities, reflecting the company's net debt burden at the period's outset. This metric typically serves as a foundation for financial analysis and is used to calculate derived indicators such as net investment for the current period.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Net Debt = Beginning Total Liabilities - Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents

nodes.name: Beginning Net Operating Assets
aliases: Net Operating Assets at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Beginning Net Operating Assets refers to the net value of assets used for business operations minus operating liabilities at the start of an accounting period. It is typically calculated from operating assets and operating liabilities rather than being a raw figure directly obtained from financial statements, and is commonly used in computing financial metrics such as the increase in net operating assets.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Net Operating Assets = Beginning Operating Assets - Beginning Operating Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Beginning Net Operating Assets = Beginning Operating Assets - Beginning Operating Liabilities

nodes.name: Beginning Net Operating Assets in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Beginning Net Operating Long-term Assets
aliases: 期初净经营长期资产总额
期初净经营非流动资产
nodes.definition: Beginning Net Operating Long-term Assets refers to the net value of long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, land, etc.) used for core business operations at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or quarter), after deducting accumulated depreciation or amortization. It reflects the scale of net capital invested in long-term operations at the beginning of the period and is an important point-in-time data item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Beginning Non-current Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning non-current assets refer to the book value of assets held by an enterprise at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter) that are not expected to be realized or consumed within one year or within one operating cycle exceeding one year.

nodes.name: Beginning Non-current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning non-current liabilities refer to the total carrying value of liabilities with a repayment period exceeding one year held by an enterprise at the start of the current accounting period (typically the beginning of the year or quarter). It is a fundamental historical data point on the balance sheet, reflecting the long-term liabilities balance at the end of the previous accounting period.

nodes.name: Beginning Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning Operating Assets refers to the book value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter) that are used for daily business operations. It is typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous period's balance sheet and serves as a fundamental data point for calculating metrics such as Net Operating Assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Operating Current Assets
aliases: 经营性流动资产期初数
经营流动资产期初余额
nodes.definition: Beginning Operating Current Assets refers to the value of current assets used for daily business operations at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a project cycle). It typically serves as a known starting point for financial analysis or project evaluation and cannot be directly calculated from other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Beginning Operating Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning operating current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations that is expected to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle, at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is a fundamental figure on the balance sheet, directly derived from the ending balance reported in the previous period's financial statements.

nodes.name: Beginning Operating Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning Operating Liabilities refers to the book value of the 'Operating Liabilities' account on a company's balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It represents the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations (such as procurement, production, and sales) that is due for repayment within one year or one operating cycle at the beginning of the period, serving as fundamental data for calculating metrics like Net Operating Assets.

nodes.name: Beginning Owner's Equity
nodes.definition: Beginning owner's equity refers to the net assets of an enterprise at the start of an accounting year, reflecting the owners' residual claim on the enterprise's assets at that point in time. It can be calculated by subtracting total liabilities at the beginning of the year from total assets at the beginning of the year, or by summing the components of beginning owner's equity (such as paid-in capital, etc.).

nodes.name: Beginning Paid-in Capital
nodes.definition: Beginning paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by shareholders or investors to the enterprise, as recorded on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the capital base formed by actual owner contributions that the enterprise possesses at the beginning of that period, typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of paid-in capital from the previous period.

nodes.name: Beginning Price
nodes.definition: Beginning price refers to the initial cost or market value of an asset, inventory, or security at the start of a specific accounting period or trading cycle. It serves as the starting point for financial records and calculations during that period, typically derived directly from bookkeeping entries rather than being calculated through formulas.

nodes.name: Beginning Principal Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning principal balance refers to the amount of principal that remains unpaid in an account at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is directly carried forward from the ending principal balance of the previous period and serves as the foundational starting point for calculating current-period interest, repayments, and other financial activities.

nodes.name: Beginning Retained Earnings
aliases: 期初未分配利润与盈余公积合计
nodes.definition: Beginning retained earnings refers to the cumulative balance of net profit carried forward from the previous accounting period at the start of the current fiscal year, which has not yet been distributed to shareholders or allocated for other specific purposes. It represents the portion of past operating results retained by the enterprise and is a significant component of owners' equity.

nodes.name: Beginning Retained Earnings Balance
nodes.definition: Beginning retained earnings balance refers to the closing amount in the retained earnings account at the start of a specific accounting period (typically a fiscal year or a quarter). It represents the cumulative net profits from past business activities that have not been distributed to shareholders and serves as the basis for calculating changes in retained earnings during the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Beginning shareholders' equity refers to the total equity shareholders hold in a company at the start of an accounting period, represented as the net value of total assets minus total liabilities. It serves as a foundational non-leaf node indicator in financial analysis for calculating metrics such as the retention ratio and the beginning equity to ending total assets multiplier.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Shareholders' Equity = Beginning Total Assets - Beginning Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Beginning Shares Outstanding
aliases: Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Beginning shares outstanding refers to the total number of common shares actually issued and circulating in the market at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year). It is a point-in-time figure reflecting the equity structure at the beginning of the period and serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as the weighted average shares outstanding.

nodes.name: Beginning Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Beginning Surplus Reserve refers to the balance in the surplus reserve account at the start of the current accounting period (e.g., the current year). It is directly carried over from the ending surplus reserve balance of the previous accounting period (e.g., the prior year). As a fundamental opening figure on the balance sheet, it is typically not calculated via a formula but serves as a given condition for computing changes in the current period's surplus reserve or the ending balance.

nodes.name: Beginning Total Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Beginning Total Accounts Receivable refers to the aggregate book value of amounts owed to a company by customers for goods sold or services rendered in the ordinary course of business, which remain uncollected at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous accounting period and serves as the baseline data for analyzing changes in accounts receivable during the current period and for calculating related financial metrics.

nodes.name: Beginning Total Assets
nodes.definition: Beginning total assets refers to the total value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending total assets of the previous accounting period. As a fundamental point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, it serves as the starting point for analyzing changes in assets during the current period and for calculating related financial metrics.

nodes.name: Beginning Total Interest-Free Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning Total Interest-Free Liabilities refers to the aggregate book value of all liabilities that do not require interest payments at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). These liabilities typically include operating liabilities such as accounts payable, deferred revenue, accrued employee compensation, and taxes payable.

nodes.name: Beginning Total Liabilities
nodes.definition: Beginning total liabilities refer to the total amount of liabilities of an enterprise at the beginning of an accounting period, representing the value of total liabilities at the starting point. It reflects the debt position of the enterprise at the beginning of the period. It is a calculable composite metric, typically derived by summing beginning current liabilities and beginning non-current liabilities, or calculated from beginning total assets and beginning total equity based on the accounting equation.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Total Liabilities = Beginning Current Liabilities + Beginning Non-current Liabilities
Beginning Total Liabilities = Beginning Total Assets - Beginning Total Equity

nodes.name: Beginning Total Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Beginning total shareholders' equity refers to the total shareholders' equity at the start of an accounting period, reflecting the net asset value attributable to shareholders at the beginning point, and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as average equity multiplier and increase in shareholders' equity.

nodes.name: Beginning Value
nodes.definition: Beginning value refers to the recorded balance of an accounting account (such as an asset, liability, or equity account) at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a month, quarter, or year). It is typically carried forward directly from the ending balance of the previous accounting period and serves as the starting point for current financial recording and calculations.

nodes.name: Beginning Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Beginning value per share refers to the value corresponding to each common share at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It typically denotes the stock's market price on the first day of the period or the book value per share calculated from the company's financial statements, serving as fundamental data for measuring the stock's value level at the period's commencement.

nodes.name: Beginning Value of Work-in-Process and Semi-Finished Goods
nodes.definition: Beginning value of work-in-process and semi-finished goods refers to the book value or cost of unfinished products on the production line and partially processed goods that have not yet become final products at the start of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). This value represents the outcome of production activities from the previous period and has already been included in the previous period's total output value. Upon completion during the current period, its value will be incorporated into the finished goods value of the current period. Therefore, when calculating the total output value for the current period, this beginning value must be deducted from the current period's total output to avoid double counting.

nodes.name: Beginning Work in Process Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Beginning Work in Process Inventory Cost refers to the total accumulated production costs of all products that are not yet completed and remain in the production process (i.e., work in process) at the start of an accounting period (typically a month). It usually includes direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead, and serves as a crucial opening figure for calculating the total cost of goods completed during the current period.

nodes.name: Beginning Work in Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost
aliases: Initial Cost of Work in Process and Semi-finished Products
Opening WIP and Semi-finished Goods Cost
nodes.definition: Beginning work in process and semi-finished goods cost refers to the accumulated production costs of all unfinished goods still in the production process at the start of an accounting period (such as a month or quarter). These costs represent the results of production activities from the previous period, already included in the previous period's output value, but will continue to be processed and ultimately converted into finished goods in the current period. Therefore, when calculating the cost of finished goods for the current period, they must be included as beginning inventory value in the current period's cost calculation process.

nodes.name: Beginning Work-in-Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost
Beginning Working Capital
nodes.definition: Beginning working capital refers to the working capital at the start of an accounting period, calculated by subtracting beginning current liabilities from beginning current assets. It is a composite metric used to assess a company's short-term solvency and working capital management efficiency, and is often utilized in calculating derived metrics such as the increase in working capital.

formulas.source_formula: Beginning Working Capital = Beginning Current Assets - Beginning Current Liabilities
Beginning Working Capital = Total Beginning Current Assets - Total Beginning Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Beginning-of-Year Investment
nodes.definition: Beginning-of-year investment refers to the funds or asset value invested at the start of each fiscal year (typically January 1st), used to support annual operations or obtain long-term returns. It serves as the original baseline data for calculating performance metrics such as return on investment.

nodes.name: Benchmark Country Equity Market Volatility
aliases: 参考国家股票市场波动性
nodes.definition: Benchmark country equity market volatility typically refers to the overall price fluctuation level of a mature, developed stock market selected as a reference standard (e.g., the United States), commonly measured by the historical return standard deviation of its stock index (e.g., S&P 500). It serves as a key input parameter when calculating the equity risk premium for other countries (especially emerging markets), used to measure market systemic risk.

nodes.name: Benchmark Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The benchmark discount rate is the rate used to discount future cash flows to their present value when evaluating investment projects or conducting asset valuation. It represents the minimum acceptable rate of return required by investors or the company for a specific project or asset, typically determined based on factors such as the risk-free rate of return, market risk premium, and the project's systematic risk (beta coefficient).

formulas.source_formula: Benchmark Discount Rate = Risk-free Rate of Return + Project Beta Coefficient × (Market Average Rate of Return - Risk-free Rate of Return)

nodes.name: Benchmark Indicator
nodes.definition: A benchmark indicator refers to a reference standard or baseline value used for comparison, measurement, or evaluation of other data, results, or performance in financial, performance, or analytical processes. It can be a budget target, industry average, historical data, or a set standard value, used to assess the quality of actual performance or the degree of deviation.

nodes.name: Benchmark Market Capitalization
nodes.definition: Benchmark market capitalization typically refers to the total market capitalization of a listed company used as a calculation or comparison benchmark in specific scenarios (such as IPO pricing or cross-market valuation comparisons). Its core calculation method is the same as that of ordinary market capitalization, i.e., the company's total shares outstanding multiplied by a specific benchmark price (e.g., the A-share price), but it emphasizes its use as a reference standard.

nodes.name: Benchmark Market Risk Premium
nodes.definition: The benchmark market risk premium refers to the excess return over the risk-free rate that investors require for bearing market systematic risk (i.e., risk that cannot be eliminated through diversification). It typically serves as a basis for measuring the overall market risk level and calculating risk premiums for other assets (such as specific countries or industries).

nodes.name: Benchmark Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The benchmark rate of return is the minimum acceptable rate of return required by investors or project decision-makers, serving as the fundamental criterion for evaluating the financial feasibility of investment projects. It is typically composed of factors such as cost of capital, risk premium, and inflation.

formulas.source_formula: Benchmark Rate of Return = (1 + Cost of Capital Rate) × (1 + Risk Discount Rate) × (1 + Inflation Rate) - 1

nodes.name: Benchmark Return Series
nodes.definition: The benchmark return series is a reference metric used to evaluate investment or project returns, calculated based on the cost of capital, risk discount rate, and inflation rate. It is a non-leaf node commonly referenced in the standard deviation analysis of asset excess returns.

operands.metric: Higher of Annual Cost of Funds Rate and Opportunity Cost

formulas.source_formula: Benchmark Return Series = (1 + Higher of Annual Cost of Funds Rate and Opportunity Cost) × (1 + Annual Risk Discount Rate) × (1 + Annual Inflation Rate) − 1

nodes.name: Benchmark Stock Price
nodes.definition: Benchmark stock price refers to a specific stock price used as the basis for calculation, comparison, or adjustment in financial transactions or financial instrument pricing. For example, in convertible bonds, it is often used as a key reference for determining the conversion price.

nodes.name: Benchmark Transportation Cost
nodes.definition: Benchmark transportation cost refers to the preset cost parameters or raw data used as the fundamental calculation basis in the cost accounting and pricing systems for multimodal transport or freight transportation. It is typically not derived through complex financial formulas but serves as a key input in cost estimation templates, such as benchmark working days, one-way kilometer distance, etc., or constitutes components of the final freight rate (e.g., base origin-destination price, base operating price).

nodes.name: Benchmark Value
nodes.definition: Benchmark value refers to a specific numerical value or standard used as a basis for comparison, evaluation, or calculation in financial, investment, or project analysis. It can be a predetermined rate of return (e.g., benchmark yield), price (e.g., benchmark price in bidding), market index, etc., used to measure the performance of other assets, projects, or indicators.

nodes.name: Beneficiary Object Consumption Quantity
nodes.definition: Beneficiary Object Consumption Quantity refers to the calculated amount of resource consumption for a specific beneficiary object, typically derived through formulas based on indicators such as workload, unit consumption, and wastage rate. It is a composite metric used in cost allocation to determine the allocated costs for the current period.

formulas.source_formula: Beneficiary Object Consumption Quantity = Net Consumption Amount ÷ (1 - Wastage Rate)
Beneficiary Object Consumption Quantity = Net Consumption × (1 + Wastage Rate)
Beneficiary Object Consumption Quantity = (Workload × Unit Consumption × Wastage Rate) ÷ (1 - Waste Rate)

nodes.name: Benefit-Cost Ratio
nodes.definition: Benefit-Cost Ratio (BCR) is a financial metric used in capital budgeting and cost-benefit analysis to evaluate the overall relationship between the relative costs and benefits of a proposed project. It is calculated by dividing the total cash benefits by the total cash costs.

formulas.source_formula: Benefit-Cost Ratio = Total Benefits ÷ Total Costs

nodes.name: Bermuda Option Premium
nodes.definition: Bermuda option premium is the estimated price of a Bermuda-style option, calculated as the average of the premiums of comparable American and European options, reflecting its hybrid exercise features.

formulas.source_formula: Bermuda Option Premium = (American Option Premium + European Option Premium) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Beta
nodes.definition: Beta (β) is a measure of the systematic risk of a specific asset or portfolio relative to the risk of the market portfolio, used in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) to calculate the expected return of an asset.

formulas.source_formula: Beta = Covariance(Stock Returns, Market Returns) ÷ Variance(Market Returns)
Beta = Covariance (Stock Returns, Market Returns) ÷ Variance (Market Returns)
Beta = Covariance(Asset Returns, Market Returns) ÷ Variance(Market Returns)
Beta = Covariance (Fund Returns, Market Returns) ÷ Variance (Market Returns)

nodes.name: Beta Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Beta coefficient measures the sensitivity of the return of an individual stock or portfolio to changes in the overall market return, used to quantify systematic risk and serving as a core parameter in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

operands.metric: Covariance of Asset Returns and Market Returns

formulas.source_formula: Beta Coefficient = Covariance of Asset Returns and Market Returns ÷ Variance of Market Returns

nodes.name: Beta Coefficient of Asset i
nodes.definition: The beta coefficient of asset i is a measure of the systematic risk of that asset (or security) relative to the volatility of the overall market (market portfolio). It quantifies the sensitivity of the asset's returns to changes in market returns.

nodes.name: Beta Coefficient of Corresponding Security
nodes.definition: Beta coefficient is an indicator measuring the systematic risk of a security or investment portfolio. It calculates the volatility of a security's returns relative to the overall market returns through statistical regression analysis, reflecting the security's sensitivity to market movements. It is not a fundamental data point but a composite indicator derived through formulas or models.

nodes.name: Beta Coefficient of the Market Portfolio
nodes.definition: The beta coefficient of the market portfolio is an indicator that measures the systematic risk of the market portfolio (typically referring to a portfolio representing the entire market, such as a broad market index) relative to itself. By definition and calculation formula, the correlation coefficient between the market portfolio and itself is 1, therefore its beta coefficient is always equal to 1. It serves as the benchmark in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) for measuring the systematic risk of other individual assets or investment portfolios.

nodes.name: Bid Price
nodes.definition: Bid price refers to the actual price paid by the buyer to the seller to acquire an asset (such as stocks, bonds, foreign exchange, etc.) in financial or commodity trading. It is typically the immediate transaction price at the time of the trade and serves as the fundamental data for recording the original cost of the asset.

nodes.name: Bid-Ask Spread
nodes.definition: Bid-ask spread refers to the difference between the buying price (bid) and selling price (ask) of an asset (such as commodities, stocks, or foreign exchange) at the same point in time. In commerce, it typically denotes the difference between the purchase cost and selling price of goods, serving as the basis for profit calculation. In financial markets, it is a key metric for measuring market liquidity and transaction costs.

formulas.source_formula: Bid-Ask Spread = Ask Price - Bid Price
supporting_source_formulas: Bid-Ask Spread = Ask Price - Bid Price

nodes.name: Bid-Ask Spread Percentage
nodes.definition: Bid-Ask Spread Percentage quantifies the bid-ask spread as a percentage of the stock price, providing a normalized measure of transaction costs and market liquidity across securities with different price levels.

formulas.source_formula: Bid-Ask Spread Percentage = (Bid-Ask Spread ÷ Stock Price) × 100

nodes.name: Bid-Ask Spread Ratio
nodes.definition: The bid-ask spread ratio is an indicator measuring market liquidity, typically referring to the percentage difference between the ask price and the bid price in financial markets relative to the bid price (or ask price). It reflects the implicit cost required to complete a transaction; a smaller spread ratio generally indicates better market liquidity.

nodes.name: Bid-Offer Spread
nodes.definition: The bid-offer spread is the difference between the offer price (the price at which units are sold to investors) and the bid price (the price at which units are repurchased from investors). In unit trusts, it represents the implicit transaction cost associated with buying and selling units; a wider spread indicates higher transaction costs.

formulas.source_formula: Bid-Offer Spread = Offer Price - Bid Price

nodes.name: Billing Mileage
nodes.definition: Billing mileage refers to the actual or agreed transportation distance used to calculate freight charges in road freight transportation. It is typically determined based on standard route maps or mutual negotiation and serves as one of the core bases for calculating transportation costs.

nodes.name: Binary Option Payout
nodes.definition: Binary option payout is the fixed return received if the option expires in-the-money, calculated as the product of the investment amount and the broker-specified payout ratio; otherwise the investor loses the entire investment.

nodes.name: Binomial Distribution Mean and Variance
nodes.definition: The binomial distribution mean and variance describe the expected value and variability of the number of successes in a fixed number of independent Bernoulli trials with constant success probability.

nodes.name: Binomial Option Pricing
nodes.definition: The binomial option pricing model is a discrete-time model that values options by creating a binomial lattice to represent possible paths the underlying asset price may take over time, incorporating risk-neutral probabilities and backward induction to determine the option's fair value.

nodes.name: Binomial Probability
aliases: Probability of k Successes in n Trials
二项分布概率质量函数
nodes.definition: Binomial probability measures the likelihood of obtaining exactly x successes in n independent Bernoulli trials, each with success probability p.

nodes.name: Bitcoin Misery Index
nodes.definition: The Bitcoin Misery Index (BMI) is a sentiment indicator for Bitcoin trading that ranges from 0 to 100, where lower values indicate greater 'misery' among traders and potential buying opportunities.

formulas.source_formula: BMI = (Win Ratio - Volatility) × 100

nodes.name: Black-Scholes Call Option Price
nodes.definition: The Black-Scholes call option price is the theoretical value of a European call option calculated using the Black-Scholes model, which incorporates the current asset price, strike price, time to expiration, risk-free rate, and volatility.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes European Call Option Price
aliases: 布莱克-舒尔斯看涨期权价格
nodes.definition: The Black-Scholes European Call Option Price is the theoretical value of a European call option on a non-dividend-paying underlying asset, derived under the Black-Scholes-Merton framework assuming continuous compounding at a constant risk-free rate, lognormal asset price dynamics with constant volatility, and no arbitrage. The price is computed using the cumulative standard normal distribution evaluated at d1 and d2.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes European Put Option Price
aliases: 黑-舒尔斯-默顿欧式看跌期权价格
黑-舒尔斯欧式看跌期权价格
nodes.definition: The Black-Scholes European put option price gives the fair value of a European-style put under the Black-Scholes-Merton framework, assuming a constant risk-free rate, constant volatility, lognormal asset dynamics, frictionless markets, and no dividends. It discounts the strike and weights terms by risk-neutral probabilities via the standard normal cumulative distribution.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes Model
nodes.definition: The Black-Scholes model is a mathematical model used for the dynamics of financial markets containing derivative financial instruments. The model assumes that the underlying asset follows geometric Brownian motion, achieves risk-neutral pricing through continuous delta hedging, and thereby provides an estimate for the theoretical price of an option, particularly suitable for pricing European options.

nodes.name: Black-Scholes Option Pricing
aliases: 布莱克-舒尔斯期权定价
nodes.definition: Black-Scholes option pricing provides the theoretical value of European call and put options under the assumptions of lognormal asset returns, constant volatility and risk-free rate, and no dividends. It derives closed-form prices using d1 and d2 parameters and the standard normal cumulative distribution function.

nodes.name: Blended Rate
nodes.definition: Blended rate is the weighted average interest rate calculated across multiple loans with different principal amounts and interest rates, representing the effective interest cost of the combined loan portfolio.

nodes.name: Bollinger Band
nodes.definition: Bollinger Bands are volatility bands placed above and below a simple moving average of price, used to identify overbought or oversold conditions and gauge market volatility.

nodes.name: Bollinger Bands
nodes.definition: Bollinger Bands are a technical analysis volatility indicator consisting of a middle band (an N-period Simple Moving Average), an upper band (SMA plus K times the standard deviation), and a lower band (SMA minus K times the standard deviation). They help identify overbought or oversold conditions, measure price volatility, and provide dynamic support and resistance.

nodes.name: Bond Annual Yield
nodes.definition: Bond annual yield, also known as current yield, represents the annual return on a bond based on its annual coupon payments and current market price, excluding any capital gains or losses.

nodes.name: Bond Assets
nodes.definition: Bond assets are standardized debt instruments issued by governments, financial institutions, or corporations to raise funds, promising to pay interest at agreed rates and repay principal at maturity. They represent a creditor-debtor relationship, where the holder is the creditor.

nodes.name: Bond Discount
nodes.definition: Bond discount is the amount by which a bond's par value exceeds its market price when the coupon rate is below the market interest rate, representing the contra-liability account that amortizes over the bond's life.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Discount = Par Value - Market Price
supporting_source_formulas: Bond Discount = Par Value - Market Price

nodes.name: Bond Discount Amortization
nodes.definition: Bond discount amortization refers to the process of systematically allocating the difference between a bond's face value and its lower issuance price (i.e., the bond discount) over the bond's entire term to maturity, using a specific method (such as the effective interest rate method or straight-line method). This process increases the periodic interest expense (for the issuer) or investment income (for the investor) and gradually adjusts the bond's carrying value to its face value at maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Discount Amortization (per period) = Beginning Book Value × Effective Interest Rate - Face Value × Coupon Rate

nodes.name: Bond Discount Percentage
nodes.definition: Bond discount percentage measures how far a bond's market price falls below its par (face) value, expressed as a percentage of par. It indicates the magnitude of pricing below par and is used in fixed-income pricing, comparison across bonds, and assessment of market-implied concessions.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Discount Percentage = (1 - Market Price ÷ Par Value) × 100%

nodes.name: Bond Discount Rate
nodes.definition: Bond discount rate measures the percentage difference between a bond's par value and its current market price, indicating the extent to which the bond is trading below its face value.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Discount Rate = (Par Value - Market Price) ÷ Par Value

nodes.name: Bond Dollar Price
nodes.definition: Bond dollar price refers to the actual monetary amount paid for a bond, calculated by converting the bond quote percentage into dollars based on the bond's face value.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Dollar Price = (Bond Quote Percentage ÷ 100) × Face Value

nodes.name: Bond Duration
nodes.definition: Bond duration measures the sensitivity of a bond’s price to changes in interest rates, expressed as the percentage change in price per percentage change in yield.

nodes.name: Bond Effective Maturity
nodes.definition: Bond effective maturity, commonly referred to as duration, is a composite measure of a bond's price sensitivity to interest rate changes, calculated as the weighted average of the present values of the bond's cash flows divided by the bond's price.

nodes.name: Bond Equivalent Yield
nodes.definition: Bond Equivalent Yield (BEY) is an annualized yield measure that allows investors to compare the return on discounted short-term bonds with traditional coupon-paying bonds that make annual interest payments.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Equivalent Yield = Return on Investment × (365 ÷ Days to Maturity)

nodes.name: Bond Future Cash Flows
nodes.definition: Bond future cash flows refer to the total sum of interest payments (coupons) expected to be paid periodically to bondholders according to the bond contract during its term, plus the principal (face value) repaid at maturity. It serves as the foundation for bond valuation, where the present value or fair value of the bond is calculated by discounting these future cash flows to the current point in time.

nodes.name: Bond Futures Price
nodes.definition: Bond futures price refers to the final settlement price of a bond futures contract at expiry, calculated by multiplying the futures price by the conversion factor and adding any accrued interest, reflecting the delivery value of the underlying bond.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Futures Price = (Futures Price × Conversion Factor) + Accrued Interest

nodes.name: Bond Interest
nodes.definition: Bond interest is the periodic interest payment made by the bond issuer to bondholders based on the bond's face value and coupon rate. It represents the cost of using funds for the bond issuer and serves as one of the primary sources of return for bondholders.

nodes.name: Bond Investment
nodes.definition: Bond investment refers to the act of purchasing and holding bonds issued by governments, financial institutions, or corporations by enterprises or individuals to obtain interest income or capital appreciation. On the balance sheet, it is typically presented as an asset account, reflecting the carrying amount or fair value of the bonds held.

nodes.name: Bond Issue Price
nodes.definition: Bond issue price is the price investors are willing to pay for a bond, calculated based on the discounting of future cash flows.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Ladder Allocation per Year = Investment Amount ÷ Number of Years

nodes.name: Bond Premium Amortization
nodes.definition: Bond premium amortization refers to the process of systematically allocating the portion of a bond's issuance price that exceeds its face value (i.e., the premium) over the bond's entire term, using a specific method (such as the straight-line method or the effective interest rate method), to periodically recognize it as interest expense or to reduce investment income. Its purpose is to adjust the bond's carrying value to its face value at maturity and to accurately reflect the actual interest cost or income for each period.

nodes.name: Bond Price
nodes.definition: Bond price refers to the sum of the present values of the bond's future cash flows, with its core valuation principle being the discounted cash flow model. The fair price that investors are willing to pay for a bond equals the sum of the present values of periodic interest payments and the present value of the principal at maturity, using the market interest rate (or required rate of return) as the discount rate.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Price = Quote × Par Value ÷ 100

nodes.name: Bond Price Change
nodes.definition: Bond price change measures the percentage fluctuation in a bond’s market price resulting from a shift in market interest rates relative to the bond’s fixed coupon rate.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Price Change = Duration × Yield Change + Convexity Adjustment

nodes.name: Bond Price Premium
nodes.definition: Bond price premium is the amount by which a bond's market price exceeds its face (par) value. A premium typically arises when the bond's coupon rate is higher than the prevailing market interest rate, causing investors to pay more than face value to receive above-market coupon payments. In valuation, the premium equals the difference between the present value of the bond's cash flows and its face value when the coupon rate exceeds the market rate.

formulas.source_formula: Bond Price Premium (Discount) = Market Value - Par Value

nodes.name: Bond Purchase Price
nodes.definition: Bond purchase price refers to the actual price paid by an investor when buying a bond in the bond market, representing the original transaction data upon trade execution. It typically differs from the bond's face value and is influenced by various factors such as market interest rates, bond credit ratings, and remaining maturity.

nodes.name: Bond Redemption Amount
nodes.definition: Bond redemption amount refers to the principal amount paid by the bond issuer to bondholders on the maturity date or early redemption date, as stipulated in the bond indenture. For bonds at maturity, it typically equals the bond's face value; for callable bonds, it may include the face value plus a certain call premium.

nodes.name: Bond Valuation
nodes.definition: Bond valuation is the process of determining the theoretical fair value or present value of a bond by discounting its expected future coupon payments and the face value at maturity using an appropriate discount rate, typically the yield to maturity.

nodes.name: Bond Value
nodes.definition: Bond value refers to the present value of the expected cash inflows an investor anticipates from a bond investment. It primarily consists of the present value of future periodic interest payments and the principal amount received at maturity or the selling price upon disposal. It is a core concept in the valuation of fixed-income securities.

nodes.name: Bond Yield
nodes.definition: Bond yield is an indicator measuring the return on investment from bonds, typically expressed as an annualized percentage. It reflects the ratio between the total return an investor receives from purchasing a bond until its maturity or sale and the initial investment principal.

nodes.name: Bonds Payable
nodes.definition: Bonds payable represent a liability arising from the issuance of marketable securities by an enterprise to raise long-term funds, with an obligation to repay principal and interest within a specified period. On the balance sheet, it is presented as a non-current liability (or the portion due within one year is reclassified as a current liability), and its amount directly reflects the actual transaction records of the bond's face value, interest adjustments (such as premium or discount), etc.

nodes.name: Bonds Payable Ending Balance
aliases: Carrying Amount of Bonds Payable at Period End
nodes.definition: Bonds Payable Ending Balance refers to the carrying value of bonds payable that have not been repaid by an enterprise as of the balance sheet date at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the amount of liability the enterprise bears due to issuing bonds at that point in time, typically calculated based on factors such as the bond's face value, interest adjustments (e.g., amortization of premium or discount), and accrued interest.

nodes.name: Bonus Depreciation
nodes.definition: Bonus depreciation is an accelerated depreciation method that allows businesses to immediately deduct a specified percentage of the cost of qualifying assets in the year they are placed in service, providing a significant tax advantage by reducing taxable income in the initial year of purchase.

formulas.source_formula: Bonus Depreciation = Asset Cost × Bonus Rate
Bonus Depreciation = Asset Cost × Bonus Depreciation Rate

nodes.name: Bonus Depreciation Allowance (Listed Property)
nodes.definition: Bonus depreciation allowance (for listed property) is the percentage of qualified property cost that can be deducted in the year placed in service under special tax depreciation rules. This allowance may phase down by fixed increments based on the property’s purchase year and applicable legislative schedule, and is subject to eligibility windows and floor limits that prevent negative allowances.

nodes.name: Bonus Depreciation Rate
nodes.definition: Bonus depreciation rate is the additional percentage of an asset's cost that can be immediately expensed in the year the asset is placed in service, as allowed by tax law, which phases out over time according to a statutory schedule.

nodes.name: Bonus Shares Issued
nodes.definition: Bonus shares issued refer to additional shares distributed free of charge to existing shareholders in proportion to their current holdings, by converting earned profits (such as retained earnings or surplus reserves) into share capital. This is a non-cash form of dividend distribution; after issuance, the company's total share capital increases while total shareholders' equity remains unchanged.

nodes.name: Book Cost
nodes.definition: Book cost refers to the original cost actually incurred when an asset or inventory is acquired or produced, as recorded in the accounting books, and serves as the fundamental data for subsequent accounting treatment and cost calculation.

nodes.name: Book Value
nodes.definition: In accounting, book value (or carrying value) refers to the value reflected by the balance of an asset in its balance sheet account. For assets, this value is based on the original cost of the asset minus accumulated depreciation, amortization, or impairment amounts. Traditionally, a company's book value equals its total assets minus intangible assets and liabilities.

formulas.source_formula: Book Value = Total Assets - Total Liabilities
Book Value = Total Assets - Intangible Assets - Liabilities

nodes.name: Book Value Per Common Share
nodes.definition: Book value per common share (BVPS) is an accounting measure that represents the per-share value of a company's common equity after deducting preferred equity. It indicates the net asset value available to common shareholders in the event of liquidation and is commonly used to assess the intrinsic value of a stock relative to its market price.

formulas.source_formula: Book Value Per Common Share = Common Equity ÷ Total Outstanding Common Shares

nodes.name: Book Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Book value per share refers to the value of net assets represented by each common share, reflecting the theoretical amount each common shareholder would receive if the company were liquidated at book value. It is an important financial metric for assessing a company's book value, financial health, and serves as the basis for calculating the price-to-book ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Book Value per Share = (Total Assets - Intangible Assets - Total Liabilities) ÷ Outstanding Shares

nodes.name: Book Value of Assets
nodes.definition: Book value of assets refers to the amount reported on the balance sheet, reflecting the net value after deducting accumulated depreciation (or amortization) and any impairment provisions from the original cost. It is an important accounting metric for measuring the current carrying value of assets.

nodes.name: Book Value of Debt
nodes.definition: Book value of debt refers to the carrying amount of various debt obligations presented on the balance sheet, typically representing their amortized cost, which reflects the historical cost-based measurement of a company's debt. For general debt, its book value can be calculated by summing relevant liability accounts; for financial liabilities such as issued bonds, the book value is the initial recognition amount adjusted for the amortization of premiums, discounts, and transaction costs using the effective interest method.

formulas.source_formula: Book Value of Debt = Short-term Borrowings + Long-term Borrowings
Book Value of Debt = Bond Face Value + Unamortized Bond Issuance Costs + Unamortized Bond Premium - Unamortized Bond Discount

nodes.name: Book Value of Equity
nodes.definition: Book value of equity refers to the residual value attributable to the company's shareholders (owners) after subtracting total liabilities from total assets on the company's balance sheet. It represents the shareholders' equity stake in the company under accounting measurement and is commonly used as a basis for calculating other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Book Value of Equity Per Share
nodes.definition: Book Value of Equity Per Share (BVPS) measures the per-share value of a company's equity available to common shareholders, calculated by dividing common equity by the total number of common shares outstanding. It indicates the net asset value backing each common share.

formulas.source_formula: BVPS = Common Equity ÷ Total Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Book Value of Equity Ratio
aliases: Book Value of Equity to Total Assets Ratio
nodes.definition: The Book Value of Equity Ratio is the ratio of the book value of shareholders' equity to the book value of total assets, reflecting the proportion of shareholders' equity in total assets. It is commonly used in capital structure analysis, financial leverage assessment, and project cost of capital calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Book Value of Equity Ratio = 1 ÷ Equity Multiplier

nodes.name: Book Value of Fixed Asset
nodes.definition: Book value of a fixed asset is the net amount at which the asset is reported on the balance sheet, calculated as its initial cost minus accumulated depreciation. It reflects the remaining un-depreciated cost of the asset under the straight-line depreciation method.

nodes.name: Book Value of Identifiable Assets
aliases: 单项可辨认资产账面价值
nodes.definition: The book value of identifiable assets refers to the value of each asset recorded on a company's financial statements at a specific point in time, such as during a merger, acquisition, or asset valuation, that can be separately identified and measured. This value is typically the net amount after deducting accumulated depreciation, amortization, and any impairment provisions from the original cost of the asset.

nodes.name: Book Value of Liabilities
nodes.definition: The book value of liabilities refers to the amount of various outstanding liabilities recorded on a company's balance sheet. It represents the economic benefits that the company expects to outflow in future periods to settle these liabilities, in accordance with accounting standards. For most liabilities (such as short-term borrowings and accounts payable), their book value is typically their principal amount or the amount payable.

nodes.name: Book Value of Old Asset
aliases: Net Book Value of Old Asset
nodes.definition: Book value of an old asset refers to its current recorded value in the accounting books, typically equal to the original acquisition cost of the asset minus the accumulated depreciation (or amortization) up to the current date and any accumulated impairment losses. It reflects the net value of the asset on the financial statements and serves as an important basis for calculating gains or losses on asset disposal, cash flows, etc.

nodes.name: Book Value of Old Equipment
aliases: Net Book Value of Old Equipment
nodes.definition: Book value of old equipment refers to the value of an old piece of equipment recorded in a company's accounting books at a specific point in time. It typically equals the equipment's original acquisition cost (historical cost) minus the accumulated depreciation up to that point. This value reflects the equipment's remaining accounting value, which may differ from its current market disposal value.

nodes.name: Book Value of Restructured Debt
aliases: Book Value of Debt Prior to Restructuring
nodes.definition: The book value of restructured debt refers to the amount recorded in the accounting books for the debt not yet repaid by the debtor on the date of debt restructuring. It typically includes the principal of the debt, accrued but unpaid interest, and other related expenses. This value serves as the benchmark for calculating gains or losses from debt restructuring.

nodes.name: Book Value of Total Capital
nodes.definition: The book value of total capital refers to the recorded value on the accounting books representing all capital sources (including shareholder contributions and retained earnings, etc.), which is the book value attributable to shareholders' equity (or owners' equity) after subtracting total liabilities from total assets according to the corporate balance sheet.

nodes.name: Book Value of a Class of Capital
nodes.definition: The book value of a class of capital refers to the amount of that capital measured and disclosed in the enterprise's financial accounting statements in accordance with accounting standards. It typically reflects the net amount of capital after deducting relevant provisions (such as depreciation, amortization, or impairment reserves) and represents the value recorded on the accounting books.

nodes.name: Book Value of a Specific Capital Type
Book-to-Bill Ratio
nodes.definition: The book-to-bill ratio is a financial metric that compares the value of new orders received to the value of orders shipped and billed during the same period, commonly used in technology and semiconductor industries to gauge demand versus supply dynamics.

formulas.source_formula: Book-to-Bill Ratio = Orders Received ÷ Orders Shipped

nodes.name: Book-to-Market Ratio
nodes.definition: The book-to-market ratio compares a company's book value (common shareholders' equity) to its market capitalization, serving as a valuation indicator to assess whether a stock is undervalued or overvalued.

nodes.name: Books and Supplies Expense
nodes.definition: Books and supplies expense refers to the expenditure incurred by an enterprise or individual for purchasing books, teaching materials, reference materials, and related stationery supplies required for business operations, employee training, or learning. In accounting treatment, it is a specific expense item, recorded in the corresponding cost or expense account based on its specific purpose.

formulas.source_formula: Borrowed Amount = Total Initial Investment − Initial Investment

nodes.name: Borrower's Own Funds
nodes.definition: Borrower's own funds refer to the portion of an enterprise's owner's equity, after deducting the part allocated to long-term assets such as fixed assets, that remains available as self-owned working capital for daily operational turnover. It is a crucial indicator for assessing an enterprise's debt repayment capacity and financial soundness.

nodes.name: Borrowing
nodes.definition: Borrowing refers to the amount of funds borrowed to finance the purchase of a stock when constructing a risk-free investment portfolio.

formulas.source_formula: Borrowing = (Downside Stock Price at Maturity × Hedge Ratio) ÷ (1 + Risk-free Rate)

nodes.name: Borrowing Base
nodes.definition: Borrowing base is the maximum loan amount a lender is willing to extend to a borrower, calculated as the collateral value multiplied by a discount factor that reflects the lender’s risk assessment.

formulas.source_formula: Borrowing Base = Collateral Value × Discount Factor

nodes.name: Bottom Line
nodes.definition: Bottom line, also known as net income or net profit, represents the final profit of a company after all expenses, including operating costs, interest, taxes, and depreciation, have been subtracted from total revenue. It is a key indicator of a company's profitability over a specific accounting period.

formulas.source_formula: Bottom Line = Total Revenue - Total Expenses

nodes.name: Box Spread Maximum Loss
nodes.definition: Box Spread Maximum Loss represents the worst-case monetary loss an investor can incur from a box spread options strategy, equal to the sum of the net premium paid and transaction commissions.

formulas.source_formula: Box Spread Maximum Loss = Net Premium Paid + Commissions

nodes.name: Box Spread Maximum Profit
nodes.definition: Box spread maximum profit is the highest potential gain achievable from a box spread options strategy, calculated as the difference between the higher and lower strike prices minus the total cost including net premium paid and commissions.

formulas.source_formula: Box Value at Expiration = Higher Strike Price - Lower Strike Price
Bracket Income = min(Income, Bracket Limit) − Previous Bracket Limit

nodes.name: Break-Even Point
nodes.definition: Break-even point is the number of units that must be sold to cover all fixed and variable costs, resulting in zero operating profit.

formulas.source_formula: Break-Even Point = Strike Price + Premium

nodes.name: Break-Even Point (Units)
nodes.definition: Break-even point in units is the sales volume at which total revenue equals total cost and profit is zero. This simplified computation divides the unit cost by the unit contribution margin (price per unit minus cost per unit) and does not incorporate fixed costs.

formulas.source_formula: Break-Even Point (Units) = Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin per Unit

nodes.name: Break-Even Point in Sales Dollars
nodes.definition: The break-even point in sales dollars is the revenue level at which total sales exactly cover total fixed costs, resulting in zero profit. It is calculated by dividing total fixed costs by the contribution margin ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Break-Even Sales = Total Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin Ratio

nodes.name: Break-Even Point in Units
nodes.definition: Break-even point in units is the number of units that must be sold so that total revenues equal total costs, resulting in zero profit. It is calculated by dividing total fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit.

formulas.source_formula: Break-Even Point in Units = Total Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin per Unit

nodes.name: Break-Even Price
nodes.definition: Break-even price is the per-unit selling price at which total revenues equal total costs (fixed plus variable), resulting in zero profit or loss.

formulas.source_formula: Break-even Price = Higher Strike Price - Net Debit
Break-Even Price (Call) = Strike Price + Premium Paid
Break-Even Price (Put) = Strike Price - Premium Paid
Break-Even Units = Cost per Unit ÷ (Price per Unit - Cost per Unit)
Break-Even Units = Fixed Cost ÷ (Unit Price - Variable Cost per Unit)

nodes.name: Break-even Lease Payment
nodes.definition: Break-even lease payment refers to the pre-tax lease amount that makes the net present value of the leasing option zero, calculated based on the discounted cash flow principle. It represents the maximum acceptable lease amount for the lessee and the minimum acceptable lease amount for the lessor, and is a composite indicator in lease decision analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Break-even Lease Payment = Fair Value of Leased Asset ÷ Ordinary Annuity Present Value Factor
Break-even Lease Payment = Fair Value of Leased Asset × [Discount Rate ÷ (1 - (1 + Discount Rate)^(-Lease Term))]
Break-even Lease Payment = (Asset Acquisition Cost - Present Value of Residual Value ÷ Ordinary Annuity Factor + Depreciation Tax Shield) ÷ (1 - Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Break-even Point Operating Rate
nodes.definition: Break-even point operating rate refers to the percentage of break-even sales volume to normal sales volume, reflecting the relationship between a company's current business scale and its break-even level.

formulas.source_formula: Break-even Point Operating Rate = Break-even Sales Volume ÷ Normal Sales Volume × 100%

nodes.name: Break-even Point Sales Quantity
nodes.definition: Break-even point sales quantity refers to the minimum product sales volume that a company must achieve in order for its total revenue to exactly equal its total costs (including fixed costs and variable costs), thereby neither making a profit nor incurring a loss.

nodes.name: Break-even Point Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Break-even point sales volume refers to the sales quantity at which a company's total revenue equals its total costs, resulting in zero profit, representing the minimum sales level for neither profit nor loss.

formulas.source_formula: Break-even Price (Call Option) = Strike Price + Premium per Share
Break-even Price (Put Option) = Strike Price - Premium per Share
Break-even Price (Short Put) = Strike Price - (Premium ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Break-even Sales
nodes.definition: Break-even sales refers to the sales volume at which total revenue equals total costs, achieving a break-even point, and is a key indicator for measuring a company's operational safety.

nodes.name: Break-even Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Break-even sales volume refers to the quantity of product sales that a company must achieve to cover all fixed and variable costs, thereby reaching a state of neither profit nor loss (i.e., zero profit).

nodes.name: Breakeven Point (Units)
nodes.definition: Breakeven point in units is the number of units that must be sold so that total revenues equal total costs, resulting in zero profit. It is calculated by dividing total fixed costs by the contribution margin per unit.

formulas.source_formula: Breakeven Point = Short Put Strike Price - Net Premium Received
Breakeven Point = Long Put Strike Price - Net Premium Paid
Breakeven Point = Short Call Strike + Premium Received
Breakeven Point = Long Call Strike Price + Net Premium Paid
Breakeven Point = Short Call Strike Price + Net Premium Received

nodes.name: Breakeven Revenue
nodes.definition: Breakeven revenue is the minimum sales revenue required to cover all fixed costs, assuming a constant gross profit margin, resulting in zero net income.

formulas.source_formula: Breakeven Revenue = Fixed Costs ÷ Gross Profit Margin

nodes.name: Breakeven Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Breakeven sales volume is the monetary value of sales required to cover all fixed and variable costs, resulting in zero profit. It is a key metric in cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis used to determine the minimum sales needed to avoid losses.

formulas.source_formula: Breakeven Sales Volume = Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin Ratio
Breakeven Units = Fixed Costs ÷ Contribution Margin per Unit

nodes.name: Brokerage Commission
nodes.definition: Brokerage commission refers to the service fee that investors must pay to a securities company (broker) when conducting securities trading (such as stocks, funds, etc.). This fee is one of the primary revenue sources for brokers, covering services such as providing trading channels, order execution, settlement, and clearing.

nodes.name: Budget Allocation Base Total
nodes.definition: Budget Allocation Base Total refers to the aggregate benchmark amount used for calculating and allocating indirect costs (such as administrative expenses, research and development expenses, etc.) during the budget preparation or cost allocation process. It is typically the sum of direct costs (such as direct labor, direct materials) or a business volume indicator (such as labor hours, production output), serving as the basis for determining the indirect cost rate.

nodes.name: Budget Appropriation
nodes.definition: Budget appropriation refers to the original funds allocated by the government or superior units to budget units for specific purposes according to the approved budget. It serves as the fundamental funding source for budget units' accounting and operational activities, typically allocated directly rather than calculated through formulas.

nodes.name: Budget Deficit
nodes.definition: Budget deficit is the excess of total expenditure over total revenue within a fiscal period, indicating that spending exceeds income. A positive deficit value signals a shortfall, whereas a negative value indicates a budget surplus.

nodes.name: Budget Surplus
nodes.definition: Budget surplus is the amount by which income (or revenue) exceeds expenditures (or spending) during a specific period, indicating a positive financial position; a negative result is termed a budget deficit.

formulas.source_formula: Budget Surplus = Income - Expenditures

nodes.name: Budget Unit Price
aliases: Unit Price in Bill of Quantities
nodes.definition: Budget unit price refers to the predetermined planned price for completing a unit of work quantity (e.g., per cubic meter, per square meter) or purchasing a unit of materials during the preparation of engineering estimates or budgets. It typically consists of labor costs, material costs, and machinery usage costs, and serves as the basis for calculating direct project costs.

nodes.name: Budget Variance
nodes.definition: Budget variance measures the difference between the approved baseline budget and actual expenses incurred for each period, serving as a key indicator in budget analysis to identify discrepancies and potential financial issues.

formulas.source_formula: Budget Variance = Actual Amount - Budgeted Amount
Budget Variance = Actual Expenses - Baseline Budget

nodes.name: Budget at Completion
nodes.definition: Budget at Completion refers to the total budgeted or approved cost planned for the entire project or engineering work before its commencement. It represents the estimated total cost upon completion of the full project scope and serves as the baseline for measuring project cost performance.

nodes.name: Budgeted Activity Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: Budgeted Activity Allocation Rate refers to the unit activity cost rate, pre-calculated based on budgeted or normal activity levels in Activity-Based Costing, used to allocate indirect costs to products or services. It helps provide stable cost information and avoids the impact of actual cost fluctuations on decision-making.

nodes.name: Budgeted Activity Cost
nodes.definition: Budgeted Activity Cost refers to the pre-estimated and allocated resource consumption costs for various planned activity executions within a specific future period (e.g., a budget cycle) under the Activity-Based Costing (ABC) framework. It serves as a critical link connecting corporate strategy, operational processes, and financial budgeting, enabling more precise planning and control of resource expenses by forecasting activity demand.

nodes.name: Budgeted Activity Cost Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The budgeted activity cost allocation rate is a distribution ratio calculated based on estimated activity costs and estimated activity output, used for planning and controlling costs.

nodes.name: Budgeted Activity Level
nodes.definition: Budgeted activity level refers to the pre-determined level or scale of business activity set as the basis for budget preparation during a specific period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It serves as the foundational data for calculating various budgets (e.g., manufacturing overhead budget, selling expense budget) and is typically expressed in quantifiable units such as production volume, sales volume, or labor hours.

nodes.name: Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead
nodes.definition: Budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead refers to the portion of indirect production costs that are pre-estimated during budget preparation for manufacturing activities in a future specific period (such as a fiscal year or a production cycle) and do not vary with changes in business volume (such as production output or labor hours). It is a key component of the manufacturing overhead budget and is used for cost control and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Budgeted Production
nodes.definition: Budgeted production refers to the quantity of goods a company plans to manufacture to meet sales forecasts and inventory targets.

formulas.source_formula: Budgeted Production = (Budgeted Sales + Budgeted Ending Inventory) - Budgeted Beginning Inventory

nodes.name: Budgeted Production Volume
nodes.definition: Budgeted production volume refers to the planned quantity of products to be manufactured during the budget period, calculated from budgeted sales volume, expected ending inventory, and beginning inventory. It is used for production budget preparation and resource planning, serving as a key indicator in budget management within financial management.

nodes.name: Budgeted Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Budgeted sales volume refers to the planned quantity of products or services to be sold in a specific future period, directly determined during the enterprise budgeting process based on market forecasts, historical sales data, and operational targets set by management. It serves as the starting point and fundamental input data for preparing the sales budget, production budget, and other components of the comprehensive budget.

nodes.name: Budgeted Total Production Worker Wages
aliases: Budgeted Total Wages for Production Workers
生产工人工资预算总额
nodes.definition: Budgeted Total Production Worker Wages refers to the total wages estimated or determined during the enterprise budgeting process, based on the production plan, projected number of workers, working hours, and wage standards, for paying workers directly involved in product production. It serves as the fundamental raw data for preparing the manufacturing overhead budget and product cost budget.

nodes.name: Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead per Unit
Bull Call Spread
nodes.definition: A bull call spread is an options strategy constructed by buying a call option with a lower strike price and selling a call option with a higher strike price on the same underlying security with the same expiration date, aiming to profit from a moderate rise in the price of the underlying asset.

operands.metric: Premium of Lower Strike Call Option
Premium of Higher Strike Call Option

formulas.source_formula: Bull Call Spread = Premium of Lower Strike Call Option - Premium of Higher Strike Call Option

nodes.name: Bull Call Spread Breakeven
aliases: 牛市看涨价差盈亏平衡点
nodes.definition: The breakeven point of a Bull Call Spread options strategy is the underlying asset price at which the strategy yields neither profit nor loss, calculated as the lower strike price plus the net premium paid for the spread.

nodes.name: Bull Call Spread Maximum Profit
aliases: Maximum Profit of Bull Call Spread
牛市看涨价差最大收益
nodes.definition: The maximum profit of a bull call spread options strategy, which involves buying a call option at a lower strike price and selling a call option at a higher strike price, realized when the underlying asset closes at or above the higher strike price.

nodes.name: Bull Put Spread
nodes.definition: A bull put spread is a vertical spread options strategy that involves selling a put option with a higher strike price and simultaneously buying a put option with a lower strike price on the same underlying asset and expiration date, resulting in a net credit received.

nodes.name: Bull Put Spread Breakeven
aliases: 牛市看跌价差盈亏平衡点
nodes.definition: The breakeven point of a Bull Put Spread options strategy is the underlying asset price at which the strategy neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss, calculated as the higher strike price minus the net credit received.

nodes.name: Bull Put Spread Maximum Profit
aliases: 牛市看跌价差最大收益
nodes.definition: The maximum profit of a bull put spread options strategy, achieved when the underlying asset closes at or above the higher strike price, equal to the net credit received when initiating the position.

nodes.name: Bullet Bond Present Value
nodes.definition: The present value of a bullet bond is the sum of all future coupon payments and the final principal repayment, each discounted at the bond’s semi-annual yield to maturity.

nodes.name: Bullet Repayment
nodes.definition: Bullet repayment is a loan structure where only periodic interest payments are made during the loan term, and the entire principal amount is repaid in a single lump sum at maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Bullet Repayment = Loan Principal + Total Interest Paid

nodes.name: Burn Rate
nodes.definition: Burn rate is the speed at which a company consumes its cash reserves to cover operating losses, typically expressed as monthly cash outflow. Gross burn rate equals total monthly operating expenses, while net burn rate deducts revenue and cost of goods sold from expenses to show net cash depletion.

nodes.name: Business Risk Premium
nodes.definition: Business risk premium refers to the additional rate of return required by investors for bearing the specific business risks of an enterprise (such as changes in market demand, intensified competition, cost fluctuations, etc.), and is an important component constituting the enterprise's cost of capital or project discount rate.

nodes.name: Business Tax
nodes.definition: Business Tax was a turnover tax levied in China on entities and individuals providing taxable services, transferring intangible assets, or selling immovable property within China, based on their turnover. It has been completely replaced by Value-Added Tax.

nodes.name: Business Tax Actually Paid in Current Period
aliases: Actual Business Tax Paid in Current Period
nodes.definition: Business Tax Actually Paid in Current Period refers to the amount of business tax calculated based on the taxable turnover and applicable tax rate during the current accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual), and actually paid to the tax authorities.

nodes.name: Business Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The Business Tax Rate refers to the specific percentage applied under China's pre-tax reform system to calculate and levy Business Tax on the turnover derived from taxpayers providing taxable services, transferring intangible assets, or selling immovable property. It was a key parameter for determining the Business Tax payable.

nodes.name: Business Tax and Surcharges
nodes.definition: Business Tax and Surcharges refer to the relevant taxes and fees borne by an enterprise for its business activities, mainly including Consumption Tax, Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, Education Surcharge, Resource Tax, Property Tax, Land Use Tax, Vehicle and Vessel Usage Tax, Stamp Duty, etc. This item is presented in the income statement and is used to calculate operating profit.

nodes.name: Business Use Percentage (Listed Property)
nodes.definition: Business Use Percentage (for listed property) measures the proportion of total use attributable to business activities and is used in tax and accounting to determine the deductible portion of expenses, depreciation, and cost recovery for mixed-use assets subject to listed property rules (e.g., vehicles, computers).

formulas.source_formula: Business Use Percentage = (Area Used ÷ Total Area) × Time Percentage
Business Use Percentage = (Business Use Measure ÷ Total Use Measure) × 100

nodes.name: Business Volume
nodes.definition: Business volume refers to the quantity of products produced, goods sold, or business operations executed by an enterprise or organization within a specific period (e.g., a reporting period). It reflects the operational activity level and business scale of the enterprise, serving as fundamental raw data for evaluating operational conditions and performance, typically obtained through direct statistical measurement.

nodes.name: Butterfly Spread Profit/Loss
nodes.definition: Butterfly Spread Profit/Loss represents the potential gain or loss from a butterfly spread options strategy, which involves three strike prices and limited risk/reward based on the underlying asset's price at expiration.

nodes.name: Buyback Ratio
nodes.definition: Buyback ratio measures the proportion of a company’s market capitalization that is returned to shareholders through share repurchases over a specific period, indicating the intensity of buyback activity relative to company size.

nodes.name: Buying Power
nodes.definition: Buying power refers to the total amount of securities that can be purchased in a margin account, calculated as the cash balance multiplied by the margin equity multiplier, representing the leverage provided by the brokerage.

formulas.source_formula: Buying Power = Cash Deposit ÷ Margin Requirement
Buying Power = Cash Balance × Margin Equity Multiplier

nodes.name: Buying on Margin
nodes.definition: Buying on margin is the practice of purchasing securities by borrowing funds from a broker, using the investor’s own equity as collateral, aiming to amplify potential returns (or losses) through leverage.

nodes.name: CAPE Ratio
nodes.definition: The CAPE Ratio is a valuation measure that compares the current share price to the 10-year average of inflation-adjusted earnings, smoothing business-cycle fluctuations to assess long-term market valuation.

formulas.source_formula: CD Rate = Base Rate - Adjustment Factor
CDS Payout = Notional Amount × (1 - Recovery Rate)

nodes.name: CFR Price
nodes.definition: CFR (Cost and Freight) is a price term in international trade, meaning the seller is responsible for delivering the goods to the named port of destination and paying the freight, but the risk transfers to the buyer once the goods pass the ship's rail at the port of shipment. This price does not include insurance.

nodes.name: CIF Price
aliases: 成本加保险费加运费价
nodes.definition: CIF (Cost, Insurance, and Freight) is a commonly used trade term in international commerce, indicating that the seller is responsible for delivering the goods to the named port of destination and paying the cost of goods, freight, and insurance. This price includes the main risks and costs during transit until the goods pass the ship's rail at the port of destination.

formulas.source_formula: CIF Value = Goods Value + Shipping Cost + Insurance Cost

nodes.name: Calculation Base
nodes.definition: Calculation base refers to the original underlying amount used in finance and accounting to compute specific expenses, taxes, or accruals. It is typically the initial data directly drawn from business records or financial statements, such as total payroll, original asset value, or operating revenue, and serves as the foundation for subsequent rate or percentage calculations.

nodes.name: Calculation Period Days
nodes.definition: Calculation period days refer to the standard number of days set for a specific calculation period (e.g., month, quarter, year) in financial analysis or calculations, or the actual number of days calculated based on specific start and end dates. It is a fundamental time parameter used to convert periodic financial data (such as sales, costs) into daily averages, or to serve as the denominator in turnover ratio calculations.

nodes.name: Call Option
nodes.definition: A call option is a financial derivative contract that grants the holder the right, but not the obligation, to buy a specified quantity of an underlying asset (such as a stock) at a predetermined price (the strike price) on or before a specific future date. The holder anticipates that the price of the underlying asset will rise, allowing them to profit by exercising the option.

formulas.source_formula: Call Option Breakeven = Strike Price + Premium

nodes.name: Call Option Breakeven Price
nodes.definition: The call option breakeven price is the underlying asset price at expiration at which a long call position results in neither profit nor loss. For a call option, the breakeven price equals the strike price plus the premium paid.

formulas.source_formula: Call Option Breakeven Price = Strike Price + Option Premium

nodes.name: Call Option Expiration Value
aliases: Long Call Option Value at Maturity
nodes.definition: The value of a long call option at expiration is equal to the maximum of the stock market price minus the strike price, or zero otherwise.

nodes.name: Call Option Intrinsic Value
nodes.definition: The intrinsic value of a call option is the amount by which the market price of the underlying security exceeds the option's strike price, representing the immediate exercise value of the option if it were exercised today.

formulas.source_formula: Call Option Max = Underlying Price
Call Option Min = 0

nodes.name: Call Option Moneyness
nodes.definition: Call option moneyness describes the relationship between the current market price of the underlying asset and the option’s strike price, classifying the option as in-the-money, at-the-money, or out-of-the-money.

nodes.name: Call Option Payoff at Expiration
aliases: Call Option Intrinsic Value at Maturity
Expiration Value of a Call Option
