nodes.definition: Cash received from investment absorption in the next period refers to the net cash amount a company expects to actually receive in the upcoming accounting period (e.g., next quarter or fiscal year) by absorbing investments from investors. This includes funds raised through methods such as issuing stocks or bonds, representing the actual cash proceeds received by the company after deducting related issuance costs (e.g., commissions).

nodes.name: Cash Received from Investment Absorption in Year k
aliases: Cash Inflow from Financing Activities (Investment Absorption)
Proceeds from Issuing Equity and Debt
nodes.definition: Cash received from investment absorption in year k refers to the net cash actually received by an enterprise during the k-th accounting year through absorbing investor contributions (such as issuing stocks, bonds, etc.). It reflects the funds directly obtained by the enterprise from owners or creditors and is an important component in calculating cash inflows.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Investment Income
aliases: Cash Received from Dividends and Interest
nodes.definition: Cash received from investment income refers to an item reported in the cash flow statement, reflecting the actual cash dividends received by the enterprise from equity investments and the actual cash interest income received from debt investments. It belongs to cash inflows from investing activities.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Investment Income for the Next Period

Cash Received from Investment Recovery in Year k

nodes.definition: Cash received from investment recovery in year k refers to the total actual cash received by an enterprise in the k-th year of a project or investment activity through the sale, transfer, or maturity recovery of short-term investments (excluding cash equivalents), long-term equity investments, and the recovery of principal from long-term debt investments. It is an important component in calculating the cash inflow for year k of the project.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Investment Returns in Next Period
aliases: Cash Received from Investments in Next Period

nodes.definition: Cash received from investment returns in the next period refers to the cash dividends expected to be received by an enterprise in the upcoming accounting period (e.g., next quarter or next fiscal year) from holding equity investments (such as stocks), as well as cash interest income obtained from holding debt investments (such as bonds). This portion of cash inflow belongs to cash flows from investing activities, but excludes non-cash forms of returns such as stock dividends.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Investment Returns in Year k

nodes.definition: Cash received from investment returns in year k refers to the total actual cash received by an enterprise in a specific year (year k) from equity investments (such as cash dividends) and debt investments (such as cash interest). It is an important component of cash inflows generated from investing activities and reflects the enterprise's ability to generate cash returns from external investments.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Investments

nodes.definition: Cash received from investments refers to the net cash amount actually received by an enterprise from investors through methods such as issuing stocks or bonds, which is the total issuance proceeds minus related issuance costs (e.g., commissions).

nodes.definition: Cash received from other financing activities in year k refers to the net cash actually received by an enterprise during the k-th accounting year from transactions or events related to financing activities, excluding major financing activities such as absorbing investments and obtaining borrowings.

aliases: Cash Inflows from Other Investing Activities

nodes.definition: This is an item in the investing activities section of a company's cash flow statement, referring to other cash inflows related to investing activities received by the enterprise, apart from major investing activities such as recovering investments and obtaining investment returns. Examples include receiving cash dividends declared but not yet collected when purchasing stocks, or receiving bond interest that has reached the payment date but not yet collected when purchasing bonds.

nodes.definition: Cash received from other investment activities in Year k refers to the cash inflows related to investment activities, other than major activities such as disposal of fixed assets or intangible assets, as reported in the company's cash flow statement for Year k. Examples include dividends or interest declared but not yet received from the purchase of stocks or bonds.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Other Operating Activities
aliases: Other Cash Received from Operating Activities
收到的其他与经营活动有关的现金
nodes.definition: This is an item under cash inflows from operating activities in the enterprise's cash flow statement, used to record all other cash receipts related to daily business operations, excluding cash received from sales of goods, rendering of services, and tax refunds. These receipts are typically not part of the enterprise's core business revenue, such as penalty income received, rental income from leasing packaging materials or equipment, deposits received, and scrap sales income.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Purchase Returns
nodes.definition: Cash received from purchase returns refers to the actual cash amount recovered by an enterprise from suppliers due to the return of previously purchased goods or materials. This cash inflow reflects the reverse cash flow of procurement activities and is a specific item of operating cash inflows when preparing the cash flow statement.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Purchase Returns in Current Period
aliases: 当期购货退回现金流入
nodes.definition: Cash received from purchase returns in the current period refers to the actual cash amounts recovered from suppliers during the current accounting period due to the return of purchased goods or materials to suppliers. This cash inflow reflects the reverse cash flow of procurement activities.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Recovery of Investments for the Next Period
Cash Received from Recovery of Investments in Next Period
aliases: Cash Received from Recovery of Investments
收回投资所收到的现金
nodes.definition: Cash received from recovery of investments in the next period refers to the total cash actually received by an enterprise in the upcoming accounting period (e.g., the next period) through the sale, transfer, or maturity recovery of short-term investments (excluding cash equivalents), long-term equity investments, and the recovery of principal from long-term debt investments.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Recovery of Investments in Year k

This cash amount excludes interest received during the investment period.

nodes.definition: Cash received from the sale or transfer of long-term equity investments refers to the actual cash inflow to the enterprise from selling or transferring its holdings of long-term equity investments (such as stock investments in other companies). This cash is a significant component of cash flows from investing activities, reflecting the cash inflow from recovering the principal of long-term equity investments or realizing investment returns.

aliases: Cash Received from Sale or Transfer of Short-term Investments (excluding Cash Equivalents)

nodes.definition: Refers to the actual cash amount received by an enterprise from the sale or transfer of short-term investments that do not qualify as cash equivalents (e.g., financial assets such as stocks and bonds held for a short period with the intent to liquidate in the near term). This cash inflow reflects the recovery of principal from short-term investments not classified as cash equivalents.

nodes.definition: Cash received from sales of goods and rendering of services refers to the actual cash received by an enterprise during the current period through operating activities such as selling goods and providing services. It is a core component of cash inflows from operating activities in the cash flow statement and reflects the enterprise's ability to generate cash from its main business operations.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Rendering of Services in Next Period

下期经营活动现金流入

nodes.definition: Cash received from sales of goods and rendering of services in the next period refers to the total cash amount a company expects to receive from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during the next accounting period (e.g., next month, next quarter, or next year). It is a crucial component for forecasting future operating cash flows.

nodes.name: Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Services
Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Services in the Next Period
Cash Requirement for a Given Period
nodes.definition: Cash requirement for a given period refers to the total amount of cash a company is projected to need to hold in order to meet the demands of its operating, investing, and financing activities during a specific future period (e.g., one year). It is typically forecasted or estimated based on fundamental data such as sales revenue, costs, and turnover rates, and serves as a key input variable for determining the optimal cash balance.

formulas.source_formula: Cash Requirement = Purchase Amount × (1 - Margin Percentage)

nodes.name: Cash Return Point
nodes.definition: The cash return point is the target level to which a company's cash balance should revert during fluctuations in the Miller-Orr stochastic cash management model, used to guide cash replenishment and conversion.

nodes.name: Cash Sales
nodes.definition: Cash sales refer to the actual sales revenue received by an enterprise in the form of cash, bank deposits, or other immediate payment methods (such as electronic payments) when selling goods or providing services. It is the most fundamental raw data in sales operations, directly reflecting the revenue realized through cash sales models.

nodes.name: Cash Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Cash sales revenue refers to income received in cash or cash equivalents (such as bank deposits) immediately upon completion of the sale of goods or provision of services. This type of revenue is recognized at the time of the transaction and is directly reflected in the company's income statement and cash flow statement.

formulas.source_formula: Cash Settlement Amount = (Notional Amount × Day Count Fraction × (Fixed Rate - Reference Rate)) / (1 + Day Count Fraction × Reference Rate)

nodes.name: Cash Surrender Value
nodes.definition: Cash surrender value is the amount of cash a policyholder receives upon voluntary termination of a permanent life insurance policy before maturity, calculated as the accumulated cash value minus surrender charges, prior withdrawals, and outstanding policy loans.

formulas.source_formula: Cash Surrender Value = Cash Value - Surrender Charges - Withdrawals - Loans

nodes.name: Cash Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: Cash Turnover Ratio measures how efficiently a company uses its working capital to generate net sales, indicating the intensity with which operating liquidity supports revenue generation.

formulas.source_formula: Cash Turnover Ratio = Net Turnover ÷ Working Capital

nodes.name: Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.definition: Cash and cash equivalents refer to assets held by an enterprise that are highly liquid, can be used for payment at any time, or can be rapidly converted into a known amount of cash. They primarily include cash on hand, bank deposits, other monetary funds, and short-term, highly liquid investments that are readily convertible to known amounts of cash and subject to an insignificant risk of changes in value (such as short-term treasury bills, money market funds, etc.).

formulas.source_formula: Cash and Cash Equivalents = Cash on Hand + Bank Deposits + Other Monetary Funds

nodes.name: Cash and Cash Equivalents of Previous Period
Cash on Hand
nodes.definition: Cash on hand refers to the banknotes and coins held by an enterprise in its finance department, managed and handled by cashiers. It is the most liquid asset of an enterprise and a key component of monetary funds, distinct from bank deposits and other forms of cash equivalents.

formulas.source_formula: Cash-Out Amount = Maximum Loan Amount - Current Mortgage Balance

nodes.name: Cash-Out Refinance Amount
nodes.definition: Cash-out refinance amount is the net cash proceeds a borrower can receive by refinancing a mortgage for more than the existing loan balance, based on the home's current market value and the lender's maximum loan-to-value ratio.

nodes.name: Cash-Out Value
aliases: 套现再融资可提取现金额
nodes.definition: Cash-Out Value is the maximum cash proceeds a borrower can obtain through a cash-out refinance. It is calculated as the lender-permitted maximum loan amount based on the property's current market value and the maximum loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, minus the outstanding loan balance, floored at zero.

nodes.name: Cash-and-Carry Arbitrage Profit
nodes.definition: Cash-and-carry arbitrage profit is the risk-free gain obtained by simultaneously buying an asset in the spot market and selling a corresponding futures contract, net of all carrying costs including storage, insurance, and financing.

formulas.source_formula: Cash-and-Carry Arbitrage Profit = Futures Price - Spot Price - Carrying Costs

nodes.name: Cash-on-Cash Return
nodes.definition: Cash-on-Cash Return is a rate of return metric used in real estate investment analysis that measures the annual pre-tax cash flow generated by a property relative to the total cash invested, expressed as a percentage.

nodes.name: Catch-up Allocation
nodes.definition: Catch-up allocation is a profit distribution mechanism in private equity and venture capital funds. After the fund's investment return reaches a pre-agreed minimum rate of return (hurdle rate), the general partner (GP) can preferentially receive most or even all of the excess profits until its cumulative performance fee reaches an agreed-upon proportion of the total profits (e.g., 20%). Thereafter, the remaining profits are distributed according to a new ratio (e.g., 80/20).

formulas.source_formula: Catch-up Allocation = (Fund Net Income - Preferred Return) × Catch-up Rate
Catch-up Allocation = Fund Net Income × Catch-up Rate - Distributed Preferred Return × Catch-up Rate

nodes.name: Catch-up Ratio
nodes.definition: Catch-up ratio is a concept in accounting and finance, particularly common in private equity and performance incentive structures. It typically refers to the mechanism where, after achieving an agreed-upon hurdle rate, the general partner (GP) or a specified party is entitled to receive a priority share of the excess returns until their cumulative share reaches a specific proportion (e.g., 20%) of the total excess returns. Thereafter, the remaining profits are distributed according to an agreed-upon split (e.g., 80/20). This concept is also commonly extended to describe the proportional relationship between recovered amounts and target total amounts in scenarios such as recovery or clawback.

formulas.source_formula: Catch-up Tranche = min(Remaining Cash, Sum of Cash Flows × Catch-up Rate)
Ceded Liability = Gross Liability × Quota Share Percentage
Celsius = (5 ÷ 9) × (Fahrenheit - 32)

nodes.name: Central Tendency
nodes.definition: Central tendency is a statistical concept referring to measures that indicate the center of a dataset, such as the mean, median, or mode. In financial management and analysis, central tendency is commonly used to calculate risk metrics (e.g., mean absolute deviation) and assess data distribution characteristics, serving as a foundation for descriptive statistics and financial modeling.

formulas.source_formula: Central Tendency = Sum of Data Points ÷ Number of Data Points

nodes.name: Certain Cash Flow in Year t
aliases: Risk-free Cash Flow in Year t
第t年肯定当量现金流量
nodes.definition: Certain cash flow in year t refers to the net cash inflow or outflow that is expected to be realized with certainty in year t (where t represents the number of years from the start of the investment) after risk adjustment in investment or project evaluation. It is typically used in conjunction with the 'certainty equivalent coefficient' to convert uncertain expected cash flows into equivalent, risk-free certain cash flows for more accurate valuation.

nodes.name: Certainty Equivalent Cash Flow
nodes.definition: The certainty equivalent cash flow is the risk-free cash flow amount that an investor considers equally desirable as a higher but uncertain expected cash flow, adjusting for risk via the risk premium.

formulas.source_formula: Certainty Equivalent Cash Flow = Expected Cash Flow ÷ (1 + Risk Premium)

nodes.name: Certainty Equivalent Coefficient of Cash Flow in Year t
nodes.definition: The certainty equivalent coefficient of cash flow in year t is a discount factor between 0 and 1, used to convert the risky projected cash flow in future year t into an equivalent, risk-free cash flow with certainty. A lower coefficient value indicates higher risk associated with the cash flow in that year.

operands.metric: Certain Cash Flow in Year t
Expected Value of Uncertain Cash Flow in Year t

formulas.source_formula: Certainty Equivalent Coefficient of Cash Flow in Year t = Certain Cash Flow in Year t ÷ Expected Value of Uncertain Cash Flow in Year t

nodes.name: Certificate of Deposit (CD)
nodes.definition: A Certificate of Deposit (CD) is a deposit certificate issued by a bank or financial institution, where a customer deposits a sum of money for a fixed term (e.g., several months or years), and the bank promises to repay the principal and pay interest at an agreed-upon rate upon maturity. It is a low-risk, fixed-income savings or wealth management instrument.

nodes.name: Change in Abscissa
nodes.definition: Change in abscissa refers to the amount of increase or decrease in the numerical value of a point's abscissa (usually denoted by X) when it moves from one position to another in a plane rectangular coordinate system. It is commonly used in measurement, geometry, and function analysis to represent horizontal displacement or variation.

nodes.name: Change in Consumption
nodes.definition: Change in consumption refers to the variation in consumption expenditure between two periods. It is a fundamental variable in the analysis of the consumption function in macroeconomics, commonly used to calculate derived indicators such as the marginal propensity to consume.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Consumption = Current Period Consumption - Previous Period Consumption

nodes.name: Change in Consumption Quantity
nodes.definition: Change in consumption quantity is a derived indicator in macroeconomics, representing the variation in consumption level. It is typically calculated as the product of the marginal propensity to consume and the change in income, reflecting the sensitivity of consumption to income changes, and is commonly used in consumption function analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Consumption Quantity = Marginal Propensity to Consume × Change in Income

nodes.name: Change in Current Assets
nodes.definition: Change in Current Assets refers to the difference between the ending balance of current assets in a given accounting period and the ending balance of the previous period. It reflects the net change in the scale of a company's current assets and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as the change in working capital.

nodes.name: Change in Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Change in Current Liabilities refers to the difference in the total amount of current liabilities between two specific points in time (typically the end and beginning of a period). It is a derived financial metric used to measure changes in a company's short-term debt repayment pressure and is commonly used in calculating changes in working capital.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Current Liabilities = Total Current Liabilities (Current Period) - Total Current Liabilities (Prior Period)
Change in Delta = Gamma × Change in Underlying Price

nodes.name: Change in EBIT
aliases: Change in Earnings Before Interest and Taxes
nodes.definition: Change in EBIT refers to the variation in Earnings Before Interest and Taxes across different accounting periods, calculated as the difference between the current period's EBIT and the prior period's EBIT. It reflects changes in the core operational profitability of an enterprise and serves as a crucial foundational metric for analyzing financial leverage effects.

formulas.source_formula: Change in EBIT = Current Period EBIT - Prior Period EBIT

nodes.name: Change in Earnings Per Common Share
aliases: Change in Earnings Per Share of Common Stock
nodes.definition: Change in Earnings Per Common Share is a composite metric measuring the variation in a company's earnings per common share between two accounting periods. It is calculated by comparing the current period's EPS with the prior period's EPS, involving changes in underlying data such as net profit, preferred stock dividends, and the number of common shares outstanding. It is commonly used in the calculation and analysis of the financial leverage coefficient.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Earnings Per Common Share = Basic EPS for Current Period - Basic EPS for Prior Period

operands.metric: Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders for Current Period
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Current Period
Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders for Prior Period
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in the Prior Period

formulas.source_formula: Change in Earnings Per Common Share = (Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders for Current Period ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Current Period) - (Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders for Prior Period ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Prior Period)

operands.metric: Preferred Stock Dividends for Current Period
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Current Period
Preferred Stock Dividends for Prior Period
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in the Prior Period

formulas.source_formula: Change in Earnings Per Common Share = (Net Profit for Current Period - Preferred Stock Dividends for Current Period) ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Current Period - (Net Profit for Prior Period - Preferred Stock Dividends for Prior Period) ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Prior Period

nodes.name: Change in Net Working Capital
nodes.definition: Change in Net Working Capital refers to the increase or decrease in net working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) of a company during a specific accounting period. This metric is a key adjustment item in calculating Free Cash Flow (FCF) and Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF), reflecting changes in the liquid funds invested in or released from supporting daily operations.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Net Working Capital = (Current Period Current Assets - Current Period Current Liabilities) - (Prior Period Current Assets - Prior Period Current Liabilities)
supporting_source_formulas: Change in Net Working Capital = (Current Period Current Assets - Current Period Current Liabilities) - (Prior Period Current Assets - Prior Period Current Liabilities)

nodes.name: Change in Ordinate
nodes.definition: Change in ordinate refers to the distance or difference a point moves in the vertical direction (y-axis direction) in a Cartesian coordinate system. It is commonly used to calculate the slope of a line, representing the magnitude of change in the y-value.

nodes.name: Change in Retained Earnings
nodes.definition: Change in Retained Earnings specifically refers to the increase in a company's retained earnings account during a specific accounting period (e.g., one year). It originates from the portion of current period net profit remaining after the appropriation of surplus reserves and the distribution of dividends to shareholders.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Retained Earnings = Net Profit - Cash Dividends
Change in Retained Earnings = Net Profit × (1 - Dividend Payout Ratio)
Change in Retained Earnings = Sales Revenue × Net Profit Margin × Retention Ratio

nodes.name: Change in Spot Exchange Rate of the Underlying Foreign Exchange Option
Change in Underlying Spot Exchange Rate of Foreign Exchange Options
nodes.definition: Refers to the numerical increase or decrease in the spot exchange rate (real-time trading price in the spot market) of a foreign currency against the domestic currency, which serves as the underlying asset of a foreign exchange option, over a period of time. This change is the fundamental data directly observed or obtained from the market and directly affects the value of the foreign exchange option, particularly its Delta.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Unemployment Rate = Okun's Coefficient × GDP Growth

nodes.name: Change in Working Capital
nodes.definition: Change in Working Capital is a composite indicator reflecting the net change in a company's current assets and current liabilities, calculated by comparing the current period's working capital with the prior period's. It is commonly used in cash flow analysis, free cash flow calculation, and financial health assessment.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Working Capital = Change in Current Assets - Change in Current Liabilities
Change in Working Capital = (Current Period Current Assets - Current Period Current Liabilities) - (Prior Period Current Assets - Prior Period Current Liabilities)

nodes.name: Change in Working Capital for Period 1
nodes.definition: Change in Working Capital for Period 1 refers to the net change in working capital (current assets minus current liabilities) from the base period (Period 0) to Period 1. It is a non-cash working capital item that requires adjustment when calculating the expected free cash flow for Period 1.

formulas.source_formula: Change in Working Capital for Period 1 = Working Capital for Period 1 - Working Capital for Base Period
Change in Working Capital for Period 1 = (Current Assets for Period 1 - Current Liabilities for Period 1) - (Current Assets for Base Period - Current Liabilities for Base Period)

nodes.name: Change in Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Change in Working Capital in the First Year of the Terminal Period
aliases: Change in Working Capital for the First Year of the Terminal Period
First Year Terminal Period Working Capital Change
后续期首年营运资本需求变动
永续期第一年营运资本变动
稳定期首年营运资本变动
nodes.definition: In financial forecasting or business valuation, this refers to the change in working capital requirement in the first year of the stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period) compared to the previous year (typically the final year of the high-growth phase). Working capital generally refers to current assets minus current liabilities, and its change reflects the additional short-term funds that need to be invested or released to support sales growth or changes in the operating model.

nodes.name: Changes in Inventories at Constant Prices
Chargeable Volume
nodes.definition: Chargeable volume is the standard volume used by carriers in international sea or air freight to calculate freight charges, based on either the actual volume of the cargo or the volumetric weight (i.e., dimensional weight). It typically takes the greater value between the actual volume of the goods and the volume converted from the volumetric weight, ensuring that carriers can reasonably cover their transportation costs.

nodes.name: Chargeable Weight
nodes.definition: Chargeable weight is the base weight unit used for calculating freight charges in the transportation industry. It is typically not the actual weight of the goods, but rather the greater of either the actual gross weight or the volumetric weight (the weight converted from the volume calculated using length, width, and height), which serves as the basis for the final freight calculation.

nodes.name: Charitable Contribution Deductible Amount
nodes.definition: The charitable contribution deductible amount is the portion of a taxpayer's donation to qualified organizations that can be claimed as an itemized deduction, subject to statutory limits expressed as a percentage of Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).

nodes.name: Chart of Accounts
nodes.definition: The Chart of Accounts refers to the classification items for the specific content of accounting elements, serving as the foundation for setting up accounts, processing accounting transactions, and preparing financial statements. It is categorized according to the nature of economic activities and management requirements, providing a standardized classification basis for recording and reflecting an enterprise's financial position, operating results, and cash flows.

nodes.name: Cheapest to Deliver
nodes.definition: Cheapest to Deliver (CTD) is the bond that minimizes the cost for the short position to fulfill delivery obligations in a Treasury futures contract, calculated as the bond’s current market price minus the futures settlement price adjusted by the conversion factor.

formulas.source_formula: CTD = Current Bond Price - (Settlement Price × Conversion Factor)

nodes.name: Chi-Square Statistic
nodes.definition: The Chi-Square statistic quantifies the aggregate squared difference between observed and expected categorical frequencies, normalized by the expected counts; it is the foundation for chi-square tests of independence and goodness-of-fit.

nodes.name: Chikou Span
nodes.definition: Chikou Span is the current closing price plotted a fixed number of periods (typically 26) into the past on the Ichimoku Kinko Hyo chart, used to visualize historical support and resistance levels relative to current price action.

nodes.name: Churn Rate
nodes.definition: Churn rate is the percentage of customers or subscribers who discontinue using a service within a specific time period, serving as a key indicator of customer retention and business sustainability.

formulas.source_formula: Churn Rate = (Subscribers Lost ÷ Total Subscribers) × 100
supporting_source_formulas: Churn Rate = (Subscribers Lost ÷ Total Subscribers) × 100

nodes.name: Circular Flow Balance
nodes.definition: Circular flow balance indicates that total injections into the economy equal total leakages from the economy, signifying a stable circular flow of income without net expansion or contraction.

nodes.name: Class Interval
nodes.definition: Class interval refers to the range of values within each data group when grouping data in statistics, specifically the difference between the upper limit and the lower limit of the group. It is a fundamental element in data grouping and frequency distribution tables.

nodes.name: Client Average Usage Limit Over Past Six Months
Closing Fee / Liquidation Fee
nodes.definition: A closing fee is a service charge paid by investors to a trading platform or broker when closing (selling or buying to offset) an existing position in a financial transaction. It is a significant component of the total transaction cost.

nodes.name: Closing Price
nodes.definition: The closing price is the final transaction price of a security at the end of a trading day. As the transaction price at a specific point in time, it is typically calculated from the closing turnover and closing volume, serving as a key reference data point for market analysis, valuation, and investment decision-making.

nodes.name: Closing Stock Price
nodes.definition: Closing stock price refers to the closing price of a stock on the last trading day of a specific reporting period (such as a fiscal year, quarter, or month) in the securities market. It is fundamental data directly obtained from market transactions, reflecting the market's valuation of the stock at that point in time.

nodes.name: Closing Turnover
nodes.definition: Closing turnover refers to the total monetary value of all shares traded at the closing time of each trading day in the stock market, calculated based on transaction prices. It reflects market capital activity and trading scale during the closing phase, serving as an important indicator of market liquidity.

nodes.name: Closing Volume
nodes.definition: Closing volume refers to the total quantity of securities or contracts traded during the closing session of a financial market (typically the final minutes of a trading day or the closing auction period), such as stocks or futures. It is fundamental raw data reflecting the trading activity level during the market close.

nodes.name: Coefficient
nodes.definition: In financial and financial analysis, a coefficient refers to a numerical value that serves as a multiplicative factor in statistical models or financial ratios, used to quantify the relationship or influence between variables, such as regression coefficients in regression analysis.

nodes.name: Coefficient of Determination
nodes.definition: The coefficient of determination, denoted R², measures the proportion of the variance in the dependent variable that is predictable from the independent variable(s). It indicates how well the regression line approximates the real data points, ranging from 0 (no explanatory power) to 1 (perfect fit).

operands.metric: Sum of All Observations in the Sample

formulas.source_formula: R² = (n × Σ(xy) − Σx × Σy)² ÷ [(n × Σx² − (Σx)²) × (n × Σy² − (Σy)²)]

nodes.name: Coefficient of Variation
nodes.definition: The coefficient of variation is the ratio of the standard deviation to the expected value (or mean), used to measure the dispersion of data relative to its average value. It is a statistical indicator for measuring relative risk.

formulas.source_formula: Coefficient of Variation = Standard Deviation ÷ Mean
supporting_source_formulas: Coefficient of Variation = Standard Deviation ÷ Mean

formulas.source_formula: Coefficient of Variation = Standard Deviation ÷ Expected Value
CV (%) = (Standard Deviation ÷ Mean) × 100
Coinsurance Cost = Pay After Deductible × Coinsurance Rate

nodes.name: Coinsurance Payment
nodes.definition: Coinsurance payment refers to the portion of medical expenses that an insured individual must pay after meeting the deductible, calculated as a percentage of the remaining costs, subject to an out-of-pocket maximum limit.

formulas.source_formula: Coinsurance Payment = Remaining Cost × Coinsurance Rate

nodes.name: Coinsurance Property Coverage
nodes.definition: Coinsurance property coverage is the minimum amount of insurance that a property owner must carry to satisfy the coinsurance clause in a property insurance policy, calculated as the property value multiplied by the coinsurance rate.

nodes.name: Collar
nodes.definition: A collar is an options strategy that combines a protective put and a covered call to limit both downside risk and upside potential, typically used to hedge long stock positions.

nodes.name: Collar Breakeven Point
nodes.definition: The collar breakeven point is the underlying stock price at which a collar options strategy results in neither profit nor loss, calculated by adjusting the stock purchase price by the net premium received or paid from the put and call options.

formulas.source_formula: Collar Breakeven = Stock Purchase Price - (Call Premium - Put Cost)
supporting_source_formulas: Collar Breakeven = Stock Purchase Price + (Put Cost - Call Premium)
Collar Breakeven = Stock Purchase Price - (Call Premium - Put Cost)

nodes.name: Collar Maximum Loss
nodes.definition: The maximum loss of a collar options strategy represents the worst-case scenario loss an investor can incur, calculated as the difference between the put strike price and the stock purchase price adjusted by the net premium received or paid.

formulas.source_formula: Collar Maximum Loss = Put Strike - Stock Purchase Price - Net Premium
Collar Maximum Loss = Put Strike - Stock Purchase Price + Net Premium

nodes.name: Collateral Coverage Ratio
nodes.definition: Collateral coverage ratio measures the current market value of collateral relative to the outstanding loan amount, indicating the extent to which the loan is secured. A higher ratio signifies stronger collateral protection and lower credit risk.

formulas.source_formula: Collateral Coverage Ratio = Current Stock Value ÷ Loan Amount

nodes.name: Collateral Value
nodes.definition: Collateral value refers to the market value or appraised value of an asset (such as real estate, securities, equipment, etc.) pledged to secure a debt or obligation in financial or guarantee business at a specific point in time. It serves as a critical basis for assessing the adequacy of collateral and calculating related risk exposures (e.g., haircut rates).

nodes.name: Collection Rate / Levy Rate
nodes.definition: The collection rate is a fixed percentage or tax rate stipulated by tax laws for calculating the tax payable of specific taxpayers (such as small-scale taxpayers). It is a fundamental policy parameter, not a composite indicator calculated from other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Collections of Prior Period Accounts Receivable in Year k
aliases: Collection of Prior Period Accounts Receivable in Year k
nodes.definition: Collections of prior period accounts receivable in year k refer to the amount of accounts receivable generated from sales made before year k (e.g., year k-1, k-2, etc.) that are actually collected by the enterprise in year k during budgeting or cash flow forecasting. It constitutes a significant component of the cash inflows in year k, reflecting the efficiency of the enterprise's credit policy implementation and the recovery of funds.

nodes.name: Combined Loan-To-Value Ratio
nodes.definition: The Combined Loan-To-Value (CLTV) ratio measures the total amount of all secured loans on a property relative to the property's appraised value, expressed as a percentage. It is used by lenders to assess the overall leverage and risk associated with a property.

formulas.source_formula: CLTV Ratio = (Total Secured Loans ÷ Property Value) × 100

nodes.name: Combined Ratio
nodes.definition: Combined ratio is a key profitability metric for insurance companies that measures underwriting performance by comparing the sum of incurred losses and expenses to earned premiums, expressed as a percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Combined Ratio = (Incurred Losses + Expenses) ÷ Earned Premium × 100
Combined Ratio = (Incurred Losses + Loss Adjustment Expenses + Other Underwriting Expenses) ÷ Earned Premiums

nodes.name: Commencement Date of the Lease
nodes.definition: The commencement date of the lease refers to the earlier of the date of the lease agreement signing and the date on which the parties to the lease commit to the principal terms of the lease. On this date, the lessee and lessor are required to classify the lease as either a finance lease or an operating lease based on the agreement terms and commence the relevant accounting recognition and measurement.

nodes.name: Commercial Paper
nodes.definition: Commercial paper is an unsecured promissory note with a fixed maturity (typically less than 270 days), issued by large corporations to meet short-term debt obligations. It is issued at a discount to its face value and is backed solely by the issuer's promise to pay. Due to its short maturity and the high credit quality of issuers, its interest rate is generally lower than that of bonds.

formulas.source_formula: Commercial Paper = Face Value × (1 - Discount Yield × Days to Maturity / 360)

nodes.name: Commission
nodes.definition: Commission refers to the compensation received by intermediaries such as agents, brokers, or distributors from principals for facilitating transactions or providing services, typically calculated as a percentage of the transaction value or a fixed amount.

formulas.source_formula: Commission = Point Value × Points × (Transaction Size ÷ 10000)

nodes.name: Commission Expense
nodes.definition: Commission expense refers to the compensation received by intermediaries (such as agents, brokers, distributors) for services provided in commercial activities, including facilitating transactions, buying and selling on behalf of others. In accounting treatment, it is an original expense directly incurred according to contracts or agreements and serves as the fundamental data for bookkeeping.

nodes.name: Commodity Futures Contract Profit
nodes.definition: Commodity futures contract profit refers to the gain or loss realized from a futures position at contract expiry, calculated as the price difference multiplied by the contract multiplier, reflecting the financial outcome of the futures trading activity.

nodes.name: Commodity Price
nodes.definition: Commodity price is the monetary expression of a commodity's value. In trade practice, it specifically refers to the final quotation calculated based on specific trade terms (such as FOB, CFR), which includes cost, expenses, and profit. It is a core accounting indicator in marketing and international trade.

formulas.source_formula: Commodity Price = Unit Variable Cost + Unit Contribution Margin
Commodity Price = Unit Cost × (1 + Cost-plus Rate)
Common Equity = Total Shareholders' Equity - Preferred Equity
Common Equity = Total Equity - Preferred Equity

nodes.name: Common Equity Tier 1 Ratio
nodes.definition: The Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) ratio is a key regulatory capital ratio under Basel III that measures a bank’s core equity capital relative to its risk-weighted assets, indicating the bank’s financial strength and capacity to absorb losses.

formulas.source_formula: CET1 Ratio = CET1 Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets

nodes.name: Common Factor
nodes.definition: Common factor refers to the underlying, unobservable but objectively existing influencing factors shared among a set of observed variables in statistical models such as factor analysis. These factors can explain the correlations among multiple variables and are used to simplify data structures by distilling multiple related variables into a few core factors.

nodes.name: Common Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Common Shareholders' Equity refers to the portion of owners' equity attributable to the company's common shareholders. It is the residual net asset value belonging to common shareholders after deducting total liabilities and preferred shareholders' equity from total assets. It represents the economic interest of common shareholders in the company and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as book value per share.

formulas.source_formula: Common Shareholders' Equity = Total Assets - Total Liabilities
Common Shareholders' Equity = Share Capital + Capital Surplus + Revenue Reserves + Retained Earnings + Other Comprehensive Income - Treasury Stock

nodes.name: Common Size Financial Statement
nodes.definition: A common size financial statement expresses each line item as a percentage of a selected base figure (e.g., total assets or net sales), enabling standardized comparison across periods or companies regardless of absolute size.

nodes.name: Common Size Income Statement
nodes.definition: A common size income statement expresses each line item as a percentage of total revenue, enabling vertical analysis and comparison of financial performance across periods or companies regardless of size.

formulas.source_formula: Common Size Percentage = (Individual Item Value ÷ Base Value) × 100
Common Size Percentage = (Income Statement Item ÷ Total Revenue) × 100

nodes.name: Common Stock Annual Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The Common Stock Annual Growth Rate is a compound metric measuring the annual growth rate of common stock dividends or value, typically calculated based on historical dividend data, stock price data, or forecast models. It is used to assess a company's growth potential and serves as a key input parameter in capital cost calculations, such as for determining the cost of retained earnings and the cost of common equity.

operands.metric: Current Year Stock Price Per Share
Prior Year Stock Price per Share

formulas.source_formula: Common Stock Annual Growth Rate = (Current Year Stock Price Per Share - Prior Year Stock Price Per Share) ÷ Prior Year Stock Price Per Share × 100%
Common Stock Annual Growth Rate = (Current Year Dividend Per Share - Prior Year Dividend Per Share) ÷ Prior Year Dividend Per Share × 100%

nodes.name: Common Stock Dividend
nodes.definition: Common stock dividend refers to the cash return distributed by a listed company to its common shareholders from its after-tax profits, after deducting preferred stock dividends. It is a primary form of return that shareholders receive from the company's earnings.

nodes.name: Common Stock Equity
nodes.definition: Common stock equity represents the amount invested by all common shareholders in the company, primarily comprising the value of common stock, retained earnings, and additional paid-in capital.

formulas.source_formula: Common Stock Equity = Common Stock + Retained Earnings + Additional Paid-in Capital

nodes.name: Common Stock Flotation Cost Rate
aliases: Flotation Cost Ratio for Common Stock
nodes.definition: The Common Stock Flotation Cost Rate refers to the percentage of the total amount raised (gross proceeds from issuance) accounted for by the total of various related expenses (such as underwriting fees, legal fees, audit fees, promotional expenses, etc.) incurred by a company during the process of raising capital through issuing common stock. It is a fundamental ratio calculated based on actual contracts and expenses, used to measure the direct cost efficiency of issuing common stock.

nodes.name: Common Stock Market Price
nodes.definition: Common stock market price refers to the real-time trading price of a company's common shares formed by buyers and sellers based on supply and demand relationships in secondary markets such as stock exchanges. It directly reflects the market's valuation of the company and fluctuates with various factors including company performance, industry conditions, macroeconomic environment, and market sentiment.

nodes.name: Common Stock Price Per Share
nodes.definition: Common stock price per share refers to the immediate price paid or received for one share of a company's common stock at a specific point in time, as agreed upon by buyers and sellers in the securities trading market. It reflects the market's collective expectations regarding the company's future profitability and risk, and serves as the basis for calculating key financial metrics such as total market capitalization and price-to-earnings ratio.

nodes.name: Company Market Value Added
nodes.definition: Company Market Value Added is a financial metric that measures the difference between a company's market value and its total invested capital, reflecting the total wealth created or destroyed for shareholders since the company's inception.

nodes.name: Company Valuation
nodes.definition: Company valuation refers to the process of assessing the overall economic value of a company at a specific point in time through a series of methods and models. It comprehensively considers various factors such as the company's financial condition, future profitability, market position, assets and liabilities, and industry prospects, providing a value reference for investment, mergers and acquisitions, financing, or internal management.

formulas.source_formula: Valuation = Revenue × Industry Multiplier
Company Valuation = Adjusted Profits × P/E Ratio

nodes.name: Comparable Companies
nodes.definition: Comparable companies are reference entities used in relative valuation methods (such as the Price-to-Earnings ratio method and the Price-to-Book ratio method). Their selection criteria are based on a series of financial drivers similar to those of the target company, such as growth rate, risk, profitability, and capital structure, rather than single data items directly obtained from financial statements.

nodes.name: Comparable Companies Average Expected Growth Rate
aliases: Average Expected Growth Rate of Comparable Firms
nodes.definition: The Comparable Companies Average Expected Growth Rate is a composite indicator obtained by calculating the expected growth rates of multiple comparable companies and taking their arithmetic mean. It is commonly used in analyses such as the Adjusted Average Revenue Multiple in business valuation, reflecting the overall growth expectations of comparable companies.

nodes.name: Comparable Companies Average Market Multiple
aliases: 可比企业平均市价比率
nodes.definition: The Comparable Companies Average Market Multiple is a commonly used relative valuation method in business valuation. It involves selecting a group of publicly traded companies in the same industry that are similar to the target company in terms of key drivers (such as growth, risk, and profitability), calculating the arithmetic average of specific market multiples (such as P/E ratio, P/B ratio, P/S ratio) for these comparable companies, and then using this average as a multiplier to estimate the market value of the target company.

nodes.name: Comparable Companies Average P/E Ratio
nodes.definition: The Comparable Companies Average P/E Ratio is a composite metric used in relative company valuation, obtained by calculating and averaging the P/E ratios of a group of comparable companies with similar business nature, size, growth stage, and risk profile. It serves as a core input parameter for estimating the value of a target company using the P/E ratio model. Calculation methods primarily include the arithmetic average method (reflecting central tendency) and the weighted average method (reflecting overall scale influence). In application, adjustments are often required to eliminate differences in key drivers (such as growth rates).

nodes.name: Comparable Company Analysis
nodes.definition: Comparable Company Analysis is a relative valuation method that compares a company's valuation multiples to those of similar peer companies to determine if the company is overvalued, undervalued, or fairly valued.

nodes.name: Comparable Company EV/EBITDA Multiple
nodes.definition: The Comparable Company EV/EBITDA Multiple is a commonly used relative valuation metric that assesses a company's market value relative to its core operating profitability (Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation, and Amortization, or EBITDA). It estimates the fair value of a target company by comparing this multiple with that of comparable companies with similar business operations, scale, and risk profiles.

nodes.name: Comparable Company Underlying Asset Price Volatility
aliases: 可比公司资产价格波动率
nodes.definition: Comparable company underlying asset price volatility is a parameter used for risk adjustment when evaluating financial instruments such as expansion options. It measures the uncertainty of future price movements by selecting comparable companies similar to the target company or underlying asset in terms of business, scale, and growth, and analyzing the volatility of historical price data of their related assets (e.g., stocks). This volatility is typically expressed as a percentage and is one of the key input variables for calculating option value or performing risk adjustments.

nodes.name: Comparable Store Sales Growth
nodes.definition: Comparable store sales growth measures the percentage change in sales revenue from retail locations that have been operating for more than one year, excluding the impact of newly opened or closed stores. This metric provides insight into the organic growth performance of existing retail locations.

formulas.source_formula: Comparable Store Sales Growth = (Current Period Existing Store Sales - Previous Period Existing Store Sales) ÷ Previous Period Existing Store Sales

nodes.name: Comparable Transaction Price
nodes.definition: Comparable transaction price refers to the actual transaction price of an asset, selected for its similarity or comparability to the subject asset in terms of function, purpose, and transaction conditions, in the recent market during asset valuation or market analysis. It serves as a crucial foundational data point for calculating the value of the subject asset when applying the market approach.

nodes.name: Comparative Annual Sales Revenue
aliases: 上年度与本年度销售收入
nodes.definition: Comparative annual sales revenue refers to the side-by-side presentation of a company's sales revenue data for two consecutive fiscal years (typically the previous year and the current year), providing a clear visual representation of the year-on-year changes in sales revenue. It serves as fundamental raw data in financial statements, used for subsequent calculations of absolute changes and percentage changes.

nodes.name: Compensating Balance
nodes.definition: A compensating balance refers to the minimum deposit balance that a bank requires a borrowing enterprise to maintain in its bank account when granting a loan, either as a fixed percentage or a fixed amount. This portion of the balance cannot be used for daily payments, thereby reducing the actual usable loan funds for the enterprise and effectively increasing the effective interest rate of the loan.

nodes.name: Compensation and Benefits
nodes.definition: Compensation and benefits refer to the total remuneration provided by an employer to employees in return for their work, including direct monetary payments (compensation) and non-monetary rewards (benefits), aimed at supporting employee well-being and satisfaction.

formulas.source_formula: Compensation and Benefits = Guaranteed Compensation + Variable Compensation + Benefits + Equity-based Compensation

nodes.name: Compensation for Construction-in-Progress Personnel
nodes.definition: Compensation for construction-in-progress personnel refers to the labor remuneration paid by an enterprise to employees directly involved in construction-in-progress projects (such as the construction, renovation, expansion, or technical transformation of fixed assets), including wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies. In accounting treatment, this portion of compensation is not recognized as a current period expense but is capitalized as part of the construction-in-progress cost.

nodes.name: Compensation of Employees
nodes.definition: Compensation of employees refers to the total remuneration that employees should receive for their participation in production activities. This includes wages, bonuses, allowances, and subsidies paid in monetary form, as well as benefits provided in kind, and social insurance contributions and housing provident fund contributions paid by the employer on their behalf.

nodes.name: Compensation of Employees in the Secondary Industry
aliases: Remuneration of Employees in Secondary Industry
工业及建筑业劳动者报酬
nodes.definition: Compensation of employees in the secondary industry refers to the total sum of monetary and in-kind remuneration received by all workers engaged in production activities within the secondary industry (primarily comprising industry and construction) during a given period, in return for their labor. It typically includes wages, salaries, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, as well as welfare expenses such as social insurance and housing provident fund contributions paid by employers on behalf of employees. It constitutes a major component of the value added of the secondary industry.

nodes.name: Compensation of Employees in the Tertiary Industry
aliases: Compensation of Employees in Tertiary Industry
nodes.definition: Compensation of employees in the tertiary industry refers to the total monetary and in-kind remuneration received by all workers engaged in production activities within the tertiary industry (service sector) during a given period for the labor they provide. It is a core component when calculating the value added of the tertiary industry using the income approach, typically sourced directly from statistical surveys or enterprise accounting data.

nodes.name: Competitive Advantage
nodes.definition: Competitive advantage refers to a company's ability to achieve sustained market leadership by possessing business systems, resources, or capabilities that are difficult for competitors to replicate or imitate, enabling it to realize lower costs or higher revenues than rivals in a specific market.

nodes.name: Completed Contract Work Volume
nodes.definition: Completed contract work volume refers to the cumulative total of the actual completed engineering quantity or output value by an enterprise at a specific point in time, based on construction contracts or similar business contracts. It is fundamental operational data obtained through on-site direct measurement, statistics, or engineering progress reports, used to measure the progress of contract execution.

formulas.source_formula: Compliance Margin = Account Equity - Minimum Equity Requirement

nodes.name: Component Company Adjusted Stock Price
nodes.definition: Component Company Adjusted Stock Price is a composite metric involving adjustments to the original stock price (such as accounting for corporate actions like stock splits and dividends), typically calculated via formulas to ensure comparability of price time series, commonly used in index construction like the Dow Jones Transportation Average and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Composite Rate (Series I Bond)
aliases: I系列储蓄债券综合利率
nodes.definition: The composite rate for a U.S. Series I Savings Bond is the bond’s effective interest rate that combines a fixed rate set at issuance with an inflation component that adjusts semiannually. The calculated rate is floored at 0% and cannot be negative.

nodes.name: Composite Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The composite tax rate refers to a total tax rate derived by consolidating multiple taxes and fees, commonly used to measure the overall tax burden level of a specific economic activity (such as rental income).

nodes.name: Compound Annual Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Compound Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) is the mean annual growth rate of an investment over a specified period longer than one year, assuming the value compounds at a constant rate each year.

formulas.source_formula: CAGR = (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1 ÷ Number of Years) - 1
CAGR = (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1 ÷ Years) - 1
Compound Annual Growth Rate = (End Value ÷ Start Value)^(1 ÷ Periods) - 1
CAGR = (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1 ÷ Number of Periods) - 1

nodes.name: Compound Interest
nodes.definition: Compound interest is the difference between the compound future value and the initial principal, representing the total interest income generated under the compound interest calculation method.

formulas.source_formula: Compound Interest Rate = Annual Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Frequency
Compounded Interest (Semiannual) = Principal × ( (1 + Annual Interest Rate ÷ 2)^(2 × Years) - 1 )

nodes.name: Compounding Frequency
aliases: Number of Compounding Periods per Year
nodes.definition: Compounding frequency refers to the number of times within a year that interest is calculated and added to the principal for subsequent interest accrual. It determines the frequency of compound growth and is a key parameter in compound interest calculations.

nodes.name: Compounding Frequency per Year
nodes.definition: Compounding frequency per year refers to the number of times within a year that the interest on an investment or loan is added to the principal, and subsequent interest is calculated on this new base. It determines the frequency of interest calculation and directly affects the final value of the investment.

nodes.name: Comprehensive Freight and Miscellaneous Charges Rate
nodes.definition: The Comprehensive Freight and Miscellaneous Charges Rate is a composite rate indicator used to calculate the total cost of goods transportation and related miscellaneous expenses. It is typically not a single freight rate, but rather a combined calculation derived from multiple components including the basic freight and miscellaneous charges rate, procurement and storage fees, transportation insurance premiums, and additional rates for special goods (such as oversized or overweight items). It is designed to more comprehensively reflect all related cost expenses incurred during the process from procurement to delivery of goods.

nodes.name: Comprehensive Income
nodes.definition: Comprehensive income is a composite financial metric, typically defined as the sum of net profit and other comprehensive income. It is used to reflect an enterprise's total earnings during a specific period, including both realized and unrealized gains, and serves as a core indicator for measuring the total change in equity.

nodes.name: Comprehensive Management Expense Ratio
nodes.definition: The Comprehensive Management Expense Ratio refers to the ratio of all management expenses incurred by an enterprise within a certain period to maintain overall operations and management activities, relative to a relevant base such as revenue or assets. It comprehensively reflects the efficiency of an enterprise's cost control in areas such as administration, human resources, and office operations.

nodes.name: Conditional Probability
nodes.definition: Conditional probability refers to the probability of event A occurring given that event B has already occurred. It is a core concept in probability theory and mathematical statistics, widely applied in financial risk assessment, Bayesian inference, and other fields.

nodes.name: Conditional Value at Risk
nodes.definition: Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), also known as Expected Shortfall, measures the expected value of portfolio losses that exceed the Value at Risk (VaR) threshold at a given confidence level, providing insight into tail risk beyond the VaR cutoff point.

nodes.name: Confidence Interval
nodes.definition: In statistics, a confidence interval (CI) is a range of values used to estimate an unknown statistical parameter (such as a population mean). It provides an estimated interval along with a corresponding confidence level (e.g., 95%), reflecting the long-term reliability of the method: if the same sampling process is repeated, approximately the corresponding percentage of the resulting intervals will contain the true parameter.

nodes.name: Confidence Interval for Mean (t-Distribution)
nodes.definition: A confidence interval for the population mean when the population standard deviation is unknown, estimated using the Student's t-distribution. Commonly applied in financial analytics and audit sampling for small samples, it quantifies the range within which the true mean is expected to fall at a specified confidence level.

nodes.name: Confidence Level
nodes.definition: Confidence level is a predetermined parameter in statistics used to measure the probability or reliability that an estimate (such as a sample statistic) falls within a certain interval of the true value of a population parameter. It is a subjectively set standard, not a calculated result, commonly used in constructing confidence intervals and assessing risk.

nodes.name: Confidence Level Coefficient
nodes.definition: The confidence level coefficient is a statistical term used to indicate the degree of certainty we have in the reliability of estimation results in sampling surveys or statistical inference. It is typically associated with a specific probability value (e.g., 90%, 95%, or 99%), which represents the likelihood that the population parameter falls within the calculated confidence interval. A higher coefficient value indicates greater confidence in the estimation results, but it may also require a larger sample size or result in a wider confidence interval.

nodes.name: Consensus Expected Net Profit
aliases: Consensus EPS (Earnings Per Share) 的底层利润指标
分析师一致预期净利润
nodes.definition: Consensus expected net profit refers to a consensus forecast figure derived from the aggregation and averaging of net profit predictions made by multiple securities analysts or research institutions for a specific future period (such as the next fiscal year or quarter) of a listed company. It reflects the market's prevailing view on the company's future profitability.

nodes.name: Consequential Loss
nodes.definition: Consequential loss refers to subsequent economic losses arising from a risk event or breach of contract that are not directly inflicted on the property itself or personal injury. It typically denotes consequential financial impacts such as reduced revenue, loss of profits, increased additional expenses, or loss of opportunities resulting from direct loss.

nodes.name: Consigned Goods for Sale
nodes.definition: Consigned goods for sale refer to goods that an enterprise receives from another entity (the consignor) to sell on their behalf. When the consignee receives the goods, ownership remains with the consignor. Therefore, the consignee accounts for them as a special type of asset (inventory), reflecting their custodial and pending-sale physical value.

nodes.name: Consigned Processing Materials
nodes.definition: Consigned processing materials refer to raw materials, semi-finished goods, or other materials owned by an enterprise that are entrusted to an external party for processing to produce inventory with new characteristics or uses. Their recorded cost primarily includes the actual cost of the materials issued, processing fees paid to the processor, round-trip transportation and miscellaneous expenses, and related taxes.

nodes.name: Consignment Goods
nodes.definition: Consignment goods refer to merchandise delivered by an enterprise (the consignor) to another entity or individual (the consignee) for sale, while ownership of the goods remains with the consignor and constitutes part of the consignor's inventory.

nodes.name: Consignment-in Payable
nodes.definition: Consignment-in payable is a liability recognized by an enterprise (the consignee) upon receiving goods for consignment sales from another entity (the consignor). It represents the future payment obligation for the goods or sales proceeds to be remitted to the consignor, and is presented as a liability on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Consolidated Financial Statements
nodes.definition: Consolidated financial statements refer to financial statements prepared by a parent company that treat the parent and all its subsidiaries as a single economic entity, comprehensively reflecting the overall financial position, operating results, and cash flows of the group.

nodes.name: Consolidated Net Profit
nodes.definition: Consolidated net profit refers to the net profit attributable to the owners of the entire group, calculated after eliminating internal transactions and unrealized profits and losses, when a parent company and all its subsidiaries are treated as a single economic entity in the preparation of consolidated financial statements.

nodes.name: Constant Dividend Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The constant dividend growth rate is a financial concept referring to the assumption, in dividend growth models (such as the Gordon Growth Model), that a company's dividends will grow at a constant rate (g) indefinitely into the future. It is a key parameter for calculating a stock's intrinsic value or the cost of equity capital.

nodes.name: Constant Price Household Consumption
nodes.definition: Constant price household consumption refers to the total value of goods and services used for final consumption by households, measured at the price level of a specific base period after eliminating the effects of price changes. It is a composite indicator obtained by adjusting current price household consumption through the price index deflation method, used to analyze changes in the actual consumption level of households.

nodes.name: Constant e
nodes.definition: Constant e is an important mathematical constant, approximately equal to 2.71828, and is an infinite non-repeating decimal (transcendental number). It serves as the base of the natural logarithm function and is widely applied in various fields including mathematics, physics, engineering, and economics.

nodes.name: Constituent Index Weight (Market-Cap-Weighted)
nodes.definition: The constituent index weight is the proportion of a company's market capitalization relative to the total market capitalization of a market-capitalization-weighted index, expressed as a percentage. It indicates the influence of a constituent on the index level and is used in indices such as the S&P 500.

formulas.source_formula: Index Weight (%) = (Company Market Capitalization ÷ Total Index Market Capitalization) × 100

nodes.name: Constituent Shares Outstanding
aliases: Number of Shares Outstanding for Free Float
nodes.definition: Constituent shares outstanding refers to the number of shares of the companies included in a stock index (such as the CSI 300 or S&P 500) that are freely tradable on the public market. It excludes shares that are long-term locked up and not freely tradable, such as those held by company insiders, governments, or strategic investors (e.g., restricted shares). This figure is fundamental for calculating index weights and reflecting the true trading scale of the market.

nodes.name: Constituent Stock Market Capitalization
nodes.definition: Constituent stock market capitalization refers to the total market value of all individual stocks that constitute a specific stock index (such as the CSI 300 or S&P 500). It is typically calculated by summing the product of each constituent stock's share price and its total shares outstanding (or free-float shares). It reflects the overall size of the market segment represented by the index.

nodes.name: Constituent Stock Price
nodes.definition: Constituent stock price refers to the real-time trading price of individual stocks selected for inclusion in a specific stock index (such as the CSI 300 Index or S&P 500 Index) in the securities market. It serves as the raw underlying data for calculating the stock index and reflects the value of each stock that constitutes the index.

nodes.name: Constituent Stock Prices
nodes.definition: Constituent stock prices refer to the real-time trading prices of each individual stock that constitutes a stock index (such as the SSE 50, CSI 300, etc.) in the secondary market. These prices are formed directly through market transactions between buyers and sellers, representing the most fundamental market trading data and serving as the basic raw data for calculating composite indicators such as stock indices and total company market capitalization.

nodes.name: Constituent Stock Prices in the Reporting Period
nodes.definition: Constituent stock prices in the reporting period refer to the actual trading prices of each individual stock that constitutes a specific stock index in the securities market during a designated reporting period (such as a trading day, a week, or a month). These prices are raw data directly generated by market transactions and serve as fundamental inputs for calculating index values, analyzing index performance, and constructing other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Construction Engineering Cost
nodes.definition: Construction engineering cost refers to all expenses incurred during the project construction process for completing the building of structures, constructions, and related works such as equipment foundations, pillars, and work platforms. It primarily includes direct costs for labor, materials, machinery usage, as well as related measure costs and indirect expenses.

nodes.name: Construction Investment
aliases: 固定资产投资总额（广义）
项目总投资（不含铺底流动资金）
nodes.definition: Construction investment refers to the total construction funds invested to form the project's fixed assets, intangible assets, and other assets. It is the main component of the total project investment and serves as the basis for calculating project cash outflows.

formulas.source_formula: Construction Investment = Construction and Installation Cost + Equipment and Tool Cost + Other Project Construction Costs + Basic Contingency Reserve + Price Contingency Reserve + Construction Period Interest

Construction Investment = Construction Engineering Cost + Installation Engineering Cost + Equipment Purchase Cost + Other Project Construction Costs + Basic Contingency Reserve + Price Contingency Reserve + Construction Period Interest

nodes.name: Construction Land Cost
nodes.definition: Construction land cost refers to all expenses incurred in a project for acquiring land use rights, land expropriation, demolition compensation, and handling related procedures. It is an important component of other construction costs.

nodes.name: Construction Loan Interest
nodes.definition: Construction loan interest is the total interest expense incurred during the construction period, calculated only on the amounts actually drawn down by the borrower, typically under an interest-only payment structure.

nodes.name: Construction Materials
nodes.definition: Construction materials refer to the value of various materials specifically reserved by an enterprise for fixed asset construction, installation, and other projects in progress, including materials for engineering, equipment not yet installed, and tools and instruments prepared for production.

nodes.name: Construction Period
nodes.definition: The construction period is a fundamental phase in the project calculation period, referring to the entire time span from the initial capital investment for construction (such as construction work, equipment procurement and installation) until the project is completed and ready for operation or commissioning. It is typically determined directly based on project planning or contracts and serves as a critical time parameter for project financial evaluation and loan term calculation.

nodes.name: Construction Period Interest
nodes.definition: Construction period interest refers to the interest expense incurred during the project construction period due to raising and utilizing debt capital, which is permitted to be capitalized and included in the original value of fixed assets according to the 'Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises'. For simplified calculation, it is typically assumed that borrowings are drawn in the middle of the year, with current-year borrowings calculated for half a year's interest, and cumulative borrowings at the beginning of the year calculated for a full year's interest.

nodes.name: Construction Project Investment Amount
nodes.definition: Construction project investment amount refers to the total actual funds invested within a specific period for completing building construction, structural engineering, and equipment installation projects, constituting a significant component of fixed asset investment.

nodes.name: Construction Settlement Profit
nodes.definition: Construction settlement profit refers to the profit realized by a construction enterprise within a certain period through the settlement of completed or finished projects with the contracting entity. It is a key indicator for measuring the profitability of the construction enterprise's main business, and its calculation is based on construction settlement revenue, costs, and related taxes.

formulas.source_formula: Construction Settlement Profit = Construction Settlement Revenue - Construction Settlement Cost - Construction Settlement Taxes and Surcharges

nodes.name: Construction Settlement Taxes and Surcharges
aliases: Tax and Surcharges on Project Settlement
nodes.definition: Construction Settlement Taxes and Surcharges refer to the collective term for various taxes and fees that construction industry enterprises are required to pay and record in the current period's profit or loss according to relevant tax regulations when settling construction projects. These mainly include Business Tax, Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, and Education Surcharge, but exclude Value-Added Tax.

nodes.name: Construction Unit Management Fee
nodes.definition: Construction Unit Management Fee refers to various administrative expenses incurred by the construction unit (i.e., the investor or owner) for organizing and managing the entire construction project, from project preparation through to the completion of final accounts.

nodes.name: Construction and Installation Costs
nodes.definition: Construction and installation costs refer to all expenses incurred during the engineering construction process for completing physical works such as building main structures, equipment installation, and pipeline laying. They mainly consist of construction engineering costs and installation engineering costs, forming a significant component of the total investment (construction investment) in a construction project.

nodes.name: Construction in Progress
nodes.definition: Construction in Progress refers to fixed asset projects that are under construction, installation, or technical renovation and have not yet reached their intended usable state. On the balance sheet, it is measured at the actual costs incurred (such as land, materials, labor, etc.) and is classified as part of non-current assets.

nodes.name: Construction in Progress Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Construction in Progress Ending Balance refers to the carrying value of actual expenditures on projects that are not yet completed or, although completed, have not undergone final completion settlement as of the balance sheet date (typically year-end or quarter-end). It reflects the actual invested cost of unfinished projects at period-end and is generally reported as the net amount of the ending debit balance in the 'Construction in Progress' account minus the ending credit balance in the 'Provision for Impairment of Construction in Progress' account.

nodes.name: Consumer Income
nodes.definition: Consumer income refers to the total monetary income received by individuals or households from various sources, forming the basis of consumer purchasing power.

nodes.name: Consumer Leverage Ratio
nodes.definition: The consumer leverage ratio measures the degree of household indebtedness by dividing total household debt by disposable income. It indicates the extent to which a household's income is leveraged by debt and is used to assess personal financial risk and short-term solvency.

formulas.source_formula: Consumer Leverage Ratio = Total Household Debt ÷ Disposable Income

nodes.name: Consumer Preference
nodes.definition: Consumer preference refers to the degree of liking consumers have for different goods or combinations of goods, which determines their ranking and selection tendencies toward these product combinations.

nodes.name: Consumer Price Index
nodes.definition: The Consumer Price Index (CPI) is a statistical estimate that measures the price level of goods and services purchased by households for consumption purposes, calculated as the weighted average price of a basket of consumer goods and services. Changes in the CPI are used to track price movements over time and serve as an indicator for measuring inflation.

operands.metric: Weighted Average Price of Market Basket in Current Period
Weighted Average Price of Market Basket in Base Period

formulas.source_formula: Consumer Price Index = (Weighted Average Price of Market Basket in Current Period) ÷ (Weighted Average Price of Market Basket in Base Period) × 100

nodes.name: Consumer Surplus
