nodes.definition: Economic Value of Equity (EVE) is the difference between the present value of expected asset cash flows and the present value of expected liability cash flows. It is a core Asset-Liability Management metric used by banks to assess structural interest rate risk and the long-term economic value impact of rate shifts on equity.

operands.metric: Present Value of Asset Cash Flows
Present Value of Liability Cash Flows

formulas.source_formula: Economic Value of Equity = Present Value of Asset Cash Flows - Present Value of Liability Cash Flows

nodes.name: Education Surcharge
nodes.definition: Education Surcharge is an additional tax levied by the state to fund local education development. It is calculated based on the actual amount of turnover taxes such as Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by taxpayers, collected by tax authorities, and its revenue is specifically allocated for educational expenditures.

nodes.name: Education Surcharge Payable
nodes.definition: Education Surcharge Payable is an additional fee that enterprises must calculate based on the actual amount of turnover taxes paid, such as Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax, according to the prescribed levy rate, and remit to the tax authorities, specifically earmarked for the development of local education.

nodes.name: Education Surcharge Rate
nodes.definition: The Education Surcharge Rate refers to the statutory percentage applied when calculating the education surcharge. It is typically calculated based on the actual amount of turnover taxes such as Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by the taxpayer, with the surcharge amount determined by applying this rate.

nodes.name: Effect of Exchange Rate Changes on Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: 汇率变动对现金的影响
汇率对现金等价物的影响
nodes.definition: The effect of exchange rate changes on cash and cash equivalents refers to the difference arising from the translation of foreign currency cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise into the reporting currency due to exchange rate fluctuations when preparing the cash flow statement. It reflects the impact of exchange rate changes on the book value of cash and cash equivalents at the end of the period and serves as a crucial reconciling item linking the cash flow statement to the monetary funds item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Effective Annual Interest Rate
nodes.definition: The Effective Annual Interest Rate (EAR) expresses the equivalent annual rate that accounts for the effects of intra-year compounding on a nominal interest rate. It represents the actual annual return or cost of borrowing when interest is compounded multiple times per year.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Annual Interest Rate = (1 + Nominal Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Periods per Year) ^ Compounding Periods per Year - 1

nodes.name: Effective Annual Rate
nodes.definition: The Effective Annual Rate is the actual annual interest rate after accounting for the compounding effect, used to accurately measure the true cost of financial products or loans. It is typically calculated from the nominal interest rate and the number of compounding periods per year, or from the actual annual financing cost paid and the actual available loan amount.

formulas.source_formula: EAR = (1 + Nominal Rate ÷ Compounding Periods) ^ Compounding Periods - 1
Effective Annual Rate = Actual Annual Financing Cost Paid ÷ Actual Available Loan Amount
Effective Annual Rate = (1 + Nominal Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Periods per Year) ^ Compounding Periods per Year - 1

nodes.name: Effective Corporate Income Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The effective corporate income tax rate refers to the ratio of the actual income tax paid by a company during a specific period to its pre-tax profit (or taxable income). It reflects the company's actual income tax burden level, which may differ from the statutory nominal tax rate due to factors such as tax incentives and tax adjustments.

nodes.name: Effective Corporate Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The effective corporate tax rate measures the actual percentage of taxable income that a corporation pays in taxes, reflecting the impact of deductions, subsidies, and tax planning strategies, and typically differs from the statutory corporate tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Tax Rate = (Total Taxes Paid ÷ Taxable Income) × 100

nodes.name: Effective Duration
nodes.definition: Effective duration measures the sensitivity of a bond's price to changes in interest rates, accounting for bonds with embedded options by comparing price changes under rising and falling yield scenarios.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Duration = (Price when Yield Decreases - Price when Yield Increases) ÷ (2 × Original Price × Change in Yield)
Effective Duration = (Bond Price Down - Bond Price Up) ÷ (2 × Bond Price × Change in Yield)

nodes.name: Effective Exchange Rate (After Service Fee)
nodes.definition: The effective exchange rate (after service fee) is the actual exchange rate a customer receives in a currency conversion after a percentage service fee is applied to the nominal (posted) exchange rate.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Exchange Rate = Base Exchange Rate × (1 - Service Fee Percentage ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Effective Expense Ratio (Leveraged ETF)
nodes.definition: Effective expense ratio (leveraged ETF) is the combined annualized cost of holding a leveraged exchange-traded fund, calculated as the sum of the fund’s stated expense ratio and any additional recurring expenses. It represents the total ongoing cost burden that reduces net returns to investors.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Expense Ratio = Leveraged ETF Expense Ratio + Additional Expenses

nodes.name: Effective Gross Income
nodes.definition: Effective Gross Income (EGI) is the total income a property is expected to generate from all sources under normal operations, calculated by adding other income to potential gross income and subtracting vacancy and credit losses. It reflects the revenue available before operating expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Gross Income = Potential Gross Income + Other Income - Vacancy Costs - Credit Costs

nodes.name: Effective Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Effective interest rate refers to the annual rate of return on a bond based on its purchase price and annual interest payments, expressing interest income as a percentage of the investment's carrying amount (purchase price).

formulas.source_formula: Effective Interest Rate = (Repurchase Price - Initial Sale Price) / Initial Sale Price × (360 / Days to Maturity)
Effective Interest Rate (%) = (Annual Interest ÷ Purchase Price) × 100

nodes.name: Effective Interest Rate (Callable Bond)
nodes.definition: The effective interest rate for a callable bond (price-based approximation) measures the annualized rate of return from face value to the call price over the years to call, assuming the bond is called at the end of the specified period and ignoring coupon payments. It provides a simplified assessment of call-driven yield for fixed-income analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Interest Rate = (Call Price - Face Value) ÷ (Face Value × Years to Call)

nodes.name: Effective Interest Rate (U.S. Savings Bonds)
nodes.definition: The effective interest rate for U.S. inflation-linked savings bonds (e.g., Series I) represents the nominal rate of return that combines a fixed interest component with an inflation adjustment. It reflects the total annualized return considering both the fixed rate and prevailing inflation, typically expressed in decimal form.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Interest Rate = Fixed Rate + Inflation Rate

nodes.name: Effective Interest Rate Method (Bond Discount Amortization)
aliases: 债券折价摊销（有效利率法）
nodes.definition: The effective interest rate method amortizes a bond discount by recognizing interest expense based on the bond’s beginning carrying amount multiplied by the market (effective) interest rate, with the amortization each period equal to the difference between interest expense and the cash coupon payment. This method ensures a constant rate of interest on the carrying amount over the bond’s life, aligning expense recognition with economic yield under IFRS and U.S. GAAP.

nodes.name: Effective Mortgage Balance (Offset Mortgage)
nodes.definition: In an offset mortgage, the effective mortgage balance is the portion of the mortgage principal on which interest is charged after deducting the balance held in linked savings accounts. It reflects the net principal used for interest calculation, thereby reducing interest costs without altering the outstanding principal on the loan agreement.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Mortgage Balance = Mortgage Principal - Linked Savings Balance
Effective NOL Carryforward = min(Net Operating Loss, Taxable Income × Limit Percentage)

nodes.name: Effective Operating Time per Unit Equipment
nodes.definition: Effective operating time per unit equipment refers to the total time a single piece of equipment is actually available for production operations within a specific period (typically one year), after accounting for necessary planned downtime (such as equipment inspection and maintenance). It is a fundamental parameter for evaluating equipment production capacity and utilization rate.

nodes.name: Effective Operating Time per Unit of Equipment
Effective Periodic Rate
nodes.definition: The effective periodic rate is the interest rate applicable to each compounding period, derived from an effective annual interest rate by accounting for intra-year compounding. It is used to discount or compound cash flows on a per-period basis (e.g., monthly, quarterly) in time value of money and capital budgeting analyses.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Periodic Rate = (1 + Annual Interest Rate)^(1 ÷ Periods per Year) - 1

nodes.name: Effective Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The effective tax rate refers to the ratio of total taxes actually paid to the total tax base (such as taxable income), expressed as a percentage. It reflects the actual tax burden level for individuals or enterprises after considering all applicable deductions, tax credits, and different statutory tax rates.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Tax Rate = Total Tax ÷ Taxable Income
Effective Tax Rate = (Total Tax ÷ Total Income) × 100
Effective Tax Rate = (Total Tax ÷ Income) × 100

nodes.name: Effective Yield
nodes.definition: Effective yield is the annualized rate of return that accounts for intra-year compounding of periodic interest or coupon payments, assuming reinvestment at the nominal rate. It reflects the true annual return compared to the stated nominal rate.

formulas.source_formula: Effective Yield = [(Face Value × Coupon Rate × Years to Maturity) + Face Value - Premium Price] ÷ (Premium Price × Years to Maturity)
Effective Yield = (1 + Nominal Interest Rate ÷ Payments per Year) ^ Payments per Year - 1
Effective Yield (Annualized) = (Face Value - Purchase Price) ÷ Purchase Price × (52 ÷ Maturity Weeks)

nodes.name: Efficiency
nodes.definition: Efficiency measures how effectively inputs are converted into outputs, commonly expressed as the ratio of useful output to total input. In financial analysis, Return on Investment (ROI) is a specific efficiency metric that evaluates the profitability of an investment by comparing the gain from the investment to its cost.

formulas.source_formula: Efficiency = Useful Output ÷ Total Input

nodes.name: Efficiency Ratio
nodes.definition: The efficiency ratio measures how effectively a bank controls its operating costs relative to revenue. It is calculated as non-interest expenses divided by revenue; a lower ratio indicates better operational efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Efficiency Ratio = Non-Interest Expenses ÷ Revenue

nodes.name: Efficient Frontier
nodes.definition: The efficient frontier is the set of mean-variance optimal portfolios that deliver the maximum expected return for a given level of risk (volatility) or the minimum risk for a given expected return. It is derived from Modern Portfolio Theory (Markowitz) using expected returns, the covariance matrix of asset returns, and portfolio weights under specified constraints.

nodes.name: Eigenvalue
nodes.definition: Eigenvalue is a core concept in linear algebra, used to describe the scaling factor of a square matrix (matrix) in certain specific directions (eigenvectors). It reflects the essential characteristics of matrix transformation and is an intrinsic numerical property of the matrix that does not depend on the choice of coordinate system.

nodes.name: Elapsed Time
nodes.definition: Elapsed time refers to the actual length of time that has passed or been consumed from a specific starting point (such as project commencement, asset activation, contract effectiveness, etc.) to the current moment.

nodes.name: Elective-Deferral Contribution Limit
nodes.definition: The elective-deferral contribution limit is the maximum amount of compensation an employee may elect to defer into a qualified defined contribution plan (such as a 401(k)) within a tax year under IRC §402(g), with an additional catch-up contribution allowed for individuals age 50 or older under IRC §414(v). The limit is set annually by the IRS and may differ by year.

nodes.name: Emergency Fund
nodes.definition: An emergency fund is a liquid reserve set aside to cover a specified number of months of essential living expenses in the event of income loss or unexpected financial shocks. It enhances household liquidity, mitigates risk, and supports financial stability.

formulas.source_formula: Emergency Fund = Monthly Living Expenses × Target Months

nodes.name: Empirical Rule
nodes.definition: The Empirical Rule states that for a normally distributed variable, approximately 68% of observations lie within ±1 standard deviation of the mean, 95% within ±2 standard deviations, and 99.7% within ±3 standard deviations. It is used to estimate dispersion and probability ranges around the mean in statistical analysis, risk assessment, and financial modeling.

nodes.name: Empirical Rule Proportions
nodes.definition: Empirical rule proportions refer to the percentages of data points that fall within one, two, and three standard deviations from the mean in a normally distributed dataset, following the 68-95-99.7 rule.

nodes.name: Employee Benefits
nodes.definition: In accounting, 'Employee Benefits' typically refers to the accrued employee welfare expenses, which are various forms of compensation and treatment provided by an enterprise to its employees beyond salaries, bonuses, and allowances. They are usually accrued at a certain percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total payroll or expensed based on actual occurrences, charged to relevant cost accounts, and used to cover employees' medical expenses, hardship allowances, collective welfare facility expenditures, etc.

nodes.name: Employee Bonus and Benefits
nodes.definition: Employee bonus and benefits refer to compensation expense items directly approved and disbursed by an enterprise to motivate and reward employees, based on company policies, performance agreements, etc. They constitute original costs and typically include various bonuses, allowances, and welfare expenses.

nodes.name: Employee Bonus and Welfare Accruals
nodes.definition: Employee Bonus and Welfare Accruals (Employee Welfare Expenses) refer to funds specifically allocated by enterprises in accordance with national regulations, calculated as a certain percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total employee payroll, and used for employee welfare purposes such as medical expenses, hardship allowances, and collective welfare facility expenditures.

formulas.source_formula: Employee Bonus and Welfare Accruals = Total Payroll × Accrual Rate

nodes.name: Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund Appropriation
aliases: Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund Provision
职工奖励及福利基金提取
nodes.definition: Employee Bonus and Welfare Fund Appropriation refers to a special fund that an enterprise pre-appropriates from costs or profits according to a specified percentage (e.g., 14% or 11%) of the total employee payroll, based on national regulations or internal bylaws, to cover various employee rewards and welfare expenses such as bonuses, medical expenses, hardship allowances, and collective welfare facilities.

nodes.name: Employee Compensation Payable
nodes.definition: Employee Compensation Payable refers to the various forms of remuneration and other related expenses that an enterprise is obligated to pay to its employees in accordance with relevant regulations. It constitutes a current obligation of the enterprise to its employees and is classified as a current liability.

nodes.name: Employee Compensation in Administrative Expenses
nodes.definition: Employee compensation in administrative expenses refers to all forms of remuneration or compensation paid by a company's administrative departments to its managerial, administrative, and other staff for organizing and managing production and operational activities. This includes salaries, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, social insurance contributions, housing provident fund contributions, labor union funds, and employee education funds. This expenditure constitutes a significant component of a company's administrative expenses.

nodes.name: Employee Compensation in Manufacturing Overhead
aliases: Indirect Labor Cost in Manufacturing Overhead
nodes.definition: Employee compensation in manufacturing overhead refers to all forms of remuneration paid by an enterprise to employees not directly engaged in product production during the manufacturing process, such as workshop management personnel and auxiliary production staff. This includes wages, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, social insurance contributions, housing provident fund, trade union funds, and employee education funds. This portion of compensation is a component of product manufacturing cost, but it is first aggregated through the manufacturing overhead account and then allocated to the production cost of specific products according to certain standards.

nodes.name: Employee Compensation in Production Costs
aliases: Labor Cost in Cost of Goods Manufactured
计入生产成本的职工薪酬
nodes.definition: Employee compensation in production costs refers to all monetary and non-monetary compensation expenses incurred by an enterprise during the production of goods or provision of services, including wages, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, social insurance contributions, housing provident fund contributions, trade union funds, and employee education funds for workers directly engaged in production and related personnel providing production services. These expenses are accumulated and allocated to specific product costs.

nodes.name: Employee Stock Option
nodes.definition: An Employee Stock Option (ESO) is a compensation contract between an employer and an employee, granting the employee a contingent right to purchase a limited number of the company's shares at a predetermined price, typically as part of their compensation package. In this arrangement, the employer holds a short position in a call option, while the employee holds the long position. The employee has no obligation to exercise the option, and unexercised options expire upon maturity or termination of employment.

nodes.name: Employee Stock Option Time Value
aliases: 员工股票期权时间价值
nodes.definition: The time value of an Employee Stock Option (ESO) is the portion of the option's fair value that exceeds its intrinsic value, capturing the value attributable to the time remaining until expiration, expected volatility, interest rates, and dividends. On a per-option basis, time value equals fair value minus intrinsic value; multiplying by the number of shares (options) yields the total time value of the ESO position.

nodes.name: Employee Stock Purchase Plan
nodes.definition: In the United States, an Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) is a program that allows employees to purchase company stock at a discount of up to 15% using payroll deductions accumulated between the offering date and the purchase date. The plan may qualify for tax advantages under Section 423 of the Internal Revenue Code, allowing for favorable tax treatment if the stock is held for at least two years from the offering date and one year from the purchase date (i.e., a qualifying disposition).

nodes.name: Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) Taxable Ordinary Income
aliases: 员工股票购买计划应税收入
nodes.definition: Taxable ordinary income from an Employee Stock Purchase Plan (ESPP) is the portion of the gain on ESPP shares treated as ordinary income for tax purposes. In this simplified model, the discounted purchase price is used to compute total gain; if the holding period meets a qualifying threshold, ordinary income equals the purchase discount applied to the purchase price times the number of shares; otherwise, the entire gain is treated as ordinary income.

nodes.name: Employment Insurance (EI) Weekly Benefit
nodes.definition: The weekly Employment Insurance (EI) benefit amount is calculated as a percentage of a claimant’s average weekly insurable earnings, commonly set at 55%, subject to a government-defined maximum insurable earnings cap.

nodes.name: Employment-to-Population Ratio
nodes.definition: The employment-to-population ratio measures the proportion of employed individuals within the working-age population, expressed as a percentage. It indicates overall labor market utilization and complements unemployment statistics by reflecting the share of the working-age population that is employed.

formulas.source_formula: Employment-to-Population Ratio (%) = (Employed Population ÷ Working-Age Population) × 100%

nodes.name: End Date
nodes.definition: End Date refers to the specific point in time when an event, activity, project, contract, or financial instrument (such as bonds, options) terminates or matures. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a fundamental input parameter for calculating periods, days, or interest.

nodes.name: End Period Number When Cash Flows Begin
End Time
nodes.definition: End Time refers to the completion point of an event, activity, or process. In financial management and operational analysis, it is typically derived through addition of the start time and the duration (or the sum of various time components), serving as a fundamental composite concept for time series analysis, efficiency evaluation, and progress control.

formulas.source_formula: End Time = Start Time + Duration
End Time = Start Time + Processing Time + Non-productive Hours

nodes.name: End Year
nodes.definition: End Year refers to a specific point in time or period endpoint preset in financial calculations or analysis, serving as the cut-off date or benchmark date for calculating indicators such as service years, depreciation, and discounted cash flows. It is a fundamental input parameter that typically cannot be derived from other financial metrics.

nodes.name: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Cost
nodes.definition: End-of-month work-in-process cost is the cost calculated by multiplying unit cost by the equivalent units of work-in-process at month-end.

operands.metric: Equivalent Units of Work-in-Process at Month-End

formulas.source_formula: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Cost = Unit Cost × Equivalent Units of Work-in-Process at Month-End

nodes.name: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Quantity
nodes.definition: End-of-month work-in-process quantity refers to the physical count of all products on the production line that have not completed the entire production process and cannot be sold as finished goods (i.e., work-in-process) at the end of an accounting period (typically a month).

nodes.name: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Quantity by Production Stage
aliases: Work-in-Process Quantity by Process at Month-End
月末各工序在产品数量
nodes.definition: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Quantity by Production Stage refers to the physical quantity of products or semi-finished goods that remain at each specific production stage at the end of each month (accounting period) in a multi-step production process, which have not completed all processing stages and cannot be transferred to finished goods inventory. It serves as critical data in cost accounting for calculating equivalent units of work-in-process and allocating production costs.

nodes.name: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Standard Material Cost
aliases: Month-end WIP Material Cost at Standard
WIP Standard Material Cost at Month-end
月末在产品标准材料成本
月末在产品直接材料定额成本
nodes.definition: End-of-month work-in-process standard material cost refers to the standard direct material cost of work-in-process calculated under the standard cost method for work-in-process, based on the quantity of work-in-process at month-end, the standard material consumption per unit of work-in-process, and the planned unit price of materials. It serves as one of the fundamental data points for allocating material costs when calculating the cost of completed products.

operands.metric: Standard Material Consumption per Unit of Work-in-Process

formulas.source_formula: End-of-Month Work-in-Process Standard Material Cost = End-of-Month Work-in-Process Quantity × Standard Material Consumption per Unit of Work-in-Process × Planned Unit Price of Materials

nodes.name: End-of-Period Debt-to-Asset Ratio
nodes.definition: The End-of-Period Debt-to-Asset Ratio refers to the ratio of total liabilities to total assets at the conclusion of a specific accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, year-end). It measures the proportion of a company's total assets financed through debt, reflecting the firm's long-term solvency and financial leverage level.

nodes.name: End-of-Period Uncredited Input VAT
nodes.definition: End-of-period uncredited input VAT refers to the amount of Value-Added Tax (VAT) that remains uncredited and can be carried forward to the next period for further deduction, resulting from the input VAT for the current period exceeding the output VAT at the end of a VAT filing period. It serves as the basis for calculating the VAT refundable under the 'exemption, credit, and refund' mechanism.

formulas.source_formula: End-of-Period Uncredited Input VAT = VAT Already Paid - Current Period VAT Payable

nodes.name: Ending Accounts Payable Balance
nodes.definition: Ending accounts payable balance refers to the total amount owed to suppliers or creditors at the balance sheet date (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) for the purchase of materials, goods, or services received but not yet paid. It is directly recorded based on the actual closing balances in the general ledger or subsidiary ledgers, reflecting the company's short-term payment obligations at a specific point in time.

nodes.name: Ending Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Ending accounts receivable refers to the net amount collectible from customers as of the balance sheet date, determined based on the debit balances of detailed accounts such as accounts receivable and advance receipts, after deducting the provision for bad debts. It is a key component in calculating ending operating current assets.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Accounts Receivable = Beginning Balance of Accounts Receivable + Debit Turnover in Current Period - Credit Turnover in Current Period

operands.metric: Debit Balance of Accounts Receivable Detailed Accounts
Debit Balance of Advance Receipts Detailed Accounts
Ending Balance of Provision for Bad Debts

formulas.source_formula: Ending Accounts Receivable = Debit Balance of Accounts Receivable Detailed Accounts + Debit Balance of Advance Receipts Detailed Accounts - Ending Balance of Provision for Bad Debts

nodes.name: Ending Accounts Receivable Balance
nodes.definition: Ending accounts receivable balance refers to the net book value of receivables arising from the sale of goods or provision of services that have not yet been collected from customers at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the amount of claims against customers at the balance sheet date and serves as fundamental data for calculating other financial metrics (such as turnover ratios).

nodes.name: Ending Accounts Receivable for Current Period
Ending Accounts Receivable for Previous Period
Ending Asset Value
nodes.definition: Ending asset value refers to the total recorded book value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the closing point of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It is directly derived from the enterprise's accounting results or asset appraisal reports, serves as the core aggregate item on the balance sheet, and reflects the overall scale of the enterprise's resources at that point in time.

nodes.name: Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Ending balance refers to the final account balance after recording all increases and decreases during a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It serves as the fundamental data for preparing financial statements and reflects the financial position of the account at the end of the period.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Balance = Current Balance - Principal Payment
Ending Balance = Beginning Balance - Principal Payment
Ending Balance = Invested Amount × (1 + Investment Rate)
Ending Balance = Beginning Balance - Debit Turnover During the Period + Credit Turnover During the Period
Ending Balance = Beginning Balance + Additions During the Period - Reductions During the Period
Ending Balance = Beginning Balance + Debit Turnover During the Period - Credit Turnover During the Period

nodes.name: Ending Balance / Period-end Data
nodes.definition: Ending balance refers to the final book balance of each accounting item in a company's financial statements at the close of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year, quarter, or month). These figures are obtained directly from accounting records like the general ledger, reflecting the company's financial position at that point in time, and serve as the fundamental raw data for calculating various financial ratios and growth rates.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Accrued Employee Benefits
aliases: Ending Balance of Employee Welfare Payable
nodes.definition: The ending balance of accrued employee benefits refers to the book balance of the 'Accrued Employee Benefits' or 'Employee Compensation Payable - Employee Benefits' account at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). According to current accounting standards, enterprises generally no longer accrue employee benefits in advance; the balance of this account primarily reflects the unused surplus carried forward from provisions made in prior years. When employee benefit expenses are incurred, they should first be offset against this credit balance. Once the balance is reduced to zero, any newly incurred employee benefit expenses are directly recognized in the current period's profit or loss.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Advances from Customers
nodes.definition: The ending balance of advances from customers refers to the amount that must be presented as a liability on the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end), arising from payments received in advance from customers for goods or services for which the related delivery or performance obligations have not yet been fulfilled or fully fulfilled. It represents an obligation that the company must settle by delivering goods or providing services in the future.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Allowance Items from Previous Period
nodes.definition: The ending balance of allowance items from the previous period refers to the closing balance of allowance accounts (such as allowance for doubtful accounts, accumulated depreciation, inventory write-down allowance, etc.) carried forward directly from the accounting books of the last accounting period (e.g., previous month, quarter, or year). It serves as the known opening data for calculating the book value of related assets or expenses in the current period, representing fundamental raw data that cannot be derived through formulas.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts
aliases: Ending Balance of Bad Debt Provision
nodes.definition: The ending balance of allowance for doubtful accounts refers to the balance of the reserve account, estimated and accrued based on the collectability of accounts receivable at the end of an accounting period, used to offset the carrying value of accounts receivable. It serves as the basis for calculating the net accounts receivable on the balance sheet.

operands.metric: Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

formulas.source_formula: Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts = Beginning Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts + Current Period Accrual - Current Period Write-offs and Reversals

operands.metric: Current Period Increase in Accounts Receivable
Current Period Decrease in Accounts Receivable

formulas.source_formula: Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts = (Beginning Balance of Accounts Receivable + Current Period Increase in Accounts Receivable - Current Period Decrease in Accounts Receivable) × Bad Debt Provision Rate

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Cash Equivalents
aliases: Closing Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents
期末现金及现金等价物余额
nodes.definition: The ending balance of cash equivalents refers to the total amount of cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It reflects the value of the most liquid assets that can be immediately utilized by the enterprise at a specific point in time.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: Closing Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance
Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance
期末现金及现金等价物余额
nodes.definition: The ending balance of cash and cash equivalents refers to the total book value of cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period (such as year-end or quarter-end), reflecting the status of the enterprise's liquidity resources at that point in time. This metric is typically calculated from the cash flow statement or balance sheet and is an important component of financial statement analysis.

operands.metric: Ending Balance of the Cash and Cash Equivalents Item on the Balance Sheet

formulas.source_formula: Ending Balance of Cash and Cash Equivalents = Ending Balance of the Cash and Cash Equivalents Item on the Balance Sheet

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Current Assets
nodes.definition: The ending balance of current assets refers to the total book value of all current asset items of an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). These assets include cash and cash equivalents, short-term investments, notes receivable, accounts receivable, inventory, etc., which are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle. This figure is a point-in-time amount directly obtained from accounting ledgers or the balance sheet at period-end.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: The ending balance of current liabilities refers to the total amount of obligations that an enterprise is expected to settle within a normal operating cycle or within one year from the balance sheet date (whichever is shorter), as recorded on the balance sheet date (period-end). It is a key indicator for measuring the short-term debt repayment pressure of an enterprise.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Deferred Tax Assets
aliases: 递延所得税资产期末数
nodes.definition: The ending balance of deferred tax assets refers to the book value of the 'Deferred Tax Assets' account at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It represents the amount of assets that a company expects to utilize in future periods to reduce taxable income and thereby decrease future income tax payable, arising from deductible temporary differences (e.g., when the book value of an asset is less than its tax base, or the book value of a liability exceeds its tax base) and deductible losses.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Deferred Tax Liabilities
Ending Balance of Deferred Tax Liability
aliases: Closing Balance of Deferred Tax Liability
递延所得税负债期末数
nodes.definition: The ending balance of deferred tax liability refers to the amount of income tax that an enterprise expects to pay to tax authorities in future periods, calculated at the balance sheet date (typically quarter-end or year-end) based on differences between accounting standards and tax regulations (primarily taxable temporary differences). It represents the cumulative carrying value at period-end of the enterprise's future tax payment obligations arising from temporary differences.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Employee Compensation Payable
aliases: 应付职工薪酬期末金额
应付职工薪酬项目期末余额
nodes.definition: The ending balance of employee compensation payable refers to the total amount of various forms of remuneration that have been incurred but not yet actually paid to employees by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end), in accordance with labor contracts and national regulations. It reflects the enterprise's liability to employees as of the balance sheet date.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Employee Compensation Payable for Construction in Progress
aliases: Accrued Payroll for CIP at Period End
在建工程人员薪酬期末余额
在建工程应付职工薪酬期末数
工程人员应付薪酬期末结余
nodes.definition: The ending balance of employee compensation payable for construction in progress refers to the cumulative total of wages, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, benefits, and other compensation items that an enterprise owes, according to labor contracts and national regulations, to employees involved in construction-in-progress projects but has not yet actually paid by the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). This compensation constitutes a liability for the enterprise and forms part of the cost of construction in progress.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Financial Assets
nodes.definition: The ending balance of financial assets refers to the total book value of various financial assets held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period. As an asset account, its value can be calculated from the opening balance and the current period's transactions, conforming to the general calculation formula for the ending balance of asset accounts. It is a calculable composite indicator, commonly used in financial analysis and the calculation of derivative indicators such as the increase in excess financial assets.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Balance of Financial Assets = Opening Balance of Financial Assets + Current Period Increase - Current Period Decrease
Ending Balance of Financial Assets = Opening Balance of Financial Assets + Current Period Debit Turnover - Current Period Credit Turnover

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Monetary Capital in the Balance Sheet
aliases: Cash and Cash Equivalents at Period End
nodes.definition: Refers to the total amount of funds held by an enterprise on the balance sheet date (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, year-end) that can be used for immediate payment, including the aggregate ending balances of accounting items such as cash on hand, bank deposits, and other monetary funds.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Net Operating Assets from Previous Period
aliases: Closing Balance of Net Operating Assets from Prior Period
Net Operating Assets at the End of Previous Period
前期净经营资产期末余额
nodes.definition: The ending balance of net operating assets from the previous period refers to the total book value of a company's net operating assets at the end of the prior accounting period (such as the previous year, quarter, or month). Net operating assets typically represent the net value of assets used for core business operations (such as operating current assets and operating long-term assets) minus operating current liabilities. This balance serves as the basis for calculating the beginning balance of net operating assets for the current period.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Notes Receivable
nodes.definition: The ending balance of notes receivable refers to the total book value of notes receivable that have not yet matured or been settled at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the amount of receivables held by the enterprise at that point in time, consisting of commercial drafts (including trade acceptance bills and bank acceptance bills).

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Operating Assets
nodes.definition: The ending balance of operating assets refers to the total book value of all assets used for daily production and business operations at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). These assets typically include cash, accounts receivable, inventory, fixed assets, etc., but exclude non-operating assets such as financial investments.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Operating Current Assets
Ending Balance of Provision for Bad Debts
Ending Balance of Retained Earnings
nodes.definition: The ending balance of retained earnings refers to the final book value of a company's retained earnings account at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). Retained earnings represent the accumulated portion of a company's after-tax profits that are retained within the business for reinvestment or future distribution, primarily consisting of two components: surplus reserves and undistributed profits.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: The ending balance of surplus reserve refers to the remaining amount in a company's surplus reserve account at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It represents the total amount of reserve funds accumulated and retained from after-tax profits up to that point in time, designated for specific purposes such as covering losses or increasing capital.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of Taxes Payable
nodes.definition: The ending balance of taxes payable refers to the total amount of various taxes and fees that a company has calculated according to tax laws and regulations as payable but not yet paid at the end of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the company's tax obligations on the balance sheet date.

nodes.name: Ending Balance of the Cash and Cash Equivalents Item on the Balance Sheet
Ending Book Balance
nodes.definition: Ending book balance refers to the calculated remaining amount of an accounting item or account at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end), based on accounting records. It reflects the final result of the account after considering the beginning balance and all additions and reductions during the current period.

nodes.name: Ending Book Value of Assets
aliases: Carrying Amount of Assets at Period End
nodes.definition: Ending book value of assets refers to the net value of various assets listed on a company's balance sheet after accounting treatments at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It typically equals the original value (acquisition cost) of the asset minus accumulated depreciation (or amortization) and any provision for asset impairment, reflecting the carrying value of the asset on the reporting date.

nodes.name: Ending Capital
nodes.definition: Ending capital refers to the book balance of owners' equity or invested capital at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the capital position of the enterprise at that specific moment, serving as the fundamental raw data for financial analysis and the calculation of other metrics (such as the weighted average cost of capital).

nodes.name: Ending Capital Employed
nodes.definition: Ending Capital Employed refers to the total amount of capital actually invested and utilized by a company to sustain its business operations at the end of a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or fiscal year). It is commonly used to measure the comprehensive usage of both debt capital and equity capital at the period-end point, serving as a key foundational data point for calculating performance metrics such as Economic Value Added (EVA).

nodes.name: Ending Capital Reserve
nodes.definition: Ending capital reserve refers to the final book balance of the 'capital reserve' account under the owners' equity section on the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the public accumulation attributable to all shareholders, formed from non-operating factors since the company's establishment, such as shareholder contributions exceeding the registered capital, donations received, and revaluation surpluses of assets.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Cash Balance = Beginning Cash Balance + Total Cash Inflows - Total Cash Outflows

nodes.name: Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: Cash and Cash Equivalents at Period End
期末现金及现金等价物
nodes.definition: Ending cash and cash equivalents refers to the total amount of funds owned by an enterprise at the cut-off point of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) that can be immediately used for payment. It is directly reported on the balance sheet by summing the ending balances of the 'Cash on Hand', 'Bank Deposits', and 'Other Cash Equivalents' accounts from the accounting ledgers, reflecting the enterprise's immediate payment capability and liquidity.

nodes.name: Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance
aliases: 现金及现金等价物期末余额
nodes.definition: Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance refers to the total book value of cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, year-end). This metric is the final result of the cash flow statement, reflecting the enterprise's immediate payment ability and liquidity position at that point in time. Its value should equal the ending balance of the 'Cash and Cash Equivalents' item on the balance sheet.

operands.metric: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance
Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents

formulas.source_formula: Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance = Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance + Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents

operands.metric: Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance
Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities
Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities

formulas.source_formula: Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance = Beginning Cash and Cash Equivalents Balance + Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities + Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities + Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities

nodes.name: Ending Common Shareholders' Equity
aliases: 普通股股东权益期末数
nodes.definition: Ending Common Shareholders' Equity refers to the total amount of owners' equity attributable to common shareholders at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It reflects the residual claim value enjoyed by common shareholders in the company's net assets at the reporting date, after deducting preferred stock equity.

nodes.name: Ending Current Assets
nodes.definition: Ending current assets refer to the total sum of assets that a company possesses at the end of an accounting period, which can be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle exceeding one year. It is a composite indicator derived by summing various current asset items and is commonly used to calculate financial metrics such as average working capital, ending total assets, and increase in working capital.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Current Assets = Current Ratio × Current Liabilities
Ending Current Assets = (Quick Ratio × Current Liabilities) + Inventory

Ending Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Accounts Receivable + Inventory + Other Receivables + Notes Receivable + Short-term Investments + Prepaid Expenses + Receivables for Subsidies + Deferred Expenses + Other Current Assets

nodes.name: Ending Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Ending current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that a company needs to repay within one year or one operating cycle at the end of an accounting period (e.g., year-end, quarter-end). It is a crucial financial metric for assessing a company's short-term solvency.

operands.metric: Current Period Incurrence of Current Liabilities
Current Period Settlement of Current Liabilities

formulas.source_formula: Ending Current Liabilities = Beginning Current Liabilities + Current Period Incurrence of Current Liabilities - Current Period Settlement of Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Ending Debit Balance of Advances from Customers
aliases: Advance from Customers Debit Balance at Period End
nodes.definition: The ending debit balance of advances from customers refers to the amount appearing on the debit side of the subsidiary accounts under the liability account 'Advances from Customers' at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). This typically indicates that the amount collected in advance from customers is less than the value of goods or services actually provided, meaning customers still owe the company money. Therefore, when preparing the balance sheet, this debit balance must be reclassified and presented under asset items such as 'Accounts Receivable'.

nodes.name: Ending Equity Multiplier
nodes.definition: The ending equity multiplier is the ratio of a company's total assets to total shareholders' equity at the end of a period, reflecting the magnification of total assets relative to shareholders' invested capital at a specific point in time. It is a key metric for measuring the degree of financial leverage and capital structure, commonly used in the DuPont analysis framework.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Equity Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 - Ending Debt-to-Assets Ratio)
Ending Equity Multiplier = Ending Total Assets ÷ Ending Total Shareholders' Equity

nodes.name: Ending Fixed Assets
aliases: 期末固定资产账面价值
nodes.definition: Ending fixed assets, also known as net fixed assets or book value, refer to the net amount of fixed assets at the balance sheet date, calculated as the original value of fixed assets minus accumulated depreciation and fixed asset impairment provisions. This reflects the remaining economic value of fixed assets after deducting value consumption and impairment.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Fixed Assets = Original Value of Fixed Assets - Accumulated Depreciation - Fixed Asset Impairment Provisions

nodes.name: Ending Inventory
nodes.definition: Ending inventory refers to the quantity of goods held in stock by an enterprise at the end of the fiscal year. It is closely related to the cost of ending inventory, which refers to the amount spent to acquire and store these goods in the warehouse. Ending inventory should be measured at the lower of cost or market value.

nodes.name: Ending Inventory Balance
nodes.definition: Ending inventory balance refers to the total book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It reflects the value of inventory items, including raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods, that have not been sold or used by the enterprise at the reporting date.

nodes.name: Ending Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Ending inventory cost refers to the total book value of all inventory items, including finished goods, work-in-progress, and raw materials, at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It represents the carrying cost of inventory on the balance sheet date and is a significant asset item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Ending Inventory Value
aliases: Inventory at the End of Period
nodes.definition: Ending inventory value refers to the book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) when preparing the balance sheet, measured according to accounting standards (such as the lower of cost or net realizable value method) and ready for presentation. It reflects the asset value of inventory at the end of the period.

nodes.name: Ending Inventory of Previous Period
aliases: 期初存货的上一期余额
nodes.definition: Ending inventory of the previous period refers to the total book value of all unsold or unconsumed inventory items, including raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods, at the close of the preceding accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or fiscal year). It serves as the direct source for calculating the beginning inventory of the current period and is a fundamental line item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Ending Inventory of Previous Quarter
nodes.definition: Ending Inventory of Previous Quarter refers to the book value or quantity of all inventory held by an enterprise at the end of the last financial quarter (i.e., the last day of that quarter). It is a specific account balance on the balance sheet, representing raw data directly obtained from accounting records or previous period financial statements, used to reflect the inventory position at a specific point in time.

nodes.name: Ending Long-term Assets
nodes.definition: Ending long-term assets refer to the total assets owned by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter) that are expected to be held for more than one year or one operating cycle. These assets are typically not intended for sale or liquidation in the short term and are primarily used for the enterprise's long-term operations and investment activities.

nodes.name: Ending Long-term Capital
nodes.definition: Ending long-term capital refers to the total amount of funding sources available for long-term use that a company possesses at the end of an accounting period (e.g., year-end, quarter-end). It typically consists of shareholders' equity, long-term liabilities, and working capital (or net working capital), reflecting the stable capital base that supports the company's long-term assets and operations.

nodes.name: Ending Long-term Liabilities
aliases: Long Term Liabilities at Period End
nodes.definition: Ending long-term liabilities refer to the total amount of debt with a repayment period exceeding one year or one operating cycle, as presented on a company's balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the debt burden that the company needs to repay over a relatively long period in the future.

nodes.name: Ending Month
nodes.definition: Ending month refers to the month in which a specific financial period (such as an accounting period, project cycle, or calculation cycle) terminates. It is a fundamental temporal identifier used to determine the endpoint of the time range covered by a calculation or report.

nodes.name: Ending Net Assets
nodes.definition: Ending net assets refer to the residual value of a company's total assets minus total liabilities at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or fiscal year), representing the total equity owned by the company's owners at that point in time.

nodes.name: Ending Net Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Ending Net Operating Assets represent the difference between a company's ending operating assets and operating liabilities, reflecting the net investment amount used for business operations. It is a composite financial metric, typically used to calculate derivative indicators such as net operating asset turnover and net investment, and belongs to a non-leaf node.

nodes.name: Ending Non-current Assets
nodes.definition: Ending non-current assets refer to the total assets held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period that are expected to be realized or consumed over one year or beyond one operating cycle. They are a key item on the balance sheet, typically calculated by directly summing all non-current asset items or by subtracting current assets from total assets.

operands.metric: Other Non-current Assets such as Available-for-sale Financial Assets

formulas.source_formula: Ending Non-current Assets = Matured Investments + Long-term Receivables + Long-term Equity Investments + Construction Materials + Investment Properties + Fixed Assets + Construction in Progress + Intangible Assets + Long-term Prepaid Expenses + Deferred Tax Assets + Other Non-current Assets such as Available-for-sale Financial Assets

nodes.name: Ending Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Ending Operating Assets refer to the total amount of assets used to support a company's core business operations at the end of a specific accounting period. It is a key metric in managerial financial statement analysis, typically derived by adjusting original balance sheet items (e.g., deducting financial assets) or summing operating asset items. It is used to evaluate the profitability and capital efficiency of the company's core business and serves as the basis for calculating Net Operating Assets.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Operating Assets = Operating Current Assets + Operating Long-term Assets

nodes.name: Ending Operating Current Assets
aliases: Operating Current Assets at End of Period
经营流动资产期末余额
nodes.definition: Ending Operating Current Assets refer to the current assets held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period that are related to daily business operations. They typically include items such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, and inventory. They are derived by aggregating or adjusting operating-related current asset items and constitute a key component in calculating net operating assets, rather than being a fundamental raw data item in financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Operating Current Assets = Ending Total Current Assets - Ending Financial Current Assets

operands.metric: Total Current Assets at Period End

formulas.source_formula: Ending Operating Current Assets = Total Current Assets at Period End - Trading Financial Assets - Other Non-operating Current Assets
Ending Operating Current Assets = Ending Cash and Cash Equivalents + Ending Accounts Receivable + Ending Inventory + Ending Prepaid Expenses + Ending Other Operating Current Assets
Ending Operating Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Accounts Receivable + Inventory + Prepaid Expenses + Other Receivables + Other Operating Current Assets

nodes.name: Ending Operating Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Ending operating current liabilities refer to the obligations directly related to daily business operations that a company is expected to settle within a normal operating cycle (typically one year) as of the balance sheet date (period-end). It is a subset of total current liabilities, excluding items related to financing activities, and is primarily used for calculating working capital and assessing a company's short-term operational solvency pressure.

nodes.name: Ending Operating Liabilities
nodes.definition: Ending operating liabilities refer to the total liabilities related to daily business operations at the end of an accounting period, typically including accounts payable, deferred revenue, accrued wages, accrued employee benefits, and taxes payable. It is a composite indicator used to calculate ending net operating assets.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Operating Liabilities = Accounts Payable + Deferred Revenue + Accrued Wages + Accrued Employee Benefits + Taxes Payable

nodes.name: Ending Operating Long-term Assets
aliases: Operating Long-term Assets at Period End
nodes.definition: Ending Operating Long-term Assets refer to the total sum of non-current assets held by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period for ongoing business operations. They are typically calculated by aggregating financial statement items such as Long-term Equity Investments, Fixed Assets, Construction in Progress, Intangible Assets, and Deferred Tax Assets. This figure is a key component in calculating ending net operating assets in financial management and is used to assess the allocation of long-term assets and operational efficiency.

nodes.name: Ending Operating Long-term Liabilities
aliases: Long-term Operating Liabilities at Period End
nodes.definition: Ending operating long-term liabilities refer to the total amount of debt directly related to daily business operations with a repayment term exceeding one year, as presented on the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., year-end or quarter-end). They typically consist of the operating-related portions of items such as long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables, and serve as fundamental data for calculating metrics like net operating assets.

nodes.name: Ending Operating Working Capital
nodes.definition: Ending Operating Working Capital refers to the net amount of operating current assets minus operating current liabilities at the end of an accounting period. It reflects the short-term funding requirements and management efficiency of a company's daily operations, serving as a key metric for assessing short-term solvency and the efficiency of working capital utilization.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Operating Working Capital = Operating Current Assets - Operating Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Ending Owner's Equity
aliases: 资产负债表日所有者权益
nodes.definition: Ending owner's equity refers to the book value of the residual interest attributable to the owners (shareholders) of an enterprise after deducting total liabilities from total assets at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It reflects the net asset position of the enterprise at the end of the period.

nodes.name: Ending Prepaid Accounts
nodes.definition: Ending prepaid accounts refer to the total amount prepaid to suppliers for goods or services not yet received, as presented on the balance sheet date at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). This amount is calculated by analyzing the debit balances of detailed ledger accounts such as 'Prepaid Accounts' and 'Accounts Payable'.

nodes.name: Ending Price
nodes.definition: Ending price refers to the market price or book value of an asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) at the end of a specific accounting period or investment horizon (e.g., at the close of a trading day, month, quarter, or year). It is a raw data point obtained directly from market transaction data or accounting records, typically serving as a fundamental input for calculating financial metrics such as returns.

nodes.name: Ending Retained Earnings
aliases: Retained Earnings Balance at Period End
nodes.definition: Ending retained earnings refers to the cumulative net profit that has not been distributed to shareholders at the end of an accounting period, reserved for reinvestment or future dividends.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Retained Earnings = Beginning Retained Earnings + Current Period Profit - Current Period Dividends

operands.metric: Credit Turnover of Current Period Retained Earnings
Debit Turnover of Current Period Retained Earnings

formulas.source_formula: Ending Retained Earnings = Beginning Retained Earnings + Credit Turnover of Current Period Retained Earnings - Debit Turnover of Current Period Retained Earnings
Ending Retained Earnings = Statutory Surplus Reserve + Public Welfare Fund + Discretionary Surplus Reserve + Undistributed Profits

nodes.name: Ending Retained Earnings Balance
nodes.definition: Ending retained earnings balance refers to the final book value of the retained earnings account at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). Retained earnings represent the accumulated after-tax profits generated by the company over the years that are retained within the business for reinvestment or future distribution, primarily consisting of two components: surplus reserves and undistributed profits.

nodes.name: Ending Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Ending shareholders' equity refers to the total residual equity attributable to the company's shareholders (owners) after subtracting total liabilities from total assets at the end of an accounting period (such as year-end or quarter-end). It represents the net asset value owned by shareholders in the company.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Shareholders' Equity = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Ending Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Ending Surplus Reserve refers to the closing balance of the surplus reserve account at the end of an accounting period (e.g., year-end), reflecting the total cumulative amount of surplus reserve that has been appropriated and retained up to that point. It is an account balance that must be calculated based on the opening balance, current period appropriations, usage, and other changes, and constitutes an important component of shareholders' equity.

operands.metric: Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period
Discretionary Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Ending Surplus Reserve = Opening Surplus Reserve Balance + Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period + Discretionary Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period + Other Additions - Amount Used in Current Period

operands.metric: Current Period Net Profit After Tax

formulas.source_formula: Ending Surplus Reserve = Opening Surplus Reserve Balance + Current Period Net Profit After Tax × Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriation Rate + Current Period Net Profit After Tax × Discretionary Surplus Reserve Appropriation Rate + Other Additions - Amount Used in Current Period

nodes.name: Ending Value of Current Assets from Previous Period
nodes.definition: The ending value of current assets from the previous period refers to the total book value of all current assets held by an enterprise at the end of the last accounting period (such as the previous quarter or the previous fiscal year). It is typically used as the baseline data for calculating the change in current assets for the current period.

nodes.name: Ending Work in Process Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Ending work in process inventory cost refers to the total accumulated costs of products that are not yet completed and remain in the processing or assembly stage on the production line at the end of an accounting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). These costs typically include direct materials, direct labor, and allocated manufacturing overhead already incurred. This cost serves as the basis for calculating the cost of goods completed during the period and is reported as part of inventory on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Ending Work in Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost
aliases: Closing WIP and Semi-finished Goods Cost
Ending Work-in-Process and Semi-finished Goods Cost
nodes.definition: Ending work in process and semi-finished goods cost refers to the total accumulated production costs of all products that are not yet completed and remain in the production process (work in process), as well as intermediate products that have completed certain production steps but are not yet final finished goods (semi-finished goods), at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end).

nodes.name: Ending Work-in-Process and Semi-finished Goods Value
aliases: Value of Work-in-Process at Period End
nodes.definition: Ending work-in-process and semi-finished goods value refers to the estimated or accounted value of all unfinished products and semi-finished goods still in the production process at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month, quarter, or year). It reflects the inventory value remaining on the production line that has not yet reached a saleable state at the period-end date.

nodes.name: Ending Working Capital
nodes.definition: Ending working capital is the difference between ending current assets and ending current liabilities, used to measure a company's short-term solvency and working capital position at a specific point in time, and is a composite indicator in financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Ending Working Capital = Ending Current Assets - Ending Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Energy Return on Investment (EROI)
nodes.definition: Energy Return on Investment (EROI) measures the ratio of usable energy obtained from an energy resource to the energy expended to extract, process, and deliver that energy. It is calculated as energy output divided by energy input; higher EROI indicates greater net energy gain and production efficiency. EROI is widely used in energy economics and project evaluation to compare energy technologies and assess long-term sustainability and cost competitiveness.

formulas.source_formula: Energy Return on Investment (EROI) = Energy Output ÷ Energy Input

nodes.name: Engel Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Engel coefficient measures the proportion of total household expenditure allocated to food, serving as a proxy for living standards and economic welfare. Rooted in Engel's Law—which posits that the share of income spent on food declines as income rises—the coefficient is widely used in poverty measurement, consumer expenditure analysis, and socio-economic assessments.

formulas.source_formula: Engel Coefficient = Food Expenditure ÷ Total Expenditure

nodes.name: Engineering Cost
nodes.definition: Engineering cost refers to the total expenses incurred during the construction process for completing project construction, equipment procurement, and installation. It typically consists of direct engineering costs, indirect costs, profit, and taxes, and is an important component of fixed asset investment.

nodes.name: Engineering Insurance Premium
nodes.definition: Engineering insurance premium refers to the fee paid to insurance companies during the construction process to transfer various risks that the project may face (such as natural disasters, accidents, third-party liability, etc.). It is a component of other construction costs.

nodes.name: Enterprise Market Value
nodes.definition: Enterprise market value refers to the overall value of a company in the public market, reflecting investors' comprehensive expectations regarding the company's future profitability and cash flow generation capacity. It is typically calculated by summing the market value of equity and the market value of net debt, or estimated using valuation models (such as discounted cash flow models or relative valuation methods), rather than being raw data directly obtained from financial statements.

nodes.name: Enterprise Multiple
nodes.definition: Enterprise multiple (EV/EBITDA) is a valuation ratio that compares a company's enterprise value to its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, reflecting the price investors are willing to pay for operating earnings irrespective of capital structure.

operands.metric: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EBITDA)

formulas.source_formula: Enterprise Multiple = Enterprise Value ÷ EBITDA

nodes.name: Enterprise Value
nodes.definition: Enterprise Value, commonly referred to as EV, is the sum of a company's equity market capitalization plus its total debt minus cash and cash equivalents. It reflects the market's valuation of the company's total assets and liabilities and is frequently used in mergers and acquisitions and valuation analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Enterprise Value = Equity Value + Debt Value
Enterprise Value = Cash Flow ÷ (Cost of Capital - Growth Rate)

operands.metric: Present Value of Forecast Period Cash Flows

formulas.source_formula: Enterprise Value = Present Value of Forecast Period Cash Flows + Present Value of Continuing Period
Enterprise Value = Initial Invested Capital + Present Value of Economic Profit
Enterprise Value = Free Cash Flow to Firm ÷ (Weighted Average Cost of Capital - Perpetual Growth Rate)
Enterprise Value = Equity Value + Total Debt + Preferred Stock + Minority Interest - Cash and Cash Equivalents

nodes.name: Enterprise Value Multiple
nodes.definition: Enterprise Value Multiple is a company valuation metric calculated by dividing enterprise value by earnings before interest and taxes, used to assess the multiple relationship between enterprise value and profitability, and is a type of relative valuation method.

formulas.source_formula: Enterprise Value Multiple = Enterprise Value ÷ EBIT

nodes.name: Enterprise Value to EBITDA Ratio
nodes.definition: Enterprise Value to EBITDA Ratio is a valuation multiple that compares the total enterprise value of a company to its earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, used to assess relative valuation independent of capital structure.

operands.metric: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EBITDA)

formulas.source_formula: EV/EBITDA Ratio = Enterprise Value ÷ EBITDA

nodes.name: Enterprise Value-to-Sales (EV/Sales)
nodes.definition: The Enterprise Value-to-Sales (EV/Sales) ratio measures a company’s enterprise value relative to its annual sales (revenue), indicating how much value the market assigns to each dollar of revenue. It is commonly used in valuation, especially for comparing companies across sectors or when earnings are negative.

nodes.name: Enterprise-Value-to-Revenue Multiple (EV/R)
nodes.definition: The Enterprise-Value-to-Revenue (EV/R) multiple measures how a company's enterprise value compares to its revenue. It is a market-based valuation metric commonly used in comparable company analysis and transactions, particularly for businesses with negative or volatile earnings. Lower EV/R values may indicate a more attractive valuation relative to peers, assuming comparable growth, margins, and risk profiles.

formulas.source_formula: Enterprise Value-to-Revenue Multiple = Enterprise Value ÷ Revenue

nodes.name: Entity Value
nodes.definition: Entity value refers to the market value of all assets of a company, including the total value of equity and debt, reflecting the total equity value enjoyed by all investors (including shareholders and creditors).

formulas.source_formula: Entity Value = Net Asset Value + Potential Growth Value + Risk-Adjusted Value

operands.metric: Present Value of Forecast Period Entity Free Cash Flow

formulas.source_formula: Entity Value = Present Value of Forecast Period Entity Free Cash Flow + Present Value of Continuing Value

nodes.name: Entity's Net Investment for the Current Year
aliases: Entity's Net Investment for the Year
nodes.definition: Entity's net investment for the current year refers to the net capital invested by an enterprise within a specific accounting period to maintain and expand its operating scale. Its core calculation formula is the increase in net operating assets, and it is a key component in calculating entity free cash flow.

operands.metric: Increase in Net Operating Long-term Assets

formulas.source_formula: Entity's Net Investment for the Current Year = Increase in Operating Working Capital + Increase in Net Operating Long-term Assets
Entity's Net Investment for the Current Year = Capital Expenditures - Depreciation and Amortization + Increase in Operating Working Capital
Entity's Net Investment for the Current Year = Increase in Net Operating Assets

nodes.name: Environmental Impact Assessment Fee
nodes.definition: Environmental Impact Assessment Fee refers to the consulting, evaluation, review, and other related costs incurred during the pre-construction phase of a project to assess its potential environmental impacts and to prepare the Environmental Impact Statement (or Report Form) or Outline. It is a component of Other Construction Costs.

nodes.name: Equal Periodic Cash Flows
nodes.definition: Equal periodic cash flows refer to a series of cash inflows or outflows of equal amounts occurring at the end (or beginning) of each period over multiple consecutive time intervals. It is a fundamental cash flow pattern in time value of money calculations, commonly used to evaluate financial activities such as investments, loans, and savings.

nodes.name: Equal Periodic Deposit Amount
nodes.definition: The equal periodic deposit amount refers to the fixed amount that must be deposited or paid each period in equal principal and interest repayment or annuity calculations. It is typically calculated using the time value of money formula based on financial metrics such as loan principal, interest rate, and number of periods, and is used for loan repayment or savings plans. It is not a raw data item in financial statements.

nodes.name: Equal Periodic Payment
nodes.definition: Equal periodic payment refers to the fixed amount paid each period in financial transactions, calculated based on present value or future value using the periodic interest rate and the number of repayment periods. It is commonly used in scenarios such as equal principal and interest loan repayments, capital recovery, or annuity investments, and is one of the core elements in time value of money calculations.

nodes.name: Equal-Weight Allocation per Stock
nodes.definition: Equal-weight allocation per stock is the per-security investment amount when constructing an equal-weight portfolio, where total capital is divided evenly across all holdings regardless of their market capitalization. It reflects a uniform allocation approach in portfolio construction and assumes a positive number of securities, excluding trading costs and taxes.

formulas.source_formula: Equal-Weight Allocation per Stock = Total Investment ÷ Number of Stocks

nodes.name: Equated Monthly Installment (EMI)
nodes.definition: Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) is the fixed monthly payment a borrower makes to amortize a loan under the reducing-balance method, covering both interest and principal over the loan term. It is calculated using the standard annuity formula based on the monthly interest rate and the total number of payments; when the interest rate is zero, EMI equals the principal divided by the number of payments.

formulas.source_formula: Equated Monthly Installment (EMI) = Principal × Monthly Interest Rate × (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(Total Payments) ÷ ((1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(Total Payments) - 1)

nodes.name: Equation of Exchange
nodes.definition: The equation of exchange is the macroeconomic identity MV = PQ linking the money supply (M), the velocity of money (V), the price level (P), and real output (Q). When nominal GDP (P × Q) and the velocity of money are known, the identity can be rearranged to infer the money supply as M = (P × Q) ÷ V.

nodes.name: Equilibrium Price
nodes.definition: The equilibrium price is the price at which the quantity of a good or service demanded by buyers equals the quantity supplied by sellers, resulting in a state of market balance where there is no tendency for price to change unless external factors alter supply or demand.

formulas.source_formula: Equilibrium Price = Supply Price
Equilibrium Price = (Demand Price per Unit × Quantity Demanded + Supply Price per Unit × Quantity Supplied) ÷ (Supply Price per Unit + Demand Price per Unit)

nodes.name: Equipment
