These items typically include depreciation, amortization, asset impairment provisions, deferred taxes, etc. The purpose of the adjustment is to convert net profit under the accrual basis to cash flow from operating activities under the cash basis.

nodes.name: First Period Return
aliases: Holding Period Yield (for the first period)
nodes.definition: First Period Return refers to the rate of return generated by an investment during the first specific time period (such as the first month, first quarter, or first year) in a multi-period investment or asset holding process. It is commonly used to measure the performance of an investment in its initial stage.

nodes.name: First Period Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: First Period Sales Revenue refers to the total revenue generated by an enterprise from its principal business activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific reporting period (typically the first financial quarter or first period). Its calculation is generally based on the product of sales volume and unit selling price during that period, reflecting the initial results of business activities for that period.

nodes.name: First Period Tax Adjustment Decrease Amount
nodes.definition: The First Period Tax Adjustment Decrease Amount refers to the amount that must be deducted from the total accounting profit when calculating the taxable income for corporate income tax in the first period, in accordance with tax regulations. These deduction items primarily include expenses deductible before tax under tax law but not recorded as current period costs or expenses in accounting records, as well as items from prior years that were subject to tax adjustment increases and can be carried forward for deduction in the current period as per tax regulations, such as prior-year losses allowed to be offset under tax law and tax-exempt income like government bond interest.

nodes.name: First Period Tax Adjustment Increase
aliases: Taxable Income Adjustment Increase for the First Period
nodes.definition: First Period Tax Adjustment Increase refers to the portion of taxable income that must be added back when calculating the first period income tax, based on tax regulations that adjust accounting profit for tax purposes. It primarily arises from differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations, such as employee welfare expenses exceeding deduction limits, trade union dues, tax penalties, and other items that are recorded as expenses in accounting but are not deductible or are subject to deduction limits when calculating taxable income.

nodes.name: First Period Taxable Income
aliases: Taxable Income for the First Period
nodes.definition: First Period Taxable Income refers to the adjusted taxable income amount for an enterprise or individual in the first calculation period of a tax year or a specific tax period (e.g., quarterly prepayment), as stipulated by tax laws, when calculating the income tax payable. It serves as the basis for calculating the first period income tax payable.

nodes.name: First Period Total Profit
aliases: Total Profit for the First Period
nodes.definition: First Period Total Profit refers to the aggregate final profit realized by an enterprise through all its operating activities (including main business, other business, and non-operating income and expenses) within a specific accounting period (such as the first quarter, first month, or first phase of a project), serving as the basis for calculating income tax for that period.

formulas.source_formula: First Resistance (R1) = (Pivot Point × 2) - Low Price
First Support (S1) = (Pivot Point × 2) - High Price
First Total Payments = First Mortgage Term (Years) × Months per Year

nodes.name: First Year Capital Expenditure in the Continuing Period
aliases: Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Terminal Period
First-Year CapEx in the Perpetuity Phase
Initial CapEx of the Continuing Period
永续期第一年资本性投资
nodes.definition: First Year Capital Expenditure in the Continuing Period refers to the cash paid by a company in the first year of entering the stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or perpetual period) in business valuation (such as the Discounted Free Cash Flow model) for investments in assets with a benefit period exceeding one year, aimed at maintaining or expanding long-term operational capacity. It is primarily used for acquiring or updating long-term assets such as fixed assets and intangible assets, and serves as a crucial deduction item when calculating the free cash flow for the first year of the continuing period.

nodes.name: First Year Continuing Period Free Cash Flow
First Year Operating Current Liabilities in the Continuing Period
aliases: First-Year Operating Current Liabilities of the Subsequent Phase
Operating Current Liabilities in the First Year of the Following Period
投产首年经营性流动负债
经营期第一年流动负债
nodes.definition: First Year Operating Current Liabilities in the Continuing Period refer to the debts arising from daily business operations (such as purchasing raw materials, receiving services, etc.) in the first year after a project or operation enters a stable phase (i.e., the starting year of the continuing period), which are expected to be repaid within one year. It is one of the key underlying data for calculating changes in operating working capital.

nodes.name: First Year of Continuing Period Capital Expenditures
First Year of Continuing Period Depreciation and Amortization
First Year of Continuing Period Equity Cash Flow
nodes.definition: First Year of Continuing Period Equity Cash Flow refers to the cash flow freely available to shareholders in the first year of the continuing period during business valuation, serving as a key metric for equity valuation using the equity cash flow discount model. It is derived from a composite calculation of financial indicators such as after-tax operating profit, increase in net operating assets, after-tax interest expense, and increase in net debt, reflecting the net cash amount available for distribution to shareholders after meeting reinvestment needs and debt obligations.

formulas.source_formula: First Year of Continuing Period Equity Cash Flow = After-tax Operating Profit - After-tax Interest Expense - Increase in Net Operating Assets + Increase in Net Debt

First Year of Continuing Period Equity Cash Flow = Net Profit + Depreciation and Amortization - Increase in Working Capital + Increase in Long-term Operating Liabilities - Increase in Long-term Operating Assets - Capital Expenditure + New Interest-bearing Debt - Debt Principal Repayment

nodes.name: First Year of Continuing Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm
aliases: Free Cash Flow to the Firm for the First Year of Subsequent Period
后续期第一年企业实体现金流量
nodes.definition: First Year of Continuing Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm is a specific instance of Free Cash Flow to the Firm in the first year of the continuing period. It is a composite metric used to calculate the present value of the continuing period value, reflecting the cash flow generated from a company's operating activities and productive asset investments. It can be calculated using financial metrics such as Net Operating Profit After Tax, depreciation and amortization, increase in operating working capital, and capital expenditures.

operands.metric: First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
First Year of Continuing Period Increase in Net Operating Assets

formulas.source_formula: First Year of Continuing Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax - First Year of Continuing Period Increase in Net Operating Assets

operands.metric: First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
First Year of Continuing Period Net Investment in Net Operating Assets

formulas.source_formula: First Year of Continuing Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax - First Year of Continuing Period Net Investment in Net Operating Assets

operands.metric: First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
Increase in Operating Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period
First Year of Continuing Period Capital Expenditures

formulas.source_formula: First Year of Continuing Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax - First Year of Continuing Period Increase in Operating Working Capital - First Year of Continuing Period Capital Expenditures

operands.metric: First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
First Year of Continuing Period Depreciation and Amortization
Increase in Operating Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period
First Year of Continuing Period Capital Expenditures

formulas.source_formula: First Year of Continuing Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax + First Year of Continuing Period Depreciation and Amortization - First Year of Continuing Period Increase in Operating Working Capital - First Year of Continuing Period Capital Expenditures

nodes.name: First Year of Continuing Period Increase in Net Operating Assets
First Year of Continuing Period Net Investment in Net Operating Assets
First Year of Continuing Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
First Year of Terminal Period Capital Expenditure
aliases: Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Subsequent Period
后续期第一年资本性支出
nodes.definition: First Year of Terminal Period Capital Expenditure refers to the cash outflow incurred in the first year of entering the stable growth stage (terminal period) in enterprise valuation or free cash flow forecasting, aimed at maintaining or expanding the scale of operating long-term assets. It is essentially the application of the capital expenditure concept at a specific forecast point in time, typically calculated based on changes in operating long-term assets and operating long-term liabilities, and is a key component in calculating the first year's entity free cash flow in the terminal period.

nodes.name: First-Period Cash Flow of the Continuing Period
aliases: First-Year Cash Flow in Terminal Period
永续期第一期现金流量
终值期第一期现金流量
nodes.definition: The first-period cash flow of the continuing period is the projected cash flow used in financial valuation to calculate the present value of the continuing period's cash flows. It is typically derived based on the cash flow of the final forecast period, the perpetual growth rate, or other financial metrics (such as revenue and costs), and serves as a key input variable in discounted cash flow models.

operands.metric: Operating Cash Flow of the Final Forecast Period

formulas.source_formula: First-Period Cash Flow of the Continuing Period = Operating Cash Flow of the Final Forecast Period × (1 + Perpetual Growth Rate)

operands.metric: Free Cash Flow of the Final Forecast Period

formulas.source_formula: First-Period Cash Flow of the Continuing Period = Free Cash Flow of the Final Forecast Period × (1 + Perpetual Growth Rate)

operands.metric: Operating Revenue of the Final Forecast Period

formulas.source_formula: First-Period Cash Flow of the Continuing Period = Operating Revenue of the Final Forecast Period × (1 + Growth Rate) × Operating Cash Flow Ratio

nodes.name: First-Year Cash Flow of the Continuing Period
aliases: First Year Cash Flow in the Terminal Period
First Year Cash Flow of Terminal Period
First Year Free Cash Flow in the Perpetuity Stage
永续增长期起点现金流
永续期第一年现金流量
稳定期第一年自由现金流
nodes.definition: First-Year Cash Flow of the Continuing Period refers to the free cash flow generated in the first year of the stable growth phase (continuing period) in corporate valuation models (such as two-stage or three-stage models). It is a composite metric calculated based on forecasted fundamental data including operating revenue, costs, depreciation, capital expenditures, and changes in working capital, and serves as a key input variable for calculating the terminal value of the continuing period.

formulas.source_formula: First-Year Cash Flow of the Continuing Period = Net Operating Profit After Tax + Depreciation and Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Increase in Working Capital
First-Year Cash Flow of the Continuing Period = Earnings Before Interest and Taxes × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation and Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Increase in Working Capital

nodes.name: First-Year Maintenance Capital Expenditure in the Terminal Period
aliases: First Year of Terminal Period Maintenance Capital Expenditure
Sustaining Capex in First Year of Perpetuity Period
后续期首年维持性投资
稳定期第一年资本性支出
nodes.definition: In financial forecasting, when a company enters the stable growth phase (i.e., the terminal or perpetual period), this refers to the cash outlay required in the first year for the acquisition, replacement, or upgrading of long-term operating assets (such as plants and equipment) to maintain the existing scale and capacity of operations. This expenditure is not for expansion but to sustain the company's current profitability and asset base.

nodes.name: Fiscal Assistance
nodes.definition: Fiscal assistance refers to funds or asset support provided by the government or other external entities to enterprises or individuals that does not require direct repayment. It is typically used to encourage specific economic activities, offset costs, or provide relief. In accounting treatment, it is generally recognized as non-operating income or deferred revenue.

nodes.name: Fiscal Deficit
nodes.definition: Fiscal deficit refers to the shortfall when a government's total expenditures exceed its total revenues (excluding borrowed funds), indicating the need for borrowing to cover the gap.

formulas.source_formula: Fiscal Deficit = Government Spending - Government Revenue
Fiscal Deficit Percentage = (Fiscal Deficit ÷ GDP) × 100

nodes.name: Fiscal Deficit as Percentage of GDP
nodes.definition: Fiscal deficit as a percentage of GDP measures the government’s fiscal shortfall relative to the size of the economy, indicating the scale of deficit in proportion to national output.

nodes.name: Fiscal Multiplier
nodes.definition: The fiscal multiplier measures the ratio of change in national income (GDP) to an exogenous change in government spending or taxation, indicating the amplification effect of fiscal policy on economic output.

formulas.source_formula: Fiscal Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 - Marginal Propensity to Consume)

nodes.name: Fiscal Year
nodes.definition: A fiscal year refers to a 12-month period used by governments, enterprises, and other organizations for accounting, budgeting, and financial reporting purposes. This period may or may not coincide with the calendar year. The fiscal year typically determines the time frame for tax calculations and the preparation of annual financial statements.

nodes.name: Fisher Transform Indicator
nodes.definition: The Fisher Transform Indicator is a technical analysis tool that converts price data into a Gaussian normal distribution, helping identify extreme price movements and potential market turning points by normalizing prices within a lookback period.

nodes.name: Five Social Insurances and One Housing Fund
aliases: 社会保险和住房公积金
nodes.definition: The Five Social Insurances and One Housing Fund is a mandatory employee benefit system stipulated by Chinese law, jointly contributed by employers and employees. The 'Five Insurances' refer to Pension Insurance, Medical Insurance, Unemployment Insurance, Work-related Injury Insurance, and Maternity Insurance. The 'One Fund' refers to the Housing Provident Fund. These contributions are typically calculated based on a percentage of the employee's wage base, withheld and remitted from the salary, and are used to provide employees with basic protections for retirement, medical care, unemployment, work-related injuries, maternity, and housing support.

nodes.name: Fixed Amount Tax Rate
nodes.definition: Fixed amount tax rate refers to a form of tax rate stipulated by tax law, where a fixed tax amount is directly levied per unit of taxable object, and does not change with the increase or decrease in the amount of the taxable object. For example, in stamp duty, certain documents are taxed per piece with a fixed amount of 5 yuan per piece, which is a type of fixed amount tax rate.

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Acquisition Cost
nodes.definition: Fixed asset acquisition cost refers to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire a fixed asset and bring it to its intended usable condition, primarily including the purchase price, transportation fees, loading and unloading charges, installation costs, and professional service fees directly related to the acquisition.

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Depreciation
nodes.definition: Fixed asset depreciation refers to the systematic and rational allocation of the original cost of a fixed asset, minus its estimated net residual value, over its estimated useful life as an expense in each accounting period, reflecting the gradual consumption of the asset's value due to usage. It is a crucial concept in financial accounting for cost allocation and asset valuation, commonly featured in professional examinations such as CPA, CFA, and ACCA.

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Depreciation of Secondary Industry in Previous Period
aliases: Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Secondary Industry of Previous Period
Previous Period Depreciation for Secondary Industry
nodes.definition: Fixed asset depreciation of the secondary industry in the previous period refers to the amount of value loss, calculated using specific methods (such as straight-line method, double-declining balance method, etc.) and recorded as cost or expense, attributable to fixed assets of the secondary industry (typically including industry and construction) during the last statistical or accounting period, due to usage, natural wear and tear, or technological obsolescence. It is a key deduction item in calculating the value added of the secondary industry for the previous period.

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Depreciation of the Secondary Industry
aliases: Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Secondary Industry
工业、建筑业固定资产折旧
nodes.definition: Fixed asset depreciation of the secondary industry refers to the process of systematically and rationally calculating and allocating the value transferred from fixed assets used in the secondary industry (industry and construction) to products or services due to wear and tear during their use. It is a component of intermediate consumption deducted when calculating the value added of the secondary industry.

operands.metric: Actual Workload in the Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Asset Depreciation of the Secondary Industry = (Original Value of Fixed Assets - Estimated Net Residual Value) ÷ Estimated Total Workload × Actual Workload in the Current Period

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Formation Rate
nodes.definition: The Fixed Asset Formation Rate is a financial metric that measures the growth or renewal scale of fixed assets within a specific period (typically an accounting period), reflecting the speed and efficiency of a company's capital investment and asset expansion.

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Investment
aliases: 资本形成总额（固定资产部分）
nodes.definition: Fixed asset investment refers to the total capital expenditure incurred by an enterprise for the acquisition, expansion, or renewal of fixed assets. It is a key metric for measuring project investment scale, calculating initial invested capital, and capital budgeting, typically accounted for based on the composition of the total investment in a construction project.

operands.metric: Purchase Investment of Equipment and Tools

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Asset Investment = Construction Project Investment + Installation Project Investment + Purchase Investment of Equipment and Tools + Other Expenses
Fixed Asset Investment = Engineering Costs + Other Construction Project Expenses + Contingency Reserve + Construction Period Interest
Fixed Asset Investment = Engineering Costs + Other Construction Project Costs + Contingency Reserve + Construction Period Interest

nodes.name: Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: Fixed Asset Turnover Ratio measures a company's efficiency in generating net sales from its investments in fixed assets, calculated by dividing net sales by the average fixed assets during a period.

nodes.name: Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Fixed assets refer to tangible assets held for the production or supply of goods and services, for rental to others, or for administrative purposes, with an expected useful life exceeding one accounting period. Such assets are not held for direct sale to customers and cannot be easily converted into cash.

nodes.name: Fixed Assets Transferred from Construction in Current Period
aliases: Current Period Transfer-in of Fixed Assets Acquired or Constructed
Fixed Assets Acquired or Constructed in Current Period
本期购建固定资产转入额
nodes.definition: Fixed Assets Transferred from Construction in Current Period refers to the total value of assets that are newly added through purchase, self-construction, or installation, reach their intended usable state within the current accounting period, and are formally transferred from accounts such as 'Construction in Progress' to the 'Fixed Assets' account for accounting purposes. It reflects the scale of fixed assets actually put into use by the enterprise during the period.

nodes.name: Fixed Conversion Cost per Securities Transaction
aliases: Fixed Transaction Cost for Securities Conversion
有价证券转换固定费用
nodes.definition: Fixed conversion cost per securities transaction refers to the fixed fee that a company must pay each time it sells securities and converts them into cash in cash management (such as the inventory model). This cost is independent of the conversion amount and typically includes transaction costs such as handling fees and commissions.

nodes.name: Fixed Cost
nodes.definition: Fixed cost refers to costs that do not vary with the level of business activity (such as production volume) within the relevant range. It typically includes expenses such as rent, equipment depreciation, and management salaries, and is a key concept in cost behavior analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Cost = Total Cost - Total Variable Cost

operands.metric: Total Cost at Lowest Production Level

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Cost = Total Cost at Lowest Production Level - Unit Variable Cost × Lowest Production Volume

operands.metric: Total Cost at Highest Production Level

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Cost = Total Cost at Highest Production Level - Unit Variable Cost × Highest Production Volume

nodes.name: Fixed Cost per Transaction
nodes.definition: Fixed cost per transaction refers to the cost that is incurred each time a transaction (such as a securities trade or cash conversion) occurs, is fixed in amount, and is independent of the number of transactions. It is a key parameter in financial models such as cash management and inventory management.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Cost per Transaction = (Total Cost - Unit Opportunity Cost × Average Cash Balance) ÷ Total Transaction Volume

nodes.name: Fixed Cost per Unit
nodes.definition: Fixed cost per unit refers to the average fixed cost allocated to each unit of product produced by an enterprise within a certain period. Fixed costs are those that do not vary with changes in production volume, such as rent, equipment depreciation, and managerial salaries.

nodes.name: Fixed Costs
nodes.definition: Fixed costs refer to expenses whose total amount does not change with variations in business volume (such as production or sales) within a certain period and a specific range of activity. Examples include rent, equipment depreciation, and management salaries. These costs remain essentially constant regardless of whether production occurs or the level of production.

nodes.name: Fixed Dividend
nodes.definition: Fixed dividend refers to the cash return paid by a company to its shareholders periodically (e.g., quarterly or annually) at a predetermined, fixed amount per share. The payment amount typically does not fluctuate with short-term variations in the company's earnings, aiming to provide investors with stable and predictable cash flow.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Dividend = Net Profit × Fixed Dividend Payout Ratio

nodes.name: Fixed Dividend Payout Ratio
nodes.definition: Fixed Dividend Payout Ratio refers to a dividend policy adopted by a company, whereby the company commits to distributing a fixed percentage of its net profit as dividends to shareholders each year. This percentage is the dividend payout ratio, which directly links dividend payments to the company's profitability level—higher profits result in higher dividends, and lower profits result in lower dividends.

nodes.name: Fixed Dividend Rate
nodes.definition: Fixed dividend rate refers to the dividend amount calculated from the current year's net profit and paid to preferred shareholders according to a predetermined, fixed dividend payout ratio. This amount is a calculated result, not a raw data item directly obtained from financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Dividend Rate = Current Year Net Profit × Fixed Dividend Payout Ratio

nodes.name: Fixed Income
nodes.definition: Fixed income refers to any type of investment where the borrower or issuer is obligated to make payments of a fixed amount on a fixed schedule. For example, the borrower may be required to pay interest at a fixed rate once a year and repay the principal at maturity. Fixed income securities (more commonly known as bonds) contrast with equity securities, which do not entail any obligation to pay dividends or any form of return.

nodes.name: Fixed Interest
nodes.definition: Fixed interest refers to the interest amount calculated based on the principal and the interest accrual period according to a predetermined fixed interest rate in financial transactions or investments. It is a core cash flow element of fixed-income instruments (such as bonds and term deposits).

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Interest = Principal × Fixed Interest Rate × Interest Accrual Period
Fixed Interest Payment = Fixed Rate × Notional Amount ÷ Payment Frequency

nodes.name: Fixed Interest Payment (Interest Rate Swap)
nodes.definition: Fixed interest payment in an interest rate swap is the periodic cash flow paid by the fixed-rate payer on the swap's notional principal. It is calculated as the fixed rate multiplied by the notional amount and adjusted by the accrual period expressed as the number of payments per year (i.e., 1 ÷ payment frequency). This represents the fixed leg coupon amount and does not involve exchange of notional principal.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Leg Payment = Notional Amount × ((1 + Fixed Rate) ^ Years - 1)

nodes.name: Fixed Interest Rate
nodes.definition: A fixed interest rate refers to an interest rate that remains unchanged throughout the term of a loan, bond, or investment. It is widely used in financial instruments such as mortgages and fixed-income securities to provide predictable interest payments.

nodes.name: Fixed Labor Cost
nodes.definition: Fixed labor cost refers to the labor expenses required to complete specific project quantities, calculated according to predetermined quota standards (such as consumption quotas) in project budgeting or cost accounting. It is typically derived by multiplying labor consumption (e.g., number of workdays) by the fixed labor unit price (budget price), and constitutes an important component of project cost.

nodes.name: Fixed Leg Present Value
aliases: Present Value of the Fixed Leg
nodes.definition: Fixed Leg Present Value is the present value of the fixed-rate cash flows in an interest rate swap. It is a composite value metric obtained by discounting and summing all future fixed interest payments and any potential principal exchange at maturity using the corresponding spot rates or discount factors for each period. In standard interest rate swap pricing, the fixed leg present value equals the floating leg present value.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Leg Present Value = Floating Leg Present Value

nodes.name: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Budget
aliases: 固定制造费用预算金额
nodes.definition: Fixed manufacturing overhead budget refers to the total predetermined manufacturing overhead costs that do not vary directly with production volume, established for the planned output during the budget period, such as managerial salaries, factory depreciation, and long-term lease expenses. It serves as a critical benchmark for cost control and variance analysis.

nodes.name: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Cost Variance
aliases: 固定制造费用成本差异
nodes.definition: Fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance is the difference between actual fixed manufacturing overhead and standard fixed manufacturing overhead, used to measure the overall control of fixed manufacturing overhead.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Cost Variance = Spending Variance + Volume Variance
Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Cost Variance = Actual Fixed Manufacturing Overhead - Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead

nodes.name: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Spending Variance
aliases: 固定制造费用耗用差异
nodes.definition: Fixed manufacturing overhead spending variance refers to the difference between the actual fixed manufacturing overhead incurred and the budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead, reflecting the effectiveness of fixed cost control.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Spending Variance = Actual Fixed Manufacturing Overhead - Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead

nodes.name: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Allocation Rate
aliases: 固定制造费用标准分配率
nodes.definition: The fixed manufacturing overhead standard allocation rate is the budgeted amount of fixed manufacturing overhead allocated per unit of standard labor hour. It is calculated based on budget data and standard hours, serving as a composite metric used for cost control and variance analysis, particularly in the calculation of fixed manufacturing overhead capacity variance.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Allocation Rate = Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Standard Direct Labor Hours

operands.metric: Total Standard Hours at Budgeted Production Level

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Allocation Rate = Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Standard Hours at Budgeted Production Level

nodes.name: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost
aliases: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Cost per Unit
单位产品固定制造费用标准成本
nodes.definition: Fixed manufacturing overhead standard cost is the fixed manufacturing overhead allocated per unit of product under the standard costing method. It is calculated from the fixed manufacturing overhead standard allocation rate and the standard hours per unit of product. It is a composite indicator, not a basic raw data point, and is commonly used in the calculation of volume variance within fixed manufacturing overhead variance analysis.

operands.metric: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Allocation Rate

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost = Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Allocation Rate × Standard Hours per Unit

operands.metric: Standard Direct Labor Hours per Unit
Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Rate per Hour

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost = Standard Direct Labor Hours per Unit × Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Rate per Hour
Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost = (Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Budgeted Hours) × Standard Hours per Unit
Fixed Monthly Payment = Principal × (Monthly Interest Rate × (1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ Number of Payments) ÷ ((1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ Number of Payments − 1)

nodes.name: Fixed Operating Costs
nodes.definition: Fixed operating costs refer to operating costs whose total amount does not change with the level of business activity within a certain period and range of activity. They constitute the portion of total costs after deducting variable costs and can be calculated using formulas such as total costs minus variable costs or the high-low point method.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Operating Costs = Lowest Activity Level Cost - Unit Variable Cost × Lowest Activity Level

nodes.name: Fixed Overhead Efficiency Variance
aliases: 固定制造费用效率差异
nodes.definition: Fixed overhead efficiency variance is the difference in fixed overhead allocation caused by the variance between actual hours and standard hours, reflecting the impact of production efficiency on fixed costs.

nodes.name: Fixed Overhead Volume Variance
aliases: 固定制造费用能量差异
nodes.definition: Fixed overhead volume variance is the difference in fixed overhead allocation caused by the variance between actual production and budgeted capacity, reflecting the degree of production capacity utilization.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed Overhead Volume Variance = (Production Capacity ÷ Standard Hours - Actual Output ÷ Standard Hours) × Standard Fixed Overhead Allocation Rate
Fixed Payment = Notional Principal × Fixed Rate

nodes.name: Fixed Price
nodes.definition: Fixed price refers to a price predetermined in a contract or agreement that remains unchanged throughout the contract period. It is not adjusted for market fluctuations, cost changes, or variations in production volume, providing both parties with a clear and stable cost or revenue expectation.

nodes.name: Fixed Transportation Cost
nodes.definition: Fixed transportation cost refers to the portion of costs in transportation operations that does not vary with changes in transportation volume (such as ton-kilometers or freight volume). These costs are typically associated with maintaining transportation capacity and must be paid regardless of whether transportation services are performed, including expenses such as vehicle depreciation, loan interest, salaries of permanent staff, insurance premiums, and fixed administrative fees.

nodes.name: Fixed-Charge Coverage Ratio
nodes.definition: Fixed-Charge Coverage Ratio measures a company's ability to cover its fixed obligations—such as lease payments and interest expense—from its earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT). A higher ratio indicates stronger capacity to service fixed charges and lower default risk.

formulas.source_formula: Fixed-Charge Coverage Ratio = EBIT ÷ Fixed Charges
Fixed-Charge Coverage Ratio = (EBIT + Fixed Charges Before Tax) ÷ (Fixed Charges Before Tax + Interest Expense)

nodes.name: Fixed-Rate Mortgage Monthly Payment
aliases: 固定利率抵押贷款月供
nodes.definition: The fixed monthly payment required to amortize a fixed-rate mortgage loan over its term, incorporating both principal repayment and interest, calculated using the annuity formula.

nodes.name: Fixed-Rate Payment
nodes.definition: Fixed-rate payment refers to the constant monthly payment required to fully amortize a loan with a fixed interest rate over a specified term, calculated using the annuity formula.

nodes.name: Fixtures
nodes.definition: Fixtures refer to permanent assets installed to enhance the functionality of a property or premises, which are difficult to move and typically cause damage upon removal, such as retail store shelving, hotel kitchen equipment, and office partitions. In accounting, they are classified as fixed assets, their value is recorded on the balance sheet, and their cost is allocated through depreciation.

nodes.name: Float
nodes.definition: Float represents the difference between a firm's available bank balance and its book balance, reflecting the net effect of checks in the process of clearing and the timing difference between cash recording and cash availability.

formulas.source_formula: Float = Available Balance - Book Balance

Float-Down Net Savings = [(Loan Amount × (Original Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12)) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Original Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12))^- (Loan Term (Years) × 12)) - (Loan Amount × (New Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12)) ÷ (1 - (1 + (New Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12))^- (Loan Term (Years) × 12))] × (Loan Term (Years) × 12) - Loan Amount × (Float-Down Fee Percentage ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Floating Interest Payment (Interest Rate Swap)
nodes.definition: The floating interest payment in an interest rate swap is the periodic coupon paid by the floating-rate leg on the notional principal. It is computed using the effective floating rate—equal to the reference rate plus the contractual spread—applied to the notional amount and prorated by the payment frequency.

formulas.source_formula: Floating Interest Payment = (Reference Rate + Spread) × Notional Amount ÷ Payment Frequency

nodes.name: Floating Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Floating interest rate is the sum of a benchmark base rate and a fixed margin, commonly used in adjustable-rate loans where the rate varies with market conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Floating Interest Rate = Base Rate + Margin

nodes.name: Floating Leg Present Value
nodes.definition: Floating Leg Present Value is the current discounted value of future cash flows calculated based on the floating rate in an Interest Rate Swap (IRS). It is derived by summing the discounted floating rate cash flows for each period using discount factors, relying on underlying data such as forward rates, accrual period lengths, notional principal, and discount rates. It is a key component in the pricing and valuation of interest rate swaps.

formulas.source_formula: Floating Payment = Notional Principal × (Floating Rate + Inflation Rate)

nodes.name: Floating Rate
nodes.definition: A floating rate refers to an interest rate in a borrowing or investment contract whose specific value is not fixed but is periodically adjusted according to changes in an agreed market benchmark rate (such as the Loan Prime Rate LPR or the London Interbank Offered Rate LIBOR). It is typically determined by adding or subtracting an agreed spread (floating points) from the benchmark rate.

nodes.name: Floating Stock
nodes.definition: Floating stock represents the number of a company's outstanding shares that are available for public trading, calculated by subtracting closely-held and restricted shares from total outstanding shares.

formulas.source_formula: Floating Stock = Total Outstanding Shares - (Closely-Held Shares + Restricted Shares)

nodes.name: Floating Strike Price (Lookback Option)
aliases: Floating Strike Lookback Option Strike Price
nodes.definition: A floating strike lookback option sets the strike at maturity to the most favorable historical price of the underlying: the minimum price over the option's life for a call and the maximum price for a put. This structure allows the holder to 'look back' over the price path to optimize the exercise level, differentiating it from fixed strike lookback options where the strike is predetermined.

nodes.name: Floor Area Ratio
nodes.definition: Floor Area Ratio (FAR) is a planning metric that measures the total usable floor area of a building divided by the total area of the lot on which the building stands, indicating the intensity of land use.

formulas.source_formula: Floor Area Ratio = Total Floor Area ÷ Lot Area

nodes.name: Floor Function
nodes.definition: The floor function is a mathematical operation that rounds a real number (which may be a decimal) down to the greatest integer less than or equal to it. For example, the floor of 5.4 is 5, and the floor of -3.7 is -4.

nodes.name: Flotation Cost Ratio
nodes.definition: The flotation cost ratio refers to the ratio of flotation costs to the total issuance amount, used to measure the financing cost in the securities issuance process. It is an indicator reflecting financing efficiency and must be considered when calculating the cost of equity capital.

formulas.source_formula: Flotation Cost Ratio = Flotation Costs ÷ Total Issuance Amount

nodes.name: Forecast Base Value
nodes.definition: Forecast base value refers to the financial data or business metric value at a specific point in time (typically the base period or current period) that serves as the starting point in a financial or business forecasting model. It forms the input foundation and initial reference for the entire forecasting process, such as revenue, assets, user count, etc., in the base period. It is usually determined based on historical actual data or currently known data, rather than being derived through formula calculations.

nodes.name: Forecast Error
nodes.definition: Forecast error is the signed difference between a forecasted value and the corresponding actual value. It quantifies overestimation (overcasting) when positive and underestimation (undercasting) when negative, and is used in financial analysis, budgeting, demand planning, and variance analysis to assess forecast accuracy and bias.

nodes.name: Forecast Net Profit
nodes.definition: Forecast net profit refers to the estimation and projection of a company's final operating results for a specific future period (e.g., the next year or several years ahead), based on assumptions such as historical financial data, business plans, and market conditions. It represents the residual profit after subtracting all costs, expenses, and taxes from revenue.

nodes.name: Forecast Period
nodes.definition: Forecast period refers to the specific years or time series set in a financial forecasting model for estimating future financial position, operating results, and cash flows. It is a fundamental time parameter used to determine the baseline point and time span of the forecast.

nodes.name: Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to Firm
Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm
aliases: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
nodes.definition: Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm refers to the cash flow generated from operating activities and productive asset investment activities during the forecast period, which is available for discretionary use by all investors (creditors and shareholders). Its calculation is based on financial metrics such as Net Operating Profit After Tax, depreciation and amortization, increases in operating working capital, and capital expenditures. It is commonly used in the Discounted Cash Flow model for enterprise valuation.

formulas.source_formula: Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Net Operating Profit After Tax - Increase in Operating Working Capital - Capital Expenditures
Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Net Operating Profit After Tax + Depreciation and Amortization - Increase in Operating Working Capital - Capital Expenditures

nodes.name: Forecast Period Fund Turnover Speed Growth Rate
aliases: Growth Rate of Forecasted Capital Turnover Speed
预测期周转速度增长率
nodes.definition: The forecast period fund turnover speed growth rate refers to the expected increase in a company's fund turnover speed (typically measured by turnover frequency or turnover days) during a future period relative to the base period or the previous period. This indicator reflects the company's expectation regarding the improvement or decline in future fund utilization efficiency.

nodes.name: Forecast Period Sales Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The forecast period sales growth rate refers to the estimated ratio of the increase in sales revenue for a future specific period (such as the next year or several years ahead), based on historical data, market analysis, and future planning. It reflects the company's anticipated business expansion speed.

nodes.name: Forecast Period Years
nodes.definition: Forecast period years refer to the length of time used for detailed year-by-year projections in financial forecasting or business valuation models. It is a preset input parameter, typically determined based on industry practice or specific valuation requirements, during which key financial metrics (such as revenue, costs, cash flow, etc.) are projected annually. After the forecast period ends, the business is usually assumed to enter a stable growth phase (terminal period).

nodes.name: Forecast Terminal Value
nodes.definition: Forecast terminal value refers to the estimated value at the end of the forecast period, calculated based on parameters such as the base period indicator and expected growth rate in financial forecasting models. It is commonly used in valuation analyses like discounted cash flow models and growth models, and serves as a composite metric referenced for calculating derived indicators such as the average expected growth rate.

formulas.source_formula: Forecast Terminal Value = Final Period Free Cash Flow × (1 + Perpetual Growth Rate) ÷ (Discount Rate - Perpetual Growth Rate)
Forecast Terminal Value = Base Period Value × (1 + Expected Compound Annual Growth Rate) ^ Forecast Period Years

nodes.name: Forecast Total Shares Outstanding
nodes.definition: Forecast total shares outstanding refers to the estimated total number of all types of shares issued by a company (such as common shares and preferred shares) at a specific future point in time, based on factors including the company's future development plans, financing plans (such as additional share issuance, rights issues, share repurchases), or equity incentive schemes. It serves as a critical foundational data point for forecasting financial metrics such as earnings per share.

nodes.name: Forecasted Cash Collections
nodes.definition: Forecasted cash collections represent the estimated cash inflows expected to be received from credit sales within a specific period, calculated by applying historical or expected collection percentages to the sales forecast.

nodes.name: Forecasted Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Forecasted Earnings Per Share is a composite metric calculated by dividing forecasted net profit by forecasted total shares outstanding, based on estimates of a company's future net profit and share capital. It serves as a crucial foundation for assessing a company's future profitability and conducting valuation analysis (e.g., calculating forward P/E ratio).

formulas.source_formula: Forecasted EPS = Forecasted Net Profit ÷ Forecasted Total Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Forecasted Net Profit
nodes.definition: Forecasted net profit refers to the estimate or projection made by a company or analysts regarding the likely final operating result (i.e., the net amount after deducting income tax expense from total profit) for a future specific accounting period (e.g., the next period), based on historical data, business plans, market conditions, and other factors.

nodes.name: Forecasted Net Profit Per Share
nodes.definition: Forecasted Net Profit Per Share refers to the estimation and projection made by analysts or investors regarding a company's net profit per share for a future period (such as the next quarter or fiscal year), based on their assessment of the company's future operating conditions, industry prospects, and market environment. It is a crucial forward-looking indicator for evaluating a company's future profitability and the potential value of its stock.

nodes.name: Forecasted Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Forecasted operating revenue refers to the estimation and projection of total sales revenue that a company is expected to achieve over a specific future period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or annually), based on historical data, market conditions, expert judgment, and other methodologies.

nodes.name: Forecasted Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Forecasted sales revenue is the expected monetary value of future sales over a planning horizon, calculated by multiplying the anticipated number of units to be sold by the selling price per unit. It supports budgeting, sales planning, and financial forecasting by translating unit sales expectations into revenue terms.

formulas.source_formula: Forecasted Sales Revenue = Anticipated Units × Selling Price per Unit

nodes.name: Forecasted Total Profit
nodes.definition: Forecasted total profit refers to the pre-estimated sum of all profits that an enterprise may achieve in a specific future period (e.g., the next period), based on assumptions and judgments about future operating conditions and using financial models or analytical methods (such as cost-volume-profit analysis). It is typically used for budgeting, performance target setting, and investment decision-making.

nodes.name: Foregone Earnings
nodes.definition: Foregone earnings represent the investment returns that an investor fails to realize because fees are deducted from the portfolio, calculated as the difference between potential earnings without fees and actual earnings received.

formulas.source_formula: Foregone Earnings = Potential Earnings - Actual Earnings
Foregone Earnings = Fee Cost₂ - Fee Cost₁

nodes.name: Foregone Earnings Due to Fund Fees
aliases: 基金费用导致的放弃收益
nodes.definition: Foregone earnings due to fund fees represent the additional investment returns that are lost by choosing a fund with higher expense ratios instead of a lower-cost alternative, calculated as the difference in fee costs applied to the same investment amount.

nodes.name: Foreign Currency Assets
nodes.definition: Foreign currency assets refer to various assets held by an enterprise that are denominated or settled in currencies other than the functional currency, such as foreign currency bank deposits, foreign currency accounts receivable, and financial assets denominated in foreign currencies. Their amounts are directly derived from records at the time of foreign currency transactions or are translated into the functional currency amount using the spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date.

nodes.name: Foreign Currency Financial Statement Translation Difference
nodes.definition: Foreign currency financial statement translation difference refers to the difference recognized in other comprehensive income that arises from translating assets, liabilities, and equity items at different exchange rates when converting the financial statements of foreign operations or those denominated in foreign currencies into the reporting currency. It reflects the impact of exchange rate fluctuations on net assets.

formulas.source_formula: Foreign Currency Financial Statement Translation Difference = Assets Translated into RMB - Liabilities Translated into RMB - Owners' Equity Translated into RMB

operands.metric: Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets
Spot Exchange Rate on Balance Sheet Date
Opening RMB Balance of Owners' Equity

formulas.source_formula: Foreign Currency Financial Statement Translation Difference = Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets × Spot Exchange Rate on Balance Sheet Date - (Opening RMB Balance of Owners' Equity + Adjusted Net Profit × Average Exchange Rate)

nodes.name: Foreign Currency Liabilities
nodes.definition: Foreign currency liabilities refer to debts that an enterprise undertakes, which are denominated and repayable in foreign currencies (such as US dollars, euros, etc.). It is a specific item on the enterprise's balance sheet, directly reflecting the amount of debt settled in foreign currency arising from business operations or financing activities.

nodes.name: Foreign Exchange
nodes.definition: Foreign exchange, as a quantifiable financial variable, refers to the net difference between foreign currency assets and foreign currency liabilities held by an enterprise or country, used to measure foreign exchange risk exposure.

nodes.name: Foreign Exchange Impact
nodes.definition: Foreign exchange impact measures the financial gain or loss resulting from fluctuations in exchange rates between the contract initiation date and the payment date for international transactions denominated in foreign currency.

formulas.source_formula: FX Impact = Final Amount - Initial Amount

nodes.name: Foreign Exchange Option Premium Variation
aliases: Change in Foreign Exchange Option Premium
nodes.definition: Foreign exchange option premium variation refers to the upward or downward fluctuation of the market price (i.e., the option premium or premium) of a foreign exchange option contract over time. This variation results from the combined effects of various factors such as market supply and demand, underlying exchange rates, volatility, and time to expiration. It is directly observed market data rather than derived from formula calculations.

nodes.name: Foreign Exchange RMB Parity
nodes.definition: Foreign Exchange RMB Parity refers to the base exchange rate data directly quoted by banks based on factors such as market supply and demand, international exchange rates, and national policies. It indicates how much Renminbi can be exchanged for a unit of foreign currency (e.g., 1 US dollar or 100 units of foreign currency) and serves as the original reference price for foreign exchange transactions and settlements.

nodes.name: Foreign Housing Exclusion
nodes.definition: Foreign housing exclusion is the amount of qualified foreign housing expenses that exceed a base housing amount (16% of the maximum foreign earned income exclusion, prorated by qualifying days) and may be excluded from U.S. taxable income for eligible taxpayers.

nodes.name: Foreign Tax Credit
nodes.definition: The Foreign Tax Credit is a nonrefundable income tax credit that reduces domestic tax liability by the amount of income taxes paid or accrued to foreign jurisdictions on foreign-source income, subject to a limitation tied to the proportion of foreign income relative to total worldwide income.

formulas.source_formula: Foreign Tax Credit = min(Foreign Tax Paid, Foreign Income ÷ Total Income)
Foreign Tax Credit = min(U.S. Tax Rate × Foreign-Source Income, Foreign Tax Rate × Foreign-Source Income)

nodes.name: Foreign Tax Credit Limit
nodes.definition: The foreign tax credit limit refers to the maximum amount of foreign income tax paid that a company is allowed to deduct from its domestic tax payable when calculating its income tax liability. Its purpose is to avoid international double taxation while preventing companies from excessively reducing their domestic tax burden through foreign losses or taxes paid in low-tax jurisdictions.

nodes.name: Foreign Tax Credit Limitation for a Specific Country (Region)
aliases: Credit Limitation for Foreign Income Tax
nodes.definition: The foreign tax credit limitation for a specific country (region) refers to the maximum amount of income tax paid in that particular country (or region) that a Chinese enterprise is allowed to credit against its Chinese corporate income tax liability calculated on its worldwide income. Its purpose is to avoid international double taxation while preventing enterprises from improperly reducing their domestic tax obligations in China by utilizing foreign tax credits.

nodes.name: Forex Margin Required
nodes.definition: Forex margin required is the amount of collateral needed to open and maintain a leveraged foreign-exchange position, calculated as the total trade value divided by the leverage ratio.

nodes.name: Forex Pip Profit/Loss
nodes.definition: Forex pip profit/loss represents the monetary gain or loss resulting from a specified number of pip movements in a foreign exchange position. It is computed as the product of the number of pips, the pip value per unit of volume, and the trade volume, translating price changes measured in pips into currency amounts for position sizing and risk management.

formulas.source_formula: Forex Pip Profit/Loss = Number of Pips × Pip Value × Trade Volume

nodes.name: Forex Profit or Loss
nodes.definition: Forex profit or loss represents the gain or loss realized from a foreign exchange transaction, calculated as the difference between the closing and opening prices of a currency pair multiplied by the traded amount.

formulas.source_formula: Forex Profit or Loss = (Close Price - Open Price) × Amount

nodes.name: Forex Rollover
nodes.definition: Forex rollover refers to the interest credit or debit applied to a trader's account for holding a currency position overnight, calculated as the interest rate differential between the two currencies divided by 365 and multiplied by the position size.

formulas.source_formula: Rollover = (Interest Rate Differential ÷ 365) × Position Size

nodes.name: Forex Spread Cost
nodes.definition: Forex spread cost is the monetary transaction cost arising from the bid–ask spread in foreign exchange trading. It is calculated as the product of the spread (often measured in pips or decimal price units) and the trade size (number of base currency units), reflecting the immediate cost incurred when opening or closing a position.

nodes.name: Forward Contract Settlement
nodes.definition: Forward contract settlement refers to the monetary amount exchanged between counterparties at the maturity of a forward contract, calculated as the difference between the spot price at settlement and the pre-agreed forward price multiplied by the contract quantity.

nodes.name: Forward Dividend Yield
nodes.definition: Forward dividend yield is the projected annual dividend payment expressed as a percentage of the current stock price, indicating the expected cash return to shareholders over the next twelve months.

formulas.source_formula: Forward Dividend Yield = (Annual Dividend ÷ Current Stock Price) × 100
Forward Dividend Yield = (Recent Dividend × Dividends per Year ÷ Stock Price) × 100

nodes.name: Forward Exchange Rate
nodes.definition: The forward exchange rate is the agreed-upon exchange rate at which two currencies will be exchanged on a specified future date, derived from the current spot rate adjusted for the interest-rate differential between the two currencies over the contract period.

formulas.source_formula: Forward Exchange Rate = Spot Exchange Rate × (1 + Interest Rate (Country C)) ÷ (1 + Interest Rate (Country B))
Forward Rate = Spot Rate × (1 + Domestic Interest Rate × Days ÷ 360) ÷ (1 + Foreign Interest Rate × Days ÷ 360)

nodes.name: Forward P/E Ratio
nodes.definition: The forward P/E ratio is a dynamic version of the price-to-earnings ratio, calculated using forecasted future earnings per share rather than historical earnings. It is a composite indicator used to assess a company's valuation level and future profit expectations, widely applied in stock valuation techniques.

formulas.source_formula: Forward P/E Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Forecasted Earnings Per Share

nodes.name: Forward Premium
nodes.definition: Forward premium (or discount) is the percentage difference between the forward exchange rate and the spot exchange rate, indicating whether the forward currency is trading at a premium (positive) or discount (negative) relative to the spot rate.

formulas.source_formula: Forward Premium = ((Forward Rate - Spot Rate) ÷ Spot Rate) × 100

nodes.name: Forward Price
nodes.definition: Forward price is the agreed-upon exchange rate for a currency transaction that will occur at a specified future date, calculated based on the spot rate and the interest rate differential between two currencies under interest rate parity.

formulas.source_formula: Forward Price = Spot Rate × (1 + Foreign Interest Rate × Time to Maturity) ÷ (1 + Domestic Interest Rate × Time to Maturity)
Forward Price = Spot Price × exp((Risk-Free Rate + Carrying Costs) × Time to Maturity)

nodes.name: Forward Price-to-Earnings
nodes.definition: Forward P/E is a valuation ratio calculated by dividing the current market price per share by the estimated future earnings per share, reflecting investors' expectations of a company's future earnings performance.

formulas.source_formula: Forward P/E = Current Share Price ÷ Estimated Future EPS

nodes.name: Forward Price-to-Earnings Ratio
nodes.definition: The forward price-to-earnings ratio is a P/E ratio calculated based on future expected earnings (such as expected earnings per share for the next year), reflecting the market's valuation of a company's future profitability and growth potential. It is a theoretical P/E ratio derived from valuation models such as the dividend discount model and is commonly used in stock valuation.

nodes.name: Forward Rate
nodes.definition: A forward rate is the expected interest rate implied in a given spot rate curve or zero-coupon bond prices, from a specific future start date to a future end date. It is used for financial instrument pricing, interest rate risk management, and investment decisions, and is a composite metric rather than a primary accounting line item.

formulas.source_formula: Forward Rate = Spot Rate × (1 + Interest Rate Country C) ÷ (1 + Interest Rate Country B)

nodes.name: Forward Rate Agreement
nodes.definition: A Forward Rate Agreement (FRA) is a derivative contract settled in cash differences, traded between two parties based on interest rate indices such as LIBOR or EURIBOR. The agreement allows both parties to lock in a fixed rate for a notional principal over a future period to hedge against or speculate on future interest rate fluctuations, without exchanging the principal.

nodes.name: Forward Rate Agreement Payment
nodes.definition: The cash settlement amount exchanged at the start of the forward period in a Forward Rate Agreement, calculated as the present value of the difference between the contracted forward rate and the realized reference rate applied to the notional principal.

nodes.name: Four Percent Rule
nodes.definition: The Four Percent Rule is a retirement planning guideline suggesting that retirees can safely withdraw 4% of their initial retirement portfolio balance in the first year, and adjust the withdrawal amount annually for inflation, without running out of money over a 30-year retirement period.

nodes.name: Fractal Indicator
nodes.definition: A technical analysis indicator that identifies potential reversal points by finding local price extremes (highs or lows) that are higher or lower than the two preceding and two succeeding periods.

nodes.name: Fractional Shares Purchased
nodes.definition: Fractional Shares Purchased refers to the quantity of stock, including fractional units, that an investor can acquire with a specified investment amount at the prevailing share price. It indicates how many shares can be bought given available capital, assuming no transaction fees or limitations and that fractional share trading is allowed.

formulas.source_formula: Fractional Shares Purchased = Investment Amount ÷ Share Price

nodes.name: Franking Credit
nodes.definition: Franking credit represents the tax already paid by a company on dividend income, which shareholders can use to offset their personal tax liability, thereby reducing double taxation of dividends under the imputation system.

formulas.source_formula: Franking Credit = (Dividend Amount ÷ (1 - Company Tax Rate)) - Dividend Amount

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Free cash flow is the residual cash flow generated from a company's operating activities, after deducting capital expenditures and changes in net working capital, that can be freely distributed to all investors. It is a core metric for valuation techniques, intrinsic value assessment, and financial health analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Free Cash Flow = Cash Flows from Operations - Capital Expenditures
Free Cash Flow = Revenue - Operating Expenses - Capital Expenditures
Free Cash Flow = Free Cash Flow to Equity + Free Cash Flow to Firm
Free Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow - Changes in Working Capital - Capital Expenditures

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow Yield
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow Yield is a financial solvency ratio that measures the cash a company generates after capital expenditures relative to its market value per share, indicating profitability and financial health.

formulas.source_formula: Free Cash Flow Yield = (Free Cash Flow per Share ÷ Market Price per Share) × 100

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow in the Final Forecast Period
aliases: Free Cash Flow at the End of Forecast Period
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow in the final forecast period refers to the cash flow generated from operating activities in the last period of the detailed forecast horizon within a business valuation or financial forecasting model, which is available for discretionary use by all capital providers (including creditors and shareholders) after meeting reinvestment needs. It serves as the basis for calculating the present value of cash flows in the terminal (perpetuity) period and is typically derived from forecasts of components such as Net Operating Profit After Tax, depreciation and amortization, changes in working capital, and capital expenditures.

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow in the Final Year of the Forecast Period
aliases: 预测期末自由现金流量
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow in the Final Year of the Forecast Period refers to the cash flow generated from operating activities in the last year of the detailed forecast period, based on corporate financial projections, which is available for discretionary use by all capital providers (including creditors and shareholders) after meeting reinvestment needs (including capital expenditures and increases in working capital). It is a key input variable for assessing the company's continuing value (terminal value).

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow in the First Year After the Forecast Period
aliases: First Year Free Cash Flow after Forecast Period
后续期第一年自由现金流量
永续期首年自由现金流
nodes.definition: Free cash flow in the first year after the forecast period refers to the estimated free cash flow for the first year following the end of the explicit forecast period (i.e., the first year entering the perpetual or stable growth phase) in business valuation (such as the two-stage growth model). It is a key input variable for calculating the continuing value (terminal value) of a business.

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow in the First Year after Forecast Period
Free Cash Flow in the First Year of the Continuing Period
aliases: First Year Terminal Period Free Cash Flow
Free Cash Flow in the First Year of the Terminal Period
永续期第一年自由现金流量
稳定期第一年自由现金流量
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow in the First Year of the Continuing Period refers to the cash flow generated in the first year after a company enters the stable growth stage (continuing period), which is available for discretionary use by all capital providers (creditors and shareholders) after meeting all reinvestment needs. It is a key input variable used to calculate the present value of the continuing period in business valuation.

operands.metric: EBIT in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Maintenance Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Incremental Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period

formulas.source_formula: Free Cash Flow in the First Year of the Continuing Period = EBIT in the First Year of the Continuing Period × (1 - Income Tax Rate) - Maintenance Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Continuing Period - Incremental Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period

operands.metric: EBIT in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Depreciation and Amortization in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Change in Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period

formulas.source_formula: Free Cash Flow in the First Year of the Continuing Period = EBIT in the First Year of the Continuing Period × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation and Amortization in the First Year of the Continuing Period - Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Continuing Period - Change in Working Capital in the First Year of the Continuing Period

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow of the Final Forecast Period
Free Cash Flow per Share
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow per Share refers to the portion of free cash flow generated from a company's operating activities, after deducting necessary capital expenditures and additions to working capital, that is available for distribution to common shareholders, divided by the number of common shares outstanding. It measures the theoretical maximum cash return that can be obtained per common share without affecting the company's normal operations and development.

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow to Equity
aliases: 归属于股东的自由现金流
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow to Equity is the residual cash flow available to a company's shareholders after paying all operating expenses, reinvestment expenditures, income taxes, and net debt payments (i.e., interest and principal payments minus the net proceeds from issuing new debt). It is a composite financial metric calculated through formulas and is commonly used to determine a company's equity value.

formulas.source_formula: FCFE = Cash from Operations - Capital Expenditures + Net Debt Issued

operands.metric: Free Cash Flow to the Firm

formulas.source_formula: Free Cash Flow to Equity = Free Cash Flow to the Firm - After-tax Interest Expense + Net Increase in Debt

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow to Firm
aliases: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow to Firm refers to the cash flow available to all claimholders (creditors and shareholders) after deducting taxes, necessary capital expenditures, and increases in working capital. It is a key composite metric for measuring a company's liquidity, financial health, and sustainable development capability.

formulas.source_formula: Free Cash Flow to Firm = Net Operating Cash Flow - Capital Expenditures
Free Cash Flow to Firm = Free Cash Flow to Equity + Free Cash Flow to Debt
Free Cash Flow to Firm = Net Profit After Tax + Interest Expense × (1 - Tax Rate) + Depreciation & Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Change in Working Capital

nodes.name: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
nodes.definition: Free Cash Flow to the Firm refers to the cash available to all capital providers of a company (including creditors and shareholders) after paying all operating expenses, taxes, and necessary capital expenditures and working capital investments. It is a key metric for assessing a company's financial health, profitability, and intrinsic value.

nodes.name: Free Float
nodes.definition: Free float refers to the number of a company’s outstanding shares that are readily available for trading by the public, excluding shares that are closely held or locked-in by insiders, promoters, or governments.

formulas.source_formula: Free-Float Shares = Total Shares - Locked-In Shares
supporting_source_formulas: Free Float = Total Shares - Locked-in Shares
Free-Float Shares = Total Shares - Locked-In Shares

nodes.name: Free Float Shares
nodes.definition: Free float shares refer to the number of outstanding shares of a listed company that are actually available for free trading in the market. Typically determined by exchanges or index providers based on the shareholding structure, it excludes shares held by specific shareholders (such as state-owned shareholders, strategic investors, company founders, etc.) whose holdings exceed a certain threshold (e.g., 5%). It serves as the fundamental data for calculating free float market capitalization.

nodes.name: Free-Float Market Capitalization
nodes.definition: Free-float market capitalization is the total market value of a company's shares that are available for public trading, calculated by multiplying the share price by the number of free-float shares (total shares minus locked-in shares).

formulas.source_formula: Free-Float Market Capitalization = Share Price × Free-Float Shares

nodes.name: Freight
nodes.definition: Freight refers to the cost incurred for transporting goods from one location to another, and is one of the core costs in logistics and supply chain management.

nodes.name: Freight Volume
nodes.definition: Freight volume refers to the actual quantity of goods transported via various modes of transportation within a specified period, typically measured in tons or ton-kilometers, serving as a key indicator for assessing the scale and efficiency of logistics and transportation.

nodes.name: Freight and Miscellaneous Charges
nodes.definition: Freight and miscellaneous charges refer to the total cost incurred during the transportation of goods, including freight charges and related miscellaneous expenses such as loading, unloading, handling, storage, and insurance. It is a key component in determining the planned unit price of materials or the replacement cost of assets.

formulas.source_formula: Freight and Miscellaneous Charges = Cargo Weight × Transportation Distance × Comprehensive Freight Rate
Freight and Miscellaneous Charges = Base Freight + Total Surcharges
Freight and Miscellaneous Charges = Base Rate × Cargo Volume + Total Surcharges

nodes.name: Frequency
nodes.definition: Frequency is the number of times a periodic event repeats per unit of time. It is a physical quantity that describes how often an event occurs, and is commonly used in financial data analysis to describe data distribution or the intensity of event occurrences.

formulas.source_formula: Frequency = 1 ÷ Period
Frequency = Number of Event Occurrences ÷ Total Time

nodes.name: Frequency Distribution
nodes.definition: Frequency distribution is a statistical representation that shows the number of observations within specified intervals (bins), illustrating how data points are spread across different ranges.

nodes.name: Frequency of Risk Event Occurrence
nodes.definition: Frequency of risk event occurrence refers to the number of times or the likelihood that a specific risk event may occur or actually occurs within a given period. It is one of the key dimensions for assessing risk level, typically determining the risk grade or value together with the severity of the risk event.

nodes.name: Front-End Debt-to-Income Ratio
nodes.definition: The front-end debt-to-income (DTI) ratio measures the percentage of a borrower’s gross monthly income that is allocated to housing-related expenses, including mortgage payments, property taxes, mortgage insurance, and homeowners insurance. It is a key metric used by lenders to evaluate a borrower’s ability to manage monthly mortgage payments relative to income.

formulas.source_formula: Front-End DTI = (Housing Expenses ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100
Front-End Debt-to-Income Ratio = Housing Expenses ÷ Gross Income × 100%

nodes.name: Front-End Load
nodes.definition: Front-end load is the sales charge or commission deducted from the initial investment amount when purchasing shares of a mutual fund or similar investment product, calculated as a percentage of the investment.

formulas.source_formula: Front-End Load = Investment Amount × (Load Percentage ÷ 100)
supporting_source_formulas: Front-End Load = Investment Amount × (Load Percentage ÷ 100)
Front-End Load = Investment Amount × Load Percentage ÷ 100

nodes.name: Front-End Ratio
nodes.definition: Front-End Ratio is the percentage of a borrower's gross monthly income that is allocated to total housing expenses, including mortgage principal and interest, property taxes, and homeowners insurance. It is a key metric used by lenders to assess mortgage affordability.

formulas.source_formula: Front-End Ratio = (Monthly Housing Expenses ÷ Monthly Income) × 100
Front-End Ratio = (Housing Expenses ÷ Monthly Gross Income) × 100
Front-End Ratio = (Total Housing Expenses ÷ Gross Monthly Income) × 100

nodes.name: Fuel Cost
nodes.definition: Fuel cost refers to the actual expenses incurred by an enterprise or individual due to the use of fuel (such as gasoline, diesel). It is typically directly allocated based on original documents like refueling invoices, fuel consumption records, or mileage traveled, and constitutes a fundamental expense in cost accounting.

nodes.name: Full Costing
nodes.definition: Full costing is an inventory valuation method in which all manufacturing costs—direct materials, direct labor, fixed manufacturing overhead, and variable manufacturing overhead—are allocated to products, ensuring that the complete cost of production is captured for financial reporting and pricing decisions.

nodes.name: Full Months
nodes.definition: Full Months refers to the number of complete calendar months contained between two specific dates. It is a fundamental unit of time measurement, commonly used in financial calculations such as determining interest period lengths, calculating depreciation and amortization, or allocating expenses across periods.

nodes.name: Full Ratchet
nodes.definition: Full ratchet is an anti-dilution provision that resets the conversion price of existing preferred shares to the lower price at which new shares are issued in a subsequent financing round, fully protecting early investors from dilution.

nodes.name: Full Replacement Cost
nodes.definition: Full replacement cost refers to the total cost required to repurchase or reconstruct a brand-new asset that is identical or functionally equivalent to the subject asset as of the valuation date. It serves as the fundamental value indicator in the replacement cost method of asset valuation.

formulas.source_formula: Full Replacement Cost = (Main Material Cost / Main Material Rate + Major Purchased Component Cost) × (1 + Cost Main Material Rate) × (1 + Non-standard Equipment Design Rate) × (1 + Comprehensive Management Rate) + Sales Tax + Non-standard Equipment Design Fee + Comprehensive Management Expenses

nodes.name: Full Truckload (FTL) Freight Rate
nodes.definition: Full Truckload (FTL) freight rate refers to the unit transportation price applicable for the one-time shipment of a full batch of goods (typically reaching the loading capacity of a full truck or railcar) in road or rail transport. It is usually calculated per ton-kilometer (CNY/(t·km)) or per ton (CNY/t) and constitutes the core pricing component of the total freight cost for a full truckload shipment.

nodes.name: Full Year Equivalent
nodes.definition: Full Year Equivalent refers to a fundamental, indivisible unit of time measurement, typically expressed in complete years (e.g., 1 year, 2 years). It serves as the original time input parameter for calculations (such as depreciation, interest, and length of service) and is not a composite metric derived from complex formulas.

nodes.name: Fully Amortizing Payment
nodes.definition: A fully amortizing payment is a periodic loan payment that, if maintained unchanged through the life of the loan, will pay off the entire principal and all accrued interest exactly by the final due date.

nodes.name: Fully Diluted Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Fully diluted earnings per share represents the earnings attributable to each share of common stock outstanding after assuming the conversion of all dilutive securities such as options, warrants, and convertible bonds.

nodes.name: Fully Indexed Rate
nodes.definition: The fully indexed rate is the actual interest rate charged on an adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) after the initial fixed-rate period, calculated by adding the ARM margin to the current benchmark or indexed rate.

formulas.source_formula: Fully Indexed Rate = Indexed Rate + ARM Margin
Fully Indexed Rate = Index Rate + Margin

nodes.name: Function Value
nodes.definition: Function value refers to the output result obtained after calculation according to specific rules or formulas when one or more input parameters (independent variables) are given. In the field of finance and accounting, it often refers to the specific numerical value calculated by a financial function (such as present value or future value function) under specific parameters.

nodes.name: Functional Adjustment Coefficient
