nodes.definition: The functional adjustment coefficient is a multiplier factor used to adjust or modify specific metrics (such as asset value or performance evaluation scores), primarily aimed at reflecting differences in functional characteristics among different objects (e.g., products, services, assets), thereby making comparisons or evaluation results more accurate and fair.

nodes.name: Functional Obsolescence
nodes.definition: Functional obsolescence refers to the loss in value of an asset being appraised due to its relative inferiority in function, performance, or efficiency caused by technological advancement. It is typically categorized into one-time functional obsolescence and operational functional obsolescence, and is a key deduction item when valuing assets using the replacement cost method.

formulas.source_formula: Functional Obsolescence = One-time Functional Obsolescence + Operational Functional Obsolescence

nodes.name: Fund Net Income
nodes.definition: Fund net income refers to the total actual profit earned by investors during the holding period of a fund, derived from changes in the net asset value per share and dividends (if any), typically after deducting related transaction costs (such as subscription fees, redemption fees) and management fees. It reflects the real return ultimately obtained by investors from the fund investment.

nodes.name: Fund Share
nodes.definition: A fund share is a certificate issued by the fund sponsor to investors, representing the holder's rights to income distribution, entitlement to residual assets after liquidation, and other related rights in proportion to their shareholding, as well as corresponding obligations. Its value is typically represented by the net asset value per share, which is the net asset value of the fund divided by the total number of fund shares.

nodes.name: Funded Debt to Net Working Capital Ratio
aliases: Funded Debt to Working Capital Ratio
Long-Term Debt to Net Working Capital Ratio
长期债务与净营运资本比率
nodes.definition: The funded debt to net working capital ratio measures the proportion of long-term debt relative to net working capital, indicating whether long-term debts are in proper proportion to a company's liquidity position.

formulas.source_formula: Funded Debt to Net Working Capital Ratio = Long-Term Debt ÷ Net Working Capital

nodes.name: Funded Status
nodes.definition: Funded status measures the net position of a defined-benefit pension plan, calculated as the fair value of plan assets minus the benefit obligation. A negative funded status indicates an underfunded plan (net pension liability), while a positive funded status indicates an overfunded plan (net pension asset). It reflects the extent to which plan assets cover the obligations owed to beneficiaries.

formulas.source_formula: Funded Status = Fair Value of Plan Assets - Accumulated Benefit Obligation

nodes.name: Funding Requirement
nodes.definition: In a financial context, funding requirement typically refers to the total amount of capital a company needs to raise to support its operations, investment, or growth plans. It is a composite metric calculated using financial indicators such as sales revenue, profit margin, growth rate, and asset turnover efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Funding Requirement = Projected Sales Revenue × Net Profit Margin × Profit Retention Rate ÷ (1 - Projected Sales Revenue × Net Profit Margin × Profit Retention Rate ÷ Projected Owners' Equity)

nodes.name: Funds From Operations
nodes.definition: Funds From Operations (FFO) is a key performance metric used primarily by Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) to measure operating cash flow. It adjusts net income by adding back non-cash charges such as depreciation and amortization, while excluding gains or losses from property sales and interest income to reflect recurring operational performance.

formulas.source_formula: Funds From Operations = Net Income + Amortization + Depreciation - Capital Gains
FFO = Net Income + Depreciation + Amortization + Property Sales Losses - Property Sales Gains - Interest Income
Funds from Operations = Net Income + Depreciation + Amortization + Tax Adjustments

nodes.name: Funds Invested in Current Assets
nodes.definition: Funds invested in current assets, commonly referred to as working capital or liquid funds, denote the portion of capital allocated by an enterprise to current assets to sustain daily operations. It reflects the short-term financial health of the enterprise and is calculated as current assets minus current liabilities. These funds support the occupation of current assets such as accounts receivable, inventory, and cash, representing essential short-term investments for normal business functioning.

nodes.name: Funds Occupied by Accounts Receivable
aliases: Funds Tied Up in Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Funds occupied by accounts receivable refer to the amount of capital tied up in accounts receivable resulting from selling goods or providing services on credit, typically calculated based on variable costs, reflecting the occupation of working capital by receivables.

nodes.name: Funds Tied Up in Incremental Accounts Receivable
Furniture, Fixtures and Equipment
nodes.definition: Furniture, Fixtures and Equipment (FF&E) refers to movable assets that are not permanently connected to a building's structure or utilities. These assets are subject to significant depreciation and are particularly important in business valuation, especially during liquidation.

nodes.name: Future Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Future cash flow refers to the expected cash inflows generated by a business or asset in future periods. It is calculated or forecasted using other financial metrics such as operating revenue and net profit, rather than being raw data directly obtained from financial statements. It serves as a core input variable in discounted cash flow valuation models.

formulas.source_formula: Future Cash Flow = Net Profit + Depreciation
Future Cash Flow = Operating Revenue - Cash Costs - Income Tax
Future Cash Flow = Earnings Per Share × Price-to-Earnings Ratio × Cash Dividend Per Share
Future Cash Flow = EBIT + Depreciation & Amortization - Capital Expenditure - Change in Working Capital

nodes.name: Future Cash Flows
nodes.definition: Future cash flows refer to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows expected to be generated by an asset or business during a specific future period. In accounting and finance, they are not raw data from financial statements but key valuation parameters that need to be calculated through forecasting, estimation, or discounting models (such as the expected cash flow method or present value formula). They are widely used in areas such as fair value measurement, asset impairment testing, and investment decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: Future Cash Flows = EBIT × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation & Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Increase in Working Capital

nodes.name: Future Cost of Asset Retirement Obligation

formulas.source_formula: Future Cost of Asset Retirement Obligation = Current Cost × (1 + Inflation Rate) ^ Years

nodes.name: Future Debt Amount
nodes.definition: Future Debt Amount refers to the estimated total value of debt that an enterprise or institution is expected to repay or assume within a specific future period (e.g., the next 3 months). It is typically derived from existing contracts, loan agreements, and forecasts of future financing needs, serving as crucial raw data for assessing an enterprise's future debt repayment pressure and financial risk.

nodes.name: Future Dividend (Constant Growth)
nodes.definition: Future dividend under the constant growth model is the expected dividend amount after a specified number of periods, calculated by compounding the current dividend at a constant growth rate. It is commonly used within dividend discount models and equity valuation to forecast dividends in stable growth environments.

formulas.source_formula: Future Dividend = Current Dividend × (1 + Growth Rate) ^ Periods

nodes.name: Future Expansion Investment Cost
nodes.definition: Future Expansion Investment Cost refers to the present value of the capital expenditure required to be invested at a future point in time to acquire future expansion opportunities (expansion options) in real options analysis or capital budgeting. It is not a standard financial statement line item but a composite concept estimated based on forecasted data such as capital expenditures and increases in working capital. It is a key input variable for evaluating the value of expansion options.

formulas.source_formula: Future Interest = Adjusted Amount × (New Rate ÷ 100) × ((12 − Months) ÷ 12)

nodes.name: Future Lease Payments
nodes.definition: Future lease payments refer to the total rental payments that a lessee is obligated to pay to the lessor over the remaining lease term as stipulated in the lease contract. In accounting treatment, it is typically used to calculate the present value of operating lease liabilities or finance lease liabilities.

formulas.source_formula: Future One-Year Rate = ((1 + Two-Year Spot Rate) × (1 + Two-Year Spot Rate) ÷ (1 + One-Year Spot Rate)) - 1
Future One-Year Rate = (1 + Two-Year Spot Rate) × (1 + Two-Year Spot Rate) ÷ (1 + Current One-Year Spot Rate)

nodes.name: Future Period Cash Flows
nodes.definition: Future period cash flows refer to a composite metric of expected cash inflows and outflows projected to occur over multiple future periods, typically forecasted using probabilistic methods such as expected cash flow method or based on business forecasting models. It involves scenario analysis and calculations of fundamental financial indicators, rather than raw data from financial statements.

nodes.name: Future Period Income Tax Expense
nodes.definition: Future Period Income Tax Expense refers to the estimated amount of income tax a company expects to pay on its operating profits for a forthcoming accounting period (e.g., the next fiscal year, next quarter) in accordance with accounting standards. It reflects the anticipated tax burden for future periods and is a crucial item for financial forecasting and budget preparation.

nodes.name: Future Selling Price
nodes.definition: Future selling price refers to the projected sales price of a product or service at a specific future period, based on factors such as market research, cost analysis, and competitive conditions. It is a key input variable in financial forecasting, investment decision-making, and valuation models (such as discounted cash flow models).

nodes.name: Future Single Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Future single cash flow refers to a specific amount of cash that a company expects to receive or pay at a particular future point in time. It is an estimate of a single future cash inflow or outflow based on current information and reasonable assumptions, serving as a fundamental element for asset valuation, investment decision-making, and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Future Value
aliases: Future Value of a Single Sum
nodes.definition: Future Value refers to the projected amount to which an initial investment or loan will grow at a given interest rate and time period, used for evaluating investment returns, calculating loan repayment schedules, and other financial decisions. It is a core concept of the time value of money.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value = Present Value × (1 + Interest Rate × Periods)
Future Value = Initial Investment × (1 + Annual Gain Rate) ^ Years
Future Value = Principal × (1 + Annual Rate ÷ Compounding Periods) ^ (Compounding Periods × Time Years)
Future Value = Periodic Payment (PMT) × (((1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(Number of Months) - 1) ÷ Monthly Interest Rate)
Future Value = Initial Investment × (1 + Interest Rate × Number of Investment Years)
Future Value = Present Value × (1 + Interest Rate ÷ Times Compounded) ^ (Times Compounded × Periods)

nodes.name: Future Value (Compound Growth)
nodes.definition: Future Value under compound growth is the amount to which a present value will accumulate when it is compounded at a constant growth rate per period for a specified number of periods. It is fundamental to time value of money analysis, investment appraisal, budgeting, and financial forecasting.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value = Present Value × (1 + Growth Rate) ^ Periods

nodes.name: Future Value (Time Deposit)
nodes.definition: Future Value (Time Deposit) is the terminal amount accumulated from a principal deposited for a fixed term under compound interest. It is calculated by compounding the periodic interest rate over the total number of compounding periods, assuming a constant annual rate, regular compounding, and no taxes or fees.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value = Principal × (1 + Compound Interest Rate)^(Total Compounding Periods)

nodes.name: Future Value Interest Factor of Annuity (FVIFA)
aliases: Future Value Interest Factor for an Annuity
Future Value Interest Factor of Annuity
等额支付系列终值系数
nodes.definition: The Future Value Interest Factor of Annuity (FVIFA) is a multiplier factor used to calculate the sum of the compound future values of equal payments received or paid at the end of each period, given a specific interest rate and number of periods. Its value is determined by the formula [(1 + interest rate) ^ number of periods - 1] / interest rate, denoted as (F/A, i, n).

nodes.name: Future Value of Annuity
nodes.definition: The future value of an annuity refers to the total future value at maturity of a series of equal periodic payments, calculated at a given interest rate over a specified period. It considers the time value of money and is a key metric in financial management for evaluating the terminal value of a series of cash flows. It can be calculated using parameters such as the periodic payment amount, interest rate, and number of periods.

nodes.name: Future Value of Annuity Due
nodes.definition: Future value of an annuity due refers to the total future amount accumulated after a certain number of periods, given equal payments made at the beginning of each period and a specified interest rate.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of Annuity Due = Cash Flow per Period × [((1 + Interest Rate)^Number of Periods - 1) ÷ Interest Rate] × (1 + Interest Rate)
Future Value of Annuity Due = Payment × ((1 + Rate)^Periods − 1) ÷ Rate × (1 + Rate)

nodes.name: Future Value of Compound Interest
nodes.definition: Future value of compound interest refers to the future principal and interest sum of a sum of money after a certain number of periods under the compound interest method, which can be calculated using indicators such as present value, interest rate, and number of periods. It is a core concept of time value in financial management.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of Compound Interest = Present Value × (1 + Annual Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Frequency) ^ (Compounding Frequency × Investment Years)

nodes.name: Future Value of Debt
nodes.definition: Future value of debt refers to the total principal and interest amount that must be repaid at a specific future date for a debt (principal), calculated according to an agreed compound interest rate. It serves as the basis for calculating the annual sinking fund.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of Debt = Annual Sinking Fund × Future Value Annuity Factor
Future Value of Debt = Debt Principal × (1 + Annual Interest Rate) ^ Number of Compounding Years

nodes.name: Future Value of Investment
nodes.definition: Future value of investment refers to the expected value of a sum of money at the present time point, calculated through compound or simple interest under specific yield (or interest rate) and time conditions, at a specific future time point. It reflects the time value of money and is a core financial metric for value comparison in areas such as project investment evaluation, personal financial planning, and stock return calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of Investment = Principal × (1 + Annual Interest Rate ÷ Compounding Frequency per Year) ^ (Number of Years × Compounding Frequency per Year)

nodes.name: Future Value of Ordinary Annuity
nodes.definition: The future value of an ordinary annuity refers to the total future amount accumulated after a certain number of periods, given equal payments made at the end of each period and a specified interest rate.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of Ordinary Annuity = Payment × ((1 + Rate)^Periods − 1) ÷ Rate

nodes.name: Future Value of Ordinary Annuity Factor
Future Value of Positive Cash Flows
Future Value of Reinvested Coupons
aliases: 再投资票息的复利价值
nodes.definition: The future value of reinvested coupons measures the compounded value of coupon cash flows when reinvested at a specified rate over a given number of periods. It isolates the reinvestment component of a bond's total return and highlights exposure to reinvestment risk, which arises when the actual reinvestment rate differs from the assumed rate.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of Reinvested Coupons = Initial Coupon Payment × (1 + Reinvestment Rate) ^ Periods

nodes.name: Future Value of an Annuity
nodes.definition: The future value of an annuity is the total value of a series of equal periodic payments compounded at a given interest rate until the end of the specified number of periods, distinguishing between ordinary annuities (payments at period-end) and annuities due (payments at period-beginning).

nodes.name: Future Value of an Ordinary Annuity (Monthly Contributions)
aliases: Future Value of an Ordinary Annuity
nodes.definition: The future value of an ordinary annuity (monthly contributions) is the accumulated value of equal payments made at the end of each month, compounded at a constant monthly rate over a given period. It is used to project the growth of regular savings or investment contributions under a fixed average annual return converted to monthly compounding.

nodes.name: Future Value with Compound Interest
nodes.definition: The future value of an investment or savings when interest is compounded periodically, calculated by applying the compound interest formula that accounts for the initial principal, annual interest rate, compounding frequency per year, and investment duration.

nodes.name: Futures Contract Value
nodes.definition: Futures contract value refers to the total notional value of the underlying asset represented by a single futures contract, calculated by multiplying the futures price by the contract multiplier (or trading unit). It serves as the basis for calculating margin requirements, assessing position risk, and conducting hedging operations.

formulas.source_formula: Futures Contract Value = Index Level × Contract Multiplier
Futures Contract Value = Futures Price × Contract Multiplier
Futures Contract Value = Futures Price × Trading Unit

nodes.name: Futures Convergence Rate
nodes.definition: Futures convergence rate measures the daily rate at which the futures price is expected to converge toward the spot price as the contract approaches expiration, reflecting market expectations about price alignment over time.

formulas.source_formula: Futures Convergence Rate = (Futures Price - Spot Price) ÷ Days to Expiry

nodes.name: Futures Cost Basis
nodes.definition: Futures cost basis is the difference between the futures contract price and the current spot price of the underlying asset, indicating the cost-of-carry or market expectations embedded in the futures price.

formulas.source_formula: Futures Cost Basis = Futures Price - Spot Price

nodes.name: Futures Position Value Change
nodes.definition: Futures position value change represents the monetary gain or loss on a futures contract resulting from the difference between the entry and exit index levels, multiplied by the contract multiplier.

nodes.name: Futures Price
nodes.definition: Futures price refers to the agreed-upon price between buyers and sellers in the futures market for the delivery of a specified quantity and quality of an underlying asset at a specific future date. It is typically formed based on the spot price plus carrying costs (such as storage fees, insurance, financing interest, etc.).

formulas.source_formula: Futures Price = Spot Price + Storage Cost + Insurance Cost + (Financing Rate × Spot Price × Term)

nodes.name: Futures Price Volatility
nodes.definition: Futures price volatility refers to the phenomenon of upward or downward price movements of futures contracts over time in the futures market, influenced by various factors such as supply and demand, macroeconomic conditions, policy changes, and market sentiment. It represents the raw price movement data directly generated in market trading and serves as the basis for calculating derivative metrics such as volatility and profit/loss.

formulas.source_formula: Futures Profit = (Final Price - Initial Price) × Contract Multiplier

nodes.name: GDP Deflator
aliases: 国内生产总值平减指数
nodes.definition: In economics, the GDP deflator (implicit price deflator) is an indicator that measures the monetary price of all newly produced, final domestic goods and services in a country's economy in a given year relative to their real value. It reflects price inflation or deflation relative to a base year, for which the deflator is set to 100. Unlike fixed-basket indices such as the CPI, the GDP deflator adjusts its basket composition annually based on current production and expenditure patterns.

nodes.name: GDP Gap
nodes.definition: GDP gap is the output gap measuring the divergence between an economy's actual GDP and its potential GDP, expressed as the proportional difference relative to potential GDP. A positive GDP gap indicates the economy is operating above potential with possible inflationary pressures, while a negative GDP gap indicates slack and underutilized capacity.

formulas.source_formula: GDP Gap = (Actual GDP - Potential GDP) ÷ Potential GDP

nodes.name: GDP Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The GDP growth rate is a core macroeconomic indicator that measures the speed of economic growth of a country or region over a specific period. It reflects the magnitude of economic expansion or contraction by calculating the percentage change between the current period's real gross domestic product and the base period's real gross domestic product. It is commonly used to assess economic cycles, policy effectiveness, and long-term development trends.

operands.metric: Current Period Real Gross Domestic Product
Base Period Real Gross Domestic Product

formulas.source_formula: GDP Growth Rate = (Current Period Real Gross Domestic Product - Base Period Real Gross Domestic Product) ÷ Base Period Real Gross Domestic Product × 100%
GDP Growth Rate (%) = (Current GDP ÷ Previous GDP - 1) × 100
GDP Growth Rate = ((Final Real GDP / Initial Real GDP) ^ (1 / Number of Years) - 1) × 100

nodes.name: GDP Price Deflator
aliases: 国内生产总值平减指数
nodes.definition: The GDP price deflator is a comprehensive measure of price inflation for all domestically produced final goods and services. It is calculated as the ratio of nominal GDP to real GDP, multiplied by 100, indicating how much of the change in GDP is due to changes in the general price level rather than real output.

formulas.source_formula: GDP Price Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100

nodes.name: GDP per Capita
nodes.definition: GDP per capita measures the average economic output produced per person in an economy, calculated as a country's gross domestic product divided by its total population. It is commonly used as a proxy for living standards and to compare economic productivity across countries and over time.

formulas.source_formula: GDP per Capita = Gross Domestic Product ÷ Population
GMWB Annual Withdrawal = Initial Investment × Withdrawal Percentage

nodes.name: Gain
nodes.definition: Realized gain is the profit recognized when an asset is sold, measured as the sale price minus the purchase price and any transaction costs. It reflects the actual increase in value realized upon disposal and is commonly used for financial reporting and tax calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Realized Gain = (Sale Price - Purchase Price) - Transaction Costs

nodes.name: Gain on Disposal of Assets
nodes.definition: Gain on disposal of assets refers to the net profit portion obtained when a company disposes of long-term assets such as fixed assets or intangible assets through sale, transfer, etc., where the disposal proceeds exceed the carrying amount of the asset and related disposal expenses.

nodes.name: Gain on Disposal of Investments
nodes.definition: Gain on disposal of investments refers to the net profit portion obtained when a company sells, transfers, or exchanges its long-term equity investments, financial assets, and other investment assets, where the disposal proceeds exceed the carrying amount of the asset and related disposal costs.

formulas.source_formula: Gain or Loss = Sale Proceeds − Borrowed Amount − Initial Investment

nodes.name: Gain or Loss on Disposal of Assets
nodes.definition: Gain or loss on disposal of assets refers to the amount of profit or loss realized by an enterprise from the disposal of long-term assets such as fixed assets and intangible assets through sale, scrapping, transfer, or other means. It is presented as a non-recurring gain or loss item in the income statement, reflecting the financial outcome of asset disposal activities.

formulas.source_formula: Gain or Loss on Disposal of Assets = Proceeds from Disposal - Original Cost of Asset - Disposal Expenses
Gain or Loss on Disposal of Assets = Proceeds from Disposal - Carrying Amount of Asset - Disposal Expenses
Gain or Loss on Disposal of Assets = Proceeds from Disposal - (Original Cost of Asset - Accumulated Depreciation - Accumulated Amortization - Impairment Provisions) - Disposal Expenses

nodes.name: Gamma
nodes.definition: Gamma is one of the option Greeks, used to measure the sensitivity of an option's Delta to changes in the price of the underlying asset. It is not a primary account in financial statements but a composite metric calculated using option pricing models (such as the Black-Scholes model) based on other indicators.

formulas.source_formula: Gamma Adjustment = Target Gamma - Portfolio Gamma

nodes.name: Gamma Neutral
nodes.definition: Gamma neutral refers to constructing an options portfolio whose net gamma is approximately zero, so the portfolio's delta remains stable with respect to small changes in the underlying asset price. By offsetting second-order sensitivity (gamma), traders reduce the need for frequent delta re-hedging caused by curvature in the price–delta relationship. Gamma-neutral positioning is typically managed alongside delta hedging and requires ongoing rebalancing as option Greeks evolve with market movements and time decay.

nodes.name: Gamma Value of Down-and-Out Options
nodes.definition: The Gamma value of a down-and-out option is a derivative metric in option pricing that measures the sensitivity of the option's Delta to changes in the underlying asset price in that state. Specifically, it is the ratio of the change in Delta to the change in the underlying asset price, or the second partial derivative of the option value with respect to the underlying asset price.

nodes.name: Gann Fans
nodes.definition: Gann fans are a technical analysis tool that plots diagonal lines (Gann angles) derived from specified price-to-time ratios to project potential support and resistance and evaluate trend direction and strength. Each angle is computed as the arctangent of the price change relative to elapsed time and expressed in degrees.

nodes.name: Gap Amount
nodes.definition: Gap amount is the difference between the outstanding auto loan balance and the vehicle's actual cash value (ACV) at the time of total loss. It represents the shortfall typically covered by gap insurance to protect the borrower from negative equity.

formulas.source_formula: Gap Amount = Loan Balance - Actual Cash Value

nodes.name: Gas (Ethereum)
nodes.definition: Ethereum gas fee is the total transaction fee, typically denominated in gwei, paid to process and include a transaction on the Ethereum blockchain. It is determined by the units of gas consumed multiplied by the sum of the network base fee and the user-specified priority fee (tip) per unit of gas.

nodes.name: Gas Guzzler Tax
nodes.definition: The Gas Guzzler Tax is a U.S. federal excise tax imposed on new passenger cars with low fuel economy. Assessed at the point of manufacture or importation, the tax is designed to discourage production and sale of vehicles with poor miles-per-gallon (MPG) performance. It applies only to passenger cars (excludes trucks, SUVs, and minivans) and is determined by statutory MPG brackets, typically ranging from $1,000 to $7,000, with no tax for vehicles achieving at least 22.5 MPG.

nodes.name: Gazelle Company
nodes.definition: A gazelle company is a high-growth firm that achieves at least a specified annual revenue growth rate (commonly 20%) for four consecutive years, starting from a minimum base revenue level. This classification emphasizes sustained top-line expansion and rapid scaling over a multi-year period.

nodes.name: Gearing
nodes.definition: Gearing measures a company's financial leverage by comparing total liabilities to shareholders' equity, indicating the proportion of financing provided by debt relative to equity. Higher gearing suggests greater leverage and potential financial risk, while lower gearing indicates a more conservative capital structure.

formulas.source_formula: Gearing = Total Liabilities ÷ Shareholders' Equity

nodes.name: Gearing Ratio
nodes.definition: The gearing ratio, commonly expressed as the debt-to-equity ratio, measures a company's financial leverage by comparing total debt to shareholders' equity. It indicates how aggressively a firm is financed through debt relative to equity, informing assessments of capital structure, risk, and solvency.

formulas.source_formula: Gearing Ratio = Total Debt ÷ Total Equity

nodes.name: General Injury Accident Lost Time
aliases: Lost Time Due to General Injury Incidents
一般伤害事故工时损失
nodes.definition: General Injury Accident Lost Time refers to the total sum of work hours lost due to general injury accidents occurring in the workplace that do not meet the statutory criteria for occupational injury recognition but result in temporary employee incapacity to work. It is a key metric in corporate safety statistics used to measure unplanned downtime and accident severity, typically calculated in hours.

nodes.name: General Ledger
nodes.definition: The general ledger is the central record of all financial transactions and account balances in a double-entry accounting system. Every journal entry posted to the general ledger must be balanced—meaning the sum of debit amounts equals the sum of credit amounts—to preserve the integrity of financial records.

nodes.name: General Risk Reserve
nodes.definition: The General Risk Reserve refers to a portion of funds directly appropriated from net profit by enterprises engaged in specific financial activities, such as securities business, in accordance with relevant national regulations or accounting policies. This fund is specifically designated to cover potential future operating losses and constitutes part of the enterprise's owners' equity.

nodes.name: General and Administrative Expense
nodes.definition: General and Administrative (G&A) expense comprises operating costs not directly tied to producing goods or generating sales, such as corporate office rent, utilities, administrative salaries, professional fees, and office supplies. G&A is often allocated across departments or business units using objective drivers (e.g., headcount, floor space, revenue) to reflect resource consumption.

nodes.name: General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.definition: General and administrative expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise in daily operations to maintain overall management and administrative functions, which are typically not directly attributable to specific production or sales activities.

nodes.name: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP)
nodes.definition: Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP) are the default set of accounting standards adopted by U.S. companies, issued and maintained by the Financial Accounting Standards Board (FASB), with specific content and authoritative provisions contained in the Accounting Standards Codification, applicable to non-governmental organizations. For government agencies and registrants of the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the legal basis for GAAP derives from federal securities laws and SEC guidance documents.

nodes.name: Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax
nodes.definition: Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax (GSTT) is a U.S. federal transfer tax imposed on certain transfers to beneficiaries who are two or more generations below the transferor (e.g., grandchildren). It is assessed in addition to estate and gift taxes when the transfer exceeds the applicable GST exemption, aiming to prevent tax avoidance by skipping a generation.

nodes.name: Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax (GSTT) - Direct Skip
nodes.definition: A direct skip under the Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax (GSTT) occurs when a transfer is made to a skip person and is immediately subject to GST tax. For non-lineal recipients, generation assignment is determined by age: if the recipient is at least 37.5 years younger than the donor, the recipient is treated as a skip person. The test computes the age difference (donor minus recipient); meeting or exceeding the 37.5-year threshold classifies the transfer as a direct skip.

nodes.name: Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax (GSTT) Taxable Transfer Amount
aliases: 隔代转移税应税转移金额
nodes.definition: The GSTT taxable transfer amount is the portion of a generation-skipping transfer that exceeds the applicable GST exemption limit and is therefore subject to the Generation-Skipping Transfer Tax under U.S. federal estate and gift tax rules.

nodes.name: Generation-Skipping Transfer Taxable Amount
aliases: 代际跳跃转移税应税额
nodes.definition: The Generation-Skipping Transfer (GST) taxable amount is the portion of a gift that exceeds the applicable GST exclusion limit and is therefore subject to the GST tax. It is computed as the excess of the gift amount over the GST exclusion, floored at zero when the exclusion fully covers the gift.

nodes.name: Genuine Progress Indicator
nodes.definition: The Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) is a comprehensive macroeconomic and sustainability accounting measure that adjusts personal consumption for income distribution, incorporates capital growth and non-market welfare contributions, and deducts defensive expenditures along with social, environmental, and natural capital costs to estimate net economic welfare.

formulas.source_formula: Genuine Progress Indicator (GPI) = Personal Consumption (Adjusted for Income Distribution) + Capital Growth + Non-market Welfare Contributions - Defensive Private Spending - Social Capital Deterioration Costs - Environmental Degradation Costs - Natural Capital Depletion Costs

nodes.name: Geometric Brownian Motion
nodes.definition: A continuous-time stochastic process in which the logarithm of the randomly varying quantity follows a Brownian motion with drift. Widely used in financial mathematics for modeling stock prices in the Black-Scholes model.

nodes.name: Geometric Mean
nodes.definition: The geometric mean is a statistical method used to calculate the average of a set of positive numbers, particularly suitable for measuring compound changes such as growth rates or ratios. It is calculated by multiplying all values together and then taking the nth root of the product, where n is the number of values, providing a more accurate reflection of long-term average trends in the data.

nodes.name: Gift of Equity
nodes.definition: Gift of equity is the portion of a property's appraised market value that exceeds the agreed sale price and is transferred to the buyer as a gift, commonly in intra-family real estate transactions. It can be applied toward the buyer's down payment and may affect loan-to-value (LTV) ratios and mortgage underwriting, subject to legal and tax considerations.

formulas.source_formula: Gift of Equity = Market Value - Sale Price

nodes.name: Gini Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Gini coefficient quantifies income or wealth inequality by comparing the Lorenz curve to the line of equality. It is defined as the area between the line of equality and the Lorenz curve divided by the area under the line of equality, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximal inequality).

formulas.source_formula: Gini Coefficient = (Area under Line of Equality - Area under Lorenz Curve) ÷ Area under Line of Equality

nodes.name: Gini Index
nodes.definition: The Gini Index is a statistical measure of income or wealth inequality within a population, ranging from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (maximum inequality), calculated based on the cumulative differences between population proportions and their corresponding income shares.

formulas.source_formula: Gini Index = (n + 1 - 2 × Lorenz Curve Area) ÷ n

nodes.name: Given Value
nodes.definition: In mathematical, statistical, or financial models, a given value refers to a predetermined or known numerical value used as an input parameter for calculations, analysis, or function operations.

nodes.name: Goal Seeking
nodes.definition: Goal seeking is a numerical technique used in financial modeling and spreadsheet analysis to determine the value of an input variable that makes a model's output equal a specified target within a defined tolerance. It is commonly applied in budgeting, break-even analysis, valuation, and scenario planning to backsolve for inputs such as required sales volume, discount rate, or price that achieve a desired financial outcome.

nodes.name: Going-Concern Value
nodes.definition: Going-concern value is the estimated value of a company as an operating entity under the assumption of continuous operations, typically exceeding liquidation value due to intangible benefits such as goodwill, reputation, customer relationships, and operational synergies.

nodes.name: Golden Cross
nodes.definition: Golden Cross is a bullish technical analysis signal that occurs when a short-term moving average rises above a long-term moving average, often referenced as the 50-day moving average crossing above the 200-day moving average. It indicates potential trend reversal to the upside and is commonly confirmed with volume and broader market context.

formulas.source_formula: Golden Cross = Short-term Moving Average - Long-term Moving Average

nodes.name: Goodness-of-Fit
nodes.definition: The goodness-of-fit chi-square statistic evaluates whether observed categorical frequencies differ significantly from expected frequencies under a specified hypothesis. In accounting and audit analytics, it helps assess conformity of transaction patterns (e.g., Benford's Law), monitor internal controls, identify anomalies, and support fraud detection and risk assessment.

nodes.name: Goods and Services Price Deflator
aliases: GDP平减指数（货物与服务部分）
货物与服务价格平减指数
nodes.definition: The Goods and Services Price Deflator is an index used to convert the nominal value of goods and services into real value based on a specific base year, measuring the overall price level changes of a basket of goods and services. It is a composite indicator calculated from other metrics.

formulas.source_formula: Goods and Services Price Deflator = (Laspeyres Price Index + Paasche Price Index) ÷ 2
Goods and Services Price Deflator = (Nominal Goods and Services Value ÷ Real Goods and Services Value) × 100

nodes.name: Goods in Transit
nodes.definition: Goods in Transit is an accounting account classified under assets, used to record the cost of goods that have been shipped by the enterprise but have not yet met the criteria for revenue recognition. It is commonly used in sales transactions involving settlement methods such as collection and acceptance, where the goods have left the enterprise's warehouse but the sale has not been finalized for recognition.

nodes.name: Goodwill
nodes.definition: Goodwill refers to the portion of the purchase price in a business acquisition that exceeds the fair value share of the identifiable net assets of the acquired entity. It represents the potential economic value of the acquired business to generate excess future profits, stemming from intangible resources that cannot be separately identified, such as brand reputation, customer relationships, and superior management teams.

operands.metric: Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets

formulas.source_formula: Goodwill = Purchase Price - Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets
Goodwill = Going-Concern Value - Liquidation Value
Goodwill = Purchase Price - Fair Value of Identifiable Assets

operands.metric: Fair Market Value of Net Identifiable Assets

formulas.source_formula: Goodwill = Purchase Price - Fair Market Value of Net Identifiable Assets

operands.metric: Net Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets

formulas.source_formula: Goodwill = Purchase Price - Net Fair Value of Identifiable Net Assets

nodes.name: Goodwill Adjustment Amount
nodes.definition: Goodwill adjustment amount refers to the difference between the merger cost paid by the acquirer and its share of the fair value of the identifiable net assets of the acquiree in a business combination, representing the present value of the acquiree's future excess earning capacity.

operands.metric: Investment Cost at Initial Investment Date
Fair Value of Subsidiary's Identifiable Net Assets at Investment Date

formulas.source_formula: Goodwill Adjustment Amount = Investment Cost at Initial Investment Date - Fair Value of Subsidiary's Identifiable Net Assets at Investment Date × Shareholding Percentage

nodes.name: Goodwill Impairment Charge
nodes.definition: Goodwill impairment charge is the expense recognized when the carrying value of goodwill exceeds its fair value. The charge equals the excess of the carrying value over the fair value, and is recorded in profit or loss in the period of impairment testing under applicable accounting standards.

nodes.name: Gordon Growth Model
aliases: 股利贴息不变增长模型
nodes.definition: The Gordon Growth Model is a dividend discount valuation model used to calculate the present value of a stock or terminal value under a stable growth phase. The model assumes perpetual dividend payments growing at a constant rate, representing a special form of the Dividend Discount Model, and is widely applied in financial management and investment analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Gordon Growth Model = First Period Dividend ÷ Discount Rate
Gordon Growth Model = First Period Dividend ÷ (Discount Rate - Dividend Growth Rate)
Gordon Growth Model = Initial Dividend × (1 + Dividend Growth Rate) ÷ (Discount Rate - Dividend Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Government Bond
nodes.definition: Government bonds are debt securities issued by the national government to finance government expenditures. They typically pay fixed interest and are backed by government credit, considered low-risk investment instruments.

nodes.name: Government Bond Market Yield Standard Deviation
aliases: Standard Deviation of Government Bond Market Yield
nodes.definition: Government Bond Market Yield Standard Deviation is a composite indicator derived from statistical calculations on a series of historical government bond yield data. It measures the dispersion or volatility of government bond market yields around their average level and serves as a crucial fundamental parameter for assessing market risk and calculating country risk premiums.

nodes.name: Government Consumption Expenditure
nodes.definition: Government consumption expenditure refers to the expenditure on goods and services incurred by government departments to provide public services (such as national defense, education, public health, etc.) for the whole society and for their own daily operations. It is an important component of final consumption expenditure in Gross Domestic Product (GDP), reflecting the scale of government spending in non-investment areas.

nodes.name: Government Consumption at Constant Prices
aliases: Government Consumption Expenditure at Constant Prices
政府最终消费支出（不变价）
nodes.definition: Government consumption at constant prices refers to government consumption expenditure measured at the price level of a fixed base period, after eliminating the effects of price changes. It reflects the real value of goods and services consumed by the government in providing public services and conducting public administration, and is a key direct component in calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at constant prices.

nodes.name: Government Expenditure
nodes.definition: Government expenditure refers to the total amount of funds spent by the government of a country or region within a specific period (usually a fiscal year) to perform its functions, provide public goods and services, make investments, and implement transfer payments, among other activities. It is a significant component of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) and reflects the scale and direction of government activities.

nodes.name: Government Subsidies
nodes.definition: Government subsidies refer to economic resources obtained by enterprises from the government without compensation, typically used to offset related costs incurred or to support specific activities. In accounting treatment, depending on whether they are related to assets or ordinary activities, they may be recorded in accounts such as deferred income, other income, or non-operating income.

nodes.name: Graded Vesting
nodes.definition: Graded vesting is a vesting method under which an employee earns nonforfeitable rights to employer-contributed benefits incrementally over time. After an initial service period with no vesting, the vested percentage increases by a fixed annual increment until reaching full vesting (100%). It is commonly used in qualified retirement plans and equity compensation arrangements and affects benefit recognition under pension and compensation accounting.

nodes.name: Graduated Payment Mortgage (GPM)
nodes.definition: A Graduated Payment Mortgage (GPM) is a fixed-rate mortgage structure in which scheduled payments start below the fully amortizing level and increase at a predetermined graduation rate for a specified number of periods, after which payments level off for the remaining term. This design shifts more of the payment burden to later years and may result in negative amortization early in the loan if initial payments are insufficient to cover accrued interest.

nodes.name: Graham Number
nodes.definition: The Graham number is an estimate of the maximum fair price per share that a defensive value investor should pay, derived from Benjamin Graham’s criteria. It combines earnings per share (EPS) and book value per share (BVPS) to set an upper valuation bound, assuming conservative limits on the price-to-earnings and price-to-book multiples.

nodes.name: Grid Size
nodes.definition: Grid size refers to the dimensions or spacing of grid cells when discretizing a continuous computational domain in fields such as numerical simulation, computational fluid dynamics, or finite element analysis. It determines computational accuracy and workload; typically, smaller grid sizes yield higher accuracy but require more computational resources.

nodes.name: Grid Trading
nodes.definition: Grid trading is an algorithmic trading strategy that places buy and sell orders at preset price intervals around a base price to capture profits from price oscillations. Order prices are computed symmetrically above and below the start price, with direction determined by the chosen trend orientation.

nodes.name: Gross Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Gross Accounts Receivable refers to the total book value of all amounts due from customers for goods sold or services rendered in the normal course of business, before deducting any allowance for doubtful accounts.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Burn Rate = Total Monthly Operating Expenses
Gross Business Income = (Net Sales - Cost of Goods Sold) + Miscellaneous Income

nodes.name: Gross Capital Formation
nodes.definition: Gross capital formation refers to the net acquisition of fixed assets and inventories by resident units during a given period. It is a core indicator measuring the scale of capital accumulation in a country or region, consisting of gross fixed capital formation and changes in inventories.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Capital Formation = Gross Fixed Capital Formation + Changes in Inventories

nodes.name: Gross Capital Formation Price Index
aliases: Price Index of Gross Capital Formation
资本形成价格平减指数
资本形成总额平减指数
nodes.definition: The Gross Capital Formation Price Index is an index used to measure changes in the price level of gross capital formation (such as fixed asset investment, inventory changes, etc.). Its primary function is to convert gross capital formation calculated at current market prices (nominal value) into constant-price gross capital formation, calculated at the prices of a fixed base period, by removing the effects of price changes through this index. This allows for a more accurate reflection of changes in the physical volume of capital formation.

nodes.name: Gross Capital Formation at Constant Prices
nodes.definition: Gross capital formation at constant prices is a composite indicator calculated by adjusting gross capital formation at current prices using a price index. It is commonly used in national economic accounting for real GDP calculation, reflecting the actual level of capital formation after removing price changes.

operands.metric: Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices

formulas.source_formula: Gross Capital Formation at Constant Prices = Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices ÷ Price Index of Gross Capital Formation

operands.metric: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices
Changes in Inventories at Constant Prices

formulas.source_formula: Gross Capital Formation at Constant Prices = Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices + Changes in Inventories at Constant Prices

nodes.name: Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices
nodes.definition: Gross Capital Formation at Current Prices refers to the total accumulation of non-financial produced assets by resident units of a country or region during a specific accounting period (usually one year), measured at current market prices. It reflects the actual investment scale and capital accumulation level of the economy during the current period and is a fundamental aggregate indicator in national economic accounting.

nodes.name: Gross Debt Service Ratio (GDS)
nodes.definition: The Gross Debt Service ratio measures the percentage of a borrower's gross income devoted to housing costs—typically principal, interest, property taxes, and utilities—and is used by lenders to assess mortgage affordability, with common underwriting guidelines targeting 28% or less.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Debt Service Ratio = (Principal + Interest + Property Taxes + Utilities) ÷ Gross Income × 100

nodes.name: Gross Domestic Income
nodes.definition: Gross Domestic Income (GDI) is the income-side measure of economic activity within a country's borders, defined as the total income earned by labor and capital from domestic production. In principle, it equals the sum of compensation of employees (wages), business operating surplus and mixed income (profits), net interest, rental income, and taxes on production and imports less subsidies, plus statistical adjustments or discrepancy. GDI is conceptually equivalent to GDP measured via the income approach.

nodes.name: Gross Domestic Product
nodes.definition: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is a monetary measure of the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country or countries during a specific period. It is commonly used to gauge the economic activity of a nation or region, serving as a statistical indicator reflecting national development and progress.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Domestic Product = Technology Level × Capital × Labor
Gross Domestic Product = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + Net Exports
supporting_source_formulas: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) = Consumption + Government Spending + Investment + Net Exports
Gross Domestic Product = Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + Net Exports

operands.metric: Total Imports of Goods and Services

formulas.source_formula: GDP = Consumption + Government Spending + Investment + (Exports - Imports)

operands.metric: Value Added of Secondary Industry in Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Gross Domestic Product = Value Added of Primary Industry + Value Added of Secondary Industry + Value Added of Tertiary Industry

nodes.name: Gross Domestic Product (Expenditure Approach)
nodes.definition: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) via the expenditure approach measures the market value of all final goods and services produced within a country's borders during a specific period by summing consumption, investment, government expenditure, and net exports.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Domestic Product = Consumption + Government Spending + Investment + Net Exports
Gross Domestic Product = Consumer Spending + Business Investment + Government Spending + Net Exports

nodes.name: Gross Earnings
nodes.definition: Gross earnings represent the excess of revenue over the cost of goods sold, indicating the basic profitability from core sales activities before deducting operating expenses, taxes, and non-operating items.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Earnings = Revenue - Cost of Goods Sold

nodes.name: Gross Exposure
nodes.definition: Gross exposure is the total market exposure of a portfolio or fund, calculated as the sum of the values of long and short positions. It reflects the scale of capital at risk irrespective of directional bias and is commonly used in risk and portfolio management.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Exposure = Long Positions + Short Positions
supporting_source_formulas: Gross Exposure = Long Positions + Short Positions

nodes.name: Gross Exposure Percentage
aliases: Gross Exposure as Percentage of Capital
nodes.definition: Gross Exposure Percentage measures the fund’s total gross exposure relative to its capital (or NAV), expressed as a percentage, indicating the degree of leverage or under-investment; values above 100% reflect the use of leverage.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Exposure Percentage = (Gross Exposure ÷ Capital) × 100%

nodes.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation
nodes.definition: Gross Fixed Capital Formation refers to the total value of fixed assets acquired by resident units of a country or region within a given period (usually one year) through purchases, self-construction, etc., minus the value of fixed assets disposed of (e.g., sold, scrapped) during the same period. These fixed assets typically have a service life of more than one year and exclude natural assets such as land. It is a key indicator for measuring the scale of investment in fixed assets in a country or region and is an essential component in calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP) using the expenditure approach.

nodes.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Base Period Prices
aliases: Constant Price Gross Fixed Capital Formation
Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices of Base Period
不变价固定资本形成总额
可比价固定资本形成总额
基期固定资本形成总额
nodes.definition: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Base Period Prices refers to the total value of new fixed assets (such as machinery and equipment, buildings, intellectual property products, etc.) added by a country or region during a specific period (e.g., one year), measured and calculated using the price level of a specific base period. It eliminates the impact of price changes to accurately reflect the real physical volume change in capital formation and serves as a crucial indicator for long-term economic analysis and comparison.

nodes.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices
aliases: Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices
固定资本形成总额（不变价）
实际固定资本形成总额
nodes.definition: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices refers to a composite indicator calculated by deflating the gross fixed capital formation at current prices (i.e., removing the effects of price changes). It reflects the actual physical value of the net increase in fixed assets acquired by resident units over a given period, after eliminating price influences. It is a core component in calculating the gross capital formation at constant prices and is considered derived data within the System of National Accounts.

operands.metric: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices in the Base Period

formulas.source_formula: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices = Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices in the Base Period × Volume Index
Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices = Gross Fixed Capital Formation ÷ Relevant Price Index

nodes.name: Gross Fixed Capital Formation at Constant Prices in the Base Period
Gross Income
nodes.definition: Gross income refers to the balance of total revenue earned by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services within a specific period, after deducting the costs directly associated with those sales or services (i.e., direct costs). It is a fundamental metric for measuring the profitability of a company's core business and reflects the profit margin of the products or services themselves.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Income = Sales Revenue - Direct Costs

nodes.name: Gross Income Multiplier
nodes.definition: Gross Income Multiplier (GIM) is a real estate valuation multiple that measures the ratio of a property's market price to its gross annual rental income. It offers a quick, expense-agnostic indicator of value and is commonly used for preliminary comparisons among income-producing properties.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Income Multiplier = Property Price ÷ Annual Rental Income
Gross Income Multiplier = Property Price ÷ Gross Annual Income

nodes.name: Gross Income Test
nodes.definition: The gross income test is a U.S. tax rule used to determine whether an individual can be claimed as a dependent, based on whether the individual's gross income is below a statutory threshold. Gross income for this test includes business gross income (net sales minus cost of goods sold plus miscellaneous income), rental income, partnership gross income, taxable Social Security benefits, unemployment compensation, and taxable grants.

nodes.name: Gross Interest
nodes.definition: Gross interest is the total interest earned before any deductions such as income taxes and fees. Net interest represents the interest retained after subtracting taxes and fees from gross interest, reflecting the effective return received.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Interest = Principal × Interest Rate

nodes.name: Gross Leverage Ratio
nodes.definition: Gross leverage ratio is an insurance solvency and risk metric that measures the extent of exposure to pricing and reserve estimation risk by comparing the sum of premiums written and net liabilities to policyholders' surplus. A higher ratio indicates greater leverage relative to surplus and potentially higher financial risk.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Leverage Ratio = (Premiums Written + Net Liabilities) ÷ Policyholders' Surplus

nodes.name: Gross Margin
nodes.definition: Gross margin is the percentage of revenue remaining after deducting cost of goods sold (COGS). It reflects a company's pricing power and production efficiency, indicating how effectively it generates gross profit from sales before operating expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Margin (%) = ((Revenue - Cost of Goods Sold) ÷ Revenue) × 100
Gross Margin (%) = (Gross Profit ÷ Sales) × 100

nodes.name: Gross Margin Return on Investment (GMROI)
nodes.definition: Gross Margin Return on Investment (GMROI) is an inventory profitability ratio that measures how much gross margin is earned for each dollar invested in inventory, indicating the effectiveness of inventory in generating profit.

formulas.source_formula: GMROI = Gross Margin ÷ Average Inventory Cost

nodes.name: Gross Merchandise Value
nodes.definition: Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) is the aggregate gross monetary value of merchandise sold through an e-commerce or marketplace platform over a specified period. It is calculated as the sales price per unit multiplied by the number of units sold and does not account for returns, discounts, cancellations, taxes, shipping fees, or platform commissions. GMV is used to indicate scale and sales throughput rather than realized revenue.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Merchandise Value = Sales Price × Number of Goods Sold

nodes.name: Gross National Income (GNI)
aliases: Gross National Income at Market Prices
nodes.definition: Gross National Income (GNI) is the total income earned by a nation’s residents and domestic institutions at market prices. It is calculated by adding Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to net foreign income earned by residents and adjusting for net taxes minus subsidies, capturing income generated both domestically and from abroad.

formulas.source_formula: Gross National Income = Gross Domestic Product + Foreign Income from Residents - Foreign Income to Foreigners + Net Taxes minus Subsidies

nodes.name: Gross National Product (GNP)
aliases: Gross National Product at Market Prices
nodes.definition: Gross National Product (GNP) measures the total market value of all final goods and services produced by a country's residents during a given period, equal to domestic production plus net factor income from abroad (income received from abroad minus income paid to foreign residents), reflecting residents' production regardless of location.

formulas.source_formula: GNP = Personal Consumption + Private Investment + Government Expenditure + Net Exports + Income from Abroad - Foreign Income Earned Domestically

nodes.name: Gross National Product (GNP) Deflator
aliases: 国民生产总值平减指数
nodes.definition: The GNP deflator is a broad measure of price inflation that reflects the change in the overall price level of all final goods and services produced by a nation's residents. It is calculated as the ratio of nominal GNP to real GNP, multiplied by 100, and is used to convert nominal values into real terms relative to a base period.

formulas.source_formula: GNP Deflator = (Nominal GNP ÷ Real GNP) × 100

nodes.name: Gross Net Written Premium Income
aliases: Premiums Net of Cancellations, Refunds and Reinsurance
nodes.definition: Gross Net Written Premium Income (GNWPI) is an insurance accounting measure representing written premiums net of cancellations, refunds, and premiums ceded to reinsurers, while remaining gross of acquisition costs and other expenses. It is commonly used as a premium base in reinsurance agreements to determine the reinsurer’s share.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Net Written Premium Income = Gross Written Premiums - Cancellations - Refunds - Reinsurance Premiums Ceded

nodes.name: Gross Operating Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Gross operating cash flow refers to the gross cash flow generated from a company's operating activities, typically calculated by adding back non-cash expenses (such as depreciation and amortization) to after-tax operating profit. It serves as the basis for calculating net operating cash flow and aligns with the definition of a non-leaf node.

nodes.name: Gross Output
nodes.definition: Gross output refers to the total value of all goods and services produced by resident units in the material production sector during a given period. It is a composite indicator measuring the overall scale of production activities, commonly used to calculate value added and Gross Domestic Product (GDP).

operands.metric: Value of Finished Products Produced in Current Period
Value Difference of Self-Produced Semi-Finished Products between Period End and Beginning

formulas.source_formula: Gross Output = Value of Finished Products Produced in Current Period + Income from External Processing Fees + Value Difference of Self-Produced Semi-Finished Products between Period End and Beginning

operands.metric: Value of Finished Products Produced in the Accounting Period
Value of Self-Produced Semi-Finished Products Sold or Ready for Sale in the Accounting Period
Value of Completed Industrial Work Undertaken for External Parties in the Accounting Period

formulas.source_formula: Gross Output = Value of Finished Products Produced in the Accounting Period + Value of Self-Produced Semi-Finished Products Sold or Ready for Sale in the Accounting Period + Value of Completed Industrial Work Undertaken for External Parties in the Accounting Period

operands.metric: Value of Finished Products in Current Period
Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Products at Period End
Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Products at Period Beginning

formulas.source_formula: Gross Output = Value of Finished Products in Current Period + Value of Services in Current Period + (Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-Finished Products at Period End - Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-Finished Products at Period Beginning)

nodes.name: Gross Output Value
nodes.definition: Gross Output Value refers to the total value of goods and services produced by resident units in the material production sector during a given period. It is a key indicator for measuring the total results of production activities, commonly referring to Industrial Gross Output Value.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Output Value = Selling Price (Excluding Tax) × Output

operands.metric: Value of Finished Products in Current Period
Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Products at Period End
Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Products at Period Beginning

formulas.source_formula: Gross Output Value = Value of Finished Products in Current Period + Value of Services in Current Period + (Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Products at Period End - Value of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Products at Period Beginning)

operands.metric: Value of Finished Products Produced in Current Period
Difference in Self-made Semi-finished Products (Ending - Beginning)

formulas.source_formula: Gross Output Value = Value of Finished Products Produced in Current Period + Income from External Processing Fees + Difference in Self-made Semi-finished Products (Ending - Beginning) + Difference in Work-in-Progress (Ending - Beginning)

nodes.name: Gross Output Value of Secondary Industry in the Same Period of Previous Year
Gross Pay
nodes.definition: Gross pay is the total earnings accrued by an employee before any deductions such as taxes, benefits, and withholdings. For hourly employees, gross pay is typically calculated as the hourly rate multiplied by the hours worked, excluding overtime or premium adjustments unless specified.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Pay = Hourly Rate × Hours Worked
Gross Pay = Net Pay ÷ (1 - Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Gross Pay per Pay Period
nodes.definition: Gross pay per pay period is the pre-tax, pre-deduction earnings attributed to a single payroll cycle, calculated by dividing the annual salary by the number of pay periods in a year. It represents the employee's compensation before withholdings such as income taxes, Social Security, Medicare, and other deductions.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Pay per Pay Period = Annual Salary ÷ Pay Periods
Gross Premium Difference = Present Value of Expense Loadings - Present Value of Future Expenses

nodes.name: Gross Processing Margin
nodes.definition: Gross Processing Margin is the difference between the revenue from selling finished products and the cost of acquiring the raw commodity, used to assess the profitability of processing activities in commodity markets such as oil (crack spread) and soybeans (crush margin).

formulas.source_formula: Gross Processing Margin = Finished Product Revenue - Raw Material Cost

nodes.name: Gross Profit
nodes.definition: For a business, gross profit refers to the difference between net sales and cost of sales before deducting indirect expenses, salaries, taxes, and interest expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Profit = Revenue - Cost of Goods Sold
supporting_source_formulas: Gross Profit = Revenue - Cost of Goods Sold

formulas.source_formula: Gross Profit = Net Sales - Cost of Sales
Gross Profit = Total Revenue - Total Cost of Goods Sold

nodes.name: Gross Profit Amount
nodes.definition: Gross profit amount is the difference between sales revenue and cost of sales over a specific period. It is a fundamental financial metric for measuring the profitability of a company's core products or services, reflecting the initial profit contribution generated from sales activities.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Profit Amount = Sales Revenue - Cost of Sales

nodes.name: Gross Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Gross profit margin is the difference between revenue and cost of goods sold (COGS) divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage. It measures the percentage of revenue that exceeds the direct costs of producing or purchasing goods, excluding indirect fixed costs such as administrative expenses or rent.

nodes.name: Gross Rate of Return
nodes.definition: Gross rate of return is the total return on an investment before deducting fees, expenses, or taxes, calculated as the change in value relative to the initial investment over a period.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Rate of Return = (Final Value - Initial Value) ÷ Initial Value

nodes.name: Gross Rent Multiplier
nodes.definition: Gross Rent Multiplier (GRM) is a real estate valuation screening metric that approximates how many months of gross rental income are required to equal the property's value. Calculated on a monthly basis here, it excludes operating expenses, vacancies, and financing effects, and should be used alongside more comprehensive cash flow and return measures.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Rent Multiplier = Property Value ÷ Monthly Rent

nodes.name: Gross Sales
nodes.definition: Gross sales refers to the total sum of all payments and additional charges collected from buyers for the sale of goods or provision of services within a specific accounting period, representing the original data before any adjustments for refunds, discounts, or taxes. It serves as the baseline for calculating other financial metrics (such as growth rates and profit margins).

nodes.name: Gross Spread
nodes.definition: Gross spread is the per-share difference between the public offering price and the underwriting price in an initial public offering (IPO). It represents the underwriters' gross compensation before expenses and allocations, reflecting the discount taken by the underwriting syndicate for distributing the new issue.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Spread = Public Offering Price - Underwriting Price

nodes.name: Gross Spread Ratio
nodes.definition: Gross Spread Ratio is the percentage of the public offering price retained by the underwriting syndicate as compensation in a securities offering (e.g., an IPO). It is calculated by dividing the gross spread per share by the public offering price per share and multiplying by 100, indicating the underwriters' discount relative to the offering price.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Spread Ratio = Gross Spread ÷ Public Offering Price × 100

nodes.name: Gross Value Added
aliases: Gross Value Added at Basic Prices
nodes.definition: Gross Value Added (GVA) measures the value of output less intermediate consumption, typically reported at basic prices. It represents the contribution of producers to the economy and links to GDP through product taxes and subsidies: GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + Taxes on Products − Subsidies on Products.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Value Added = Gross Domestic Product + Subsidies on Products - Taxes on Products

nodes.name: Gross Value of Operating Long-term Assets Acquired in Current Period
Gross Value of Operating Long-term Assets Disposed of in Current Period
Gross Working Capital
nodes.definition: Gross working capital is the total book value of a company's current assets expected to be converted into cash within one year. It is used to assess short-term liquidity and resource availability but excludes current liabilities and therefore does not reflect net working capital.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Working Capital = Cash + Cash Equivalents + Short-term Investments + Accounts Receivable + Inventory + Other Current Assets

nodes.name: Gross Yield
nodes.definition: Gross yield is the annual return before taxes and expenses divided by the current market price of the investment, expressed as a percentage. It measures the pre-expense income-generating efficiency of an asset and does not account for taxes, fees, or other costs.

formulas.source_formula: Gross Yield (%) = Annual Coupon Payment ÷ Par Value × 100
Gross Yield = (Annual Coupon Payment ÷ Current Market Price) × 100
Gross Yield (%) = (Annual Return ÷ Current Price) × 100

nodes.name: Gross-Up
nodes.definition: Gross-up is the process of increasing a payment to a pre-tax (gross) amount such that, after withholding at a specified tax rate, the recipient obtains a targeted net amount. It is commonly applied to bonuses, relocation benefits, and executive compensation to neutralize tax effects.

nodes.name: Grouping Interval
nodes.definition: A grouping interval is a predefined framework in data analysis that categorizes data into different classes or levels based on specific rules or criteria (such as numerical ranges, percentages, etc.). It is not a calculated metric itself, but rather a fundamental tool for data classification, frequency statistics, or subsequent analysis.

nodes.name: Growing-Equity Mortgage
nodes.definition: A growing-equity mortgage (GEM) is a fixed-rate mortgage structured so that scheduled payments increase at a predetermined growth rate each period. The increasing payments accelerate principal amortization, potentially reducing the loan's effective term and total interest paid compared to a level-payment mortgage, while the interest rate remains constant.

nodes.name: Growth Amount
nodes.definition: Growth amount is the absolute difference between the reporting period level and the base period level, used to measure the absolute change in a specific indicator between two different periods (reporting period and base period). It is a fundamental metric for time series analysis and comparison.

formulas.source_formula: Growth Amount = Reporting Period Level - Base Period Level

nodes.name: Growth Potential
nodes.definition: Growth potential refers to the possibility and capability of a company, industry, or economy to achieve scale expansion, revenue growth, or value appreciation over a future period. It is typically based on a comprehensive assessment of factors such as market space, technological development, management capability, financial condition, and competitive advantages.

nodes.name: Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Growth rate is a percentage metric that measures the magnitude of change in financial or non-financial indicators from a base period to a reporting period. It is calculated using the formula (Final Value - Initial Value) / Initial Value, and is widely applied in financial analysis, economics, and corporate management to assess growth trends and forecast future performance. Depending on the base period, it can be categorized into year-on-year growth rate, quarter-on-quarter growth rate, etc. In professional fields, it also includes concepts such as internal growth rate and sustainable growth rate.

formulas.source_formula: Growth Rate = (Current Value - Base Value) ÷ Base Value
Growth Rate = (New Subscribers ÷ Total Subscribers) × 100
Growth Rate = (Final Value - Initial Value) ÷ Initial Value × 100%
Growth Rate = (Ending Value - Beginning Value) ÷ Beginning Value × 100

nodes.name: Growth Rate of Owners' Equity
nodes.definition: The Growth Rate of Owners' Equity is a financial metric that measures the growth rate of owners' equity (i.e., net assets) over a specific period (typically one year or an accounting period). It reflects the company's ability to create value for shareholders and the enhancement of its financial strength through retained earnings from operations and shareholder contributions.

nodes.name: Growth Rate of Value Added of the Secondary Industry in the Current Period
Growth Stage Free Cash Flow to the Firm
aliases: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
nodes.definition: Growth Stage Free Cash Flow to the Firm refers to the total after-tax cash flow available to all investors (including creditors and shareholders) after meeting the reinvestment needs for operating assets when a company is in an expansion or growth phase. This metric is a core composite indicator for assessing the entity value and investment value of a company.

formulas.source_formula: Growth Stage Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Net Operating Profit After Tax - Increase in Net Operating Assets
Growth Stage Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Operating Cash Flow - Investing Cash Flow

operands.metric: Increase in Net Operating Long-term Assets

formulas.source_formula: Growth Stage Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Net Operating Cash Flow - Increase in Net Operating Long-term Assets - Depreciation and Amortization
Growth Stage Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Net Operating Profit After Tax + Depreciation and Amortization - Increase in Operating Working Capital - Capital Expenditures

nodes.name: Guarantee Coefficient
nodes.definition: The guarantee coefficient is the ratio of the bank guarantee amount to the value of the collateral, used to measure the extent to which the collateral covers the bank's guaranteed debt. It is an important indicator for assessing credit risk.

formulas.source_formula: Guarantee Coefficient = Bank Guarantee Amount ÷ Collateral Value × 100%

nodes.name: Guaranteed Compensation
nodes.definition: Guaranteed compensation refers to a fixed portion of remuneration that an employer commits to paying an employee according to the employment contract or company policy, which is not affected by performance, attendance (except for statutory absences), or the company's operational conditions. It constitutes the foundational guarantee of an employee's income and is typically explicitly stipulated in the labor contract.

nodes.name: Guaranteed Lifetime Withdrawal Benefit (GLWB)
nodes.definition: A Guaranteed Lifetime Withdrawal Benefit (GLWB) is an annuity rider that provides a contractually guaranteed annual withdrawal amount for life, regardless of market performance. The guaranteed withdrawal is typically determined by applying a stated withdrawal rate to the greater of the benefit base (which may increase via roll-up or step-up provisions) or the current cash value of the annuity.

nodes.name: Guaranteed Minimum Withdrawal Benefit (GMWB)
nodes.definition: A Guaranteed Minimum Withdrawal Benefit (GMWB) is an annuity rider that guarantees the policyholder a fixed annual withdrawal, typically expressed as a percentage of a defined benefit base (often the initial premium), regardless of market performance, subject to contract limits and fees. It provides predictable retirement income and downside protection.

nodes.name: Guppy Multiple Moving Average (GMMA)
