formulas.source_formula: Intrinsic Value = (EPS × (8.5 + 2 × Growth Rate) × 4.4) ÷ Bond Yield

nodes.name: Intrinsic Value (Option)
nodes.definition: Intrinsic value of an option is the immediate exercise value based on the current underlying price and the strike price: for a call it is the positive difference between the underlying price and the strike price, and for a put it is the positive difference between the strike price and the underlying price. Negative values are floored at zero.

nodes.name: Intrinsic Value (Put Option)
nodes.definition: Intrinsic value of a put option is the immediate exercise value, measured as the positive difference between the strike price and the underlying asset price; if the underlying price exceeds the strike price, the intrinsic value is zero. It reflects only the in-the-money amount and excludes any time value component.

nodes.name: Intrinsic Value After Down Then Up Movement
Intrinsic Value of Employee Stock Option
aliases: 员工股票期权内在价值
nodes.definition: The intrinsic value of an Employee Stock Option equals the positive difference between the underlying stock’s market price and the exercise (strike) price, multiplied by the number of shares. If the option is at-the-money or out-of-the-money (market price less than or equal to the exercise price), its intrinsic value is zero.

nodes.name: Intrinsic Value of a Call Option
nodes.definition: The intrinsic value of a call option refers to the present value of the gain obtainable if the option were exercised immediately, reflecting the economic value derived from exercising the option's right given the current market price of the underlying asset. It is calculated as the greater of the difference between the current market price of the underlying asset and the strike price, or zero.

nodes.name: Intrinsic Value of an Option
nodes.definition: The intrinsic value of an option is the amount by which the option is in-the-money, representing the immediate economic value if the option were exercised now. For a call option it equals the stock price minus the strike price when positive; for a put option it equals the strike price minus the stock price when positive.

nodes.name: Intrinsic Value with a Decline Followed by a Rise
nodes.definition: Intrinsic value with a decline followed by a rise refers to the pattern where the intrinsic value of a stock or other asset first decreases and then increases over time. Intrinsic value is typically calculated as the present value of future cash flows and is a core concept of absolute valuation methods or discounted earnings models, used to assess the economic value of an asset.

formulas.source_formula: Intrinsic Value with a Decline Followed by a Rise = Next Period Dividend ÷ (Discount Rate - Dividend Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Invalid Hours
nodes.definition: Invalid hours refer to time periods that are excluded from the calculation of total working hours or time efficiency according to specific rules, such as rest periods, non-business hours, or invalid recorded intervals.

nodes.name: Inventory
nodes.definition: Inventory refers to finished goods or merchandise held for sale, work-in-process, and materials or supplies consumed in the production process or service provision. It is classified as a current asset, its book value is calculated through specific formulas in financial statements, and it is a significant composite indicator in financial analysis.

nodes.name: Inventory Balance
nodes.definition: Inventory balance refers to the total book value of all inventory held by an enterprise at a specific point in time (e.g., the end of an accounting period) that is intended for sale or use in the production process. It reflects the scale of the enterprise's inventory assets at that point in time.

nodes.name: Inventory Balance at End of Year
Inventory Balance at Start of Year
Inventory Change at Constant Prices
nodes.definition: Inventory change at constant prices refers to the market value of changes in the physical volume of inventories held by resident units during a given period. It is calculated by adjusting the opening and closing inventory values and eliminating the effects of price changes during the period (i.e., holding gains), and is a key component in calculating total capital formation at constant prices.

nodes.name: Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Inventory cost refers to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire inventory and bring it to a condition ready for sale or use, primarily including purchase costs, production costs, and related expenses such as processing, transportation, and storage. It serves as the basis for measuring the inventory item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Inventory Level
nodes.definition: Inventory level typically refers to the quantity or value of goods, raw materials, or products physically stored by an enterprise or warehouse at a specific point in time. It is a key metric for measuring warehousing capacity and inventory management status, directly impacting storage costs and operational efficiency.

nodes.name: Inventory Quantity
nodes.definition: Inventory quantity refers to the physical count of goods, finished products, semi-finished products, etc., actually held by an enterprise at a specific point in time (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end) and intended for sale or production processes. It is a fundamental data point obtained directly through physical counts or primary methods such as inbound/outbound records, serving as the core basis for calculating inventory value, assessing inventory status, and making inventory management decisions.

nodes.name: Inventory Turnover
nodes.definition: Inventory turnover reflects the speed at which a company sells its goods within a given period, indicating the frequency at which inventory is sold and replaced.

formulas.source_formula: Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory
supporting_source_formulas: Inventory Turnover = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory

formulas.source_formula: Inventory Turnover = Sales Revenue ÷ Inventory

nodes.name: Inventory Turnover Period
nodes.definition: The inventory turnover period refers to the average number of days required for a company's inventory to complete one turnover cycle. It is used to measure the speed of inventory turnover and the efficiency of inventory management. Its calculation formula relies on financial metrics such as inventory turnover ratio, average inventory balance, and cost of goods sold. It is an important analytical tool in working capital management.

nodes.name: Inventory Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: Inventory turnover ratio is the ratio of a company's cost of goods sold (or operating revenue) to its average inventory balance over a certain period, used to measure the speed of inventory turnover, liquidity, and management efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Operating Revenue ÷ Average Inventory Balance
Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory
supporting_source_formulas: Inventory Turnover Ratio = Cost of Goods Sold ÷ Average Inventory

nodes.name: Inventory Value
nodes.definition: Inventory value refers to the total value of a company's stock of goods, typically calculated based on cost, and reflects the asset value of inventory on the balance sheet. As a non-leaf node, it can be derived from financial metrics such as unit cost and inventory quantity, and is widely applied in inventory management and carrying cost analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Inventory Value = Unit Cost × Inventory Quantity

nodes.name: Inventory Write-Down
nodes.definition: Inventory write-down is the reduction in the carrying amount of inventory on the balance sheet when its fair market value falls below its original book value, reflecting the lower-of-cost-or-market principle.

formulas.source_formula: Inventory Write-Down = Book Value - Market Value

nodes.name: Inventory Write-Off
nodes.definition: Inventory write-off refers to the direct reduction of inventory value on the balance sheet when the inventory no longer holds economic value due to obsolescence, damage, theft, or other reasons, with the write-off amount recognized as an expense in the income statement.

nodes.name: Inventory Year-end Balance
nodes.definition: Inventory year-end balance refers to the total book value of all inventory items presented on a company's balance sheet at the end of a specific fiscal year (typically December 31st). It reflects the amount of inventory held by the company on the annual cutoff date, including raw materials, work-in-progress, finished goods, and other stock intended for sale or production processes.

nodes.name: Inventory to Revenue Ratio
nodes.definition: The Inventory to Revenue Ratio reflects the proportion of a company's inventory scale relative to its sales revenue, indicating the efficiency of capital occupied by inventory.

formulas.source_formula: Inventory to Revenue Ratio = Inventory ÷ Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Inverse Leveraged ETF Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Inverse leveraged ETF ending balance refers to the terminal value of an investment after applying daily inverse leveraged returns to the underlying index, assuming daily rebalancing. The product multiplies the initial investment by a series of daily factors that reflect the leverage ratio applied to the negative of each day's index return, capturing path-dependent compounding effects typical of inverse leveraged ETFs.

nodes.name: Inverted Yield Curve
nodes.definition: An inverted yield curve occurs when short-term Treasury bond yields exceed long-term Treasury bond yields, typically interpreted as a signal of potential economic recession.

nodes.name: Invested Capital
nodes.definition: Invested capital is the total capital provided by investors (including creditors and shareholders) to support a company's business operations, representing the long-term capital actually employed by the enterprise. It serves as the core denominator for calculating key performance and valuation metrics such as Return on Invested Capital (ROIC), Economic Value Added (EVA), and Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF), reflecting the company's capital scale and capital structure.

formulas.source_formula: Invested Capital = Operating Working Capital + Net Operating Long-term Assets
Invested Capital = Fixed Assets + Working Capital
Invested Capital = Total Assets - Current Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Invested Capital = Total Assets - Current Liabilities

formulas.source_formula: Invested Capital = Fixed Assets + Net Working Capital
Invested Capital = Total Assets - Cash - Non-Interest-Bearing Liabilities
Invested Capital = Initial Cash Investment + Long-term Assets
supporting_source_formulas: Invested Capital = Initial Cash Investment + Long-term Assets

formulas.source_formula: Invested Capital = Total Assets - Non-interest-bearing Current Liabilities - Cash and Cash Equivalents

nodes.name: Invested Value
nodes.definition: Invested Value is a financial analysis metric, typically referring to the value derived by deducting necessary capital investments from the cash flow generated by a company's current operating activities, used to measure the company's true value creation capability. It reflects the net cash return that operating activities can provide to investors after meeting reinvestment needs.

nodes.name: Investing Activities Cash Inflow in Year k
Investment
nodes.definition: Investment is traditionally defined as the allocation of resources into an asset with the expectation that its value will increase over time. In financial terminology, investment refers to the commitment of funds with the expectation of obtaining more funds in the future, with the objective of generating returns. These returns may include capital gains, income (such as dividends, interest, rent), or foreign exchange gains.

nodes.name: Investment Amortization
nodes.definition: Investment amortization refers to the accounting process of systematically allocating the cost of long-term investments (including depreciation of tangible assets and amortization of intangible assets) over their expected useful lives, reflecting the consumption of asset value and the matching principle of revenues and expenses. Common calculation methods include the straight-line method and accelerated depreciation methods (such as the double-declining balance method), which form the basis for calculating financial metrics like average annual cost.

nodes.name: Investment Amount
nodes.definition: Investment amount refers to the total funds invested to obtain future returns. In financial analysis, it often refers to the future value determined by the initial investment amount, investment return rate, and investment period after considering the time value of money.

nodes.name: Investment Amount in Security j
nodes.definition: Refers to the amount of funds allocated by an investor to purchase a specific security j (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) when constructing an investment portfolio. It serves as the basis for calculating the proportion of this security in the total investment amount.

nodes.name: Investment Amount of State-owned Enterprises
nodes.definition: Investment amount of state-owned enterprises refers to the total funds invested by state-owned enterprises (i.e., enterprises owned by the whole people) for fixed asset construction during a specific period (usually one year). It is a key component in calculating indicators such as 'enterprise investment proportion' and is used to analyze the investment scale and structure of the state-owned economic sector.

nodes.name: Investment Amount of a Specific Investor
nodes.definition: The investment amount of a specific investor refers to the total funds contributed by that particular investor in a given investment project or enterprise. It serves as the basis for calculating the investor's investment proportion or shareholding ratio.

nodes.name: Investment Banking
nodes.definition: Investment banking is an advisory-focused financial service for institutional investors, corporations, governments, and similar clients. Its activities include helping companies raise capital through underwriting or acting as an agent for issuing debt and equity securities, providing mergers and acquisitions (M&A) advisory services, and offering ancillary services such as market making, derivatives and equity trading, FICC services (fixed income instruments, currencies, and commodities), and research. Unlike commercial banks, investment banks do not accept deposits and primarily generate revenue through transaction-based fees.

formulas.source_formula: Investment Banking = Advisory Fees + Underwriting Fees + Trading Revenue + Asset Management Fees

nodes.name: Investment Capital Increase
nodes.definition: Investment capital increase refers to the additional capital invested by a company during a specific period to maintain or expand operations, typically including working capital increase and net capital expenditures (capital expenditures minus depreciation).

formulas.source_formula: Investment Carrying Amount = Initial Investment + Share of Profit or Loss

nodes.name: Investment Carrying Amount (Equity Method)
aliases: Carrying Amount under the Equity Method
权益法下的投资账面价值
nodes.definition: Under the equity method, the carrying amount of an investment is measured at initial cost and subsequently adjusted each period by adding the investor’s proportionate share of the investee’s net income and subtracting the investor’s share of dividends received, reflecting changes in the investee’s net assets attributable to the investor.

nodes.name: Investment Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Investment cash flow refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by a company during a specific accounting period from purchasing or selling long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, securities investments, etc.) and other non-current investment projects. It reflects the company's cash activities in expanding or contracting its long-term asset scale.

nodes.name: Investment Center
nodes.definition: An organizational unit whose manager is accountable for its profit and the capital employed to generate that profit; performance is evaluated by comparing the center’s return on investment (ROI) to its cost of capital.

nodes.name: Investment Cost
nodes.definition: Investment cost refers to the total sum of all expenses required to complete a specific investment activity, typically including interest, taxes, fees, commissions, and other related expenditures. It is a comprehensive estimation or calculation metric used for investment decision analysis and return rate calculation, rather than a single raw data item directly obtained from financial statements.

nodes.name: Investment Cost at Initial Investment Date
Investment Days
nodes.definition: Investment days refer to the actual number of days elapsed from the initial capital investment until the capital is recovered or the investment concludes. It serves as a crucial temporal basis for calculating investment interest, returns, or assessing investment efficiency.

nodes.name: Investment End Date
nodes.definition: Investment End Date refers to the predetermined, formal termination date or time point of an investment activity or project. It serves as the fundamental time parameter required for calculating investment holding periods, evaluating investment returns, and other financial analyses.

nodes.name: Investment Expenditure
nodes.definition: Investment expenditure refers to the net cash outlay by a company for the purchase of fixed assets over a specific period, calculated as the final investment amount minus the initial investment amount, where the final investment amount is the total cash purchase of fixed assets at the end of the period, and the initial investment amount is the total fixed assets at the beginning of the period. This metric is commonly used in corporate capital budgeting and for calculating nominal GDP in macroeconomics.

formulas.source_formula: Investment Expenditure = Final Investment Amount - Initial Investment Amount

nodes.name: Investment Expenses Attributable to Other Assets
aliases: Costs of Investments Attributable to Other Assets
Investment Costs Capitalized to Other Assets
其他资产相关投资成本
nodes.definition: Investment expenses attributable to other assets refer to various expenditures incurred by an enterprise during specific investment activities that should not be directly recognized in current profit or loss. Instead, they should be treated as part of the investment cost and ultimately included in the carrying amount of the relevant other assets (such as investments in other equity instruments, investments in other debt instruments, etc.). These expenses typically include directly related costs such as transaction fees and handling charges. Their accounting treatment differs from that of financial assets at fair value through profit or loss (where transaction costs are recognized in investment income).

nodes.name: Investment Horizon
nodes.definition: Investment horizon refers to the length of time from the beginning to the end of an investment, typically measured in years. It is a key time input parameter for financial calculations such as computing future value, present value, or rate of return.

nodes.name: Investment Impairment Loss
nodes.definition: Investment impairment loss refers to the accounting loss recognized when the recoverable amount of various investment assets held by an enterprise (such as long-term equity investments, debt investments, etc.) falls below their carrying value due to reasons such as sustained market price declines or deterioration in the operating conditions of the investee.

nodes.name: Investment Income
nodes.definition: Investment income refers to the returns obtained by an enterprise or individual through external investment activities, including but not limited to interest, dividends, bonuses, and capital gains or losses generated from asset disposals. It is a key financial indicator for measuring investment effectiveness and profitability.

operands.metric: Income from External Investments (Profits, Dividends, Bond Interest, etc.)

formulas.source_formula: Investment Income = Income from External Investments (Profits, Dividends, Bond Interest, etc.) - Investment Losses
Investment Income = Investment Revenue - Investment Cost
Investment Income = (Ending Value of Principal - Beginning Value of Principal) ÷ Beginning Value of Principal × 100%

operands.metric: Sale Proceeds of Trading Financial Assets
Initial Carrying Cost of Trading Financial Assets

formulas.source_formula: Investment Income = (Sale Proceeds of Trading Financial Assets - Transaction Fees at Sale) - Initial Carrying Cost of Trading Financial Assets

nodes.name: Investment Initial Value
nodes.definition: Investment initial value refers to the capital value required to acquire or evaluate an asset or enterprise at a specific valuation reference date. It is a composite concept that can be calculated using book value, replacement value, or realizable value based on different valuation purposes and underlying data.

formulas.source_formula: Investment Initial Value = Replacement Value
Investment Initial Value = Book Value
Investment Initial Value = Realizable Value

nodes.name: Investment Loss
nodes.definition: Investment loss refers to the outflow of economic benefits incurred by an enterprise or individual from external investment activities, resulting from factors such as operating losses of the investee, asset impairment, decline in market value, or disposal proceeds lower than the cost, which lead to a reduction in the carrying value of the investment or actual recovery amount being lower than the initial investment cost.

nodes.name: Investment Management Fees
nodes.definition: Investment management fees refer to the relevant fees paid by investors for entrusting professional institutions or individuals to manage their investment assets, typically including management fees, advisory fees, custody fees, etc., representing a direct cost expenditure in investment activities.

nodes.name: Investment Multiplier
nodes.definition: The investment multiplier quantifies the total increase in national income resulting from an initial autonomous investment, determined by the marginal propensity to consume (MPC). It reflects how consumption spending propagates through the economy, amplifying the initial investment's impact on GDP.

formulas.source_formula: Investment Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 - Marginal Propensity to Consume)

nodes.name: Investment Period
nodes.definition: Investment period refers to the predetermined number of specific time intervals used for capital investment, cost incurrence, or revenue generation in project investment or financial analysis. It is typically a fundamental time parameter in project planning, contractual agreements, or financial models, serving as a known input condition for calculating financial metrics such as net present value and payback period.

nodes.name: Investment Principal
nodes.definition: Investment principal refers to the total amount of funds initially invested by an investor into a specific investment or loan, serving as the original base amount for calculating returns, interest, or profits.

nodes.name: Investment Property
nodes.definition: Investment property refers to real estate held by an enterprise to earn rental income, capital appreciation, or both, such as leased land use rights and leased buildings, and is a long-term asset of the enterprise.

nodes.name: Investment Proportion
nodes.definition: Investment proportion refers to the ratio of a specific investor's investment amount to the total relevant investment amount, used to measure that investor's share or importance in the total investment. In specific contexts, such as corporate investment analysis, it specifically refers to the ratio of the fixed asset investment amount of state-owned enterprises to the total fixed asset investment of state-owned units during the same period.

operands.metric: Total Fixed Asset Investment of Whole People-Owned Units

formulas.source_formula: Investment Proportion = State-owned Enterprise Investment Amount ÷ Total Fixed Asset Investment of State-owned Units × 100%
Investment Proportion = Specific Investor's Investment Amount ÷ Total Investment Amount × 100%

nodes.name: Investment Requirement
nodes.definition: Investment requirement refers to the total amount of new capital a company needs to invest during a specific period to support its expected growth and operational activities. It typically manifests as the projected increase in net operating assets and is a core composite metric in financial forecasting and financing planning.

formulas.source_formula: Investment Requirement = Projected Net Operating Assets - Base Period Net Operating Assets
Investment Requirement = Base Period Net Operating Assets × Operating Revenue Growth Rate
Investment Requirement = (Projected Operating Assets - Projected Operating Liabilities) - (Base Period Operating Assets - Base Period Operating Liabilities)
Investment Return = Investment Amount × Investment Return Rate

nodes.name: Investment Securities
nodes.definition: Investment securities refer to securities acquired for investment purposes, distinct from those obtained by brokers or financial intermediaries for resale or short-term speculation. Under U.S. law, investment securities are specifically governed by Article 8 of the Uniform Commercial Code (UCC), which clarifies ownership and transfer mechanisms within centralized, dematerialized systems managed by central securities depositories (such as the Depository Trust Company (DTC) and the Federal Reserve).

formulas.source_formula: Investment Securities = Purchase Cost + Gains/Losses from Fair Value Changes
Investment Securities = Equity Investments + Bond Investments + Other Security Investments

nodes.name: Investment Start Date
nodes.definition: Investment Start Date refers to the specific date on which an investor formally commits capital and begins to accrue investment returns or assume investment risks. It marks the commencement of the investment cycle and serves as the basis for subsequent calculations of holding periods, return on investment, and other metrics.

nodes.name: Investment Tax Credit
nodes.definition: The Investment Tax Credit (ITC) is a tax incentive that allows taxpayers to offset a certain percentage of the cost of eligible assets (such as renewable energy equipment) against their income tax liability. This credit directly reduces the amount of income tax owed on a dollar-for-dollar basis.

formulas.source_formula: Investment Tax Credit = Eligible Investment Amount × Credit Rate

nodes.name: Investment in Equipment and Tool Acquisition
nodes.definition: Investment in equipment and tool acquisition refers to the expenses incurred by the construction unit (or its entrusted unit) for purchasing or self-manufacturing equipment meeting fixed asset standards according to the project design document requirements, as well as for configuring the first set of tools, instruments, and production furniture for new or expansion projects. It is an important component of fixed asset investment.

nodes.name: Investment in Subsidiary's Local Currency
aliases: Investment Denominated in Host Country Currency
跨国子公司当地货币投资
nodes.definition: Refers to an investment made by a parent company in its foreign subsidiary using the currency of the country or region where the subsidiary is located (i.e., the local currency). This investment method involves cross-border capital flows and exchange rate risks. When preparing consolidated financial statements, related monetary items require specific accounting treatment and the elimination of exchange differences.

nodes.name: Investment in Year t
nodes.definition: Investment in Year t refers to the total amount of capital invested in a specific year (typically denoted as t, such as Year 1, Year 2, etc.) in project investment or corporate operations. It is commonly used in financial analysis and investment decision-making to calculate metrics such as Net Present Value and Internal Rate of Return, and is a key component of cash flow forecasting.

nodes.name: Investment-Related Expenses
nodes.definition: Investment-related expenses refer to all necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise during investment activities (such as purchasing fixed assets, investment projects, etc.) for acquiring, constructing, or improving long-term assets, including direct investment cash outlays as well as related transaction fees, taxes, consulting fees, etc.

nodes.name: Investor Contribution
nodes.definition: Investor contribution refers to the total amount of funds actually invested by investors (such as shareholders) into a company in exchange for equity or shares, typically including share capital and any premium over par value, serving as a crucial source of corporate capital.

nodes.name: Investor Equity Percentage
nodes.definition: Investor equity percentage is the proportion of total post-money equity allocated to an investor in a financing round, calculated as the investor's new equity investment divided by the company's post-money valuation and expressed as a percentage. It indicates the ownership stake received and is fundamental to cap table modeling and dilution analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Investor Equity Percentage = New Equity ÷ Post-Money Valuation × 100

nodes.name: Invoice Financing Advance Amount
nodes.definition: Invoice financing advance amount is the immediate cash provided by a lender to a borrower based on a percentage of the outstanding invoice value, enabling businesses to access working capital before the invoice is paid by the customer.

formulas.source_formula: Advance Amount = Invoice Amount × Advance Rate

nodes.name: Iron Butterfly Potential Profit
nodes.definition: Iron Butterfly potential profit represents the maximum possible profit from an iron butterfly options strategy, calculated by subtracting the differences between strike prices from the initial net credit received when initiating the trade.

nodes.name: Issuance Date / Date Outstanding
nodes.definition: The issuance date, or date outstanding, refers to the specific date on which a company's shares or securities are formally issued and begin trading. In calculating the weighted average number of shares, this date is used to determine the time-weighting of newly issued or repurchased shares during the reporting period.

nodes.name: Issuance Expenses
nodes.definition: Issuance expenses refer to the various cash payments made by a company directly to intermediaries such as underwriters, law firms, and accounting firms during the process of issuing securities (e.g., stocks, bonds). These expenses represent the direct costs of issuing securities and are typically accounted for in financial statements by either reducing capital reserves (such as share premium) or recognizing them in current period profit or loss (e.g., as financial expenses).

nodes.name: Issue Date
nodes.definition: Issue Date refers to the specific date on which securities such as stocks or bonds are formally issued or sold to investors. It is a fundamental point-in-time data point, typically sourced directly from issuance announcements or relevant legal documents, and serves as a crucial input value for subsequent financial calculations such as weighted average number of shares.

nodes.name: Issue Price
nodes.definition: Issue price refers to the price per share determined by a company when selling shares to investors during an initial public offering (IPO) or a seasoned equity offering (SEO). It serves as a critical nexus connecting the company's financing needs with capital market valuation. Its determination is typically based on the company's fundamentals, market conditions, and regulatory requirements, and can be calculated using various financial models and metrics.

formulas.source_formula: Issue Price = Net Earnings Per Share × Issue P/E Ratio
Issue Price = Total Proceeds Raised ÷ Total Number of Shares Issued

nodes.name: Issued Shares
nodes.definition: Issued shares refer to the total number of shares that a company has issued and registered in the names of shareholders (including public investors, company insiders, etc.) since its establishment, through methods such as initial public offerings and additional share issuances. It reflects the company's total share capital scale and serves as fundamental data for analyzing the company's capital structure, market capitalization, and per-share metrics.

nodes.name: Itemized Deduction
nodes.definition: Itemized deductions are specific eligible expenses that taxpayers can subtract from their adjusted gross income to reduce taxable income, such as mortgage interest, state and local taxes, and charitable contributions.

nodes.name: Itemized Quantities
nodes.definition: Itemized quantities refer to the specific calculated quantities of individual work items (such as concrete pouring, steel reinforcement binding, masonry work, etc.) that constitute the physical project, determined according to design drawings, technical specifications, and quantity take-off rules. They serve as the fundamental data for preparing bills of quantities, conducting project valuation, and performing cost accounting.

nodes.name: Japanese Yen (JPY) to U.S. Dollar (USD) Conversion
aliases: Japanese Yen to U.S. Dollar Conversion
nodes.definition: JPY to USD conversion calculates the equivalent amount in U.S. dollars (USD) for a given amount of Japanese yen (JPY) using an exchange rate quoted as USD per JPY. In this formulation, the USD amount is computed by dividing the JPY amount by the exchange rate, which must be greater than zero.

nodes.name: Jensen's Alpha
nodes.definition: Jensen's Alpha measures a portfolio's excess return over the expected return predicted by the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), isolating manager skill after adjusting for market risk (beta) and the risk-free rate.

formulas.source_formula: Jensen's Alpha = Average Asset Return - (Risk-free Rate + Beta × (Average Benchmark Return - Risk-free Rate))

nodes.name: Jensen's Measure
nodes.definition: Jensen's Measure (Jensen's Alpha) evaluates a portfolio's risk-adjusted performance by measuring the excess return over the expected return implied by the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), given the portfolio's beta, the market return, and the risk-free rate.

formulas.source_formula: Jensen's Alpha = Realized Return - (Risk-free Rate + Beta × (Market Return - Risk-free Rate))

nodes.name: Johannesburg Interbank Average Rate (JIBAR)
aliases: 约翰内斯堡同业拆借平均利率
约翰内斯堡银行同业拆借平均利率
nodes.definition: The Johannesburg Interbank Average Rate (JIBAR) is South Africa’s benchmark short-term money market reference rate. It is calculated from participating banks’ bid and offer submissions by first deriving mid-rates as the average of each bid and offer pair, then excluding the two highest and two lowest mid-rates, and finally averaging the remaining mid-rates. JIBAR is widely used to price floating-rate loans, notes, and derivatives in the South African financial markets.

formulas.source_formula: JIBAR = Sum of Trimmed Mid-Rates ÷ Number of Trimmed Mid-Rates

nodes.name: Joint Commissioning and Trial Run Costs
nodes.definition: Joint commissioning and trial run costs refer to the various expenses incurred during the joint debugging and trial operation of the entire production system before the official commissioning of a newly constructed or expanded/renovated engineering project.

nodes.name: Joint Cost
nodes.definition: Joint cost refers to the cost incurred jointly in the production process for manufacturing multiple products or serving multiple departments, which needs to be allocated among these products or departments. It typically occurs before the split-off point of joint products and serves as the basis for cost accumulation and allocation.

nodes.name: Joint Probability
nodes.definition: Joint probability refers to the probability of two or more random events occurring simultaneously in statistics and probability theory. It describes the likelihood of multiple events co-occurring.

nodes.name: Joint Probability Density Function of Random Variable X and Random Variable Y
aliases: 二维随机变量概率密度函数
nodes.definition: The joint probability density function describes the likelihood of two random variables (such as X and Y) simultaneously taking specific values. It gives the probability that the random point (X, Y) falls within a certain region in the plane, serving as the foundation for studying the relationship between two random variables.

nodes.name: Joint Probability of Random Variable X and Random Variable Y
nodes.definition: The joint probability of random variable X and random variable Y refers to the probability that, within the same probability model, random variable X and random variable Y simultaneously take specific values (or fall within specific intervals). It describes the statistical regularity of these two random variables as a whole.

formulas.source_formula: Joint Tax Liability = Joint Income - Sum of Credits - Sum of Deductions

nodes.name: Jordanian Dinar (JOD)
nodes.definition: The Jordanian Dinar (JOD) is the official currency of Jordan and is commonly converted under a fixed exchange rate framework (e.g., the JOD/USD peg). In financial accounting and treasury operations, currency conversion under a fixed exchange rate computes the target currency amount by multiplying the source currency amount by the exchange rate (expressed as units of target currency per unit of source currency), assuming no transaction fees.

nodes.name: K-Percent Rule Money Supply
aliases: K百分比规则货币供应量
nodes.definition: The K-Percent Rule Money Supply refers to the adjustment of money supply by applying a constant percentage growth rate aligned with GDP growth, as proposed by the K-Percent Rule in monetary economics.

nodes.name: K-Ratio
nodes.definition: The K-ratio is a performance metric that measures the consistency of an equity's returns over time by analyzing the slope of the cumulative return series relative to its standard error, scaled by the square root of the number of observations.

formulas.source_formula: KYD Amount = USD Amount ÷ Exchange Rate

nodes.name: Kairi Relative Index
nodes.definition: The Kairi Relative Index (KRI) measures the percentage deviation of an asset's current closing price from its simple moving average (SMA), used to identify potential buy or sell signals based on price divergence from the average.

formulas.source_formula: Kairi Relative Index = (Close Price - Simple Moving Average) ÷ Simple Moving Average × 100

nodes.name: Kappa
nodes.definition: Kappa (also known as vega) measures the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in the implied volatility of the underlying asset, expressed as the price change per 1% change in implied volatility.

formulas.source_formula: Kappa = Option Price Change ÷ Implied Volatility Change Percent

nodes.name: Kelly Criterion
nodes.definition: Kelly Criterion is a mathematical formula used to determine the optimal size of a series of bets or investments in order to maximize the logarithmic growth rate of wealth over time, based on the probability of winning and the win/loss ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Kelly Fraction = Win Probability - ((1 - Win Probability) ÷ Win/Loss Ratio)

nodes.name: Keltner Channel
nodes.definition: Keltner Channel is a technical analysis indicator consisting of three lines: a middle line (exponential moving average), an upper band (middle line plus a multiple of average true range), and a lower band (middle line minus a multiple of average true range), used to assess price volatility and trend direction.

nodes.name: Kenney Rule
nodes.definition: The Kenney Rule is a financial metric used to evaluate the financial health of an insurance company by comparing its policyholders' surplus to its unearned premium reserves. A common benchmark is a 2-to-1 ratio, indicating strong financial stability.

formulas.source_formula: Kenney Ratio = Policyholders' Surplus ÷ Unearned Premiums

nodes.name: Key Performance Indicator Score
nodes.definition: The Key Performance Indicator (KPI) score is a specific numerical value obtained through quantitative assessment of the performance of an individual, department, or organization during a specific evaluation period, based on predefined Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) and calculated using specific formulas or evaluation methods. This score is typically used for performance appraisal, objective management, and performance improvement.

nodes.name: Key Rate Duration
nodes.definition: Key rate duration measures the sensitivity of a bond's price to a 1% change in yield for a specific maturity, used to evaluate how yield curve shifts affect bond prices, particularly for non-parallel shifts.

nodes.name: Kickback
nodes.definition: A kickback refers to a portion of funds or benefits secretly returned by one party (typically a supplier) to another party (usually the decision-maker or agent of the purchasing side) in a commercial transaction to facilitate the deal or obtain favorable terms. This practice is typically covert and non-public, with the beneficiary often being an individual rather than their employing company.

nodes.name: Kiddie Tax
nodes.definition: Kiddie tax is a U.S. federal tax levied on a child’s unearned income above certain thresholds, taxing the excess at the parent’s marginal tax rate to prevent income shifting to minors.

nodes.name: Kijun Line
nodes.definition: The Kijun Line, or Base Line, is a component of the Ichimoku Cloud indicator that represents the midpoint of the highest and lowest prices over a specified period, typically 26 periods, used to identify trends and generate trading signals.

formulas.source_formula: Kijun Line = (Highest Price + Lowest Price) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Kijun-Sen
nodes.definition: Kijun-sen is the Base Line component of the Ichimoku Kinko Hyo technical indicator, representing a key support and resistance level calculated as the midpoint of the highest high and lowest low over a specified period, typically 26 periods.

formulas.source_formula: Kijun-sen = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2
supporting_source_formulas: Kijun-Sen = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2
Kijun-sen = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Kimchi Premium
nodes.definition: The Kimchi Premium is the percentage difference between the price of a cryptocurrency on South Korean exchanges and its price on foreign exchanges, reflecting local supply-demand imbalances and potential arbitrage opportunities.

formulas.source_formula: Kimchi Premium = (Price Korea - Price Foreign) ÷ Price Foreign × 100

nodes.name: Klinger Oscillator
nodes.definition: The Klinger Oscillator is a technical indicator that measures the long-term trend of money flow while remaining sensitive to short-term fluctuations by comparing volume flowing through securities with the security's price movements.

formulas.source_formula: Klinger Oscillator = EMA₁(Volume Force) - EMA₂(Volume Force)

nodes.name: Know Sure Thing
nodes.definition: Know Sure Thing (KST) is a momentum oscillator that combines the smoothed rate-of-change (ROC) of four different periods into a single weighted sum to identify trend strength and reversals in price movements.

formulas.source_formula: KST = RCMA₁ + RCMA₂ + RCMA₃ + RCMA₄

nodes.name: Kolmogorov-Smirnov Statistic
aliases: 科尔莫戈洛夫-斯米尔诺夫统计量
nodes.definition: The Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic measures the maximum absolute deviation between a sample's empirical distribution function and a specified reference cumulative distribution function, and is widely used in financial risk modeling and model validation to assess goodness-of-fit for distributional assumptions (e.g., returns, losses, or residuals). A larger KS statistic indicates poorer fit.

nodes.name: Kurtosis
nodes.definition: Kurtosis is a statistical measure that describes the degree to which a distribution is more or less peaked than a normal distribution, indicating the presence of outliers or extreme values in the tails.

formulas.source_formula: Kurtosis = (Fourth Moment ÷ (Second Moment²)) - 3

nodes.name: LIFO Gain/Loss
nodes.definition: LIFO gain/loss represents the capital gain or loss recognized when selling securities under the Last In, First Out cost basis method, calculated by summing the difference between the sale price and the purchase price for the most recently acquired lots, multiplied by the number of shares sold from each lot, until the total shares sold are allocated.

nodes.name: LIFO Liquidation
nodes.definition: LIFO liquidation refers to the reduction of inventory quantities under the Last-In, First-Out cost flow assumption such that older inventory layers (often lower-cost) are released to cost of goods sold. This can temporarily depress COGS and inflate gross profit and reported earnings. Analysts monitor LIFO liquidation to assess earnings quality and the sustainability of margins when units sold exceed recent LIFO layers.

nodes.name: LIFO Reserve
nodes.definition: LIFO reserve is the cumulative difference between inventory valued under the FIFO method and the LIFO method. It is used to reconcile inventory and cost of goods sold for financial reporting, facilitate comparability across companies using different cost flow assumptions, and support conversions from LIFO to FIFO. Changes in the LIFO reserve can indicate inflationary effects, cost trends, and purchasing patterns.

formulas.source_formula: LIFO Reserve = FIFO Inventory - LIFO Inventory

nodes.name: Labor Cost
nodes.definition: Labor cost refers to the expenses incurred for wages, bonuses, allowances, etc., for workers directly engaged in construction or production activities in engineering projects or production operations. In engineering cost estimation, it is typically calculated based on the quantity of work items and the corresponding standard labor unit price, constituting a significant component of direct project costs.

nodes.name: Labor Cost Variance
nodes.definition: Labor cost variance is the sum of the labor rate variance and the labor efficiency variance, reflecting the overall deviation of labor costs.

formulas.source_formula: Labor Cost Variance = Actual Labor Cost - Standard Labor Cost
Labor Cost Variance = Labor Rate Variance + Labor Efficiency Variance

nodes.name: Labor Efficiency Variance
nodes.definition: Labor efficiency variance refers to the cost variance arising from the difference between actual hours worked and standard hours allowed.

formulas.source_formula: Labor Efficiency Variance = (Actual Hours - Standard Hours) × Standard Rate

nodes.name: Labor Force Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Labor force growth rate is an indicator measuring the relative change in the size of the labor force or working-age population over a specific period. It is commonly used in macroeconomic analysis, potential GDP growth forecasting, and the estimation of a company's sustainable growth rate.

formulas.source_formula: Labor Force Growth Rate = (Current Period Employment - Prior Period Employment) ÷ Prior Period Employment × 100%
Labor Force Growth Rate = (Current Period Labor Force - Prior Period Labor Force) ÷ Prior Period Labor Force × 100%

nodes.name: Labor Output Elasticity
nodes.definition: Labor output elasticity is an economic concept that measures the degree to which total output or production changes in response to a proportional change in labor input. It reflects the contribution and efficiency of labor as a factor of production.

nodes.name: Labor Productivity
nodes.definition: Labor productivity measures the amount of real economic output produced per unit of labor input, typically expressed as real GDP per labor hour. It reflects the efficiency of labor in generating output and is used across national, sectoral, and firm levels to assess performance and competitiveness.

formulas.source_formula: Labor Productivity = Real GDP ÷ Labor Hours

nodes.name: Labor Productivity Growth
nodes.definition: Labor productivity growth measures the percentage change in output per labor hour between two periods, commonly proxied by GDP per labor hour. It indicates improvements or declines in efficiency and is used to assess economic performance across time at national, sectoral, or firm levels.

formulas.source_formula: Labor Productivity Growth (%) = (New GDP per Labor Hour - Old GDP per Labor Hour) ÷ Old GDP per Labor Hour × 100

nodes.name: Labor Rate Variance
nodes.definition: Labor rate variance refers to the cost difference arising from the discrepancy between the actual wage rate paid and the standard wage rate.

formulas.source_formula: Labor Rate Variance = Actual Hours × (Actual Rate - Standard Rate)

nodes.name: Labor Rate per Hour
nodes.definition: Labor rate per hour refers to the estimated or predetermined direct labor cost per hour required to complete a unit of product (or unit of operation) under standard costing or budgeting. It is typically calculated based on the ratio of the total estimated wages payable to direct production workers to the estimated total standard labor hours, serving as a key metric for measuring and controlling labor costs.

nodes.name: Labor Safety and Health Assessment Fee
aliases: Occupational Safety and Health Evaluation Cost
劳动安全卫生预评价费
nodes.definition: Labor Safety and Health Assessment Fee refers to the costs incurred for conducting a pre-assessment of labor safety and health in construction projects, in accordance with relevant national regulations, to predict and analyze potential occupational hazards and risk factors.

nodes.name: Labor Wages and Benefits
nodes.definition: Labor wages and benefits refer to the various forms of compensation and related expenses paid by an enterprise to employees in exchange for their services, primarily including base salary, bonuses, allowances, subsidies, and various benefit expenses (such as social insurance contributions, housing provident fund, union dues, employee education funds, etc.).

nodes.name: Labor and Unemployment Insurance Premiums and Taxes in Administrative Expenses
aliases: Administrative Expenses: Taxes and Social Insurance
Labor and Unemployment Insurance and Taxes in Administrative Expenses
管理费中的社保与税金
管理费用-税金及保险费
行政费用中的劳动待业保险与税金
nodes.definition: Labor and unemployment insurance premiums and taxes in administrative expenses are specific cost line items incurred by the enterprise's administrative departments for organizing and managing production and operational activities. Among these, 'Taxes' primarily refer to property tax, vehicle and vessel usage tax, land use tax, stamp duty, and other taxes recorded under administrative expenses; 'Labor and Unemployment Insurance Premiums' include the labor insurance and unemployment insurance premiums paid by the enterprise for its employees. These expenses are directly recorded in the accounting books based on their actual occurrence and serve as fundamental raw data for calculating indicators such as value added in the construction industry.

nodes.name: Labor, Unemployment, Pension, and Medical Insurance Expenses
Labor, Unemployment, Pension, and Medical Insurance Premiums
nodes.definition: Labor, unemployment, pension, and medical insurance premiums refer to mandatory contributions paid by employers and employees according to state regulations, based on the total employee wages or contribution base wage, at specified rates for social insurance programs such as pension, medical, and unemployment. These constitute a significant component of enterprise labor costs.

formulas.source_formula: Labor, Unemployment, Pension, and Medical Insurance Premiums = Contribution Wage Base × (Pension Insurance Contribution Rate + Medical Insurance Contribution Rate + Unemployment Insurance Contribution Rate)

Labor, Unemployment, Pension, and Medical Insurance Premiums = Pension Insurance Contribution Base × Pension Insurance Contribution Rate + Medical Insurance Contribution Base × Medical Insurance Contribution Rate + Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base × Unemployment Insurance Contribution Rate

nodes.name: Laddering
nodes.definition: Laddering is a fixed-income investment strategy that allocates capital evenly across bonds with staggered maturities. By spreading purchases over successive maturity dates, investors aim to manage interest rate and reinvestment risk while maintaining periodic liquidity as bonds mature.

nodes.name: Lagging Span
nodes.definition: Lagging Span (Chikou Span) is the current closing price plotted a fixed number of periods (typically 26) back on the chart, used in Ichimoku Cloud analysis to visualize the relationship between current and historical prices and gauge market sentiment.

nodes.name: Lambda
nodes.definition: Lambda (also known as omega or option elasticity) measures the percentage change in an option's price for a 1% change in the underlying asset's price, reflecting the leverage inherent in options. It is calculated as Delta multiplied by the ratio of the stock price to the option price.

formulas.source_formula: Lambda = Delta × (Stock Price ÷ Option Price)

nodes.name: Land Use Tax
nodes.definition: Land Use Tax is a type of property tax levied by the state on entities and individuals using land within the scope of cities, county towns, designated towns, and industrial and mining districts, based on the actual area of land occupied.

nodes.name: Large Cap (Big Cap)
nodes.definition: Large Cap (Big Cap) refers to companies with a high market capitalization, typically well-established and widely traded firms. Classification is based on market capitalization, which is calculated as the number of shares outstanding multiplied by the current share price. In many markets (e.g., U.S.), companies with market capitalization above commonly cited thresholds (such as USD 10 billion) are considered Large Cap, though exact cutoffs vary by index provider and region. Large Cap stocks often exhibit greater liquidity, broader analyst coverage, and relatively lower volatility compared to smaller-cap segments, but their size does not imply undervaluation or growth prospects.

nodes.name: Laspeyres Price Index
nodes.definition: The Laspeyres Price Index is an indicator that measures changes in the price level of a basket of goods and services over time. It uses a fixed base-period quantity as weights to calculate price changes in the reporting period relative to the base period. This method assumes that consumer purchase quantities remain unchanged after the base period, thus primarily reflecting the impact of pure price movements.

nodes.name: Last In, First Out (LIFO)
nodes.definition: Last In, First Out (LIFO) is an inventory cost flow assumption whereby the most recently purchased units are assumed to be sold first, assigning the latest costs to Cost of Goods Sold and the oldest costs to ending inventory.

nodes.name: Last Twelve Months (LTM)
nodes.definition: Last Twelve Months (LTM) refers to the aggregation of a financial metric (e.g., revenue, EBITDA, net income) over the most recent 12 consecutive months. It provides a current, rolling view of performance that smooths seasonality and is widely used in trend analysis, benchmarking, and valuation multiples.

formulas.source_formula: Last Twelve Months (LTM) Figure = Monthly Figure (t) + Monthly Figure (t-1) + Monthly Figure (t-2) + Monthly Figure (t-3) + Monthly Figure (t-4) + Monthly Figure (t-5) + Monthly Figure (t-6) + Monthly Figure (t-7) + Monthly Figure (t-8) + Monthly Figure (t-9) + Monthly Figure (t-10) + Monthly Figure (t-11)

nodes.name: Latest Total Shares Outstanding
nodes.definition: Latest total shares outstanding refers to the sum of all shares issued by a company at a specific point in time (typically the most recent reporting period), serving as a fundamental quantitative metric measured in 'shares'.

nodes.name: Lead Time
nodes.definition: Lead time is the total elapsed time from the initiation of a process or order to its completion, encompassing the preparatory phase, the core processing phase, and the finishing or delivery phase. It is a key operations and managerial accounting metric used to plan production, manage inventory, and assess process efficiency across manufacturing and supply chains.

formulas.source_formula: Lead Time = Pre-processing Time + Processing Time + Post-processing Time

nodes.name: Lead Time Days
nodes.definition: Lead time days refer to the number of calendar days required in advance from placing an order or initiating production to receiving goods or completing product output. It is an important time-quantity standard used for planning and controlling production or procurement activities.

nodes.name: Leading Span A
nodes.definition: Leading Span A is a component of the Ichimoku Cloud indicator, calculated as the average of the Conversion Line and the Base Line, typically plotted 26 periods ahead to forecast future support and resistance levels.

formulas.source_formula: Leading Span A = (Conversion Line + Base Line) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Leading Span B
nodes.definition: Leading Span B (Senkou Span B) is a component of the Ichimoku Cloud indicator, calculated as the average of the highest high and the lowest low over a specified period (typically 52), used to identify long-term support and resistance levels.

formulas.source_formula: Leading Span B = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Learning Curve
aliases: 累计平均时间学习曲线
nodes.definition: The learning curve is a managerial accounting concept that models how labor time or cost per unit decreases as cumulative production increases. In the cumulative average-time form, the cumulative average time per unit declines according to a constant learning percentage, supporting forecasting of production efficiency, labor budgeting, and cost estimation.

nodes.name: Lease Commencement Date
nodes.definition: The lease commencement date is the date on which the lease contract formally takes effect or begins execution, typically referring to the earlier of the lease agreement signing date and the date on which the parties commit to the principal terms. It serves as the baseline date for determining the lease term, calculating lease payments, and performing related accounting treatments.

nodes.name: Lease End Date
nodes.definition: The lease end date refers to the specific date explicitly stipulated in the lease contract when the lease relationship terminates, the lessee is required to return the leased asset, or the lease right expires. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics such as the lease term and total lease payments.

nodes.name: Lease Expense
nodes.definition: Lease expense refers to the periodic payments made by a business or individual to the lessor for the right to use an asset (such as equipment, property, etc.) as stipulated in the lease agreement. It represents a direct, fundamental cash outflow under the lease contract and typically cannot be derived from other financial statement line items.

nodes.name: Lease Payment
nodes.definition: Lease payment refers to the amount the lessee is required to pay the lessor each period under a lease agreement. It is typically determined through calculation formulas based on parameters such as the cost of the leased asset, the discount rate, and the lease term, and is a key metric in finance lease accounting and debt analysis.

nodes.name: Lease Period Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Lease period cash flow refers to the cash flow generated by the lessee or lessor from leasing activities during the lease term, including rent, tax deductions, and depreciation effects.

formulas.source_formula: Lease Period Cash Flow = Rent - Tax Shield from Rent + Tax Shield from Depreciation

nodes.name: Lease Principal
nodes.definition: Lease principal refers to the cost paid by the lessor to acquire the leased asset in a finance lease transaction, or the initial value of the asset corresponding to the right of use obtained by the lessee through the lease arrangement. It serves as the basis for calculating periodic lease payments (rent) and typically excludes interest and other charges incurred during the lease term.

nodes.name: Lease Term
nodes.definition: The lease term is the duration from the commencement date to the expiration date of a lease contract, typically expressed in years, months, or number of payment periods. It is a key parameter for calculating financial metrics such as lease payments, present value of the asset at the end of the lease, and present value of the residual asset value.

nodes.name: Lease Term Cash Flow Discount Rate
aliases: Discount Rate for Lease Cash Flows
nodes.definition: The lease term cash flow discount rate is the interest rate used in lease accounting to discount future lease payments for calculating the present value of lease liabilities or right-of-use assets. It typically employs the lessee's incremental borrowing rate or the implicit lease rate, and in financial valuation, it may be adjusted based on the after-tax cost of debt.

formulas.source_formula: Lease Term Ratio = Lease Term ÷ Asset Useful Life

nodes.name: Lease Term in Years
nodes.definition: Lease term in years refers to the effective period of a lease contract, expressed in years. It is typically calculated from the lease commencement date to the lease end date and is used in financial valuation scenarios such as present value calculations for assets in finance leases.

nodes.name: Leased Asset Acquisition Cost
aliases: Initial Direct Cost of Leased Asset
nodes.definition: Leased asset acquisition cost refers to the total direct costs paid by the lessor to acquire the leased asset (e.g., equipment) in a leasing transaction. It typically includes the purchase price of the equipment, transportation fees, insurance premiums, tariffs, and other necessary expenditures incurred to bring the asset to its intended usable condition. It serves as the fundamental data for calculating lease payments and conducting lease financial analysis.

nodes.name: Leased Asset Cost
aliases: 租赁负债初始计量金额
nodes.definition: Leased asset cost refers to the present value, discounted at a specific interest rate to the commencement date of the lease, of all future payments (such as lease payments, bargain purchase option price, etc.) that the lessee is required to make to obtain the right to use an asset over the lease term. It represents the initial amount at which the lessee recognizes both the asset and the liability under a finance lease.

nodes.name: Leased Asset Purchase Price
nodes.definition: The leased asset purchase price refers to the total price paid by the lessor (e.g., a leasing company) to acquire the leased asset (e.g., equipment) in a finance lease transaction. It typically includes the equipment's purchase price, transportation costs, insurance premiums, installation and commissioning fees, and related taxes. This amount serves as the basis for calculating periodic lease payments.

nodes.name: Leased Asset Valuation
nodes.definition: Leased asset valuation refers to the process of assessing the value of assets acquired through leasing arrangements (such as finance leases or operating leases) at specific points in time (e.g., at lease inception, termination, or for rental calculation purposes). Its core objective is to estimate the economic value of the leased asset, typically calculated based on factors such as the present value of future lease payments, the asset's remaining useful life, expected rental growth rates, and an appropriate discount rate.

nodes.name: Least Squares Criterion
nodes.definition: The least squares criterion is a statistical estimation method that determines the linear regression parameters by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between observed and fitted values. In finance and accounting analytics, it is used to quantify relationships (e.g., estimating beta, forecasting revenues or costs) and to obtain the slope and intercept of the best-fit line for predictive modeling.

nodes.name: Least Squares Method
nodes.definition: The Least Squares Method is a statistical estimation technique that fits a linear relationship between an independent variable and a dependent variable by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. In finance and accounting, it is widely used for cost estimation, forecasting, sensitivity analysis, and risk modeling (e.g., estimating beta in the Capital Asset Pricing Model).

nodes.name: Ledger Balance
nodes.definition: Ledger balance is the end-of-day account balance recorded in the bank's ledger after posting all processed credits and debits to the opening balance. It excludes pending or unprocessed transactions and serves as the opening balance for the next business day.

formulas.source_formula: Ledger Balance = Opening Balance + Credits - Debits

nodes.name: Legal Lending Limit
nodes.definition: The legal lending limit is the maximum amount a national bank or savings association may lend to a single borrower, calculated as a percentage of the institution's capital and surplus. Under U.S. regulatory standards, the base limit is 15% of capital and surplus, which may increase by an additional 10% when the credit is fully secured by readily marketable securities.

formulas.source_formula: Legal Lending Limit = (Capital + Surplus) × (15% + 10% × Secured by Readily Marketable Securities (Indicator))

nodes.name: Lehman Formula
nodes.definition: The Lehman Formula is a tiered commission schedule used primarily in investment banking to calculate advisory fees on transaction value. It applies specified percentage rates to successive portions of the transaction amount defined by tier limits, with any amount above the final tier charged at the final tier rate.

nodes.name: Level 1 Assets
nodes.definition: Level 1 Assets are a core concept in liquidity risk management, specifically referring to assets that can be quickly and easily converted into cash with minimal or no loss of value under stress scenarios. These assets typically possess extremely high credit quality and market liquidity, and are key components for financial institutions to meet regulatory requirements such as the Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR).

nodes.name: Level 2 Assets
nodes.definition: Level 2 assets refer to the asset category in the liquidity asset classification that ranks below Level 1 assets (such as cash and government bonds). They generally possess good liquidity, but compared to Level 1 assets, their market depth may be shallower, and their valuation may involve more model assumptions or rely on quotes from inactive markets. Therefore, when calculating high-quality liquid assets, their value may need to be subject to a certain percentage haircut according to regulatory requirements.

nodes.name: Level Coupon Bond Value
nodes.definition: Level coupon bond value refers to the value of a bond that pays interest periodically and repays principal at maturity, calculated as the sum of the present values of all interest payments and principal discounted at the periodic discount rate.

operands.metric: Sum of Present Values of Periodic Interest Payments

formulas.source_formula: Level Coupon Bond Value = Sum of Present Values of Periodic Interest Payments + Present Value of Face Value
Level Coupon Bond Value = Periodic Interest × Present Value Annuity Factor + Face Value × Present Value Factor

operands.metric: Number of Interest Payments per Year

formulas.source_formula: Level Coupon Bond Value = (Face Value × Coupon Rate) / Number of Interest Payments per Year × Present Value Annuity Factor + Face Value × [1 ÷ (1 + Annual Discount Rate)^Years to Maturity]

nodes.name: Leverage Contribution Ratio
nodes.definition: The leverage contribution ratio represents the additional return generated by a company through financial leverage, reflecting the enhancement effect of debt financing on shareholder returns.

formulas.source_formula: Leverage Contribution Ratio = (Net Operating Asset Profit Margin - Net Interest Rate) × Net Financial Leverage

nodes.name: Leverage Effect
nodes.definition: Leverage effect in options trading measures how many times the invested capital is represented by the position’s final value. In this implementation, it is calculated as the ratio of the final value of the option position to the initial investment, indicating capital efficiency and exposure amplification. Values greater than 1 indicate beneficial leverage. This definition assumes no transaction costs, margin requirements, or financing effects.

formulas.source_formula: Leverage Effect = Final Value ÷ Initial Investment
Leverage Effect (%) = (Theoretical Gain ÷ Option Cost) × 100

nodes.name: Leverage Effect (Options on Futures)
nodes.definition: The leverage effect for options on futures measures the percentage market exposure gained per dollar of option premium based on the underlying index move and the contract multiplier. It indicates how much notional exposure an option controls relative to its cost, abstracting from time value and volatility dynamics.

nodes.name: Leverage Ratio
nodes.definition: The consumer leverage ratio measures household indebtedness relative to the income available after taxes. It is calculated as total household debt divided by disposable personal income and indicates the household sector's debt burden, leverage, and sensitivity to changes in income and interest rates.

formulas.source_formula: Leverage Ratio = Total Household Debt ÷ Disposable Personal Income
Leverage Ratio = Notional Value ÷ Market Value

nodes.name: Leveraged ETF
aliases: 杠杆型交易型开放式指数基金
nodes.definition: A leveraged ETF is an exchange-traded fund that seeks to deliver a multiple (e.g., 2×, 3×) of the daily return of an underlying index through the use of derivatives and/or debt. Leveraged ETFs rebalance daily, causing returns to compound based on the sequence of daily index moves, which can lead to path dependency, volatility decay, and divergence from long-term multiples of index performance. They are generally intended for short-term tactical exposure rather than long-term buy-and-hold investing.

nodes.name: Leveraged Lease
nodes.definition: A leveraged lease is a finance lease structure in which the lessor acquires the leased asset using significant third-party, typically nonrecourse, debt alongside the lessor’s equity. Lease classification for accounting purposes follows finance (capital) lease criteria, such as transfer of ownership, bargain purchase option, lease term being a major part of the asset’s economic life, or the present value of lease payments being substantially all of the asset’s fair value.

nodes.name: Levered Free Cash Flow (LFCF)
nodes.definition: Levered free cash flow represents the cash available to equity holders after covering operating needs and mandatory debt service, specifically after accounting for changes in net working capital and capital expenditures. It indicates a company’s capacity to distribute cash to shareholders, repurchase shares, or reduce debt while honoring required debt payments.

operands.metric: Earnings Before Interest, Taxes, Depreciation and Amortization (EBITDA)

formulas.source_formula: Levered Free Cash Flow = EBITDA - Change in Net Working Capital - Capital Expenditures - Debt Payments

nodes.name: Liabilities
nodes.definition: Present obligations arising from past transactions or events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits.

nodes.name: Liability Translation to Renminbi
nodes.definition: Liability translation to Renminbi refers to the process by which an enterprise converts foreign currency-denominated liability items into its functional currency (Renminbi) using a specified exchange rate (such as the spot rate on the balance sheet date or the historical rate). This is a critical step in the translation of foreign currency financial statements, aimed at preparing consolidated financial statements with Renminbi as the uniform unit of measurement.

nodes.name: Liability Value
nodes.definition: Liability value refers to the economic value of debts or obligations undertaken by an enterprise at a specific point in time. From an accounting perspective, it typically refers to the book value of liabilities, i.e., the amount recorded on financial statements; from the perspective of financial management and markets, it may involve the discounted calculation of future cash outflows to reflect its fair market value.

formulas.source_formula: Life Insurance Coverage (Needs Approach) = Lump Sum Needs + Future Income Needs

nodes.name: Lifetime Cost
nodes.definition: Lifetime cost represents the total cost of ownership of an asset over its useful life, encompassing the initial purchase price, cumulative operating costs, maintenance expenses, and debt repayments. It is commonly used in cost accounting and capital budgeting to evaluate long-term affordability and economic efficiency. Unless explicitly considered, it typically excludes opportunity costs and residual/salvage value at the end of the asset’s life.

formulas.source_formula: Lifetime Cost = Purchase Price + Total Operating Costs + Total Maintenance Costs + Total Debt Repayments

nodes.name: Lifetime Learning Credit
nodes.definition: The Lifetime Learning Credit (LLC) is a nonrefundable U.S. federal income tax credit that allows taxpayers to claim 20% of up to $10,000 in qualified tuition and related expenses per return (maximum $2,000), subject to a Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) phase-out determined by filing status. The credit phases down proportionally within the applicable MAGI range and is eliminated above the upper threshold.

nodes.name: Likelihood
nodes.definition: Likelihood is a core concept in statistics that measures the probability of observing the current sample data given a set of parameters. In Bayesian statistics, it is combined with prior probability to calculate posterior probability via Bayes' theorem.

nodes.name: Likelihood of Occurrence
nodes.definition: Likelihood of occurrence refers to the probability or chance of a specific accident or hazardous event happening under given environmental conditions and circumstances. It is a key qualitative or semi-quantitative indicator in risk assessment, used to measure the ease with which a risk event may occur.

nodes.name: Limit
nodes.definition: The limit is a core concept in calculus, describing a definite value that a function value (or term value) approaches infinitely as the independent variable (or term number) approaches a specific value. It serves as the foundation for understanding concepts such as derivatives and integrals.

nodes.name: Limit Down
nodes.definition: Limit down refers to the maximum allowable decline in the trading price of a security or futures contract within a specified period, set by exchanges to curb excessive volatility. When the price falls to the limit down price, trading may be halted or restricted according to exchange rules.

formulas.source_formula: Limit Down Price = Reference Price × (1 - Limit Percentage)
Limit Down Threshold Price = Closing Price × (1 - Threshold Percentage)

nodes.name: Limit Order
nodes.definition: A limit order is an order instruction to buy a security at a price not higher than a specified price, or to sell a security at a price not lower than a specified price (both directions are referred to as 'or better'). This allows traders to control the execution price; however, the order may not be filled. A buy limit order can only be executed at the limit price or lower, while a sell limit order can only be executed at the limit price or higher.

nodes.name: Limit Price
nodes.definition: A limit price is a specific price pre-set by a trader when placing an order; the trade will only be executed when the market price reaches or is better than this pre-set price. It is one of the most fundamental order types in financial trading, primarily used to control transaction costs or lock in profits.

nodes.name: Limited Net Operating Loss (NOL)
nodes.definition: The limited Net Operating Loss (NOL) is the amount of NOL that may be applied in a tax period subject to the statutory cap, which generally restricts the NOL deduction to 80% of taxable income. It equals the lesser of the available NOL carryforward and 80% of taxable income.

nodes.name: Limited Partner Total Committed Capital
aliases: 有限合伙人承诺出资总额
有限合伙人认缴出资总额
nodes.definition: Limited Partner Total Committed Capital refers to the total amount of capital that all limited partners collectively commit to contribute to the limited partnership as stipulated in the limited partnership agreement. This represents the maximum capital contribution obligation that each limited partner is required to fulfill in the future according to the agreement, and serves as the core foundational data for the fund's fundraising size.

nodes.name: Limited Partnership
nodes.definition: A Limited Partnership (LP) is a form of partnership that includes general partners and limited partners. General partners possess management rights and assume unlimited liability for the partnership's debts; limited partners do not have management rights but assume limited liability for the partnership's debts only to the extent of their capital contributions. A limited partnership differs from a limited liability partnership, in which all partners enjoy limited liability.

formulas.source_formula: Limited Partnership = Total Assets - Total Liabilities
Line Item Percentage = (Line Item Amount ÷ Base Figure) × 100

nodes.name: Line of Best Fit
nodes.definition: The line of best fit, estimated via Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), is the linear relationship that minimizes the sum of squared residuals between observed values and fitted values. In financial analysis and accounting, it is used to estimate cost functions, forecast revenues or expenses, derive factor sensitivities (betas), and model relationships among financial variables.

nodes.name: Linear Cost Function
nodes.definition: A linear cost function expresses Total Cost as the sum of a fixed cost component and a variable cost component proportional to the activity level (e.g., units produced or hours worked). It is used in cost accounting to model mixed costs for forecasting, budgeting, and decision-making.

nodes.name: Linear Interpolation
nodes.definition: Linear interpolation is a method of estimating an unknown value that lies between two known data points by assuming a straight-line relationship between them, commonly used in financial time-series analysis and valuation.

nodes.name: Linear Regression
nodes.definition: Linear regression is a statistical analysis method used to model the linear relationship between a dependent variable and one or more independent variables. It calculates the intercept and slope using the least squares method and is widely applied in financial and accounting fields such as financial forecasting and stock beta coefficient calculation.

nodes.name: Linear Regression (OLS)
nodes.definition: Linear regression (OLS) estimates a linear relationship between a dependent variable and an independent variable by minimizing the sum of squared residuals. In finance and accounting, it is used to model cost behavior, forecast revenues or expenses, estimate asset betas, and analyze drivers of financial performance.

nodes.name: Linear Relationship
