nodes.definition: In financial analysis and accounting-related analytics, a linear relationship (affine transformation) maps one variable to another using a constant scale factor and offset. Such transformations are used for index rebasing, unit conversions, and normalization of financial metrics to comparable scales. The provided example demonstrates a linear transformation converting degrees Fahrenheit to degrees Celsius.

nodes.name: Linearly Weighted Moving Average
nodes.definition: The Linearly Weighted Moving Average (LWMA) is a technical analysis indicator that assigns linearly decreasing weights to historical prices over a specified lookback period, emphasizing more recent observations. It is calculated as the sum of each price multiplied by its corresponding linear weight divided by the sum of all weights, producing a moving average that is more responsive to recent price changes than the Simple Moving Average (SMA).

formulas.source_formula: Linearly Weighted Moving Average = Weighted Sum of Prices ÷ Sum of Weights

nodes.name: Lintner's Model
nodes.definition: Lintner's model is an empirical dividend policy framework in which firms smooth dividends by partially adjusting the current period dividend toward a target dividend. The adjustment is governed by a partial adjustment coefficient (speed of adjustment), includes a constant intercept, and may include an error term to capture unexpected variations.

nodes.name: Liquid Funds
nodes.definition: Liquid funds represent the portion of a company's current assets that exceeds its current liabilities, used to measure short-term solvency and the adequacy of operating funds, serving as a core indicator for assessing corporate financial liquidity.

formulas.source_formula: Liquid Funds = Current Assets - Current Liabilities
Liquid Funds = Annual Operating Revenue × Operating Revenue to Funds Ratio

nodes.name: Liquidation Expenses
nodes.definition: Liquidation expenses refer to the various necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise during the liquidation process to complete the liquidation work. These expenses typically include asset disposal fees, financial audit fees, administrator remuneration, litigation costs, public announcement fees, etc., and should be paid preferentially from the liquidation assets.

nodes.name: Liquidation Margin
nodes.definition: Liquidation margin is the amount of equity in a margin account attributable to immediately realizable cash and the current market values of long and short positions. It is used to assess whether the account can meet margin requirements and withstand forced liquidation thresholds.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidation Margin = Cash Deposits + Long Position Value - Short Position Value

nodes.name: Liquidation Value
nodes.definition: Liquidation value refers to the residual value available for distribution to owners (shareholders) after deducting all expenses incurred during the liquidation process and repaying all liabilities from the total revenue obtained by selling all assets when a company ceases operations and undergoes asset liquidation. It serves as the basis for evaluating equity value in the event of corporate bankruptcy or liquidation.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidation Value = Total Proceeds from Asset Sales - Liquidation Expenses - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Liquidity
nodes.definition: Liquidity is a concept in economics concerning the convertibility of assets and liabilities, encompassing market liquidity (the ease of selling an asset), accounting liquidity (the ability to meet cash payment obligations at maturity), funding liquidity (the availability of credit support to finance asset purchases), liquid capital (cash held by a company), and liquidity risk (the risk of impaired market liquidity).

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
Liquidity = (Current Assets - Inventory) ÷ Current Liabilities
Liquidity = Marketable Equivalent Value ÷ Illiquid Equity Value

nodes.name: Liquidity Adjustment Factor
nodes.definition: The Liquidity Adjustment Factor is a composite parameter used to quantify the value adjustment or risk compensation required for assets or portfolios due to lack of market liquidity. It is typically derived from specific rules or models based on underlying metrics such as liquidity ratios, asset classes, market depth, and bid-ask spreads, and serves as a key input variable for calculating liquidity discount rates or adjusting Value at Risk models.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity Adjustment Factor = 1 ÷ (1 + Liquidity Risk Premium)
Liquidity Adjustment Factor = 1 - (Bid-Ask Spread Rate × Asset Class Adjustment Coefficient)
Liquidity Adjustment Factor = Liquidity Ratio ÷ Market Benchmark Liquidity Ratio

nodes.name: Liquidity Coverage Ratio
nodes.definition: The Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) is a regulatory requirement under Basel III, designed to ensure that banks hold sufficient high-quality liquid assets (HQLA) to cover their total net cash outflows over a 30-day stress period, thereby enhancing short-term resilience to liquidity risk.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity Coverage Ratio = (Total Cash and Liquid Assets ÷ Net Cash Outflows over 30 Days) × 100
Liquidity Coverage Ratio (LCR) = (High-Quality Liquid Assets ÷ Total Net Cash Outflows) × 100

nodes.name: Liquidity Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The liquidity discount rate refers to the additional required rate of return or value discount ratio applied in valuation models due to the lack of liquidity of an asset or equity interest. It is commonly used to adjust the expected return or present value of illiquid assets. As a composite metric, it is typically estimated based on indicators such as market liquidity premium and risk premium.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity Discount Rate = Market Liquidity Premium
Liquidity Discount Rate = 1 - (Illiquid Equity Value ÷ Liquid Equity Value)
Liquidity Discount Rate = Risk Premium × Liquidity Adjustment Factor

nodes.name: Liquidity Premium
nodes.definition: In economics, the liquidity premium is used to explain the difference between two financial securities that are identical in all characteristics except liquidity. It reflects the additional return required by investors for holding securities with lower liquidity (more difficult to sell), especially over longer time horizons. This premium causes the yield curve to slope upward, and it is higher for illiquid assets such as unlisted stocks or restricted corporate bonds.

operands.metric: Price at End of Restriction Period

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity Premium = Highest Price During Restriction Period - Price at End of Restriction Period

nodes.name: Liquidity Ratio
nodes.definition: The liquidity ratio is a key financial metric for measuring a company's short-term solvency. It assesses whether a company has sufficient liquid assets to repay its maturing debts in the short term (typically within one year or one operating cycle) by comparing its current assets to its current liabilities.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Liquidity Ratios
nodes.definition: Liquidity ratios are financial metrics used to measure a company's ability to pay off its short-term debts as they come due, using current assets. They provide insight into the firm's short-term financial strength and operational efficiency.

nodes.name: Liquidity Risk Premium
nodes.definition: Liquidity risk premium refers to the additional rate of return or compensation required by investors for bearing the extra risk associated with holding less liquid assets (i.e., assets that cannot be quickly and cost-effectively converted into cash). It reflects the impact of asset liquidity differences on price or yield.

nodes.name: Liquidity-Adjusted Equity Value
aliases: 流动性调整后权益价值
非流动性折价后权益价值
nodes.definition: Liquidity-adjusted equity value refers to the assessed value of equity market value after applying a liquidity discount adjustment, considering factors such as insufficient market liquidity or restrictions on equity transfer. It reflects the realizable value of equity assets under conditions of imperfect market liquidity, commonly used in scenarios such as valuation of non-listed companies and assessment of restricted shares.

formulas.source_formula: Liquidity-Adjusted Equity Value = Equity Market Value × (1 - Liquidity Discount Rate)
Liquidity-Adjusted Equity Value = Net Profit ÷ Cost of Equity × (1 - Liquidity Discount Rate)

nodes.name: Listed Company Bond Yield to Maturity
nodes.definition: Listed company bond yield to maturity refers to the annualized rate of return an investor can achieve by purchasing a bond at a specific market price and holding it until its maturity date. It is the discount rate that equates the present value of the bond's future cash flows (including periodic interest payments and the principal at maturity) to its current purchase price. It serves as a core indicator for evaluating bond investment value and measuring the compensation rate for bond credit risk.

formulas.source_formula: Listed Company Bond Yield to Maturity = [Bond Face Value × (1 + Coupon Rate × Bond Effective Term) - Bond Purchase Price] ÷ (Bond Purchase Price × Remaining Years to Maturity) × 100%

nodes.name: Living Expenses
nodes.definition: Living expenses refer to the total of various basic expenditures incurred by individuals or households to maintain daily life, typically including specific consumption items such as rent, food and beverage, transportation, utilities, communication, and daily necessities. In a financial context, it is an expenditure item composed of multiple original consumption categories, rather than a composite indicator calculated through formulas.

nodes.name: Living Wage
nodes.definition: Living wage is the level of income required for an individual or household to afford basic needs (including housing, food, healthcare, childcare, taxes, and transportation) without falling into poverty. It is often calibrated so that housing costs do not exceed a specified share of total income.

formulas.source_formula: Living Wage = Cost of Basic Needs ÷ (1 - Housing Percentage)

nodes.name: Load Factor
nodes.definition: Load factor is an airline operating efficiency metric that measures the percentage of available seat capacity utilized by revenue passengers. It is calculated as Revenue Passenger Miles divided by Available Seat Miles and expressed as a percentage, indicating capacity utilization and demand relative to supply.

formulas.source_formula: Load Factor (%) = (Revenue Passenger Miles ÷ Available Seat Miles) × 100

nodes.name: Loading and Unloading Charges
nodes.definition: Loading and unloading charges refer to the actual or payable expenses incurred by an enterprise during the transportation of goods for operations such as loading goods onto transport vehicles or unloading them from transport vehicles. It is an original cost in accounting, directly allocated to the cost of relevant assets (such as inventory) or recognized as a current period expense.

nodes.name: Loan
nodes.definition: In finance, a loan refers to a transaction where one party lends funds to another, with an agreement for repayment. The borrower thereby incurs a debt and typically pays interest for the use of the funds. The relevant terms are generally specified in a promissory note, detailing the principal amount, interest rate, and repayment date.

nodes.name: Loan Amount
nodes.definition: Loan amount refers to the total sum of funds actually borrowed by an individual or enterprise from banks, financial institutions, or other lenders. It is typically determined based on the borrower's creditworthiness, income level, collateral value, and the lending institution's policies, and serves as the basis for calculating interest and repayment schedules.

formulas.source_formula: Loan Amount = Purchase Price - Down Payment

nodes.name: Loan Constant
nodes.definition: Loan constant is the annual debt service divided by the total loan principal, typically expressed as a percentage, indicating the annual cost of carrying a fixed-rate loan and enabling comparison of borrowing costs across loans.

formulas.source_formula: Loan Constant = Annual Debt Service ÷ Total Loan Amount

nodes.name: Loan Default Status
nodes.definition: Loan default status is a binary assessment indicating whether a loan is considered in default based on whether the days past due meet or exceed a specified default threshold. It is used in credit risk management, portfolio monitoring, regulatory reporting, and provisioning.

nodes.name: Loan Interest Income
nodes.definition: Loan interest income refers to the interest compensation collected by financial institutions (such as banks) or enterprises from borrowers for extending loans, and is one of their primary revenue sources.

nodes.name: Loan Life Coverage Ratio (LLCR)
nodes.definition: Loan Life Coverage Ratio (LLCR) is a project finance solvency ratio that measures a project's ability to repay its outstanding debt over the loan term. It is calculated as the net present value of cash flows available for debt service, discounted at the weighted average cost of capital, plus the debt service reserve, divided by the outstanding debt balance.

formulas.source_formula: Loan Life Coverage Ratio = (NPV of Cash Flows + Debt Service Reserve) ÷ Outstanding Debt

nodes.name: Loan Loss Provision
nodes.definition: Loan loss provision is the estimated amount recognized to cover expected credit losses on a loan portfolio. In this simplified approach, the provision is measured as the sum of each loan's exposure multiplied by its historical default rate and is recorded as an expense that increases the allowance for loan losses.

nodes.name: Loan Loss Reserve
aliases: Allowance for Loan and Lease Losses
nodes.definition: A loan loss reserve is a contra-asset account maintained by lending institutions to absorb expected credit losses on their loan portfolio. It represents the estimated portion of total loans not expected to be collected, typically determined by applying an expected default rate to outstanding loans, supporting prudent risk management and financial reporting.

formulas.source_formula: Loan Loss Reserve = Total Loans × Estimated Default Rate

nodes.name: Loan Principal
nodes.definition: Loan principal refers to the original amount borrowed by the borrower from a lending institution (such as a bank), which is used to calculate interest and determine the repayment schedule. It is a core element in the loan agreement and serves as the foundation for all subsequent financial calculations.

nodes.name: Loan Repayment Amount
nodes.definition: Loan repayment amount refers to the total principal or principal plus interest actually paid by an enterprise or individual to creditors (e.g., banks) within a specific period, as stipulated in the loan agreement. It is a specific figure of cash outflow, directly sourced from contract execution records or bank statements, reflecting actual debt settlement activities that have occurred.

nodes.name: Loan Servicing Fee
nodes.definition: A loan servicing fee is the portion of each periodic loan payment retained by the loan servicer as compensation for administering the loan. It is typically calculated as a fixed percentage of the periodic payment and recognized as servicing revenue.

formulas.source_formula: Servicing Fee = Periodic Payment × Servicing Fee Rate

nodes.name: Loan Term
nodes.definition: Loan term refers to the agreed-upon duration for which a borrower obtains funds from a lending institution, typically measured in years. It is a key parameter for calculating loan interest and determining the repayment schedule.

nodes.name: Loan Term (Years)
nodes.definition: Loan Term (Years) refers to the total duration, typically measured in years, explicitly stipulated in the loan contract or borrowing agreement, during which the borrower is required to repay the entire principal and interest. It serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating loan interest and formulating repayment plans.

nodes.name: Loan-to-Cost Ratio (LTC)
nodes.definition: The Loan-to-Cost (LTC) ratio measures the proportion of a project's construction cost financed by debt. It is calculated as the loan amount divided by the construction cost and is used by lenders to assess leverage and construction lending risk. A higher LTC indicates greater lender risk and lower borrower equity contribution.

formulas.source_formula: Loan-to-Cost Ratio (LTC) = Loan Amount ÷ Construction Cost

nodes.name: Loan-to-Deposit Ratio (LDR)
nodes.definition: Loan-to-Deposit Ratio (LDR) is a banking liquidity metric that measures the proportion of a bank’s total deposits that have been deployed as loans. It assesses balance sheet liquidity and funding stability, with higher values indicating more aggressive lending relative to available deposits and potentially lower liquidity.

formulas.source_formula: Loan-to-Deposit Ratio = (Total Loans ÷ Total Deposits) × 100

nodes.name: Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio
nodes.definition: The Loan-to-Value (LTV) ratio measures the proportion of a loan or mortgage relative to the appraised value of the collateral property. It is a key lending risk indicator used by financial institutions; mortgages with an LTV above common thresholds (e.g., 80%) are often classified as high-ratio loans and may require mortgage insurance.

formulas.source_formula: Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio = Loan Amount ÷ Property Value
Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio (%) = Mortgage Amount ÷ Appraised Property Value × 100
supporting_source_formulas: Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio (%) = Mortgage Amount ÷ Appraised Property Value × 100
Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio = (Mortgage Amount ÷ Appraised Property Value) × 100%

nodes.name: Loan-to-Value Ratio
nodes.definition: Loan-to-Value Ratio (LTV) typically refers to the ratio of the loan amount to the appraised value of the collateral, used to measure the risk exposure of the loan. For example, an LTV of 70% means the loan amount is 70% of the collateral value.

formulas.source_formula: Loan-to-Value Ratio = Loan Amount ÷ Market Value
Loan-to-Value Ratio = Loan Amount ÷ Property Value × 100%

nodes.name: Loan-to-Value Ratio (LTV)
nodes.definition: The loan-to-value ratio is the ratio between the principal or total principal and interest of a mortgage loan and the appraised value of the collateral, used to measure loan risk and determine the value of collateral a borrower must provide to secure loan repayment.

nodes.name: Local Education Surcharge
nodes.definition: The Local Education Surcharge is a local government fund levied in accordance with national regulations to increase local education funding and promote the development of local education. Its revenue is primarily used to supplement local education expenditures.

nodes.name: Local Education Surcharge Rate
aliases: Rate of Local Education Fee Surcharge
地方教育费附加征收率
nodes.definition: The Local Education Surcharge Rate refers to the percentage applied by local governments to collect local education surcharges from entities and individuals who pay Value-Added Tax (VAT) and Consumption Tax, based on a certain proportion of the actual VAT and Consumption Tax paid, for the purpose of raising education funds. The current nationwide uniform rate is 2%.

nodes.name: Log Old Price
nodes.definition: Log old price refers to the value obtained by taking the natural logarithm or common logarithm of the price of an asset or commodity at a specific historical point in time (i.e., the old price). In financial analysis, logarithmic prices are often used to calculate price change percentages or returns under continuous compounding, eliminating the influence of price levels and simplifying calculations.

nodes.name: Log Price
nodes.definition: Log price refers to the value obtained by taking the natural logarithm (usually base e) of the price of a commodity or financial asset. In financial analysis, using log prices simplifies calculations, particularly when computing continuously compounded returns or price change percentages. The log return (i.e., the difference in log prices) approximates the percentage change in price and exhibits superior statistical properties, such as approximate normal distribution.

nodes.name: Log-Normal Distribution
nodes.definition: In quantitative finance, the log-normal distribution models positive-valued variables whose natural logarithm is normally distributed, such as asset prices under geometric Brownian motion. It is widely used for option pricing, risk modeling, and portfolio simulations due to its ability to capture skewness and non-negativity in returns or prices.

nodes.name: Logarithmic Price Scale
nodes.definition: A logarithmic price scale represents price movements in percentage terms rather than absolute units. In the given implementation, it computes sequential percentage price changes (arithmetic returns) between consecutive observations, which is useful for analyzing relative volatility and performance over time.

nodes.name: London Interbank Offered Rate
aliases: 伦敦银行同业拆放利率
nodes.definition: The London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) is an average interest rate calculated from estimated data submitted by major banks in London, representing the rate at which banks estimate they could borrow from other banks. LIBOR served as a major global benchmark rate, covering short-term rates for five currencies and seven maturities (from overnight to one year). The rate was phased out by the end of 2021 and officially ceased on June 30, 2023, being replaced by risk-free rates such as SOFR and SARON.

nodes.name: Long Butterfly Spread
nodes.definition: A long butterfly spread is an options strategy combining bull and bear spreads with three strike prices, designed to profit from low volatility; maximum profit occurs when the underlying asset price equals the middle strike at expiration.

formulas.source_formula: Long Butterfly Spread P&L = Middle Strike - Lower Strike - Premium Cost

nodes.name: Long Call Option Expiration Value
aliases: Terminal Value of a Long Call
nodes.definition: Long call option expiration value, also known as call option exercise net income, refers to the theoretical cash inflow that an investor holding a long call option can obtain by exercising the option at expiration. It equals the difference between the underlying asset's market price at expiration and the option's strike price, but is zero when this difference is negative, as the option holder would choose not to exercise. This value does not deduct the initial purchase cost of the option (premium).

nodes.name: Long Call Option Net Profit/Loss
aliases: Net Payoff of Long Call Option
Net Profit of Long Call Option
nodes.definition: The net gain or loss of a long call option at expiration, equal to its expiration date value minus the option purchase price.

nodes.name: Long Hedge
nodes.definition: A long hedge is a risk management strategy in which a firm buys futures contracts to protect against rising spot prices for inputs or commodities. By taking a long position in futures, the firm aims to lock in purchase costs and offset adverse spot price movements. Hedge effectiveness can be evaluated by the net cost change, combining the change in the physical (spot) market cost and the profit or loss realized on the futures contract.

nodes.name: Long Jelly Roll
nodes.definition: A long jelly roll is an options calendar arbitrage strategy constructed at a single strike across two maturities. It exploits mispricing between the call calendar spread and the put calendar spread. The theoretical value reflects the cost of carry across maturities; a long jelly roll profits when the put calendar spread is priced richer than the call calendar spread, net of transaction costs.

nodes.name: Long Put Profit
nodes.definition: Long put profit refers to the net profit or loss realized from purchasing a put option, calculated as the option’s intrinsic value at expiration minus the premium paid, multiplied by the contract size (shares per option). It evaluates the financial outcome of a bearish options strategy where the underlying asset is expected to decline.

nodes.name: Long Straddle
nodes.definition: A long straddle is an options strategy that involves purchasing a call and a put option with the same strike price and expiration on the same underlying asset. The strategy profits from large price movements in either direction. At expiration, the profit equals the absolute move of the underlying price relative to the strike, minus the net premium paid. The maximum loss is limited to the net premium paid when the underlying price closes at the strike. Break-even points occur at the strike price plus and minus the net premium paid.

formulas.source_formula: Long Straddle Profit (Down Move) = Option Strike Price - Underlying Price at Expiration - Net Premium Paid
Long Straddle Profit (Up Move) = Underlying Price at Expiration - Option Strike Price - Net Premium Paid

nodes.name: Long Synthetic (Synthetic Put)
aliases: 卖空股票+买入看涨期权
nodes.definition: A Long Synthetic (Synthetic Put) replicates the payoff of a long put by shorting the underlying stock and purchasing a call option on the same underlying. The strategy’s worst-case outcome is capped when the underlying price is at or above the call strike; ignoring transaction costs, the maximum loss (expressed as the worst-case profit/loss) equals the short sale price minus the call option strike price minus the call option premium, under the assumption that the short sale price is equal to or higher than the strike price.

nodes.name: Long-Term Capital Gain or Loss
nodes.definition: Long-term capital gain or loss is the net profit or loss realized from selling a capital asset held for more than 12 months, calculated as the sale price minus the purchase price. It reflects investment performance and is often subject to preferential tax treatment compared to short-term gains in many jurisdictions.

formulas.source_formula: Long-Term Capital Gain or Loss = Sale Price - Purchase Price

nodes.name: Long-Term Capital Gains Tax
nodes.definition: Long-term capital gains tax is the tax levied on profits realized from the sale of assets held for more than one year, calculated based on the gain, the taxpayer’s taxable income, and filing status.

formulas.source_formula: Long-Term Capital Gains Tax = Capital Gain × Applicable Tax Rate
Long-Term Capital Gains Tax = Net Long-Term Capital Gain × Long-Term Capital Gains Tax Rate
Long-Term Capital Gains Tax = Long-Term Capital Gains × Long-Term Capital Gains Tax Rate

nodes.name: Long-Term Capital Gains Tax Liability
nodes.definition: Long-Term Capital Gains Tax Liability refers to the amount of income tax owed on realized long-term capital gains, calculated by applying the applicable capital gains tax rate to the gain. It quantifies the taxpayer's financial obligation arising from the appreciation and subsequent disposition of capital assets held for the long-term holding period defined by tax regulations.

formulas.source_formula: Long-Term Capital Gains Tax Liability = Long-Term Capital Gain × Capital Gains Tax Rate

nodes.name: Long-Term Capital Loss Deduction
nodes.definition: Long-term capital loss deduction refers to the portion of a taxpayer's capital loss that can be applied against taxable income or capital gains in the current tax year, subject to a statutory annual cap. Any excess loss beyond the cap may be carried forward to subsequent tax years in accordance with tax regulations.

formulas.source_formula: Long-Term Capital Loss Deduction = min(Capital Loss, Maximum Deductible Amount)

nodes.name: Long-Term Debt to Capitalization Ratio
nodes.definition: The long-term debt to capitalization ratio is a solvency and capital structure metric that measures the proportion of a company's total capitalization financed by long-term debt. It is calculated as long-term debt divided by the sum of long-term debt, preferred stock, and common stock; higher values indicate greater financial leverage and potentially higher insolvency risk.

formulas.source_formula: Long-Term Debt to Capitalization Ratio = Long-Term Debt ÷ (Long-Term Debt + Preferred Stock + Common Stock)

nodes.name: Long-Term Debt to Total Assets Ratio
aliases: 长期负债与总资产比率
长期负债占总资产比率
nodes.definition: The Long-Term Debt to Total Assets Ratio measures the proportion of a company's total assets financed by long-term debt. It is calculated as long-term debt divided by total assets and is used to assess solvency, financial leverage, and capital structure risk.

formulas.source_formula: Long-Term Debt to Total Assets Ratio = Long-Term Debt ÷ Total Assets

nodes.name: Long-Term Equity Anticipation Securities (LEAPS) Option Premium
aliases: 长期股票预期证券期权权利金
nodes.definition: LEAPS option premium is the total price paid to acquire a long-dated call option on an equity or equity index. It equals the sum of the option’s intrinsic value and time value; for a call, intrinsic value is the positive difference, if any, between the underlying’s market price and the strike price.

formulas.source_formula: Option Premium = Intrinsic Value + Time Value

nodes.name: Long-term Asset Impairment Provision
aliases: Provision for Impairment of Long-term Assets
长期资产减值损失准备
nodes.definition: Long-term asset impairment provision is a reserve pre-accrued by an enterprise to address potential declines in value or the inability to recover the full carrying amount of its long-term assets (such as long-term equity investments, fixed assets, intangible assets, etc.). It reflects the difference between the recoverable amount of an asset and its carrying amount, serving as a significant deduction in the calculation of net asset value.

nodes.name: Long-term Assets
nodes.definition: Long-term assets refer to assets that an enterprise plans to hold for more than one year or one complete operating cycle, which are expected to generate long-term economic benefits for the enterprise. They primarily include plant and equipment, land use rights, patents, long-term equity investments, etc.

nodes.name: Long-term Borrowings
nodes.definition: Long-term borrowings refer to various loans obtained by an enterprise from banks or other financial institutions with a repayment term exceeding one year (excluding one year). It constitutes a significant non-current liability for the enterprise, primarily used to fund long-term asset investments and business expansion.

nodes.name: Long-term Borrowings Due Within One Year (Prior Period)
aliases: Current Portion of Long-term Debt from Prior Period
Long-term Borrowings Due within One Year of Previous Period
上期一年内到期长期负债
前期一年内到期的长期借款
前期一年内到期长期借款
nodes.definition: Long-term borrowings due within one year (prior period) refers to the principal portion of long-term borrowings that was classified as current liabilities on the balance sheet of the previous reporting period (e.g., the prior fiscal year or quarter) and is due for repayment within the upcoming year. It reflects the portion of short-term debt pressure faced by the enterprise at the end of the prior reporting period that originated from the reclassification of long-term borrowings.

nodes.name: Long-term Borrowings Due within One Year
aliases: Long-Term Debt Due Within One Year
nodes.definition: Long-term borrowings due within one year refer to the principal portion of borrowings originally with a term exceeding one year that will mature and require repayment within the next 12 months. When preparing the balance sheet, this amount must be separated from the 'Long-term Borrowings' item and reclassified to be presented separately under current liabilities as 'Non-current Liabilities Due within One Year'.

nodes.name: Long-term Borrowings Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Long-term borrowings ending balance refers to the total carrying value of all borrowings with a repayment term exceeding one year that remain outstanding as of the balance sheet date (typically the end of an accounting period). On the balance sheet, this item is reported based on the general ledger account balance after deducting the portion due within one year.

nodes.name: Long-term Borrowings Opening Balance
nodes.definition: Long-term borrowings opening balance refers to the total book value of all borrowings with a repayment term exceeding one year that remain outstanding at the beginning of an accounting period (typically a fiscal year or an accounting period). It reflects the level of long-term debt obligations borne by the enterprise at the period's commencement.

nodes.name: Long-term Capital
nodes.definition: Long-term capital refers to the capital used by a company for long-term investments, typically composed of long-term liabilities and total shareholders' equity. It is an intermediate derived concept used in calculating financial metrics such as working capital and net operating assets.

nodes.name: Long-term Debt
nodes.definition: Long-term debt refers to obligations undertaken by an enterprise with a repayment period exceeding one year (or one operating cycle). It represents funds borrowed to raise long-term capital, typically used for long-term purposes such as fixed asset investments and project development, and constitutes a significant component of the enterprise's capital structure.

nodes.name: Long-term Debt Investments
nodes.definition: Long-term debt investments refer to investments in bonds or other debt instruments that an enterprise intends to hold for more than one year (or one operating cycle) with the objective of earning interest income. Their initial cost is typically recorded at the actual purchase price (net of related expenses and accrued but unpaid interest) and are presented as non-current assets on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Long-term Debt to Capital Ratio
nodes.definition: The Long-term Debt to Capital Ratio reflects the proportion of long-term debt in a company's long-term capital, measuring its long-term debt pressure and the stability of its capital structure.

nodes.name: Long-term Equity Investment
nodes.definition: Long-term equity investment refers to equity investments held by an enterprise to exercise control, joint control, or significant influence over the investee, with the objective of obtaining long-term returns. It is an independent asset whose value is recognized and measured based on actual transaction costs and subsequent accounting policies (such as the equity method).

nodes.name: Long-term Government Bond Yield to Maturity
nodes.definition: Long-term government bond yield to maturity refers to the annualized internal rate of return that investors can obtain by holding long-term government bonds until maturity. It is a composite indicator calculated based on fundamental data such as bond market price, coupon rate, face value, and remaining term, reflecting market expectations for the long-term risk-free rate, and is commonly used to calculate a company's credit risk premium.

nodes.name: Long-term Investment Book Value
aliases: 长期股权投资账面价值
nodes.definition: Long-term investment book value refers to the value recorded on the books for various investments (such as long-term equity investments and debt investments) that a company expects to hold for more than one year, calculated according to accounting standards (e.g., cost method or equity method) as of the balance sheet date. It reflects the historical cost or adjusted value of these long-term investments and is a key indicator for assessing the company's long-term asset position.

nodes.name: Long-term Investment Impairment Provision
aliases: Provision for Impairment of Long-term Investments
长期股权投资减值准备
nodes.definition: Long-term Investment Impairment Provision is an asset contra-account that an enterprise pre-establishes to address the risk of potential value decline (i.e., impairment) of its long-term investments, such as long-term equity investments. When the carrying amount of an investment exceeds its recoverable amount, the enterprise must recognize an impairment loss and establish this provision to reflect the asset's value more accurately.

nodes.name: Long-term Investments
nodes.definition: Long-term investments refer to equity or debt investments held by an enterprise that are not intended to be liquidated within one year or one operating cycle. Their book value is directly presented on the balance sheet and represents asset allocation undertaken to obtain long-term returns or achieve strategic objectives.

nodes.name: Long-term Liabilities
nodes.definition: Long-term liabilities refer to debts that a company is obligated to repay over a period exceeding one year or one operating cycle. They are a significant item on the balance sheet, primarily including long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables, reflecting the company's financial obligations requiring long-term repayment.

nodes.name: Long-term Liabilities Due Within One Year
aliases: Long-Term Debt Due Within One Year
一年内到期的非流动负债
nodes.definition: Long-term liabilities due within one year refer to the portion of a company's long-term liabilities that must be repaid within one year (including one year) from the date of the balance sheet preparation. Although this portion may still be recorded under long-term liability accounts such as 'long-term loans' in the accounting system, its nature has transformed into current liabilities and must be separately presented in the current liabilities section of the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Long-term Payables
nodes.definition: Long-term payables refer to various payable items with a repayment period exceeding one year or one operating cycle longer than a year, and constitute an independent liability account on the balance sheet. Their amounts are directly sourced from accounting records, such as actual unpaid amounts for installment purchases of assets or financing leases of fixed assets.

nodes.name: Long-term Prepaid Expenses
nodes.definition: Long-term prepaid expenses refer to costs that have been actually paid or incurred by an enterprise, but whose benefit period exceeds one year, requiring amortization over the current and subsequent multiple accounting periods. They are classified as a non-current asset of the enterprise, commonly seen in capitalized expenditures such as renovation expenses and fixed asset improvement costs.

nodes.name: Long-term Prepaid Expenses Amortization
nodes.definition: Long-term prepaid expenses amortization refers to the accounting process by which a company systematically allocates various expenses that have been paid but have benefit periods exceeding one year into the costs or expenses of each period, according to the determined amortization period and method.

nodes.name: Long-term Receivables
nodes.definition: Long-term receivables refer to receivables with an expected collection period exceeding one year (or one operating cycle), typically associated with non-routine business activities such as finance leases, installment sales of goods, or provision of services. Their amounts are determined by discounting the future cash flows stipulated in the contracts.

nodes.name: Lookback Option
nodes.definition: A lookback option is a path-dependent exotic option that allows the holder to reference the extreme prices of the underlying asset over the option’s life when determining the payoff. For a fixed strike lookback option, the strike is set at initiation. A call pays the difference between the maximum underlying price observed and the strike (floored at zero), while a put pays the difference between the strike and the minimum underlying price observed (floored at zero). For a floating strike lookback option, the strike is set at maturity equal to the final underlying price; the payoff structure is otherwise analogous, substituting the final price as the strike.

nodes.name: Lorenz Curve Area
nodes.definition: Lorenz Curve Area is the integral (approximated by trapezoidal summation) under the Lorenz curve that plots the cumulative share of income or wealth against the cumulative share of the population. It is a foundational quantity for inequality measurement and is used to derive the Gini coefficient (Gini Coefficient = 1 - 2 × Area under Lorenz Curve), reflecting how far a distribution deviates from perfect equality.

nodes.name: Loss
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, loss refers to the reduction in economic value or increase in costs due to various reasons (such as poor management, asset impairment, accidents, investment failures, etc.). It reflects the negative financial outcome suffered by an enterprise or individual during a specific period or in specific activities.

nodes.name: Loss Amount
nodes.definition: Loss amount refers to the original, directly observable or measurable numerical value of economic losses actually incurred during a specific event or period. It serves as fundamental data in risk management, insurance claims settlement, and financial analysis, used for subsequent calculation of derived metrics such as loss ratios and expected losses.

nodes.name: Loss Carryforward
nodes.definition: Loss carryforward refers to carrying net operating losses (NOLs) into future periods to offset net income, typically subject to statutory limitations (e.g., an 80% offset cap per year), thereby reducing future income and potentially giving rise to deferred tax assets.

nodes.name: Loss Carryforward Order
nodes.definition: Loss carryforward order refers to the sequence, as stipulated by tax laws or accounting standards, in which a company uses profits from future years to offset losses incurred in prior years. Typically, the order specifies whether the earliest losses or the most recent losses are offset first, which directly affects the company's taxable income and income tax expense for the current year.

nodes.name: Loss Development
nodes.definition: Loss development is an actuarial technique used in insurance accounting to adjust reported claims by a loss development factor (LDF) to estimate ultimate loss, reflecting expected changes in claim amounts as they mature and are finalized.

nodes.name: Loss Distribution
aliases: 损失频率与严重度联合分布
nodes.definition: Loss distribution is a statistical/probabilistic modeling concept used to describe the possible values of losses and their associated probabilities. It is not a primary account in financial statements but rather a composite result obtained through statistical fitting or modeling of underlying loss data (such as single loss amounts, loss frequency, etc.). In risk measurement, it often serves as an intermediate step for calculating metrics like Value at Risk (VaR).

nodes.name: Loss Frequency
nodes.definition: Loss frequency refers to the number of times or probability of losses occurring within a specific time period for a given number of risk units. It is a key metric for measuring risk characteristics in risk management, commonly used to assess the likelihood of risk occurrence.

nodes.name: Loss Given Default
nodes.definition: Loss Given Default (LGD) refers to the proportion of loss incurred on an asset when a borrower defaults. It is a key parameter in credit risk modeling, used to calculate expected loss, economic capital, and regulatory capital under Basel II.

formulas.source_formula: Loss Given Default = Loss Amount / Exposure at Default
Loss Given Default (Dollar Amount) = Exposure at Default × (1 - Recovery Rate)
Loss Given Default (LGD) = 1 - (Potential Sale Proceeds ÷ Outstanding Debt)

nodes.name: Loss Ratio
nodes.definition: Loss ratio measures the percentage of total incurred losses relative to total collected insurance premiums, indicating the profitability of an insurer's underwriting operations before considering expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Loss Ratio = (Incurred Losses ÷ Collected Premiums) × 100
Loss Ratio (%) = ((Insurance Claims + Loss Adjustment Expenses) ÷ Total Earned Premiums) × 100

nodes.name: Loss Severity
nodes.definition: Loss severity refers to the degree of economic loss or the monetary amount caused by a single risk event or accident within a specific period. It is used to measure the actual financial impact scale following an accident or risk event, serving as a crucial indicator in risk assessment and management.

nodes.name: Loss Value of Current Assets
aliases: 流动资产盘亏毁损价值
nodes.definition: Loss value of current assets refers to the net loss amount determined after adjustment (such as deducting residual value, recoverable insurance compensation, and compensation from responsible parties) when assets held by an enterprise, which are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle (such as raw materials, finished goods, work-in-progress, etc.), partially or completely lose their utility value or market value due to natural disasters, long-term overstocking, inventory shortages, damage, or other reasons.

nodes.name: Loss on Disposal of Assets
aliases: 资产处置损益（损失部分）
nodes.definition: Loss on disposal of assets refers to the deficit arising when the proceeds from the sale, transfer, or retirement of long-term assets such as fixed assets or intangible assets are lower than the net book value of the asset and related disposal expenses. It reflects the economic loss incurred by the enterprise from asset disposal activities.

nodes.name: Loss on Disposal of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Loss on disposal of fixed assets refers to the difference between the carrying amount of a fixed asset (original cost minus accumulated depreciation and impairment provisions) and the net proceeds from its disposal (residual value income minus relevant taxes and disposal expenses) when the asset is retired due to reaching the end of its useful life, technological obsolescence, or damage. When the carrying amount exceeds the net disposal proceeds, the resulting net loss is recorded as non-operating expenses.

nodes.name: Loss on Retirement of Fixed Assets
Lost Time
nodes.definition: Lost time refers to the working hours that are not utilized for effective product production due to defective products, unplanned equipment downtime, safety incidents, or other non-productive activities. It is a crucial operational metric for measuring production efficiency, safety management levels, and production plan execution, typically calculated from basic production data or incident statistics.

formulas.source_formula: Lost Time = Quantity of Lost Products × Standard Time per Unit
Lost Time = Unplanned Work Stoppage Lost Time + Minor Injury Incident Lost Time + Occupational Injury Lost Time

nodes.name: Lost Time Due to Work Injury
nodes.definition: Lost time due to work injury refers to the total time employees are unable to work normally as a result of occupational accidents, typically measured in hours. It is a key indicator for assessing the severity of occupational accidents and the level of corporate safety management.

nodes.name: Low Discount Rate
nodes.definition: Low discount rate is a qualitative description of the level of the discount rate, referring to a relatively low rate used to discount future expected returns to their present value. The discount rate is a comprehensive indicator measuring the time value of money and risk compensation, and its level directly affects asset valuation and investment decisions.

nodes.name: Low Point Activity Level
nodes.definition: Low point activity level refers to the data point with the lowest activity volume (such as production output, sales volume, or labor hours) within the selected observation period in cost behavior analysis (e.g., the high-low method). It is one of the key parameters used to separate mixed costs and calculate the unit variable cost and total fixed cost.

nodes.name: Low-Point Activity Level Cost
nodes.definition: Low-point activity level cost refers to the total cost corresponding to the lowest activity level selected from historical cost data in the high-low method. It is a raw observation value directly read from historical records, used for subsequent calculation of unit variable cost and total fixed cost.

nodes.name: Low-point Shipment Volume
nodes.definition: Low-point shipment volume refers to the minimum or a specific data point of transportation quantity occurring within a given period (such as a single shipment task, a planning cycle, or a cost analysis scenario) in logistics or supply chain management. It is a fundamental raw operational data point, commonly used in quantitative analyses like transportation problem optimization and cost function construction to determine the most economical shipping solution or to assess cost variations.

nodes.name: Low-point Total Transportation Cost
nodes.definition: Low-point total transportation cost refers to the sum of basic cost data obtained through direct allocation in transportation cost calculation. It primarily includes original expenditures directly traceable to transportation activities, such as vehicle expenses and operational overheads, and serves as the starting point for subsequent cost analysis and calculations (e.g., variable transportation costs).

nodes.name: Low-value Consumables
nodes.definition: Low-value consumables refer to non-fixed asset items held by an enterprise with a unit value below a specified limit (e.g., 2,000 or 5,000 yuan) or a short useful life (typically within one year), which are prone to damage or consumption. Such items usually include office supplies, cleaning tools, small tools, packaging containers, etc., and are managed and accounted for as part of inventory in accounting.

nodes.name: Low-value Consumables Expense
aliases: Expense for Low-value and Perishable Articles
nodes.definition: Low-value consumables expense refers to the cost incurred by an enterprise during production and operation due to the use of non-fixed asset items with low unit value, short service life, and high susceptibility to wear and tear (such as office supplies, cleaning tools, etc.). The value of these items is typically below a certain threshold (e.g., 5,000 yuan), and their cost is recognized in the current period's profit or loss through amortization or one-time expense recognition.

formulas.source_formula: Lower Band = Middle Band - (Number of Standard Deviations × Standard Deviation)
Lower Band = Middle Line - (Multiplier × Average True Range)
Lower Band = Simple Moving Average (SMA) - (Multiplier (K) × Standard Deviation (σ))
Lower Breakeven (Strangle) = Put Strike Price - Total Premium
Lower Breakeven Point = Lower Strike Price - Maximum Profit Points
Lower Envelope = Simple Moving Average × (1 - Percentage)

nodes.name: Lower Limit of Integration
nodes.definition: In mathematics, the lower limit of integration is a parameter in definite integral calculation, representing the starting value from which the integration variable begins to accumulate. In finance and accounting, it is sometimes extended to refer to the minimum guaranteed value or threshold set for calculation results (such as bonuses or performance points), below which predetermined rules apply (e.g., guaranteed minimum payout or prohibition of deductions).

nodes.name: Lower Limit of the Modal Class
nodes.definition: In statistics, when data is grouped into class intervals, the mode is the value that appears most frequently. The 'lower limit of the modal class' refers to the starting value of the class interval that contains this most frequent data. It is a key parameter required when calculating the mode for grouped data using the lower limit formula.

formulas.source_formula: Lower Shadow = min(Open Price, Close Price) - Low Price

nodes.name: Lower of Cost or Market (LCM/LOCOM)
nodes.definition: In accounting, the Lower of Cost or Market (LCM or LOCOM) is a conservative method for valuing and reporting inventory. Typically, ending inventory is reported at historical cost. However, when the original cost of ending inventory exceeds its net realizable value, the inventory should be written down to its current market price. The resulting loss, if not material in amount, is included in 'Cost of Goods Sold'; if material, it is separately reported as 'Loss on Write-down of Inventory to Lower of Cost or Market'.

nodes.name: Lower of Cost or Market Method
aliases: Lower of Cost or Market Rule
nodes.definition: The lower of cost or market (LCM) method is an inventory valuation approach under U.S. GAAP where inventory is reported at the lower of its historical cost or market value. Market is defined as replacement cost constrained by a ceiling (Net Realizable Value) and a floor (Net Realizable Value minus Normal Profit Margin). This ensures inventory is not overstated and reflects recoverable amounts.

nodes.name: Lowest Activity Level
nodes.definition: Lowest Activity Level refers to the minimum level of business activity (such as production volume, sales volume, etc.) directly observed or selected from a company's historical operational data. It serves as a fundamental data point in cost behavior analysis (e.g., the High-Low Method), used as an original input value for calculating parameters such as variable cost per unit.

nodes.name: Lowest Price
nodes.definition: The lowest price refers to the minimum transaction price reached by a stock, fund, or other financial asset within a specific time period (such as a trading day, week, month, or since listing). It reflects the lower price limit of the asset in the market and serves as an important indicator for measuring its price volatility and risk.

nodes.name: Luhn Algorithm
nodes.definition: The Luhn algorithm (Modulus 10 check) is a checksum method widely used in payment processing and financial operations to validate identification numbers such as credit card numbers. It helps detect common data entry errors and ensures basic format integrity but does not verify account ownership or credit risk.

formulas.source_formula: Luhn Check = Total Adjusted Digit Sum ÷ 10

nodes.name: Lump-Sum Payment
nodes.definition: A lump-sum payment (commuted value) is the present cash equivalent of a stream of future annuity or pension payments, determined by discounting the value over the relevant period at a specified discount rate. It is used to convert periodic payments into a single payment at a point in time under time value of money principles.

formulas.source_formula: Commuted Value = Present Value ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Years

nodes.name: Luxury Tax
nodes.definition: Luxury tax is a selective excise applied to the portion of a good's price exceeding a statutory threshold. The liability equals the excess over the threshold multiplied by the applicable tax rate, with no tax due when the price is at or below the threshold.

nodes.name: M1 Money Supply
nodes.definition: M1 money supply is a measure of the most liquid components of the money supply, consisting of currency in circulation, demand deposits, and other liquid deposits that can be quickly converted into cash for transactions.

formulas.source_formula: M1 Money Supply = Currency in Circulation + Demand Deposits + Other Liquid Deposits

nodes.name: MACD Histogram
aliases: 指数平滑异同移动平均线柱状图
nodes.definition: The MACD histogram is a momentum indicator that represents the difference between the MACD line and the signal line. It visually depicts the rate of change in trend momentum, where positive values indicate the MACD line is above the signal line and negative values indicate it is below.

formulas.source_formula: MACD Histogram = MACD Line - Signal Line
supporting_source_formulas: MACD Histogram = MACD Line - Signal Line

nodes.name: MACD Signal Line
nodes.definition: The MACD Signal Line is the N-period exponential moving average (EMA) of the MACD line, typically set to 9 periods. It serves as a smoothing benchmark for MACD and is used to generate trading signals based on crossovers with the MACD line.

nodes.name: MACRS Depreciation
aliases: Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System Depreciation
修改后的加速成本回收系统折旧
nodes.definition: MACRS depreciation is the U.S. tax depreciation method under the Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System that allocates the cost of tangible personal property over a statutory recovery period using accelerated rates, typically under the General Depreciation System (GDS) with the half-year convention. The annual depreciation expense equals the asset's tax basis multiplied by the applicable MACRS percentage for the specified recovery period and year.

formulas.source_formula: MACRS Depreciation Expense = Cost Basis × MACRS Depreciation Rate

nodes.name: MBS Age
aliases: 抵押贷款支持证券年限
nodes.definition: MBS Age refers to the number of years elapsed since the issuance (vintage year) of a mortgage-backed security, used to assess its remaining maturity and associated risk profile.

formulas.source_formula: MBS Age = Current Year - Vintage Year

nodes.name: MCF to BTU Conversion
nodes.definition: MCF to BTU conversion translates a volume of natural gas measured in thousand cubic feet (MCF) into its energy content in British Thermal Units (BTU). This conversion is commonly used by energy analysts, commodity traders, and oil & gas accountants to align volumetric production, transportation, and sales data with energy-based pricing, valuation, and hedging models.

nodes.name: Macaulay Duration
nodes.definition: Macaulay Duration is the weighted average time until a bond's cash flows are received, where the weights are the present value of each cash flow as a proportion of the bond's price. It measures the bond's average maturity and interest rate risk.

nodes.name: Machined Diameter
nodes.definition: Machined diameter refers to the final diameter dimension achieved by a workpiece after machining, serving as a key parameter for measuring machining accuracy and meeting design requirements.

nodes.name: Machining Length
nodes.definition: Machining length refers to the actual axial length of a workpiece that requires cutting or processing during mechanical machining. It is a fundamental parameter for calculating machining time, determining cutting parameters (such as feed rate, rotational speed), and establishing time standards.

nodes.name: Main Material Rate
nodes.definition: Main Material Rate refers to the ratio of main material costs to total costs, used to measure the impact of main materials on overall costs. In fields such as equipment valuation, it is often a key parameter for calculating full manufacturing costs.

nodes.name: Maintenance
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, maintenance primarily refers to the ongoing management, upkeep, and investment required to ensure the continuous normal operation and stable value of financial systems, data, assets, customer relationships, and compliance status. It is typically reflected as actual incurred maintenance expenses or costs, serving as a fundamental raw data point in financial accounting.

nodes.name: Maintenance Capital Expenditure
nodes.definition: Maintenance capital expenditure refers to the capital outlays or working capital investments that an enterprise must make during normal operations to sustain the continuous and stable functioning of existing production or service capacity. These investments are typically used for equipment maintenance, renewal, technological upgrades, or replenishing necessary working capital, ensuring the enterprise can consistently generate revenue and cash flow. It is not an ordinary operating expense but rather an essential investment project required to maintain long-term operational capability.

nodes.name: Maintenance Capital Expenditure in the First Year of the Continuing Period
Maintenance Expense
nodes.definition: Maintenance expense refers to the costs incurred by an enterprise to maintain or restore assets such as fixed assets, equipment, and vehicles to their normal operating condition. It typically includes expenditures on labor, materials, and spare parts. In management accounting, it is often treated as a mixed cost for cost behavior analysis to decompose into fixed and variable components.

nodes.name: Maintenance Margin
nodes.definition: Maintenance margin is the minimum amount of equity that must be maintained in a margin account to keep a futures position open, calculated as a percentage of the total trade value.

formulas.source_formula: Maintenance Margin = Total Trade Value × Margin Requirement Percentage
Maintenance Margin = Securities Value × Margin Requirement

nodes.name: Maintenance Margin Call Threshold
nodes.definition: The minimum account equity level at which a margin call is triggered, calculated as the product of the initial deposit and the maintenance margin rate.

formulas.source_formula: Maintenance Margin Call Threshold = Initial Deposit × Maintenance Margin Rate

nodes.name: Maintenance Margin Equity
nodes.definition: Maintenance margin equity is the minimum equity level an investor must maintain in a margin account to comply with the brokerage's maintenance margin requirement, calculated as the product of the current market value of securities and the maintenance margin percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Maintenance Margin Equity = Security Value × Maintenance Margin Requirement

nodes.name: Maintenance Requirement
nodes.definition: Maintenance requirement is the minimum dollar amount of equity that must be maintained in a margin account to avoid a margin call, calculated as the current market value of securities multiplied by the maintenance margin percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Maintenance Requirement = Security Value × Maintenance Margin

nodes.name: Maintenance and Renovation Fee
nodes.definition: The Maintenance and Renovation Fee is a fund extracted from costs by enterprises in specific industries (such as mining and forestry) according to stipulated standards, specifically used for fixed asset renewal, technological transformation, and extension projects to maintain production scale and sustain simple reproduction.

nodes.name: Major Purchased Components Cost
nodes.definition: Major Purchased Components Cost refers to the expenses incurred in production or engineering projects to acquire key externally purchased parts, raw materials, or components essential for constituting the final product or equipment. It typically includes the purchase price (invoice price) of these purchased components as well as related procurement expenses, such as transportation fees, loading/unloading charges, insurance premiums, customs duties, and inspection fees. In the calculation of replacement cost, it constitutes a significant component of the equipment or asset value.

nodes.name: Major Repair Fund
nodes.definition: The Major Repair Fund is a special source of funds that enterprises pre-withdraw and accumulate from production costs according to state-prescribed withdrawal rates, specifically designated for covering large-scale, periodic repair expenses of fixed assets (such as machinery, equipment, buildings, and structures).

nodes.name: Make-Whole Call Price
nodes.definition: The make-whole call price is the present value of a bond’s remaining scheduled coupon and principal payments, discounted at the sum of a comparable Treasury yield plus a contractually specified spread, representing the amount an issuer must pay bondholders to exercise an early call under a make-whole provision.

nodes.name: Malthusian Population Growth
nodes.definition: The Malthusian population growth model estimates future population size under a constant discrete compounding growth rate, yielding exponential growth analogous to the compound interest formula. It projects the population size by applying a fixed growth rate per period to the initial population.

nodes.name: Management Expense Ratio
nodes.definition: The Management Expense Ratio is the ratio of management expenses to core operating revenue, used to measure the proportion of expenses incurred for organizing and managing production and operational activities relative to core business revenue. It is an important financial indicator for evaluating management efficiency.

nodes.name: Management Fee
nodes.definition: Management fee is a periodic charge levied by an investment fund, calculated as a percentage of assets under management (AUM), compensating the fund manager for portfolio management and administrative services.

formulas.source_formula: Management Fee = Assets Under Management × Fee Percentage
Management Fee = Assets under Management × Management Fee Rate
Management Fee = Assets Under Management (End of Year) × Management Fee Rate
Management Fee = Portfolio Value × Management Fee Percentage ÷ 100

nodes.name: Manufacturing Cost
nodes.definition: Manufacturing cost refers to all expenses incurred by an enterprise in producing goods, primarily including materials directly used in production (direct materials), compensation for workers directly engaged in production (direct labor), and various indirect expenses incurred for organizing and managing production activities (manufacturing overhead).

nodes.name: Manufacturing Labor Rate
nodes.definition: Manufacturing labor rate refers to the standard or unit price of labor costs required to complete a specific product or process in the manufacturing industry. It is typically calculated based on wage levels, workload, and potential adjustment factors (such as region, technical difficulty), serving as a crucial foundation for the direct labor cost component within product production costs.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead
nodes.definition: The manufacturing overhead allocated to a product is the result of multiplying the actual labor hours used by the overhead allocation rate.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead Allocation
nodes.definition: Manufacturing overhead allocation refers to the process of reasonably distributing various indirect costs incurred during the production process (such as workshop management salaries, equipment depreciation, utilities, etc.) that cannot be directly attributed to specific product costs, to various cost objects (such as different products, batches, or production stages) according to certain standards and methods. This is a key step in calculating the actual cost of products.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Amount
nodes.definition: Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Amount refers to the specific amount allocated to individual cost objects (such as products, orders, or production steps) from the total actual or planned manufacturing overhead incurred during a specific accounting period, based on predetermined allocation bases (e.g., direct labor hours, machine hours, direct labor wages) and allocation rates. It is a critical step in incorporating indirect production costs into the total product cost.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The manufacturing overhead allocation rate is the ratio used to allocate total manufacturing overhead costs to products based on the proportion of actual labor hours (standard or machine hours) used.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead Quantity Standard
nodes.definition: Manufacturing Overhead Quantity Standard is the predetermined benchmark for manufacturing overhead consumption per unit of product established by an enterprise when setting standard costs. It is typically expressed in time units such as direct labor hours or machine hours. It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating standard manufacturing overhead costs.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead Rate Standard
nodes.definition: The manufacturing overhead rate standard refers to the predetermined amount of manufacturing overhead allocated per unit of direct labor hour (or machine hour) for producing a unit of product or completing a unit of activity under standard costing. It is a predetermined allocation rate calculated based on the total budgeted manufacturing overhead and the total budgeted hours, used to allocate manufacturing overhead to products or cost centers. It serves as a fundamental parameter for establishing standard costs and conducting cost variance analysis.

nodes.name: Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost
nodes.definition: Manufacturing overhead standard cost refers to the manufacturing overhead that should occur per unit of product under standard production conditions. It is a decomposable composite indicator calculated from the manufacturing overhead price standard (or standard manufacturing overhead allocation rate) and the manufacturing overhead quantity standard (or standard hours), and is a component of the standard cost per unit product.

formulas.source_formula: Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost = Manufacturing Overhead Price Standard × Manufacturing Overhead Quantity Standard
Manufacturing Overhead Standard Cost = Standard Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate × Standard Hours

nodes.name: Manufacturing Value Added
nodes.definition: Manufacturing Value Added refers to the final monetary result of production activities by manufacturing enterprises within a reporting period; it is the total output of all production activities minus the value of material products and services consumed or transferred during the production process; it represents the newly created value in the production process and is commonly used to measure the manufacturing sector's contribution to Gross Domestic Product.

formulas.source_formula: Manufacturing Value Added = Total Output - Intermediate Input + Value-Added Tax Payable
Manufacturing Value Added = Depreciation of Fixed Assets + Compensation of Employees + Net Taxes on Production + Operating Surplus

nodes.name: Margin Account Equity
nodes.definition: Margin account equity represents the net value of an investor's position in a margin account, calculated as the current market value of securities minus the outstanding loan amount. It reflects the investor's actual ownership value excluding borrowed funds.

formulas.source_formula: Margin Account Equity = Security Value - Loan Amount

nodes.name: Margin Buying Power
nodes.definition: Margin buying power is the maximum amount of securities that can be purchased in a margin account, calculated by dividing the cash balance by the initial margin requirement.

formulas.source_formula: Margin Buying Power = Cash Balance ÷ Initial Margin Requirement

nodes.name: Margin Call Amount
nodes.definition: Margin call amount is the additional funds that must be deposited into a margin account when the account's equity falls below the maintenance margin requirement, ensuring compliance with broker-imposed minimum equity levels.

formulas.source_formula: Margin Call Amount = Required Equity - Current Equity

nodes.name: Margin Call Deposit
nodes.definition: The total deposit required to cover a margin call, representing the cash or marginable securities that must be added to a margin account to restore the equity requirement percentage.

nodes.name: Margin Call Requirement
aliases: Required Deposit to Meet Maintenance Margin
nodes.definition: Margin call requirement is the additional cash or collateral an investor must deposit to restore the account to the maintenance margin level when the account's equity has fallen below the required threshold.

nodes.name: Margin Call Threshold
nodes.definition: Margin call threshold is the critical account equity level below which a margin call is triggered, requiring the investor to deposit additional funds or liquidate positions to maintain the margin account.

formulas.source_formula: Margin Call Threshold = Account Equity × (1 - Maintenance Margin)

nodes.name: Margin Call Trigger
nodes.definition: A margin call trigger occurs when the equity in a margin account falls below the required maintenance margin, prompting the broker to demand additional funds or securities to cover potential losses.

nodes.name: Margin Debt
nodes.definition: Margin debt is the amount of money an investor borrows from a broker to purchase securities, secured by the investor's existing securities in the margin account.

nodes.name: Margin Loan Availability
nodes.definition: Margin loan availability refers to the dollar amount that an investor can still borrow against the current market value of securities held in a margin account, after satisfying the broker’s maintenance margin requirement.

formulas.source_formula: Margin Loan Availability = Securities Value × (1 - Maintenance Margin)
Margin Required = Trade Value ÷ Leverage Ratio

nodes.name: Margin Requirement
nodes.definition: Margin requirement is the minimum amount of funds that must be deposited by an investor to open and maintain a position in a futures contract, calculated as a percentage of the total contract value.

formulas.source_formula: Margin Requirement = Position Value × Margin Percentage
Margin Requirement = Trade Value ÷ Leverage Ratio
Margin Requirement = Contract Value × Margin Percentage

nodes.name: Margin Trading Profit or Loss
nodes.definition: The net gain or loss resulting from trading securities on margin, calculated as the proceeds from the sale of margined securities minus the initial investment, borrowed funds, and interest expense incurred on the borrowed amount.

nodes.name: Margin of Error
nodes.definition: Margin of error refers to the maximum possible deviation between a sample statistic and the population parameter when estimating population parameters in statistical inference. It is typically associated with the confidence level and is a key component in constructing confidence intervals.

formulas.source_formula: Margin of Error = Critical Value × Standard Error

nodes.name: Margin of Safety
nodes.definition: Margin of safety refers to the portion by which actual sales exceed break-even sales, indicating the extent to which sales can decline before the company incurs a loss.

nodes.name: Margin of Safety Ratio
nodes.definition: The margin of safety ratio is the percentage of the margin of safety to normal sales revenue, used to measure the safety level of a business's operations. A higher ratio indicates greater business safety.

nodes.name: Margin of Sampling Error
nodes.definition: The margin of sampling error refers to the maximum possible deviation between a sample statistic (such as the sample mean or sample proportion) and the population parameter at a specified confidence level. It is a key statistical measure for assessing the precision of sampling results.

nodes.name: Marginal Analysis
nodes.definition: Marginal analysis is the technique of evaluating the additional benefits of an activity compared to its additional costs, used to determine the optimal production or consumption level where marginal revenue equals marginal cost.

nodes.name: Marginal Benefit
nodes.definition: Marginal benefit is the additional satisfaction or utility that a consumer receives from consuming one more unit of a good or service, used to determine optimal consumption where marginal benefit equals price.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Benefit = Total Additional Benefit ÷ Total Additional Goods Consumed

nodes.name: Marginal Cost
nodes.definition: In economics, marginal cost (MC) refers to the change in total cost resulting from an increase in output, i.e., the cost of producing one additional unit of output. It includes only variable costs that change with the production level, excluding fixed costs. Marginal cost can be defined as the derivative of the total cost function with respect to quantity (for continuous functions), or as the ratio of the change in total cost to the change in quantity (for discrete changes).

nodes.name: Marginal Cost Function
nodes.definition: The marginal cost function is a mathematical function that describes the increase in total cost corresponding to each additional unit of output. It reflects the instantaneous rate of change of cost with respect to output, serving as a core tool in economics and financial management for analyzing production decisions, pricing, and profit maximization.

nodes.name: Marginal Cost of Production
nodes.definition: Marginal cost of production is the additional cost incurred to produce one more unit of output, calculated by dividing the change in total expenses by the change in quantity produced.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Cost = Change in Total Expenses ÷ Change in Quantity

nodes.name: Marginal Probability
nodes.definition: Marginal probability refers to the probability distribution of one or several random variables within a joint probability distribution involving multiple random variables, while ignoring the influence of other variables. Simply put, it is the probability obtained by 'marginalizing out' the variables of no interest from the overall probability distribution.

nodes.name: Marginal Profit
nodes.definition: Marginal profit is the additional profit earned from producing and selling one more unit of output, calculated as the difference between marginal revenue and marginal cost.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Profit = Marginal Revenue - Marginal Cost
supporting_source_formulas: Marginal Profit = Marginal Revenue - Marginal Cost

nodes.name: Marginal Propensity to Consume
nodes.definition: In economics, the Marginal Propensity to Consume (MPC) is a metric used to quantify induced consumption, which refers to the increase in consumer spending triggered by an increase in personal disposable income. It represents the proportion of additional disposable income that an individual allocates to consumption rather than saving.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Propensity to Consume = Change in Consumption / Change in Disposable Income
Marginal Propensity to Consume = Change in Consumption ÷ Change in Income
supporting_source_formulas: MPC = Change in Consumption ÷ Change in Income
Marginal Propensity to Consume = Change in Consumption ÷ Change in Income

formulas.source_formula: MPC = Change in Spending ÷ Change in Income

nodes.name: Marginal Propensity to Import
nodes.definition: Marginal Propensity to Import (MPM) is the ratio of the change in imports to the change in disposable income, indicating how much additional imports are induced by each unit increase in disposable income.

formulas.source_formula: MPM = Change in Imports ÷ Change in Disposable Income

nodes.name: Marginal Propensity to Save
nodes.definition: Marginal Propensity to Save (MPS) is the proportion of an additional unit of income that is saved rather than spent, measuring how much saving increases when income rises by one unit.

formulas.source_formula: MPS = Change in Saving ÷ Change in Income

nodes.name: Marginal Rate of Substitution
nodes.definition: The Marginal Rate of Substitution (MRS) measures the rate at which a consumer is willing to give up units of one good to obtain an additional unit of another good while maintaining the same level of utility.

formulas.source_formula: MRS = Marginal Utility of Good X ÷ Marginal Utility of Good Y

nodes.name: Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution
nodes.definition: Marginal Rate of Technical Substitution (MRTS) measures the rate at which one input (e.g., labor) can be substituted for another input (e.g., capital) while maintaining the same level of output, reflecting the slope of an isoquant curve.

formulas.source_formula: MRTS = Marginal Product of Labor ÷ Marginal Product of Capital
supporting_source_formulas: MRTS = Marginal Product of Labor ÷ Marginal Product of Capital

nodes.name: Marginal Rate of Transformation
nodes.definition: Marginal Rate of Transformation (MRT) is the opportunity cost of producing one additional unit of a good (good X) in terms of the amount of another good (good Y) that must be foregone, calculated as the ratio of the marginal cost of good X to the marginal cost of good Y.
