formulas.source_formula: MRT = Marginal Cost of Good X ÷ Marginal Cost of Good Y

nodes.name: Marginal Revenue
nodes.definition: Marginal revenue refers to the incremental change in total revenue resulting from the sale of one additional unit of product, representing the additional revenue generated by the last unit sold, which can be positive or negative. It is a key concept in microeconomics, often used in conjunction with marginal cost for profit maximization decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Revenue = Marginal Cost
Marginal Revenue = Change in Revenue ÷ Change in Quantity

nodes.name: Marginal Revenue Product
nodes.definition: Marginal Revenue Product (MRP) is the additional revenue generated from employing one more unit of a productive resource, calculated as the product of the marginal physical product and the marginal revenue per unit of output.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Revenue Product = Marginal Physical Product × Marginal Revenue

nodes.name: Marginal Social Cost
nodes.definition: Marginal Social Cost (MSC) is the total cost to society of producing an additional unit of a good or service, comprising the marginal private cost borne by the producer plus any marginal external cost (or minus external benefits) imposed on third parties.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Social Cost = Marginal Private Cost + Marginal External Cost

nodes.name: Marginal Tax Rate
nodes.definition: Marginal tax rate refers to the statutory tax rate corresponding to the specific income bracket into which a taxpayer's taxable income falls under a progressive tax system. It is the tax rate directly applied when calculating the tax payable, typically used in conjunction with a quick calculation deduction to simplify the tax computation process.

nodes.name: Marginal Utility
nodes.definition: Marginal utility is the additional satisfaction or usefulness a consumer receives from acquiring one more unit of a good or service, measured as the change in total utility divided by the change in quantity consumed.

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Utility = Current Utility - Previous Utility
Marginal Utility = Change in Total Utility ÷ Change in Quantity
supporting_source_formulas: Marginal Utility = Change in Total Utility ÷ Change in Quantity

nodes.name: Marginal Utility (between units n and n-1)

formulas.source_formula: Marginal Utility (between units n and n-1) = Total Utility (n) - Total Utility (n-1)

nodes.name: Mark to Market (MTM)
nodes.definition: Mark to Market (MTM) is an accounting practice that values an asset or liability at its current market price rather than its historical cost, reflecting real-time gains or losses in financial statements.

nodes.name: Mark-to-Market Gain
nodes.definition: Mark-to-market gain represents the unrealized profit on a Section 1256 contract calculated as the difference between its fair market value at year-end and its initial purchase value, recognized for tax purposes regardless of actual sale.

formulas.source_formula: Mark-to-Market Gain = End of Year Value - Initial Value

nodes.name: Markdown Percentage
nodes.definition: Markdown percentage measures the reduction in selling price from the original price to a reduced price, expressed as a percentage of the original price. It is commonly used in retail to quantify promotional discounts or clearance reductions.

formulas.source_formula: Markdown Percentage = (Original Price - Reduced Price) ÷ Original Price × 100

nodes.name: Market Approach
nodes.definition: The market approach is a valuation method that estimates the fair value of an asset by comparing it to similar assets that have recently been sold in the market, adjusting for differences in features, size, and condition.

nodes.name: Market Average Return
nodes.definition: Market average return refers to the average profit level of the entire market (typically represented by the stock market) or a representative portfolio (such as the CSI 300 Index or S&P 500 Index) over a specific period. It reflects the overall profitability of the market and serves as a fundamental benchmark for measuring systematic investment returns.

nodes.name: Market Average Return Rate
nodes.definition: The market average return rate is an indicator measuring the overall investment return level of the market, typically derived by calculating the average historical return of a market index or all investment instruments. It is used in financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model as a benchmark for assessing asset risk and return.

formulas.source_formula: Market Average Return Rate = (Expected Asset Return Rate - Risk-Free Rate) ÷ Beta Coefficient + Risk-Free Rate

nodes.name: Market Average Return on Investment
nodes.definition: Market Average Return on Investment refers to the average return level of all investment targets or portfolios in the entire market or a representative market index (such as the CSI 300 Index) over a specific period. It is commonly used as a benchmark for measuring investment performance or calculating the opportunity cost of investment.

nodes.name: Market Benchmark Liquidity Ratio
nodes.definition: The Market Benchmark Liquidity Ratio is a reference standard or target value used to measure and compare the short-term solvency of an enterprise or the overall market. It is typically established based on industry averages, historical data, or specific market conditions to assess whether a specific entity's liquidity position meets or exceeds the prevailing market level.

nodes.name: Market Benchmark Rate of Return
aliases: Required Rate of Return on Equity
nodes.definition: The market benchmark rate of return is the minimum rate of return required by investors for an asset or project with a specific risk level, serving as a key reference standard for evaluating investment opportunities, conducting capital budgeting, and asset pricing. It is typically calculated by compounding factors such as the risk-free rate, market risk premium, and the specific asset's risk coefficient.

formulas.source_formula: Market Benchmark Rate of Return = (1 + Annual Cost of Capital Rate) × (1 + Annual Risk Discount Rate) × (1 + Annual Inflation Rate) - 1

nodes.name: Market Benchmark Retail Price
nodes.definition: Market benchmark retail price is the selling price of goods to end consumers at the retail stage, typically calculated based on cost-plus or wholesale price-plus methods, serving as a composite financial indicator reflecting market supply-demand dynamics and competitive conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Market Benchmark Retail Price = Product Cost × (1 + Average Profit Margin)
Market Benchmark Retail Price = Wholesale Price + Freight & Miscellaneous Charges + Interest + Retail Profit

nodes.name: Market Breadth
nodes.definition: Market breadth measures the proportion of stocks trading above a specified moving average, indicating the underlying strength or weakness of a market trend.

operands.metric: Number of Stocks Above Moving Average

formulas.source_formula: Market Breadth = (Number of Stocks Above Moving Average ÷ Total Number of Stocks) × 100

nodes.name: Market Cannibalization Rate
nodes.definition: Market cannibalization rate measures the percentage of new product sales that are offset by lost sales of an existing product, indicating the degree to which a new product erodes the sales of older products within the same company.

formulas.source_formula: Cannibalization Rate = (Lost Sales ÷ New Product Sales) × 100

nodes.name: Market Capitalization
nodes.definition: Market capitalization refers to the total value of outstanding common shares held by shareholders of a listed company, calculated as the market price per common share multiplied by the number of outstanding common shares.

formulas.source_formula: Market Capitalization = Share Price × Total Shares Outstanding
Market Capitalization = Enterprise Value - Market Value of Debt
Market Capitalization = Shares Outstanding × Share Price
supporting_source_formulas: Market Capitalization = Share Price × Shares Outstanding
Market Capitalization = Shares Outstanding × Share Price

formulas.source_formula: Market Capitalization = Share Price × Number of Shares Outstanding
Market Capitalization = Price per Share × Shares Outstanding
Market Capitalization = Stock Price × Shares Outstanding
Market Capitalization = Market Price Per Share × Total Shares Outstanding
supporting_source_formulas: Market Capitalization = Market Price Per Share × Total Shares Outstanding
Market Capitalization = Market Price per Share × Total Shares Outstanding

formulas.source_formula: Market Capitalization = Share Price × Outstanding Shares
Market Capitalization = (Total Shares Outstanding - B Shares Outstanding) × A Share Price + B Shares Outstanding × B Share Price

nodes.name: Market Capitalization Weight
nodes.definition: Market capitalization weight refers to the proportion of a company's (or asset's) market value relative to the total market value of its market or portfolio. It is commonly used to calculate the average return of market indices or investment portfolios. Companies with larger market capitalizations typically have higher weights and exert greater influence on the overall indicator.

nodes.name: Market Capitalization of the k-th Security
nodes.definition: Market capitalization of the k-th security refers to the total value of that security (typically a stock) at a specific point in time, calculated based on its market price and the total number of shares outstanding. It is an indicator measuring the overall market scale of that security.

nodes.name: Market Capitalization to GDP Ratio
nodes.definition: The Market Capitalization-to-GDP Ratio, also known as the Buffett Indicator, measures the total value of all publicly traded stocks in a market relative to the economy's gross domestic product (GDP). It is used to assess whether a market is undervalued or overvalued relative to historical averages.

formulas.source_formula: Market Capitalization-to-GDP Ratio = (Stock Market Capitalization ÷ GDP) × 100

nodes.name: Market Competitive Price
nodes.definition: Market competitive price refers to the price formed through market competition. In a perfectly competitive market under long-run equilibrium, it equals the minimum average total cost, or it is determined by referencing the market benchmark retail price of similar products through the market comparison method. It is a composite concept in target costing.

formulas.source_formula: Market Competitive Price ≈ Market Benchmark Retail Price
Market Competitive Price = Minimum Average Total Cost

nodes.name: Market Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The market discount rate refers to the interest rate used to discount future cash flows to their present value. It reflects the time value of money and investment risk, serving as a key parameter in financial markets for evaluating asset prices and investment project feasibility.

nodes.name: Market Entry Costs
nodes.definition: Market entry costs refer to the various direct expenditures incurred by a company in the initial phase to successfully introduce and penetrate a new product, new service, or new business into the target market. These expenditures are primarily used to overcome market barriers, establish initial brand awareness and sales channels, laying the foundation for subsequent sustainable operations.

nodes.name: Market Excess Return
nodes.definition: Market excess return refers to the portion by which the return of a portfolio or asset exceeds the market benchmark return or the risk-free rate. It is used to evaluate investment performance, calculate risk-adjusted returns, and derive financial analysis metrics such as beta in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

formulas.source_formula: Market Excess Return = Investment Return - Market Benchmark Return
Market Excess Return = Daily Stock Return - Daily Index Return

nodes.name: Market Expected Rate of Return
nodes.definition: Market expected rate of return refers to the anticipated average rate of return that investors expect to obtain from a specific asset or investment portfolio in the future, given the assumption of specific risks. It is a composite indicator calculated based on probability distributions or asset pricing models, used for evaluating investment opportunities and conducting asset pricing.

nodes.name: Market Exposure
nodes.definition: Market exposure measures the proportion of a portfolio's total value that is invested in a specific asset, sector, or market, expressed as a percentage, and is used to assess concentration risk and diversification.

formulas.source_formula: Market Exposure = (Investment Value ÷ Portfolio Value) × 100

nodes.name: Market Index
nodes.definition: A market index is a statistical indicator used to measure and reflect the overall price level movements of a specific stock market or a segment of its stocks. It is typically constructed from the prices of a representative group of stocks using specific calculation methods (such as weighted averaging) and serves as a crucial benchmark for investors to observe market trends and evaluate investment performance.

nodes.name: Market Index Closing Value
nodes.definition: Market Index Closing Value refers to the raw point or price figure obtained directly from securities market trading data at the end of a specific reporting period (such as a trading day, month, or year), reflecting the overall price level of a specific stock portfolio. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating metrics such as market returns.

nodes.name: Market Index Daily Return
nodes.definition: Market index daily return refers to the percentage reflecting the overall price movement amplitude of a specific stock market (such as the Shanghai Composite Index, Shenzhen Component Index, etc.) within a single trading day. It is typically calculated by comparing the index's closing price on the current day with that of the previous trading day, serving as a fundamental indicator for measuring short-term market performance and volatility.

nodes.name: Market Index Historical Return Rate
nodes.definition: Market index historical return rate refers to the investment return rate calculated by analyzing the point changes of a specific market index (such as the Shanghai Composite Index or S&P 500 Index) over a past period (e.g., one year, five years, or ten years). It reflects the average performance of the overall market or specific sectors during historical periods and serves as fundamental data for evaluating market trends and conducting investment analysis.

nodes.name: Market Index Opening Value
nodes.definition: Market Index Opening Value refers to the original numerical value of a market index at the selected starting point when calculating market performance over a specific period (such as an accounting period or an investment cycle). It is typically directly published by stock exchanges or professional index compilers (e.g., China Securities Index Co., Ltd., Shenzhen Securities Information Co., Ltd.) and serves as the benchmark starting point for measuring market fluctuations during that period.

nodes.name: Market Index Return
nodes.definition: Market index return refers to the investment return rate of the overall market or a specific sector over a corresponding period, calculated by comparing the price changes of a specific market index (such as the Shanghai Composite Index, CSI 300 Index, etc.) at two different points in time. It is a fundamental indicator for measuring overall market performance and is commonly used as a benchmark for evaluating the relative performance of individual stocks or investment portfolios.

nodes.name: Market Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Market interest rate is the price of funds borrowing and lending in financial markets, typically composed of the pure interest rate, inflation premium, and various risk premiums aggregated. It serves as a core benchmark for asset valuation and investment/financing decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Market Interest Rate = Pure Interest Rate + Inflation Premium + Liquidity Premium + Default Risk Premium + Maturity Risk Premium

nodes.name: Market Liquidity Premium
nodes.definition: Market liquidity premium refers to the additional return required by investors for holding less liquid assets, compensating for the time, cost, and uncertainty involved in converting the asset into cash. It is a crucial adjustment factor in asset pricing models, reflecting the impact of liquidity risk on an asset's expected return.

nodes.name: Market Momentum
nodes.definition: Market momentum (price momentum) measures the absolute change in an asset's price between the latest observation and a prior reference period, indicating the direction and strength of the price trend. A positive value signals upward momentum, while a negative value signals downward momentum. It is widely used in momentum investing and technical analysis to gauge trend persistence.

formulas.source_formula: Market Momentum = Latest Price - Past Price

nodes.name: Market Participant
nodes.definition: A market participant refers to a buyer or seller in the principal market (or most advantageous market) for the relevant asset or liability, who is independent, knowledgeable, willing, and able to transact. They are hypothetical ideal counterparties assumed when determining the fair value of an asset or liability.

nodes.name: Market Penetration Rate
nodes.definition: Market penetration rate is the percentage of the total target market that has been reached by a company's product or service, calculated as the number of unique customers divided by the total potential market size.

formulas.source_formula: Market Penetration Rate = (Customers Number ÷ Total Target Market Size) × 100

nodes.name: Market Portfolio
nodes.definition: In the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), the market portfolio is a theoretical investment portfolio that includes all risky assets weighted by their respective market values. Its return, calculated via a weighted average formula, serves as a benchmark for overall market performance and is used in computing financial metrics such as stock beta coefficients.

nodes.name: Market Portfolio Average Return Rate
nodes.definition: The market portfolio average return rate refers to the expected return calculated as the weighted average of all risky assets in the market based on their market values. It represents the average return level of the entire market (or a representative market index, such as the CSI 300 Index) and serves as a key benchmark for measuring overall market performance and calculating asset risk premiums (such as the market risk premium in the Capital Asset Pricing Model, CAPM).

nodes.name: Market Portfolio Return
nodes.definition: Market portfolio return refers to the weighted average return of all assets in the market, reflecting the overall return level of the entire market. It is a key parameter in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), used to calculate risk-adjusted metrics such as the beta coefficient.

nodes.name: Market Portfolio Return under Corresponding Scenario
nodes.definition: Market Portfolio Return under Corresponding Scenario refers to the weighted average return of all risky assets in the market determined according to a specific scenario (such as historical data, expectations, or the market portfolio in the CAPM model), serving as a core benchmark indicator in financial theories like the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

formulas.source_formula: Market Portfolio Return under Corresponding Scenario = Risk-Free Rate + Beta of Market Portfolio × (Expected Return of Market Portfolio - Risk-Free Rate)

nodes.name: Market Portfolio Risk Premium
aliases: 市场组合平均风险报酬率
nodes.definition: The market portfolio risk premium refers to the difference between the expected return of the market investment portfolio and the risk-free rate, which compensates investors for bearing market systematic risk and serves as a key parameter in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) for calculating the required rate of return on assets.

formulas.source_formula: Market Portfolio Risk Premium = Expected Return of Market Portfolio - Risk-Free Rate

nodes.name: Market Price
nodes.definition: Market price, typically referring to the price per share, is the real-time transaction price at which a stock is bought and sold on public securities exchanges. It is determined by market supply and demand, reflecting investors' immediate assessment of the company's current and future value, and is one of the most fundamental and direct trading data in capital markets.

formulas.source_formula: Market Price = PV of Coupons + PV of Principal
Market Price = Coupon × (1 - (1 + Zero-Coupon Rate ÷ 2)^(-Periods)) ÷ (Zero-Coupon Rate ÷ 2) + Par Value ÷ (1 + Zero-Coupon Rate ÷ 2)^Periods

nodes.name: Market Price Per Share
nodes.definition: Market price per share refers to the real-time transaction price of a listed company's stock formed through continuous bidding by buyers and sellers in secondary markets such as securities exchanges. It reflects the market investors' comprehensive assessment of the company's current value and future expectations, and is dynamically changing.

nodes.name: Market Price Per Share After Stock Dividend
aliases: 股利分配后的每股市价
nodes.definition: Market price per share after stock dividend refers to the trading price of each share of stock in the market after a company issues a stock dividend, which typically declines due to the increase in share capital.

nodes.name: Market Price Per Share at Exercise
nodes.definition: Market price per share at exercise refers to the per-share trading price of the underlying asset (typically stock) in the public market when the holder of an option or warrant actually exercises the right to purchase or sell the underlying asset.

nodes.name: Market Price Per Share of Common Stock
nodes.definition: Market price per share of common stock refers to the transaction price per share formed by real-time trading between buyers and sellers on secondary markets such as stock exchanges for a listed company's common stock. It reflects the market's assessment of the company's value at a specific moment and serves as the direct basis for investors to buy and sell shares.

nodes.name: Market Price of Comparable Assets
nodes.definition: The market price of comparable assets refers to the actual transaction price or market quotation of assets that are similar or comparable to the asset being appraised in terms of industry, scale, risk, growth potential, etc., in the open market. It serves as the fundamental raw data for valuation under the market comparison approach.

nodes.name: Market Price of Debt Instruments
nodes.definition: Market price of debt instruments refers to the real-time transaction price determined by supply and demand when various debt instruments such as bonds and notes are bought and sold in the secondary market (e.g., stock exchanges, interbank markets). It reflects the market's current assessment of the future cash flows and risks associated with that debt instrument and is raw data directly observed from market transactions.

nodes.name: Market Price of Long-term Debt Securities
nodes.definition: Market price of long-term debt securities refers to the trading price of debt instruments such as long-term bonds in the secondary market. It is typically calculated by discounting future cash flows (including periodic interest payments and principal repayment at maturity), reflecting the required rate of return by investors (cost of debt capital). It serves as a crucial indicator for debt valuation and cost of capital estimation.

nodes.name: Market Price of an Option
nodes.definition: The market price of an option, also known as the option premium or option price, refers to the real-time transaction price formed between buyers and sellers for an option contract in the open trading market. It is the actual amount paid or received by investors to obtain the rights (to buy or sell the underlying asset) conferred by the option contract. It is a fundamental data point observed directly from the market, not derived from formulaic calculation.

nodes.name: Market Price of the Relevant Asset
aliases: Market Price of the Underlying Asset
nodes.definition: The market price of the relevant asset refers to the transaction price that an asset can obtain at a specific point in time in an open, active, and orderly market where buyers and sellers voluntarily engage in trading. It reflects the consensus of market participants on the value of the asset.

nodes.name: Market Return
nodes.definition: Market return refers to the total return of an asset or market portfolio over a specific period, calculated as ending value minus beginning value plus interim income. It is a key metric for measuring overall market performance and is commonly used in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) as the basis for calculating beta coefficients.

formulas.source_formula: Market Return = Ending Value - Beginning Value + Interim Income

nodes.name: Market Return Rate
nodes.definition: Market return rate refers to the total rate of return of the entire market (typically represented by a representative stock market index, such as the CSI 300 Index) over a specific period (e.g., one year), including capital gains from price fluctuations and dividend income received during the period. It reflects the average return level achievable by investing in the market as a whole.

formulas.source_formula: Market Return Rate = Investment Return ÷ Investment Principal × 100%
Market Return Rate = (Asset Selling Price - Asset Purchase Price + Holding Period Income) ÷ Asset Purchase Price × 100%

nodes.name: Market Return Rate of Government Bond
Market Return Rate of Government Bonds
nodes.definition: The market return rate of government bonds refers to the yield to maturity or the yield implied by the trading price of government bonds (such as treasury bonds) with a specific maturity, directly observed from the financial market. It is a raw market data point, typically used as a fundamental input for calculating financial metrics such as corporate debt cost.

nodes.name: Market Return Series
nodes.definition: A market return series refers to a sequence of return data calculated from the price data of a market index (such as the CSI 300 Index or S&P 500 Index) at consecutive time points using specific methods (such as percentage return or logarithmic return), arranged in chronological order. It is one of the most fundamental time series data in financial modeling, risk analysis, and asset pricing.

nodes.name: Market Return Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Market return standard deviation is a statistical measure of the volatility or risk of the overall market return, typically represented by the return of a market index such as the CSI 300 Index. It reflects the average extent to which market returns deviate from their mean value. A larger standard deviation indicates greater volatility and higher risk in market returns.

nodes.name: Market Return Variance
nodes.definition: Market return variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of possible values of market returns (or asset returns) from their expected value, used to quantify market risk. It is calculated based on historical or expected return data and serves as the basis for calculating market standard deviation.

nodes.name: Market Return in the Given Scenario
nodes.definition: Market return in the given scenario typically refers to the estimated expected or historical average return level of the overall market (e.g., a stock market index) within a specific analysis or calculation context. It is a key input variable in financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), used to measure the overall risk and return level of the market and serves as a benchmark for calculating the required return or risk premium of individual assets (e.g., stocks).

nodes.name: Market Risk Coefficient of Listed Company Stock
nodes.definition: The market risk coefficient (Beta coefficient) of a listed company's stock is calculated through statistical regression analysis. It measures the volatility of a single stock's return relative to the overall market return (such as a market index) and is a key input variable in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) used to calculate the cost of equity capital.

nodes.name: Market Risk Premium
aliases: 市场投资组合的风险溢价
nodes.definition: Market risk premium refers to the portion by which the expected return of the market portfolio exceeds the risk-free rate, representing the additional compensation investors require for bearing average market risk. It is a core parameter in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), used to measure the extra return for systematic risk.

nodes.name: Market Risk-Free Rate
nodes.definition: The market risk-free rate refers to the interest rate that can be obtained by investing funds in an investment vehicle with no risk, typically benchmarked against government bond yields. It serves as an ideal investment return indicator and functions as a fundamental parameter in financial theories such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model.

nodes.name: Market Risk-Free Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The market risk-free rate of return refers to the theoretical rate of return an investor can obtain from an investment with no default risk. It is generally regarded as the minimum expected return benchmark for all other risky investments, consisting of the pure time value of money and inflation compensation. In practice, short-term government bond yields or bank deposit rates are often used as its approximations.

nodes.name: Market Sentiment Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Market Sentiment Coefficient is an indicator used to quantify the psychological state of investors or the market as a whole (such as optimism, pessimism, excitement, or fear). It is calculated by analyzing multiple data sources including survey data, social media sentiment, financial news sentiment, or market trading behavior, and is commonly used to predict market trends and assess asset price volatility.

nodes.name: Market Share
nodes.definition: Market share refers to the proportion of a company's sales volume or sales revenue within the total sales of similar products in a specific market. It is a key composite indicator for measuring a company's market competitiveness, market position, and control capabilities, typically calculated as the ratio of the company's data to the total market data.

formulas.source_formula: Market Share = (Company Sales Revenue ÷ Total Market Sales Revenue) × 100%

nodes.name: Market Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Market standard deviation is a measure of the dispersion or volatility of market returns, typically calculated based on historical market return data. It is used to assess market risk and to calculate the beta coefficient in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

nodes.name: Market Value
nodes.definition: Market value refers to the overall valuation of a company in the public market, which can be calculated through formulas and reflects investors' expectations of the company's future cash flows and profitability. It is not an original accounting figure and is typically composed of the sum of equity market value and debt market value, and is referenced by concepts such as intrinsic value.

nodes.name: Market Value Added
nodes.definition: Market Value Added is the difference between total market value and total capital, measuring the value added portion where a company's market value exceeds its invested capital. It is an important composite indicator for assessing a company's value creation capability and financial performance.

formulas.source_formula: Market Value Added = Equity Value Added + Debt Value Added
Market Value Added = Total Market Value - Total Capital
Market Value Added = (Market Value of Equity - Capital Employed for Equity) + (Market Value of Debt - Capital Employed for Debt)

nodes.name: Market Value Weight of Assets
nodes.definition: Market value weight of assets refers to the proportion of an individual asset's (or liability's, or equity's) market value to the total market value of the portfolio to which it belongs. It is a key parameter in financial analysis for calculating the weighted average cost of capital and constructing market portfolios, typically calculated based on market value data rather than accounting book values.

nodes.name: Market Value Weights of Individual Assets
nodes.definition: Market value weights of individual assets refer to the weights determined by the proportion of each asset's total market value (e.g., total market capitalization of a stock) to the total value of the entire market portfolio when calculating the market portfolio return. They reflect the relative importance of each asset within the overall market.

nodes.name: Market Value Weights of Individual Risky Assets
aliases: Market Value Weights of Risky Assets
nodes.definition: Market value weights of individual risky assets refer to the proportion of each risky asset's market value relative to the total market value of the entire investment portfolio composed of multiple risky assets. It reflects the relative importance of each asset within the portfolio and serves as a key input parameter for calculating the portfolio's overall risk and return (such as the expected return of the market portfolio).

nodes.name: Market Value of All Managed Financial Assets
aliases: Market Value of Managed Financial Assets
Total Market Value of Financial Assets Under Management
资产管理规模市场价值
nodes.definition: Market Value of All Managed Financial Assets refers to the total fair value sum of a portfolio of financial assets for which an investment management institution is responsible for investment and management, calculated based on current market prices, fair value valuation models, or other professional assessment methods. It is commonly used to measure the market performance of Assets Under Management (AUM).

nodes.name: Market Value of Asset Class i
aliases: Current Market Price of Asset i
Fair Value of Asset Class i
nodes.definition: The market value of asset class i refers to the prevailing transaction price agreed upon by willing buyers and sellers in an open, active, and orderly market on the valuation date, for the i-th category of assets after dividing the portfolio's assets into different classes based on specific criteria (such as stocks, bonds, real estate, etc.). It serves as the core foundational data for asset allocation, financial reporting, and risk management.

nodes.name: Market Value of Debt
nodes.definition: Market value of debt refers to the current fair market value of a company's debt, reflecting market expectations and pricing of debt risk. It typically refers to net debt market value, which is the value of the company's total debt market value minus cash and cash equivalents, and is a key metric for assessing a company's capital structure and calculating enterprise value.

formulas.source_formula: Market Value of Debt = Enterprise Value - Equity Value
Market Value of Debt = Total Capital Market Value × Debt Capital Proportion
Market Value of Debt = Book Value of Debt × (Market Trading Price of Debt ÷ Face Value of Debt)

operands.metric: Total Market Value of Long-term Bonds
Total Market Value of Short-term Debt

formulas.source_formula: Market Value of Debt = Total Market Value of Long-term Bonds + Total Market Value of Short-term Debt - Cash and Cash Equivalents

nodes.name: Market Value of Each Asset
nodes.definition: Market value of each asset refers to the current price at which an asset can be bought or sold in an active, open market. It reflects the consensus of market participants on the value of the asset and serves as fundamental data directly used in asset valuation, financial analysis, and investment decision-making.

nodes.name: Market Value of Equity
nodes.definition: The market value of equity is the fair value of all common shares of a company in the capital market, typically estimated through discounted expected cash flows or the Capital Asset Pricing Model.

nodes.name: Market Value of Individual Asset
aliases: Fair Market Value of an Asset
nodes.definition: Market value of an individual asset refers to the price that could be obtained for selling a specific asset in an open and active market, under conditions of fair transaction and rational behavior by both willing buyers and sellers. It reflects the asset's immediate liquidity under current market conditions and serves as a crucial basis for financial valuation, investment decision-making, and asset weighting calculations.

nodes.name: Market Value of Interest-Bearing Debt
nodes.definition: Market Value of Interest-Bearing Debt refers to the total value of all debt instruments requiring interest payments, calculated based on their fair market value. It is typically derived by summing the market prices of debt instruments or using a discounted cash flow model for future payments. As a composite metric, it is commonly used in enterprise valuation and capital structure analysis.

nodes.name: Market Value of Inventory
nodes.definition: Market value of inventory refers to the estimated value that can be obtained through sale or use in the normal course of business for inventory held by an enterprise on the balance sheet date. In accounting practice, it is typically measured using the lower of cost or net realizable value principle to reflect potential inventory impairment. It is not derived from formula calculations but is determined as raw data based on accounting records or professional valuation.

nodes.name: Market Value of Repurchase Assets
nodes.definition: Market value of repurchase assets refers to the market price of the assets (such as securities, stocks, etc.) serving as the transaction subject in a repurchase agreement at a specific point in time. It serves as the basis for calculating the repurchase price and is typically used to determine the initial value or reference value of the repurchase transaction.

nodes.name: Market Value of Securities Sold Short
Market Value of Total Capital
nodes.definition: Market value of total capital refers to the aggregate market value of all issued securities of a company, primarily including common equity and debt. It is typically calculated by summing the market value of equity capital and the market value of debt capital, reflecting the market's assessment of the company's overall value.

nodes.name: Market Value of Tradable Equity
nodes.definition: Market Value of Tradable Equity refers to the total value of common shares issued by a listed company in the public trading market (i.e., shares that can be freely bought and sold) calculated based on the current market price. It reflects the market's overall pricing of this portion of equity and is an important component of the market value of equity capital.

formulas.source_formula: Market Value of Tradable Equity = Market Value of Equity Capital - Value of Non-Tradable Equity

nodes.name: Market Value of a Class of Capital
nodes.definition: The market value of a class of capital, typically referring to equity capital (such as common stock), is the total price investors are willing to pay in the open market to acquire all of a company's equity. It reflects the market's comprehensive assessment of the company's future profitability and growth potential.

nodes.name: Market Value of a Specific Capital Type
Market Value of an Individual Asset
nodes.definition: The market value of an individual asset refers to the estimated amount for which the asset would be exchanged between a willing buyer and a willing seller in an arm's length transaction in an open and active market. It reflects the immediate value of the asset under current market conditions, rather than its historical cost or book value.

nodes.name: Market Value of the k-th Security
Market Weight
nodes.definition: Market weight refers to the proportion of a specific asset (e.g., a stock) within a particular market portfolio (e.g., an index), typically calculated based on the ratio of the asset's market value to the total market value of the portfolio. It is a key metric for measuring the relative importance of an asset within a portfolio and is commonly used in financial analysis, such as calculating the portfolio's return.

formulas.source_formula: Market Weight = Market Value of Individual Asset ÷ Total Value of Market Portfolio

nodes.name: Marketable Securities Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Marketable securities interest rate refers to the rate set at the issuance of marketable securities (such as bonds, notes, etc.) for calculating their periodic interest payments, typically expressed as an annualized percentage. It is a key metric for measuring the fixed income level obtainable from holding such securities and is commonly used in financial analysis to assess the opportunity cost of holding cash.

nodes.name: Marketable Securities Yield
nodes.definition: Marketable securities yield refers to the interest return rate that investors can obtain by holding securities such as bonds and notes, usually expressed as a percentage, and is a key indicator for measuring investment returns and opportunity costs of securities.

nodes.name: Marketing Expenses
nodes.definition: Marketing expenses refer to the various direct costs incurred by an enterprise in the process of promoting and selling its products or services. These typically include advertising fees, promotional expenses, market research costs, sales personnel salaries, and travel expenses. These costs are directly allocated based on actual occurrences and are used to reflect the investment costs in the enterprise's marketing activities.

nodes.name: Markup
nodes.definition: Markup is the percentage amount added to the cost price of a product to determine its selling price, representing the profit margin relative to cost.

formulas.source_formula: Markup Percentage = (Selling Price - Cost Price) ÷ Cost Price × 100

nodes.name: Markup Allocated to Goods Sold in Current Period
Markup Amount
nodes.definition: Markup amount refers to the additional amount added to the cost of a product or service to generate profit. It is typically calculated as a percentage of the cost or selling price (i.e., the markup rate) and constitutes a key component of the final selling price.

nodes.name: Markup Rate
nodes.definition: The markup rate is the percentage of profit added to the relevant cost when a company sets product prices. It is the core parameter of cost-plus pricing and reflects the company's expected profit level.

formulas.source_formula: Markup Rate = Markup Amount ÷ Relevant Cost

nodes.name: Married Filing Jointly vs Separately Comparison
aliases: 夫妻合并申报与分别申报比较
nodes.definition: A comparison method to determine whether married taxpayers should file their tax returns jointly or separately by evaluating which filing status results in a lower overall tax liability after accounting for respective incomes, deductions, and credits.

nodes.name: Married Put Breakeven Price
aliases: 保护性看跌期权盈亏平衡点
nodes.definition: The married put breakeven price is the stock price at which a married put strategy (holding a long stock position plus a protective put option) neither gains nor loses money, calculated as the sum of the stock purchase price and the put option premium paid.

nodes.name: Material Consumption Quota per Unit Product
aliases: Material Consumption Standard per Unit Product
单位产品原材料消耗定额
单位产品材料消耗定额
单位产品材料消耗标准
nodes.definition: Material consumption quota per unit product refers to the standard quantity of materials that must be consumed to produce one qualified unit of product under current production technology and management conditions. It is typically composed of the net weight of the unit product and various process-related losses, and is used for material cost control, cost accounting, and quota management.

operands.metric: Total Weight of Various Process-Related Losses

formulas.source_formula: Material Consumption Quota per Unit Product = Net Weight of Unit Product + Total Weight of Various Process-Related Losses

operands.metric: Total Material Consumption in the Past Three Years
Total Product Output in the Past Three Years

formulas.source_formula: Material Consumption Quota per Unit Product = Total Material Consumption in the Past Three Years ÷ Total Product Output in the Past Three Years

nodes.name: Material Consumption Quota per Unit of Work-in-Process
aliases: Unit Material Consumption Standard for WIP
单位产品材料消耗定额
在产品材料定额消耗量
nodes.definition: Material Consumption Quota per Unit of Work-in-Process refers to the predetermined standard quantity of a specific raw material that should be consumed to complete one unit of work-in-process (i.e., unfinished products) during the production process. It serves as an important basis for enterprise cost accounting (such as the quota proportion method), material cost allocation, and work-in-process cost calculation.

nodes.name: Material Cost
nodes.definition: Material cost refers to the value of raw materials, auxiliary materials, and other supplies consumed by an enterprise in the process of producing goods or providing services. It is a significant component of product cost, reflecting the primary consumption in the production phase, and serves as the foundation for cost control and product pricing.

nodes.name: Material Cost Allocated to Finished Goods
aliases: Direct Materials Cost Allocated to Finished Products
Materials Cost Allocated to Finished Goods
分摊至完工产品的材料成本
完工产品应分配的材料成本
nodes.definition: Material cost allocated to finished goods refers to the portion of total material costs apportioned to completed products based on the material cost allocation rate.

operands.metric: Standard Material Cost of Finished Products

formulas.source_formula: Material Cost Allocated to Finished Goods = Standard Material Cost of Finished Goods × Material Cost Allocation Rate

nodes.name: Material Cost Allocated to Work-in-Process at Month-End
aliases: 月末在产品材料成本分配
nodes.definition: Material cost allocated to work-in-process at month-end refers to the portion of total material costs allocated to unfinished products based on the material cost allocation rate.

operands.metric: Standard Material Cost of Work-in-Process at Month-End

formulas.source_formula: Material Cost Allocated to Work-in-Process at Month-End = Standard Material Cost of Work-in-Process at Month-End × Material Cost Allocation Rate

nodes.name: Material Cost Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: Material Cost Allocation Rate is the ratio used to allocate the actual total material consumption or cost proportionally based on the standard material consumption quotas of various products.

operands.metric: Actual Material Cost of Beginning Work-in-Process
Actual Material Cost Incurred in Current Month
Standard Material Cost of Finished Products
Standard Material Cost of Ending Work-in-Process

formulas.source_formula: Material Cost Allocation Rate = (Actual Material Cost of Beginning Work-in-Process + Actual Material Cost Incurred in Current Month) ÷ (Standard Material Cost of Finished Goods + Standard Material Cost of Ending Work-in-Process)

nodes.name: Material Cost Variance
nodes.definition: Material cost variance refers to the difference between the actual cost of materials and the planned standard cost. It is a key indicator under standard costing used to measure the effectiveness of cost control in material procurement or consumption. A variance where actual cost exceeds planned cost is an unfavorable variance, while the opposite is a favorable variance.

nodes.name: Material Original Price
nodes.definition: Material original price refers to the price stated on the original invoice provided by the production unit or supplier when a company purchases materials. It serves as the fundamental data for material cost calculation and typically excludes subsequent additional expenses such as transportation and storage.

nodes.name: Material Planned Unit Price
nodes.definition: Material planned unit price is the predetermined unit cost of materials established by an enterprise for a planning period, used for the planned cost accounting of material receipts, issues, and inventory. This price is comprehensively calculated based on cost elements such as the original material price, transportation and miscellaneous expenses, off-site transportation loss rate, and procurement and storage fee rate. It serves as a crucial foundational indicator for determining the standard material cost of finished products and for cost control.

formulas.source_formula: Material Planned Unit Price = (Original Material Price + Transportation and Miscellaneous Expenses) × (1 + Off-site Transportation Loss Rate)
Material Planned Unit Price = (Original Material Price + Transportation and Miscellaneous Expenses) × (1 + Off-site Transportation Loss Rate) × (1 + Procurement and Storage Fee Rate)

nodes.name: Material Price Standard
nodes.definition: Material price standard refers to the pre-determined, approved per-unit price for direct materials consumed in producing one unit of product under standard costing. It is typically determined based on comprehensive factors including market conditions, supplier contracts, and full cost elements such as freight, insurance, and inspection fees, serving as one of the foundational data points for calculating direct material standard cost.

nodes.name: Material Price Variance
nodes.definition: Material price variance refers to the cost difference arising from the discrepancy between the actual purchase price and the standard price.

formulas.source_formula: Material Price Variance = Actual Quantity × (Actual Price - Standard Price)

nodes.name: Material Procurement Costs
nodes.definition: Material procurement costs refer to the total expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire materials such as raw materials and components required for production or operations. These typically include the purchase price of materials, transportation fees, insurance premiums, loading and unloading charges, warehousing fees, customs duties, and other related taxes and costs directly associated with procurement activities.

nodes.name: Material Quantity Allocated to a Specific Product
nodes.definition: Material quantity allocated to a specific product refers to the quantity of materials calculated by multiplying the standard material consumption of that product by the material cost allocation rate.

nodes.name: Material Quantity Variance
nodes.definition: Material quantity variance refers to the cost difference arising from the discrepancy between the actual quantity of materials used and the standard quantity.

formulas.source_formula: Material Quantity Variance = (Actual Quantity - Standard Quantity) × Standard Price

nodes.name: Material Standard Consumption Quantity
aliases: 单位产品材料消耗标准
nodes.definition: Material standard consumption quantity refers to the predetermined quantity standard of a specific material allowed for consumption in producing one unit of qualified product under conditions of reasonable material usage. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and material management.

nodes.name: Material Standard Cost
nodes.definition: Material standard cost refers to the predetermined cost standard for materials, calculated under a quota management system based on the pre-established material consumption quota per unit of product, the planned unit price of materials, and the quantity of products. It serves as the foundation for the standard costing method in cost accounting and is used for cost control, variance analysis, and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Material Standard Price
aliases: Standard Price per Unit of Material
nodes.definition: Material standard price refers to the predetermined unit price that an enterprise should pay for a specific material consumed in producing one unit of product under normal operating conditions, within the standard costing system. It serves as the basis for calculating direct material standard costs and conducting cost variance analysis.

nodes.name: Material Standard Unit Price
aliases: Standard Price per Unit of Material
nodes.definition: Material standard unit price refers to the predetermined base price per unit of material established for setting cost standards under a standard costing system. It typically includes all necessary expenditures such as purchase price, freight and miscellaneous charges, transportation losses, and procurement and storage costs, serving as fundamental input data for calculating composite indicators like direct material standard cost.

nodes.name: Material Unit Price
nodes.definition: Material unit price refers to the comprehensive average price of materials after they are transported from their source to the site warehouse or designated storage location. It serves as the basis for calculating product material standard costs or standard sales quantities, and is typically composed of the material base price, freight and miscellaneous charges, transportation loss costs, and procurement and storage expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Material Unit Price = (Material Base Price + Freight and Miscellaneous Charges) × (1 + Transportation Loss Rate) × (1 + Procurement and Storage Expense Rate)

nodes.name: Material Wastage Rate
nodes.definition: Material wastage rate refers to the percentage of material loss caused by accidents, human operations, or natural factors during production or construction processes, relative to the planned net usage of that material. It is a key metric for measuring material usage efficiency and cost control, commonly used in establishing material consumption quotas.

nodes.name: Materials Procurement
nodes.definition: Materials procurement refers to the actual expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire raw materials, auxiliary materials, and other supplies required for production and operation. These expenditures are typically recorded and recognized directly based on original documents such as invoices and freight bills, constituting a significant component of inventory cost.

nodes.name: Materials and Supplies Cost
nodes.definition: Materials and supplies cost refers to all expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire materials required for production or operations, including raw materials, auxiliary materials, fuel, spare parts, and other supplies. It typically includes the purchase price of materials, related taxes and duties, transportation fees, loading and unloading charges, insurance premiums, and other costs attributable to the procurement of materials.

nodes.name: Maternity Insurance
nodes.definition: Maternity insurance is a social insurance system established by the government or social institutions, designed to provide medical services and certain financial compensation to employees or citizens during childbirth, in order to alleviate the potential economic difficulties faced by individuals and families due to childbirth, and to safeguard the health and well-being of mothers and infants.

nodes.name: Mathematical Expectation
nodes.definition: Mathematical expectation is a concept in probability theory and statistics, defined as the sum (or integral) of all possible values of a random variable multiplied by their corresponding probabilities. It is a composite indicator calculated through specific formulas, used to reflect the average value of a random variable.

nodes.name: Mathematical Expectation of Random Variable X
nodes.definition: The mathematical expectation of random variable X is the weighted average of all possible values of the random variable, with their corresponding probabilities as weights. It is the most important numerical characteristic describing the central location of the random variable's values. For discrete random variables, it is defined as the sum of each possible value multiplied by its corresponding probability; for continuous random variables, it is defined as the integral of the value multiplied by the probability density function.

nodes.name: Mathematical Expectation of Random Variable Y
nodes.definition: Mathematical expectation is a core concept in probability theory and mathematical statistics, representing the weighted average of all possible values of a random variable with their corresponding probabilities as weights. It is the most important characteristic number describing the central tendency of a random variable. It is not directly observable raw data but rather a result calculated or derived based on the probability distribution of the random variable.

nodes.name: Mathematical Expectation of the Product of Random Variable X and Random Variable Y
aliases: Expectation of the Product of Random Variables X and Y
nodes.definition: The mathematical expectation of the product of random variable X and random variable Y is the expected value of their product. It reflects the average level of their product under the joint distribution of X and Y, and serves as the foundation for calculating statistical measures such as covariance.

nodes.name: Maturity
nodes.definition: Maturity refers to the remaining length of time from the current date to the final principal repayment date stipulated in the contract for a financial instrument (such as a bond or loan), typically measured in years.

nodes.name: Maturity Date
nodes.definition: Maturity date refers to the specific date, as directly stipulated in the terms of contracts, agreements, financial products, or certificates, on which their validity or obligations terminate. It is a fundamental, original date datum, not derived through calculation.

nodes.name: Maturity Date Change
nodes.definition: Maturity date change refers to the alteration of the specific expiration date stipulated in contracts, financial products, or derivative contracts (such as options, futures). It is a fundamental date data point, typically obtained directly from contract terms or product specifications, used to determine the final effective period of rights or obligations.

nodes.name: Maturity Principal and Interest
aliases: Future Value of Principal and Interest
nodes.definition: Maturity principal and interest refers to the total sum of principal and accumulated interest formed at the end of the agreed investment or loan term, calculated according to the agreed interest rate in financial investment or lending activities.

nodes.name: Maturity Risk Premium
nodes.definition: Maturity risk premium refers to the interest rate differential arising from varying maturities of bonds or other financial instruments, serving as compensation to investors for bearing the risk of future market interest rate fluctuations. Generally, the longer the maturity, the greater the interest rate uncertainty faced by investors, and thus the higher the required maturity risk premium.

nodes.name: Maturity Value
nodes.definition: Maturity value refers to the total amount payable to the holder of a financial instrument (such as a note or bond) at its maturity date. For interest-bearing notes, it equals the face value plus interest calculated based on the coupon rate and term; for non-interest-bearing notes, the maturity value equals the face value. It serves as the basis for calculating discount interest and evaluating bond value.

formulas.source_formula: Maturity Value = Face Value
Maturity Value = Principal × (1 + Annual Interest Rate)^(Years)
Maturity Value = Face Value × (1 + Interest Rate ÷ Compound Frequency) ^ (Compound Frequency × Years)
Max Profit = Initial Credit - (Target Strike Price - Low Strike Price) - (High Strike Price - Target Strike Price)

nodes.name: Maximum Cash Limit
nodes.definition: The maximum cash limit is the upper bound of cash balance set by an enterprise under the random model, beyond which excess cash should be converted into marketable securities.

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Cash Limit = 3 × Cash Return Line - 2 × Minimum Cash Balance

nodes.name: Maximum Daily Requirement
nodes.definition: Maximum Daily Requirement refers to the highest consumption or demand volume within a specific period (e.g., one day). It is a key metric in financial management used for inventory management, safety stock calculation, and other scenarios, typically derived from historical data or forecasting models.

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Deductible Amount = Adjusted Gross Income × Maximum Deductible Percentage

nodes.name: Maximum Delivery Time
nodes.definition: Maximum Delivery Time refers to the latest permissible point or deadline for completing the delivery of products or services, as stipulated by suppliers, manufacturers, or contract terms in supply chain, production, or trade agreements. It typically serves as fundamental business data for production scheduling, logistics planning, or performance evaluation (e.g., calculating delivery achievement rates) and is not derived through formulaic calculation.

nodes.name: Maximum Drawdown
nodes.definition: Maximum Drawdown (MDD) refers to the maximum decline from a historical peak to a subsequent trough for an investment or portfolio since its inception, representing the most severe peak-to-trough loss in value experienced before a new high is reached.

nodes.name: Maximum Expected Profit from Foregone Alternatives
Maximum Expected Profit of Abandoned Alternatives
aliases: Maximum Expected Profit of Forgone Alternatives
机会成本中的放弃收益
nodes.definition: In decision analysis, when selecting one alternative from multiple options, the maximum expected profit of abandoned alternatives refers to the profit value of the alternative with the highest expected return among all unselected options. It represents the potential benefit that could have been gained from the best foregone alternative due to choosing the current option, serving as a key foundational data point for calculating opportunity cost.

nodes.name: Maximum Frequency
nodes.definition: Maximum frequency is the count of the most frequently occurring value in a dataset, a statistical measure obtained by calculating the frequency of each value and taking the maximum, used to describe the central tendency of data distribution and often serves as a reference indicator for central point analysis.

nodes.name: Maximum Gain (Synthetic Put)
nodes.definition: Maximum Gain (Synthetic Put) is the upper bound of profit for the synthetic put options strategy, constructed by shorting the underlying stock and purchasing a call option on the same underlying. Assuming the stock price can fall to zero and excluding transaction costs, the maximum gain equals the short sale price minus the call option premium.

nodes.name: Maximum Garnishment
nodes.definition: Maximum garnishment refers to the legally permitted upper limit of wages that can be withheld from an employee’s disposable income, typically governed by the Consumer Credit Protection Act (CCPA). The cap is the lesser of a fixed percentage of disposable income and the amount by which disposable income exceeds a threshold tied to the minimum wage.

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Home Purchase Cost = Annual Household Income × Income Multiple

nodes.name: Maximum Inventory Level
nodes.definition: Maximum inventory level refers to the peak inventory value reached after a batch of goods is delivered, as inventory is consumed concurrently with delivery.

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Inventory Level = Order Quantity per Batch - (Order Quantity per Batch ÷ Daily Delivery Quantity) × Daily Consumption Quantity
Maximum Loan Amount = Home Value × Loan-to-Value Ratio
Maximum Loan Amount = Collateral Value × Leverage Limit
Maximum Loan Amount = Property Value × Loan-to-Value (LTV) Ratio
Maximum Loan Amount = Advance Rate × Collateral Value

nodes.name: Maximum Loan Amount (Asset-Based Lending)
aliases: 资产为基础的贷款额度
资产抵押贷款最高贷款额
nodes.definition: In asset-based lending, the maximum loan amount is determined by multiplying the collateral's appraised value by the applicable advance rate, which reflects the lender's expected recovery from the collateral. Typical advance rates are higher for liquid collateral (e.g., cash, marketable securities) and lower for illiquid collateral (e.g., specialized equipment, inventory).

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Loss = Spread Credit - (Higher Strike - Lower Strike)
Maximum Loss = Net Premium Paid
supporting_source_formulas: Maximum Loss = Net Premium Paid

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Loss = Premium Cost
Maximum Loss = Buy Price - Sell Price
Maximum Loss = (Sell Strike - Buy Strike) - Net Credit
Maximum Loss = Long Put Strike Price - Short Put Strike Price - Net Premium Received
Maximum Loss = Long Call Strike Price - Short Call Strike Price - Net Premium Received
Maximum Loss = (Long Call Strike − Short Call Strike) − Premium Received
Maximum Loss = Upper Strike - Lower Strike - Premium Received
Maximum Loss = (Purchase Price - Put Strike Price) × Shares per Contract - Net Cost or Credit

nodes.name: Maximum Output
nodes.definition: Maximum output refers to the production level that maximizes profit, derived through mathematical optimization methods (such as setting the first derivative of the profit function to zero) given cost and revenue functions. It is a key concept in enterprise production decision-making and financial management, used to determine the optimal production scale, commonly applied in cost management, production optimization, and microeconomic analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Output = (Demand Function Intercept - Demand Function Slope × Unit Variable Cost) ÷ 2
Maximum Profit = Net Credit Received
Maximum Profit = Net Credit
Maximum Profit = Premium Received
supporting_source_formulas: Maximum Profit = Premium Received

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Profit = Net Premium Received
supporting_source_formulas: Maximum Profit = Net Premium Received

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Profit = Premium Received + Price Appreciation
Maximum Profit = Box Value at Expiration - (Net Premium Paid + Commissions)
Maximum Profit = Short Put Strike Price - Long Put Strike Price - Net Premium Paid
Maximum Profit = Short Call Strike Price - Long Call Strike Price - Net Premium Paid
Maximum Profit = Middle Strike - Lower Strike - Premium Cost
Maximum Profit = (Higher Strike Price - Lower Strike Price) × Shares per Contract - Net Cost of Spread
Maximum Profit = (Call Strike Price - Purchase Price) × Shares per Contract + Net Cost or Credit
Maximum Profit (Net Credit) = Call Strike Price - Stock Purchase Price + Net Premium
Maximum Profit (Net Debit) = Call Strike Price - Stock Purchase Price - Net Premium

nodes.name: Maximum Value
nodes.definition: Maximum value is the largest number in a set of data or numerical collection, typically determined through comparison operations, serving as a fundamental statistical measure in financial analysis, data processing, and model calculations.

formulas.source_formula: Maximum Value = MIN(Preset Upper Limit, Original Calculation Result)

nodes.name: Maximum Velocity
nodes.definition: Maximum velocity refers to the highest instantaneous or average speed that an object can achieve under specific conditions (such as over a specific distance or time period). In physics and kinematics, it typically denotes the peak speed of an object during its motion.

nodes.name: Mean
nodes.definition: The mean is a statistical measure obtained by dividing the sum of a set of values by their count, used to describe the central tendency of data. In financial and investment analysis, it is commonly used to calculate derived metrics such as average growth rate, average cost, and average return.

formulas.source_formula: Mean = Sum of All Data ÷ Number of Data Points
Mean = n × p

operands.metric: Sum of All Observations in the Sample

formulas.source_formula: Mean = Σx ÷ n

nodes.name: Mean Absolute Deviation
nodes.definition: Mean Absolute Deviation (MAD) is the average of the absolute deviations of a set of data from a central point (typically the mean). It is a measure of statistical dispersion that indicates the average absolute distance between data points and the central value.

nodes.name: Mean-Variance Analysis
nodes.definition: Mean-Variance Analysis is a core framework of Modern Portfolio Theory that evaluates and constructs portfolios by trading off expected return (mean) against risk (variance). It aggregates asset expected returns with portfolio weights to obtain the portfolio's expected return and uses asset volatilities and their correlations to compute portfolio variance, enabling efficient diversification and risk-return optimization.

nodes.name: Mean-Variance Model
nodes.definition: The Mean-Variance Model is the core model of modern portfolio theory, proposed by Harry Markowitz. This model quantifies a portfolio's expected return (mean) and risk (variance or standard deviation), helping investors seek the highest expected return for a given level of risk, or the lowest risk for a given expected return, thereby determining the optimal asset allocation proportions.

nodes.name: Measures and Methods Cost
nodes.definition: Measures and methods cost refers to the expenses incurred for non-entity project items before and during the construction process of a building project, which are necessary to complete the project construction. These costs typically arise from essential measures taken to ensure project quality, safety, environmental protection, and civilized construction.

nodes.name: Median
nodes.definition: The median, also known as the middle position, is a statistical measure used to represent the central tendency of a set of numerical values. It is calculated by arranging the values in ascending order and selecting the value at the middle position; if the number of values is even, the average of the two middle values is taken. In Excel, it is calculated using the MEDIAN function and is widely applied in financial data analysis, risk assessment, and descriptive statistics.

nodes.name: Medical Cost Ratio (MCR)
nodes.definition: Medical Cost Ratio (MCR) measures the proportion of insurance premiums spent on medical claims and related healthcare costs. It is calculated as total medical expenses divided by total premiums collected and is used to assess an insurer’s cost efficiency, profitability, and compliance with regulatory standards such as the Affordable Care Act.

formulas.source_formula: Medical Cost Ratio = Total Medical Expenses ÷ Total Premiums Collected

nodes.name: Medical Insurance
nodes.definition: Medical insurance is a social security system designed to establish a fund through contributions from individuals and employers, providing compensation for medical expenses to insured individuals in case of illness or injury, thereby alleviating their financial burden.

nodes.name: Medical Insurance Contribution Base
nodes.definition: The Medical Insurance Contribution Base refers to the base amount used to calculate the monthly medical insurance premiums payable by the insured (typically employees) and their employers. It is generally determined based on the insured individual's wage income, but is subject to upper and lower limits, which are usually linked to the local average monthly wage of employees in the previous year.

nodes.name: Medical Insurance Contribution Rate
aliases: 医保个人单位缴费比例
nodes.definition: The Medical Insurance Contribution Rate refers to the percentage rate at which individuals and employers calculate and pay medical insurance premiums based on the employee's wages when participating in social medical insurance. It is typically shared by the individual and the employer, with specific ratios determined by each pooling region according to policy.

formulas.source_formula: Medicare Tax = Net Earnings × Medicare Tax Rate
Medicare Tax = Gross Income × Medicare Rate

nodes.name: Member Competency
nodes.definition: Member competency refers to the aggregate of knowledge, skills, qualities, and behavioral characteristics required by organizational members (such as finance personnel, analysts, etc.) in the accounting and finance field to effectively perform their job responsibilities and achieve work objectives. It is typically defined and assessed through competency models or qualification systems, covering multiple dimensions such as professional foundation, thinking ability, and interpersonal collaboration.

nodes.name: Merchandise Export Value
nodes.definition: Merchandise export value refers to the total value of all goods sold abroad by a country or region within a specific period. This value is typically calculated on a Free On Board (FOB) basis, meaning the value of the goods when they are loaded onto the vessel at the port of the exporting country, ready for shipment overseas. It includes the cost of the goods and transportation to the port, but excludes subsequent international freight and insurance costs.

nodes.name: Merchandise Markup
nodes.definition: Merchandise markup refers to the difference between the selling price and the purchase price of goods in merchandising enterprises using the retail inventory method. This metric serves as the basis for calculating the cost of goods sold and the cost of ending inventory, typically allocated through the markup rate.

operands.metric: Markup Allocated to Goods Sold in Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Merchandise Markup = (Beginning Inventory Markup + Current Period Purchases Markup) - Markup Allocated to Goods Sold in Current Period
Merchant Discount Fee = Transaction Amount × Merchant Discount Rate ÷ 100

nodes.name: Merchant Discount Rate
nodes.definition: Merchant Discount Rate is the percentage charged to merchants by acquiring banks or payment processors for card transactions. It typically covers interchange, assessment, and processing costs. The fee for a given transaction is calculated by multiplying the transaction amount by the Merchant Discount Rate.

nodes.name: Merchant Risk Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Merchant Risk Coefficient is a comprehensive metric used by financial institutions or payment platforms to quantify the potential risk level of partner merchants. It is typically calculated based on multi-dimensional data including the merchant's operational stability, transaction behavior, compliance records, and credit status, and is used to assist in formulating risk management strategies, such as setting transaction monitoring thresholds, adjusting settlement cycles, or determining partnership eligibility.

nodes.name: Merchant Transaction Limit Setting
nodes.definition: Merchant transaction limit setting refers to the maximum payment amount restriction established by a merchant or payment service provider for a single transaction or cumulative transactions within a specific period, aimed at controlling transaction risk, managing cash flow, or complying with specific regulations.

nodes.name: Merton Model
nodes.definition: The Merton model is a structural credit risk framework that models a firm's equity as a European call option on its assets. It uses option-pricing theory to value equity and infer default risk based on firm asset value, asset volatility, debt face value, risk-free rate, and time to maturity.

nodes.name: Micro E-mini S&P 500 Contract Notional Value
aliases: Micro E-mini S&P 500 Futures Notional Value
微型E-mini 合约名义价值
微型E-mini 标普500期货合约名义价值
nodes.definition: The Micro E-mini S&P 500 contract notional value represents the monetary exposure of one Micro E-mini S&P 500 futures contract, calculated by multiplying the S&P 500 index level by the Micro E-mini contract multiplier (USD per index point). It is used for position sizing, margin planning, and risk management.

formulas.source_formula: Micro E-mini S&P 500 Contract Notional Value = S&P 500 Index Level × Micro E-mini Contract Multiplier
Middle Donchian Band = (Upper Donchian Band + Lower Donchian Band) ÷ 2
Middle Line = Exponential Moving Average

nodes.name: Midpoint of Integration Interval
nodes.definition: The midpoint of an integration interval is a concept in numerical integration, referring to the center point of each subinterval after dividing the total integration interval into several subintervals. In numerical integration methods (such as the midpoint rule), the function value at this midpoint is typically used to approximate the average function value over the entire subinterval, thereby calculating the approximate integral value for that subinterval.

nodes.name: Military Base Pay
nodes.definition: Military base pay is the foundational salary paid to military personnel before any allowances or special pays, determined by pay grade and years of service, and adjusted for Employment Cost Index (ECI) increases.

nodes.name: Mill Levy
nodes.definition: Mill levy is the property tax rate applied to the total assessed property value, typically expressed in mills (per $1,000 of assessed value). It is calculated to meet the revenue requirements of taxing jurisdictions such as the school district, county, and city.

nodes.name: Mill Rate
nodes.definition: Mill rate is a property tax rate expressed per $1,000 of assessed (taxable) property value. One mill equals $1 of tax for every $1,000 of assessed value. Jurisdictions use the mill rate to calculate property tax liabilities by applying the rate to the property's taxable value.

nodes.name: Millage Rate
nodes.definition: Millage rate is a property tax rate expressed in mills, meaning the amount of tax per $1,000 of assessed taxable value. It is used by local governments to compute property tax liabilities: Property Tax = Millage Rate × Taxable Value ÷ 1,000.

nodes.name: Mine Maintenance and Simplification Fee
aliases: 矿山维持简单再生产费用
nodes.definition: The Mine Maintenance and Simplification Fee is a special fee accrued by mining enterprises (such as coal mines), similar in nature to the Work Safety Fee, specifically earmarked for expenditures to maintain simple reproduction and for work safety facilities.

nodes.name: Minimum Average Total Cost
nodes.definition: Minimum Average Total Cost is the lowest point on the Average Total Cost curve, indicating the minimum total cost per unit of output at a specific production scale. This point serves as a key reference for determining a firm's long-term competitive price and optimal production scale.

formulas.source_formula: Minimum Average Total Cost = min(Total Cost ÷ Output Quantity)

nodes.name: Minimum Cash Balance
nodes.definition: Minimum cash balance refers to the minimum amount of cash that a company must hold to maintain daily operational turnover and meet basic payment requirements. It is a key parameter in cash management models and is typically used in conjunction with concepts such as the cash return line and maximum cash limit.

formulas.source_formula: Minimum Equity = Stock Value × Maintenance Margin

nodes.name: Minimum Interest Amount (AFR)
aliases: 最低利息额（适用联邦利率）
适用联邦利率最低利息额
nodes.definition: Minimum Interest Amount (AFR) is the required interest to be charged on a loan to comply with the IRS Applicable Federal Rate, calculated as principal multiplied by the AFR and the loan term in years, helping avoid imputed interest and below-market loan tax consequences.

formulas.source_formula: Minimum Interest Amount = Principal × Applicable Federal Rate (AFR) × Loan Term (Years)

nodes.name: Minimum Monthly Payment
nodes.definition: Minimum monthly payment is the lowest amount a borrower must pay each billing cycle on a revolving credit account (e.g., credit cards) to keep the account current.
