It is commonly calculated as a fixed percentage of the outstanding credit balance and may not fully amortize principal. A related measure, Total Interest Paid, reflects the cumulative interest expense over a specified period given fixed monthly payments and monthly compounding.

formulas.source_formula: Minimum Monthly Payment = Credit Balance × Minimum Payment Rate

nodes.name: Minimum Production Volume
nodes.definition: Minimum production volume refers to the quantity of production or sales required for an enterprise to reach the break-even point or achieve a specific target profit. It can be calculated through formulas and is a core composite indicator in cost-volume-profit analysis in financial management.

formulas.source_formula: Minimum Production Volume = Fixed Costs ÷ (Unit Price - Unit Variable Cost)
Minimum Production Volume = (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) ÷ (Unit Price - Unit Variable Cost)
Minimum Production Volume = [Fixed Costs + After-tax Profit ÷ (1 - Income Tax Rate)] ÷ (Unit Price - Unit Variable Cost)

nodes.name: Minimum Required Collateral
nodes.definition: Minimum Required Collateral refers to the minimum value of pledged assets that a creditor or counterparty requires a debtor to provide in a financial transaction (such as a loan or derivative contract) to mitigate counterparty default risk. This minimum value is typically determined based on risk assessment and serves as the fundamental threshold for maintaining the transaction or obtaining financing.

formulas.source_formula: Minimum Required Collateral = Loan Amount ÷ Collateral Ratio
Minimum Required Collateral = Loan Amount ÷ Loan-to-Value Ratio

nodes.name: Mining Industry Labor Compensation
aliases: Wages and Salaries in Mining Industry
nodes.definition: Mining industry labor compensation refers to the total sum of all forms of remuneration paid to all personnel engaged in mining and related activities (including production workers, management personnel, technical personnel, etc.) in the cost accounting of mining enterprises. It is typically reflected as the aggregate of personnel wages and constitutes an important component of the value added in the mining industry.

nodes.name: Mining Industry Operating Surplus
nodes.definition: Mining industry operating surplus measures the residual income available for primary distribution that mining enterprises obtain from their core production and operating activities within a certain period. It is an important component in calculating the value added of the mining industry.

operands.metric: Wages and Benefits Paid from Profits
Public Welfare Funds Withdrawn from After-tax Profits

formulas.source_formula: Mining Industry Operating Surplus = Operating Profit + Production Subsidies - Wages and Benefits Paid from Profits - Public Welfare Funds Withdrawn from After-tax Profits

nodes.name: Mining Industry Value Added
nodes.definition: Mining Industry Value Added is a derived indicator in economic statistics used to measure the new value created by mining production activities within a specific period. It is typically calculated using the production approach (output minus intermediate consumption) or the income approach formula, constitutes a significant component of secondary industry value added, and is not an original accounting item in financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Mining Industry Value Added = Gross Output Value of Mining - Intermediate Consumption of Mining

operands.metric: Net Taxes on Production in Mining
Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Mining

formulas.source_formula: Mining Industry Value Added = Compensation of Employees in Mining + Net Taxes on Production in Mining + Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Mining + Operating Surplus of Mining

nodes.name: Minority Interest
aliases: Minority Interest in Profit or Loss
nodes.definition: In accounting, minority interest (or non-controlling interest) refers to the portion of a subsidiary's equity that is not held by the parent company. It represents the equity and net profit attributable to shareholders other than the parent company, and is presented in the consolidated balance sheet and consolidated income statement.

formulas.source_formula: Minority Interest = Total Shareholders' Equity of Subsidiary × Minority Shareholding Percentage

nodes.name: Minority Interest Eligible for Inclusion
nodes.definition: Minority interest eligible for inclusion refers to the portion of equity in subsidiaries attributable to investors other than the parent company, as presented in consolidated financial statements, which may be included in the calculation of the group's Common Equity Tier 1 capital in accordance with regulatory requirements.

operands.metric: Parent Company's Shareholding Percentage in Subsidiary

formulas.source_formula: Minority Interest Eligible for Inclusion = Total Owners' Equity of Subsidiary × (1 - Parent Company's Shareholding Percentage in Subsidiary)

operands.metric: Parent Company's Shareholding Percentage in Subsidiary

formulas.source_formula: Minority Interest Eligible for Inclusion = Total Equity of Subsidiary × (1 - Parent Company's Shareholding Percentage in Subsidiary)
Minority Interest Eligible for Inclusion = Total Owners' Equity of Subsidiary × Minority Shareholding Percentage
Minority Interest Eligible for Inclusion = Total Equity of Subsidiary × Minority Shareholding Percentage

nodes.name: Minority Interest Ratio
nodes.definition: The minority interest ratio refers to the proportion of shares held by non-controlling shareholders (i.e., minority shareholders) to the total share capital of a company (typically a subsidiary consolidated in the parent company's financial statements). It is a fundamental metric derived directly from the company's ownership structure, reflecting the minority shareholders' ownership stake in the company.

nodes.name: Minority Interest Share of Net Profit

formulas.source_formula: Minority Interest Share of Net Profit = Net Profit of Subsidiary × Minority Shareholding Percentage

nodes.name: Minority Interest Value
nodes.definition: Minority interest value refers to the net assets or equity value of a subsidiary attributable to minority shareholders in consolidated financial statements, reflecting the economic interests of minority shareholders in the subsidiary. It is typically a key composite metric in enterprise valuation and consolidated statement preparation.

formulas.source_formula: Minority Interest Value = Equity Value × Minority Interest Percentage

nodes.name: Misery Index
nodes.definition: The Misery Index is a macroeconomic indicator calculated as the sum of the unemployment rate and the inflation rate, used to gauge the economic discomfort experienced by the public due to labor-market slack and rising price levels.

formulas.source_formula: Misery Index = Unemployment Rate + Inflation Rate

nodes.name: Mixed Cost
nodes.definition: Mixed cost (semi-variable cost) is a cost that contains both fixed and variable components. It can be modeled with a linear cost function where total mixed cost equals a fixed cost plus a variable cost rate multiplied by the activity level. This representation is widely used in cost behavior analysis, budgeting, and cost-volume-profit (CVP) analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Mixed Cost = Variable Cost per Unit × Activity Level + Fixed Cost

nodes.name: Modal Class Frequency
nodes.definition: In grouped data, modal class frequency refers to the number of data points occurring within the class interval that contains the mode (the value with the highest frequency in the dataset). It is a key parameter when calculating the mode for grouped data.

nodes.name: Mode
nodes.definition: The mode refers to the value that appears most frequently in a dataset, and is one of the statistical measures used to describe the central tendency of data. A dataset may have no mode, one mode, or multiple modes.

operands.metric: Lower Limit of the Modal Class

formulas.source_formula: Mode = Lower limit of modal class + (Frequency of modal class - Frequency of preceding class) ÷ ((Frequency of modal class - Frequency of preceding class) + (Frequency of modal class - Frequency of succeeding class)) × Class width

nodes.name: Modified Accelerated Cost Recovery System (MACRS)
aliases: 修正加速成本回收系统
nodes.definition: MACRS is the U.S. tax depreciation system that assigns accelerated depreciation rates to asset classes over specified recovery periods under the General Depreciation System (GDS) or the Alternative Depreciation System (ADS). Annual depreciation expense is determined by applying IRS-prescribed MACRS percentages to the asset's cost basis for each year of the recovery period.

nodes.name: Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI)
nodes.definition: Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI) is an income measure derived from Adjusted Gross Income (AGI) by adding back specific exclusions and deductions. It is used to determine eligibility for tax benefits, credits, deductions, and program qualifications (e.g., IRA contribution eligibility and certain premium tax credits).

nodes.name: Modified Dietz Return
nodes.definition: The Modified Dietz Return is a money-weighted performance measure that approximates the internal rate of return by accounting for the timing and magnitude of external cash flows. It weights each cash flow by the fraction of the period it is invested, providing a robust estimate of portfolio performance over a specific interval when full daily valuation is unavailable.

formulas.source_formula: Modified Dietz Return = (Ending Market Value - Beginning Market Value - Weighted Cash Flows) ÷ (Beginning Market Value + Weighted Cash Flows)

nodes.name: Modified Duration
nodes.definition: Modified duration is a measure of the sensitivity of a bond's price to changes in interest rates, calculated from Macaulay duration and yield, used to estimate the percentage change in bond price when interest rates change.

formulas.source_formula: Modified Duration = Macaulay Duration ÷ (1 + Yield to Maturity)
Modified Duration = Macaulay Duration ÷ (1 + Periodic Yield)
Modified Duration = Macaulay Duration ÷ (1 + Yield Rate)

nodes.name: Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR)
nodes.definition: Modified Internal Rate of Return (MIRR) is a capital budgeting metric that measures the annualized return of a project by compounding positive cash inflows at a specified reinvestment rate and discounting negative cash outflows at a finance (cost of capital) rate, thereby addressing the reinvestment assumption and multiple-solution issues present in IRR.

operands.metric: Future Value of Positive Cash Flows
Absolute Present Value of Negative Cash Flows

formulas.source_formula: MIRR = (Future Value of Positive Cash Flows ÷ Absolute Present Value of Negative Cash Flows)^(1 ÷ (Number of Periods - 1)) - 1

nodes.name: Monetary Base
nodes.definition: Monetary base refers to the total amount of currency issued by the central bank, which serves as the foundation for the money supply. It primarily consists of cash held by the public (banknotes and coins) and reserve deposits held by commercial banks at the central bank (including required reserves and excess reserves). It is the starting point for credit creation and money multiplication within the entire financial system.

formulas.source_formula: Monetary Base = Currency in Circulation + Required Reserves + Excess Reserves
Monetary Base = Currency in Circulation + Total Reserve Deposits

nodes.name: Monetary Payment Amount
nodes.definition: Monetary payment amount refers to the total cash actually paid or receivable/payable in monetary form (including cash, electronic transfers, mobile payments, etc.) in economic transactions, which directly reflects the actual fund flow situation in the transaction.

nodes.name: Money Factor
nodes.definition: Money factor is the lease finance charge rate expressed as a monthly decimal, widely used in vehicle and equipment leasing to determine rent charges. It is commonly derived from the annual percentage rate (APR, in percent) by dividing by 2,400.

formulas.source_formula: Money Factor = Lease Charge ÷ ((Capitalized Cost + Residual Value) × Lease Term)

nodes.name: Money Flow
nodes.definition: Money flow measures the dollar value of traded shares over a period by multiplying trading volume by the typical price (the average of high, low, and closing prices). It is a core input to money flow-based indicators (e.g., Money Flow Index) and helps assess buying versus selling pressure.

formulas.source_formula: Money Flow = Trading Volume × Typical Price

nodes.name: Money Flow Index
nodes.definition: The Money Flow Index (MFI) is a volume-weighted momentum oscillator that uses price and volume data to measure buying and selling pressure, oscillating between 0 and 100 to identify potential overbought and oversold conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Money Flow Multiplier = ((Close - Low) - (High - Close)) ÷ (High - Low)

nodes.name: Money Flow Ratio
aliases: Ratio of Positive to Negative Money Flow
nodes.definition: Money Flow Ratio is the quotient of total positive money flow divided by total total negative money flow over a specified period. It measures buying pressure relative to selling pressure and is a core component used to compute the Money Flow Index (MFI), typically over 14 periods.

formulas.source_formula: Money Flow Ratio = Positive Money Flow ÷ Negative Money Flow

nodes.name: Money Illusion
nodes.definition: Money illusion is the behavioral tendency to evaluate wealth and prices in nominal terms rather than real terms, neglecting the effects of inflation on purchasing power. Adjusting nominal amounts to real values helps analysts and decision-makers compare values across time consistently by removing inflation effects.

nodes.name: Money Market Yield
nodes.definition: Money market yield is an annualized yield measure for short-term discount securities, computed by scaling the holding period yield to a 360-day year. It estimates the investor's return based on the purchase price, face value, and time to maturity, and is commonly used for Treasury bills and other highly liquid money market instruments.

formulas.source_formula: Money Market Yield = ((Face Value - Purchase Price) ÷ Purchase Price) × (360 ÷ Time to Maturity)
Money Market Yield = Bank Discount Yield × (Face Value ÷ Purchase Price)

nodes.name: Money Multiplier
nodes.definition: The money multiplier quantifies the maximum potential expansion of the money supply in a fractional-reserve banking system for a given reserve requirement ratio. It is defined as the inverse of the reserve requirement ratio, indicating how many units of total money can be created per unit of reserves.

formulas.source_formula: Money Multiplier = 1 ÷ Reserve Requirement Ratio

nodes.name: Money Purchase Plan Contribution
aliases: 固定金额购买养老金计划缴费额
nodes.definition: Money Purchase Plan Contribution represents the maximum permissible employer contribution to a money purchase pension plan for a participant, determined as the lesser of a fixed percentage of eligible employee compensation and the annual IRS dollar contribution limit, ensuring compliance with defined contribution plan regulations.

formulas.source_formula: Money Purchase Plan Contribution = min(Employee Compensation × Percentage Limit, Contribution Limit)
Money Supply = Nominal GDP ÷ Velocity of Money

nodes.name: Money Supply Reserve Multiplier
nodes.definition: The money supply reserve multiplier quantifies the maximum potential expansion of the money supply resulting from an additional unit of reserves in a fractional-reserve banking system. Under the simple model with no currency drain and no excess reserves, it equals the reciprocal of the required reserve ratio, indicating how changes in reserve requirements affect money supply growth.

formulas.source_formula: Money Supply Reserve Multiplier = 1 ÷ Required Reserve Ratio (RRR)

nodes.name: Money Supply–Velocity Product (MV)
aliases: 货币供给与流通速度乘积
nodes.definition: The Money Supply–Velocity Product (MV) represents nominal money expenditure derived from the equation of exchange, defined as the product of the money supply (M) and the velocity of money (V). In monetarist theory, MV is used to assess aggregate demand and the price level, with velocity often treated as relatively stable in the short run.

formulas.source_formula: Money Supply–Velocity Product (MV) = Money Supply × Velocity of Money

nodes.name: Money Wage Rate
nodes.definition: Money wage rate refers to the amount of wages expressed in monetary terms that a worker receives per unit of time (such as per hour, day, week, or month), serving as a fundamental unit for measuring labor compensation efficiency.

nodes.name: Money-Weighted Rate of Return
aliases: Internal Rate of Return (IRR) for cash flows
nodes.definition: Money-weighted rate of return is an application of the internal rate of return (IRR) used to measure investment performance by considering the timing of cash flows. It is calculated as the discount rate that equates the present value of all cash inflows to the present value of all cash outflows, and is a key concept in professional examinations such as the CFA.

formulas.source_formula: Moneyness Spread = Underlying Asset Price - Strike Price

nodes.name: Monte Carlo Simulation
nodes.definition: Monte Carlo simulation is a stochastic modeling technique used to project possible future asset price paths by repeatedly sampling random shocks under specified statistical assumptions. In finance, a common implementation assumes geometric Brownian motion, where returns are normally distributed with constant drift and volatility, producing lognormally distributed prices.

nodes.name: Monte Carlo Simulation (Investment Value)
nodes.definition: Monte Carlo simulation is a stochastic modeling technique used to forecast the distribution of possible investment outcomes by repeatedly compounding random period returns. In this context, the investment's value evolves by multiplying the initial value by successive (1 + period return) terms over a specified time horizon, with each return drawn from a specified distribution characterized by an expected rate of return and volatility.

nodes.name: Monthly Aggregate Deductible per Employee
aliases: 总体止损每人每月免赔额
nodes.definition: The monthly aggregate deductible per employee in an aggregate stop-loss insurance arrangement represents the per-member-per-month threshold of claim costs that must be borne by the employer before aggregate stop-loss coverage begins to reimburse. It is typically calculated by applying the stop-loss attachment multiplier (aggregate attachment factor) to the estimated claims per employee per month.

operands.metric: Estimated Claims per Employee per Month

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Aggregate Deductible per Employee = Estimated Claims per Employee per Month × Stop-Loss Attachment Multiplier

nodes.name: Monthly Amortizing Payment
nodes.definition: The fixed monthly payment amount required to fully amortize a loan over its term, covering both principal repayment and interest charges.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Annual MIP = Annual MIP ÷ 12
Monthly Base Pay = Base Pay × (1 + ECI Increase)

nodes.name: Monthly Collection Amount
nodes.definition: Monthly Collection Amount refers to the total amount of cash or cash equivalents actually recovered by a business or individual within a calendar month or accounting month through various means (such as sales collection, rental income, return of investment principal or earnings, etc.). It is a key metric for measuring monthly cash inflow.

nodes.name: Monthly Depreciation Charge
nodes.definition: Monthly depreciation charge represents the portion of an asset's cost allocated as expense each month under the straight-line method, reflecting the systematic allocation of the depreciable base over the asset's useful life.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Depreciation = Annual Depreciation ÷ 12

nodes.name: Monthly Depreciation Expense
nodes.definition: Monthly depreciation expense refers to the amount of depreciation cost allocated evenly to each month over the estimated useful life of a fixed asset, based on its cost (net of estimated residual value) in accordance with accounting standards. It is a significant item in calculating a company's monthly costs and profits.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Homeowners Insurance = Annual Homeowners Insurance ÷ 12

nodes.name: Monthly Income
nodes.definition: Monthly income refers to the total sum of all cash or cash equivalents received by an individual or household from various sources within a calendar month. It typically includes wages, bonuses, allowances, benefits, investment returns, rental income, etc., and is a core indicator for measuring the short-term financial inflow status of an individual or household.

nodes.name: Monthly Installment Payment
nodes.definition: Monthly installment payment refers to the fixed amount paid each month to repay an amortized loan over a specified term, calculated using the annuity formula that accounts for principal and interest.

nodes.name: Monthly Interest Payment
nodes.definition: Monthly interest payment is the portion of a fixed-rate mortgage payment that covers only the interest charged on the outstanding loan balance for that month, calculated by applying the monthly interest rate to the remaining principal.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Interest = Average Daily Balance × Daily Periodic Rate × Billing Cycle Days

nodes.name: Monthly Interest Rate
nodes.definition: Monthly interest rate refers to the interest rate calculated based on a one-month interest accrual period, i.e., the ratio of the interest amount within one month to the principal of a deposit or loan, typically expressed in parts per thousand of the principal. It is a crucial compound indicator in financial calculations that connects the annual interest rate and the daily interest rate.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Interest Rate = Daily Interest Rate × 30
Monthly Interest Rate = Annual Nominal Interest Rate ÷ 12
Monthly Interest Rate = Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12
supporting_source_formulas: Monthly Interest Rate = Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Rate = Fully Indexed Rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100
Monthly Interest Rate = Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100
Monthly Interest-Only Payment = Loan Amount × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12)

nodes.name: Monthly Lease Payment
nodes.definition: Monthly lease payment is the periodic cash outflow due under a lease contract, typically composed of the depreciation portion (the asset's value consumed over the lease term) and a financing charge based on the lease rate (money factor), allocated on a monthly basis.

nodes.name: Monthly MBS Payout
nodes.definition: The monthly payout of a mortgage-backed security (MBS) represents the cash flow distributed to investors each month, comprising both interest and scheduled principal repayment, calculated using the standard amortizing-loan formula.

nodes.name: Monthly Mortgage Payment
nodes.definition: Monthly mortgage payment is the fixed periodic payment on a fixed-rate mortgage that amortizes the loan principal and interest over the loan term. It is calculated using the annuity payment formula based on the principal, monthly interest rate, and total number of payments, and typically excludes taxes, insurance, and other fees.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Mortgage Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Term Months))
Monthly Mortgage Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Total Number of Payments))
Monthly Mortgage Payment = Loan Amount × Monthly Interest Rate ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^-Number of Payments)
Monthly Mortgage Payment = Principal × Monthly Interest Rate ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^-Number of Payments)
Monthly Mortgage Payment = Principal × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12)) ^ -(Years × 12))
supporting_source_formulas: Monthly Mortgage Payment = Principal × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12)) ^ -(Years × 12))
Monthly Mortgage Payment = Principal × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 100 ÷ 12))^- (Years × 12))

nodes.name: Monthly Payment
nodes.definition: Monthly payment refers to the fixed periodic amount required to amortize a loan with a constant interest rate over a specified number of months. It is computed by converting the annual interest rate to a monthly rate and applying the level-payment annuity formula, assuming equal monthly installments and monthly compounding.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Periods))
Monthly Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ (-Number of Payments))
supporting_source_formulas: Monthly Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ (-Number of Payments))
Monthly Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Number of Payments))
Monthly Payment = Principal × Monthly Interest Rate ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Number of Payments))

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Payment = (Loan Amount × Monthly Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Rate) ^ (-Number of Payments))
supporting_source_formulas: Monthly Payment = (Loan Amount × Monthly Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Rate) ^ (-Number of Payments))
Monthly Payment = Loan Amount × Monthly Interest Rate ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Number of Payments))

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Payment = (Premium × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 − (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(−Total Periods))
Monthly Payment = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate × (1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ Number of Payments) ÷ ((1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ Number of Payments - 1)
Monthly Payment = (Loan Amount × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12)) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12)) ^ -(Loan Term Years × 12))
Monthly Payment = (Principal × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12)) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12))^(-Total Payments))
Monthly Payment = Principal × (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12))^(-Term Months))
Monthly Payment (5-6 Hybrid ARM) = Principal × [(Fully Indexed Rate ÷ 12) × (1 + Fully Indexed Rate ÷ 12)^(Loan Term Months)] ÷ [(1 + Fully Indexed Rate ÷ 12)^(Loan Term Months) - 1]

nodes.name: Monthly Payment (Amortized Loan)
nodes.definition: Monthly Payment (Amortized Loan) is the fixed periodic installment required to fully repay a loan over its term, calculated using the monthly interest rate derived from the annual interest rate and the total number of payments, reflecting the time value of money and the amortization structure.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Payment = Loan Amount × (Monthly Interest Rate × (1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ Number of Payments) ÷ ((1 + Monthly Interest Rate) ^ Number of Payments - 1)
Monthly Payout = Years of Service × Benefit per Year
Monthly Periodic Interest Rate = Annual Nominal Interest Rate ÷ 12
Monthly Periodic Rate = Purchase Annual Percentage Rate (APR) ÷ 12
Monthly Principal and Interest = Principal ÷ Number of Payments
Monthly Principal and Interest = (Principal × Monthly Interest Rate) ÷ (1 - (1 + Monthly Interest Rate)^(-Number of Payments))
Monthly Property Tax = Annual Property Tax ÷ 12

nodes.name: Monthly Recurring Revenue
nodes.definition: Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) is the predictable, subscription-based revenue a company earns each month, calculated by multiplying the number of paying users by the average revenue per user. It is a key metric for assessing the momentum and stability of subscription businesses.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly Recurring Revenue (MRR) = Number of Users × Average Revenue per User (ARPU)

nodes.name: Monthly Return
nodes.definition: Monthly return refers to the ratio of the profit earned by an investment asset or portfolio within one month to the initial investment principal, commonly used to measure the short-term profitability of an asset.

formulas.source_formula: Months Early = (Full Retirement Age - Claiming Age) × 12
Months Remaining = Term Months - ((Year - 1) × 12)

nodes.name: Months Since Issuance
nodes.definition: Months Since Issuance refers to the number of complete months that have elapsed from the official issuance date of a security (such as stocks or bonds) to a specific calculation date. It is a fundamental time-based data point calculated from specific dates, used to measure the time span since the security's issuance.

nodes.name: Months of Repurchase
nodes.definition: Months of Repurchase refers to the weighted average length of time, expressed in months, during which repurchased shares are no longer outstanding, used to calculate the weighted average number of common shares outstanding. It is an intermediate metric calculated from share repurchase transaction data (such as the number of shares repurchased and the timing of repurchases), rather than a raw figure directly obtained from financial statements.

nodes.name: Months of Shares in Circulation
nodes.definition: Months of Shares in Circulation refers to the total duration, typically measured in months, during which a stock has been freely tradable from the date of its initial public offering or the lifting of trading restrictions to the current date. It is a time-based fundamental data point, not a financial metric derived from calculations using financial statement line items.

nodes.name: Morbidity Rate
nodes.definition: Morbidity rate measures the frequency of new cases of a specified illness or disease in a defined population over a given period, typically expressed as a percentage. It is widely used in public health and actuarial analysis to assess population health risk, inform health insurance pricing, and support reserving and risk management decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Morbidity Rate = (New Cases ÷ Population) × 100

nodes.name: Mortgage Interest Deduction
nodes.definition: Mortgage Interest Deduction is a tax provision allowing taxpayers to deduct interest paid on qualified residence mortgage debt, subject to statutory debt limits based on acquisition date and filing status. If total mortgage debt exceeds the applicable limit, the deductible interest is proportionally reduced in line with the ratio of the debt limit to the mortgage debt.

nodes.name: Mortgage Payment Breakdown
nodes.definition: Mortgage payment breakdown refers to the allocation of a periodic mortgage payment into interest and principal components. For each month, the interest portion is calculated on the outstanding principal balance using the periodic interest rate, while the principal portion equals the scheduled payment minus the interest. This breakdown underpins loan amortization schedules and helps borrowers understand how their payments reduce the loan balance over time.

nodes.name: Mortgage Rate Lock Float Down
aliases: 抵押贷款利率锁定下调
按揭利率锁定浮动下调
nodes.definition: A mortgage rate lock float down is an option that allows a borrower who has locked a mortgage rate to reduce (float down) to a lower available rate before closing if market rates decline. The economic value of exercising the float down equals the reduction in total scheduled principal-and-interest payments over the loan term due to the lower rate, minus the float-down fee.

nodes.name: Mortgage Recast
nodes.definition: Mortgage recast is a process by which a lender recalculates the amortization schedule of an existing fixed-rate mortgage after a substantial principal reduction. The interest rate and maturity typically remain unchanged, but the monthly payment is lowered based on the reduced principal and the remaining term.

nodes.name: Mortgage Servicing Rights (MSR)
nodes.definition: Mortgage servicing rights (MSR) represent an intangible asset that entitles the holder to service mortgage loans and collect servicing fees and ancillary income. The value of MSRs is typically measured as the present value of expected servicing cash flows, adjusted for anticipated prepayments and discounted at an appropriate rate to reflect time value of money and risk.

nodes.name: Most Likely Future Cash Flows of an Asset
nodes.definition: Refers to the net amount of a series of cash inflows and outflows that an asset is most likely to generate during a forecast period under normal operating conditions. It serves as the core forecast data for future cash conditions when assessing asset value, conducting impairment testing, and making investment decisions.

nodes.name: Most Recent Dividend
nodes.definition: The most recent dividend refers to the per-share cash dividend that a company has actually declared and paid to shareholders in its latest period (typically the previous payment cycle). It is a known historical fact and serves as the foundational starting point for future dividend forecasts and stock valuation calculations.

nodes.name: Movable Furniture
nodes.definition: Movable furniture refers to furniture assets purchased by an enterprise to meet daily office or operational needs, which can be relatively easily moved or rearranged, such as office desks and chairs, filing cabinets, sofas, etc. In accounting, it is typically classified as part of fixed assets, and its initial value (original cost) is primarily confirmed directly based on original documents such as purchase invoices.

nodes.name: Moving Average
nodes.definition: Moving Average is a statistical calculation used to analyze data points by creating a series of averages of different subsets of the full data set, commonly applied to stock prices to smooth out short-term fluctuations and identify trends.

formulas.source_formula: Simple Moving Average = Sum of Prices over Period ÷ Period

nodes.name: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD)
aliases: 指数平滑异同移动平均线
nodes.definition: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) is a trend-following momentum indicator that measures the relationship between two Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs) of a security’s price. The MACD line is calculated as the short-period EMA minus the long-period EMA, typically using the 12-period and 26-period EMAs, respectively.

formulas.source_formula: MACD = Short-period Exponential Moving Average (EMA) - Long-period Exponential Moving Average (EMA)

nodes.name: Moving Average Cost
aliases: 移动加权平均单位成本
nodes.definition: Moving average cost refers to the unit cost recalculated after each purchase based on the total cost and total quantity of inventory, under the perpetual inventory system using the moving average method for inventory issuance valuation. It reflects the latest cost information, is applicable to continuous and dynamic cost flow assumptions, and is used in relevant asset valuation techniques.

operands.metric: Actual Cost of Existing Inventory on Hand
Quantity of Existing Inventory on Hand

formulas.source_formula: Moving Average Cost = (Actual Cost of Existing Inventory on Hand + Actual Cost of Current Purchase) ÷ (Quantity of Existing Inventory on Hand + Quantity of Current Purchase)

nodes.name: Moving Average Envelope
nodes.definition: A moving average envelope is a technical analysis indicator that plots two bands at fixed percentage distances above and below a simple moving average (SMA) to define a dynamic price range, helping identify potential overbought and oversold conditions and assess trend strength.

nodes.name: Multi-Factor Model
nodes.definition: A multi-factor model estimates a security's expected return as the sum of an intercept, the product of market beta and market return, the weighted contributions of multiple risk factors (each factor's beta times its return), and an idiosyncratic error term. It generalizes single-factor models like CAPM to capture broader sources of systematic risk.

nodes.name: Multimodal Transport
nodes.definition: In financial management, multimodal transport refers to the strategy of optimizing total transportation costs or time by combining two or more modes of transportation, commonly used in supply chain cost control and efficiency evaluation.

formulas.source_formula: Multimodal Transport = Benchmark Transportation Cost - Actual Multimodal Transport Cost
Multimodal Transport = Total Transportation Cost ÷ Transportation Distance
Multimodal Transport = Rail Freight Cost + Road Freight Cost + Sea Freight Cost

nodes.name: Multiple
nodes.definition: A multiple is a financial ratio calculated by dividing one valuation or performance metric by another, used to assess relative valuation and compare companies across peers or time periods (e.g., price-to-earnings, EV/EBITDA, EV/sales).

formulas.source_formula: Multiple = Numerator ÷ Denominator

nodes.name: Multiple Linear Regression
nodes.definition: Multiple Linear Regression (MLR) estimates the relationship between a dependent variable and multiple independent variables using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). In finance and econometrics, it is used to quantify how predictors (e.g., macroeconomic indicators, firm characteristics) jointly explain outcomes such as asset returns, sales, or costs by minimizing the sum of squared residuals.

nodes.name: Multiplier
nodes.definition: The multiplier measures the change in equilibrium national income resulting from a one-unit change in autonomous expenditure. In the simple Keynesian model (closed economy without taxes or other leakages), the multiplier equals 1 divided by 1 minus the marginal propensity to consume (MPC), indicating how initial spending propagates through the economy via induced consumption.

formulas.source_formula: Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 - Marginal Propensity to Consume)
Price-to-Earnings Ratio = Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share

nodes.name: Multiplier Effect
nodes.definition: The multiplier effect is the ratio of the change in aggregate income (output) to the change in autonomous spending that initiated it. It measures how an injection or withdrawal of spending (such as investment or government expenditure) amplifies through the economy, indicating the effectiveness of fiscal actions or investment in influencing total economic activity.

formulas.source_formula: MPC Multiplier = 1 ÷ (1 - Marginal Propensity to Consume)
Multiplier Effect = Change in Income ÷ Change in Spending

nodes.name: Mutual Fund
nodes.definition: A mutual fund is an investment fund that pools money from numerous investors to purchase securities, commonly used in the United States, Canada, and India. Similar structures in Europe are SICAVs, and in the UK, OEICs. Mutual funds are classified by primary investment objectives (e.g., money market, bond, equity, hybrid) and management style (active or passive). Their advantages include risk diversification, strong liquidity, professional management, and economies of scale, but they incur related fees and expenses. Mutual funds are regulated and must disclose performance, fees, and holdings.

formulas.source_formula: Mutual Fund = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: My Balance
nodes.definition: My balance typically refers to the total remaining funds in an individual's or enterprise's bank account, e-wallet, or other financial account at a specific point in time (e.g., at the time of inquiry). It reflects the amount of funds available for use or investment after deducting all expenditures and fees.

nodes.name: NAV Return
nodes.definition: NAV return measures the percentage change in a fund's net asset value (NAV) over a period, calculated as the ending NAV relative to the beginning NAV. It is commonly used to assess mutual fund and ETF performance and typically excludes distributions, fees, and other cash flows unless explicitly incorporated.

formulas.source_formula: NAV Return (%) = (Final NAV - Initial NAV) ÷ Initial NAV × 100%
NDF Settlement Amount = (NDF Rate - Spot Rate) × Notional Amount

nodes.name: NIIP to GDP Ratio
aliases: Net International Investment Position to GDP Ratio
净国际投资头寸占GDP比率
国际投资头寸净额占GDP比率
nodes.definition: The NIIP to GDP Ratio expresses a country's Net International Investment Position as a percentage of its Gross Domestic Product, indicating the relative size of its net external asset or liability position compared to the economy.

formulas.source_formula: NIIP to GDP Ratio (%) = Net International Investment Position ÷ Gross Domestic Product × 100

nodes.name: NIIP to Total Financial Assets Ratio
aliases: Net International Investment Position to Total Financial Assets Ratio
净国际投资头寸/金融资产比率
净国际投资头寸占金融资产比率
nodes.definition: The NIIP to Total Financial Assets Ratio measures the Net International Investment Position as a percentage of a country's total financial assets, indicating external wealth relative to the size and depth of domestic financial markets.

formulas.source_formula: NIIP to Total Financial Assets Ratio = Net International Investment Position (NIIP) ÷ Total Financial Assets × 100

nodes.name: NYSE Composite Index
aliases: 纽约证券交易所综合指数
nodes.definition: The NYSE Composite Index is a stock market index that encompasses all common stocks listed on the New York Stock Exchange, including American Depositary Receipts, Real Estate Investment Trusts, tracking stocks, and stocks of foreign listed companies. The index covers all ten industry sectors of the Industry Classification Benchmark and is calculated using a free-float market capitalization weighting methodology.

nodes.name: Naked Call Breakeven Point
aliases: 裸卖出看涨期权盈亏平衡价
裸卖出看涨期权盈亏平衡点
nodes.definition: The naked call breakeven point is the stock price at which a call option writer who is not covered by the underlying asset (naked) neither makes a profit nor incurs a loss. It equals the call option's strike price plus the premium received, excluding transaction costs and taxes.

formulas.source_formula: Naked Call Breakeven Point = Strike Price + Premium Received

nodes.name: Naked Call Loss
nodes.definition: Naked Call Loss represents the per-unit monetary loss incurred by a writer of an uncovered call option when the underlying price exceeds the strike price, net of the premium received. The loss is zero when the underlying price is at or below the strike and increases linearly above the strike, reflecting the strategy’s theoretically unlimited risk.

nodes.name: Naked Call Profit
nodes.definition: Naked call profit refers to the profit or loss realized by an option writer from an uncovered (naked) short call position at expiration. It equals the premium received minus the call’s intrinsic value, if any, when the underlying price exceeds the strike price. The writer’s downside is theoretically unlimited as the underlying price rises.

nodes.name: Nanny Tax
nodes.definition: Nanny tax refers to the U.S. federal payroll and unemployment taxes that a household employer must withhold and pay on wages paid to a household employee, primarily including Social Security and Medicare (FICA) taxes for both the employee and employer shares, and Federal Unemployment Tax (FUTA). It typically excludes state unemployment or other state/local taxes.

nodes.name: Nasdaq Composite Index
nodes.definition: The Nasdaq Composite Index is a market capitalization-weighted stock market index that covers nearly all stocks listed on the Nasdaq Stock Exchange, with a significant weighting towards information technology companies. The index is calculated by summing the product of each constituent security's closing price and its index share, then dividing by a divisor for scaling.

nodes.name: National Average Wage Index
nodes.definition: The National Average Wage Index (NAWI), also known as the Average Wage Index (AWI), measures the average wages of U.S. workers covered by Social Security for a given year. It is published by the Social Security Administration and is used to index past earnings, adjust benefit computation parameters (such as bend points), and inform contribution and benefit bases. The index for the current year is typically derived by applying the percentage change in average wages to the prior year's index.

formulas.source_formula: NAWI-Indexed Earnings = Original Earnings × Wage Indexing Factor
National Average Wage Index (Current Year) = National Average Wage Index (Previous Year) × (1 + Percentage Change in Average Wages)

nodes.name: National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO)
nodes.definition: The National Best Bid and Offer (NBBO) is the consolidated quote across all U.S. exchanges and eligible venues that displays the highest available bid price and the lowest available ask (offer) price for a security at a given moment, representing the tightest composite bid-ask spread and informing best execution and trade-through protections.

nodes.name: National Disposable Income
nodes.definition: National Disposable Income refers to the total income available to all resident units (including households, enterprises, and the government) of a country or region within a given period (usually one year) after primary and secondary distribution, which can ultimately be used for final consumption and savings. It reflects the total amount of economic resources that the nation can freely allocate for consumption and accumulation.

nodes.name: Natural Increase in Liabilities
nodes.definition: Natural increase in liabilities typically refers to the automatic or endogenous growth in the amount of a company's liabilities resulting from the expansion of business scale or changes in operational needs during daily business activities, rather than from active financing decisions (such as new borrowings). For example, as sales revenue increases, operating liabilities such as accounts payable and deferred revenue may increase correspondingly, and this incremental amount can be considered a natural increase in liabilities.

nodes.name: Natural Logarithm
nodes.definition: The natural logarithm is a logarithmic function with the mathematical constant e (approximately equal to 2.71828) as its base. In finance, it is commonly used for non-linear transformation of financial indicators to process growth rates, volatility, or construct specific models (such as Rho value calculation in option pricing models).

nodes.name: Natural Real Interest Rate
nodes.definition: The natural real interest rate refers to the level of the real interest rate when the economy is in an ideal state of full employment and price stability, and savings and investment are in equilibrium. It excludes the effects of inflation, reflects the true cost and scarcity of capital, and serves as an important reference benchmark for central banks in formulating monetary policy and for economists in analyzing economic conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Natural Real Interest Rate = (1 + Nominal Interest Rate) ÷ (1 + Inflation Rate) - 1
Natural Real Interest Rate ≈ Nominal Interest Rate - Inflation Rate

nodes.name: Necessary Equipment Setup Time per Unit
Neckline
nodes.definition: The neckline is a key chart level in technical analysis that connects swing points within patterns such as head and shoulders or inverse head and shoulders. It serves as the breakout confirmation level and is often used to derive a projected price target by adding the pattern’s height to the neckline after a breakout.

nodes.name: Needs Approach
nodes.definition: The needs approach is a life insurance planning method that determines the required amount of coverage by summing immediate cash needs at death and the present value of future income needed to support dependents.

nodes.name: Negative Amortization
nodes.definition: Negative amortization occurs when a loan's periodic payment is insufficient to cover accrued interest, causing the unpaid interest to be added to the outstanding principal balance. This increases the loan balance over time until payments exceed interest or the amortization schedule changes.

nodes.name: Negative Arbitrage
nodes.definition: Negative arbitrage is a fixed‑income condition, common in advance refundings, where the yield earned on escrowed investments is lower than the coupon rate on the outstanding bonds. This negative carry increases the economic cost of refinancing unless escrow earnings are sufficient to cover the higher interest payments on the refunded debt or are supplemented by additional funds.

nodes.name: Negative Arbitrage Cost
nodes.definition: Negative arbitrage cost is the opportunity cost incurred when the yield earned on invested bond proceeds is lower than the interest cost on the issued bonds. It quantifies the rate differential applied to the principal for a consistent time period.

formulas.source_formula: Negative Arbitrage Cost = Principal × (Issued Rate - Invested Rate)

nodes.name: Negative Bond Yield
nodes.definition: Negative bond yield refers to an annualized percentage yield on a bond that is less than zero, indicating the investor expects to receive back less, on an annualized basis, than the amount invested when accounting for coupon income and redemption at face value. This simplified annualized measure aggregates coupon income and capital gain or loss relative to the purchase price over the holding period to maturity, excluding taxes, inflation adjustments, fees, and reinvestment effects.

nodes.name: Negative Carry
nodes.definition: Negative carry is the amount by which the financing or holding cost of an investment exceeds the income generated by that investment over the same period. It indicates that the position costs more to maintain than it earns, commonly arising when the cost of funds (e.g., borrowing rate) is higher than the asset's yield.

formulas.source_formula: Negative Carry = Cost of Funds - Income Earned

nodes.name: Negative Convexity
nodes.definition: Negative convexity is a property of certain fixed-income securities, typically those with embedded call or prepayment options, where the price-yield relationship curves downward. As yields decline, effective duration shortens and price appreciation is dampened; as yields rise, price declines can be larger than predicted by duration alone. Practitioners refine price-change estimates using a convexity adjustment in conjunction with duration for small yield changes.

nodes.name: Negative Directional Indicator (-DI)
nodes.definition: The Negative Directional Indicator (-DI) is a component of Welles Wilder’s Directional Movement System that quantifies the strength of downward price movement. It is computed by scaling Smoothed Negative Directional Movement (-DM) by the Average True Range (ATR) and expressing the result as a percentage, typically over a 14-period lookback. -DI is commonly used alongside +DI and ADX to assess trend direction and strength.

formulas.source_formula: Negative Directional Indicator (-DI) = (Smoothed Negative Directional Movement (-DM) ÷ Average True Range (ATR)) × 100

nodes.name: Negative Equity
nodes.definition: Negative equity refers to the condition in which the outstanding mortgage balance exceeds the current market value of the property. It quantifies the shortfall by measuring the portion of debt not covered by the property's value, indicating the property is underwater.

nodes.name: Negative Gap
nodes.definition: Negative gap is an asset-liability management measure indicating that interest-sensitive liabilities exceed interest-sensitive assets over a given repricing horizon. It reflects a liability-sensitive position in which net interest income typically decreases if market interest rates rise and increases if rates fall.

formulas.source_formula: Negative Gap = Interest-Sensitive Liabilities - Interest-Sensitive Assets

nodes.name: Negative Goodwill
nodes.definition: Negative goodwill, also known as a bargain purchase gain, arises in a business combination when the fair value of the acquired assets exceeds the purchase price (consideration transferred). After required reassessments, the excess is recognized as a gain in profit or loss at the acquisition date under acquisition accounting.

formulas.source_formula: Negative Goodwill = Fair Value of Acquired Assets - Purchase Price

nodes.name: Negative Income Tax (NIT)
nodes.definition: Negative Income Tax (NIT) is a tax-transfer mechanism in which individuals with income above a specified threshold pay tax on the excess at a marginal tax rate, while individuals with income below the threshold receive a cash benefit (negative tax) that declines with income at a benefit reduction rate. The resulting tax amount can be positive (tax liability) or negative (benefit/transfer).

nodes.name: Negative Return
nodes.definition: Negative return refers to a loss on an investment or portfolio over a period, occurring when the total ending value is less than the total initial investment. It is measured as the aggregate final value minus the aggregate initial investment; a negative result indicates a negative return.

formulas.source_formula: Negative Return = Total Final Value - Total Initial Investment
Negative Return = Final Value - Initial Value

nodes.name: Negative Volume Index
nodes.definition: The Negative Volume Index (NVI) is a cumulative technical indicator that adjusts only on days when current trading volume is lower than the previous day's volume, reflecting price changes influenced by low-volume trading activity.

nodes.name: Net Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: Net accounts receivable refers to the amount of a company's total accounts receivable after deducting the allowance for doubtful accounts. It reflects the expected realizable value of accounts receivable and is an important indicator for assessing the quality of current assets and operational efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Net Accounts Receivable = Total Accounts Receivable - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

nodes.name: Net Accounts Receivable at Period End
nodes.definition: Net accounts receivable at period end refers to the net amount of accounts receivable after deducting the allowance for doubtful accounts at the end of an accounting period, reflecting the estimated collectible value of receivables. It is a current asset item on the balance sheet, calculated from the debit balance of the accounts receivable subsidiary ledger, the debit balance of the advance receipts subsidiary ledger, and the ending balance of the allowance for doubtful accounts. It is commonly used in financial ratio analysis, such as the accounts receivable turnover ratio.

operands.metric: Debit Balance of Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger
Debit Balance of Advance Receipts Subsidiary Ledger
Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

formulas.source_formula: Net Accounts Receivable at Period End = Debit Balance of Accounts Receivable Subsidiary Ledger + Debit Balance of Advance Receipts Subsidiary Ledger - Ending Balance of Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

nodes.name: Net Accounts Receivable of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Net accounts receivable of the previous period refers to the actual collectible amount of a company's total accounts receivable at the end of the last accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter), after deducting the corresponding allowance for doubtful accounts. It reflects the value of accounts receivable that the company actually possessed and expected to collect at the end of the previous period.

nodes.name: Net Amount at Risk
nodes.definition: Net Amount at Risk (NAR) is the portion of a life insurance policy's death benefit that exceeds the retention limit held by the primary insurer, reduced by any accumulated cash value. It represents the actual risk transferred to the reinsurer.

nodes.name: Net Asset Value
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value refers to the balance of owners' equity in an enterprise, calculated as total assets minus total liabilities, reflecting the economic benefits enjoyed by owners in the enterprise's assets. It includes components such as paid-in capital, capital reserves, surplus reserves, and undistributed profits.

nodes.name: Net Asset Value Increase
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value Increase is a composite metric representing the absolute increase in net asset value over a specific period. It is typically calculated by subtracting the beginning net asset value from the ending net asset value, or based on portfolio returns minus portfolio expenses. It is commonly used for performance evaluation of investment funds such as hedge funds.

operands.metric: Net Asset Value at Period End

formulas.source_formula: Net Asset Value Increase = Ending Net Asset Value - Beginning Net Asset Value
Net Asset Value Increase = Portfolio Returns - Portfolio Expenses

nodes.name: Net Asset Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value Per Share is the ratio of shareholders' equity to the total number of shares outstanding, reflecting the present asset value owned by each share. It is a key indicator for measuring a company's financial foundation and valuation level, commonly used in valuation techniques, intrinsic value analysis, and price-to-book ratio comparisons.

formulas.source_formula: Net Asset Value per Share (NAVPS) = Net Asset Value ÷ Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Net Asset Value at Period End
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value at Period End refers to the net value of an enterprise's total assets minus total liabilities at the end of a specific accounting period, representing owners' equity, including paid-in capital, capital reserves, surplus reserves, and undistributed profits. In comprehensive strength evaluation, to reflect the enterprise's sustainable and stable development, the three-year year-end average is often used for calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Net Asset Value at Period End = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

operands.metric: Net Asset Value from Two Years Prior

formulas.source_formula: Net Asset Value at Period End = (Current Year-end Net Asset Value + Previous Year-end Net Asset Value + Net Asset Value from Two Years Prior) ÷ 3

nodes.name: Net Asset Value at Prior Year-End
aliases: Net Asset Value at the End of Previous Year
上年度期末所有者权益
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value at Prior Year-End refers to the book value of net assets owned by an enterprise at a specific point in time marking the end of the previous fiscal year (i.e., December 31 of the prior year). It is directly derived from the balance sheet at that date, representing the total amount of owners' equity, and reflects the total equity attributable to owners after deducting total liabilities from total assets as of the end of the prior year.

nodes.name: Net Asset Value at the End of the Year Two Years Ago
aliases: Closing Net Assets Two Years Prior
Net Asset Value at the End of Two Years Ago
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value at the End of the Year Two Years Ago refers to the book value of a company's total assets minus total liabilities at the close of the fiscal year (i.e., December 31) two years prior to the present date. It represents the total equity owned by shareholders at that specific historical point in time and is commonly used to calculate composite metrics such as the three-year average net asset value.

nodes.name: Net Asset Value from Two Years Prior
Net Asset Value of Fund
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value (NAV) of a fund refers to the value of the fund's total assets minus its total liabilities, reflecting the actual value of the fund at a specific point in time. It is typically expressed as the NAV per unit, representing the net asset value corresponding to each fund share.

nodes.name: Net Asset Value per Unit
nodes.definition: Net Asset Value per Unit represents the price of each unit in a unit trust or similar collective investment scheme, calculated by dividing the fund’s net asset value (NAV) by the number of units outstanding. It is used to value investor holdings and price subscriptions and redemptions, typically excluding transaction, management, and other fees.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Price = Net Asset Value (NAV) ÷ Units Outstanding

nodes.name: Net Assets
nodes.definition: Net assets refer to the net amount of total assets minus total liabilities, equivalent to owners' equity. It reflects the economic benefits that owners enjoy in the enterprise's assets, including components such as paid-in capital (or share capital), capital reserve, surplus reserve, and undistributed profits. It is a core indicator for measuring a company's financial soundness and the scale of its own capital.

formulas.source_formula: Net Assets = Total Assets - Total Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Net Assets = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Net Assets Employed
nodes.definition: Net assets employed refers to the residual equity net amount attributable to owners after deducting total liabilities from total assets. It is a core financial metric for measuring the scale of a company's own capital and serves as a key calculation basis in valuation models such as residual income.

formulas.source_formula: Net Assets Employed = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Net Beginning Operating Long-term Assets
aliases: Net Book Value of Operating Long-term Assets at Beginning of Period
经营性长期资产期初净额
经营长期资产期初净值
长期经营资产期初账面价值
nodes.definition: Net beginning operating long-term assets refers to the net book value of long-term assets (such as plants, equipment, land use rights, etc.) used for ongoing business activities at the start of an accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year or quarter), after deducting accumulated depreciation or amortization. It reflects the scale of capital invested in long-term business activities at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Net Book Value
nodes.definition: Net book value is the value of an asset as reported on the balance sheet, calculated as the original cost of the asset minus any accumulated depreciation, amortization, or impairment charges. It represents the current carrying amount of the asset after accounting for contra accounts.

formulas.source_formula: Net Book Value = Original Value - Contra Value

nodes.name: Net Book Value of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Net book value of fixed assets refers to the remaining value after subtracting the accumulated depreciation accrued up to the current accounting period from the original acquisition cost (original value) of the fixed assets. It reflects the current book value of fixed assets after deducting value impairment.

nodes.name: Net Borrowing
nodes.definition: Net borrowing refers to the net increase in a company's borrowings over a specific period, calculated as new borrowings minus debt repayments. It is a key adjustment item in the calculation of Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE) and is a composite metric, not a primary accounting line item.

formulas.source_formula: Net Borrowing = Total Debt at Period End - Total Debt at Period Start
Net Burn Rate = (Monthly Revenue - Cost of Goods Sold) - Total Monthly Operating Expenses
Net Capital = Net Short-term Capital + Net Long-term Capital

nodes.name: Net Capital Gain
nodes.definition: Net capital gain is the excess of total capital gains over total capital losses for a given period, computed as capital gains minus capital losses. It is commonly used in tax accounting and investment reporting to determine the taxable portion of gains from the disposal of capital assets.

formulas.source_formula: Net Capital Gain = Capital Gains - Capital Losses

nodes.name: Net Capital Gains
nodes.definition: Net capital gains represent the residual gain or loss after offsetting total capital gains with total capital losses within the same holding-period category (short-term or long-term), used to determine taxable capital gains or allowable capital losses for tax reporting.

nodes.name: Net Capital Gains Tax
aliases: Capital Gains Tax Payable (Net of Losses)
nodes.definition: Net capital gains tax is the tax payable on capital gains after offsetting allowable capital losses, calculated as the non-negative net capital gain multiplied by the applicable capital gains tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Net Capital Loss = Capital Loss - Capital Gain
Net Capital Loss = Capital Losses - Capital Gains

nodes.name: Net Cash
nodes.definition: Net cash represents the excess of a company's total cash over its total liabilities, indicating the residual cash available after settling all obligations. It is used to assess liquidity and short-term financial strength.

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash = Gross Cash - Cash Outflows
Net Cash = Total Cash - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Net cash flow refers to the balance of total cash and cash equivalents inflows minus total outflows over a specific period, reflecting the net cash income or expenditure of the enterprise during the period. It is a core indicator of the cash flow statement.

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow = Net Profit + Depreciation
Net Cash Flow = Income - Expenses

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow Available for Loan Repayment During Forecast Period
aliases: Net Cash Flow Available for Debt Service in Forecast Period
Projected Net Cash Flow for Loan Repayment
可用于还贷的预测净现金流
预测期偿债现金流净额
nodes.definition: Refers to the projected net cash amount, specifically expected to be available for repaying loan principal and interest, calculated by forecasting the cash inflows and outflows from a client's (typically a corporate entity's) future operating, investing, and financing activities over a defined future period (the forecast period) set by a bank or financial institution. It serves as a crucial basis for assessing a client's debt repayment capacity and determining loan limits.

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow by Period
nodes.definition: Net cash flow by period refers to the difference between the total inflow and total outflow of cash and cash equivalents during a specific accounting period (such as a year or a quarter). It reflects the net increase or decrease in cash ultimately generated by the enterprise through operating, investing, and financing activities during that period, serving as a core indicator for assessing the enterprise's liquidity, earnings quality, and financial health.

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow for the Period
aliases: Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents
nodes.definition: Net cash flow for the period refers to the net increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents of an enterprise during a specific accounting period. It is calculated as the difference between total cash inflows and total cash outflows, or reflected in the cash flow statement as the sum of net cash flows from operating, investing, and financing activities. It is a key financial metric for measuring the overall change in an enterprise's cash flow.

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow for the Period = Total Cash Inflows - Total Cash Outflows

operands.metric: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities
Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow for the Period = Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities + Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities + Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities
aliases: 筹资活动产生的现金流量净额
融资活动现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from financing activities refers to the difference between cash inflows generated from financing activities such as absorbing investments and obtaining borrowings, and cash outflows generated from financing activities such as repaying debts and distributing dividends. It reflects the net amount of cash obtained by an enterprise through financing activities over a specific period and is one of the three major net cash flow items in the cash flow statement.

operands.metric: Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities
Cash Paid for Dividends, Profit Distribution, or Interest Payments

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities = Cash Received from Capital Contributions + Cash Received from Borrowings + Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities - Cash Paid for Debt Repayment - Cash Paid for Dividends, Profit Distribution, or Interest Payments

operands.metric: Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities
Cash Paid for Dividends, Profit Distribution, or Interest Payments
Other Cash Paid Related to Financing Activities

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities = Cash Received from Capital Contributions + Cash Received from Borrowings + Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities - Cash Paid for Debt Repayment - Cash Paid for Dividends, Profit Distribution, or Interest Payments - Other Cash Paid Related to Financing Activities

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities for the Next Period
aliases: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities
下期筹资活动现金净流量
下期融资活动现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from financing activities for the next period refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by an enterprise in a future accounting period due to activities that cause changes in the scale and composition of its capital and debt (such as absorbing investments, obtaining borrowings, repaying debts, distributing dividends, etc.). This indicator is an important composite metric for predicting the future cash position of a company's financing activities.

operands.metric: Cash Received from Investments Absorbed in the Next Period
Cash Received from Borrowings in the Next Period
Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period
Cash Paid for Debt Repayment in the Next Period
Cash Paid for Dividends, Profits or Interest Payments in the Next Period
Other Cash Paid Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities for the Next Period = Cash Received from Investments Absorbed in the Next Period + Cash Received from Borrowings in the Next Period + Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period - Cash Paid for Debt Repayment in the Next Period - Cash Paid for Dividends, Profits or Interest Payments in the Next Period - Other Cash Paid Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities in the Next Period
Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from investing activities refers to the net difference between cash inflows and cash outflows generated by a company's investing activities. It reflects the impact on net cash from activities such as purchasing and selling long-term assets and recovering investments, and is one of the core components of the cash flow statement.

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities = Cash Inflows from Investing Activities - Cash Outflows from Investing Activities

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities for the Next Period
aliases: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities
投资活动现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from investing activities for the next period refers to the difference between cash inflows and cash outflows generated by a company's investing activities during a specific future period. It reflects the net cash change resulting from the acquisition or disposal of long-term assets and external investments, serving as a key indicator for evaluating the company's future investment expansion, asset renewal, and capital allocation efficiency.

operands.metric: Subtotal of Cash Inflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period
Subtotal of Cash Outflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities for the Next Period = Subtotal of Cash Inflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period - Subtotal of Cash Outflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period

operands.metric: Cash Received from Recovery of Investments for the Next Period
Cash Received from Investment Income for the Next Period
Net Cash Received from Disposal of Fixed Assets, etc. for the Next Period
Net Cash Received from Disposal of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units for the Next Period
Other Cash Received Related to Investing Activities for the Next Period
Cash Paid for Acquisition and Construction of Fixed Assets, etc. for the Next Period
Cash Paid for Investments for the Next Period
Net Cash Paid for Acquisition of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units for the Next Period
Other Cash Paid Related to Investing Activities for the Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities for the Next Period = (Cash Received from Recovery of Investments for the Next Period + Cash Received from Investment Income for the Next Period + Net Cash Received from Disposal of Fixed Assets, etc. for the Next Period + Net Cash Received from Disposal of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units for the Next Period + Other Cash Received Related to Investing Activities for the Next Period) - (Cash Paid for Acquisition and Construction of Fixed Assets, etc. for the Next Period + Cash Paid for Investments for the Next Period + Net Cash Paid for Acquisition of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units for the Next Period + Other Cash Paid Related to Investing Activities for the Next Period)

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities in the Next Period
Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
aliases: 经营活动现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from operating activities refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by a company's daily business operations during a specific accounting period. It is a core indicator in the cash flow statement, used to assess the ability of a company's core business to generate cash and its financial health.

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities (Direct Method)
aliases: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
经营活动现金流量净额（直接法）
nodes.definition: Under the direct method of the cash flow statement, net cash flow from operating activities is calculated as total cash receipts from operating activities minus total cash payments for operating activities during the reporting period. This approach presents gross cash inflows and outflows, providing a transparent view of cash collections from customers and cash disbursements to suppliers, employees, and other operating parties.

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities = Total Cash Inflows - Total Cash Outflows

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities for the Next Period
aliases: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
未来期间经营现金流净额
预计经营活动现金流净额
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from operating activities for the next period refers to the net amount resulting from the total cash inflows minus total cash outflows generated by a company's core, ongoing daily business operations (such as sales of goods, provision of services, payments to suppliers, and employee compensation) in the upcoming accounting period (e.g., next fiscal quarter or fiscal year), based on forecasts or budgets. It reflects the company's ability to generate cash from its principal business activities in the future period.

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities for the Period
aliases: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
经营活动现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Net cash flow from operating activities for the period refers to the difference between the total cash inflows and total cash outflows generated by a company's core, day-to-day business operations (such as sales of goods, provision of services, payments to suppliers, and employee compensation) during a specific accounting period (e.g., a quarter or a year). It reflects the company's ability to generate cash from its principal business activities and is a key indicator for assessing financial health and earnings quality.

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities in Current Period
Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities in Period 1
aliases: First Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
第一期经营现金流净额
首期经营活动现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities in Period 1 refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated by a company's normal operating activities during the first specific reporting period. It is a key indicator for measuring the ability of a company's core business to generate cash and can be calculated using either the direct or indirect method.

operands.metric: Cash Inflows from Operating Activities in Period 1
Cash Outflows from Operating Activities in Period 1

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities in Period 1 = Cash Inflows from Operating Activities in Period 1 - Cash Outflows from Operating Activities in Period 1

operands.metric: Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Period 1
Amortization of Intangible Assets in Period 1
Adjustments for Other Non-Cash Items in Period 1

formulas.source_formula: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities in Period 1 = Net Profit in Period 1 + Asset Impairment Provisions in Period 1 + Depreciation of Fixed Assets in Period 1 + Amortization of Intangible Assets in Period 1 + Adjustments for Other Non-Cash Items in Period 1

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow from Previous Period
aliases: Net Cash Flow of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Net Cash Flow from Previous Period refers to the net increase or decrease in cash and cash equivalents reported on the cash flow statement at the end of the prior accounting period (e.g., previous quarter or fiscal year). It is a historical figure directly taken from the prior period's cash flow statement, reflecting the combined effect of operating, investing, and financing activities on the company's cash position in that period.

nodes.name: Net Cash Flow in Year k
nodes.definition: Net cash flow in year k refers to the difference between all cash inflows and all cash outflows of an enterprise in a specific year (year k). It reflects the final outcome of the enterprise's cash activities for that year and is a key indicator for evaluating the financial performance of investment projects and making financial decisions.

nodes.name: Net Cash Outflow
nodes.definition: Net cash outflow refers to the difference between total cash outflows and total cash inflows over a specific period, serving as a key indicator of a company's cash payment pressure.

nodes.name: Net Cash Paid for Acquisition of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units
aliases: 取得子公司现金净流出
收购子公司支付的现金净额
nodes.definition: Net cash paid for acquisition of subsidiaries and other business units refers to the net outflow amount resulting from the actual cash purchase price paid by an enterprise when acquiring subsidiaries or other business units, minus the cash and cash equivalents held by the acquired unit on the acquisition date. It reflects the net cash expenditure incurred by the enterprise to obtain control.

nodes.name: Net Cash Paid for Acquisition of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units for the Next Period
Net Cash Paid for Acquisition of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units in the Next Period
aliases: Net Cash Paid for Acquisition of Subsidiaries and Other Business Units
取得子公司支付的现金净额
收购子公司现金净流出
nodes.definition: Net cash paid for acquisition of subsidiaries and other business units in the next period refers to the net outflow amount resulting from the actual cash purchase price paid by an enterprise for acquiring subsidiaries or other business units in a future period (e.g., the next reporting period), minus the cash and cash equivalents held by the acquired entity on the acquisition date. It reflects the net cash expenditure arising from the enterprise's merger and acquisition activities.

nodes.name: Net Cash Proceeds from Disposal of Fixed Assets in Next Period
aliases: Net Cash Inflow from Disposal of Long-lived Assets (Next Period)
