aliases: Net Cash Received from Bond Issuance
债券实际募集资金净额
nodes.definition: Net proceeds from bond issuance refer to the total cash actually received by a company when issuing bonds, after deducting all issuance costs (such as underwriting fees, legal fees, audit fees, etc.). It is a fundamental data item under the 'Cash Received from Investments' line in the cash flow statement, directly sourced from transaction records.

nodes.name: Net Proceeds from Financing Activities
nodes.definition: Net proceeds from financing activities refer to the net income obtained by an enterprise through financing activities (such as absorbing investments, borrowing, etc.), minus expenses paid for financing activities (such as debt repayment, dividend distribution, interest payments, etc.). It reflects the net outcome after a company raises funds through financing channels and pays related costs, and is one of the important indicators for measuring the efficiency of corporate financing.

nodes.name: Net Proceeds from Issuance of Shares
aliases: Net Cash Received from Issuance of Stock
吸收投资收到的现金净额
nodes.definition: Net proceeds from issuance of shares refers to the net cash amount actually received by an enterprise from raising funds through issuing shares, after deducting directly paid commissions, fees, and other expenses incurred during the issuance process. This metric is a core component of the 'Cash Received from Investments' item in the cash flow statement, reflecting the actual cash inflow from equity financing.

operands.metric: Total Cash Received from Share Issuance

formulas.source_formula: Net Proceeds from Issuance of Shares = Total Cash Received from Share Issuance - Issuance Costs

operands.metric: Total Cash Received from Share Issuance

formulas.source_formula: Net Proceeds from Issuance of Shares = Total Cash Received from Share Issuance × (1 - Issuance Cost Rate)

nodes.name: Net Production Taxes in Mining Industry
aliases: Net Production Tax of Mining Industry
nodes.definition: Net production taxes in the mining industry refer to the net amount of various production taxes paid by mining enterprises to the government during the production process, minus production subsidies received from the government. It is an important component in calculating the value added of the mining industry and reflects the net contribution of the mining sector to government finances during production activities.

nodes.name: Net Production Taxes of Secondary Industry in Previous Period
aliases: Net Production Tax of Secondary Industry in Previous Period
Previous Period Secondary Industry Net Production Tax
上期第二产业生产税净值
前期第二产业生产税净额
第二产业上期生产税净额
nodes.definition: Net production taxes of the secondary industry in the previous period refer to the net amount obtained by subtracting production subsidies granted by the government from the total amount of various production taxes paid to the government by production units in the secondary industry (mainly including industry and construction) during their production and operating activities in the last statistical or accounting period. It reflects the share of primary income the government obtains from the value added created by that industry in the previous period.

nodes.name: Net Production Taxes of the Secondary Industry
aliases: Net Production Tax of Secondary Industry
nodes.definition: Net production taxes of the secondary industry refer to the net amount of various production taxes levied by the government on the production, sales, and operating activities of the secondary industry, minus the production subsidies provided by the government. It reflects the share of primary income the government obtains from the value added created by the secondary industry, serves as a crucial component in calculating the value added of the secondary industry, and represents the specific application of the net production taxes indicator from the System of National Accounts within the secondary industry.

nodes.name: Net Production Taxes of the Tertiary Industry
aliases: Net Taxes on Production of Tertiary Industry
nodes.definition: Net production taxes of the tertiary industry refer to the net amount of production taxes payable by production units in the tertiary industry for engaging in production, sales, and business activities (after deducting production subsidies). It reflects the share of primary income that the government obtains from the value added created by the tertiary industry in the current period and is an important component in calculating the value added of the tertiary industry using the income approach.

operands.metric: Production Taxes of the Tertiary Industry
Production Subsidies of the Tertiary Industry

formulas.source_formula: Net Production Taxes of the Tertiary Industry = Production Taxes of the Tertiary Industry - Production Subsidies of the Tertiary Industry
Net Profit (Protective Put) = Quantity × (Stock Sale Price - Stock Purchase Price - Put Option Premium)

nodes.name: Net Profit After Tax
nodes.definition: Net profit after tax refers to the final profit of an enterprise after deducting income tax expenses within a specific accounting period, reflecting the net profitability of the enterprise and serving as the basis for calculating financial indicators such as return on equity.

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit After Tax = Total Profit × (1 - Income Tax Rate)
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit After Tax = Total Profit × (1 - Income Tax Rate)

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit After Tax = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit After Tax = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Net Profit After Tax for the Period
nodes.definition: Net profit after tax for the period refers to the amount of profit ultimately attributable to the owners of the enterprise within a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year), after deducting all costs, expenses, and income tax expenses.

nodes.name: Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders
aliases: Net Income Attributable to Common Shareholders
归属于普通股股东的净利润
nodes.definition: Net profit attributable to common shareholders refers to the portion of a company's net profit realized during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) that ultimately belongs to common shareholders after deducting dividends payable to preferred shareholders. It is a fundamental item on the income statement, directly reflecting the operating results attributable to common shareholders for that period.

nodes.name: Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders for Current Period
Net Profit Attributable to Common Shareholders for Prior Period
Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders (Pre-change)
Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders (Previous Period)
Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders for the Next Period
aliases: Future Period Net Income to Common Equity
Net Income Attributable to Common Shareholders for Next Period
下期普通股股东净利润
预期普通股股东净利润
nodes.definition: Net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders for the next period refers to the portion of net profit that a company expects to achieve in the next accounting period (such as the next quarter or the next fiscal year) and that ultimately belongs to the company's ordinary shareholders. It serves as a key underlying data point for calculating metrics such as earnings per share for the next period, reflecting the company's expected future ability to generate profits for its ordinary shareholders.

nodes.name: Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders for the Prior Period
aliases: Net Income Attributable to Common Shareholders of Previous Period
Prior Period Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders
上期归属普通股净利润
上期归属普通股股东净利
上期普通股股东净利润
前期归属于普通股股东的净利润
前期普通股股东净利润
nodes.definition: Net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders for the prior period refers to the portion of a company's net profit from its operating results in the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or prior quarter) that ultimately belongs to the company's ordinary shareholders. It is a directly reported item on the income statement, reflecting the company's actual profit level attributable to ordinary shareholders after deducting all costs, expenses, taxes, and preferred stock dividends (if any).

nodes.name: Net Profit Attributable to Parent Company Shareholders
aliases: Net Income Attributable to Parent Company Shareholders
Net Profit Attributable to Equity Holders of the Parent
归属于母公司所有者的净利润
nodes.definition: Net profit attributable to parent company shareholders refers to the portion of consolidated net profit that belongs to the ordinary shareholders of the parent company. It excludes profits or losses attributable to non-controlling interests and is a core indicator for measuring the actual profitability of parent company shareholders and evaluating the overall operating efficiency and financial condition of the enterprise.

nodes.name: Net Profit Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Net Profit Growth Rate is an important composite indicator measuring a company's profitability, reflecting the growth magnitude of current period net profit compared to the previous period's net profit. A higher indicator value signifies stronger corporate profitability. The calculation formula is Net Profit Growth Rate = (Current Period Net Profit - Previous Period Net Profit) / Previous Period Net Profit × 100%.

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit Growth Rate = ( (Current Period Total Profit - Current Period Income Tax) - (Previous Period Total Profit - Previous Period Income Tax) ) ÷ (Previous Period Total Profit - Previous Period Income Tax) × 100%

nodes.name: Net Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Net profit margin reflects the proportion of each unit of sales revenue that ultimately converts into net profit, serving as a key indicator for measuring a company's ultimate profitability. This metric comprehensively considers the impact of all costs, expenses, taxes, and non-recurring items.

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit Margin = Net Profit ÷ Sales Revenue
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit Margin = Net Profit ÷ Sales Revenue

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit Margin = Net Income ÷ Revenue
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit Margin = Net Income ÷ Revenue

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit Margin (%) = Net Income ÷ Revenues × 100
Net Profit Margin (%) = (Net Income After Taxes ÷ Revenue) × 100
Net Profit Margin = (Net Income ÷ Revenue) × 100%
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit Margin = (Net Income ÷ Revenue) × 100
Net Profit Margin = (Net Income ÷ Revenue) × 100%

nodes.name: Net Profit Margin on Core Business Revenue
aliases: Net Profit Margin on Core Business
nodes.definition: Net Profit Margin on Core Business Revenue is the ratio of a company's net profit to its net core business revenue, used to measure the company's ability to generate net profit from its core operations. It is a key indicator reflecting the company's core profitability.

nodes.name: Net Profit Margin on Operating Revenue
Net Profit for the Period
nodes.definition: Net profit for the period refers to the net income realized by an enterprise within a specific accounting period. It is the remaining portion after deducting income tax expense from total profit, reflecting the final operating results of the enterprise and is commonly used in financial analysis and performance evaluation.

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit for the Period = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit for the Period = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit for the Period = Total Profit × (1 - Income Tax Rate)
Net Profit for the Period = (Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses) - Income Tax Expense
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit for the Period = (Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses) - Income Tax Expense
Net Profit for the Period = Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses - Income Tax Expense

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit for the Period = (Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Business Taxes and Surcharges - Selling Expenses - Administrative Expenses - Financial Expenses - Asset Impairment Losses + Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Investment Income + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses) - Income Tax Expense
supporting_source_formulas: Net Profit for the Period = (Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Business Taxes and Surcharges - Selling Expenses - Administrative Expenses - Financial Expenses - Asset Impairment Losses + Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Investment Income + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses) - Income Tax Expense

Net Profit for the Period = Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Business Taxes and Surcharges - Selling Expenses - Administrative Expenses - Financial Expenses - Asset Impairment Losses + Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Investment Income + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses - Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Net Profit for the Year
nodes.definition: Net profit for the year refers to the final operating result generated by an enterprise through operating activities, investment activities, and non-recurring items within a complete fiscal year. It is the net amount after deducting all costs, expenses, taxes, and losses from total revenue, serves as the basis for profit distribution, and is classified as an owners' equity account.

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit for the Year = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Net Profit in the Final Period of the Forecast Horizon
aliases: Net Profit of the Final Forecast Period
nodes.definition: Net profit in the final period of the forecast horizon refers to the projected net profit amount expected to be achieved in the last forecast period (e.g., the final year) within a specified forecast timeframe (such as the next 3, 5, or 10 years) in a corporate financial forecast or valuation model. It reflects the company's operating results at the end of the forecast period and serves as a critical input data point for calculating terminal value or discounting cash flows.

formulas.source_formula: Net Profit or Loss = Gross Sales Price - Cost Basis
Net Profit or Loss = Stock Value at Sale - Investment - Borrowed Funds - Interest Paid

nodes.name: Net Profit or Loss from Sale of Business Property
aliases: Net Gain or Loss on Sale of Business Asset
nodes.definition: Net profit or loss from the sale of business property represents the taxable gain or deductible loss computed as the excess of the gross sales price over the property’s adjusted cost basis (purchase cost less accumulated depreciation), reported on IRS Form 4797.

nodes.name: Net Property Income
nodes.definition: Net property income refers to the net income received by households or enterprises for surrendering the use of their financial assets, non-financial assets, and natural resources to other institutional units, households, or individuals, after deducting related expenses. It is one of the important components of disposable income and reflects the net return from property-related activities.

operands.metric: Net Income from Renting Other Assets
Net Rental Value of Owner-occupied Houses

formulas.source_formula: Net Property Income = Operating Revenue - Operating Expenses - Depreciation of Productive Fixed Assets - Production Taxes + Net Income from Renting Houses + Net Income from Renting Other Assets + Net Rental Value of Owner-occupied Houses

nodes.name: Net Property, Plant, and Equipment (Net PP&E)
nodes.definition: Net PP&E represents the carrying amount of tangible fixed assets on the balance sheet, calculated as gross PP&E plus capital expenditures minus accumulated depreciation. It indicates the net book value of property, plant, and equipment after recognizing investment in assets and the wear-and-tear costs through depreciation.

formulas.source_formula: Net PP&E = Gross PP&E + Capital Expenditures - Accumulated Depreciation

nodes.name: Net Realizable Value
nodes.definition: Net realizable value refers to the net value obtained by subtracting the estimated costs to completion, estimated selling expenses, and relevant taxes from the estimated selling price of inventory in the ordinary course of business. It is a key measurement attribute for impairment testing under the lower of cost or market method for inventory.

formulas.source_formula: Net Realizable Value = Expected Selling Price - Total Production and Selling Costs
Net Realizable Value = Estimated Selling Price - Estimated Selling Expenses - Estimated Relevant Taxes and Fees
Net Realizable Value = Estimated Selling Price of Inventory - Estimated Costs to Completion - Estimated Selling Expenses - Relevant Taxes
Net Realizable Value = Estimated Selling Price - Estimated Costs to Completion - Estimated Selling Expenses - Relevant Taxes

nodes.name: Net Receivables
nodes.definition: Net receivables represent the realizable value of accounts receivable after deducting the allowance for doubtful accounts, indicating the amount expected to be collected.

formulas.source_formula: Net Receivables = Gross Receivables - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts

nodes.name: Net Receivables Percentage
aliases: Net Realizable Value of Accounts Receivable Percentage
nodes.definition: Net Receivables Percentage measures the proportion of accounts receivable expected to be collected, calculated as 100% minus the allowance for doubtful accounts percentage. It reflects credit risk and collection efficiency in receivables management.

formulas.source_formula: Net Receivables Percentage = 100% - Allowance for Doubtful Accounts Percentage

nodes.name: Net Rental Income
aliases: Net Operating Income from Rental Property
nodes.definition: Net rental income refers to the actual profit obtained from renting out a property after deducting all related operating expenses and losses. It is typically calculated by subtracting vacancy losses, rental delinquency losses, and operating costs such as property management, maintenance, and taxes from the gross rental income.

nodes.name: Net Rental Income of Owner-occupied Dwellings
aliases: Net Rental Income from Owner-Occupied Housing
nodes.definition: Net rental income of owner-occupied dwellings refers to the implied net income that individuals or households receive by owning and occupying their own homes without paying market rent. In national economic accounting, it is treated as imputed income, used to measure the value of housing services provided by owner-occupied housing. Its calculation is typically based on the market rent of comparable properties minus relevant imputed operating costs (such as depreciation, maintenance expenses, etc.).

nodes.name: Net Rental Value of Owner-occupied Houses
Net Repayment of Interest-bearing Debt
nodes.definition: Net repayment of interest-bearing debt refers to the difference between the total principal amount of interest-bearing debt repaid and the total amount of newly borrowed interest-bearing debt by a company during a specific period. It is a composite financial metric used in calculating indicators such as Free Cash Flow to Equity.

formulas.source_formula: Net Repayment of Interest-bearing Debt = Debt Principal Repaid - Newly Borrowed Interest-bearing Debt

nodes.name: Net Residual Value of Fixed Asset
Net Residual Value of Intangible Assets
nodes.definition: The net residual value of an intangible asset refers to the amount, net of estimated disposal costs, that an entity expects to obtain from the disposal of the asset at the end of its estimated useful life. According to accounting standards, the net residual value of an intangible asset with a finite useful life is generally assumed to be zero, unless there is a commitment by a third party to purchase the asset at the end of its life, or unless there is an active market from which the residual value can be determined based on market information.

formulas.source_formula: Net Returns = Total Returns − (Number of Trades × Trading Cost)

nodes.name: Net Revenue from Principal Operations
nodes.definition: Net revenue from principal operations refers to the net amount of income generated from a company's core business activities during the current period, after deducting sales discounts and allowances. It is a key figure for calculating efficiency metrics such as total asset turnover and is typically sourced from the income statement.

nodes.name: Net Sales
nodes.definition: Net sales refers to the total revenue actually obtained by an enterprise from its principal business activities, such as selling goods and providing services, during a specific period, after deducting sales returns, sales allowances, and sales discounts. It serves as the basis for calculating financial indicators such as asset turnover ratio and cost of sales ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Net Sales = Total Sales Revenue - Sales Returns - Sales Allowances - Sales Discounts
Net Sales = Gross Sales - Sales Allowances - Sales Returns - Sales Discounts

nodes.name: Net Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Net sales revenue refers to the actual revenue earned by an enterprise from its principal business activities, such as selling goods and providing services, during a specific accounting period. It equals the gross sales revenue minus sales discounts and allowances, as well as sales returns. It serves as the basis for calculating key financial indicators such as accounts receivable turnover ratio and asset turnover ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Net Sales Revenue = Sales Revenue - Sales Returns - Sales Discounts - Sales Allowances
Net Sales Revenue = Sales Revenue - Sales Returns - Quantity Discounts - Sales Allowances

nodes.name: Net Sales Revenue of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Net sales revenue of the previous period refers to the total revenue earned by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services during the last accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter), after deducting items such as sales discounts, sales allowances, and sales returns incurred during that period. It reflects the actual results of the enterprise's sales activities in the previous period and serves as the base data for calculating financial metrics such as the accounts receivable turnover ratio of the previous period.

nodes.name: Net Salvage Value Rate
nodes.definition: Net salvage value rate is a financial metric that measures the proportion of an asset's residual value (after deducting disposal costs) to its original acquisition cost at the end of its estimated useful life, commonly used for depreciation calculation.

nodes.name: Net Salvage Value of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Net salvage value of fixed assets refers to the net amount of the estimated residual value recoverable by the enterprise at the end of the asset's estimated useful life, minus the estimated disposal costs. It represents the estimated net realizable value of the asset upon retirement.

formulas.source_formula: Net Settlement Amount (NDS) = (Spot Rate - Contract Rate) × Notional Amount ÷ Contract Rate
Net Short-Term Gain/Loss = Short-Term Capital Gains - Short-Term Capital Losses
Net Short-term Capital = Short-term Capital Gain - Short-term Capital Loss

nodes.name: Net Tangible Assets
nodes.definition: Net tangible assets represent the value of a company's tangible asset base after deducting total liabilities and removing intangible assets such as goodwill. It indicates the residual value attributable to physical and other tangible assets, reflecting the firm's tangible net worth.

formulas.source_formula: Net Tangible Assets = Total Assets - Total Liabilities - Intangible Assets - Goodwill

nodes.name: Net Tangible Assets per Share
nodes.definition: Net Tangible Assets per Share measures the tangible book value attributable to common shareholders on a per-share basis. It is calculated by dividing net tangible assets (total shareholders' equity minus intangible assets and sometimes preferred equity) by the number of common shares outstanding, providing a per-share indicator of tangible value.

formulas.source_formula: Net Tangible Assets per Share = Net Tangible Assets ÷ Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Net Tax Liability or Refund (After Tax Credit)
nodes.definition: Net Tax Liability or Refund (After Tax Credit) represents the resulting tax payable or refund amount after applying tax credits to the initial tax liability. Refundable tax credits can reduce liability below zero and generate a refund, while nonrefundable credits can only reduce liability to a minimum of zero.

nodes.name: Net Taxable Income After Capital Gain-Loss Offset
aliases: Net Taxable Income After Gain-Loss Offset
Net Taxable Income Post Gain-Loss Harvesting
Taxable Income After Capital Loss Deduction
税收损益对冲后的应税收入
资本利得亏损抵扣后的应税收入
nodes.definition: Net Taxable Income After Capital Gain-Loss Offset represents the taxable amount remaining after capital losses are applied to offset capital gains, with any excess loss deduction constrained by the maximum deductible loss permitted against ordinary income under applicable tax regulations.

nodes.name: Net Taxes on Production
nodes.definition: Net taxes on production refer to the net amount of various taxes, surcharges, and fees levied by the government on enterprises or production units during the reporting period for their production, sales, and operating activities, after deducting production subsidies. It reflects the share of primary income obtained by the government from the value added created in the current period and is a key component in calculating value added.

nodes.name: Net Taxes on Production in Mining
Net Taxes on Production in the Secondary Industry
Net Transfer Income
nodes.definition: Net transfer income refers to the net amount of total transfer income received by residents or households from the government, enterprises, other institutions, or households during the reporting period, after deducting total transfer payments made externally. It is a key component in calculating disposable income.

formulas.source_formula: Net Transfer Income = Transfer Income - Transfer Payments

nodes.name: Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA)
aliases: Net Unrealized Appreciation of Employer Securities
nodes.definition: Net Unrealized Appreciation (NUA) is the increase in value of employer securities held within a qualified retirement plan above their cost basis. Under the NUA strategy, at a qualifying distribution, the cost basis portion is subject to ordinary income tax, while the NUA portion may be eligible for long-term capital gains tax treatment when the shares are subsequently sold. The provided computation estimates the total tax liability assuming the NUA portion is taxed at capital gains rates and the cost basis is taxed at ordinary income rates.

nodes.name: Net Value of Operating Long-term Assets at Period End
Net Volume
nodes.definition: Net Volume is a technical analysis indicator that measures the difference between the volume traded on price upticks and the volume traded on price downticks, indicating the balance of buying versus selling pressure. A positive Net Volume suggests bullish sentiment, while a negative Net Volume suggests bearish sentiment.

formulas.source_formula: Net Volume = Uptick Volume - Downtick Volume
supporting_source_formulas: Net Volume = Uptick Volume - Downtick Volume

nodes.name: Net Weight per Unit
nodes.definition: Net weight per unit refers to the actual physical weight of an individual product after removing all packaging materials, containers, or other non-product substances. It is a fundamental physical attribute of the product, typically obtained through direct measurement rather than calculated via financial formulas.

nodes.name: Net Working Capital
nodes.definition: Net working capital is the difference between a company's current assets and current liabilities, used to measure its short-term liquidity and solvency. This indicator reflects, in absolute terms, the scale of net current assets invested to maintain normal operations; a larger value typically indicates stronger short-term debt repayment capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Net Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Net Working Capital Investment in the Final Forecast Period
aliases: Final Period Net Working Capital Investment
Net Working Capital Investment at the End of Forecast Period
预测期最后一期营运资本净额
预测期末营运资本净投资
预测期结束营运资本净投资
nodes.definition: Net working capital investment in the final forecast period refers to the projected net working capital amount at the end of the last period (e.g., Year 5) within a defined forecast timeframe (e.g., the next 5 years) in business valuation or project investment analysis. It typically equals the difference between operating current assets (such as accounts receivable and inventory, excluding excess cash) and operating current liabilities (such as accounts payable and accrued expenses) at the end of that period, reflecting the net liquid capital required to maintain normal operations at the forecast horizon.

nodes.name: Net Working Capital in Old State
aliases: 旧设备相关净营运资金
nodes.definition: In capital budgeting or project investment decisions, this specifically refers to the net working capital that a company needs to invest in or occupy in order to maintain the existing (old) operating state before the project begins or before equipment replacement decisions. It is typically used to calculate the net occupancy of current assets and current liabilities when continuing to use old equipment or maintain the old business model, and is an important component in calculating relevant cash flows.

nodes.name: Net Working Capital under Old Status
Net Worth
nodes.definition: Net worth, also known as net assets, is the residual value after subtracting total liabilities from total assets. It represents the actual wealth level of an enterprise or individual and is a core indicator for measuring solvency and financial strength.

formulas.source_formula: Net Worth = Total Assets - Total Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Net Worth = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

formulas.source_formula: Net Worth = Total Assets - (Current Liabilities + Long-term Liabilities)
Net Wealth = Total Wealth - Liabilities
Net Worth = Total Assets (Excluding Primary Residence) - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Net of Tax
nodes.definition: Net of tax refers to the amount remaining after deducting taxes from a gross amount, commonly used to assess income, profit, or cash flows after accounting for tax expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Net of Tax = Gross Amount - Taxes Paid

nodes.name: Net-Net Working Capital
nodes.definition: Net-Net Working Capital (NNWC) is a conservative, liquidation-oriented measure popularized in deep value investing that estimates a company’s residual value by applying haircuts to certain current assets and subtracting total liabilities. It assigns reduced realizable values to accounts receivable and inventory to reflect potential collection and liquidation risk.

nodes.name: Netback
nodes.definition: Netback is a per-barrel profitability metric in the oil and gas industry, calculated as the sales price per barrel minus royalties, production costs, and transportation costs. It approximates gross margin per barrel and is a non-GAAP operating measure used to assess upstream operational efficiency and cost competitiveness.

nodes.name: Netting
nodes.definition: Netting is the process of offsetting reciprocal financial obligations to determine a single net amount payable or receivable, thereby reducing gross settlement flows, counterparty exposure, and operational complexity. In bilateral netting, a party’s receivables and payables with a single counterparty are offset to one net payment. In multilateral netting, obligations among multiple parties are aggregated and offset to produce net balances for each participant, often used in treasury centers, clearing systems, and derivatives operations.

nodes.name: New Accounts Receivable Amount
nodes.definition: New accounts receivable amount refers to the total amount of newly added accounts receivable during a specific accounting period, arising from business activities such as sales of goods or provision of services for which customers have not yet made payment. It reflects the growth of credit sales during that period.

formulas.source_formula: New Annual Depreciation Expense = Original Annual Depreciation Expense - (Write-Down Amount ÷ Remaining Useful Life)
New Balance = Previous Balance + Daily Gain/Loss
New Balance = Current Balance - Total Payments + Total New Charges
New Benefit = Previous Benefit × (1 + COLA Percentage)

nodes.name: New Borrowing Amount
aliases: 新增流动资金贷款额度
nodes.definition: New borrowing amount refers to the planned incremental loan amount that an enterprise intends to obtain to meet its working capital needs, typically referring to the incremental working capital loan facility. It can be calculated using financial indicators such as working capital requirement, the borrower's own funds, existing working capital loans, and working capital provided through other channels.

formulas.source_formula: New Loan Amount = New Purchase Price - Original Mortgage Balance

operands.metric: Working Capital Provided Through Other Channels

formulas.source_formula: New Borrowing Amount = Working Capital Requirement - Borrower's Own Funds - Existing Working Capital Loans - Working Capital Provided Through Other Channels

nodes.name: New Capital Investment
nodes.definition: New capital investment refers to the initial cash outflow required by a company for new assets or investment projects. It is typically calculated based on factors such as capital expenditures, changes in net working capital, proceeds from the sale of old assets, and related tax liabilities, and is a key concept in capital budgeting and intrinsic value assessment.

formulas.source_formula: New Capital Investment = Initial Cash Outflow
New Carrying Value = Initial Carrying Value - Impairment Loss

nodes.name: New Cash Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The new cash discount rate refers to a newly established or adjusted price reduction percentage offered by a company to customers for early payment within a specified period, based on the original credit policy, in order to accelerate collection of receivables and improve cash flow. It is typically expressed in the format 'discount rate/payment period', such as '2/10, n/30', meaning the customer can enjoy a 2% price discount if payment is made within 10 days.

formulas.source_formula: New Cash Discount Rate = (Original Price of Goods - Discounted Cash Price) ÷ Original Price of Goods × 100%

nodes.name: New Common Shares Issued During Period

formulas.source_formula: New Conversion Price = (Old Conversion Price × Outstanding Shares Before Issuance + Total Consideration Received) ÷ (Outstanding Shares Before Issuance + New Shares Issued)

nodes.name: New Debt
nodes.definition: New debt refers to the incremental increase in debt over a specific period, calculated by comparing the total debt at the beginning and end of the period. It is a key composite metric in financial analysis used to measure changes in debt and assess a company's financing activities, and can be derived from the balance sheet or cash flow statement.

formulas.source_formula: New Debt = Total Debt at Period End - Total Debt at Period Beginning

nodes.name: New Debt Borrowings
nodes.definition: New debt borrowings refer to the debt formed by funds newly raised or borrowed by an enterprise or entity within a specific period through channels such as banks, financial institutions, or the bond market. It is part of corporate financing activities, used to supplement working capital, undertake capital investments, or repay existing debt.

nodes.name: New Debt Issuance
nodes.definition: New debt issuance refers to the total cash proceeds actually raised by a company from investors through the issuance of debt instruments such as bonds in the primary market. This represents a significant cash inflow in the company's financing activities and is directly recorded in the financing activities section of the cash flow statement.

nodes.name: New Earnings Per Share After Buyback
nodes.definition: New earnings per share (EPS) after a company repurchases a portion of its outstanding shares, calculated by adjusting the pre-buyback EPS for the reduction in share count.

formulas.source_formula: New EPS = Current EPS ÷ (1 - Shares Repurchase Percentage)

nodes.name: New Enterprise Value
nodes.definition: New Enterprise Value refers to the present value of future cash flows brought to investors under improved management and operational strategies after corporate control changes or restructuring, or the overall enterprise value calculated based on post-restructuring financial data. It is a composite metric used to evaluate control premium, representing the value attainable by controlling investors, distinct from the current enterprise value.

operands.metric: Present Value of Post-restructuring Forecast Period Free Cash Flow
Present Value of Post-restructuring Terminal Value

formulas.source_formula: New Enterprise Value = Present Value of Post-restructuring Forecast Period Free Cash Flow + Present Value of Post-restructuring Terminal Value
New Enterprise Value = Post-restructuring Equity Market Value + Post-restructuring Debt Market Value - Post-restructuring Cash and Cash Equivalents

nodes.name: New Fixed Capital Investment
nodes.definition: New fixed capital investment refers to the additional cash outflow incurred by an enterprise within a specific period (such as a project or a fiscal year) to acquire, construct, or upgrade long-term tangible assets (e.g., plants, equipment, land). It typically constitutes a significant component of the initial project investment or capital budgeting decisions, aimed at expanding production capacity, replacing obsolete equipment, or implementing technological upgrades.

nodes.name: New Highs-Lows Ratio
nodes.definition: The New Highs-Lows Ratio is a market breadth indicator that measures the number of stocks hitting new 52-week highs relative to those hitting new 52-week lows, used to assess overall market sentiment and potential reversal points.

formulas.source_formula: New Highs-Lows Ratio = New Highs ÷ New Lows

nodes.name: New Highs-New Lows Ratio
nodes.definition: The New Highs-New Lows Ratio measures the number of securities hitting new highs relative to those hitting new lows, serving as a breadth indicator to gauge overall market strength or weakness.

formulas.source_formula: New Highs-New Lows Ratio = New Highs ÷ New Lows

nodes.name: New Interest-bearing Debt
nodes.definition: New interest-bearing debt refers to the increase in a company's total interest-bearing debt during a specific period compared to the previous period. It reflects the additional financing scale obtained by the company through increasing interest-bearing liabilities (such as long-term loans, bonds payable, etc.) and is a key intermediate variable for calculating metrics like Free Cash Flow to Equity.

operands.metric: Total Interest-bearing Debt in Current Period
Total Interest-bearing Debt in Prior Period

formulas.source_formula: New Interest-bearing Debt = Total Interest-bearing Debt in Current Period - Total Interest-bearing Debt in Prior Period
New Inventory Value = Inventory Value - Write-Off Amount
New Money Supply = Current Money Supply × (1 + GDP Growth Rate)
New Monthly Rate = New Interest Rate ÷ 12 ÷ 100

nodes.name: New Price
nodes.definition: New price refers to the transaction price reset for goods, services, or assets after changes in market conditions, cost structures, competitive strategies, or policies. It is typically used to reflect the latest market conditions or corporate decisions and serves as the basis for calculating price change percentages.

formulas.source_formula: New Price per Share = Old Price per Share ÷ Reverse Split Ratio

nodes.name: New Product Development
nodes.definition: New Product Development in finance refers to the total cost or total investment incurred by an enterprise for launching new products, including expenditures in stages such as research and development, design, testing, and market introduction, used for financial evaluation, return on investment calculation, and project decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: New Product Development = Initial Investment Amount + Total Subsequent Development Costs
New Product Development = R&D Expenses + Design Expenses + Testing Expenses + Market Introduction Expenses

nodes.name: New Program Peak Activity Level
aliases: Maximum Business Volume under New Scheme
Peak Activity Level of New Plan
nodes.definition: New Program Peak Activity Level refers to the highest level of business activity expected or actually achieved after implementing a new business program or plan. In financial management, particularly in cost behavior analysis (such as the high-low method) or program comparison, this metric is often used as a key data point to calculate or evaluate costs, revenues, or profitability under the new program.

nodes.name: New Proportion of Customers Taking Cash Discount
New Sales Level
nodes.definition: The new sales level is a projected or adjusted sales metric calculated based on benchmark sales data by considering factors such as sales growth rate, discount policy adjustments, or other market factors. It is commonly used in financial forecasting, cash discount cost analysis, and sales performance evaluation.

formulas.source_formula: New Sales Level = Benchmark Sales Level × (1 + Sales Growth Rate)
New Sales Level = Benchmark Sales Level × (1 - Sales Discount Rate)

nodes.name: New Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: New sales revenue refers to the revenue generated for the first time by an enterprise within a specific period through the sale of products or services to new customers, or through the sale of new products/services. It excludes repeat purchases or renewal income from existing customers and is a key metric for measuring a company's market expansion capability and growth potential.

nodes.name: New Sales Volume
nodes.definition: New sales volume typically refers to the quantity or value of sales that are newly added or exceed the base period level within a specific period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter), used to measure the direct results of business growth and market expansion.

nodes.name: New Scheme Highest Activity Level Cost
nodes.definition: New Scheme Highest Activity Level Cost refers to the total cost corresponding to the highest activity level under the new scheme when using the high-low method for cost behavior analysis. It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating the unit variable cost and total fixed cost.

nodes.name: New Share Issuance
nodes.definition: New share issuance refers to the process in which a company sells its shares to the public for the first time to raise capital. The issue price is a composite indicator determined by comprehensively considering factors such as the company's financial condition, market environment, capital raising needs, and underwriter negotiations, rather than a basic raw data point.

formulas.source_formula: New Share Issuance = Total Funds Raised ÷ Total Number of Shares Issued

operands.metric: Total Trading Volume of Both Markets This Week

formulas.source_formula: New Share Issuance = (Total Trading Volume of Both Markets This Week × Market Sentiment Coefficient + Benchmark Market Capitalization × 100 × Industry P/E Ratio) × (1 + Expected Oversubscription Multiple × Price Adjustment Coefficient)

nodes.name: New Shareholder Capital Contribution
nodes.definition: New Shareholder Capital Contribution refers to the total amount of funds actually invested by a new investor into the company in exchange for equity ownership, typically through methods such as capital increase and share expansion. These funds are usually used to increase the company's registered capital or capital reserve in return for a corresponding shareholding percentage.

formulas.source_formula: New Shares = Old Shares × Reverse Split Ratio
New Shares = Preferred Shares × (Conversion Ratio Increase - 1)

nodes.name: New Store Daily Sales
nodes.definition: New store daily sales typically refer to the daily sales revenue generated by a company's newly opened branches, stores, or business units during their initial operating period (especially on the opening day or within the first month). It is often used as a key performance indicator for evaluating the launch effectiveness and initial operational performance of new ventures.

nodes.name: New Value
nodes.definition: New Value refers to the net revenue generated by new business, calculated as sales revenue minus direct costs and indirect costs. It is a composite metric commonly used in enterprise valuation and new business value ratio analysis, conforming to the definition of a non-leaf node.

formulas.source_formula: New Value = Sales Revenue - Direct Costs - Indirect Costs

nodes.name: Newly Borrowed Interest-bearing Debt
nodes.definition: Newly borrowed interest-bearing debt refers to debt that is newly incurred during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year) and requires interest payments. This includes newly obtained bank loans, newly issued bonds, newly generated finance lease liabilities, etc., but excludes interest-bearing debt that existed and carried over from prior periods. It is an important component when calculating metrics such as 'Net Repayment of Interest-bearing Debt'.

nodes.name: Newness Rate
nodes.definition: Newness rate is an indicator reflecting the degree of newness and remaining useful life of an asset, typically expressed as the ratio of the asset's current value to its replacement cost in new condition, used in asset appraisal and financial management.

nodes.name: Next Group Frequency
nodes.definition: In grouped statistical data, specifically refers to the frequency of the group immediately following the current group, i.e., the number of occurrences of data within that group.

nodes.name: Next Period After-tax Interest Expense
nodes.definition: Next period after-tax interest expense refers to the net amount of a company's interest expense in future periods after considering the impact of income tax, reflecting the actual after-tax cost of the company's debt financing.

nodes.name: Next Period Amortization of Intangible Assets
aliases: Amortization Expense of Intangible Assets for Next Period
下一会计期间无形资产摊销
未来期间无形资产摊销额
nodes.definition: Next period amortization of intangible assets refers to the amount to be allocated to profit or loss in the next accounting period (typically monthly) for finite-lived intangible assets under the straight-line method, calculated based on their original cost, estimated net residual value, accumulated impairment provisions, and amortization period.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Amortization of Intangible Assets = (Original Cost of Intangible Assets - Residual Value of Intangible Assets - Impairment Provision for Intangible Assets) ÷ Amortization Period ÷ 12

nodes.name: Next Period Amortization of Long-term Deferred Expenses
aliases: Amortization of Long-term Deferred Expenses in Next Period
Long-term Prepaid Expenses Amortization for Next Period
下期长期待摊费用摊销额
未来期间长期待摊费用摊销
nodes.definition: Next Period Amortization of Long-term Deferred Expenses refers to the amortization amount calculated by an enterprise based on accounting policies and relevant contracts or estimates (such as the book value of long-term deferred expenses and the estimated amortization months) that should be included in costs or expenses in the next accounting period (e.g., next month, next quarter, or next year). It is a fundamental data point in accounting used to reflect the consumption of long-term deferred expenses in future periods.

nodes.name: Next Period Capital Expenditure
nodes.definition: Next period capital expenditure refers to a company's planned investment expenditure on operating long-term assets (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, etc.) for the upcoming period. It is a key component in forecasting the next period's entity free cash flow and is typically a composite indicator calculated through other financial metrics.

operands.metric: Increase in Net Operating Long-term Assets

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Capital Expenditure = Increase in Net Operating Long-term Assets + Depreciation and Amortization
Next Period Capital Expenditure = Increase in Operating Long-term Assets - Increase in Operating Long-term Liabilities

operands.metric: Increase in Gross Value of Operating Long-term Assets

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Capital Expenditure = Increase in Gross Operating Long-term Assets - Increase in Operating Long-term Liabilities

nodes.name: Next Period Carrying Value of Assets
aliases: Future Period Book Value of Asset
未来期间资产账面价值
nodes.definition: Next period carrying value of assets refers to the value at which an asset is expected to be reported on the balance sheet at the end of the next accounting period (e.g., the next fiscal year or quarter), in accordance with accounting standards. It is typically calculated based on the asset's current or expected original cost, accumulated depreciation (or amortization), and the estimated impairment provision to be recognized, reflecting the projected net amount of the asset at a future point in time.

nodes.name: Next Period Cash Cost
nodes.definition: Next period cash cost refers to the costs that a company expects to actually pay in cash during a specific future period (such as the next accounting period or the next phase of a project) for its operating or investment activities. It excludes non-cash expenses such as depreciation and amortization, and is directly related to the company's future cash flow planning and fund arrangement.

nodes.name: Next Period Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Next period cash flow refers to the forecasted or estimated value of cash flow for a specific future period (typically the next fiscal year or period). It is a key input variable in business valuation, capital budgeting, and risk premium calculations, usually derived through methods such as the expected cash flow approach or adjustments to accounting profits, rather than directly from historical financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Cash Flow = Net Profit + Depreciation and Amortization
Next Period Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow + Investing Cash Flow + Financing Cash Flow
supporting_source_formulas: Next Period Cash Flow = Operating Cash Flow + Investing Cash Flow + Financing Cash Flow

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Cash Flow = EBIT × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation and Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Increase in Working Capital
Next Period Cash Flow = EBIT × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation & Amortization - Increase in Working Capital - Capital Expenditures

nodes.name: Next Period Cash Inflows from Operating Activities
Next Period Cash Outflows from Operating Activities
Next Period Contribution Margin
nodes.definition: Next period contribution margin refers to the expected contribution amount formed by subtracting estimated variable costs from projected sales revenue during a specific future operating period (such as the next month, next quarter, or next fiscal year). It reflects the expected contribution capacity of sales activities in that period to cover fixed costs and generate profits, serving as an important basis for forecasting next period earnings before interest and taxes (EBIT).

nodes.name: Next Period Cost of Goods Sold
Next Period Decrease in Deferred Expenses
Next Period Depreciation Expense
nodes.definition: Next period depreciation expense refers to the amount of fixed asset value consumption that an enterprise pre-calculates and plans to accrue for the next accounting period (such as the next month, next quarter, or next fiscal year) based on the estimated useful life, original cost, residual value, and selected depreciation method (e.g., straight-line method, double-declining balance method, sum-of-the-years'-digits method). It is a crucial component of forecasting future non-cash expenses.

nodes.name: Next Period Depreciation and Amortization
nodes.definition: Next Period Depreciation and Amortization refers to the depreciation and amortization expenses that an enterprise expects to accrue in the next accounting period, calculated according to established accounting policies (such as the straight-line method) based on the original value of fixed assets and intangible assets, estimated net residual value (or net residual value rate), and estimated useful life. This indicator is a calculable composite metric that directly affects the forecasting and evaluation of next period's entity cash flow.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Depreciation and Amortization = Original Value of Fixed Assets × (1 - Estimated Net Residual Value Rate) ÷ Estimated Useful Life
Next Period Depreciation and Amortization = Original Value of Fixed Assets × (1 - Estimated Net Residual Value Rate) ÷ (Estimated Useful Life × 12)

nodes.name: Next Period Depreciation of Fixed Assets
Next Period Dividend
nodes.definition: Next period dividend refers to the amount of cash dividend per share that a company is expected to pay to its common shareholders in the upcoming period (typically the next accounting period). It is the forecasted or declared result of the company's dividend policy and is often used as a known baseline forecast input in financial valuation models, such as the Dividend Discount Model.

nodes.name: Next Period Dividend Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Next period dividend cash flow refers to the expected cash amount of dividends to be paid in the next period. It is typically calculated based on the current dividend and expected growth rate, or derived from earnings per share and the dividend payout ratio. It is a key input variable in the dividend discount model and perpetual growth rate calculations.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Dividend Cash Flow = Current Dividend × (1 + Expected Growth Rate)
Next Period Dividend Cash Flow = Earnings Per Share × Dividend Payout Ratio

nodes.name: Next Period Dividend Per Share
nodes.definition: Next Period Dividend Per Share refers to the forecasted or estimated value of cash dividends that a company is expected to distribute to each common shareholder over a specific future period (typically the next fiscal year). It is a forward-looking metric derived from comprehensive factors such as the company's dividend policy, earnings forecasts, retained earnings plans, and share capital structure, rather than historical financial statement data. It is commonly used in valuation models such as the cost of equity capital.

operands.metric: Estimated Total Dividends for Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Dividend Per Share = Estimated Total Dividends for Next Period ÷ Number of Common Shares Outstanding

operands.metric: Dividend Per Share for the Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Dividend Per Share = Current Period Dividend Per Share × (1 + Estimated Dividend Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Next Period EBIT
nodes.definition: Next Period EBIT refers to a company's profit before deducting interest expenses and income taxes for a specific future period. It reflects the profitability of the company's core operating activities and is a key metric for calculating free cash flow, evaluating operating performance, and conducting financial leverage analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period EBIT = Next Period Total Profit + Next Period Interest Expense
Next Period EBIT = Next Period Contribution Margin - Next Period Fixed Operating Costs
Next Period EBIT = Next Period Net Profit + Next Period Income Tax Expense + Next Period Interest Expense

nodes.name: Next Period Earnings
nodes.definition: Next Period Earnings is a forecasted value or calculation step in the income approach to valuation, referring to the expected earnings for the first forecast period after the valuation date. It is typically derived by forecasting future net profit and discounting it, rather than being directly taken from raw financial statement line items.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Earnings = Forecasted Net Profit × Discount Factor
Next Period Earnings = Forecasted Net Profit ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Period

nodes.name: Next Period Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Next Period Earnings Per Share is a projected or future period's earnings per share. Its calculation logic is the same as basic earnings per share, relying on metrics such as net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders and the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding for calculation. It is a composite indicator.

operands.metric: Next Period Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders
Next Period Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Earnings Per Share = Next Period Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders ÷ Next Period Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Next Period Equity Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Next period equity cash flow is the cash flow that can be freely distributed to equity investors in the future period. It is a composite indicator calculated based on fundamental data such as net profit, depreciation, capital expenditures, and changes in working capital through formulas, and is used for equity valuation.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Equity Cash Flow = Entity Cash Flow - Debt Cash Flow
Next Period Equity Cash Flow = Net Profit - (1 - Debt Ratio) × Entity Net Investment
Next Period Equity Cash Flow = Net Profit - Increase in Shareholders' Equity

nodes.name: Next Period Expected Dividend Per Share
nodes.definition: Next Period Expected Dividend Per Share refers to the amount of cash dividend per common share that investors or analysts forecast a company will pay in the next payment cycle (typically the next year). It is a future value estimated based on factors such as the company's current dividend, earnings expectations, and dividend policy, and serves as a key input variable in stock valuation models like the Dividend Discount Model.

nodes.name: Next Period Fixed Asset Depreciation
nodes.definition: Next Period Fixed Asset Depreciation refers to the estimated depreciation amount to be charged for fixed assets in the next accounting period (e.g., next month, next quarter, or next year), calculated based on the original value of the enterprise's existing fixed assets, estimated useful life, estimated net residual value, and the selected depreciation method (such as the straight-line method). It is a crucial foundational data point in financial forecasting and budgeting.

nodes.name: Next Period Fixed Costs
nodes.definition: Next period fixed costs refer to the costs that a company expects to incur in the next accounting period (such as the next month, quarter, or year) that do not vary with changes in business volume (e.g., production or sales volume). These costs remain relatively stable within the relevant range of business activity, such as rent, administrative salaries, depreciation of fixed assets, and long-term loan interest.

nodes.name: Next Period Fixed Operating Costs
aliases: Fixed Operating Cost for Next Period
未来期间固定经营费用
nodes.definition: Next period fixed operating costs refer to the operational costs that a company expects to incur in the next operating period (such as the next month, quarter, or year) and that do not vary with changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume). These costs are essential for maintaining the basic operations of the enterprise, such as rent, administrative salaries, and depreciation of fixed assets.

nodes.name: Next Period Free Cash Flow
aliases: Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF)
nodes.definition: Next Period Free Cash Flow refers to the estimated residual cash flow that a company is expected to generate in the next accounting or forecast period, after meeting reinvestment needs (such as capital expenditures and increases in working capital), which is available for distribution to all capital providers (creditors and shareholders). It is a key input variable used in business valuation to calculate the present value of the terminal value in the stable growth stage.

nodes.name: Next Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm
nodes.definition: Next Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm is a composite metric calculated based on forecasted future revenues, expenses, capital expenditures, and other fundamental data. It reflects the net cash flow generated from the company's future operating activities. It cannot be obtained directly but must be derived through formulas or models, serving as a core input variable for entity valuation.

operands.metric: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities - Next Period Capital Expenditures

operands.metric: Next Period Gross Operating Cash Flow
Next Period Increase in Operating Working Capital

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Next Period Gross Operating Cash Flow - Next Period Increase in Operating Working Capital - Next Period Capital Expenditures

operands.metric: Next Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
Next Period Increase in Operating Working Capital

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm = Next Period Net Operating Profit After Tax + Next Period Depreciation and Amortization - Next Period Increase in Operating Working Capital - Next Period Capital Expenditures

nodes.name: Next Period Gross Operating Cash Flow
aliases: Operating Cash Flow before Working Capital Changes
nodes.definition: Next Period Gross Operating Cash Flow refers to the projected gross cash flow generated from operating activities in the next period, calculated using metrics such as after-tax operating revenue, after-tax variable costs, after-tax fixed costs, and depreciation & amortization. It serves as a foundational non-leaf node indicator for calculating the next period's entity free cash flow and is used to assess the enterprise's cash generation capacity from operations in the upcoming period.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Gross Operating Cash Flow = After-tax Operating Net Profit + Depreciation & Amortization
Next Period Gross Operating Cash Flow = After-tax Operating Revenue - After-tax Variable Costs - After-tax Fixed Costs + Depreciation & Amortization

nodes.name: Next Period Income Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The next period income tax rate refers to the base rate used to calculate income tax expenses for the next accounting period (such as the next fiscal year or quarter), as stipulated by national tax laws or set by the enterprise based on future operational forecasts and budgets. It is a pre-determined policy or forecast parameter, not calculated from current financial data.

nodes.name: Next Period Increase in Operating Working Capital
Next Period Interest Expense
nodes.definition: Next Period Interest Expense refers to the estimated interest cost that a company is expected to incur in a specific future accounting period (such as the next quarter or the next fiscal year) due to the use of external borrowings (e.g., bank loans, bonds). It is a crucial component for forecasting future financial conditions and calculating related profit metrics (such as next period EBIT).

nodes.name: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities
Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
aliases: 下期经营现金流量净额
nodes.definition: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities refers to the net amount of cash inflows and outflows generated from a company's operating activities in the future period. It is a key indicator for forecasting future cash liquidity, assessing operating performance, and evaluating financial health, typically calculated from other financial metrics.

operands.metric: Next Period Cash Inflows from Operating Activities
Next Period Cash Outflows from Operating Activities

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities = Next Period Cash Inflows from Operating Activities - Next Period Cash Outflows from Operating Activities

operands.metric: Next Period Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents
Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities for the Next Period
Next Period Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities = Next Period Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents - Next Period Net Cash Flow from Financing Activities - Next Period Net Cash Flow from Investing Activities

operands.metric: Next Period Net Increase in Operating Assets
Next Period Net Decrease in Non-Interest-Bearing Liabilities

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities = Next Period Net Operating Income + Next Period Non-Cash Expenses - Next Period Net Increase in Operating Assets - Next Period Net Decrease in Non-Interest-Bearing Liabilities

operands.metric: Next Period Provision for Asset Impairment
Next Period Depreciation of Fixed Assets
Next Period Amortization of Intangible Assets
Next Period Amortization of Long-term Deferred Expenses
Next Period Decrease in Deferred Expenses

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities = Next Period Net Profit + Next Period Provision for Asset Impairment + Next Period Depreciation of Fixed Assets + Next Period Amortization of Intangible Assets + Next Period Amortization of Long-term Deferred Expenses + Next Period Decrease in Deferred Expenses

nodes.name: Next Period Net Debt
nodes.definition: Next Period Net Debt refers to the projected or planned net debt amount that an enterprise expects to hold in the next accounting period (such as the next fiscal quarter or fiscal year). It is commonly used for financial forecasting and budgeting. It represents the difference between financial liabilities and financial assets, reflecting the net debt capital the enterprise plans to invest in production and operations in the future.

nodes.name: Next Period Net Decrease in Non-Interest-Bearing Liabilities
Next Period Net Increase in Cash and Cash Equivalents
Next Period Net Increase in Operating Assets
Next Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
aliases: Forecasted Net Operating Profit After Tax
nodes.definition: Next Period Net Operating Profit After Tax (NOPAT) is the forecasted net operating profit after tax for a future period, reflecting a company's operating profitability excluding the impact of financing structure. It serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as next period free cash flow to the firm. Its calculation formula is the same as that for NOPAT, i.e., net profit after tax plus after-tax interest expense, or earnings before interest and tax multiplied by (1 minus the income tax rate).

operands.metric: Next Period Net Profit After Tax

formulas.source_formula: Next Period NOPAT = Next Period Net Profit After Tax + Next Period After-Tax Interest Expense
Next Period NOPAT = Next Period EBIT × (1 - Next Period Income Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Next Period Net Profit
nodes.definition: Next Period Net Profit refers to the final net income generated from both operating and non-operating activities of an enterprise in a specific future accounting period. It is a key indicator for measuring the profitability of the enterprise in the future period. Its calculation logic is the same as that of current period net profit, i.e., deducting income tax expense from total profit, or derived by adding net non-operating income to operating profit and then deducting income tax expense.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Net Profit = Next Period Total Profit × (1 - Next Period Income Tax Rate)
Next Period Net Profit = Next Period Total Profit - Next Period Income Tax Expense
Next Period Net Profit = Next Period Operating Profit + Next Period Non-operating Income - Next Period Non-operating Expenses - Next Period Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Next Period Net Profit After Tax
aliases: Next Period Net Income After Tax
nodes.definition: Next Period Net Profit After Tax refers to the final retained profit after the total profit from business activities in a future specific period (e.g., the next accounting period) is subject to income tax according to regulations. It is a core indicator for measuring a company's future profitability and the distributable earnings available to shareholders.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Net Profit After Tax = Next Period Total Profit × (1 - Next Period Income Tax Rate)
Next Period Net Profit After Tax = Next Period Total Profit - Next Period Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Next Period Net Profit Attributable to Ordinary Shareholders
Next Period Non-Cash Expenses
nodes.definition: Next period non-cash expenses refer to costs incurred by an enterprise in a specific future operating period that are not directly paid in cash. They typically consist of accounting allocation items such as depreciation and amortization, and serve as key adjustments for calculating metrics like net cash flow from operating activities in the next period.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Non-Cash Expenses = Next Period Total Costs - Next Period Cash Costs

operands.metric: Amortization Amount of Deferred Expenses for Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Non-Cash Expenses = Next Period Depreciation Expense + Next Period Intangible Assets Amortization + Next Period Prepaid Expenses Amortization + Next Period Other Non-Cash Expenses

nodes.name: Next Period Non-operating Income
nodes.definition: Next period non-operating income refers to various revenues expected to occur in the next accounting period (such as the next fiscal year, next quarter, or next month) that are not directly related to the enterprise's daily production and operating activities. Such income is typically incidental or non-recurring, for example, gains from disposal of non-current assets, government grants, inventory surplus gains, donation gains, etc.

nodes.name: Next Period Non-operating Net Income
aliases: Non-operating Net Income for Next Period
未来期间非经营净收益
nodes.definition: Next period non-operating net income refers to the net income generated by a company from non-core business activities during a specific future accounting period (such as the next fiscal quarter or fiscal year). It typically arises from activities such as investments, financing, or asset disposals, rather than from the daily sale of goods or provision of services.

nodes.name: Next Period Operating Cost
nodes.definition: Next period operating cost refers to the total expenses that an enterprise expects to incur for production activities, such as manufacturing products or providing services, in the next accounting period (e.g., the next fiscal year, quarter, or month), which are attributable to product costs or service costs. It typically includes estimated main business costs and other business costs, and is a key component in forecasting the next period's net operating income.

nodes.name: Next Period Operating Expenses
aliases: 下一会计期间营业费用
nodes.definition: Next period operating expenses refer to the various expense outlays directly related to daily business operations that an enterprise expects to incur in the next accounting period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual), primarily including selling expenses, administrative expenses, research and development expenses, and financial expenses, but excluding cost of sales.

nodes.name: Next Period Operating Net Income
aliases: Next Period Operating Profit After Tax
nodes.definition: Next Period Operating Net Income refers to the net profit obtained by an enterprise through its principal operating activities in a future specific period (e.g., the next accounting period), after deducting all related costs, expenses, and income taxes. It reflects the future profitability of the enterprise's core business and is a key foundational indicator for forecasting the net cash flow from operating activities in the next period.

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Operating Net Income = Next Period Net Profit - Next Period Non-operating Net Income

operands.metric: Next Period Cost of Goods Sold
Taxes and Surcharges Payable in Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Next Period Operating Net Income = Next Period Operating Revenue - Next Period Cost of Goods Sold - Next Period Operating Expenses - Next Period Taxes and Surcharges - Next Period Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Next Period Operating Profit
nodes.definition: Next period operating profit refers to the profit that a company expects to achieve from its normal business operations in a specific future accounting period (such as the next quarter or the next fiscal year), based on current operating conditions and market expectations. It reflects the anticipated profitability from core business activities after deducting operating costs, taxes, and various period expenses, serving as a key leading indicator for forecasting future net profit and assessing the company's going concern capability.

nodes.name: Next Period Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Next Period Operating Revenue refers to the total revenue a company expects to generate from its principal business activities and other operations in the next accounting period (e.g., next quarter, next fiscal year). It is a crucial indicator for forecasting future operating performance and conducting financial planning.

nodes.name: Next Period Provision for Asset Impairment
Next Period Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Next period sales revenue refers to the total revenue a company expects to earn from selling goods or providing services in the next accounting period (e.g., next month, next quarter, or next fiscal year). It serves as a crucial basis for sales budgeting and cash flow forecasting.

nodes.name: Next Period Variable Cost
nodes.definition: Next period variable cost refers to costs that change in direct proportion to changes in business volume (such as production or sales volume) during the next accounting period or budget period. It serves as a crucial foundational data point for forecasting financial metrics such as EBIT for the upcoming period.

nodes.name: Next Period Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding
Next Quarter Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Next quarter sales volume refers to the forecasted or planned quantity of product sales for the upcoming financial quarter, serving as fundamental data for preparing sales budgets and operating budgets.

nodes.name: Next-In, First-Out (NIFO) Profit
nodes.definition: NIFO Profit measures margin under the Next-In, First-Out inventory valuation convention, where the cost of goods sold is based on the current replacement cost (i.e., the cost of the next unit to be acquired) rather than the historical cost. It is used primarily for internal managerial analysis, especially during inflationary periods, and is not permitted under GAAP or IFRS for external financial reporting.

formulas.source_formula: NIFO Profit = Selling Price - Replacement Cost
Nisab (Gold) = 87.48 × Gold Price per Gram
Nisab (Silver) = 612.36 × Silver Price per Gram

nodes.name: Nominal Effective Exchange Rate
nodes.definition: The Nominal Effective Exchange Rate (NEER) is the trade-weighted average of a domestic currency’s bilateral exchange rates against a basket of foreign currencies. Weights reflect the relative trade shares with partner countries. NEER is not adjusted for inflation differentials and serves as an indicator of a currency’s nominal external competitiveness.

nodes.name: Nominal GDP
nodes.definition: Nominal GDP refers to the total market value of all final goods and services produced in an economy, measured using current-year (or current-period) market prices. This indicator reflects both changes in the total output of the economy and changes in the price level, serving as a nominal value measure of the total economic activity scale of a country or region over a specific period.

formulas.source_formula: Nominal GDP = Consumption + Investment + Government Expenditure + Net Exports

nodes.name: Nominal GDP for the Reporting Period
nodes.definition: Nominal GDP for the reporting period refers to the total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country or region during a specific period (typically a quarter or a year), calculated at current market prices. It does not exclude the effects of price changes (inflation or deflation) and directly reflects the scale of total economic output measured at current prices.

nodes.name: Nominal Goods and Services Value
aliases: Nominal Value of Goods and Services
nodes.definition: Nominal goods and services value refers to the total value of all final goods and services calculated at current market prices within a given period, without removing the effects of price changes (inflation or deflation).

nodes.name: Nominal Gross Domestic Product
nodes.definition: Nominal Gross Domestic Product is the gross domestic product calculated at current market prices, reflecting the total market value of all final goods and services produced by resident units in a country or region during a given period, which can be measured using the income approach, expenditure approach, or production approach.

formulas.source_formula: Nominal GDP = Total Output - Intermediate Input
Nominal GDP = Compensation of Employees + Consumption of Fixed Capital + Net Taxes on Production + Operating Surplus

nodes.name: Nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP)
nodes.definition: Nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the aggregate market value of all final goods and services produced within an economy during a specific period measured at current prices, unadjusted for inflation. It can be derived by multiplying real GDP by the GDP deflator, a price index that reflects the change in the overall price level relative to a base year.

formulas.source_formula: Nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP) = Real Gross Domestic Product (GDP) × GDP Deflator

nodes.name: Nominal Growth Amount
nodes.definition: Nominal growth amount (or nominal growth rate) refers to the absolute or relative change in an indicator (such as Gross Domestic Product) calculated at current market prices between two periods. It reflects the growth in nominal value without removing the effects of price changes and is an important composite indicator for measuring changes in the monetary value of economic activity.

formulas.source_formula: Nominal Growth Amount = Current Period Value - Base Period Value
Nominal Growth Amount = Base Period Value × Nominal Growth Rate

nodes.name: Nominal Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The nominal growth rate is a ratio measuring the magnitude of change in nominal values from the base period to the reporting period, calculated via formulas rather than from original accounting line items, commonly used to analyze changes in economic or financial indicators such as disposable income

formulas.source_formula: Nominal Growth Rate = (Nominal Value in Reporting Period - Nominal Value in Base Period) ÷ Nominal Value in Base Period

nodes.name: Nominal Income
