nodes.name: Original Plan Total Cost
nodes.definition: Original Plan Total Cost refers to the total sum of all costs initially established for developing or evaluating a project, plan, or technical solution, without considering subsequent changes or adjustments. It typically serves as a benchmark for cost comparison and decision analysis.

nodes.name: Original Plan Variable Cost per Unit
aliases: Original Scheme Variable Cost per Unit
nodes.definition: Original plan variable cost per unit refers to the cost incurred for producing or selling each unit of product under the enterprise's original production or operational plan, which changes in direct proportion to the level of business activity (such as production volume or sales volume). It serves as a critical foundational data point for cost-volume-profit analysis, cost control, and plan comparison.

nodes.name: Original Price
nodes.definition: Original price refers to the initial selling price of a good or service before any discounts, promotions, or price adjustments, serving as the base reference price for calculating discounts, profit margins, and other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Original Price of Goods
nodes.definition: Original price of goods refers to the initial selling price before any discounts, promotions, or price adjustments, typically serving as the base price for calculating discounts, profits, or costs.

nodes.name: Original Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Original sales revenue refers to the total income obtained by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during a specific accounting period. It is typically calculated based on the product of sales volume and unit selling price, serving as a key indicator for measuring the scale and performance of the enterprise's core business.

nodes.name: Original Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Original sales volume typically refers to the initially set or actually achieved quantity of product sales by an enterprise during a specific period (such as a financial cycle or planning period), serving as a baseline or reference data for subsequent revenue, profit, or budget analysis.

nodes.name: Original Share Capital
nodes.definition: Original share capital refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and subscribed by founding shareholders or initial investors at the time of a company's establishment or initial public offering. It represents the initial source of corporate capital and historical factual data, typically determined by multiplying the par value per share (e.g., 1 yuan) by the total number of shares initially issued.

nodes.name: Original Stock Price
nodes.definition: Original stock price refers to the initial stock price used as the starting point for calculation in stock market trading, which is unadjusted or not derived from further calculations. It serves as the fundamental raw data for market transactions and is typically used to compute derivative metrics such as stock price change percentages.

nodes.name: Original Value
nodes.definition: In financial accounting, original value typically refers to the total reasonable and necessary expenditures incurred to acquire or construct an asset and bring it to its intended usable condition, representing the initial recorded amount of the asset in the accounting books.

nodes.name: Original Value of Assets at Beginning of Period
aliases: Initial Asset Cost at Period Start
Opening Historical Cost of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Original value of assets at the beginning of the period refers to the original acquisition cost of fixed assets at the start of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month), including the purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, installation expenses, and all other necessary expenditures incurred to bring the asset to its intended usable condition. It is a fundamental historical data point obtained directly from accounting ledgers or asset cards, serving as the starting point for subsequent depreciation calculations and the determination of net asset value.

nodes.name: Original Value of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: The original value of fixed assets refers to the total sum of all reasonable and necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire a specific fixed asset and bring it to its intended usable condition. It represents the initial book entry value of the fixed asset in the accounting records, reflecting the actual investment scale in fixed assets and serving as the basis for subsequent depreciation calculations.

nodes.name: Original Value of Fixed Assets Disposed or Transferred Out
aliases: Book Value of Assets Transferred Out for Disposal
Original Value of Disposed Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Original value of fixed assets disposed or transferred out refers to the original carrying value of fixed assets, intangible assets, or other long-term assets before they are transferred to the disposal process, i.e., the recorded acquisition cost when the assets were initially purchased or obtained.

nodes.name: Original Value of Intangible Assets
nodes.definition: The original value of intangible assets refers to the initial cost or historical cost recognized and recorded on the books according to accounting standards when an enterprise acquires or forms an intangible asset. It serves as the basis for calculating subsequent amortization, impairment, and determining the net book value of intangible assets.

nodes.name: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets
aliases: Historical Cost of Operating Non-current Assets
nodes.definition: Original value of operating long-term assets refers to the historical cost or book value at initial acquisition of tangible assets (such as plants, machinery, equipment, land use rights, etc.) purchased or constructed by an enterprise for its principal business activities, with an expected useful life exceeding one accounting year. It reflects the original cost incurred by the enterprise to obtain these long-term operating resources, without deducting subsequent accumulated depreciation or amortization.

nodes.name: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets Acquired in Current Period
aliases: Cost of Long-lived Operating Assets Purchased This Period
当期购置长期经营资产原值
本期购入经营长期资产原值
经营用长期资产本期购置原值
nodes.definition: The original value of operating long-term assets acquired in the current period refers to the initial recognized cost at acquisition of tangible assets (such as plants, equipment, vehicles, etc.) purchased or constructed for business operations during the current accounting period (e.g., the current year or quarter), with an expected useful life exceeding one year, excluding subsequent depreciation or impairment.

nodes.name: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets Disposed in Current Period
aliases: Book Value of Long-lived Assets Disposed
Original Value of Disposed Operating Long-term Assets in Current Period
处置经营长期资产账面原值
本期处置固定资产原值
本期清理长期资产原值
nodes.definition: Original Value of Operating Long-term Assets Disposed in Current Period refers to the historical cost value at initial recognition of fixed assets, intangible assets, and other long-term assets used in the enterprise's daily business operations that were disposed of during the current accounting period (such as the current quarter or fiscal year) through means such as sale, scrapping, damage, external investment, non-monetary asset exchange, or debt restructuring. It reflects the scale of historical cost of long-term assets withdrawn from operating activities during the current period.

nodes.name: Origination Fee
nodes.definition: An origination fee is a lender-charged fee at the initiation of a loan, typically expressed as a percentage of the loan amount, to compensate for processing, underwriting, and administrative costs. It is usually calculated as a fixed rate applied to the total loan principal.

formulas.source_formula: Origination Fee = Loan Amount × Origination Fee Rate
supporting_source_formulas: Origination Fee = Loan Amount × Origination Fee Rate

nodes.name: Origination Points Fee
nodes.definition: Origination points fee is the lender's charge for processing and underwriting a mortgage, typically quoted in points where 1 point equals 1% of the loan amount. The fee is calculated by applying the origination points percentage to the mortgage principal.

nodes.name: Orphan Drug Credit
nodes.definition: The orphan drug credit is a U.S. federal income tax credit that allows eligible pharmaceutical companies to reduce tax liability by a specified percentage of qualified clinical testing expenses incurred in developing treatments for rare diseases.

formulas.source_formula: Orphan Drug Credit = Qualified Clinical Testing Expenses × Credit Rate

nodes.name: Oscillator of a Moving Average (OsMA)
nodes.definition: The Oscillator of a Moving Average (OsMA) is a technical analysis indicator that measures the deviation of an oscillator from its own moving average. It highlights momentum shifts and potential trend reversals by quantifying the difference between the oscillator and its smoothed value.

formulas.source_formula: Oscillator of a Moving Average (OsMA) = Oscillator - Moving Average of Oscillator

nodes.name: Other Adjustments
nodes.definition: In financial accounting and tax treatment, it refers to the amount of items that require additional adjustments in financial statements or tax returns due to differences between accounting regulations and tax laws that cannot be classified into specific adjustment categories. Commonly used during corporate income tax final settlement to address differences not explicitly listed, such as deemed sales and special asset treatments.

nodes.name: Other Alternative Investment Assets
aliases: 非交易性权益工具投资
nodes.definition: Other alternative investment assets, in accounting, typically refer to non-trading equity instrument investments held by an enterprise that are designated as measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. They belong to a category of alternative investments, distinct from traditional assets such as stocks, bonds, and cash, and represent a specific asset account on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Other Asset Investments
nodes.definition: Other asset investments refer to the allocation of corporate funds into financial or physical assets beyond traditional stocks, bonds, and cash, such as long-term equity investments, real estate, commodities, artwork, or intangible assets, typically falling under the category of long-term investments.

nodes.name: Other Assets
nodes.definition: Other Assets is an aggregated accounting item on the balance sheet, used to consolidate long-term asset items that are unique in nature, occur infrequently or irregularly, and cannot be clearly classified into major asset categories such as current assets, fixed assets, or intangible assets.

nodes.name: Other Attributable Costs
nodes.definition: Other attributable costs refer to various costs in financial accounting that can be clearly and directly attributed to a specific cost object (such as a product, project, or department) but are not separately listed under major cost categories (such as direct materials or direct labor). They represent raw data in the cost accumulation process, used for more accurately calculating the true cost of a specific object.

nodes.name: Other Business Income and Expenses
aliases: Non-operating Income and Expenses (in a broad sense)
nodes.definition: Other business income and expenses refer to the revenue generated and corresponding cost expenditures from business activities other than the main operations of an enterprise. It is directly derived from accounting records and serves as a fundamental line item on the income statement, used to account for the operating results of non-core business activities such as material sales and asset leasing.

nodes.name: Other Capital Reserves
aliases: 资本公积-其他资本公积
nodes.definition: Other capital reserves is a detailed account under capital reserves, primarily recording gains and losses directly attributable to owners' equity other than capital premium (or share premium). It arises from specific accounting events, such as equity-settled share-based payments, changes in other equity of investees under the equity method excluding net profit or loss, etc. Its amount is directly recognized and not derived through calculation.

nodes.name: Other Cash Paid Related to Financing Activities
Other Cash Paid Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period

nodes.definition: Refers to cash payments related to financing activities, as reported in the cash flow statement, other than principal repayments of debt, dividend or profit distributions, and interest payments. These expenditures typically do not constitute the main part of financing activities but are nevertheless related to raising funds or changes in capital structure.

nodes.definition: Other cash payments related to financing activities in the next period refer to other cash payments associated with financing activities that an enterprise expects to occur in future periods (e.g., the next accounting period), excluding major financing cash outflows such as debt repayment, dividend or profit distribution, and interest payments. These payments typically include audit fees, consulting fees directly paid for raising funds, lease payments for finance leases, and cash payments for capital reduction (e.g., share repurchases).

nodes.name: Other Cash Payments Related to Investing Activities in the Next Period
aliases: Future Period Other Investing Cash Outflows

nodes.definition: Other cash payments related to investing activities in the next period refer to other cash outflows associated with investing activities that an enterprise expects to incur in the next accounting period (such as the next fiscal year or quarter), excluding the net cash paid for the purchase of fixed assets, intangible assets and other long-term assets, and for obtaining subsidiaries and other business units. These expenditures generally do not constitute major investing activities but are components of cash flows from investing activities.

nodes.definition: Other cash received related to financing activities is an item in the cash flow statement that reflects various other cash inflows related to financing activities received by an enterprise, apart from major items such as absorbing investments and obtaining borrowings, for example, receiving cash donations.

nodes.name: Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities in Year k
Other Cash Received Related to Financing Activities in the Next Period
aliases: Future Period's Other Financing Cash Inflows
Other Cash Received from Financing Activities in Next Period
下期筹资活动其他现金流入
未来期间收到的其他筹资现金
nodes.definition: Refers to other cash inflows related to financing activities that an enterprise expects to receive in future accounting periods (e.g., next period, next fiscal year), excluding primary financing methods such as capital absorption and borrowing. Examples include expected cash donations received and refunds of deposits related to finance leases.

nodes.name: Other Cash Received Related to Investing Activities for the Next Period
Other Cash Received Related to Investing Activities in Year k
Other Cash Received Related to Investment Activities in the Next Period

Other Cash Received from Investing Activities in Next Period

nodes.definition: Other cash received related to investment activities in the next period refers to other cash inflows related to investment activities received in the enterprise's cash flow statement for the next accounting period (e.g., next period, next quarter, or next fiscal year), excluding major items such as the net cash received from the disposal of fixed assets, intangible assets, and other long-term assets, and cash received from investment returns. Examples may include dividends or interest received that were paid but not yet collected when purchasing stocks or bonds.

nodes.name: Other Cash Received Related to Operating Activities in Next Period
aliases: Next Period's Other Operating Cash Receipts
Other Cash Received from Operating Activities in the Next Period
下期其他经营现金流入
下期收到的其他经营现金
下期经营活动其他现金收入
nodes.definition: Other cash received related to operating activities in the next period refers to other cash inflows related to daily operations that an enterprise expects to receive in the next accounting period (such as the next quarter or fiscal year), excluding major operating activities such as sales of goods and provision of services. These inflows typically include non-core business cash receipts such as penalty income, rental income, scrap sales revenue, and refunds of deposits received.

nodes.name: Other Cash Received Related to Operating Activities in Year k
aliases: Other Cash Received from Operating Activities
收到的其他与经营活动有关的现金
经营活动其他现金流入
nodes.definition: Other cash received related to operating activities in year k refers to cash inflows received by an enterprise during its operating activities in year k, apart from main business operations such as sales of goods and provision of services. These inflows typically include non-recurring or secondary cash receipt items such as penalty income, deposit refunds, rental income (non-core business), and cash overages.

nodes.name: Other Comprehensive Income
nodes.definition: Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) refers to the difference between comprehensive income and net profit, representing certain gains and losses of an enterprise that are not recognized in the current period's profit or loss. These items are directly recorded in the equity account 'Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income' (AOCI) and include unrealized gains/losses on available-for-sale financial assets, the effective portion of cash flow hedges, foreign currency translation adjustments, actuarial gains/losses on defined benefit plans, and revaluation surplus.

formulas.source_formula: Other Comprehensive Income = Comprehensive Income - Net Profit
Other Comprehensive Income = Total Comprehensive Income - Operating Net Profit

operands.metric: Foreign Currency Financial Statement Translation Difference
Fair Value Change of Investment Property

formulas.source_formula: Other Comprehensive Income = Foreign Currency Financial Statement Translation Difference + Fair Value Change of Investment Property + Revaluation Change of Financial Assets

nodes.name: Other Comprehensive Income by Scenario
nodes.definition: Other comprehensive income by scenario refers to the gains and losses that, according to accounting standards, are directly recorded in changes of owners' equity but not recognized in the current period's income statement, excluding net profit generated from ordinary business activities during a specific accounting period. It primarily reflects unrealized or temporary gains and losses, which do not affect current period net profit but impact total comprehensive income.

nodes.name: Other Comprehensive Income for the Period
aliases: 其他综合收益本期发生额
nodes.definition: Other Comprehensive Income for the Period refers to the gains and losses recognized in a specific accounting period, as stipulated by accounting standards, that are not included in the current period's profit or loss but are directly recorded in owners' equity. It is a component of the statement of changes in owners' equity and a key element in calculating total comprehensive income.

operands.metric: Fair Value Changes on Investment Properties

formulas.source_formula: Other Comprehensive Income for the Period = Foreign Currency Translation Differences + Fair Value Changes on Investment Properties + Revaluation Changes on Financial Assets + Other Qualifying Items

nodes.name: Other Construction Costs
nodes.definition: Other Construction Costs are a significant component of the construction investment within the total investment estimate for a construction project. They refer to various expenses incurred during the construction period that are related to land use rights acquisition, the entire construction process, and future production and operation, but are not classified under construction engineering costs, installation engineering costs, or equipment purchase costs. They are aggregated from a series of independently measurable specific cost items and are ultimately capitalized into the original value of fixed assets.

nodes.name: Other Costs Attributable to Inventory Procurement
Other Costs Attributable to Inventory Purchase
aliases: Other Costs Attributable to Inventory Acquisition
nodes.definition: Refers to other necessary and reasonable expenditures incurred by an enterprise during the inventory procurement process, beyond the purchase price, related taxes, transportation fees, loading/unloading fees, and insurance premiums, to bring the inventory to its intended salable or usable condition. These costs form part of the total inventory purchase cost and must be capitalized into the initial cost of inventory.

nodes.name: Other Costs Directly Attributable to Inventory Acquisition
aliases: 其他可归属于存货采购成本的费用
nodes.definition: Refers to other expenditures, besides the purchase price, related taxes, transportation fees, loading and unloading charges, and insurance premiums, that are necessarily incurred by an enterprise during the inventory acquisition process to bring the inventory to the location and condition necessary for it to be saleable or usable, and that can be directly attributed to the acquisition of that specific inventory.

nodes.name: Other Current Assets
nodes.definition: Other current assets is a specific line item under current assets on the balance sheet, referring to short-term assets that do not belong to major current asset categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory, but are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle.

nodes.name: Other Current Assets as Percentage of Total Current Assets
aliases: OCA as Percentage of Current Assets
Other Current Assets to Current Assets Ratio
其他流动资产占流动资产比率
nodes.definition: A composition ratio that measures the proportion of Other Current Assets within Total Current Assets, indicating the materiality and mix of less common current asset categories in a firm's liquidity profile.

formulas.source_formula: Other Current Assets as Percentage of Total Current Assets = (Other Current Assets ÷ Total Current Assets) × 100%

nodes.name: Other Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Other current liabilities refer to the aggregate of short-term debts that a company must repay within one year or one operating cycle, which do not fall under major current liability items such as short-term borrowings, accounts payable, or employee compensation payable. It is a collective account used to summarize short-term obligations that are either unique in nature or relatively insignificant in amount, making separate presentation impractical.

nodes.name: Other Debt Investments
aliases: Financial Assets at Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVOCI)
Financial Assets at Fair Value through Other Comprehensive Income (FVOCI) - Debt Instruments
指定为以公允价值计量且其变动计入其他综合收益的金融资产
nodes.definition: Other debt investments are a type of financial asset held by an enterprise, typically referring to investments in debt instruments such as bonds that are held with the objective of both collecting contractual cash flows and selling the financial asset. In accounting treatment, they are designated as measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. Their carrying amount is directly formed through initial recognition and subsequent measurement (such as fair value changes and amortization of interest adjustments).

nodes.name: Other Deductions
aliases: Other Deductions as Prescribed by Law
个人所得税其他扣除项
nodes.definition: Other Deductions refer to additional items, as stipulated by China's Individual Income Tax Law, that can be legally deducted when calculating the taxable income of a resident individual's comprehensive income, apart from the basic deductions, special deductions, and special additional deductions. They are original deduction items explicitly listed in the tax law, with specific content determined according to relevant laws and regulations, and cannot be derived or calculated through other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Other Direct Costs
nodes.definition: Other direct costs refer to additional expenditures, beyond primary raw material costs and direct labor costs, that can be directly attributed to a specific cost object (such as a product, project, or service) during the production, construction, or service provision process. These costs are typically directly related to production or service activities and can be clearly traced and allocated to specific cost objects.

nodes.name: Other Direct Operating Costs
nodes.definition: Other direct operating costs refer to other necessary expenditures directly related to the provision of products or services, beyond primary costs such as direct materials and direct labor, incurred by an enterprise in its daily business operations. These costs typically cannot be directly attributed to a specific production process or product but are indispensable components of operating activities. In accounting, they are treated as basic or detailed items under cost and expense categories.

nodes.name: Other Equity Instrument Investments
aliases: 以公允价值计量且变动计入其他综合收益的权益投资
指定为FVOCI的权益工具投资
非交易性权益工具投资
nodes.definition: Other equity instrument investments refer to non-trading equity instrument investments that an enterprise actively designates as measured at fair value with changes in fair value recognized in other comprehensive income, in accordance with accounting standards. They are a type of financial asset whose value fluctuates directly with market fair value, and the holding purpose is typically for long-term strategic holding rather than short-term trading gains.

nodes.name: Other Equity Instruments
nodes.definition: Other equity instruments refer to various financial instruments issued by an enterprise, other than ordinary shares, that are classified as equity instruments. They are used to account for funds raised by the enterprise through the issuance of these special financial instruments (such as perpetual bonds, preferred shares, etc.) that constitute part of the owner's equity.

nodes.name: Other Expenses
nodes.definition: In financial statements (such as the income statement), 'Other Expenses' is an independent primary account used to aggregate and present various incidental or non-recurring expenditures that cannot be classified into major expense categories (such as Selling Expenses, Administrative Expenses, and Financial Expenses). It belongs to fundamental financial data and typically cannot be directly derived through calculations from other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Other Financial Current Assets
nodes.definition: Other financial current assets is a specific line item under current assets on the balance sheet, referring to short-term assets with financial characteristics held by an enterprise that do not belong to major current asset categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory. These assets are typically expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle and represent fundamental financial data directly obtained from accounting records.

nodes.name: Other Freight Charges
nodes.definition: Other freight charges refer to the aggregate of various additional costs incurred during the freight transportation process, excluding basic freight (such as air freight, road tonnage charges) and declared value surcharges. These charges are typically applied to cover the costs of specific operations or services within the transportation service.

nodes.name: Other Income
nodes.definition: Other income refers to various non-recurring or secondary revenues obtained by an enterprise or administrative unit in accordance with regulations, beyond its main business or primary appropriation income. In financial statements, it is typically presented as an independent revenue item directly, rather than derived through calculation.

nodes.name: Other Increases
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, 'Other Increases' typically refers to the incremental amount in a specific statement or account (such as surplus reserves) that results from items not separately presented or classified, apart from the main, clearly defined components. It is an aggregated, supplementary item used to reflect increases that are not conveniently or separately disclosed within the primary items.

nodes.name: Other Interest-bearing Current Liability Items
nodes.definition: Other interest-bearing current liability items refer to debts that a company must repay within one year or one operating cycle and on which interest must be paid. These items exclude major categories such as short-term borrowings and current portion of long-term debt, and constitute a part of interest-bearing current liabilities.

nodes.name: Other Investment Expenses
nodes.definition: Other investment expenses refer to the various necessary costs incurred to complete a project's construction, beyond the main direct costs such as equipment purchase costs and construction engineering costs, during the preparation of project investment estimates or design budget estimates. These expenses typically include construction unit management fees, survey and design fees, engineering supervision fees, etc., and constitute an important component of the total project investment.

nodes.name: Other Investments
nodes.definition: Other investments refer to long-term investments made directly by an enterprise in other entities in the form of monetary funds, physical assets, or intangible assets, typically not constituting control over the investee. In accounting, it is presented as a separate asset item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Other Items Meeting Regulatory Requirements
nodes.definition: In financial statements, this specifically refers to items that comply with accounting standards or regulatory provisions but cannot be classified under major standard categories, and are therefore presented separately in specific statement line items (such as other comprehensive income for the period).

nodes.name: Other Long-term Assets
nodes.definition: Other long-term assets refer to those long-term asset items on a company's balance sheet that are of a special nature, occur infrequently, or have an amortization period exceeding one year, and are not classified under specific categories such as current assets, long-term equity investments, fixed assets, or intangible assets. They typically include items like long-term prepaid expenses that cannot be categorized under the aforementioned major asset classes.

nodes.name: Other Long-term Assets Book Value
aliases: Book Value of Other Long-term Assets
Net Book Value of Other Long-term Assets
其他长期资产账面余额净额
其他长期资产账面净值
nodes.definition: Other long-term assets book value refers to the net amount of other long-term assets presented on the balance sheet, excluding major long-term assets such as fixed assets, intangible assets, and long-term equity investments, after deducting relevant impairment provisions or allowance items. It reflects the actual accounting value of these assets on the books.

nodes.name: Other Monetary Funds
nodes.definition: Other monetary funds refer to various monetary funds deposited in banks or other financial institutions for specific purposes, excluding cash on hand and bank deposits, in the daily business operations of an enterprise.

nodes.name: Other Non-Cash Expenses for Next Period
aliases: 未来期间其他非现金支出
nodes.definition: Other non-cash expenses for the next period refer to expense items that a company expects to incur in the next accounting period but do not involve actual cash outflow or inflow in the current period. These expenses are recognized under the accrual basis of accounting, affecting current period profits, while their cash impact occurs in future periods, such as prepaid expenses or deferred costs that require future amortization.

nodes.name: Other Non-Operating Activity Adjustments in the Final Forecast Period
aliases: Non-Recurring Items Adjustment at Forecast Horizon
预测期最后一期非经常性项目调整
预测期末非经营性调整
nodes.definition: Other non-operating activity adjustments in the final forecast period refer to the cash inflow or outflow items considered when adjusting the cash flow statement for the final period of the forecast horizon (typically the ending year of the detailed forecast period) in a financial forecast or valuation model. These items are not part of the company's regular operating activities and are of a non-recurring or one-time nature. The adjustments aim to make the cash flow in the final period better reflect the normalized operating condition of the company as it enters a stable or perpetual growth phase, thereby providing a more reasonable basis for subsequent terminal value calculation. Common adjustment items may include non-recurring gains or losses, significant asset disposals or acquisitions, one-time restructuring charges, litigation settlements, and other cash impacts unrelated to operations.

nodes.name: Other Non-cash Adjustments
nodes.definition: Other Non-cash Adjustments is an aggregate adjustment item in the supplementary information of the cash flow statement, used to reflect all other non-cash adjustment items not separately listed during the process of reconciling net profit to cash flows from operating activities, apart from the explicitly enumerated items (such as asset impairment provisions, depreciation of fixed assets, etc.). It serves as a catch-all item to ensure the completeness of the reconciliation process.

nodes.name: Other Non-current Assets
nodes.definition: Other non-current assets refer to long-term assets with a turnover or realization period exceeding one year, excluding those separately presented on the balance sheet (such as fixed assets, intangible assets, long-term equity investments, etc.). These assets typically do not meet the criteria for separate presentation or have relatively unique characteristics.

nodes.name: Other Non-current Assets such as Available-for-sale Financial Assets
Other Non-current Financial Assets
aliases: 其他非流动资产-金融资产
其他非流动资产金融资产
非流动金融资产其他项
nodes.definition: Other non-current financial assets are items in the balance sheet used to aggregate financial assets that are not separately presented in the financial statements and have a holding period exceeding one year. They typically include infrequent or immaterial long-term financial assets that are not practical to present separately.

nodes.name: Other Non-current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Other non-current liabilities are items on the balance sheet used to aggregate long-term debts or obligations that cannot be classified into standard long-term liability categories such as long-term borrowings, bonds payable, and long-term payables. They form part of non-current liabilities and typically refer to non-standard liabilities with a repayment period exceeding one year.

nodes.name: Other Non-operating Assets
nodes.definition: Other Non-operating Assets is a line item on the balance sheet used to aggregate various non-current assets held by an enterprise that are not directly related to its daily operating activities and are expected to be realized or consumed over a period exceeding one year (or one normal operating cycle). It typically includes specific assets with longer amortization periods, such as contract acquisition costs, contract fulfillment costs (net of the portion to be recovered within one year), and costs of expected returns.

nodes.name: Other Non-operating Current Assets
aliases: 非经营性其他流动资产
nodes.definition: Other non-operating current assets refer to short-term assets presented on a company's balance sheet that do not fall into major operating current asset categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory, are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, but are not directly related to primary business activities.

nodes.name: Other Operating Costs
nodes.definition: Other Operating Costs is an enterprise accounting item used to record the direct costs incurred from operating activities other than the main business operations, such as the cost of selling materials, depreciation of leased fixed assets, amortization of leased intangible assets, and the cost of leased packaging materials.

nodes.name: Other Operating Current Assets
nodes.definition: Other operating current assets refer to the operational portion under the 'Other Current Assets' account on the balance sheet. These are short-term assets arising from daily business operations that do not fall into major categories such as cash, accounts receivable, or inventory. They typically include prepayments, deferred expenses, etc., and are expected to be realized or consumed within one year or one operating cycle.

nodes.name: Other Operating Current Assets at Period End
nodes.definition: Other operating current assets at period end refer to other current assets, excluding major items such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, and inventory, that are used in daily business operations and are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle, as presented in the balance sheet at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end).

nodes.name: Other Operating Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Other operating current liabilities refer to other short-term debts arising from a company's daily business operations that are due within one year or one operating cycle, excluding major items such as accounts payable and employee compensation payable. It is a specific line item on the balance sheet used to account for and report these non-major operating short-term liabilities.

nodes.name: Other Operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Other operating expenses refer to various expenditures related to business activities incurred by an enterprise in its daily operations, excluding main business costs and primary operating expenses (such as selling expenses, administrative expenses, and financial expenses). These expenses are typically accounted for under operating costs or operating expense accounts.

nodes.name: Other Operating Payables
nodes.definition: Other operating payables are a current liability item on the balance sheet, referring to various amounts payable or temporarily received by an enterprise in its daily operating activities, excluding notes payable, accounts payable, advances from customers, employee compensation payable, taxes payable, interest payable, dividends payable, etc. The reported amount must be calculated and recorded based on an analysis of the balances of relevant subsidiary ledger accounts, involving reclassification adjustments.

operands.metric: Total Credit Balance of Other Receivables Subsidiary Ledger Accounts
Total Credit Balance of Other Payables Subsidiary Ledger Accounts

formulas.source_formula: Other Operating Payables = Total Credit Balance of Other Receivables Subsidiary Ledger Accounts + Total Credit Balance of Other Payables Subsidiary Ledger Accounts

nodes.name: Other Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Other operating revenue refers to the income realized by an enterprise from other operating activities besides its main business in daily operations, such as selling materials, leasing assets, and providing non-core business services.

nodes.name: Other Owners' Equity Items of Subsidiaries
nodes.definition: Other owners' equity items of subsidiaries refer to the equity interests in the net assets of subsidiaries attributable to investors other than the parent company (i.e., non-controlling interests) as presented in consolidated financial statements. They represent the portion of the subsidiary's owners' equity that does not belong to the parent company.

nodes.name: Other Owners' Equity Items of Subsidiary
Other Payables
aliases: Other Funds in Conformity with Paying
nodes.definition: Other payables refer to various amounts payable or temporarily received from other entities or individuals that occur in the course of daily business operations, excluding major transactions such as purchasing goods or accepting services. It is an account under current liabilities on the balance sheet, reflecting debts related to non-core business operations that the enterprise needs to repay or settle.

nodes.name: Other Payables (Non-interest Bearing Portion)
nodes.definition: Other payables (non-interest bearing portion) refer to amounts payable or temporarily received from other entities or individuals arising from transactions or events not directly related to the principal business operations in the course of daily business activities, and which do not accrue interest according to relevant contracts or agreements. It is a significant component of a company's non-interest bearing current liabilities, and its amount is directly sourced from accounting book records.

nodes.name: Other Payables - Prior Period
nodes.definition: Other payables - prior period refer to various payable and temporarily received amounts, excluding those arising from main business operations such as accounts payable and notes payable, that remained unpaid or unsettled as of the balance sheet date of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous fiscal year or quarter).

nodes.name: Other Payments to Individuals
aliases: 支付给个人的其他款项
nodes.definition: Refers to various non-fixed or non-recurring expenses paid by an enterprise to individuals (such as sales personnel, consultants, freelancers, etc.) within intermediate inputs like selling expenses, excluding regular wages, bonuses, and commissions. Examples include travel allowances, business entertainment reimbursements, and temporary service remunerations.

nodes.name: Other Policy Tax Reduction Amount
nodes.definition: Other Policy Tax Reduction Amount refers to the portion of tax reduction already granted by other independent tax incentive policies (such as employment of disabled persons, entrepreneurship of retired soldiers, etc.) that must be deducted from the tax payable in advance when calculating the tax reduction amount for a specific tax incentive (e.g., halved individual income tax on business income of sole proprietorships). It is used to ensure accurate calculation when multiple tax incentives are applied cumulatively and to avoid duplicate reductions.

nodes.name: Other Procurement Expenses
nodes.definition: Other procurement expenses refer to other necessary expenditures incurred by an enterprise during the procurement of materials or goods, in addition to direct costs such as purchase price, main transportation fees, and related taxes. These expenses typically include packaging fees, warehousing fees, loading and unloading fees, insurance premiums, inspection fees, etc., and constitute part of the total cost of inventory procurement.

nodes.name: Other Property Loss Value
nodes.definition: Other Property Loss Value refers to the monetary measurement of economic losses incurred due to damage, destruction, or depreciation of various properties other than major assets such as buildings, structures, and equipment (e.g., inventory, office supplies, intangible assets) in specific events such as accidents, fires, etc.

nodes.name: Other Receivables
nodes.definition: Other receivables refer to various amounts receivable or temporarily paid to other entities or individuals by an enterprise in its daily operations, excluding those arising from principal operating activities such as accounts receivable, notes receivable, and prepayments. Examples include travel advances to employees, petty cash funds, various deposits collected, insurance claims receivable, or fines receivable. On the balance sheet, it is presented as part of current assets.

nodes.name: Other Receivables - Prior Period
nodes.definition: Other Receivables - Prior Period refers to the carrying value of various receivables and temporary payments due from other entities or individuals at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the prior year or quarter), excluding major receivable items such as accounts receivable, notes receivable, and prepayments. It is typically presented as the net amount of the ending balance in the 'Other Receivables' account from the prior period, less the corresponding provision for bad debts.

nodes.name: Other Related Expenses
nodes.definition: Other related expenses refer to the directly associated, necessary additional expenditures incurred in specific economic activities (such as asset disposal or procurement), apart from the primary cost or revenue. These expenses typically do not constitute core costs but are essential for the complete accounting of the transaction.

nodes.name: Other Securities Investments
nodes.definition: Other Securities Investments is a composite metric in financial statements, representing the total value of securities held by an enterprise beyond major categories (such as equities and bonds). It is typically derived by aggregating or calculating data from underlying securities investments and is used to reflect the diversification of the enterprise's investment portfolio and non-core investment activities.

nodes.name: Other Short-term Borrowings
nodes.definition: Other short-term borrowings refer to non-core operating loans obtained by an enterprise from financial institutions such as banks, with a repayment period of one year or less. They are typically used for temporary working capital needs, specific project financing, or as bridge financing, and are separately presented as a current liability in the financial statements.

nodes.name: Other Short-term Liabilities Related to Operating Activities
aliases: Other Current Liabilities Related to Operating Activities
经营活动相关短期负债
nodes.definition: Other short-term liabilities related to operating activities refer to various short-term debts that a company incurs in its daily business operations, excluding major items such as accounts payable and notes payable, which are due for repayment within one year or one operating cycle. They typically include liabilities directly related to core business operations, such as accrued employee compensation, deferred revenue, dividends payable, and short-term borrowings.

nodes.name: Other Statutory Deductions
aliases: Other Deductions as Prescribed by Law
nodes.definition: Other statutory deductions refer to specific expenditure items that individuals are permitted to deduct from their comprehensive income according to relevant national laws and regulations, in addition to basic deductions, special deductions, and special additional deductions, when calculating the taxable income for individual income tax purposes.

nodes.name: Other Taxes and Fees Paid
aliases: Payment of Other Taxes and Fees
nodes.definition: Other taxes and fees paid refer to the actual cash disbursements made by an enterprise for various taxes and fees other than major tax categories (such as corporate income tax and value-added tax), including stamp duty, property tax, land use tax, vehicle and vessel tax, etc. It constitutes a significant component of the 'Cash Paid for Taxes' item in the cash flow statement and represents fundamental cash outflow data directly sourced from accounting records.

nodes.name: Other Tier 1 Capital Instruments and Their Premiums
aliases: Additional Tier 1 Capital Instruments and Premiums
nodes.definition: Other Tier 1 capital instruments and their premiums are direct components of a commercial bank's capital structure, referring to capital instruments, other than common equity and retained earnings, that meet regulatory requirements and have the capacity to absorb losses on a going concern basis, along with the premium portion exceeding their par value at issuance. Common examples include preferred shares and their issuance premiums.

nodes.name: Out of The Money (OTM)
nodes.definition: Out of the Money (OTM) describes an option with no intrinsic value. A call option is OTM when the underlying asset's market price is below the strike price; a put option is OTM when the underlying asset's market price is above the strike price. OTM options have zero immediate exercise value and consist solely of time value.

nodes.name: Out-of-Pocket Cost
nodes.definition: Out-of-pocket cost refers to the expenses that a company needs to pay in cash during operational decision-making, directly impacting cash flow management, and is commonly used in production/operational decisions and cash flow analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Out-of-Pocket Cost = Cost - Depreciation
Out-of-Pocket Cost = Operating Cost - Depreciation and Amortization
Out-of-Pocket Cost = Total Cost - Interest - Depreciation and Amortization
Out-of-Pocket Cost = Out-of-Pocket Production Cost + Paid Expenses + Paid Relevant Taxes and Fees

nodes.name: Out-of-Pocket Expenses
nodes.definition: Out-of-pocket expenses are direct payments made by an individual for goods or services that are not reimbursed by an employer, insurer, or other payer. In accounting and finance, they are tracked to evaluate personal spending, employee expense claims, and patient cost burden in healthcare.

nodes.name: Out-of-Pocket Limit
nodes.definition: The out-of-pocket limit (out-of-pocket maximum) is the annual cap on cost sharing a policyholder must pay for covered healthcare services, including deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance. Once this limit is reached, the insurance plan pays 100% of covered, in-network allowed charges for the remainder of the year, excluding premiums and non-covered or out-of-network costs.

nodes.name: Outcome Probability
nodes.definition: Outcome probability refers to the likelihood of a specific financial result or market event occurring in the future within financial and accounting activities, typically expressed as a percentage or a value between 0 and 1. It is a fundamental data point estimated based on historical data, statistical models, or expert judgment.

formulas.source_formula: Probability of Outcome = Frequency of Outcome ÷ Total Frequency

nodes.name: Outcome Value
nodes.definition: Outcome value refers to the final economic value of a project or decision calculated through financial models (such as discounted cash flow or probability-weighted analysis) after considering future uncertainties. It is a core evaluation metric for capital budgeting and investment decision analysis and typically does not directly equate to the book value in financial statements.

nodes.name: Output
nodes.definition: Output refers to the physical quantity of qualified products produced by an enterprise, production line, equipment, or worker within a specific period. It is the most fundamental physical measure or operational data in the production process, typically obtained through direct counting, weighing, or measurement, and is used to gauge the scale and efficiency of production activities.

nodes.name: Output Gap
nodes.definition: Output gap measures the deviation of actual GDP from potential GDP, expressed as a percentage of potential GDP. A positive output gap indicates the economy is operating above potential (inflationary pressure), while a negative output gap indicates slack or underutilized capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Output Gap (%) = (Actual GDP - Potential GDP) ÷ Potential GDP × 100

nodes.name: Output VAT
nodes.definition: Output VAT is the value-added tax amount calculated based on sales revenue and the tax rate stipulated by tax laws, collected from the buyer when a taxpayer sells goods or provides taxable services. It is a key component in VAT calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Output VAT = Tax-exclusive Sales Revenue × Tax Rate

nodes.name: Output VAT Amount
nodes.definition: Output VAT amount refers to the value-added tax calculated based on the current period's sales revenue and the prescribed VAT rate, which is charged to the buyer by a general taxpayer when selling goods, providing taxable services, or engaging in deemed sales activities. It is a key component in calculating the enterprise's current period VAT payable.

nodes.name: Output VAT Payable
nodes.definition: Output VAT payable refers to the value-added tax amount calculated based on sales revenue and the prescribed VAT rate, which a general taxpayer should collect from the buyer when selling goods, providing taxable services, or engaging in taxable activities. It is a key component in calculating the enterprise's current-period VAT payable.

nodes.name: Output VAT for the Current Period
nodes.definition: Output VAT for the current period refers to the amount of Value-Added Tax (VAT) that a taxpayer is required to collect from purchasers during the current tax period (e.g., a month or a quarter) arising from taxable sales activities, such as the sale of goods, provision of taxable services, intangible assets, or immovable property. It serves as one of the fundamental components for calculating the enterprise's VAT payable for the current period.

nodes.name: Output Value
nodes.definition: Output value refers to the total market value of all goods and services created by an enterprise or individual through production activities within a specific period. It is an important economic indicator for measuring the scale and results of production activities, reflecting the final outcome of the production process, but it is not equivalent to profit, as production costs have not yet been deducted.

nodes.name: Output per Shift (Month)
nodes.definition: Output per shift (month) refers to the actual quantity of products completed by a production team or individual within one work shift or one month, serving as important raw data for measuring production efficiency and capacity.

nodes.name: Output per Unit Time
nodes.definition: Output per unit time refers to the quantity of products produced or the amount of work completed within a specific time period (such as per hour, day, or week), serving as a fundamental metric for measuring production efficiency.

nodes.name: Outright Forward
nodes.definition: An outright forward is a foreign exchange forward contract that locks in a single all-in forward exchange rate for settlement on a future date. The outright forward rate (forward outright) is computed by adjusting the spot exchange rate with forward points, which reflect the covered interest rate differential; positive points indicate a forward premium and negative points a forward discount. It is used to hedge or manage exchange rate risk.

nodes.name: Outright Option
nodes.definition: An outright option is a standalone position in a single call or put option, not combined with other option legs. The net profit or loss for a long outright option position equals the option's intrinsic value minus the premium paid, evaluated at a given spot price and strike, ignoring transaction costs and time value.

nodes.name: Outstanding Amount of Long-term Debt Securities
aliases: 长期债务证券发行在外的数量
长期债务证券在外流通数
长期债务证券流通份额
nodes.definition: Outstanding amount of long-term debt securities refers to the total number of units or certificates of long-term debt securities (such as long-term bonds) that have been issued by an issuer (e.g., government, corporation) and are currently being traded among investors in the financial market, not yet matured or redeemed. It is a fundamental statistical value directly obtained from market records or issuer data, reflecting the supply scale of the security in the secondary market.

nodes.name: Outstanding Balance
nodes.definition: Outstanding balance refers to the total amount in an account that has not been paid or settled at a specific point in time (e.g., statement date or reporting date). It typically includes unpaid principal, accrued interest, and other related charges, serving as fundamental data reflecting the current debt level.

nodes.name: Outstanding Common Shares
nodes.definition: Outstanding common shares refer to the total number of common stock shares issued by a company and actually held by investors in the public market. It excludes shares repurchased and held as treasury stock by the company, serving as fundamental data for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share.

nodes.name: Outstanding Invoices
nodes.definition: Outstanding invoices refer to sales invoices issued to customers for which payment has not yet been received, or purchase invoices received from suppliers for which payment has not yet been completed. They represent a state of receivables or payables where the transaction has been confirmed but funds have not yet been settled.

nodes.name: Outstanding Principal Balance
nodes.definition: Outstanding principal balance refers to the portion of the original loan principal that has not been repaid by the borrower at a specific point in time for an installment loan or debt. It serves as the basis for calculating current interest and is a core indicator for measuring the remaining liability scale of the debtor. It can be calculated through methods such as the total loan amount minus the present value of cumulative principal repaid or the present value of future repayment amounts.

nodes.name: Outstanding Shares
nodes.definition: Outstanding shares refer to all shares that have been authorized by the company, issued, and purchased and held by investors. They are distinguished from treasury shares, which are shares held by the company itself and do not carry exercisable rights. The sum of outstanding shares and treasury shares equals the total number of issued shares.

formulas.source_formula: Outstanding Shares = Issued Shares - Treasury Stock
Outstanding Shares = Issued Shares - Treasury Shares
supporting_source_formulas: Outstanding Shares = Issued Shares - Treasury Shares

nodes.name: Outward Arbitrage Profit
nodes.definition: Outward arbitrage profit is the gain realized by borrowing domestically at a given interest rate and lending the proceeds abroad at a higher foreign interest rate for the same period, ignoring transaction costs, taxes, and other frictions.

nodes.name: Over and Short
nodes.definition: Over and Short (Cash Over and Short) is a general ledger account and reconciliation measure that records the discrepancy between the recorded cash sales expected to be collected and the actual cash received. A positive amount indicates a cash over situation (excess cash on hand), while a negative amount indicates a cash short situation (cash deficiency), typically arising from cash-handling errors, timing issues, or recording mistakes. It is used in cash-intensive operations to monitor internal control effectiveness and reconcile cash drawers to sales records.

formulas.source_formula: Over and Short = Actual Cash Received - Expected Sales

nodes.name: Overall Capture Ratio
nodes.definition: Overall capture ratio measures an investment manager's relative performance in rising versus declining markets. It is defined as the up-market capture ratio divided by the down-market capture ratio, indicating how effectively the manager participates in gains compared to losses. A value greater than 1 suggests stronger participation in up-markets relative to down-markets.

formulas.source_formula: Overall Capture Ratio = Up-Market Capture Ratio ÷ Down-Market Capture Ratio

nodes.name: Overall Credit Utilization Ratio
nodes.definition: Overall Credit Utilization Ratio measures the percentage of total outstanding revolving balances relative to total revolving credit limits across all credit cards. It is calculated by dividing the sum of balances by the sum of credit limits and is a key factor in credit scoring and credit risk assessment.

formulas.source_formula: Overall Credit Utilization Ratio = Total Outstanding Balance ÷ Total Credit Limit

nodes.name: Overall Current Period Amount
nodes.definition: Overall current period amount refers to the actual value of a specific indicator during the current statistical or analytical period. It is a fundamental concept in data analysis and can be calculated using the base period amount combined with the growth amount or growth rate.

formulas.source_formula: Overall Current Period Amount = Base Period Amount × (1 + Growth Rate)
Overall Current Period Amount = Base Period Amount + Growth Amount

nodes.name: Overall Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Overall Growth Rate refers to the proportional increase in quantity or value over a specified period, serving as a fundamental composite metric for measuring the magnitude of change in scale or level, widely applied in financial, economic, and business analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Overall Growth Rate = (Current Value - Original Value) ÷ Original Value × 100%

nodes.name: Overall Labor Productivity
nodes.definition: Overall labor productivity measures the ratio of labor output (such as total output value or GDP) created by all employees in a country, region, sector, or enterprise over a specific period (typically one year) to the corresponding labor input (such as average annual number of employees or total labor hours), used to evaluate the overall input-output efficiency of the labor factor.

nodes.name: Overall Liquidity Ratio
nodes.definition: The overall liquidity ratio measures an institution’s capacity to meet outstanding liabilities using assets on hand. It is calculated as total assets divided by net liabilities (total liabilities minus conditional reserves) and is commonly used in solvency assessment for insurers and financial institutions.

formulas.source_formula: Overall Liquidity Ratio = Total Assets ÷ (Total Liabilities - Conditional Reserves)

nodes.name: Overall Ratio
nodes.definition: Overall ratio is a type of financial analysis metric, calculated by dividing the amount of a specific item in the financial statements by a relevant total base amount and multiplying by 100%, used to reflect the composition or proportion of that item within the total.

nodes.name: Overall Recorded Amount
nodes.definition: Overall Recorded Amount refers to the total book value or aggregate amount recorded for a specific account, transaction category, or financial statement item during financial auditing or analysis. It serves as the base figure for calculating financial metrics such as misstatement rates and composition ratios.

nodes.name: Overcapitalization
nodes.definition: Overcapitalization occurs when a company's capital employed exceeds the capitalized value of its maintainable earnings at the required rate of return, resulting in inadequate returns on capital and potential impairment of shareholder value. The capitalized value (fairly capitalized capital) is commonly estimated as earnings divided by the required rate of return.

nodes.name: Overcollateralization (OC)
nodes.definition: Overcollateralization (OC) is a credit enhancement technique in which the value of pledged collateral exceeds the outstanding exposure. The Overcollateralization Ratio, also called the collateralization or collateral coverage ratio, measures the extent of coverage by comparing collateral value to loan value; a ratio greater than 1 indicates overcollateralization, while a ratio less than 1 indicates undercollateralization. It is widely used in lending, structured finance, and securitizations to assess credit protection and resilience against losses.

formulas.source_formula: Overcollateralization Ratio = Collateral Value ÷ Loan Value

nodes.name: Overextension
nodes.definition: Overextension is a condition in which an individual or corporation assumes a debt burden that is unsustainably high relative to income, typically indicated by a debt service ratio at or above a defined threshold (here, one-third of net income). It signals elevated credit risk and potential stress on liquidity and repayment capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Overextension Ratio = Debt Payments ÷ Net Income

nodes.name: Overfunded Pension Plan
aliases: 资金充足的养老金计划
超额资助的养老金计划
nodes.definition: An overfunded pension plan is a defined benefit plan whose fair value of plan assets exceeds its pension obligations (liabilities). The condition is assessed by the funded ratio, calculated as total plan assets divided by total plan liabilities and expressed as a percentage; a funded ratio greater than 100% indicates an overfunded plan, around 100% indicates fully funded, and less than 100% indicates underfunded.

formulas.source_formula: Funding Ratio (%) = Total Plan Assets ÷ Total Plan Liabilities × 100

nodes.name: Overhang
nodes.definition: Overhang is a dilution metric that measures the potential future shareholder dilution from stock-based compensation plans. It is calculated as the total of granted stock options and authorized but unissued stock options relative to total shares outstanding, expressed as a percentage. Companies and investors use it to assess equity compensation impact and dilution risk.

formulas.source_formula: Overhang Percentage = (Stock Options Granted + Authorized but Unissued Stock Options) ÷ Total Shares Outstanding × 100

nodes.name: Overhead Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The overhead allocation rate is a calculated ratio used to allocate indirect costs (such as manufacturing overhead), representing the amount of indirect cost to be borne per unit of allocation base (e.g., labor hours, machine hours, direct labor cost, etc.). Its core calculation formula is the total amount of indirect costs to be allocated divided by the total allocation base of all allocation objects.

nodes.name: Overhead Rate
nodes.definition: The overhead rate is a predetermined allocation rate used to distribute total indirect costs to specific cost objects (such as products or projects). It is typically established based on historical data, budgets, or industry standards and serves as a key calculation parameter in cost accounting and management accounting.

formulas.source_formula: Overhead Rate = Indirect Costs ÷ Allocation Base
Overhead Rate = Total Budgeted Indirect Costs ÷ Total Budgeted Allocation Base

nodes.name: Overhead Ratio
aliases: 运营费用与平均资产比率
非利息费用与平均资产比率
nodes.definition: The overhead ratio measures a bank’s noninterest expenses relative to its average assets, indicating the institution’s cost efficiency in managing operating expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Overhead Ratio = Noninterest Expense ÷ Average Assets
Overhead Ratio = Operating Expenses ÷ (Taxable Interest Income + Operating Income)
Overhead Variance = Actual Overhead - Budgeted Overhead

nodes.name: Overhead to be Allocated
aliases: Total Indirect Costs to be Allocated
nodes.definition: Overhead to be allocated refers to the total amount of indirect costs that need to be apportioned to various cost objects (such as products, projects, or departments) according to specific allocation bases during the cost accounting process. It is typically aggregated from multiple common expenses that cannot be directly attributed to specific cost objects (such as management salaries, office expenses, utilities, depreciation, etc.) and serves as the basis for calculating the overhead allocation rate.

formulas.source_formula: Overhead to be Allocated = Overhead Allocation Rate × Total Allocation Base

nodes.name: Overleveraged
nodes.definition: Overleveraged refers to a condition in which a company has an excessive amount of debt relative to its equity and earnings capacity, elevating refinancing, liquidity, and default risks. A primary indicator is the Debt-to-Equity Ratio, which compares total debt to shareholders’ equity; higher values signal greater financial leverage and potential overleveraging.

nodes.name: Overnight Index Swap
nodes.definition: An Overnight Index Swap (OIS) is an interest rate swap where the floating leg is linked to a compounded overnight rate over the accrual period, while the fixed leg pays a predetermined rate. The benefit calculated here represents the incremental gain from compounding at the overnight index rate over the swap horizon relative to the initial one-day accrual (adjusted for weekend conventions), using a 360-day money market day-count convention.

nodes.name: Oversold
nodes.definition: Oversold refers to a market condition in which an asset has experienced sustained selling pressure, driving its price lower and momentum indicators (commonly the Relative Strength Index, RSI) to levels that suggest the decline may be overextended. A typical technical benchmark flags oversold when RSI falls below a predefined threshold (e.g., 30), signaling potential mean reversion risk but not guaranteeing a price rebound.

nodes.name: Overtime Pay
nodes.definition: Overtime pay is the portion of wage expense compensated at a premium rate for hours worked beyond the standard workweek (commonly 40 hours). It represents incremental labor cost recognized when employees exceed standard hours under statutory or company policy.

nodes.name: Overwriting Yield
nodes.definition: Overwriting yield measures the combined income rate generated by a dividend-paying stock when call options are written against the position (covered call). It is calculated as the sum of the stock's dividend yield and the option premium yield over the same period, typically expressed as a fraction.

formulas.source_formula: Overwriting Yield = Dividend Yield + Option Premium Yield

nodes.name: Own Price of a Good
nodes.definition: The own price of a good refers to the monetary amount a consumer must pay to purchase one unit of the good, serving as a direct factor influencing consumer purchasing decisions and market demand.

nodes.name: Owner Earnings Run Rate
aliases: 所有者收益年化运行率
nodes.definition: Owner earnings run rate is an extrapolated measure that annualizes or scales recent owner earnings over a chosen forecast horizon, assuming consistent performance. It estimates future owner-oriented cash generation based on observed periods and is useful for forward-looking valuation and budgeting, but it may be unreliable for highly seasonal or volatile businesses.

formulas.source_formula: Owner Earnings = Reported Earnings + Depreciation and Amortization + Other Non-Cash Charges - Average Maintenance Capital Expenditures + Change in Working Capital

nodes.name: Owner's Equity Translated into Renminbi
nodes.definition: Owner's Equity Translated into Renminbi refers to the process, when an enterprise prepares consolidated financial statements or translates foreign currency financial statements, of converting owner's equity items denominated in foreign currency (such as paid-in capital, capital reserve, surplus reserve, and undistributed profits) into amounts denominated in Renminbi, in accordance with specific accounting standards (such as China's Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises) and exchange rates (such as the spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date, historical exchange rates, etc.). This process is a crucial component of foreign currency financial statement translation, and its results affect the balance of the translated statements and the calculation of translation differences.

nodes.name: Owners' Equity
nodes.definition: Owners' equity refers to the residual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities, representing the owners' claim on the net assets. It reflects the financial position and operating results of an enterprise at a specific date, also known as shareholders' equity or net assets.

nodes.name: Owners' Equity at the Beginning of the Year
P/E 10 Ratio
nodes.definition: The P/E 10 Ratio, also known as the CAPE or Shiller P/E, measures equity market valuation by dividing the current index level by the average of inflation-adjusted earnings per share (EPS) over the past 10 years. It smooths short-term earnings volatility and uses CPI-based adjustments to express historical EPS in current-year dollars.

formulas.source_formula: P/E 10 Ratio = Current Index Level ÷ Average Real EPS (10 Years)
P/E Ratio = Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share (EPS)

nodes.name: PDCA Cycle
nodes.definition: The PDCA Cycle is an iterative four-stage management method widely used in quality management and process improvement. It drives continuous improvement and optimization of work or projects through the cyclical repetition of the four stages: Plan, Do, Check, and Act.

nodes.name: Paasche Price Index
nodes.definition: The Paasche Price Index is a price index calculated using the quantities of the reporting period (current period) as weights, used to measure the average change in prices of a basket of goods and services from the base period to the reporting period. It reflects the impact of price changes on total cost or total expenditure under the current consumption or production structure.

nodes.name: Packaging Costs
nodes.definition: Packaging costs refer to all expenditures related to packaging materials incurred by an enterprise during the production, sales, or transportation of products, for the purposes of protection, decoration, storage, transportation, and sales facilitation. These expenditures typically include the procurement cost of packaging materials, labor costs for packaging operations, and related indirect expenses.

nodes.name: Paid-Up Capital
nodes.definition: Paid-up capital is the amount of equity that shareholders have actually contributed to the company in exchange for issued shares. It equals the sum of the par (nominal) value of issued shares and the share premium (additional paid-in capital) received over par, and is presented within shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Paid-Up Capital = (Par Value × Number of Shares) + ((Issue Price - Par Value) × Number of Shares)

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital
nodes.definition: Paid-in capital refers to the total amount of capital actually received from shareholders, reflecting the funds that shareholders have actually contributed. It represents the paid-up portion of the company's registered capital and is a significant component of shareholders' equity on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital Eligible Portion
nodes.definition: The Paid-in Capital Eligible Portion refers to the capital actually contributed by shareholders to the enterprise and already credited to the account. This portion of capital forms the foundation of the enterprise's owner's equity, reflects the actual capital contribution by shareholders, and serves as a crucial component in calculating regulatory capital such as Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1).

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital at Beginning of Year
aliases: Paid-in Capital at the Beginning of the Year
nodes.definition: Paid-in capital at the beginning of the year refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by shareholders to the enterprise at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1st), in accordance with laws or the company's articles of association. It includes various forms of contributions such as cash, physical assets, intellectual property rights, and land use rights. It is a point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, reflecting the enterprise's capital base at the beginning of the year.

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital at End of First Quarter
aliases: Paid-in Capital at the End of Q1
nodes.definition: Paid-in capital at the end of the first quarter refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and received by shareholders or investors as of the close of the first quarter (typically January 1 to March 31), reflecting the status of registered capital actually paid up by the company at the end of the first quarter.

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital at End of Q2
aliases: Paid-in Capital at the End of Q2
nodes.definition: Paid-in capital at the end of the second quarter refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed and received by all investors as of the close of the second quarter (typically April 1 to June 30), reflecting the status of registered capital actually paid up at the mid-year point.

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital at Period End
nodes.definition: Paid-in capital at period end refers to the total amount of capital actually contributed by all shareholders and recorded in the accounts at the end of an accounting period. It is a core component of owners' equity. Its value is calculated from the opening balance, additions during the period, and reductions during the period, reflecting the final outcome of shareholders' actual investment in the enterprise.

operands.metric: Additions to Paid-in Capital during the Period
Reductions to Paid-in Capital during the Period

formulas.source_formula: Paid-in Capital at Period End = Opening Balance of Paid-in Capital + Additions to Paid-in Capital during the Period - Reductions to Paid-in Capital during the Period

nodes.name: Paid-in Capital at the End of the First Quarter
Paid-in Registered Capital Ratio
nodes.definition: The Paid-in Registered Capital Ratio refers to the proportion of a new shareholder's capital contribution to the company's total capital after capital increase (or company valuation) following an equity investment through capital increase. It is a key intermediate variable for calculating accounting items such as subsidiary capital surplus.

formulas.source_formula: Paid-in Registered Capital Ratio = New Shareholder's Investment Amount ÷ Company Valuation
Paid-in Registered Capital Ratio = New Shareholder's Investment Amount ÷ Total Capital After Capital Increase

nodes.name: Pair Trade Profit (Long-Short Equity)
nodes.definition: Pair trade profit in long-short equity is the net profit or loss from concurrently holding a long position in one stock and a short position in another, computed as the sum of the long-leg gain and the short-leg gain. The measure typically assumes simultaneous closure of both legs and excludes transaction costs, financing charges, and taxes.

formulas.source_formula: Pair Trade Profit = (Long Price Final - Long Price Initial) × Long Shares + (Short Price Initial - Short Price Final) × Short Shares

nodes.name: Paired t-Statistic
nodes.definition: The paired t-statistic measures the standardized mean difference between two related samples (matched pairs or repeated measures). In financial and accounting analysis, it is used to test whether pre- and post-event metrics (e.g., returns, costs, or efficiency measures) differ significantly, assuming normally distributed paired differences and independence across pairs.

nodes.name: Par Value
nodes.definition: Par value is the stated face value of a bond that is repaid to the holder at maturity. It serves as the benchmark for assessing whether a bond is trading at par, at a premium, or at a discount by comparing the bond's current market value to its par value.

nodes.name: Par Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Par value per share refers to the legal price per share set in the company's articles of association when a joint-stock company issues shares, usually denominated in yuan/share. It represents the amount of legal capital corresponding to each share and serves as the basis for share issuance and accounting. In China's A-share market, the par value per share for the vast majority of stocks is fixed at 1 RMB, with exceptions for individual companies (such as Zijin Mining).

nodes.name: Par Value of Preferred Stock
nodes.definition: Par value of preferred stock refers to the nominal value per share explicitly stated on the stock certificate or in the company's articles of incorporation at the time of issuance.
