nodes.definition: Planned production output refers to the predetermined quantity of products that an enterprise plans to manufacture within a specific planning period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual), based on factors such as market demand, production capacity, and resource availability. It serves as a crucial basis for production management and budget preparation.

nodes.name: Planned Production Volume
nodes.definition: Planned production volume refers to the predetermined quantity of products a company aims to complete within a specific production cycle (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or annual), based on factors such as market demand, production capacity, and resource availability. It serves as a critical foundational data point for production planning and budget formulation.

nodes.name: Planned Production and Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Planned production and sales volume refers to the quantitative targets set by an enterprise during the budgeting or planning stage for the expected production and sales of a specific product over a future period (e.g., monthly, quarterly, or annual). It serves as fundamental input data for formulating production and sales plans, production budgets, and sales budgets.

nodes.name: Planned Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Planned profit margin refers to the pre-determined, expected ratio of profit to relevant revenue or cost set by an enterprise during project or business planning. It reflects the enterprise's anticipated target for profitability over a specific period and is commonly used in project budgeting, cost control, and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Planned Sales Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Planned Sales Growth Rate is the percentage increase in planned sales revenue for the current year compared to the previous year's sales revenue. It is a core financial metric for measuring a company's market expansion capability and growth potential, commonly used in financial forecasting and budgeting.

formulas.source_formula: Planned Sales Growth Rate = (Current Year Sales - Previous Year Sales) ÷ Previous Year Sales

nodes.name: Planned Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Planned sales revenue is an expected revenue indicator calculated based on sales forecasts for future periods, derived from planned sales volume and planned unit selling price. It belongs to composite budget data in management accounting, used for corporate financial planning, performance evaluation, and profit forecasting, and often serves as the basis for calculating derivative indicators such as planned net profit margin on sales.

formulas.source_formula: Planned Sales Revenue = Planned Sales Volume × Planned Unit Selling Price
supporting_source_formulas: Planned Sales Revenue = Planned Sales Volume × Planned Unit Selling Price

formulas.source_formula: Planned Sales Revenue = Previous Year's Sales Revenue × (1 + Planned Sales Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Planned Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Planned sales volume refers to the number of units of products or services that a company plans or expects to sell during a specific budget or forecast period (such as a fiscal year or quarter). It serves as the fundamental raw data for developing sales budgets, revenue forecasts, and resource allocation.

nodes.name: Planned Selling Expenses
nodes.definition: Planned selling expenses refer to the total estimated and approved expenditures for various marketing and sales activities, pre-planned by an enterprise within the budget period to achieve its sales targets. It is a fundamental data item in the enterprise's budget statements, typically serving as the starting point for budget preparation or as a direct input item.

nodes.name: Planned Selling Price per Unit
nodes.definition: Planned selling price per unit refers to the predetermined expected selling price set for each unit of product or service when formulating sales budgets or making pricing decisions. It is typically determined based on a comprehensive analysis of factors such as market research, cost analysis, competitive strategy, and profit targets, and serves as the foundational data for calculating planned sales revenue and sales volume.

nodes.name: Planned Target Figures
nodes.definition: Planned target figures refer to the specific quantitative targets, in terms of number or value, pre-established by an enterprise or organization within a particular planning or budgeting period, used to measure and evaluate future operating results, financial conditions, or management performance.

nodes.name: Planned Tax Incentive Reduction Amount
nodes.definition: Planned Tax Incentive Reduction Amount refers to the total sum of various tax incentives, reductions, or refunds that an enterprise expects to enjoy during a specific future period, based on current tax laws, regulations, and policies, when preparing financial budgets or plans.

nodes.name: Planned Taxable Income
nodes.definition: Planned taxable income refers to the pre-estimated amount of income that an enterprise or taxpayer expects to realize in a future specific period (such as an accounting year) and that is subject to corporate income tax, as part of financial budgeting or tax planning. It serves as the basis for calculating planned income tax expense.

nodes.name: Planned Taxes and Surcharges
nodes.definition: Planned Taxes and Surcharges refer to various taxes and surcharge expenses that an enterprise estimates in advance and includes in the planned total profit when preparing financial budgets or operating plans, based on projected data such as operating revenue and profit.

nodes.name: Planned Total Profit
nodes.definition: Planned Total Profit refers to the sum of all profits a company expects to achieve within a specific planning period (e.g., annual, quarterly). It is a core indicator for measuring the overall profitability of the enterprise during the planning period and serves as the basis for calculating Planned Net Profit.

formulas.source_formula: Planned Total Profit = Planned Operating Profit + Planned Non-operating Income - Planned Non-operating Expenses

nodes.name: Planned Unit Selling Price
nodes.definition: Planned Unit Selling Price refers to the pre-determined, expected market sales price set by an enterprise for each unit of product during operational planning. It is a fundamental planning parameter established based on a comprehensive analysis of market conditions, product costs, competitive landscape, and corporate strategic objectives (such as market share and profit targets), used for subsequent revenue forecasting, profit planning, and budget preparation.

nodes.name: Planned Usage
nodes.definition: Planned usage refers to the predetermined quantity or monetary amount of raw materials, energy, labor, or other resources that an enterprise or project is expected to consume within a specific period, based on production plans, budgets, or operational schemes. It serves as a crucial benchmark for cost control, inventory management, and efficiency evaluation.

nodes.name: Planned Value-Added Tax
nodes.definition: Planned Value-Added Tax refers to the estimated amount of VAT calculated in advance and included in the planned business tax and surcharges item during the preparation of financial budgets or operating plans, based on projected taxable sales and applicable tax rates. It reflects the enterprise's anticipated VAT liability for a specific future period.

nodes.name: Planned Variable Cost Per Unit
nodes.definition: Planned variable cost per unit refers to the predetermined unit cost that varies proportionally with product output or sales volume within a specific planning or budgeting period, set to achieve established operational objectives (such as target profit). It is a key parameter in cost-volume-profit analysis, budget preparation, and cost control.

nodes.name: Plowback Ratio
nodes.definition: The plowback ratio (retention ratio) measures the proportion of a company's earnings that is retained and reinvested rather than distributed as dividends. It equals one minus the dividend payout ratio and indicates a firm’s reinvestment policy and potential for internal growth.

formulas.source_formula: Plowback Ratio = 1 - (Dividends per Share ÷ Earnings per Share)

nodes.name: Point-and-Figure (P&F) Chart
nodes.definition: A point-and-figure chart is a price-only technical analysis chart that plots columns of Xs (rising prices) and Os (falling prices) to filter out minor price fluctuations and highlight trend direction and breakouts. The O-column addition condition evaluates whether the current price has declined by at least one box size from the last recorded O, thereby warranting the plotting of a new O to extend the downward column.

nodes.name: Point-and-Figure Add X Signal
aliases: 点数图上升箱体阈值差
nodes.definition: The Point-and-Figure Add X Signal quantifies how far the current price exceeds the upward box threshold in an X column. It is computed as the current price minus the sum of the last recorded X price and the box size. A non-negative signal indicates that the price movement is sufficient to add a new X to the current column under standard Point-and-Figure charting rules.

nodes.name: Point-and-Figure Reversal Amount
nodes.definition: The Point-and-Figure (P&F) reversal amount is the price change required to reverse the direction of columns (from X to O or O to X) on a P&F chart. It is calculated as the product of the box size and a chosen multiplier, commonly three for a three-box reversal, and determines the sensitivity of the chart to price reversals.

nodes.name: Poisson Distribution
nodes.definition: The Poisson distribution models the probability of observing a given number of discrete events within a fixed interval when events occur independently at a constant average rate. In finance and risk management, it is applied to event counts such as defaults, claim arrivals, operational loss incidents, system failures, or customer arrivals, supporting frequency modeling and loss forecasting.

nodes.name: Poisson Probability
nodes.definition: Poisson probability quantifies the likelihood of observing exactly a specified number of events in a fixed interval given an average event rate, assuming independent occurrences. In finance, it is used to model rare-event counts such as credit defaults, insurance claims, fraud incidents, or operational losses.

nodes.name: Policy Sensitivity Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Policy Sensitivity Coefficient is a quantitative measure that gauges the sensitivity of key performance indicators (such as profit, revenue, valuation, etc.) of a specific industry or company to changes in particular policy factors (such as interest rates, tax rates, industry regulations, etc.). It indicates the percentage change in the performance indicator resulting from a one percent change in the policy factor.

nodes.name: Pool Factor
nodes.definition: Pool factor is the ratio of the current face value (remaining principal) to the original face value (initial principal) of a mortgage-backed security (MBS), indicating the proportion of principal still outstanding.

formulas.source_formula: Pool Factor = Current Face Value ÷ Original Face Value

nodes.name: Population Mean
nodes.definition: The population mean is the average of all data points in a population in statistics, calculated as the sum of all observations divided by the number of observations. Also known as the population mathematical expectation, it is used to describe the central tendency of a dataset and serves as the basis for calculating statistics such as standard deviation.

nodes.name: Population Mean Return of Security j
aliases: Average Rate of Return for Security j
第j种资产的平均收益率
证券j的预期回报率均值
nodes.definition: The population mean return of security j refers to the expected value obtained by taking the probability-weighted average of all possible future returns (or yields) that could be realized for security j (or asset j) in statistics and finance. It represents an investor's expectation of the average future return level for that security after considering all possible outcomes and their probabilities of occurrence.

nodes.name: Population Mean of Random Variable
aliases: Expected Value of a Random Variable
nodes.definition: The population mean of a random variable, also known as the mathematical expectation or expected value of the population, is an indicator that describes the average level of all possible values of the random variable. It represents the average outcome of the random variable over the long term or in a large number of repeated trials.

nodes.name: Population Size
aliases: Total Number of Observations in Population
nodes.definition: Population size refers to the total number of individuals, units, or observations in the population of a study or statistical analysis. It serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating statistical measures such as population variance and is typically denoted by the uppercase letter N.

formulas.source_formula: Population Size = Initial Population × (1 + Growth Rate) ^ Time Periods

nodes.name: Population Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Population standard deviation is a statistical measure used to quantify the dispersion or volatility of all data points in a complete dataset (i.e., the population) relative to its population mean. A larger value indicates a more dispersed data distribution, while a smaller value indicates a more concentrated data distribution.

nodes.name: Population Standard Deviation of Random Variable
aliases: Standard Deviation of a Random Variable
nodes.definition: The population standard deviation of a random variable is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion or volatility between all possible values of the random variable and its population mean. It represents the average magnitude of fluctuation in the random variable's values; a larger value indicates greater dispersion of the random variable's values and higher uncertainty or risk.

nodes.name: Population Variance
nodes.definition: Population variance is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of all data points in a population from the population mean, reflecting the volatility or risk level of the population data. In financial analysis, it is commonly used to measure the overall volatility risk of asset returns.

nodes.name: Portfolio Beginning Value
nodes.definition: Portfolio beginning value refers to the total market value of all assets (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.) held within a portfolio at the start of a specific analysis or reporting period. It serves as the baseline data for measuring portfolio size, calculating period returns, or conducting performance analysis.

nodes.name: Portfolio Beta
nodes.definition: The portfolio beta is the weighted average of the beta coefficients of the individual securities in the portfolio, reflecting the overall sensitivity of the portfolio to market fluctuations.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Beta = Asset Weights × Asset Betas

nodes.name: Portfolio Cost
nodes.definition: Portfolio cost refers to the total expenses required to construct or maintain an investment portfolio, including transaction costs, management fees, cost of capital, etc. It is typically calculated through specific expense items rather than being a direct fundamental data point, and is commonly used in financial analysis for evaluations such as option valuation.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Cost = Weighted Average Cost of Capital × Portfolio Market Value

nodes.name: Portfolio Current Net Value
nodes.definition: Portfolio current net value refers to the net amount obtained by subtracting all related liabilities (such as borrowings, accrued expenses, etc.) from the total current market value of all assets (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) in an investment portfolio at a specific valuation point in time. It reflects the actual value of the portfolio at the present moment and is a key metric for measuring investment performance and risk exposure.

nodes.name: Portfolio Diversification
nodes.definition: Portfolio diversification is the process of allocating total investment across multiple asset categories in specified proportions to reduce financial exposure and mitigate risk.

nodes.name: Portfolio Duration
nodes.definition: Portfolio duration refers to the estimated number of years a retirement portfolio can sustain constant inflation-adjusted withdrawals before depletion, given initial balance, withdrawal rate, expected return, and inflation rate.

nodes.name: Portfolio Ending Value
aliases: 投资组合期末预期价值
nodes.definition: Portfolio ending value refers to the expected total value of a portfolio at the end of a specific evaluation period. It is calculated by summing the expected ending values of all constituent securities (i.e., the number of shares held for each security multiplied by its expected per-share ending value). This serves as a fundamental composite metric for measuring the future value performance of a portfolio and calculating portfolio returns.

nodes.name: Portfolio Expected Return
nodes.definition: Portfolio expected return refers to the average rate of return that a portfolio is likely to achieve in the future, calculated as the weighted average of the expected returns of its constituent assets based on their respective weights in the portfolio. It is a core metric for measuring the return level of an investment portfolio.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Expected Return = Risk-Free Rate + Portfolio Beta × (Market Portfolio Expected Return - Risk-Free Rate)

nodes.name: Portfolio Expenses
nodes.definition: Portfolio expenses refer to the cumulative costs incurred during the management and trading of a portfolio, including periodic fees calculated based on the market value of held assets (such as management fees) and transaction costs (such as commissions and stamp duties). They are typically deducted when calculating net asset value, consistent with the definition of a non-leaf node.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Expenses = Total Transaction Commissions + Total Stamp Duties + Total Other Transaction Costs

nodes.name: Portfolio Market Value
nodes.definition: Portfolio market value refers to the total value of all assets in a portfolio calculated at current market prices, obtained by summing the market values of individual assets. It is a decomposable composite metric commonly used in financial analysis such as portfolio cost calculation.

nodes.name: Portfolio Return
nodes.definition: Portfolio return refers to the rate of return on an investment portfolio over a specific period, typically calculated as the weighted average of individual asset returns or the change in portfolio value. It reflects the overall profitability of the portfolio, is a composite metric, and is commonly used to evaluate investment performance and the increase in net asset value.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Return = (Portfolio Ending Value - Portfolio Beginning Value) ÷ Portfolio Beginning Value
Portfolio Return = Risk-Free Rate + ((Market Return - Risk-Free Rate) ÷ Market Standard Deviation) × Portfolio Standard Deviation
Portfolio Return = Stock Allocation × Stock Return + Bond Allocation × Bond Return

nodes.name: Portfolio Return Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Portfolio return standard deviation is a composite risk metric calculated using data such as the returns, weights, standard deviations, and correlation coefficients of the assets within the portfolio. It is used to measure the volatility or risk level of the overall portfolio return.

nodes.name: Portfolio Risk (Standard Deviation)
nodes.definition: Portfolio risk (standard deviation) measures the volatility of portfolio returns. Under Modern Portfolio Theory, it is computed as the square root of the double-sum of pairwise covariances, using asset weights, asset standard deviations (derived from variances), and their correlation coefficients.

nodes.name: Portfolio Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Portfolio standard deviation is a measure of the overall risk of an investment portfolio, taking into account the covariance relationships among individual securities.

nodes.name: Portfolio Turnover
nodes.definition: Portfolio turnover measures the rate at which a fund's holdings are bought and sold over a period. It is commonly calculated as the lesser of total purchases or total sales divided by average assets, and reported as a percentage. Higher turnover may indicate more active trading, potentially leading to higher transaction costs and tax implications.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Turnover Rate (%) = (min(Total Purchases, Total Sales) ÷ Average Monthly Assets) × 100

nodes.name: Portfolio Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: Portfolio turnover ratio measures the proportion of a portfolio's holdings traded during a specific period, indicating the level of trading activity and management intensity. It is commonly computed as the value of securities sold divided by the portfolio's total assets at the beginning of the period.

formulas.source_formula: Portfolio Turnover Ratio = Sale Proceeds ÷ Total Assets

nodes.name: Portfolio Variance
nodes.definition: Portfolio variance is the quantitative measure of the total risk of an investment portfolio under Modern Portfolio Theory. It aggregates asset volatilities and their co-movements via the covariance matrix, reflecting how diversification and correlation among assets influence overall portfolio risk.

nodes.name: Portfolio Vega
nodes.definition: Portfolio vega measures the aggregate sensitivity of an options portfolio to changes in implied volatility, calculated as the sum of vega from long positions minus the sum of vega from short positions.

nodes.name: Portfolio Weight
nodes.definition: Portfolio weight refers to the proportion of the market value of each asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) within a portfolio relative to the total market value of the entire portfolio. It measures the importance and influence of each asset in the portfolio and serves as key foundational data for asset allocation, risk management, and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Portion of Annual Taxable Income Exceeding 1 Million Yuan but Not Exceeding 3 Million Yuan
aliases: Taxable Income Portion between 1 million and 3 million RMB
小微企业所得税优惠区间
nodes.definition: Refers to the portion of calculated taxable income for a qualified small and low-profit enterprise within a tax year that is greater than 1 million yuan but less than or equal to 3 million yuan. According to preferential tax policies, this portion of income is eligible for specific reductions or exemptions when calculating corporate income tax.

nodes.name: Portion of Annual Taxable Income Not Exceeding 1 Million Yuan
aliases: Annual Taxable Income Not Exceeding 1 Million CNY
小微企业所得税优惠区间
nodes.definition: Refers to the portion of calculated annual taxable income that is less than or equal to 1 million RMB for eligible small and low-profit enterprises or individual businesses. This portion of income is typically subject to special preferential tax policies, such as being included in taxable income at a reduced percentage and taxed at preferential rates.

nodes.name: Portion of Taxable Income from Individual Industrial and Commercial Household Business Operations Not Exceeding RMB 1 Million
aliases: Portion of Individual Business Operating Income Taxable Income Not Exceeding 1 Million Yuan
Taxable Income Portion ≤ 1 Million for Individual Businesses
个体工商户年应纳税所得额不超100万部分
个体户应纳税所得额100万以下部分
个体户经营所得100万以内部分
nodes.definition: Refers to the portion of the taxable income from business operations calculated according to tax laws for an individual industrial and commercial household within a tax year that is less than or equal to RMB 1 million. This amount serves as the basis for enjoying the specific preferential policy of halving the individual income tax.

nodes.name: Portion of Taxable Income from Individual Industrial and Commercial Household Business Operations Not Exceeding RMB 2 Million
aliases: Portion of Individual Business Income Taxable Income Not Exceeding 2 Million Yuan
Taxable Business Income of Individual Industrial and Commercial Households Within 2 Million
应纳税所得额200万以内减半部分
nodes.definition: Refers to the portion of taxable income from business operations of an individual industrial and commercial household in a tax year, after calculation, that does not exceed RMB 2 million. According to current preferential tax policies, this portion of taxable income is eligible for a 50% reduction in individual income tax.

nodes.name: Position Opening Fee
nodes.definition: Position opening fee refers to the fee paid by investors to brokers or exchanges for establishing new trading positions (buying or selling) in financial markets such as stocks, futures, and foreign exchange.

nodes.name: Position Quantity
nodes.definition: Position quantity refers to the specific number or units of a particular financial asset (such as stocks, bonds, fund shares, futures contracts, etc.) held in an investor's trading account or investment portfolio at a specific point in time. It serves as fundamental data for calculating profit and loss, risk assessment, and asset allocation.

nodes.name: Position Size
nodes.definition: Position size is the number of shares or contracts allocated to a trade based on a predefined fraction of account capital at risk. In swing trading risk management, it ensures the dollar risk on a trade equals a set percentage of the account, divided by the per-trade risk (e.g., entry-to-stop distance). Practitioners commonly round the resulting quantity down to the nearest whole unit to comply with trading constraints.

formulas.source_formula: Position Size = (Account Size × Risk Percentage) ÷ Risk per Trade
Position Value Change = (Exit Index Level - Entry Index Level) × Contract Multiplier

nodes.name: Positive Correlation
nodes.definition: Positive correlation describes a relationship in which two variables move in the same direction: increases in one variable are associated with increases in the other, and decreases with decreases. In finance, it indicates that asset returns, sales, or economic indicators tend to co-move. The strength and direction are quantified by the correlation coefficient (r), ranging from -1 to +1; r > 0 denotes positive correlation, with r = +1 indicating a perfect positive linear relationship.

nodes.name: Positive Volume Index
nodes.definition: Positive Volume Index (PVI) is a technical indicator that adjusts its value only when the current trading volume is higher than the previous day's volume, reflecting price movements influenced by increased trading activity.

formulas.source_formula: PVI = PVI_previous
PVI = PVI_previous + ((Closing Price_today - Closing Price_yesterday) ÷ Closing Price_yesterday × PVI_previous)

nodes.name: Possible Rate of Return
nodes.definition: Possible rate of return refers to the return that an asset may achieve within a single investment period, typically consisting of two components: the return generated from interest or dividend income received during the holding period, and the return resulting from changes in asset price (capital gains or losses). It serves as the basis for calculating the expected rate of return on an asset.

nodes.name: Possible Returns of Market Portfolio under Various Scenarios
aliases: 市场组合预期收益率情景
nodes.definition: Possible returns of the market portfolio under various scenarios refer to the potential returns that may be achieved by the market portfolio, which consists of all risky assets in the market, under different economic or market conditions (such as boom, normal, recession, etc.). It reflects the performance of the market portfolio under different future scenarios and serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating market portfolio risk (e.g., standard deviation) and asset pricing (e.g., the CAPM model).

formulas.source_formula: Post-Acquisition EPS = (Initial Earnings + Acquisition Earnings) ÷ (Initial Shares + New Shares)

nodes.name: Post-Credit Tax Liability
nodes.definition: Post-Credit Tax Liability is the amount of tax owed after applying all eligible tax credits. It is calculated by subtracting the total tax credits from the tax liability before credits, typically constrained to be no less than zero under tax compliance rules.

formulas.source_formula: Post-Credit Tax Liability = Tax Liability Before Credits - Total Tax Credits

nodes.name: Post-Money Valuation
nodes.definition: Post-money valuation refers to the assessment of a company's total enterprise value based on newly injected capital after completing a round of equity financing. It equals the sum of the pre-money valuation and the total amount raised in the financing round, serving as the basis for determining the equity stake acquired by new investors.

formulas.source_formula: Post-money Valuation = Pre-money Valuation + Investment Amount
Post-Money Valuation = Pre-Money Valuation + New Equity

nodes.name: Post-Restructuring Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: Cash and Cash Equivalents after Restructuring
nodes.definition: Post-restructuring cash and cash equivalents refer to the amount of cash and cash equivalents presented in a company's financial statements after completing a restructuring (such as debt restructuring, business reorganization, or mergers and acquisitions). It reflects the actual holdings of cash on hand, bank deposits, other monetary funds, and short-term investments meeting the definition of cash equivalents (short-term, highly liquid, readily convertible to known amounts of cash, and subject to insignificant risk of value changes) that are available for immediate payment following a specific restructuring event.

nodes.name: Post-Restructuring Continuing Value Present Value
aliases: Present Value of Continuing Period Value
nodes.definition: Post-Restructuring Continuing Value Present Value refers to the present value, discounted to the current point in time, of the value of a restructured enterprise after it enters a stable perpetual growth phase following the forecast period. It is typically calculated based on free cash flow, discount rate, and perpetual growth rate, and is used in business valuation to determine the total enterprise value.

operands.metric: First Year Continuing Period Free Cash Flow

formulas.source_formula: Post-Restructuring Continuing Value Present Value = First Year Continuing Period Free Cash Flow ÷ (Discount Rate - Perpetual Growth Rate) ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Forecast Period Years

operands.metric: Final Year Forecast Free Cash Flow

formulas.source_formula: Post-Restructuring Continuing Value Present Value = [Final Year Forecast Free Cash Flow × (1 + Perpetual Growth Rate) ÷ (Discount Rate - Perpetual Growth Rate)] ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Forecast Period Years

nodes.name: Post-Restructuring Equity Market Value
nodes.definition: Post-restructuring equity market value is the total market value of a company's equity calculated after completing a restructuring (such as a merger, acquisition, or asset restructuring). It is derived either based on its expected profitability (e.g., net profit) and market valuation multiples (e.g., P/E ratio), or according to its stock price and total shares outstanding. This metric is a composite indicator rather than a fundamental raw data point. It is commonly used to assess the overall value of a restructured enterprise and serves as a basis for calculating the new enterprise value.

formulas.source_formula: Post-Restructuring Equity Market Value = Post-Restructuring Net Profit × P/E Ratio

nodes.name: Post-Restructuring Free Cash Flows by Period
aliases: Free Cash Flow to the Firm
nodes.definition: Post-restructuring free cash flows by period refer to the free cash flows in each future forecast period after a corporate merger or restructuring, used to assess the new enterprise value. It is a composite metric calculated based on the Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) model, reflecting the cash flow generation capacity created by the restructured enterprise for all capital providers.

formulas.source_formula: Post-Restructuring Free Cash Flows by Period = EBIT × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation and Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Increase in Working Capital
Post-Restructuring Free Cash Flows by Period = Net Profit After Tax + Interest Expense × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Depreciation and Amortization - Capital Expenditures - Increase in Working Capital

nodes.name: Post-Rise Option Value
aliases: Call Option Value after Price Rise
上涨状态看涨期权价格
nodes.definition: Post-rise option value refers to the value of a call option calculated based on its intrinsic value after the stock market price has risen, reflecting the minimum return that option holders can obtain at expiration or under specific conditions, commonly used in option pricing and financial derivatives analysis.

nodes.name: Post-change Value
nodes.definition: Post-change value refers to the new value obtained after a specific change (such as a percentage increase/decrease or adjustment) is applied to an original value (e.g., cost, revenue, assets) in financial analysis or calculation. It is commonly used in sensitivity analysis, budgeting, and performance evaluation to measure the impact of parameter changes on outcomes.

formulas.source_formula: Adjusted Value = Base Value × (1 + Percentage Change ÷ 100)
Adjusted Value = Base Value × (1 + Percentage Change × Sensitivity Factor ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Post-promotional Monthly Payment
aliases: Monthly Payment after 0% APR Promotional Period
促销期后的每月还款额
零利率促销期后每月还款额
nodes.definition: Post-promotional monthly payment is the fixed payment required to amortize an outstanding balance after an introductory zero percent interest promotional period, calculated using the standard level-payment annuity formula based on the post-promotional annual interest rate and an assumed 12-month repayment term.

formulas.source_formula: Post-promotional Monthly Payment = Outstanding Balance × (Post-promotional Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12) ÷ (1 - (1 + (Post-promotional Annual Interest Rate ÷ 12))^-Repayment Period)

nodes.name: Post-restructuring Debt Market Value
nodes.definition: Post-restructuring debt market value refers to the fair value of debt redetermined according to the terms of a restructuring agreement (including settlement assets, equity conversion arrangements, and contingent payment obligations, etc.) in a debt restructuring transaction. It reflects the market value of the restructured debt on the measurement date and is a key parameter for revaluing debt when calculating enterprise value.

operands.metric: Fair Value of Non-cash Settlement Assets
Present Value of Contingent Payment Amount

formulas.source_formula: Post-restructuring Debt Market Value = Book Value of Restructured Debt - (Cash Settlement + Fair Value of Non-cash Settlement Assets + Fair Value of Equity Conversion) + Present Value of Contingent Payment Amount

nodes.name: Posterior Probability
nodes.definition: Posterior probability refers to the updated and revised probability of a hypothesis or event occurring after obtaining new evidence or data. It is a core concept in Bayesian statistics, calculated by combining prior probability with new observational information.

formulas.source_formula: Posterior Probability = (Prior Probability × Likelihood) ÷ Marginal Probability
Potential Earnings = Actual Earnings ÷ (1 - Fee Percent ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Potential Employment
nodes.definition: Potential employment is a macroeconomic concept referring to the highest sustainable level of employment an economy can achieve without triggering accelerating inflation, given the existing technological level, capital stock, and institutional environment. It is typically associated with the calculation of potential GDP and reflects the degree of labor utilization in the long-run equilibrium state of the economy.

nodes.name: Potential GDP
nodes.definition: Potential GDP refers to the sustainable maximum output level an economy can achieve under existing technological conditions, at full employment (i.e., all factors of production, particularly labor, are fully utilized) and with stable prices. It is a theoretical estimate used to measure an economy's long-term growth trend and output gap.

formulas.source_formula: Potential GDP = Total Factor Productivity × (Capital Stock ^ Capital Output Elasticity) × (Potential Employment ^ Labor Output Elasticity)

nodes.name: Potential GDP Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Potential GDP growth rate refers to the maximum growth rate of the total volume of goods and services an economy can achieve under conditions where all resources (such as labor, capital, and technology) are optimally and fully utilized. It reflects the economy's long-term sustainable growth capacity without inflationary pressures.

nodes.name: Potential Growth Value
nodes.definition: Potential Growth Value refers to the present value sum of future cash flows that a company can generate after entering a stable growth phase following the forecast period. It is a significant component of the entity value of a company, typically evaluated using the perpetual growth model or exit multiple method, reflecting the company's long-term, sustainable profitability.

nodes.name: Potential Loss from Writing an Option
nodes.definition: Option writer loss measures the monetary outcome per option contract for a short option position at expiration. It equals the option’s intrinsic value at expiry minus the premium received, multiplied by the number of shares per contract. A positive result represents a loss; a negative result represents profit. For a call, intrinsic value at expiry is max(0, Stock Price at Expiry − Strike Price); for a put, intrinsic value at expiry is max(0, Strike Price − Stock Price at Expiry).

formulas.source_formula: Option Writer Loss = (Intrinsic Value at Expiry - Premium Received) × Shares

nodes.name: Potential Risk Exposure
nodes.definition: Potential Risk Exposure refers to the maximum potential loss amount that may be faced in financial transactions or credit activities in the future due to counterparty default, changes in market conditions, or other risk events. It measures the unrealized but possible loss exposure before the occurrence of a risk event.

nodes.name: Pre-Adjusted Stock Price
nodes.definition: Pre-adjusted stock price refers to the market trading price of a stock before corporate actions such as ex-rights, ex-dividends, rights issues, or stock splits, typically the closing price on the last trading day prior to the event. It is the original, unadjusted price data used to calculate adjustment factors to maintain comparability in the price series.

nodes.name: Pre-collected Revenue from Previous Period
aliases: Advance from Customers of Prior Period
nodes.definition: Pre-collected revenue from the previous period refers to the liability formed when a company has received payment from customers for goods or services by the end of the prior accounting period (e.g., previous month, quarter, or year), but has not yet fulfilled or completely fulfilled the related obligations to deliver the goods or provide the services. It reflects the company's obligation for advance receipts from customers at the end of the prior period.

nodes.name: Pre-money Valuation
nodes.definition: Pre-money valuation refers to the total equity or overall value of a company before it receives external investment or financing. This valuation is calculated prior to the injection of new capital into the company's balance sheet and is used to determine the equity stake that investors receive in exchange for their capital contribution.

nodes.name: Pre-reciprocal Allocation Costs
aliases: 交互分配前发生费用额
辅助生产车间原始费用
nodes.definition: Pre-reciprocal allocation costs refer to the total expenses directly accumulated by each auxiliary production department (such as power supply and maintenance workshops) before mutual service provision when using the reciprocal allocation method to distribute auxiliary production costs. These costs typically originate directly from raw cost data such as materials and labor, and serve as the foundational data for subsequent reciprocal allocation.

nodes.name: Pre-tax Accounting Profit
nodes.definition: Pre-tax accounting profit refers to the total profit calculated according to accounting standards before computing and paying income tax. It reflects the net amount obtained by an enterprise from operating activities, investment activities, and financing activities within a certain accounting period, after deducting all related costs, expenses, and losses. It serves as the basis for calculating the current period's income tax payable.

nodes.name: Pre-tax Cost of Borrowing
nodes.definition: Pre-tax cost of borrowing is the after-tax required rate of return demanded by the bank divided by (1 - income tax rate), representing the borrowing cost the company needs to pay before taxes.

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Cost of Borrowing = After-tax Required Rate of Return ÷ (1 - Income Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Pre-tax Cost of Debt
nodes.definition: The pre-tax cost of debt refers to the internal rate of return that a company must pay when issuing bonds or borrowing, in order to make the bond price equal to its present value, i.e., the rate of return required by investors, reflecting the actual cost of using debt financing.

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Cost of Debt = Interest Expense ÷ Total Debt

operands.metric: Yield to Maturity of Comparable Company's Long-term Bond

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Cost of Debt = Yield to Maturity of Comparable Company's Long-term Bond
Pre-tax Cost of Debt = Yield to Maturity of Bond

operands.metric: Market Return Rate of Government Bond

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Cost of Debt = Market Return Rate of Government Bond + Company's Credit Risk Premium Rate
Pre-tax Cost of Debt = Market Return on Government Bonds + Company's Credit Risk Premium
supporting_source_formulas: Pre-tax Cost of Debt = Market Return on Government Bonds + Company's Credit Risk Premium

nodes.name: Pre-tax Cost of Debt for Next Period
aliases: 未来期间税前债务成本
预期税前债务资本成本
nodes.definition: Pre-tax cost of debt for the next period refers to the total cost, expressed as a rate or amount before deducting the impact of income tax, that a company expects to incur for raising and using debt capital (such as loans or bond issuance) during a future period (e.g., the next accounting period or budget cycle). It reflects the rate of return required by creditors for the company's debt in the upcoming period and is typically calculated based on the risk-free rate (e.g., government bond yield) plus a spread compensating for the company's credit risk.

nodes.name: Pre-tax Income
nodes.definition: Pre-tax income refers to the total income of an individual or enterprise calculated according to relevant accounting standards before paying income tax. For individuals, it typically means the total salary and wages before deducting special items such as social security and housing funds; for enterprises, it refers to the total profit before deducting corporate income tax expenses. It serves as the basis for calculating taxable income.

nodes.name: Pre-tax Operating Profit
nodes.definition: Pre-tax operating profit is a company's operating profit before deducting income tax but excluding financial gains and losses, reflecting the profitability of core business activities. It is a composite metric calculated by adjusting total profit or by removing non-operating items from operating profit, commonly used in managerial income statements and financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Operating Profit = Net Operating Profit After Tax ÷ (1 - Income Tax Rate)
Pre-tax Operating Profit = Total Profit + "Interest Expense" in Managerial Income Statement

operands.metric: Net Gains on Fair Value Changes

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Operating Profit = Operating Profit - Other Income - Gains on Asset Disposal - Exchange Gains - Net Investment Income - Net Gains on Fair Value Changes

nodes.name: Pre-tax Profit/Loss After Offering Cash Discount
aliases: Pre-tax Profit from Cash Discount Policy
现金折扣政策的税前利润
nodes.definition: Pre-tax profit/loss after offering cash discount refers to the net income resulting from the difference between increased revenue and increased costs/expenses after a company implements a cash discount policy.

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Profit/Loss After Offering Cash Discount = Increased Revenue - Increased Costs/Expenses

nodes.name: Pre-tax Profit/Loss from Credit Period Change
aliases: Incremental Pre-tax Impact of Credit Period Change
Pre-tax Profit from Credit Period Adjustment
信用期调整的税前利润
nodes.definition: Pre-tax profit/loss from credit period change refers to the change in pre-tax profit calculated by comparing incremental benefits (such as contribution margin from increased sales) and incremental costs (such as bad debt losses, accounts receivable opportunity costs, etc.) after a company adjusts the credit period in its credit policy. It is used to evaluate the financial impact of credit period decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Profit/Loss from Credit Period Change = Increase in Revenue - Increase in Costs and Expenses
Pre-tax Profit/Loss from Credit Period Change = (New Sales - Original Sales) × (1 - Variable Cost Ratio) - Increase in Bad Debt Losses - Increase in Opportunity Costs

nodes.name: Pre-tax Rent
nodes.definition: Pre-tax rent refers to the original rental payment amount in finance leases or operating leases before deducting any related taxes and fees (such as value-added tax, income tax, etc.). It serves as a fundamental input value for calculating financial metrics like the net present value of leases and after-tax cash flows.

nodes.name: Pre-tax Rental Income
nodes.definition: Pre-tax rental income refers to the total rental payments received from lessees before deducting any taxes, loan interest, depreciation, or other costs when leasing assets (such as real estate or equipment). It reflects the original cash inflow generated by leasing activities and serves as a fundamental metric for assessing the initial earning capacity of an asset.

formulas.source_formula: Pre-tax Rental Income = After-tax Rental Income ÷ (1 - Composite Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Predetermined Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The predetermined discount rate is a ratio set in advance based on factors such as market interest rates, the company's cost of capital, and project-specific risks, before conducting financial valuation or investment decisions. It is used to discount future cash flows to their present value and serves as a key input parameter for calculating metrics like net present value, rather than being derived from a fixed formula.

nodes.name: Predetermined Overhead Rate
nodes.definition: The predetermined overhead rate is a budget-based allocation rate used in cost accounting to apply manufacturing overhead to cost objects. It is calculated by dividing budgeted overhead costs by the budgeted level of the chosen activity base (e.g., direct labor hours or machine hours) prior to the period.

formulas.source_formula: Predetermined Overhead Rate = Budgeted Overhead ÷ Budgeted Activity
Predicted Value (Ŷ) = Intercept (a) + Slope (b) × Independent Variable (X)

nodes.name: Preference Shares
nodes.definition: Preference shares (preferred stock) are equity securities that have priority over common stock in dividend distributions and liquidation. For cumulative preferred shares, missed dividends accrue and must be paid before any dividends to common shareholders. The cumulative dividends per share quantify the total unpaid dividends owed to cumulative preferred shareholders by multiplying the periodic (quarterly) dividend per share by the number of missed dividend payments.

nodes.name: Preference Shares Quarterly Dividend
nodes.definition: The quarterly dividend for preference shares is the periodic cash distribution calculated by applying the annual fixed dividend rate to the par value and dividing by four, representing the cash payout to preferred shareholders each quarter for fixed-rate preferred stock.

nodes.name: Preferential Tax Amount
nodes.definition: Preferential tax amount refers to the amount of tax that taxpayers can directly reduce, deduct, or refund when calculating the tax payable in accordance with national tax laws, regulations, and relevant policies. It reflects the actual reduction in tax burden resulting from preferential tax policies.

nodes.name: Preferential Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The preferential tax rate is a key parameter used to calculate preferential tax amounts or tax reductions based on specific tax incentive policies. It is typically not a fixed statutory rate, but rather a percentage determined or calculated according to policy provisions (such as taxable income brackets, enterprise type, etc.), serving as the basis for calculating the reduction in tax payable.

formulas.source_formula: Preferential Tax Rate = Preferential Tax Amount ÷ Taxable Income
Preferential Tax Rate = (Taxable Income × Statutory Tax Rate - Tax Payable) ÷ Taxable Income

nodes.name: Preferred Dividend
nodes.definition: Preferred dividend refers to the dividend compensation paid by a company to preferred shareholders according to the preferred stock charter, based on an agreed fixed dividend rate or amount.

formulas.source_formula: Preferred Dividend = Preferred Stock Par Value × Fixed Dividend Rate
Preferred Dividend = Number of Preferred Shares × Preferred Stock Par Value × Fixed Dividend Rate

nodes.name: Preferred Return
nodes.definition: Preferred return refers to the right of preferred shareholders or specific investors (e.g., in private equity funds) to receive a specific proportion or amount of investment return before common shareholders or general partners during profit distribution or liquidation of a company. This is typically a protective provision ensuring that specific investors recover their invested principal and obtain an agreed minimum return before distributions are made to ordinary participants.

formulas.source_formula: Preferred Return = min(Remaining Cash, Sum of Cash Flows × Preferred Rate)

nodes.name: Preferred Stock
nodes.definition: Preferred stock is a component of equity capital that combines characteristics of both equity and debt, making it a hybrid instrument. In terms of asset claims and dividend distribution, preferred stock ranks above common stock but below bonds in the order of priority. Preferred shareholders typically enjoy preference in dividend payments and distribution of assets upon liquidation, with specific terms governed by the company's articles of incorporation.

formulas.source_formula: Preferred Stock = Par Value per Share × Number of Shares Issued
Preferred Stock = Annual Preferred Dividend ÷ Preferred Stock Discount Rate

nodes.name: Preferred Stock Amount
nodes.definition: The Preferred Stock Amount is an account presented in the shareholders' equity section of the balance sheet, representing the total amount of outstanding preferred stock calculated at par value or issue price. It is a fundamental, raw data item directly sourced from the company's capital records, not a composite metric derived from other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Preferred Stock Discount Rate
aliases: Required Rate of Return for Preferred Stock
Required Rate of Return on Preferred Stock
nodes.definition: The preferred stock discount rate is the minimum annualized rate of return required by investors when purchasing or holding preferred stock, based on market expectations or contractual agreements. It is a key input parameter in preferred stock valuation models (such as the dividend discount model), used to discount the expected future cash flows of preferred stock dividends to their present value.

nodes.name: Preferred Stock Dividend
nodes.definition: Preferred stock dividend is the compensation paid by a company to preferred shareholders according to the preferred stock charter, based on an agreed fixed or floating dividend rate. It is typically calculated based on the par value of the preferred stock and the dividend rate, and is commonly used in financial analysis to calculate metrics such as net income per share.

nodes.name: Preferred Stock Dividend Rate
nodes.definition: The preferred stock dividend rate is a fixed or floating rate benchmark, explicitly stipulated in the contract or corporate bylaws at the time of issuance, used to calculate the dividends payable to preferred shareholders. It serves as a direct input value for calculating preferred stock dividends and is not derived from other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Preferred Stock Dividends for Current Period
Preferred Stock Dividends for Prior Period
Preferred Stock Equity
nodes.definition: Preferred stock equity is a separate line item within the shareholders' equity section of a company's balance sheet, representing the claim of preferred shareholders on the company's net assets (i.e., the residual portion after total liabilities are subtracted from total assets). This figure is typically sourced directly from the company's financial statements as a fundamental financial datum, not derived from calculations involving other metrics.

nodes.name: Preferred Stock Value
nodes.definition: Preferred stock value refers to the market value or assessed value of preferred stock at a specific point in time. It reflects the price investors are willing to pay for the rights represented by preferred stock, such as fixed dividend payments and priority in asset liquidation. Its value is typically influenced by factors including the dividend rate, market interest rates, the company's creditworthiness, and redemption terms.

nodes.name: Premium Bond
nodes.definition: A premium bond is a fixed-income security that trades above its face value because its coupon rate exceeds the prevailing market interest rate. Investors pay a premium to receive higher periodic coupon payments relative to market rates, resulting in a lower yield compared to the bond's coupon rate when purchased at a premium price.

formulas.source_formula: Premium Bond Price = Face Value × (Coupon Rate ÷ Market Interest Rate)

nodes.name: Premium Multiple
nodes.definition: Premium multiple typically refers to the ratio of a company's post-financing (or post-issuance) valuation to its pre-financing (or pre-issuance) valuation during a financing or issuance process, used to measure the magnitude of valuation growth.

nodes.name: Premium of Call Option with Higher Strike Price
aliases: Call Option Premium with Higher Exercise Price
Premium of Higher Strike Price Call Option
高执行价看涨期权权利金
高行权价看涨期权价格
nodes.definition: The premium of a call option with a higher strike price refers to the trading price of a call option contract in the options market where the strike price is above the current market price of the underlying asset. This price is directly formed by market transactions, reflecting the fee paid by the buyer to the seller for obtaining the right to purchase the asset at a specific higher price in the future. Its specific value is influenced by various factors such as market supply and demand, underlying asset price, strike price, volatility, and time to expiration, and must be obtained directly from real-time market quotes or historical trading data.

nodes.name: Premium of Higher Strike Call Option
Premium of Lower Strike Call Option
Premium of Lower Strike Price Call Option
aliases: 低执行价看涨期权权利金
低行权价看涨期权价格
nodes.definition: The premium of a lower strike price call option refers to the fee that an investor pays to the option seller in order to obtain the right to purchase an asset (such as a stock) at a predetermined price (the strike price) that is below the current market price at a future date. Because this purchase price is more favorable than the market price, such an option has intrinsic value (known as an in-the-money option), and therefore its premium is typically higher.

nodes.name: Prepaid Accounts Balance
nodes.definition: Prepaid accounts balance refers to the balance of an asset account on the balance sheet date, arising from payments made in advance to suppliers or service providers, reflecting the company's right to receive goods or services in the future.

nodes.name: Prepaid Accounts Ending Debit Balance
aliases: Prepaid Accounts Detail Ending Debit Balance
Prepayment Detail Debit Balance at Period End
预付账款明细借方期末数
预付账款明细科目借方余额
预付账款明细账借方余额
nodes.definition: The prepaid accounts ending debit balance refers to the aggregate amount of balances in debit positions across all subsidiary ledger accounts under the 'Prepaid Accounts' general ledger account at the end of an accounting period (e.g., month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It represents the amount of funds the enterprise has paid but has not yet received corresponding goods or services for.

nodes.name: Prepaid Accounts from Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prepaid accounts from the previous period refer to the balance of payments made in advance to suppliers or service providers by the end of the last accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year), for which corresponding goods or services have not yet been received. It reflects the utilization of prepaid funds at the end of the previous period.

nodes.name: Prepaid Expense Amortization (Straight-Line)
nodes.definition: Prepaid expense amortization is the systematic recognition of a prepaid asset as expense over the periods that benefit from it, typically using the straight-line method to allocate an equal amount to each period in accordance with accrual accounting and the matching principle.

nodes.name: Prepaid Expenses
nodes.definition: Prepaid expenses refer to payments made in advance by a company for which the economic benefits or services have not yet been received or fully received, and which need to be allocated to costs or expenses over a specific future period. Examples include prepaid rent and insurance premiums.

nodes.name: Prepaid Expenses / Prepayments
nodes.definition: Prepaid expenses refer to the amounts paid in advance by an enterprise to suppliers according to purchase or service contracts. They are presented as current assets on the balance sheet. The reported amount must be calculated and filled in based on an analysis of the detailed balances of relevant accounting accounts.

nodes.name: Prepaid Expenses Turnover Days
nodes.definition: Prepaid Expenses Turnover Days measures the average number of days required for funds prepaid to suppliers to be recovered or consumed through sales activities. It reflects the duration of funds being tied up by upstream suppliers and is an important component of working capital management efficiency analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Prepaid Expenses Turnover Days = 360 × Average Prepaid Expenses Balance ÷ Cost of Sales
Prepaid Expenses Turnover Days = 360 × Average Prepaid Expenses Balance ÷ Operating Costs
Prepaid Expenses Turnover Days = 360 × Average Prepaid Expenses Balance ÷ Cost of Main Business

nodes.name: Prepaid Expenses for the Current Period
nodes.definition: Prepaid expenses for the current period refer to payments made by an enterprise to suppliers or service providers in advance for the purchase of goods or receipt of services within the current accounting period. It reflects the cash outflow from the enterprise's operating activities during the current period and is typically associated with future delivery of goods or completion of services.

nodes.name: Prepaid Rent Adjustment Factor
nodes.definition: The prepaid rent adjustment factor is an adjustment factor or calculation ratio used to allocate a lump-sum prepaid rent amount reasonably and systematically across the respective benefit periods (e.g., months or years) within an accounting period. It is typically related to factors such as rent escalation clauses, lease term, and discount rate, and is used to calculate the rent expense to be recognized in each period, ensuring that expenses are matched with revenues on a timely basis.

nodes.name: Preparation Time Coefficient
nodes.definition: The preparation time coefficient is an adjustment factor in work hour quota calculation, used to convert or adjust the standard work hour quota based on the complexity or required time of pre-production preparations (such as tools, cutters, equipment debugging, etc.), in order to more accurately reflect the total work hours actually required for production.

nodes.name: Prepayment Penalty
nodes.definition: A prepayment penalty is a contractual fee charged by a lender when a borrower repays a loan, typically a mortgage, before its scheduled term. It is commonly calculated as a percentage of the remaining mortgage balance and is intended to compensate the lender for lost interest revenue.

formulas.source_formula: Prepayment Penalty = Remaining Mortgage Balance × Prepayment Penalty Rate

nodes.name: Prepayments
nodes.definition: Prepayments refer to funds paid in advance by an enterprise to suppliers or other entities according to contractual agreements in the course of daily business operations, constituting a current asset of the enterprise. When preparing the balance sheet, its value is calculated by aggregating the ending debit balances of all subsidiary accounts under the two general ledger accounts: 'Prepaid Accounts' and 'Accounts Payable'.

nodes.name: Prepayments Beginning Balance
nodes.definition: Prepayments beginning balance refers to the book value of the 'Prepayments' account on the balance sheet at the start of a fiscal year (typically January 1st). It reflects the amount of funds already paid in advance to suppliers or service providers at the beginning of the year for which corresponding goods or services have not yet been received.

nodes.name: Prepayments Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Prepayments ending balance refers to the total book value of payments made in advance to suppliers or service providers by an enterprise as of the balance sheet date (typically month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the funds utilized by the enterprise for goods or services not yet received but paid for in advance at the end of the reporting period.

nodes.name: Prepayments Opening Balance
nodes.definition: Prepayments opening balance refers to the book value of payments made in advance to suppliers for which corresponding goods or services have not yet been received at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or month). It reflects the company's prepaid funds position with external parties at the period start and constitutes part of current assets on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Present Value
nodes.definition: Present Value refers to the current worth of a future cash flow or series of cash flows, discounted to the present point in time using the principle of the time value of money and a selected discount rate. Its core concept is that money has time value, meaning a given amount of money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. This metric is a fundamental tool for investment decision-making, asset valuation, and liability measurement.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value = Future Payment ÷ (1 + Annual Discount Rate) ^ (Periods ÷ 365)
Present Value = Annuity × Present Value Annuity Factor
Present Value = Future Single Cash Flow × Present Value Interest Factor
supporting_source_formulas: Present Value = Future Single Cash Flow × Present Value Interest Factor

nodes.name: Present Value (Single Sum)
aliases: Present Value of a Future Lump Sum
Present Value of a Single Sum
nodes.definition: Present value (single sum) is the current worth of a fixed amount to be received at a specified future date, discounted at a periodic rate over the number of periods, reflecting the time value of money.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value (Single Sum) = Future Value ÷ (1 + Discount Rate)^(Periods)
Present Value (Whole Life Annuity Due) = Payment × (1 + Interest Rate per Period)

nodes.name: Present Value Annuity Factor
aliases: Present Value Interest Factor of Annuity
等额支付系列现值系数
nodes.definition: The present value annuity factor is the discount factor for converting a series of future equal payments of one monetary unit into its present value at a given interest rate and number of periods. It is a core tool in financial mathematics for time value of money calculations.

nodes.name: Present Value Annuity Factor (m periods)
aliases: Present Value Interest Factor of Annuity
等额支付系列现值系数
nodes.definition: The present value annuity factor refers to the total present value of one unit of equal payment received or paid at the end of each period over a specified future period at a given discount rate. It is a key composite indicator for calculating the present value of an annuity and is widely used in the valuation of financial instruments such as deferred annuities and perpetuities.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value Annuity Factor (m periods) = 1 ÷ Discount Rate - 1 ÷ [Discount Rate × (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of Periods]

nodes.name: Present Value Annuity Factor (m+n periods)
aliases: Annuity Present Value Factor for (m+n) periods
nodes.definition: The Present Value Annuity Factor (m+n periods) is a composite metric used to calculate the present value of an equal cash flow stream lasting for n periods starting from period m+1 in a deferred annuity. It equals the ordinary annuity present value factor for the total periods (deferral periods plus annuity payment periods) minus the ordinary annuity present value factor for the deferral periods. Based on the time value of money principle, it is widely applied in finance, accounting, and investment decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value Annuity Factor (m+n periods) = [ (1 + Interest Rate) ^ (-Deferral Periods) - (1 + Interest Rate) ^ (-(Deferral Periods + Annuity Payment Periods)) ] ÷ Interest Rate

nodes.name: Present Value Annuity Factor (n periods)
aliases: Present Value Interest Factor of Annuity
等额支付系列现值系数
nodes.definition: The Present Value Annuity Factor (n periods) is a composite metric used in finance and accounting to calculate the present value of a series of equal future payments at a specific point in time. It is derived from a formula based on a specified periodic interest rate and the number of payment periods, reflecting the time value of money. It is widely applied in investment appraisal, lease contracts, pension planning, and other areas.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value Annuity Factor (n periods) = [1 - (1 + Periodic Interest Rate) ^ (-Number of Payment Periods)] ÷ Periodic Interest Rate
Present Value Factor = (1 − (1 + Treasury Yield)^(−Remaining Months ÷ 12)) ÷ Treasury Yield

nodes.name: Present Value Index
nodes.definition: The Present Value Index is the ratio of the present value of future cash inflows to the present value of cash outflows for an investment project, used to measure the profitability per unit of investment.

nodes.name: Present Value Interest Factor (PVIF)
nodes.definition: The Present Value Interest Factor (PVIF) is the discounting factor used under compound interest to convert a future sum of money (future value) at a specific point in time to its equivalent value at the present time (present value). Its numerical value equals the present value of 1 unit of future value discounted at a given interest rate over a specified number of periods.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value Interest Factor = Present Value ÷ Future Value
Present Value Interest Factor (m periods) = 1 ÷ (1 + Periodic Interest Rate) ^ Number of Periods

nodes.name: Present Value Interest Factor of Annuity (PVIFA)
aliases: Present Value Interest Factor of Annuity
nodes.definition: The Present Value Interest Factor of Annuity (PVIFA) is the discount factor used to determine the present value of a series of equal cash flows (ordinary annuity) occurring at regular intervals, given a constant interest rate over a specified number of periods.

formulas.source_formula: PVIFA = (1 - (1 + Interest Rate)^-Number of Periods) ÷ Interest Rate

nodes.name: Present Value Interest Factor of a Single Sum (m periods)
nodes.definition: The Present Value Interest Factor of a Single Sum (PVIF) refers to the multiplier used to discount a future sum of money to its present value under compound interest. Its value equals the present value of a unit future value discounted at a given interest rate over a specified number of periods.

nodes.name: Present Value and Future Value
nodes.definition: Present Value and Future Value are core concepts in financial management and finance, used to measure the value of money at different points in time. Present Value refers to the current worth of a future cash flow discounted at a specific discount rate; Future Value refers to the value of a current cash flow compounded at a specific interest rate to a future point in time. They form the foundation of valuation methods such as the Discounted Cash Flow model.

nodes.name: Present Value of After-Tax Cash Flows During Lease Term
aliases: Present Value of After-Tax Lease Cash Flows
租赁期税后现金流量现值
nodes.definition: The present value of after-tax cash flows during the lease term is the sum of the present values obtained by discounting the lessor's after-tax cash flows during the lease period at the after-tax borrowing cost.

nodes.name: Present Value of After-Tax Terminal Asset Cash Flow
aliases: Present Value of Terminal Asset After-Tax Cash Flow
期末资产税后现金流量现值
nodes.definition: The present value of after-tax terminal asset cash flow is the current value of the after-tax cash flow from asset disposal at the end of a lease, discounted at the project's cost of capital.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of After-Tax Terminal Asset Cash Flow = After-Tax Terminal Asset Cash Flow ÷ (1 + Cost of Capital)^Number of Periods

nodes.name: Present Value of Annuity
nodes.definition: The present value of an annuity refers to the total current value of a series of equal, periodic cash flows (i.e., an annuity) discounted to the present point in time at a specified interest rate (discount rate). It reflects the current economic value of these future cash flows.

nodes.name: Present Value of Annuity Due
nodes.definition: The present value of an annuity due refers to the total value of a series of equal cash flows received or paid at the beginning of each period, discounted to the present point in time.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Annuity Due = Present Value of Ordinary Annuity × (1 + Discount Rate)
Present Value of Annuity Due = Cash Flow per Period × ( (1 - (1 + Interest Rate)^-Number of Periods) ÷ Interest Rate ) × (1 + Interest Rate)

nodes.name: Present Value of Asset Cash Flows
Present Value of Cash Inflows
nodes.definition: Present value of cash inflows refers to the total current value of expected future cash inflows received at different time points, discounted to the present moment using a specific discount rate (reflecting the time value of money and risk). It is a key metric for assessing the current value of future returns when evaluating investment projects, asset values, or financing options.

nodes.name: Present Value of Cash Outflows
nodes.definition: Present Value of Cash Outflows refers to the total current value of a series of projected future cash outflows (such as investment costs, operating expenses, etc.) discounted at a specific discount rate. It is a key component in evaluating investment projects or asset values, used for calculating metrics like Net Present Value or Present Value Index.

nodes.name: Present Value of Compound Interest
nodes.definition: Present value of compound interest refers to the current value of a sum of money to be received at a future point in time, discounted at a compound interest rate, reflecting the time value of money.

nodes.name: Present Value of Contingent Consideration
nodes.definition: The present value of contingent consideration refers to the current value, discounted at an appropriate rate, of potential future payments in transactions such as business reorganizations, where the occurrence and amount of payment depend on specific conditions (e.g., future performance, occurrence of specific events). It reflects the current value of potential future payment obligations and is commonly used to assess the fair value of post-reorganization liabilities.

nodes.name: Present Value of Contingent Payment Amount
Present Value of Continuing Cash Flows
aliases: Present Value of Continuing Period Cash Flows
nodes.definition: The Present Value of Continuing Cash Flows refers to the sum of the values of all future cash flows, discounted to the present point in time at a specific discount rate (e.g., Weighted Average Cost of Capital), after a company enters a stable growth phase following the end of a detailed forecast period. This metric is a core component in evaluating a company's equity value or entity value using discounted cash flow models (such as the two-stage growth model).

operands.metric: Sum of Present Values of Continuing Cash Flows

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Continuing Cash Flows = Sum of Present Values of Continuing Cash Flows ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of Forecast Years

operands.metric: Cash Flow in First Year of Continuing Period

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Continuing Cash Flows = Cash Flow in First Year of Continuing Period ÷ (Discount Rate - Perpetual Growth Rate) ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of Forecast Years

nodes.name: Present Value of Continuing Value
nodes.definition: The present value of continuing value is a key component in the discounted cash flow model, representing the value of infinite future cash flows discounted to the present point in time after the detailed forecast period enters a stable growth phase. It is crucial for assessing equity value or entity value.

nodes.name: Present Value of Deferred Annuity
nodes.definition: The present value of a deferred annuity refers to the total value, discounted to the present point in time at a given interest rate, of a series of equal payments that begin at the end of each period after a specified deferral period (m).

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Deferred Annuity = Periodic Payment Amount × Present Value Annuity Factor (n periods) × Present Value Factor (m periods)
Present Value of Deferred Annuity = Periodic Payment Amount × [ Present Value Annuity Factor (m+n periods) － Present Value Annuity Factor (m periods) ]

nodes.name: Present Value of Dividends
nodes.definition: The present value of dividends is the current worth of a series of future dividend payments, discounted at the risk-free rate to reflect the time value of money. It is used to adjust forward prices for dividend-paying assets.

nodes.name: Present Value of Dividends in High-Growth Phase
Present Value of Dividends in High-Growth Stage
nodes.definition: Present Value of Dividends in the High-Growth Stage refers to the sum of the present values of all dividends a stock is expected to pay during its high-growth phase in the Dividend Discount Model. It is a composite metric calculated via formulas involving fundamental data such as dividend growth rate and discount rate, used for stock valuation and classified as a non-leaf node.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Dividends in High-Growth Stage = Expected First-Year Dividend × [1 - (1 + Dividend Growth Rate) ^ Number of High-Growth Periods ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of High-Growth Periods] ÷ (Discount Rate - Dividend Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Present Value of Each Period's Cash Flows
nodes.definition: Present Value of Each Period's Cash Flows refers to the value of expected future cash flows for each period, discounted back to the current point in time (valuation date) using a specific discount rate. It is a composite metric that must be calculated via formulas and serves as the core foundation for evaluating investment projects, conducting enterprise value analysis, and pricing financial assets (e.g., DCF models, bond pricing).

nodes.name: Present Value of Economic Profit
nodes.definition: The present value of economic profit is the sum of the discounted values of future economic profits from each period, brought back to the present point in time using a discount rate. It is used to assess the entity value of a company. Economic profit is typically defined as net profit minus capital cost, reflecting the residual income that exceeds the opportunity cost of capital.

nodes.name: Present Value of Estimated Future Cash Flows of an Asset
aliases: Present Value of Estimated Future Cash Flows
Present Value of Future Cash Flows
nodes.definition: The present value of estimated future cash flows of an asset refers to the total current value of all expected cash inflows that an asset is projected to generate during its future use and final disposal, discounted to the present point in time using an appropriate discount rate. It serves as a crucial basis for assessing the current value of an asset, conducting impairment tests, and making investment decisions.

nodes.name: Present Value of Estimated Selling Price
aliases: Present Value of Expected Selling Price
nodes.definition: The present value of the estimated selling price refers to the current value calculated by discounting the projected selling price of an asset (such as a stock) at a future point in time. It involves forecasting the future selling price and discounting it at an appropriate discount rate, commonly used in the terminal value calculation within stock valuation models.

nodes.name: Present Value of Exercise Price
nodes.definition: The present value of the exercise price refers to the current value of an option's strike price (the price to be paid or received upon exercising the option in the future), discounted to the present point in time using the risk-free interest rate.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Exercise Price = Underlying Asset Price - Call Option Price + Put Option Price
Present Value of Exercise Price = Exercise Price ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Time

nodes.name: Present Value of Expansion Investment Cost
nodes.definition: Present Value of Expansion Investment Cost refers to the current value of future investment costs required for expansion projects, discounted to the present point in time using a specific discount rate. It is a composite financial metric commonly used in evaluating expansion options or capital budgeting decisions, involving the time value of money and risk adjustments.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Expansion Investment Cost = Future Expansion Investment Cost ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Investment Period

nodes.name: Present Value of Expected Cash Flows
Present Value of Expected Economic Profit
aliases: Present Value of Estimated Economic Profit
Present Value of Projected Economic Profit
nodes.definition: The present value of expected economic profit is the sum of the discounted present values of economic profits over a future forecast period. It involves projecting revenues minus costs and applying a discount rate to convert future values to present value. It is used to assess the portion of enterprise value that exceeds the cost of capital and is commonly applied in business valuation analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Expected Economic Profit = Enterprise Value - Invested Capital

nodes.name: Present Value of Expense Loadings
