nodes.definition: Present value of expense loadings represents the portion of the gross premium allocated to cover expense loadings, measured as the difference between the gross premium and the net premium minus the present value of future expenses. It quantifies the provision for acquisition, administration, and maintenance expenses embedded in the premium at the valuation date.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Expense Loadings = Gross Premium - Net Premium - Present Value of Future Expenses

nodes.name: Present Value of Forecast Period Cash Flows
aliases: Present Value of Forecasted Cash Flows
Present Value of Future Cash Flows
资产预计未来现金流量的现值
预测期内现金流量现值
预计未来现金流量现值
nodes.definition: The present value of forecast period cash flows refers to the sum of the values of estimated future cash flows discounted to the present point in time using a discount rate, used to assess the intrinsic value of an asset or investment project. It is a composite metric derived through discounting calculations, reflecting the time value of money, and is widely applied in financial valuation and capital budgeting.

nodes.name: Present Value of Forecast Period Entity Free Cash Flow
Present Value of Forecast Period Equity Cash Flows
aliases: PV of Equity Cash Flows during Forecast Period
Present Value of Forecasted Equity Cash Flows
股权现金流量预测期现值
预测期股权现金流现值
nodes.definition: The Present Value of Forecast Period Equity Cash Flows is a composite metric in business valuation, referring to the sum of the present values of each period's equity cash flows (such as dividends or free cash flow to equity) during the forecast period, discounted at the cost of equity, used to calculate equity value.

nodes.name: Present Value of Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm
aliases: Present Value of Forecast Period FCFF
Present Value of Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to Firm
nodes.definition: The Present Value of Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to the Firm refers to the cumulative present value obtained by discounting the forecasted future periodic free cash flows to the firm during the detailed forecast period of a business valuation, using the corresponding Weighted Average Cost of Capital. It represents the current value of the firm's free cash flow generation capacity during the explicitly forecastable period.

nodes.name: Present Value of Free Cash Flow to Equity
nodes.definition: The present value of free cash flow to equity is a composite metric calculated by discounting and summing the forecasted free cash flow to equity for each future period using an appropriate discount rate (cost of equity capital), used to assess a company's equity value. Its calculation relies on other financial data (such as net profit, capital expenditures, changes in working capital, etc.) and the discount rate, and is not a raw, fundamental data item from financial statements.

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Cash Flows
aliases: 资产未来现金流量现值
预计未来现金流量现值
nodes.definition: Present Value of Future Cash Flows refers to the current value of expected future cash flows discounted at a specific discount rate. It is a composite metric calculated through formulas and is widely used in financial valuation, investment decision-making, cost of capital estimation (e.g., pre-tax cost of debt), and other areas to measure the current economic value of an asset, project, or investment.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Future Cash Flows = Equal Periodic Cash Flow ÷ Discount Rate
Present Value of Future Cash Flows = Equal Periodic Cash Flow × [1 - (1 + Discount Rate) ^ -Number of Periods] ÷ Discount Rate

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Cash Inflows
aliases: Present Value of Future Cash Flows
资产未来现金流量现值
预计未来现金流量现值
nodes.definition: Present Value of Future Cash Inflows refers to the total current value of the expected cash inflows from an asset or investment in different future periods, discounted to the present point using an appropriate discount rate. It reflects the current worth of future cash inflows after considering the time value of money.

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Net Cash Flows
aliases: Present Value of Expected Future Cash Flows
Present Value of Future Cash Flows
资产预计未来现金流量现值
nodes.definition: The present value of future net cash flows refers to the total current value calculated by discounting the estimated net cash flows generated by an asset or investment project in each future period, using a discount rate that reflects its risk and time value. It is a core composite metric for assessing asset value and investment project feasibility, and serves as the basis for calculating net present value.

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Payment
aliases: Discounted Value of Future Cash Flow
nodes.definition: The present value of a future payment is the current worth of a future sum of money or stream of cash flows given a specified rate of return (discount rate), accounting for the time value of money.

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Payments
nodes.definition: The present value of future payments refers to the total current value of all remaining payments (including principal and interest) for a loan or debt over its remaining term, discounted at a specific discount rate (typically the loan's interest rate). Under equal principal and interest payments or equal principal payment methods, this value typically equals the current outstanding principal balance.

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Periodic Payments
nodes.definition: The present value of future periodic payments refers to the sum of the values, discounted to the current point in time at a specific discount rate (typically the loan interest rate or market rate), of all amounts required to be repaid in future payment periods (e.g., monthly, quarterly) for a loan or debt. It represents the theoretical total amount of funds needed at the current point in time to settle all future debt obligations, commonly used to calculate the outstanding principal balance of a loan or to evaluate prepayment options.

nodes.name: Present Value of Future Salary Increases
nodes.definition: The present value of future salary increases refers to the current value, discounted at a specified rate, of the incremental benefit obligations arising from employees' expected future salary growth (e.g., due to inflation, promotion, performance, etc.) in the accounting measurement of long-term employee benefits such as pension liabilities. It reflects the impact of future compensation changes on the current assessment of liabilities.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Growing Perpetuity = First Period Cash Flow ÷ (Discount Rate - Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Present Value of Growth Opportunities (PVGO)
nodes.definition: The Present Value of Growth Opportunities (PVGO) refers to the current value of a company's future growth opportunities, equal to the stock price minus the value under a no-growth scenario (i.e., earnings per share divided by the discount rate). It reflects the market's valuation of the company's future growth potential and is commonly used in intrinsic value analysis of stocks.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Growth Opportunities = Stock Price - (Earnings Per Share ÷ Discount Rate)

nodes.name: Present Value of Growth Period Cash Flows
aliases: Present Value of Cash Flows during Growth Period
明确的预测期间现金流量现值
nodes.definition: Present Value of Growth Period Cash Flows refers to the sum of the discounted values of projected cash flows for each period during the growth phase (explicit forecast period) to the present point in time, using a discount rate, in business valuation. It is a key component of the Discounted Cash Flow model and is commonly used in equity valuation.

nodes.name: Present Value of Initial Investment
nodes.definition: The present value of initial investment refers to the total present value of initial investment amounts occurring at different points in time, discounted back to the project's inception using a specified discount rate. It is not a fundamental data point directly obtained from financial statements, but rather a composite metric used for capital budgeting decisions (such as calculating net present value and present value index).

nodes.name: Present Value of Interest
nodes.definition: Present Value of Interest refers to the total current value of a series or single future interest payments, discounted to the present point in time using a specific discount rate. It is a core calculation metric for valuing fixed-income securities such as bonds, conducting investment project analysis, and measuring the time value of money, reflecting the current economic value of future interest income.

nodes.name: Present Value of Interest Payments
aliases: Sum of Present Value of Interest Payments
nodes.definition: The present value of interest payments refers to the composite metric obtained by discounting the future cash flows of periodic interest payments at a discount rate (e.g., market interest rate) and summing their present values. It is commonly used in bond valuation and investment analysis and is a core component in calculating the value of a plain vanilla bond.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Interest Payments = Periodic Interest Amount × [1 - (1 + Discount Rate) ^ (-Number of Periods)] ÷ Discount Rate

nodes.name: Present Value of Investment
nodes.definition: Present Value of Investment refers to the current value of the cash flows an investment is expected to generate at a future point in time, discounted back to the present using a specific discount rate (or interest rate). It reflects the current worth of future funds and is one of the core metrics for evaluating the feasibility of an investment project.

nodes.name: Present Value of Lease Cash Flows
nodes.definition: The present value of lease cash flows is the total current value of cash flows during the lease period, discounted at the discount rate.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Lease Cash Flows = Periodic Lease Payment × Present Value Annuity Factor

nodes.name: Present Value of Lease Payments
nodes.definition: The present value of lease payments represents the current worth of all future lease obligations discounted at an appropriate rate, used to determine whether a lease qualifies as a capital lease under accounting standards.

nodes.name: Present Value of Lease Period Cash Flows
Present Value of Liability Cash Flows
Present Value of Loss Reserve
nodes.definition: Present value of loss reserve is the discounted value of expected future claim payments, reflecting the time value of money. Insurers use it to estimate the economic value of reserves required to settle unpaid losses and claims obligations over time.

nodes.name: Present Value of Minimum Lease Payments
nodes.definition: Present value of minimum lease payments is the discounted current value of contractual lease payments over the lease term plus the discounted residual value, using an appropriate discount rate. It is used in lease accounting and financial analysis to measure the current obligation associated with future lease cash flows.

nodes.name: Present Value of Minimum Lease Receipts
nodes.definition: The present value of minimum lease receipts refers to the value, as of the lease commencement date, of the minimum lease receipts that the lessor is certain to receive in future periods, discounted at the lease's implicit interest rate (or the contractually stipulated rate, incremental borrowing rate, etc.). It serves as the basis for the lessor's lease accounting, recognition of long-term receivables, and unearned finance income.

nodes.name: Present Value of Ordinary Annuity
aliases: Present Value of an Ordinary Annuity
nodes.definition: The present value of an ordinary annuity refers to the total value of a series of equal cash flows received or paid at the end of each period, discounted to the present point in time.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Ordinary Annuity = Payment × (1 - (1 + Discount Rate) ^ -Number of Periods) ÷ Discount Rate
Present Value of Ordinary Annuity = Payment × (1 - (1 + Discount Rate)^(-Periods)) ÷ Discount Rate
Present Value of Ordinary Annuity = Periodic Payment (PMT) × (1 - (1 + Interest Rate per Period (r))^-Number of Periods (n)) ÷ Interest Rate per Period (r)

nodes.name: Present Value of Original Investment Amount
Present Value of Perpetuity
nodes.definition: The present value of a perpetuity refers to the total current value of an infinite series of future cash flows from an annuity, discounted at a specified rate.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Perpetuity = Periodic Payment Amount ÷ Periodic Interest Rate + Periodic Payment Amount
Present Value of Perpetuity = Periodic Payment Amount ÷ Periodic Interest Rate
Present Value of Perpetuity = Cash Flow ÷ Discount Rate

nodes.name: Present Value of Post-Reorganization Forecast Period Free Cash Flow
aliases: Present Value of Post-Reorganization Forecast Period Free Cash Flows
并购后目标公司预测期自由现金流现值
nodes.definition: In the context of corporate mergers, acquisitions, or restructuring, this refers to the sum of the present values, discounted to the valuation date using an appropriate discount rate, of the annual free cash flows generated by the target company during a specified future forecast period. This metric serves as the basis for evaluating acquisition transaction prices and calculating incremental corporate value.

nodes.name: Present Value of Post-restructuring Forecast Period Free Cash Flow
Present Value of Post-restructuring Terminal Value
Present Value of Principal
aliases: Present Value of Future Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Present value of principal refers to the current worth of a sum of money to be received at a specific future date, discounted at a given rate. It is a core concept in the time value of money calculation and is widely applied in bond pricing, project valuation, and fair value measurement.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Principal = Future Cash Flow × Present Value Interest Factor

nodes.name: Present Value of Principal Repaid
nodes.definition: The present value of principal repaid refers to the total value, discounted to a specific point in time (typically the current date or an evaluation reference date) at a certain discount rate (such as the loan interest rate or market rate), of the principal amounts that have already been repaid in financial activities like loans or bonds. It reflects the current value of the principal portion the borrower has actually repaid, taking into account the time value of money.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Remaining Payments = Present Value Factor × Remaining Balance

nodes.name: Present Value of Rental Inflows
nodes.definition: Present Value of Rental Inflows refers to the total current value of a series of future rental cash inflows, discounted to the present point in time using an appropriate discount rate. It serves as the foundation for evaluating the value of leased assets or lease contracts and is a key component in calculating metrics such as Net Present Value.

nodes.name: Present Value of Repaid Loan Principal
nodes.definition: The present value of repaid loan principal refers to the total value, discounted to the loan origination date or a specific valuation date at a certain discount rate (typically the loan interest rate), of all principal portions already repaid by the borrower during the loan term. It reflects the time value of the loan principal that the borrower has actually repaid.

nodes.name: Present Value of Repaid Principal Portion
Present Value of Residual Asset Value
nodes.definition: Present Value of Residual Asset Value is a composite metric calculated by discounting the estimated residual value of an asset at the end of the lease term to the present point in time using a specific discount rate. It involves discounting formulas and is commonly used in lease accounting and break-even rental analysis.

nodes.name: Present Value of Residual Value Inflows
nodes.definition: Present Value of Residual Value Inflows refers to the current value of the estimated salvage value or terminal value of an investment project at the end of its life, discounted to the present point in time at a specific discount rate. It is a significant component of discounted future cash inflows in Net Present Value calculation and is classified as a non-leaf node.

nodes.name: Present Value of Selling Price
aliases: Present Value of Future Sale Proceeds
nodes.definition: Present Value of Selling Price refers to the current value of an asset's estimated future selling price at a specific point in time, discounted to the present using an appropriate discount rate. It is a composite metric calculated through discounting, whose value depends on future cash flows and the discount rate, and is not directly sourced from financial statements. It is commonly used to assess the intrinsic value of financial or physical assets such as bonds and fixed assets.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Selling Price = Future Selling Price ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Holding Period

nodes.name: Present Value of Terminal Asset
nodes.definition: Present Value of Terminal Asset is a component in calculating the lessee's net present value in finance leases. It represents the present value, discounted to the beginning of the lease term at an appropriate discount rate, of the estimated residual value of the leased asset at the end of the lease term (estimated based on factors such as asset cost and depreciation rate). It is used to assess the financial feasibility of the lease transaction.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Terminal Asset = Estimated Terminal Asset Residual Value ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of Lease Periods
Present Value of Terminal Asset = (Asset Cost - Annual Depreciation Amount × Number of Lease Years) ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of Lease Periods

nodes.name: Present Value of Terminal Period Cash Flows
Present Value of Terminal Value in Stable Growth Stage
aliases: Gordon Growth Model Terminal Value Present Value
PV of Stable Growth Terminal Value
戈登增长模型终值现值
永续增长阶段终值现值
nodes.definition: The present value of terminal value in the stable growth stage refers to the value, based on stock valuation models (such as the Gordon Growth Model), of discounting the terminal value of perpetual cash flows after entering the stable growth stage back to the current point in time. It is a composite financial metric calculated through formulas involving fundamental data such as future cash flows, growth rates, and discount rates, used to assess the intrinsic value of a company or stock.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of Terminal Value in Stable Growth Stage = Next Period Dividend ÷ (Required Rate of Return - Stable Growth Rate)
Present Value of Terminal Value in Stable Growth Stage = Next Period Free Cash Flow ÷ (Discount Rate - Perpetual Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Present Value of Terminal Value in Stable-Growth Phase
Present Value of Transition Period Cash Flows
aliases: Present Value of Conversion Period Cash Flows
nodes.definition: Present Value of Transition Period Cash Flows refers to the sum of the discounted values of future cash flows during the transition period, brought to the present point in time using an appropriate discount rate. It is a composite metric used in financial analysis such as equity valuation.

nodes.name: Present Value of Unguaranteed Residual Value
nodes.definition: The present value of unguaranteed residual value refers to the current value, discounted to the beginning of the lease term at a specified discount rate (typically the implicit interest rate in the lease), of the unguaranteed residual value of a leased asset at the end of the lease term (i.e., the portion of the estimated residual value not guaranteed by the lessee or a third party). It is a significant factor for lessors when calculating the net investment in the lease and determining the implicit interest rate in the lease.

nodes.name: Present Value of Zero-Coupon Swap
aliases: Net Present Value of Zero-Coupon Swap
nodes.definition: The present value of a zero-coupon swap is the valuation of its expected net cash flows discounted to today using the corresponding spot rates for each period. In a zero-coupon swap, the fixed leg typically makes a single lump-sum payment at maturity, while the floating leg accrues over time; valuing the swap entails discounting each expected cash flow by its appropriate term spot rate to obtain the net present value.

nodes.name: Present Value of a Growing Perpetuity
aliases: 增长型永续现金流现值
nodes.definition: The present value of a growing perpetuity is the current value of an infinite stream of cash flows that grow at a constant rate g and are discounted at rate r. It is calculated as the first-period cash flow divided by the difference between the discount rate and the growth rate (r - g), and is valid when r > g.

nodes.name: Present Value of an Annuity
aliases: Present Value of an Ordinary Annuity
nodes.definition: The present value of an ordinary annuity measures the current worth of a series of equal cash flows paid at the end of each period, discounted at a specified rate. It is used to value annuity cash streams in areas such as retirement planning, loan amortization, and bond coupon valuation.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of an Ordinary Annuity = Annuity Payment × (1 - (1 ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Number of Periods)) ÷ Discount Rate

nodes.name: Present Value of an Annuity Due
nodes.definition: Present Value of an Annuity Due is the current worth of a series of equal cash flows paid at the beginning of each period, discounted at a specified rate over a fixed number of periods. It equals the present value of an ordinary annuity multiplied by (1 + discount rate), reflecting the earlier timing of each payment.

formulas.source_formula: Present Value of an Annuity Due = Payment × (1 - (1 + Discount Rate)^(-Periods)) ÷ Discount Rate × (1 + Discount Rate)

nodes.name: Preset Upper Limit
nodes.definition: A preset upper limit refers to the maximum allowable value or boundary pre-established for a specific numerical value, result, or variable in financial calculations, data analysis, or model settings. When the actual calculated value exceeds this limit, the system or formula typically constrains it to this upper bound to ensure results remain within a controllable or reasonable range.

nodes.name: Pretax Earnings
nodes.definition: Pretax earnings represent a company's profit before income taxes, measuring profitability prior to tax effects. In this implementation, pretax earnings are calculated as total sales minus operating expenses and interest expenses for the same reporting period.

formulas.source_formula: Pretax Earnings = Total Sales - Operating Expenses - Interest Expenses

nodes.name: Pretax Earnings Margin
nodes.definition: Pretax earnings margin is the percentage of earnings before tax (EBT) relative to total sales (revenue), indicating how efficiently a company generates pretax profit from its sales, independent of tax rates or tax strategies.

nodes.name: Pretax Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Pretax profit margin measures the percentage of profit earned before income taxes relative to total revenue. It is calculated as pretax profit (revenue minus all expenses excluding taxes) divided by total revenue, expressed as a percentage. This ratio assesses operational profitability and cost efficiency before the impact of taxation.

formulas.source_formula: Pretax Profit Margin = (Total Revenue - Total Expenses (excluding taxes)) ÷ Total Revenue × 100
Pretax Profit Margin = Earnings Before Taxes ÷ Total Revenues × 100%

nodes.name: Previous Close Price
nodes.definition: Previous Close Price refers to the final transaction price of a stock at the close of the most recently completed trading day (typically the previous trading day). It is raw trading data directly recorded and provided by the exchange, serving as a crucial benchmark price for calculating the day's price change percentage, ex-rights/ex-dividend reference price, etc.

nodes.name: Previous Closing Price
nodes.definition: The previous closing price refers to the final transaction price of a stock or security at the end of the last formal trading day. It is the consensus price reached by market trading activities at the close of that day and serves as a crucial benchmark for calculating the day's price change, opening reference price, and other metrics.

nodes.name: Previous Day's Closing Price
nodes.definition: Previous day's closing price refers to the final transaction price of a stock at the end of the most recently completed trading day (i.e., yesterday). It serves as a crucial benchmark price for calculating indicators such as the day's price change and return rate.

nodes.name: Previous Group Frequency
nodes.definition: In grouped statistical data, 'previous group frequency' refers to the frequency of the group immediately preceding the current group in the ordered sequence of data groups. Frequency refers to the number of data points falling within a specific group.

nodes.name: Previous Level Quick Deduction
nodes.definition: The Previous Level Quick Deduction refers to the quick deduction amount corresponding to the immediately lower tax bracket, which is referenced when calculating the quick deduction for the current tax bracket under a progressive tax rate system (such as individual income tax). It serves as one of the foundational data points for recursively calculating quick deductions for all tax brackets, with the quick deduction for the first bracket typically being 0.

nodes.name: Previous Month Figure
nodes.definition: The Previous Month Figure refers to the relevant values, amounts, or data from the month immediately preceding the current reporting period (this month) used for description or comparison in financial or management reports. It typically serves as a reference benchmark for current period indicators to analyze month-to-month change trends.

nodes.name: Previous Period Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio
aliases: 上期应收账款周转次数
nodes.definition: The Previous Period Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio is an indicator calculated by applying the accounts receivable turnover ratio formula to data from the preceding accounting period. It measures the average number of times accounts receivable were converted into cash during the previous period, reflecting the efficiency and liquidity of accounts receivable management in that period.

operands.metric: Previous Period Average Accounts Receivable Balance

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio = Previous Period Accounts Receivable Collections ÷ Previous Period Average Accounts Receivable Balance

operands.metric: Previous Period Average Accounts Receivable Balance

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio = Previous Period Net Sales Revenue ÷ Previous Period Average Accounts Receivable Balance

nodes.name: Previous Period Administrative Expenses
aliases: Prior Period General and Administrative Expenses
nodes.definition: Previous period administrative expenses refer to the total amount of various expenses actually incurred by an enterprise for organizing and managing production and operating activities during the last accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental historical data item in the income statement, directly sourced from the accounting records of the previous period.

nodes.name: Previous Period Average Accounts Receivable Balance
Previous Period Business Tax Payable
nodes.definition: Previous Period Business Tax Payable refers to the amount of business tax calculated based on the business turnover or sales revenue of an enterprise during the preceding accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) according to the applicable business tax rate, which is payable to the tax authorities.

nodes.name: Previous Period Business Tax and Surcharges
nodes.definition: Previous Period Business Tax and Surcharges refer to the tax burden calculated and recognized by an enterprise in the preceding accounting period based on turnover taxes (such as Business Tax, Value-Added Tax, and Consumption Tax) generated from its operating activities and corresponding surcharges (such as Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, Education Surcharge, and Local Education Surcharge). This account has been adjusted to 'Taxes and Surcharges' after the 'Business Tax to VAT Reform', but may still be referenced in historical data analysis and specific comparisons.

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Business Tax and Surcharges = Previous Period Business Tax Amount × Previous Period Operating Revenue Amount - Previous Period Preferential Deduction Amount + (Surcharge Rate × Previous Period Preferential Deduction Amount)

operands.metric: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Business Tax and Surcharges = (Previous Period Business Tax Amount + Previous Period VAT Amount + Previous Period Consumption Tax Amount) × (Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate + Education Surcharge Rate + Local Education Surcharge Rate)

nodes.name: Previous Period Cash and Cash Equivalents
aliases: Cash and Cash Equivalents at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Previous period cash and cash equivalents refer to the total amount of assets held in monetary form by an enterprise at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous year, quarter, or month), primarily including cash on hand, bank deposits, and other monetary funds.

nodes.name: Previous Period Consumption Amount
nodes.definition: Previous Period Consumption Amount typically refers to the total consumption expenditure from the last comparable period (e.g., the same period in the previous fiscal year) used for comparison with the current period's consumption amount in financial statements (such as the Cash Flow Statement). It is directly sourced from historical ledgers or statements and serves as the foundational data for reflecting consumption changes.

nodes.name: Previous Period Consumption Expenditure
nodes.definition: Previous Period Consumption Expenditure refers to the total amount spent by individuals, households, or businesses on purchasing goods and services during the last statistical period (e.g., previous month, previous quarter, or previous year). It serves as fundamental data for measuring past consumption levels, conducting budget comparisons, and calculating consumption variations.

nodes.name: Previous Period Consumption Tax Amount
nodes.definition: Previous Period Consumption Tax Amount refers to the amount of consumption tax calculated and payable to the tax authority by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) in accordance with relevant tax laws and regulations. It reflects the enterprise's consumption tax liability arising from the sale of taxable consumer goods or provision of taxable services during the previous tax period.

nodes.name: Previous Period Consumption Unit Price
nodes.definition: Previous Period Consumption Unit Price refers to the average amount corresponding to each unit of consumption in the previous statistical period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental metric used to measure historical consumption levels and typically serves as a reference benchmark for analyzing consumption trends and variations.

nodes.name: Previous Period Demand
nodes.definition: Previous period demand refers to the actual purchase quantity or intended purchase quantity of a specific good or service by the market or consumers during a defined time period prior to the current period. It serves as crucial historical reference data for conducting demand analysis, forecasting future demand, and calculating demand change percentages.

nodes.name: Previous Period Employment
nodes.definition: Previous period employment refers to the total number of all employed persons in a country or region during a prior statistical period (such as the previous quarter or year), which serves as the comparative benchmark when calculating indicators like labor force growth rate.

nodes.name: Previous Period Ending Book Balance
nodes.definition: Previous period ending book balance refers to the closing amount of an accounting account at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It is a point-in-time figure directly derived from the previous period's accounting records and settlement, serving as the basis for calculating the current period's transactions and ending balance.

nodes.name: Previous Period Equity Per Share
aliases: Previous Period Book Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Previous Period Equity Per Share is a composite financial indicator that reflects the net assets per share attributable to common shareholders at the end of the previous period. It is calculated by dividing the previous period's shareholders' equity by the total number of shares outstanding at the end of the previous period, and is used to measure the book equity per share enjoyed by shareholders in the last accounting period.

operands.metric: Total Shares Outstanding at End of Previous Period

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Equity Per Share = Previous Period Shareholders' Equity ÷ Total Shares Outstanding at End of Previous Period

nodes.name: Previous Period Financial Expenses
aliases: 上一会计期间财务费用
nodes.definition: Previous period financial expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise during the last accounting period (such as the previous quarter or fiscal year) related to financing activities, primarily including interest expenses, exchange losses, and related handling fees. It is a historical data item on the income statement, reflecting the enterprise's financing costs from the previous period.

nodes.name: Previous Period Indicator
nodes.definition: "Previous Period Indicator" is a temporal qualifier used to denote the historical value of a specific financial metric (such as operating revenue, net profit, etc.) in the preceding accounting period (e.g., previous month, previous quarter, or previous year). It is not an independent calculation formula itself, but rather a temporal reference point for the underlying financial metric.

nodes.name: Previous Period Labor Force
nodes.definition: Previous period labor force refers to the total population meeting the national statutory working age (typically males aged 16-60 and females aged 16-55) and possessing working capacity in the preceding statistical period (such as the previous year, quarter, or month), which serves as the comparative benchmark when calculating indicators like labor force growth rate.

nodes.name: Previous Period Operating Surplus of Secondary Industry
aliases: Operating Surplus of Secondary Industry in Previous Period
Previous Period Secondary Industry Operating Surplus
上期第二产业营业利润余额
前期第二产业营业盈余
第二产业上期营业盈余
nodes.definition: Previous Period Operating Surplus of Secondary Industry refers to the residual value remaining after deducting costs such as compensation paid to laborers, net production taxes, and depreciation of fixed assets from the value added created by production units in the secondary industry (primarily comprising industry and construction) during the previous statistical or accounting period. It reflects the net income obtained by this industry through production and operating activities in the preceding period.

nodes.name: Previous Period Operating Working Capital
nodes.definition: Previous Period Operating Working Capital is the value of operating working capital from the prior period, representing the net current assets required by the enterprise to sustain daily operations in the previous period. It reflects short-term solvency and working capital status, serves as the basis for calculating the increase in operating working capital, and is a composite metric.

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Operating Working Capital = Previous Period Operating Current Assets - Previous Period Operating Current Liabilities
Previous Period Operating Working Capital = Previous Period Current Assets - Previous Period Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Previous Period Price
nodes.definition: Previous Period Price refers to the original price or amount data from the preceding accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or the same period in the prior year) used for comparison with current period data in financial statements. It is a fundamental historical benchmark value, not a calculated composite metric, primarily used for deriving indicators such as price changes.

nodes.name: Previous Period Price Index
nodes.definition: The Previous Period Price Index is a statistical indicator that reflects the overall price level of a basket of goods and services during a specific base period or the previous statistical cycle (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It is typically set at a benchmark of 100 or 1000 and is used to measure price changes in subsequent periods, serving as the fundamental raw data for calculating economic indicators such as the inflation rate.

nodes.name: Previous Period Repurchase Time
nodes.definition: Previous Period Repurchase Time refers to the duration or contractual period of share repurchase activities that occurred in the preceding reporting period, which is referenced when calculating the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding for that period. It is used to measure the time span over which the repurchase activity affects the number of ordinary shares.

nodes.name: Previous Period Sales Revenue
aliases: 上一会计期间销售收入
nodes.definition: Previous period sales revenue refers to the total income earned by an enterprise from selling goods or providing services during the preceding accounting period (e.g., previous month, quarter, or fiscal year). It is typically sourced directly from financial statements such as the income statement and serves as fundamental historical data for budgeting and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Previous Period Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Previous period sales volume refers to the quantity or monetary value of products or services actually sold by an enterprise during the last statistical period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It is a historical actual figure, often used as a benchmark for forecasting future sales or calculating sales variations.

nodes.name: Previous Period Secondary Industry Compensation of Employees
Previous Period Secondary Industry Consumption of Fixed Capital
Previous Period Secondary Industry Gross Output
aliases: Secondary Industry Total Output of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Previous Period Secondary Industry Gross Output refers to the total value of all goods and services produced by all production units in the secondary industry within a given territory or region during the previous statistical period (such as the previous quarter or the previous year). The secondary industry primarily includes industry and construction.

nodes.name: Previous Period Secondary Industry Intermediate Input
Previous Period Secondary Industry Labor Compensation
aliases: Labor Compensation of Secondary Industry in Previous Period
Previous Period Secondary Industry Employee Compensation
上期第二产业人工成本
上期第二产业工资总额
前期第二产业劳动报酬
nodes.definition: Previous Period Secondary Industry Labor Compensation refers to the total compensation payable to all resident units' laborers for services provided during the production process in the secondary industry (primarily comprising industry and construction) in a comparable period prior to a statistical period (such as a quarter or year). It constitutes an important component in calculating the previous period's secondary industry value added.

nodes.name: Previous Period Secondary Industry Net Taxes on Production
Previous Period Secondary Industry Value Added
aliases: Base Period Secondary Industry Value Added
nodes.definition: Previous Period Secondary Industry Value Added refers to the final outcome of production activities by all resident units in the secondary industry during the reference period (typically the previous statistical cycle). It is a core indicator for measuring the total production volume and growth of the secondary industry during that period. Its calculation follows the principles of the System of National Accounts (SNA) and can be derived through two equivalent approaches: the production approach or the income approach.

operands.metric: Previous Period Secondary Industry Gross Output
Previous Period Secondary Industry Intermediate Input

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Secondary Industry Value Added = Previous Period Secondary Industry Gross Output - Previous Period Secondary Industry Intermediate Input

operands.metric: Previous Period Secondary Industry Compensation of Employees
Previous Period Secondary Industry Net Taxes on Production
Previous Period Secondary Industry Consumption of Fixed Capital
Previous Period Operating Surplus of Secondary Industry

formulas.source_formula: Previous Period Secondary Industry Value Added = Previous Period Secondary Industry Compensation of Employees + Previous Period Secondary Industry Net Taxes on Production + Previous Period Secondary Industry Consumption of Fixed Capital + Previous Period Secondary Industry Operating Surplus

nodes.name: Previous Period Selling Expenses
nodes.definition: Previous period selling expenses refer to the various costs actually incurred by an enterprise in the prior accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) for selling goods or providing services, including sales personnel compensation, advertising and promotion expenses, transportation and handling fees, etc. It is a fundamental historical data item on the income statement, reflecting past sales-related expenditures.

nodes.name: Previous Period Short-term Borrowings
aliases: 前期流动负债中的短期借款
nodes.definition: Previous period short-term borrowings refer to the total amount of various borrowings obtained by an enterprise from banks or other financial institutions at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous year, quarter, or month), with a repayment term of one year or less (including one year). It constitutes a significant component of the previous period's current liabilities and reflects the level of short-term debt obligations borne by the enterprise at the end of the previous period.

nodes.name: Previous Period Statistical Data
nodes.definition: Previous period statistical data refers to the raw data recorded in the corresponding prior time period (e.g., previous month, previous quarter, previous year) in accounting or statistics, relative to the current reporting period. It serves as the foundational historical value for conducting trend analysis such as year-over-year and period-over-period comparisons, and for calculating growth rates.

nodes.name: Previous Period Stock Price
nodes.definition: Previous period stock price refers to the final transaction price, i.e., the closing price, of a specific stock at the end of the trading period immediately preceding the current trading session (typically the previous trading day) in financial markets. It is fundamental data directly obtained from historical trading records and is used to calculate derived metrics such as returns.

nodes.name: Previous Period Technology Level Indicator Value
aliases: Previous Period Technical Level Indicator Value
nodes.definition: The Previous Period Technology Level Indicator Value refers to the quantified numerical value of the technology level corresponding to the previous period (e.g., the previous year, the previous quarter) used as a benchmark for comparison when calculating the technology level growth rate. It reflects the technological capability or achievement level at a specific past point in time and is used to measure the starting point of technological progress.

nodes.name: Previous Period VAT Amount
nodes.definition: Previous Period VAT Amount refers to the amount of Value-Added Tax calculated in accordance with tax regulations and payable to the tax authority by an enterprise during the previous tax filing period (typically the previous month or quarter). It reflects the enterprise's VAT tax liability arising from business activities such as sales of goods and provision of services during the preceding period.

nodes.name: Previous Period Volatility
nodes.definition: Previous period volatility refers to a financial or market data volatility indicator calculated based on data from the preceding period, typically used to measure historical risk levels or as a basis for calculating volatility changes.

nodes.name: Previous Reporting Period Date
nodes.definition: Previous Reporting Period Date refers to the specific accounting period corresponding to the 'Previous Period Amount' in financial statements, i.e., the comparable period immediately preceding the current reporting period. For example, when preparing annual statements, if the current period is from January 1 to December 31, 2023, the previous reporting period date is typically from January 1 to December 31, 2022; when preparing monthly statements, if the current period is September 2023, the previous reporting period date is typically August 2023. It serves as the fundamental temporal reference for comparative financial data analysis.

nodes.name: Previous Tax Bracket Rate
nodes.definition: In a progressive tax rate system, this refers to the tax rate corresponding to the income bracket immediately below the current applicable rate. It is typically used to calculate the quick deduction amount to simplify the computation of progressive taxation on excess amounts.

nodes.name: Previous Trading Day Closing Price
nodes.definition: The previous trading day closing price refers to the final transaction price of a stock at the end of the most recently completed trading day (i.e., the previous trading day). It serves as an important benchmark for calculating the day's price change percentage, opening reference price, and other metrics.

nodes.name: Previous Underlying Asset Price
aliases: Underlying Asset Price at Prior Date
nodes.definition: Previous underlying asset price refers to the market price or fair value of the underlying asset observed or recorded at a specific historical point in time (such as the beginning of the calculation period, contract signing date, or valuation reference date). It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating price changes, returns, and other derivative metrics.

nodes.name: Previous Year Discount Factor
nodes.definition: The previous year discount factor is a specific form of discount factor, calculated based on the discount rate and the time period of the previous year. It is used to discount cash flows from the previous year to their present value at the current or an earlier point in time, serving as a crucial parameter in discounting calculations within financial management.

formulas.source_formula: Previous Year Discount Factor = 1 ÷ (1 + Discount Rate)

nodes.name: Previous Year's Operating Revenue
nodes.definition: Previous year's operating revenue refers to the total income earned by an enterprise from its principal business activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, during the last complete fiscal year. It typically includes revenue from main operations, other business operations, and deemed sales revenue.

nodes.name: Previous Year's Sales Profit Margin
aliases: Prior Year Profit Margin on Sales
nodes.definition: The previous year's sales profit margin is a core financial metric that measures a company's ability to generate profit from sales activities during the last complete fiscal year. It is specifically expressed as the ratio of the previous year's total profit to the previous year's operating revenue, reflecting the overall sales profitability level after deducting all costs and expenses (excluding income tax).

formulas.source_formula: Previous Year's Sales Profit Margin = Previous Year's Total Profit ÷ Previous Year's Operating Revenue × 100%

nodes.name: Price
nodes.definition: Price is the monetary expression of the value of goods or services. In financial management and international trade, its composition typically includes elements such as cost, expenses, and profit, serving as a core variable influencing corporate revenue, profit, and market decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Price = Cost + Profit

nodes.name: Price 1
nodes.definition: Price 1 typically refers to the average price of an asset, product, or service during a specific historical period, used for cost analysis, valuation, or performance comparison.

nodes.name: Price 2
nodes.definition: Price 2 typically refers to the second price data point used as a reference or input value in specific analyses or calculations. According to the provided reference information, it is used to calculate the historical price average, which involves averaging multiple price data points over a past period to reflect their general level or trend.

nodes.name: Price Adjustment Factor
nodes.definition: The Price Adjustment Factor is a multiplier used to adjust a base price in specific contexts (such as contract execution, new share issuance, or project budgeting). It is calculated according to predetermined rules or formulas (e.g., based on market prices, cost changes, or comparisons of specific indicators) to reflect the extent to which the price should be increased or decreased.

nodes.name: Price Change Rate
nodes.definition: The Price Change Rate is an indicator that measures the magnitude of change in the overall price level of goods and services over a specific period (such as a year or a month), usually expressed as a percentage. It reflects changes in the purchasing power of money and serves as crucial foundational data for calculating real interest rates, assessing economic conditions, and conducting financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Price Change_t = Price_t - Price_{t-1}

nodes.name: Price Contingency
nodes.definition: Price contingency refers to a provision estimated and included in the total investment to address the risk of potential cost overruns due to changes in price factors (i.e., price differentials) such as interest rates, exchange rates, and material/equipment prices during the project or construction period. It is typically calculated using the compound interest method, based on the price level of the estimation year and in accordance with the national composite investment price index.

nodes.name: Price Count
nodes.definition: Price count refers to the number of independent price data points contained within a specific dataset or analysis scope. For example, when calculating the historical average price, it is necessary to count the number of all historical prices used in the calculation.

formulas.source_formula: Price Decline Percentage = 1 - (Current Price ÷ Previous Closing Price)

nodes.name: Price Decrease Value
nodes.definition: Price Decrease Value is the amount of price reduction calculated by comparing current period price data with previous period price data. It can be expressed as an absolute amount or a percentage, serving as a composite indicator for measuring the magnitude of price changes, commonly used in financial analysis, market pricing, and investment evaluation.

nodes.name: Price Deviation
nodes.definition: Price deviation refers to the difference between a current price and the mean (average) price, quantifying how far the price is from its central tendency. It is commonly used in mean reversion analysis to identify potential overvaluation or undervaluation relative to the average.

formulas.source_formula: Price Difference = End Price - Start Price

nodes.name: Price Elasticity of Demand
nodes.definition: Price elasticity of demand measures the sensitivity of the quantity demanded of a good to changes in its price, defined as the ratio of the percentage change in quantity demanded to the percentage change in price, ceteris paribus. Due to the law of demand, this value is typically negative; an absolute value greater than 1 indicates elastic demand, less than 1 indicates inelastic demand, and equal to 1 indicates unit elasticity.

formulas.source_formula: Price Elasticity of Demand = (Percentage Change in Quantity Demanded) ÷ (Percentage Change in Price)
supporting_source_formulas: Price Elasticity of Demand = (Percentage Change in Quantity Demanded) ÷ (Percentage Change in Price)
Price Elasticity of Demand = Percentage Change in Quantity Demanded ÷ Percentage Change in Price

nodes.name: Price Elasticity of Supply
nodes.definition: Price elasticity of supply measures the responsiveness of the quantity supplied to a change in price, expressed as the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price.

formulas.source_formula: Price Elasticity of Supply = Percentage Change in Quantity Supplied ÷ Percentage Change in Price
supporting_source_formulas: Price Elasticity of Supply = Percentage Change in Quantity Supplied ÷ Percentage Change in Price

nodes.name: Price Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Price growth rate is an indicator that measures the rate of change in price levels over a specific period, commonly used to analyze trends in the prices of goods, services, or assets. In sales analysis, it can be calculated based on changes in unit price (price/sales volume).

formulas.source_formula: Price Growth Rate = (Current Period Value - Base Period Value) ÷ Base Period Value

nodes.name: Price Increase Amount
nodes.definition: Price Increase Amount refers to the absolute increase in the price of a commodity or asset from the base period to the reporting period within a specific timeframe, serving as a fundamental indicator for measuring the absolute scale of price level changes.

formulas.source_formula: Price Increase Amount = Current Period Price - Base Period Price

nodes.name: Price Increase Rate
nodes.definition: Price increase rate refers to the growth magnitude of the price of goods, services, or assets over a specific period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually), typically expressed as a percentage, used to measure the trend of price level changes.

nodes.name: Price Index
nodes.definition: A price index is a composite indicator calculated using the weighted average method by collecting price data for a basket of representative goods and services. It is used to measure changes in the overall price level over time. It is not an original account in financial statements but is derived from base prices and weight calculations. In macroeconomic analysis, it is commonly used to calculate indicators such as real GDP.

nodes.name: Price Index Adjustment Factor
nodes.definition: The Price Index Adjustment Factor is a ratio directly obtained from officially published price indices (such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI), Producer Price Index (PPI), or specific industry price indices). It is used to adjust historical costs or values to their value at the current point in time, reflecting the impact of inflation or specific market price changes.

formulas.source_formula: Indexation Factor = CPI Final ÷ CPI Initial
Price Level = (Money Supply × Velocity of Money) ÷ Real Expenditures

nodes.name: Price Rate of Change (ROC)
nodes.definition: The Price Rate of Change (ROC) is a momentum indicator that measures the percentage change in price between the current period and a prior period. It quantifies the speed of price movements to help identify accelerating trends, potential overbought or oversold conditions, and shifts in market momentum.

formulas.source_formula: Price Rate of Change (ROC) = ((Current Price - Previous Price) ÷ Previous Price) × 100
Price Rate of Change (ROC) = ((Current Price - Past Price) ÷ Past Price) × 100%

nodes.name: Price Return
nodes.definition: Price return is the percentage change in an asset's market price over a specified period, excluding the impact of cash distributions such as dividends or interest. It measures price-only performance and is commonly used for evaluating securities or indices when cash flows are not considered.

formulas.source_formula: Price Return = ((Final Price - Initial Price) ÷ Initial Price) × 100

nodes.name: Price Sensitivity
nodes.definition: Price sensitivity (price elasticity of demand) measures how responsive the quantity demanded is to changes in price. It is calculated as the percentage change in quantity demanded divided by the percentage change in price, indicating demand elasticity for pricing and revenue management decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Price Sensitivity = Percentage Change in Quantity Demanded ÷ Percentage Change in Price

nodes.name: Price Target
nodes.definition: Price target is an analyst’s estimated fair value for a stock based on fundamental inputs. Using the price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio method, the price target is calculated by multiplying an appropriate P/E ratio by the company’s earnings for a specified period (e.g., trailing twelve months), serving as a benchmark for valuation and investment decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Price Target = Neckline + Pattern Height
Target Price = Breakout Level + Cup Height
Price Target = P/E Ratio × Earnings

nodes.name: Price Value of a Basis Point
aliases: Dollar Value of a Basis Point
nodes.definition: Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP) is the dollar change in a bond’s price resulting from a 1 basis point (0.01%) change in yield. It quantifies interest rate sensitivity and is calculated as modified duration times the bond’s dirty price times 0.0001.

nodes.name: Price Variance
nodes.definition: Price variance refers to the cost difference resulting from the discrepancy between actual price and standard price under standard costing. It is a component of variable cost variance in cost variance analysis and is commonly used in analyzing direct materials, direct labor, and variable manufacturing overhead.

formulas.source_formula: Price Variance = (Actual Price - Standard Price) × Actual Quantity

nodes.name: Price at End of Restriction Period
Price at the End of the Restriction Period
aliases: Price at the End of Lock-up Period
nodes.definition: Price at the end of the restriction period refers to the market price of a stock at the specific point in time (typically the lock-up expiration date) when the share lock-up period concludes and the relevant shares become freely tradable on the market. This price is a direct market-derived or contractually agreed-upon base figure used for assessing share value or calculating related financial derivatives, rather than a composite value computed through other financial formulas.

nodes.name: Price of Complementary Goods
nodes.definition: The price of complementary goods refers to the price of goods that must be used together with another product to satisfy the same consumer need. Examples include cars and gasoline, household appliances and electricity. Generally, the demand for a product moves inversely with the price of its complementary goods; that is, when the price of a complementary good rises, the demand for the product decreases.

nodes.name: Price of Tax-exempt Purchased Raw Materials
Price per Square Foot
nodes.definition: Price per square foot is a valuation metric calculated by dividing the total price of an asset by its area in square feet, commonly used in real estate to compare property values on a standardized basis.

formulas.source_formula: Price per Square Foot = Total Price ÷ Square Feet

nodes.name: Price to Free Cash Flow
aliases: Price to Free Cash Flow Ratio
nodes.definition: Price to Free Cash Flow (P/FCF) is a valuation ratio that compares a company's market capitalization to its free cash flow. It indicates how much investors are willing to pay for each unit of free cash flow and is used to assess equity valuation relative to cash generation capacity. Lower values may suggest undervaluation and higher values may suggest overvaluation, contingent on industry norms and company context.

nodes.name: Price to Tangible Book Value (PTBV)
aliases: 市价对有形账面价值比
nodes.definition: Price to Tangible Book Value (PTBV) is a valuation ratio that compares a company’s market price per share to its tangible book value per share, indicating how the market values the firm’s tangible net assets. It is particularly relevant for asset-intensive industries where tangible assets comprise a significant portion of total value.

formulas.source_formula: Price to Tangible Book Value = Share Price ÷ Tangible Book Value per Share

nodes.name: Price-Earnings Ratio
nodes.definition: The Price-Earnings (P/E) ratio measures the price investors are willing to pay for each dollar of a company's earnings, serving as a key indicator of market expectations and stock valuation.

formulas.source_formula: Price-Earnings Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Earnings per Share
supporting_source_formulas: Price-Earnings Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Earnings per Share

nodes.name: Price-Weighted Index
nodes.definition: A price-weighted index is a type of stock market index calculated by summing the current market prices of all its constituent stocks and then dividing by a divisor (or adjustment factor). The level of the index is directly dependent on the stock prices of its constituents, with higher-priced stocks exerting a greater influence on the index. The Dow Jones Industrial Average is a classic example of a price-weighted index.

formulas.source_formula: Price-Weighted Index = Sum of Constituent Stock Prices ÷ Divisor

nodes.name: Price-to-Book Ratio
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Book Ratio is the ratio of a stock's price to the company's book value per share (or net assets), reflecting the market's valuation level of the company's net assets and used to measure whether a stock is overvalued or undervalued.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Book Ratio = (Dividend × (1 + Growth Rate)) ÷ (Cost of Equity - Growth Rate) ÷ Book Value per Share
Price-to-Book Ratio = (Return on Equity × Dividend Payout Ratio × (1 + Growth Rate)) ÷ (Cost of Equity - Growth Rate)
Price-to-Book Ratio = Market Price ÷ Net Assets
Price-to-Book Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Book Value per Share
supporting_source_formulas: Price-to-Book Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Book Value per Share

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Book Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Book Value per Share
supporting_source_formulas: P/B Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Book Value per Share
Price-to-Book Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Book Value per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Book Ratio (P/B Ratio)
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Book (P/B) ratio compares a company’s market price per share to its book value per share, indicating how the market values the company’s net assets. A lower P/B may suggest undervaluation relative to the firm’s book value, while a higher P/B may reflect growth expectations or asset-light business models. This implementation uses an adjusted book value per share that excludes intangible assets.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Book Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Book Value per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Book Ratio Multiple
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Book Ratio Multiple is a valuation metric that measures a stock's market value relative to its book value (net assets), reflecting the price multiple investors are willing to pay for each unit of the company's net assets per share.

nodes.name: Price-to-Cash Flow Ratio
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Cash Flow (P/CF) ratio measures a company's valuation relative to the cash it generates from operations. It is calculated either on a per-share basis as the market price per share divided by operating cash flow per share, or on a company-wide basis as market capitalization divided by total operating cash flow. The ratio helps assess valuation using cash flows, which are less susceptible to accounting adjustments than earnings.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Cash Flow Ratio = Share Price ÷ Operating Cash Flow per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio measures how much investors are willing to pay per dollar of a company's earnings. It is calculated by dividing the market price per share by the earnings per share (EPS) and is widely used in equity valuation and comparative analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Earnings per Share (EPS)
Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio = Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Earnings Ratio
nodes.definition: The price-to-earnings ratio is the ratio of a stock's market price to its earnings per share, used to assess stock valuation levels. It is a key metric in valuation techniques and comparable company analysis, reflecting the price investors pay per unit of earnings.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Earnings Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Net Profit per Share
Price-to-Earnings Ratio = Market Price per Common Share ÷ Earnings per Common Share
P/E Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share
supporting_source_formulas: P/E Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share
Price-to-Earnings Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share

formulas.source_formula: P/E Ratio = Stock Price ÷ Earnings per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Earnings Ratio (P/E Ratio)
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio is a valuation multiple that measures the market price per share relative to earnings per share (EPS), indicating how much investors are willing to pay for each unit of a company’s earnings. It is widely used to compare valuations across companies, industries, and market indexes, and is meaningful primarily when EPS is positive.

formulas.source_formula: P/E Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Earnings per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Earnings Ratio at Issuance
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Earnings Ratio at Issuance refers to the ratio of a company's stock offering price to its earnings per share (typically referring to the EPS of the last full fiscal year prior to issuance) during its initial public offering (IPO). It is a key metric for evaluating the reasonableness of new stock pricing and assessing the company's valuation level.

nodes.name: Price-to-NAV Ratio
nodes.definition: The Price-to-NAV Ratio compares a fund's market price to its Net Asset Value (NAV) to indicate whether the fund trades at a premium (ratio > 1) or discount (ratio < 1) relative to its underlying net assets. It is commonly used for ETFs and closed-end funds to assess investor sentiment and potential pricing inefficiencies.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-NAV Ratio = Market Price ÷ Net Asset Value (NAV)

nodes.name: Price-to-Rent Ratio
nodes.definition: The price-to-rent ratio measures the relationship between a property's purchase price and its annual rental income. It is calculated as the median home price divided by the median annual rent and is used to assess housing valuation, affordability, and whether buying or renting is more economical in a given market. Higher ratios generally indicate buying may be less favorable relative to renting, while lower ratios suggest potential buying attractiveness.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Rent Ratio = Median Home Price ÷ Median Annual Rent

nodes.name: Price-to-Sales (P/S)
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Sales (P/S) ratio is a valuation metric that measures how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of a company's sales. It is calculated by dividing the market value (price) per share by the sales per share, and is commonly used to compare relative valuation across companies, especially in sectors where earnings may be volatile or negative.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Sales (P/S) = Market Value per Share ÷ Sales per Share

nodes.name: Price-to-Sales Ratio
nodes.definition: The Price-to-Sales Ratio is a financial ratio used to evaluate stock valuation levels, reflecting the relationship between a stock's market value and the company's revenue. This metric is commonly used to value companies that are not yet profitable or have unstable earnings.

formulas.source_formula: Price-to-Sales Ratio = Market Price per Share ÷ Revenue per Share

nodes.name: Price/Earnings to Growth (PEG) Ratio
aliases: 市盈率相对盈利增长比率
nodes.definition: The PEG ratio is a valuation metric that adjusts the Price-to-Earnings (P/E) ratio by the expected earnings growth rate to assess whether a stock’s price is reasonable relative to its growth prospects. Commonly used in GARP (Growth at a Reasonable Price) investing, a PEG near 1 is often interpreted as fair value, while values above or below 1 may indicate overvaluation or undervaluation relative to growth.

formulas.source_formula: PEG Ratio = P/E Ratio ÷ Earnings Growth Rate
PEG Ratio = Price-to-Earnings (P/E) Ratio ÷ Earnings Growth Rate

nodes.name: Prime Cost
nodes.definition: Prime cost refers to the costs incurred in the production or provision of services that can be directly and clearly attributed to specific products or services, primarily including direct materials and direct labor—original expenditures that can be directly traced to the product. It represents the most fundamental cost data in accounting records and serves as the starting point for subsequent cost calculation and analysis.

nodes.name: Prime Rate
nodes.definition: The prime rate, or base lending rate, is an interest rate used by banks, typically representing the rate at which they lend to their most creditworthy customers. This rate serves as a benchmark for various floating-rate financial products, such as adjustable-rate mortgages, credit cards, and home equity lines of credit.

formulas.source_formula: Prime Rate = Federal Funds Rate + Spread

nodes.name: Principal
nodes.definition: Principal refers to the original amount of a loan, deposit, or investment before interest is calculated, serving as the basis for determining derived values such as interest and future value in financial calculations.

formulas.source_formula: Principal = Interest ÷ Interest Rate ÷ Time

nodes.name: Principal Amount
nodes.definition: Principal amount refers to the original sum of money initially invested or borrowed in financial calculations (such as calculating interest, future value, or present value). It serves as the basis for computing financial metrics like interest and future value, typically functioning as a known input variable rather than a calculated result.

nodes.name: Principal Component
nodes.definition: Principal components are a small number of new, mutually uncorrelated variables obtained through linear combinations of multiple correlated original variables (indicators) using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). These new variables retain the maximum possible information from the original data and are used to simplify data structure and reduce dimensionality.

formulas.source_formula: Principal Payment (Monthly) = Scheduled Monthly Payment - Interest Payment (Monthly)

nodes.name: Principal Present Value
nodes.definition: Principal Present Value refers to the value of the original capital invested at the beginning of an investment or financial calculation at the calculation point in time. When considering the time value of money, it typically refers to the discounted present value of the principal corresponding to a future series of cash flows, serving as the basis for calculating investment returns and future values.

nodes.name: Principal Repayment Amount
nodes.definition: The principal repayment amount refers to the portion of the loan principal that a borrower repays in each installment. It is a key component of the total debt repayment, and its calculation depends on the loan principal, interest rate, repayment term, and repayment method (such as equal principal or equal principal and interest). It is a core concept in financial management and financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Principal Repayment Amount = Periodic Repayment Amount - Periodic Interest

nodes.name: Principal Repayment Portion
nodes.definition: In the repayment process of debts such as loans or bonds, the portion of each periodic payment that is used to reduce the original principal amount (i.e., the initial debt amount). It does not include the interest portion.

nodes.name: Principal Terminal Value
nodes.definition: Principal terminal value refers to the total value achieved by the initially invested principal at the end of a specific investment period, after appreciation over time (such as through interest, dividends, or capital gains). It reflects the final outcome of the principal after considering the time value of money and investment returns.

nodes.name: Principal and Interest of Debt Maturing in Current Period
Principal, Interest, Taxes, Insurance (PITI)
nodes.definition: PITI is the total monthly mortgage payment comprising principal and interest, plus the monthly portions of property taxes and homeowners insurance. It is used to evaluate housing affordability and underwriting metrics such as the debt-to-income ratio for fixed-rate mortgages.

formulas.source_formula: Monthly PITI Payment = Monthly Principal and Interest + Monthly Property Tax + Monthly Homeowners Insurance

nodes.name: Prior Period Accounting Profit
nodes.definition: Prior period accounting profit refers to the total profit or net profit ultimately realized by an enterprise through operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities in the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It serves as a reference data for comparison when preparing the current period's income statement.

nodes.name: Prior Period Accounts Receivable Turnover Ratio
Prior Period Amount
nodes.definition: The prior period amount is a benchmark figure directly entered in financial statements (such as the income statement or cash flow statement) for comparison with current period data. It represents the actual amount incurred for the corresponding item in the previous accounting period (e.g., the same period last year or the prior period). It is typically obtained directly from historical financial data by specifying an accounting period (e.g., 'Year-1' or 'Month-1'), rather than being derived through formula calculation.

nodes.name: Prior Period Applicable Income Tax Rate
aliases: Applicable Income Tax Rate of Previous Period
nodes.definition: The prior period applicable income tax rate refers to the statutory corporate income tax rate actually applied to an enterprise's taxable income when calculating the income tax expense for the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter).

nodes.name: Prior Period Asset Impairment Loss
nodes.definition: Prior period asset impairment loss refers to the loss recognized by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) due to the recoverable amount of an asset being lower than its carrying value. This loss reflects the decline in the economic value of the asset during the prior period and is deducted as an expense when calculating the total profit for the prior period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Business Taxes and Surcharges
Prior Period Cost of Sales
aliases: Cost of Sales of Prior Period
nodes.definition: Prior Period Cost of Sales refers to the total direct costs incurred by an enterprise for its daily business operations, such as selling goods and providing services, during the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year or quarter). It is typically taken directly from the 'Cost of Sales' line item in the income statement of the prior period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Current Assets
nodes.definition: Prior period current assets refer to the total amount of current assets presented on a company's balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous quarter or fiscal year). It represents the aggregate of assets that the company owned at the end of the prior period and are expected to be converted into cash or consumed within one year or one operating cycle. This is a fundamental data point directly obtained from historical financial statements.

nodes.name: Prior Period Current Income Tax
aliases: Income Tax Payable of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prior period current income tax refers to the amount of income tax determined and payable to tax authorities, calculated in accordance with tax laws and regulations for transactions and events that occurred in the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter). It is one of the components used to calculate the prior period income tax expense.

nodes.name: Prior Period Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Prior period current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt that an enterprise is obligated to settle within one normal operating cycle or within one year from the balance sheet date, as recorded at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous fiscal year or quarter). Its calculation logic is the same as that for current period current liabilities, and it serves as fundamental data for calculating financial metrics such as changes in working capital and increases in liabilities.

operands.metric: Prior Period Long-term Borrowings Due Within One Year

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Current Liabilities = Prior Period Short-term Borrowings + Prior Period Accounts Payable + Prior Period Advances from Customers + Prior Period Employee Benefits Payable + Prior Period Taxes Payable + Prior Period Other Payables + Prior Period Long-term Borrowings Due Within One Year + Prior Period Other Current Liabilities

operands.metric: Non-current Liabilities Due within One Year (Prior Period)

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Current Liabilities = Prior Period Short-term Borrowings + Prior Period Notes Payable + Prior Period Accounts Payable + Prior Period Advances from Customers + Prior Period Employee Benefits Payable + Prior Period Taxes Payable + Prior Period Other Payables + Prior Period Non-current Liabilities Due Within One Year + Prior Period Other Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Prior Period Deferred Tax
aliases: Deferred Income Taxes of Last Period
nodes.definition: Prior period deferred tax refers to the net combined amount of deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities recognized according to accounting standards at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or prior quarter). It reflects the tax amounts from temporary differences in the prior period that are expected to affect income tax expense in future periods.

nodes.name: Prior Period Deferred Tax Asset
aliases: Deferred Tax Asset of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prior period deferred tax asset refers to the amount of assets formed at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) due to deductible temporary differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations, which are expected to be used to reduce taxable income in future periods. It reflects the recognition of future tax benefits at the end of the prior period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Deferred Tax Liability
aliases: Deferred Tax Liability of Previous Period
上期应纳税暂时性差异负债
