nodes.definition: Prior period deferred tax liability refers to the amount of income tax calculated at the applicable tax rate, based on taxable temporary differences between the carrying amount of assets and their tax base at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or prior quarter), which is expected to be payable to tax authorities in future periods. It reflects the future tax obligation recognized in the previous period's financial statements.

nodes.name: Prior Period Dividend
nodes.definition: Prior period dividend refers to the dividend that a company has actually paid or declared to its shareholders during a specific past accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). It reflects the company's historical profit distribution and serves as an important reference for analyzing the company's dividend policy and forecasting future dividends.

nodes.name: Prior Period EBIT
nodes.definition: Prior Period EBIT refers to the earnings before interest and taxes achieved by an enterprise in the previous accounting period, i.e., profit before deducting interest expenses and income tax expenses. It is a fundamental composite indicator in financial analysis used to evaluate business operating performance, financial leverage, and calculate financial ratios such as the EBIT change rate.

nodes.name: Prior Period Ending Contra Account Balance
Prior Period Expenses
nodes.definition: Prior period expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise during the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) for organizing and managing production and operating activities, selling goods, or providing services, which cannot be directly attributed to the cost of a specific product or service. These expenses are generally directly recognized in the profit or loss of the period in which they occur and constitute a significant deduction item in calculating the total profit of the prior period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Fair Value Change Gains
aliases: Fair Value Change Income of Previous Period
上期公允价值变动损益
前期公允价值变动损益
前期公允价值变动收益
nodes.definition: Prior Period Fair Value Change Gains refer to the unrealized gains or losses arising from changes in the fair value of assets measured at fair value (such as trading financial assets, investment properties, etc.) held by an enterprise during the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year or quarter). These gains or losses are included in the total profit of the prior period, reflecting the changes in the book value of assets due to market price fluctuations during that period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Income Tax
nodes.definition: Prior period income tax refers to the income tax expense calculated, actually paid, or accrued by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter) in accordance with tax laws and regulations. It is a historical actual amount, serving as fundamental raw data in financial statements, typically used for comparative analysis with current period data.

nodes.name: Prior Period Income Tax Expense
nodes.definition: Prior period income tax expense refers to the income tax expense recognized by an enterprise in the previous accounting period, which is related to the total profit of that period. Its calculation logic is consistent with the current period income tax expense and it is an important component in calculating the prior period net profit.

operands.metric: Income Tax Payable for Prior Period

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Income Tax Expense = Prior Period Income Tax Payable + Prior Period Deferred Tax Liability - Prior Period Deferred Tax Asset
Prior Period Income Tax Expense = Prior Period Current Income Tax + Prior Period Deferred Income Tax

nodes.name: Prior Period Indicator Value
nodes.definition: Prior period indicator value refers to the numerical value of a specific financial or business metric from the previous comparable period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) used for comparison with current period data in financial or operational analysis. It serves as the baseline reference data for calculating changes such as growth amount and growth rate.

nodes.name: Prior Period Investment Income
nodes.definition: Prior period investment income refers to the net income or return realized by an enterprise from external investment activities (such as purchasing stocks, bonds, funds, or other equity or debt investments) during the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year, quarter, or month).

nodes.name: Prior Period Long-term Borrowings Due Within One Year
Prior Period Net Income
nodes.definition: Prior period net income refers to the final financial result generated from business operations in the previous accounting period (e.g., previous quarter, previous fiscal year), representing the profit amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes. It reflects the operating performance of the enterprise in the prior period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Net Operating Assets
aliases: Net Operating Assets of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prior period net operating assets refer to the net value of a company's operating assets minus operating liabilities at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). It represents the net capital scale actually invested and occupied by the company in its operating activities during the prior period and serves as the basis for calculating dynamic indicators such as net investment in net operating assets for the current period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Net Profit
nodes.definition: Prior period net profit refers to the net profit achieved by an enterprise in the previous accounting period. It is the historical value of net profit, a composite metric that can be calculated from income statement items, commonly used in financial comparative analysis and metric change calculations (such as change in earnings per common share).

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Net Profit = Prior Period Total Profit - Prior Period Income Tax Expense
Prior Period Net Profit = Prior Period Total Profit × (1 - Period Income Tax Rate)

operands.metric: Prior Period Business Taxes and Surcharges

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Net Profit = Prior Period Operating Revenue - Prior Period Operating Cost - Prior Period Business Taxes and Surcharges - Prior Period Selling Expenses - Prior Period Administrative Expenses - Prior Period Financial Expenses - Prior Period Income Tax

nodes.name: Prior Period Non-current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Prior period non-current liabilities refer to the total amount of liabilities with a repayment period exceeding one year or one normal operating cycle that an enterprise bears as of the balance sheet date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). They are directly sourced from the financial statements of the prior period and serve as fundamental data for financial analysis and comparison.

nodes.name: Prior Period Non-operating Expenses
nodes.definition: Prior period non-operating expenses refer to various losses or expenditures incurred by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter) that are not directly related to its daily production and operating activities. These expenses are typically incidental, such as losses from damage or scrapping of fixed assets, charitable donations, fines, extraordinary losses, etc.

nodes.name: Prior Period Non-operating Income
nodes.definition: Prior period non-operating income refers to various revenues generated by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year) that are not directly related to its daily production and operating activities.

nodes.name: Prior Period Operating Current Assets
nodes.definition: Prior Period Operating Current Assets is a composite metric calculated based on prior period financial data, specifically the portion of total current assets excluding trading financial assets, used to measure the level of operating current assets in the prior period.

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Operating Current Assets = Prior Period Total Current Assets - Prior Period Trading Financial Assets

nodes.name: Prior Period Operating Current Liabilities
aliases: Operating Current Liabilities of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prior period operating current liabilities refer to the total amount of debt arising from daily business operations that is expected to be repaid within a normal operating cycle (typically within one year), as of the closing date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter). They generally include short-term liability items directly related to core business operations, such as accounts payable, deferred revenue, accrued employee compensation, and taxes payable.

nodes.name: Prior Period Operating Long-term Liabilities
aliases: Operating Long-term Liabilities of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prior period operating long-term liabilities refer to debts with a repayment term exceeding one year that an enterprise bears at the end of the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) to support its long-term operating activities. These liabilities are typically related to the core business operations of the enterprise, such as long-term borrowings and bonds payable, but exclude portions due within a short term (usually within one year).

nodes.name: Prior Period Operating Revenue Amount
nodes.definition: Prior period operating revenue amount refers to the total revenue earned by an enterprise through its principal operating activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, during the previous comparable accounting period (e.g., previous month, previous quarter, or previous fiscal year). In the income statement, it is typically presented as the 'prior period amount' column for comparison with the current period amount to analyze revenue trend changes.

nodes.name: Prior Period Other Comprehensive Income
aliases: Other Comprehensive Income of Prior Period
nodes.definition: Prior period other comprehensive income refers to the various gains or losses that were directly recorded in the changes of owners' equity but not included in the current period's net profit during the previous accounting period. It reflects changes in asset values or equity adjustments that occurred in the prior period but were not presented in the income statement.

nodes.name: Prior Period Other Current Liabilities
aliases: Other Current Liabilities of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Prior Period Other Current Liabilities refer to various obligations of an enterprise at the balance sheet date of the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter) that are expected to be settled within one year or one normal operating cycle (whichever is longer), and are not separately presented under major current liability items (such as short-term borrowings, accounts payable, etc.).

nodes.name: Prior Period Permanent Differences
nodes.definition: Prior period permanent differences refer to differences arising in the previous accounting period (such as the prior year or quarter) due to fundamental discrepancies between accounting standards and tax laws in the recognition of revenues and expenses, resulting in irreconcilable variances between pre-tax accounting profit and taxable income that cannot be reversed or eliminated in future periods. Such differences only affect the income tax expense of the period in which they occur and do not give rise to deferred tax assets or liabilities.

nodes.name: Prior Period Preferential Reduction Amount
aliases: Tax Abatement Amount of Previous Period
nodes.definition: The Prior Period Preferential Reduction Amount refers to the amount directly reduced or credited from the tax payable by an enterprise in the previous accounting period (such as the previous fiscal year or quarter) according to applicable tax preferential policies. It reflects the actual scale of tax benefits enjoyed by the enterprise in the prior period and is one of the adjustment items to be considered when calculating the current period's actual tax burden.

nodes.name: Prior Period Preferred Stock Dividends
nodes.definition: Prior period preferred stock dividends refer to the compensation distributed to preferred shareholders in the previous accounting period according to the provisions of the preferred stock issuance terms, based on the agreed dividend rate or amount. It is a non-leaf node indicator that must be deducted when calculating the change in earnings per common share.

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Preferred Stock Dividends = Preferred Stock Par Value × Fixed Dividend Rate
Prior Period Preferred Stock Dividends = Number of Preferred Shares × Preferred Stock Par Value × Preferred Stock Dividend Rate

nodes.name: Prior Period Price
nodes.definition: Prior period price typically refers to the historical transaction price or cost of an asset, commodity, or service before a specific point in time or period. In financial analysis, it is often used as a benchmark for evaluating current price movements, calculating returns, or analyzing market trends.

nodes.name: Prior Period Reported Amount
nodes.definition: The Prior Period Reported Amount refers to financial data from the previous comparable period used for comparison with current period amounts in financial statements. It is typically not raw data taken directly from the books, but rather derived through retrieval operations on specific accounting items for a designated period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year), fitting the definition of being calculable via formulas from other metrics.

nodes.name: Prior Period Reported Improvement Quantity
nodes.definition: Prior Period Reported Improvement Quantity refers to the absolute change calculated by comparing the values of the same indicator in the current period and prior period financial statements, used to measure the degree of improvement in financial or operational performance, and typically serves as the basis for calculating derivative metrics such as the improvement percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Reported Improvement Quantity = Current Period Reported Value - Prior Period Reported Value
Prior Period Reported Improvement Quantity = Prior Period Reported Value × Reported Improvement Percentage ÷ 100

nodes.name: Prior Period Revenue
aliases: 上一会计期间营业收入
nodes.definition: Prior period revenue refers to the total revenue recognized by an enterprise from its principal operating activities, such as sales of goods and provision of services, during the previous accounting period (e.g., previous month, quarter, or fiscal year). It is historical data directly obtained from the accounting records of the prior period and serves as the foundation for financial comparison and analysis.

nodes.name: Prior Period Sales
nodes.definition: Prior period sales refers to the total revenue amount generated by a company from selling goods or providing services during a specific period preceding the current period (e.g., the previous fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is a fundamental historical financial data point, typically obtained directly from the company's accounting records or financial statements, and is used for comparative analysis with current period data.

nodes.name: Prior Period Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Prior period shareholders' equity refers to the total shareholders' equity of an enterprise in the previous accounting period, typically calculated based on balance sheet items using the formula: Shareholders' Equity = Total Assets - Total Liabilities. As a historical value, it is used in financial analysis and ratio calculations, such as the shareholders' equity growth rate, and is categorized as a non-leaf node concept.

formulas.source_formula: Prior Period Shareholders' Equity = Prior Period Total Assets - Prior Period Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Prior Period Taxes and Surcharges
aliases: Taxes and Surcharges of Previous Period
上期主营业务税金及附加
nodes.definition: Prior Period Taxes and Surcharges refer to the total amount of various related taxes and fees attributable to business activities, as presented in the income statement for the previous accounting period (such as the previous year or quarter). These taxes and fees typically include Consumption Tax, Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, Education Surcharge, Resource Tax, Property Tax, Urban Land Use Tax, Vehicle and Vessel Tax, Stamp Duty, etc.

nodes.name: Prior Period Trading Financial Assets
aliases: Trading Financial Assets of Previous Period
上期交易性金融资产余额
上期末交易性金融资产
nodes.definition: Prior period trading financial assets refer to the carrying amount of trading financial assets presented on the balance sheet at the end of the previous accounting period (e.g., the previous year or quarter). They reflect the fair value of financial assets (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.) held by the enterprise for short-term trading purposes at the end of the prior period.

nodes.name: Prior Period Value
nodes.definition: Prior period value refers to the numerical value from the previous accounting period in financial reports, used for comparative analysis. It typically denotes the amount of line items from the preceding period in statements such as the income statement, which can be obtained or calculated through accounting ledger functions. In financial analysis, it is often used as a benchmark for calculating metrics such as growth rates.

nodes.name: Prior Probability
nodes.definition: Prior probability refers to the initial estimated probability of an event occurring, based on prior experience, historical data, logical analysis, or theoretical deduction, before considering any new evidence or data.

nodes.name: Prior Year Amount
nodes.definition: In accounting and financial reporting, 'Prior Year Amount' typically refers to the financial data as of the end of the last complete fiscal year. For example, when preparing the current year's income statement, the 'Prior Year Amount' column reflects the operating results for the same period of the previous year, used for year-over-year comparative analysis.

nodes.name: Prior Year Credit Sales Amount
nodes.definition: Prior Year Credit Sales Amount refers to the total sales revenue from goods or services achieved through credit sales (i.e., allowing customers deferred payment) within the previous fiscal year. It is typically sourced directly from the company's sales records or income statement and serves as fundamental historical data for analyzing accounts receivable turnover and the effectiveness of credit policies.

nodes.name: Prior Year Dividend Per Share
nodes.definition: Prior Year Dividend Per Share is a composite financial metric calculated using the prior fiscal year's financial data, representing the dividend amount received per common share. It reflects the company's dividend distribution level in the previous year and is commonly used in calculations such as the dividend growth rate.

nodes.name: Prior Year Operating Current Assets
nodes.definition: Prior Year Operating Current Assets refers to the total amount of current assets used for daily business operations at the end of the previous fiscal year. It is typically calculated by combining operational items such as accounts receivable, inventory, and prepayments, and serves as a key foundational metric for calculating the prior year's operating working capital.

nodes.name: Prior Year Operating Current Liabilities
nodes.definition: Prior Year Operating Current Liabilities refer to the debts related to daily business operations that are expected to be repaid within one year or one operating cycle at the end of the previous fiscal year. They are typically calculated by combining balance sheet items such as accounts payable, advances from customers, employee compensation payable, taxes payable, etc., and are a key component in calculating financial metrics like operating working capital.

nodes.name: Prior Year Operating Working Capital
aliases: Operating Working Capital of Previous Year
上年经营营运资本余额
nodes.definition: Prior Year Operating Working Capital refers to the balance of operating working capital at the end of the previous accounting year, which is the difference between operating current assets and operating current liabilities. It is a composite metric commonly used in calculating financial analysis indicators such as the increase in operating working capital, reflecting the short-term operating fund status of the enterprise in the prior year.

formulas.source_formula: Prior Year Operating Working Capital = Prior Year Operating Current Assets - Prior Year Operating Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Prior Year Revenue
nodes.definition: Prior year revenue refers to the total revenue amount realized by an enterprise through its ordinary business activities, such as sales of goods, provision of services, and transfer of asset usage rights, during the previous complete fiscal year (typically from January 1 to December 31). It is an important historical data item in financial statements, used for comparative analysis with current year revenue.

nodes.name: Prior Year Sales
nodes.definition: Prior year sales refers to the total revenue amount generated by a company from the sale of goods or provision of services during the previous complete fiscal year. It is a fundamental historical business data point that reflects the company's past operational scale and performance level.

nodes.name: Prior Year Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Prior year sales revenue refers to the total revenue amount obtained by an enterprise through its principal operating activities, such as selling goods or providing services, during the previous complete fiscal year. It reflects the company's past operating scale and performance level, serving as important historical data for financial analysis and forecasting.

nodes.name: Prior Year Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Prior year sales volume refers to the total quantity of products or services sold by an enterprise through the sale of goods or provision of services during the previous complete fiscal year. It serves as a critical foundational data point for conducting year-over-year sales comparisons, calculating sales growth rates, and performing related analyses.

nodes.name: Prior Year Stock Price per Share
aliases: Previous Year's Stock Price per Share
Prior Year Closing Price per Share
nodes.definition: Prior year stock price per share refers to the market price of a listed company's stock at the end of the previous complete fiscal year, typically based on the closing price on the last trading day of that year. It reflects the market's assessment of the company's value at a specific point in time and serves as fundamental data for calculating metrics such as stock returns and growth rates.

nodes.name: Private Equity
nodes.definition: Private Equity (PE) refers to equity in non-publicly traded companies that is not issued to the general public but rather to specialized investment funds and limited partnerships, which actively participate in the management and structure of the enterprises. As a financial product, private equity funds utilize private capital to finance long-term investment strategies for illiquid companies, typically involving leveraged buyouts, operational restructuring, and value creation through revenue growth, margin improvement, debt repayment, and multiple expansion.

formulas.source_formula: Private Equity = Contributed Equity

nodes.name: Private Equity Fund
nodes.definition: A private equity fund is a collective investment vehicle used to invest in various equity (and, to a lesser extent, debt) securities according to investment strategies related to private equity. It typically takes the form of a limited partnership with a lifespan of 10 years (often extendable by one to two years), raised and managed by a private equity firm acting as the general partner.

formulas.source_formula: Private Equity Fund = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Pro Rata
nodes.definition: Pro rata refers to allocating amounts proportionally based on an entity's share of the total, commonly used to distribute costs, dividends, interest, payroll, or benefits according to applicable units relative to total units.

formulas.source_formula: Pro Rata = Applicable Units ÷ Maximum Quantity

nodes.name: Probability
nodes.definition: Probability is a numerical measure of the likelihood of a random event occurring, with a value between 0 and 1. A value of 0 indicates the event is impossible, while 1 indicates the event is certain. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a known weight or base data for calculating metrics such as expected rate of return.

formulas.source_formula: Probability (Discrete Uniform) = 1 ÷ Number of Discrete Outcomes

nodes.name: Probability Corresponding to Each Market Return
nodes.definition: In financial risk and return analysis, 'Probability Corresponding to Each Market Return' refers to the likelihood (i.e., probability) assigned to each possible outcome of market return (or portfolio return) when calculating the expected value, variance, and standard deviation of market returns. It serves as the fundamental data point for constructing the probability distribution of returns and measuring risk (such as standard deviation).

nodes.name: Probability Corresponding to the Expected Rate of Return
nodes.definition: In calculating the expected rate of return on an investment, this concept refers to the likelihood of occurrence for each possible rate of return outcome (such as high return, low return, or loss) in the forecast, typically expressed as a percentage or decimal. It serves as the key weighting factor for calculating the weighted average of various possible return scenarios to derive the overall expected value.

nodes.name: Probability Density Function
nodes.definition: The probability density function describes the density of the probability distribution of a continuous random variable around various possible value points. Its function value itself is not a probability, but its integral over a certain interval equals the probability that the random variable falls within that interval.

nodes.name: Probability Density Function Value
nodes.definition: The probability density function (PDF) value refers to the output value of the probability density function for a continuous random variable corresponding to a specific input value (e.g., x). It describes the relative likelihood of the random variable taking values near that point. It is not a probability itself, but the probability over an interval can be obtained by integrating the PDF over that interval.

nodes.name: Probability Density Function of Random Variable X
nodes.definition: The probability density function is a non-negative real-valued function that describes the distribution of a continuous random variable X. It is not a probability itself, but its integral over any interval equals the probability that random variable X falls within that interval.

nodes.name: Probability Distribution Function
nodes.definition: The probability distribution function, typically referring to the cumulative distribution function, describes the probability that a random variable takes a value within a specific interval (usually less than or equal to a certain value). It fully characterizes the statistical regularity of the random variable.

nodes.name: Probability of A or B (Mutually Exclusive Events)

formulas.source_formula: Probability of A or B (Mutually Exclusive Events) = Probability of Event 1 + Probability of Event 2

nodes.name: Probability of Default
nodes.definition: Probability of Default (PD) is a financial term used to describe the likelihood of a default occurring within a specific time frame. It provides an estimate of the possibility that a borrower will fail to fulfill its debt obligations.

nodes.name: Probability of Each Scenario
nodes.definition: Probability of each scenario refers to the assignment of a numerical value to each possible future occurrence (or state) of an event in decision analysis, investment evaluation, or risk management, quantifying the likelihood of that scenario occurring. The sum of the probabilities of all possible scenarios equals 1.

nodes.name: Probability of Economic Scenarios
nodes.definition: Probability of economic scenarios refers to the numerical estimation of the likelihood of different economic conditions (such as boom, recession, normal, etc.) occurring in the future, used in risk assessment and financial decision-making. These probabilities are fundamental input data, typically directly assigned based on historical statistics, expert judgment, or market expectations, and are used to calculate metrics such as expected return and risk.

formulas.source_formula: Probability of Either Event (Non-Mutually Exclusive) = Probability of Event 1 + Probability of Event 2 - Probability of Both Events

nodes.name: Probability of Occurrence
nodes.definition: Probability of occurrence is a numerical measure describing the likelihood of a random event happening in the future, with its value ranging between 0 and 1. A value of 0 indicates the event is impossible, while 1 indicates the event is certain. It serves as a fundamental input for risk assessment, financial modeling, and investment decision-making.

nodes.name: Probability of Occurrence of Each State
nodes.definition: The probability of occurrence of each state refers to the measure of likelihood, derived through statistical or model analysis, that a specific event or business condition may occur in the future. It serves as the basis for calculating financial metrics such as the expected rate of return on assets, and is typically calculated based on historical data, sample statistics, or specific probability distribution models (e.g., binomial distribution).

operands.metric: Number of Occurrences of That State

formulas.source_formula: Probability of Occurrence of Each State = Number of Occurrences of That State ÷ Total Sample Size

nodes.name: Probability of Occurrence of Scenario i in Year t
aliases: Occurrence Probability of Case i in Year t
Occurrence Probability of Event i in Year t
Probability of Scenario i in Year t
第t年特定情况i的可能性
nodes.definition: In financial forecasting or risk assessment models, this refers to the likelihood of a specific scenario i (e.g., favorable, average, or poor market conditions) actually occurring in future year t. This probability is typically set directly based on historical statistical data, expert judgment, or model assumptions, and serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating derived metrics such as expected values.

nodes.name: Probability of Occurrence of the Return
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, particularly when assessing investment risk and return, 'Probability of Occurrence of the Return' refers to the likelihood that a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) will achieve a particular level of return in the future under given market or economic conditions. It is one of the fundamental data points required for calculating an asset's expected return and measuring risk (e.g., variance).

nodes.name: Probability of Risk Event Occurrence
nodes.definition: Probability of risk event occurrence refers to the likelihood that an adverse or uncertain event will actually occur in the future under specific conditions, and is one of the core elements for measuring risk severity.

nodes.name: Probability of the Value
nodes.definition: Probability of the value refers to the likelihood that a random variable takes a specific value or falls within a specific interval, with its value ranging between 0 and 1, where 0 indicates an impossible event and 1 indicates a certain event.

nodes.name: Probability of the i-th Scenario
nodes.definition: In probability theory and statistics, 'Probability of the i-th Scenario' refers to the likelihood of the occurrence of a specific i-th scenario or outcome among multiple possible scenarios or outcomes, typically represented by a numerical value between 0 and 1.

nodes.name: Proceeds from Disposal of Existing Fixed Assets
aliases: Proceeds from Disposal of Fixed Assets
nodes.definition: Proceeds from disposal of existing fixed assets refer to the cash income obtained by a company when disposing of its original, no longer used fixed assets (such as through sale, scrapping, or dismantling during renovation or replacement). This income represents a cash inflow item that must be considered when calculating the initial investment of a project or the cost of asset replacement.

formulas.source_formula: Proceeds from Option Exercises = In-the-money Options and Warrants × Exercise Price

nodes.name: Proceeds from Sale of Old Assets
Proceeds from Sale of Old Equipment
Proceeds from Sale of Trading Financial Assets
aliases: 交易性金融资产出售收入
出售交易性金融资产实收款
nodes.definition: Proceeds from sale of trading financial assets refer to the actual amount received by an enterprise from the buyer when selling financial assets held for short-term trading purposes (such as stocks, bonds, funds, etc.). This amount serves as the basis for calculating investment gains or losses arising from the disposal of such assets and typically equals the net amount of fair value at the time of sale minus relevant transaction taxes and fees.

nodes.name: Proceeds from Sale of Used Assets
nodes.definition: Proceeds from the sale of used assets refer to the cash or cash equivalents obtained by an enterprise through the sale or disposal of assets such as used fixed assets, second-hand goods, or old properties. In accounting treatment, it is typically recorded as an original inflow and serves as the basis for calculating relevant taxes and fees (such as value-added tax and income tax).

nodes.name: Processing Time
nodes.definition: Processing time refers to the time required to complete a specific processing operation for a product or component, serving as essential data for calculating production costs, scheduling production plans, and evaluating production efficiency.

nodes.name: Processing Weight
nodes.definition: Processing weight refers to the total weight of raw materials or semi-finished products input for processing at the initial stage of a production or manufacturing process. It serves as fundamental data for calculating yield rates, loss rates, and conducting cost accounting.

nodes.name: Procurement
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, procurement primarily refers to the total price actually paid or payable by an enterprise to acquire materials such as raw materials and goods for production or sales, as well as directly related expenses such as transportation, handling, insurance, and taxes. It forms the basis of the initial cost of inventory and directly impacts subsequent cost of sales and profit.

nodes.name: Procurement Cost
nodes.definition: Procurement cost refers to all expenditures incurred by an enterprise to acquire raw materials, goods, or services, including the direct purchase price paid to obtain inventory as well as incidental costs such as related taxes, transportation, loading/unloading, and insurance. It is a core component of the initial measurement of inventory.

formulas.source_formula: Procurement Cost = Material Cost + Freight + Other Related Expenses

nodes.name: Procurement and Storage Fee Rate
nodes.definition: The procurement and storage fee rate is a predetermined percentage rate set by an enterprise to compensate for various expenses incurred during material procurement, inspection, storage, and safekeeping (such as purchasing staff salaries, travel expenses, warehouse rent, and losses). It is typically determined directly based on historical data, industry practices, or contractual agreements and serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating the specific amount of procurement and storage fees.

nodes.name: Producer Price Index
nodes.definition: The Producer Price Index is an index that measures the trend and degree of changes in the ex-factory prices of industrial enterprises' products. It is an important economic indicator reflecting price changes in the production sector during a specific period and serves as a key basis for calculating the inflation rate.

nodes.name: Producer Surplus
nodes.definition: Producer surplus is the difference between the total revenue received from selling goods and the marginal cost of producing those goods, representing the benefit to producers from pricing above marginal cost.

formulas.source_formula: Producer Surplus = Total Revenue - Marginal Cost

nodes.name: Product Actual Labor Hours
nodes.definition: Product actual labor hours refer to the direct labor working time actually consumed in the manufacturing process to produce specific products. It is fundamental data obtained through on-site recording, measurement, or estimation, primarily used to allocate direct labor costs and manufacturing overhead to individual products, serving as a crucial basis for cost accounting.

nodes.name: Product Cost
nodes.definition: Product cost refers to the total expenses incurred by an enterprise from the input of raw materials to the completion and warehousing of a specific product throughout the entire production process. These expenses primarily include materials directly used for the product (direct materials), wages of workers directly involved in production (direct labor), and various indirect expenses incurred for organizing and managing production (manufacturing overhead, such as factory rent, equipment depreciation, etc.).

operands.metric: Production Costs Incurred in Current Period
Ending Work in Process Inventory Cost

formulas.source_formula: Product Cost = Beginning Work-in-Process Inventory Cost + Production Costs Incurred in Current Period - Ending Work-in-Process Inventory Cost
Product Cost = Total Fixed Costs + Variable Cost per Unit × Total Product Quantity

nodes.name: Product Output
nodes.definition: Product output refers to the quantity of finished goods produced by an enterprise within a specific accounting period. It serves as a fundamental metric for measuring production scale, calculating costs, conducting break-even analysis, and formulating sales plans.

formulas.source_formula: Product Output = Production Capacity × Capacity Utilization Rate × Actual Production Time

nodes.name: Product Quantity
nodes.definition: Product quantity refers to the specific number of completed or unfinished products obtained through physical methods such as direct counting, weighing, or measurement during the production process. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting, production management, and inventory management.

nodes.name: Product Sales Mix Ratio
nodes.definition: Product sales mix ratio refers to the percentage of a specific product's sales revenue within the enterprise's total sales revenue. It serves as key foundational data for measuring product portfolio structure, analyzing revenue source composition, and calculating composite metrics such as the weighted average contribution margin ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Product Sales Mix Ratio = (Sales Revenue of the Product ÷ Total Sales Revenue) × 100%

nodes.name: Product Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Product sales revenue refers to the total income obtained by an enterprise through the sale of its manufactured or purchased products, serving as one of the core indicators for measuring the scale and performance of business operations. It is typically calculated directly based on the actual sales volume and unit price of the products.

nodes.name: Product Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Product sales volume refers to the specific unit quantity of a particular product sold by an enterprise within a specified period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It serves as fundamental data for calculating sales revenue, analyzing sales performance, and determining market share.

nodes.name: Production Capacity
nodes.definition: Production capacity refers to the maximum quantity of a specific product or service that an enterprise's productive fixed assets can produce within a given period under established organizational and technological conditions. It is a key indicator for formulating production plans, making investment decisions, and evaluating operational efficiency.

operands.metric: Effective Operating Time per Unit of Equipment

formulas.source_formula: Production Capacity = Effective Operating Time per Unit of Equipment × Number of Equipment Units × Output Quota

operands.metric: Effective Operating Time per Unit of Equipment

formulas.source_formula: Production Capacity = (Effective Operating Time per Unit of Equipment × Number of Equipment Units) ÷ Time Quota

nodes.name: Production Cost
nodes.definition: Production cost refers to the various production expenses incurred by an enterprise for manufacturing products or providing services, which can be directly attributed to specific cost objects, and constitutes the core component of inventory cost.

formulas.source_formula: Production Cost = Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead

nodes.name: Production Cost of Inventory Goods
nodes.definition: Production cost of inventory goods refers to the total of all expenses incurred by an enterprise during the production process for manufacturing finished products or goods available for sale. It primarily includes directly consumed raw materials (direct materials), compensation for workers directly involved in production (direct labor), and indirect expenses incurred for organizing and managing production (manufacturing overhead). These costs are accumulated and recorded as part of the carrying value of inventory when the finished products are completed and accepted into the warehouse.

nodes.name: Production Costs
nodes.definition: Production costs (product costs) are the costs incurred to manufacture goods, comprising direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. These costs are capitalized into inventory and recognized as cost of goods sold when the goods are sold, and exclude period costs such as selling, general, and administrative expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Production Costs = Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead

nodes.name: Production Costs Incurred in Current Period
nodes.definition: Production costs incurred in the current period refer to the various production expenditures, expressed in monetary terms, that are actually incurred by an enterprise during the current accounting period for producing goods or providing services. They primarily include expenses such as direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead.

nodes.name: Production Costs Incurred in the Current Month
aliases: Production Costs Incurred in Current Month
nodes.definition: Production costs incurred in the current month refer to the total of all expenses actually incurred by an enterprise within the current accounting month for producing goods or providing services. It is directly aggregated from source documents such as material requisition forms, payroll sheets, and depreciation calculation tables, and serves as the foundational data for subsequent allocation in cost accounting.

nodes.name: Production Efficiency
nodes.definition: Production efficiency is a productivity metric that measures the actual output rate relative to the standard output rate, expressed as a percentage. It indicates how effectively a production process utilizes resources to achieve expected performance under normal operating conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Production Efficiency (%) = (Output Rate ÷ Standard Output Rate) × 100%

nodes.name: Production Expenses Incurred in Current Period
aliases: Production Expenses Incurred in the Period
nodes.definition: Production expenses incurred in the current period refer to the total of various actual expenditures made by an enterprise during the current accounting period for producing goods or providing services. It reflects the value of resources invested in production activities during the period and serves as an important basis for calculating product costs and evaluating current operational efficiency.

nodes.name: Production Preparation Costs
nodes.definition: Production preparation costs refer to the expenses incurred for production preparation activities, such as training maintenance personnel and familiarizing with process flows and equipment performance, before a project or new production line is officially put into operation.

nodes.name: Production Quota
nodes.definition: Production quota refers to the standard quantity of qualified products that a worker or work team should complete per unit of time (such as a workday or an hour) under normal technical conditions, reasonable use of production tools, and correct labor organization. It is an important indicator for measuring labor efficiency and production capacity.

nodes.name: Production Requirement
nodes.definition: Production requirement refers to the total quantity of raw materials or components required to be consumed within a given period to fulfill a specific production plan. It is a core intermediate variable in production planning and material management, typically calculated based on the planned production output and the material consumption quota per unit product. It serves as the foundation for preparing procurement budgets and determining estimated purchase quantities.

operands.metric: Material Consumption Quota per Unit Product

formulas.source_formula: Production Requirement = Planned Production Output × Material Consumption Quota per Unit Product

nodes.name: Production Subsidies of the Tertiary Industry
Production Subsidy
nodes.definition: Production subsidy refers to economic assistance or financial support provided directly by the government or relevant institutions to enterprises to support specific production activities or industries. It is typically used to reduce production costs, encourage the production of specific goods, or achieve specific socio-economic objectives.

nodes.name: Production Tax
nodes.definition: Production tax refers to the collective term for various taxes, surcharges, and fees levied by the government on production units for their production, sales, and business activities, as well as for the use of certain factors of production (such as land, labor, capital) in these activities. It is a primary data item directly generated from production and operating activities and serves as the basis for calculating net production tax.

nodes.name: Production Taxes of the Tertiary Industry
Production Volume
nodes.definition: Production volume refers to the quantity of products actually manufactured and completed by an enterprise or production unit within a specific period, which is available for sale or use. It is the most fundamental raw data in the production process, typically obtained directly through production records, statistical reports, etc., rather than being calculated from other financial or efficiency indicators.

nodes.name: Production Worker Wage Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The production worker wage allocation rate is the ratio used to allocate the total wages of production workers proportionally based on the actual labor hours consumed by various products.

nodes.name: Production and Sales Volume Change Rate
aliases: Change Rate of Production and Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Production and Sales Volume Change Rate is a composite indicator used to measure the degree of change in production volume and sales volume of an enterprise or industry. It is typically calculated by comparing current period data with base period data, serving as a crucial foundational variable for analyzing operating leverage effects.

operands.metric: Current Period Production and Sales Volume
Base Period Production and Sales Volume

formulas.source_formula: Production and Sales Volume Change Rate = (Current Period Production and Sales Volume - Base Period Production and Sales Volume) ÷ Base Period Production and Sales Volume

nodes.name: Production or Procurement Cost
nodes.definition: Production or procurement cost refers to all expenditures incurred by an enterprise from the start of production or procurement until the inspection and acceptance of products or goods into inventory. For purchased goods, it primarily includes purchase price, related taxes and fees, transportation costs, loading and unloading fees, and insurance premiums. For self-produced products, it mainly comprises direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead. It is one of the fundamental components constituting the selling price of goods.

nodes.name: Production/Purchase Cost Price
nodes.definition: Production/Purchase Cost Price refers to the direct and fundamental costs incurred by an enterprise for producing or purchasing a single unit of goods, excluding subsequent domestic expenses, freight, insurance, and profit. In trade terms, it serves as the foundational component constituting export prices such as FOB, CFR, and CIF.

nodes.name: Productivity
nodes.definition: Productivity is an indicator measuring the efficiency ratio between the input of production factors (such as labor, capital) and the output of goods or services produced. It reflects the effectiveness of resource utilization and serves as a key foundation for evaluating economic or enterprise performance.

formulas.source_formula: Productivity = Total Output ÷ Total Input
Productivity Increase = (1 ÷ 3) × Capital Deepening Growth + Technology-Driven Productivity Growth

nodes.name: Products Received into Warehouse
nodes.definition: Products Received into Warehouse refers to the physical quantity of finished goods or merchandise that an enterprise receives and stores in its warehouse within a specific period through means such as procurement or production completion. It is a core data point in inventory management, used to track inventory inflows.

nodes.name: Profit
nodes.definition: Profit is the difference between total revenue earned from selling products or providing services and total costs over a specific period, reflecting the operating results of a business.

formulas.source_formula: Profit = Margin of Safety × Contribution Margin Ratio
Profit = Sales Revenue - Total Cost
Profit = Sales Revenue - Variable Cost - Fixed Cost
Profit = Profit per Share × Contract Multiplier
Profit = Sales Volume × Unit Contribution Margin - Target Cost
Profit (Call Option) = Intrinsic Value (Call) - Premium Paid

nodes.name: Profit Available for Distribution to Investors
aliases: 可向投资者分配的利润
nodes.definition: Profit available for distribution to investors refers to the portion of profit that can actually be distributed to the owners of the enterprise (such as shareholders, partners, etc.) after a series of statutory and internal allocations (such as appropriation to surplus reserves) during a specific accounting period. It is a key stage in the profit distribution process, reflecting the ultimate return that owners can obtain from the enterprise's earnings.

nodes.name: Profit Available for Distribution to Shareholders
aliases: 可供投资者分配的利润
nodes.definition: Profit available for distribution to shareholders refers to the portion of profit remaining after the company has appropriated necessary retained earnings such as statutory surplus reserve and discretionary surplus reserve. This remaining profit can be used to pay dividends to shareholders (including both preferred and common shareholders) or for other forms of distribution. It reflects the amount of profit, both current and accumulated, that can genuinely be returned to shareholders.

nodes.name: Profit Before Tax (PBT)
nodes.definition: Profit before tax (PBT) is the earnings a company generates after operating profit is adjusted for net interest—subtracting interest expense and adding interest income—but before income tax expense. It indicates profitability prior to tax obligations.

formulas.source_formula: Profit Before Tax = Operating Profit - Interest Paid + Interest Earned

nodes.name: Profit Change Rate
aliases: 普通股每股收益变动率
nodes.definition: Profit change rate is a financial metric that measures the degree of change in a company's profit relative to a base period, commonly used to analyze the impact of operating leverage or financial leverage on profit fluctuations.

operands.metric: Rate of Change in Earnings Per Share of Common Stock

formulas.source_formula: Profit Change Rate = Earnings Per Share Change Rate ÷ Financial Leverage Ratio
Profit Change Rate = Operating Leverage Ratio × Sales Revenue Change Rate
Profit Change Rate = Operating Leverage Ratio × Sales Volume Change Rate

nodes.name: Profit Distributed to Investors in Current Period
nodes.definition: Profit distributed to investors in the current period refers to the amount of cash dividends determined to be distributed to shareholders (investors) after calculating net profit, appropriating statutory surplus reserves, etc., in accordance with the profit distribution resolution of the board of directors or shareholders' meeting. It is the result of the profit distribution process, representing a decision-based or calculation-based composite metric that depends on distributable profit, distribution policy, and specific resolutions.

operands.metric: Profit Available for Distribution to Investors

formulas.source_formula: Profit Distributed to Investors in Current Period = Profit Available for Distribution to Investors × Dividend Payout Ratio

nodes.name: Profit Distributed to Shareholders
nodes.definition: Profit distributed to shareholders refers to the portion allocated from the company's distributable profits, as resolved by the board of directors, and paid directly to shareholders in forms such as cash. This is the specific outcome of the company's profit distribution action, with its amount determined by corporate decisions rather than calculated through a fixed formula.

formulas.source_formula: Profit Due = Contract Value × Profit Percentage × Completion Percentage

nodes.name: Profit Function
nodes.definition: The profit function is a key financial function describing a company's profitability, typically referring to total profit or net profit. It is calculated from other financial indicators such as operating profit, non-operating income and expenses, and income tax expense through explicit formulas, serving as a core metric for measuring a company's financial performance over a specific period, rather than being a fundamental raw data point.

formulas.source_formula: Profit Function = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense
Profit Function = Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses

nodes.name: Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Profit margin is a financial ratio used to measure the percentage of a company's profit relative to its revenue. Expressed as a percentage, it reflects the amount of profit a company earns per dollar of revenue generated.

formulas.source_formula: Profit Margin = (100 × (Sales Revenue - Total Expenses)) ÷ Revenue
Profit or Loss = (Opening Price - Closing Price) × Bet Size
Profit or Loss = Number of Ticks × Tick Value

nodes.name: Profit or Loss Value
nodes.definition: Profit or loss value refers to the final numerical figure of profit or loss generated by a company's operating activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It reflects the difference between revenue and costs/expenses and is a core indicator for measuring a company's financial performance.

nodes.name: Profit or Loss from Tick Movements
nodes.definition: Profit or loss from tick movements quantifies the monetary outcome resulting from price changes measured in ticks for a traded instrument. It is computed as the product of the number of ticks moved and the tick value (the currency amount per tick), and is widely used by traders in markets with defined tick size and contract specifications to estimate gains or losses.

formulas.source_formula: Profit per Share = Put Calendar Spread Price - Call Calendar Spread Price

nodes.name: Profit-Sharing Plan
nodes.definition: A profit-sharing plan is an employee compensation arrangement in which a company distributes a portion of its profits to employees. Under the comp-to-comp method, each employee’s allocation is proportional to their compensation relative to the total compensation of all eligible employees, ensuring a fair and formula-driven distribution of profits.

formulas.source_formula: Profit/Loss = (Exit Price - Entry Price) × Contract Multiplier
Profit/Loss per Contract = Total Profit/Loss ÷ Number of Contracts

nodes.name: Profitability Index
nodes.definition: Profitability Index (PI) is a capital budgeting metric that equals the present value of expected future cash inflows divided by the initial investment. It measures the value created per unit of investment, where PI > 1 indicates an investment that is expected to generate value above its cost.

operands.metric: Present Value of Future Cash Flows

formulas.source_formula: Profitability Index = Present Value of Future Cash Flows ÷ Initial Investment

nodes.name: Profitability Ratios
nodes.definition: Profitability ratios are financial metrics used to evaluate a company's ability to generate profit relative to its revenue, operating costs, balance sheet assets, or shareholders' equity. These ratios are essential in fundamental analysis to assess financial performance and efficiency in generating profits from operations and investments.

formulas.source_formula: Progress Billing Amount = Contract Amount × Percentage of Completion

nodes.name: Progress Billings
nodes.definition: Progress billings refer to invoicing a client for a portion of the contract value based on the percentage of completion of a long-term project. It aligns cash collection with project progress, commonly used in construction and other industries with long-duration contracts. The billed amount is typically calculated by multiplying the total contract amount by the verified percentage of completion, subject to contractual terms, retainage, and compliance with agreed measurement of progress.

nodes.name: Progressive Tax
nodes.definition: Progressive tax is a taxation system in which the marginal tax rate increases as taxable income rises, resulting in higher-income taxpayers paying a larger proportion of their income in taxes. The total tax liability is computed by applying different marginal rates to successive portions of income defined by tax brackets.

nodes.name: Progressive Tax Liability
nodes.definition: Progressive tax liability is the total tax owed under a progressive tax system where tax rates increase as income crosses successive bracket thresholds, ensuring vertical equity by imposing higher effective rates on higher income earners.

nodes.name: Project Beta Coefficient
nodes.definition: The project beta coefficient is a measure of the systematic risk or volatility of a project relative to the overall market (typically represented by the market portfolio). It reflects the sensitivity of the project's returns to changes in the overall market returns. A beta coefficient greater than 1 indicates the project's risk is higher than the market average, while a beta less than 1 indicates risk lower than the market average.

nodes.name: Project Commissioning Year
nodes.definition: The project commissioning year refers to the year in which an investment project completes construction and officially commences production operations, beginning to generate cash inflows. It marks the starting point of the operational period within the project's calculation period (typically including the construction period and the operational period), signifying the transition of the project from the capital investment phase to the revenue recovery phase.

nodes.name: Project Cost of Capital
aliases: 项目加权平均资本成本
nodes.definition: Project cost of capital is a composite metric used to evaluate the feasibility of investment projects, typically referring to the discount rate used to discount project cash flows. It is calculated based on the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) or other methods, involving fundamental data such as debt cost, equity cost, and tax rate. It is a key parameter in capital budgeting and investment decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: Project Cost of Capital = Debt Book Value Proportion × Cost of Debt × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Equity Book Value Proportion × Cost of Equity

nodes.name: Project Duration
nodes.definition: Project duration refers to the total time length required to complete an engineering project or specific work task, typically calculated from the project commencement date to the date when the project is fully completed and passes acceptance inspection. It is a core metric for measuring progress and efficiency in project management.

nodes.name: Project Expected Value
nodes.definition: Project Expected Value is the weighted average of all possible outcomes calculated by their respective probabilities of occurrence in uncertain decision-making, used to measure the anticipated economic value of a project.

nodes.name: Project Life
nodes.definition: Project life, also known as the project calculation period, refers to the entire time span from the construction start point to the end of the production and operation phase. It is derived by adding the construction period and the production and operation period, serving as a key parameter for cash flow estimation and analysis in project investment decisions.

nodes.name: Project Quantity Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The Project Quantity Growth Rate is an indicator that measures the degree of change in the number of projects over a specific period (e.g., one year, one quarter). It is commonly used to assess the activity level of business expansion, market development, or investment activities. Its core calculation logic is the ratio of the increase in the number of projects in the current period relative to the base period (previous period) to the number of projects in the base period.

nodes.name: Project Required Rate of Return
aliases: Required Rate of Return for Project
nodes.definition: The project required rate of return refers to the minimum rate of return required by investors or a company for a specific investment project. It is commonly used as the discount rate in capital budgeting to evaluate the net present value of a project. It is a composite metric, typically calculated based on methods such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) or the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC).

nodes.name: Project Risk-Adjusted Discount Rate
nodes.definition: The project risk-adjusted discount rate refers to the discount rate obtained by adding a risk premium to the risk-free rate of return in order to reflect the inherent risk level of a project when evaluating investment projects. It is used to discount the project's future expected cash flows to their present value, with higher-risk projects using a higher discount rate to compensate investors for the additional risk undertaken.

nodes.name: Project Settlement
nodes.definition: Project settlement refers to the revenue recognized by a construction enterprise when settling the project payment with the client (owner) upon project completion or reaching specific milestones, as stipulated in the contract. It constitutes the primary source of operating revenue for construction enterprises and reflects the value of completed or finished projects.

nodes.name: Project Settlement Cost
nodes.definition: Project settlement cost refers to the total cost calculated and recognized by a construction enterprise upon completion of a specific project or reaching a contractually agreed settlement milestone, based on the actual expenditures directly related to the project. It is a key component in calculating project settlement profit.

nodes.name: Project Settlement Revenue
nodes.definition: Project settlement revenue refers to the price income obtained by a construction enterprise from the client unit for settlement of completed or finished construction projects according to contract agreements. It is a core component for recognizing the operating revenue of a construction enterprise.

nodes.name: Project Termination Year
nodes.definition: The project termination year refers to the final year in which an investment project or construction project concludes, marking the end of its economic or physical life. It signifies the completion of the project's operational period and serves as a critical time node for conducting project financial evaluations, calculating metrics such as the payback period and net present value.

nodes.name: Project Value
nodes.definition: Project value refers to the present value sum of the perpetual cash flows generated by a project in the future, discounted at an appropriate discount rate.

formulas.source_formula: Project Value = Perpetual Cash Flow ÷ Discount Rate

nodes.name: Projected AMT Exemption
nodes.definition: Projected AMT Exemption refers to the future value of the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exemption amount, indexed by a constant annual inflation rate over a specified number of years. It is used in tax planning and forecasting to estimate the inflation-adjusted exemption that offsets income subject to the AMT.

formulas.source_formula: Future AMT Exemption = Current AMT Exemption × (1 + Inflation Rate) ^ Years

nodes.name: Projected Annual Sales Revenue Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The Projected Annual Sales Revenue Growth Rate is a financial metric that measures the expected percentage increase in a company's sales revenue for a future fiscal year relative to a comparison year, used for forecasting, budgeting, and financial modeling.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Annual Sales Revenue Growth Rate = (Projected Sales Revenue - Comparison Year Sales Revenue) ÷ Comparison Year Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Projected Cash Flows by Period
nodes.definition: Projected cash flows by period refer to the direct estimates of cash inflows and outflows for specific future periods (such as monthly, quarterly, or annual) in financial forecasting. These estimates are typically derived directly from underlying assumptions such as business plans, sales forecasts, and cost budgets, and constitute the most fundamental input data for cash flow projection statements.

nodes.name: Projected Debt-to-Asset Ratio
nodes.definition: The Projected Debt-to-Asset Ratio is the ratio of total projected liabilities to total projected assets, calculated based on future forecast data, used to assess a company's future capital structure, debt repayment risk, and financial leverage level.

nodes.name: Projected Dividend Payout Ratio
nodes.definition: The projected dividend payout ratio is the percentage of total planned cash dividends to projected net profit for a future period, based on a company's dividend policy. It is an important forward-looking indicator for measuring a company's future dividend distribution intention and financial policy, commonly used in financial planning models such as external financing requirement forecasts.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Dividend Payout Ratio = Projected Dividend Per Share ÷ Projected Earnings Per Share × 100%

operands.metric: Estimated Total Dividends for Next Period

formulas.source_formula: Projected Dividend Payout Ratio = Projected Total Dividends ÷ Projected Net Profit × 100%

nodes.name: Projected Equity
nodes.definition: Projected equity refers to the estimated value of owners' equity at a future point in time (e.g., quarter-end, year-end), based on the company's future business plans, financial forecasts, or specific assumptions. It reflects the estimated residual interest expected to be attributable to the owners after deducting liabilities from assets at the forecast date.

nodes.name: Projected Financial Assets
nodes.definition: Projected financial assets refer to the forecasted or estimated value or scale of financial instruments (such as stocks, bonds, derivatives, etc.) that an enterprise or individual may hold at a specific future point or period, measured at fair value with changes recognized in profit or loss, based on current information, market trends, and financial models.

nodes.name: Projected Income Tax
nodes.definition: Projected income tax refers to the estimated amount of income tax that a company or analyst anticipates needing to pay in a specific future period (such as the next fiscal year or quarter), based on expectations of future revenue, profits, applicable tax rates, and tax regulations. It is a key item in financial forecasting and budgeting.

nodes.name: Projected Increase in Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Projected increase in operating assets refers to the additional amount of operating assets a company needs to invest in to support expected sales growth. It is a key intermediate variable for forecasting external financing needs and financial planning.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Increase in Operating Assets = Base Period Operating Assets × Sales Growth Rate

nodes.name: Projected Increase in Operating Liabilities
nodes.definition: Projected Increase in Operating Liabilities refers to the forecasted incremental amount of spontaneous operating liabilities (such as accounts payable, accrued wages, and taxes payable) that are expected to automatically increase with revenue growth in future periods, based on the percentage of sales method or other forecasting models. It is a key component in calculating composite metrics such as external financing needs.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Increase in Operating Liabilities = Base Period Operating Liabilities × Projected Operating Revenue Growth Rate

nodes.name: Projected Increase in Retained Earnings
nodes.definition: Projected increase in retained earnings refers to the amount of additional retained earnings accumulated through internal operations during the forecast period, calculated based on projected sales revenue, net profit margin, and dividend policy in financial forecasting (e.g., the percentage of sales method). It is a key intermediate variable for determining external financing needs.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Increase in Retained Earnings = Projected Net Profit × Retention Ratio
Projected Increase in Retained Earnings = Projected Sales Revenue × Net Profit Margin × Retention Ratio
Projected Increase in Retained Earnings = Projected Sales Revenue × Net Profit Margin × (1 - Dividend Payout Ratio)

nodes.name: Projected Net Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Projected Net Operating Assets is the future-period value of net operating assets calculated based on forecasted operating assets and operating liabilities. It is a key composite metric used for business valuation, free cash flow forecasting, and financial planning.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Net Operating Assets = Projected Operating Assets - Projected Operating Liabilities

nodes.name: Projected Net Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Projected Net Profit Margin refers to the percentage of net profit to sales revenue calculated based on forecast data. It is a core financial ratio that measures a company's profitability per unit of sales revenue in future periods, commonly used in financial forecasting and external financing requirement analysis.

nodes.name: Projected Operating Assets
nodes.definition: Projected Operating Assets refer to the total amount of operating assets for future periods, calculated based on base-period financial statement data and future operating revenue forecasts, using predictive assumptions such as the percentage of sales method. It is a key component in financial forecasting and planning models, used to calculate the total external financing requirement.

operands.metric: Base-period Operating Assets as a Percentage of Sales

formulas.source_formula: Projected Operating Assets = Projected Operating Revenue × Base-period Operating Assets as a Percentage of Sales
Projected Operating Assets = Projected Operating Revenue × (Base-period Operating Assets ÷ Base-period Operating Revenue)

nodes.name: Projected Pension Benefit Payments
nodes.definition: Projected Pension Benefit Payments refer to the total sum or sequence of pension amounts expected to be paid to pension recipients in future periods (e.g., monthly, annually) based on a pension plan or insurance contract under specific actuarial assumptions (such as discount rate, mortality rate, salary growth rate, etc.). It serves as the basis for assessing the present value of pension liabilities.

nodes.name: Projected Sales Growth Rate
aliases: 预计销售收入年增长率
nodes.definition: The Projected Sales Growth Rate is the growth ratio between a company's projected sales revenue and the sales revenue of the comparison year (or base period). It is used to measure the expected growth level of future sales revenue and is a key indicator in financial forecasting, budget preparation, and performance evaluation.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Sales Growth Rate = (Projected Sales Revenue - Comparison Year Sales Revenue) ÷ Comparison Year Sales Revenue × 100%
Projected Sales Growth Rate = Projected Sales Increase ÷ Comparison Year Sales Revenue × 100%

nodes.name: Projected Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Projected sales revenue refers to the forecasted total revenue expected to be generated from the sale of products or provision of services over a specific future period (such as a quarter or a year), based on methods including historical sales data, market trend analysis, and expert judgment. It serves as a critical foundational data point for corporate financial budgeting and operational decision-making.

nodes.name: Projected Total Assets
nodes.definition: Projected Total Assets refers to the estimated total assets at a future point in time based on forecasts or assumptions, and is not an original line item in financial statements. It is typically derived through forecasting models or relationships with other projected financial metrics (such as Projected Shareholders' Equity and Projected Equity Multiplier), and is used for financial forecasting, valuation analysis, and capital structure planning.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Total Assets = Projected Current Assets + Projected Non-current Assets
Projected Total Assets = Projected Total Liabilities + Projected Total Shareholders' Equity
Projected Total Assets = Base Period Total Assets × (1 + Projected Asset Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Projected Total Ether Supply
nodes.definition: Projected total ether supply is the estimated total number of ether (ETH) units outstanding after a specified number of days, assuming a constant daily issuance rate and excluding burns or other supply adjustments.

formulas.source_formula: Projected Total Ether Supply = Initial Ether Supply + Daily Issuance × Days

nodes.name: Projected Total Financial Assets at Period End
Projected Total Misstatement
nodes.definition: Projected total misstatement refers to the estimated value of the total misstatement that may exist in the entire audit population, inferred by applying specific methods (such as the ratio method or difference method) based on the misstatement amounts found in the sample during audit sampling.

nodes.name: Projected Total Shareholders' Equity
nodes.definition: Projected Total Shareholders' Equity refers to the forecasted total equity of a company at a specific future point in time, calculated by subtracting projected total liabilities from projected total assets. It reflects the scale of anticipated proprietary capital and is a core metric in financial forecasting and valuation analysis.

nodes.name: Property Income
nodes.definition: Property income refers to the income earned by individuals or households through owning, managing, and operating their movable assets (such as bank deposits, securities) and immovable assets (such as houses, land, vehicles). Its core sources include asset appreciation, granting the right to use assets (such as interest, rent), and participating in property operations (such as dividends).

nodes.name: Property Loss Value
nodes.definition: Property loss value refers to the direct monetary loss amount of a house or building resulting from destruction, damage, smoke, water damage, demolition, etc., caused by a specific event (such as fire, natural disaster, or accident). It is typically calculated based on the full replacement value, considering factors such as depreciation, to measure the economic loss.

nodes.name: Property Tax
nodes.definition: Property tax is a type of property tax levied on the owners of property rights, with houses, structures, and other buildings as the taxable objects. The tax base is typically the original value of the property or rental income, and the tax payable is calculated according to different assessment methods (such as ad valorem or rental-based assessment).

formulas.source_formula: Property Tax = Assessed Value × Millage Rate ÷ 1000
Property Value = Gross Income Multiplier × Gross Annual Income

nodes.name: Property Value (Income Approach)
nodes.definition: The Income Approach estimates a property's value by capitalizing its Net Operating Income (NOI) at an appropriate capitalization rate (Cap Rate), reflecting the relationship between income and value for income-generating real estate.

nodes.name: Proportion Invested in Risky Portfolio
nodes.definition: The proportion invested in a risky portfolio refers to the percentage of an investor's total capital allocated to risky assets (such as stocks, high-yield bonds, etc.) relative to the net asset value of the fund. It is a core metric in asset allocation decisions, used to measure the risk exposure of an investment portfolio and serves as the basis for calculating the total expected rate of return.

formulas.source_formula: Proportion Invested in Risky Portfolio = Current Net Value of Portfolio ÷ Fund Net Asset Value × 100%
Proportion Invested in Risky Portfolio = Amount Invested in Risky Assets ÷ Total Fund Value × 100%
Proportion Invested in Risky Portfolio = Amount Invested in Risky Assets ÷ Fund Net Asset Value × 100%
Proportion Invested in Risky Portfolio = Current Net Value of Portfolio ÷ Total Fund Value × 100%

nodes.name: Proportion of New Customers Taking Cash Discount
aliases: New Customer Cash Discount Take-up Rate
Percentage of Customers Availing Cash Discount
Proportion of Customers Taking Cash Discount
享受现金折扣的顾客比例
新客户现金折扣接受率
nodes.definition: The proportion of new customers taking cash discount refers to the percentage of credit customers who choose to pay within the discount period to avail the cash discount under a new credit policy (e.g., offering cash discounts). This proportion is one of the key variables in calculating the cost of cash discounts.

formulas.source_formula: Proportion of New Customers Taking Cash Discount = Cost of Cash Discount ÷ (Credit Sales × Discount Rate)

nodes.name: Proportion of Old Customers Taking Cash Discount
aliases: Historical Customer Cash Discount Take-up Rate
Historical Percentage of Customers Taking Cash Discount
Proportion of Existing Customers Taking Cash Discount
历史客户折扣享受比例
原有客户现金折扣使用率
原有现金折扣客户比率
