formulas.source_formula: Shareholder Value Added = Net Operating Profit After Tax - Cost of Capital
Shareholders' Equity After Repurchase = Shareholders' Equity Before Repurchase - Treasury Stock at Cost

nodes.name: Shareholders' Equity Attributable to Parent Company Common Shareholders
Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate is a financial metric that measures the growth degree of a company's shareholders' equity over a specific period, usually expressed as a percentage. It reflects the company's ability to expand its net assets through operational accumulation or financing activities, and is used to assess the company's growth potential and financial sustainability. It often serves as the basis for calculating the sustainable growth rate.

formulas.source_formula: Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate = Return on Equity × Retention Ratio ÷ (1 - Return on Equity × Retention Ratio)
Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate = (Current Period Shareholders' Equity - Prior Period Shareholders' Equity) ÷ Prior Period Shareholders' Equity × 100%

operands.metric: Increase in Shareholders' Equity in Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate = Increase in Shareholders' Equity in Current Period ÷ Beginning Shareholders' Equity × 100%

operands.metric: Beginning Equity to Total Assets Multiplier

formulas.source_formula: Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate = Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × Retention Ratio × Beginning Equity to Ending Total Assets Multiplier
Shareholders' Equity Reduction (Cost Method) = Number of Shares Repurchased × Repurchase Price Per Share
Shareholders' Equity Reduction (Par Value Method) = Number of Shares Repurchased × Par Value Per Share + Number of Shares Repurchased × (Repurchase Price Per Share - Par Value Per Share)

nodes.name: Shareholding Ratio
nodes.definition: Shareholding ratio refers to the proportion of a shareholder's (or investor's) capital contribution to the total registered capital of a company, used to measure the size of their equity stake in the company.

nodes.name: Shares Outstanding
nodes.definition: Shares outstanding refers to the actual number of common shares circulating in the market during a specific reporting period. The calculation must consider share issuance, repurchases, and their respective time-weighting to reflect the average number of shares during the reporting period, which is used to determine key financial metrics such as earnings per share and net asset value per share.

formulas.source_formula: Shares Outstanding = Issued Shares - Treasury Shares
Shares Outstanding = Total Issued Common Shares - Treasury Shares

operands.metric: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period
Number of Newly Issued Common Shares in the Current Period
Repurchased Common Shares in Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Shares Outstanding = Beginning Outstanding Common Shares + Newly Issued Common Shares in Current Period × (Days Outstanding ÷ Days in Reporting Period) - Repurchased Common Shares in Current Period × (Days Since Repurchase ÷ Days in Reporting Period)
Shares to Hedge = Delta × Number of Options Contracts × Contract Size

nodes.name: Sharpe Ratio
nodes.definition: In finance, the Sharpe ratio is used to measure the risk-adjusted performance of an investment (such as a security or portfolio) relative to a risk-free asset. Its calculation formula is: the difference between the investment return rate and the risk-free return rate divided by the standard deviation of the investment return rate. This ratio indicates the excess return an investor can obtain per unit of additional risk assumed.

formulas.source_formula: Sharpe Ratio = Excess Return ÷ Volatility
Sharpe Ratio = (Portfolio Expected Return Rate - Risk-Free Rate) ÷ Standard Deviation of Portfolio Returns
Sharpe Ratio = (Portfolio Return - Risk-free Rate) ÷ Standard Deviation of Returns
Sharpe Ratio = (Expected Return - Risk-Free Rate) ÷ Standard Deviation
supporting_source_formulas: Sharpe Ratio = (Expected Return - Risk-Free Rate) ÷ Standard Deviation
Sharpe Ratio = (Expected Return - Risk-free Rate) ÷ Standard Deviation

formulas.source_formula: Sharpe Ratio = (Expected Return - Risk-free Rate) ÷ Standard Deviation of Returns

nodes.name: Shipment Value
nodes.definition: Shipment value refers to the total value of goods or products actually sold and delivered to customers by an enterprise within a specific period. It reflects the direct results of sales activities and serves as fundamental data for business operations and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Short Butterfly Spread
nodes.definition: A short butterfly spread is an options strategy that involves selling one lower-strike option, buying two middle-strike options, and selling one upper-strike option, resulting in limited profit potential equal to the net premium received and limited loss potential equal to the difference between strikes minus the premium received.

formulas.source_formula: Short Butterfly Spread P&L = Lower Strike - Upper Strike + Premium Cost

nodes.name: Short Call
nodes.definition: A short call is an options strategy in which an investor writes (sells) a call option and receives a premium, profiting if the underlying asset's price remains at or below the strike price at expiration. The maximum profit is limited to the premium received, while potential losses are theoretically unlimited if the underlying price rises significantly. The net profit or loss per contract equals the premium received minus the option's intrinsic value, multiplied by the contract size.

nodes.name: Short Call Net Profit/Loss
aliases: Net Profit of Short Call Option
nodes.definition: The net profit or loss of a short call option equals its expiration date value plus the option premium.

nodes.name: Short Call Option Value at Expiration
aliases: Value of Short Call at Expiration
空头看涨期权到期价值
nodes.definition: Short call option value at expiration refers to the net income received or payment obligation assumed by the option seller upon expiration due to the potential exercise of the call option. Its value depends on the relationship between the stock market price and the strike price, calculated as the negative of the greater of the difference between the stock market price and the strike price and zero.

nodes.name: Short Covering Profit or Loss
nodes.definition: Short covering profit or loss measures the monetary outcome realized when closing a short position by buying back previously shorted shares. A profit occurs if the buy-to-cover price is lower than the original short sale price; a loss occurs if it is higher. This measure typically excludes transaction costs, financing costs, and taxes unless otherwise specified.

formulas.source_formula: Short Covering Profit or Loss = (Short Sale Price - Cover Price) × Shares Sold Short

nodes.name: Short Float Percentage
aliases: Short Interest as a Percentage of Float
nodes.definition: Short float percentage measures the proportion of a company’s public float that has been sold short, indicating bearish sentiment and potential short-squeeze risk. It is calculated as shares sold short divided by float shares, expressed as a percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Short Float Percentage = (Shares Sold Short ÷ Float Shares) × 100%

nodes.name: Short Interest Percentage
aliases: Short Interest as % of Shares Outstanding
Short Interest as a Percentage of Shares Outstanding
nodes.definition: Short interest percentage measures the proportion of a company's shares outstanding that have been sold short, expressed as a percentage. It indicates the scale of short-selling activity relative to total shares outstanding and is commonly used as a market sentiment indicator.

formulas.source_formula: Short Interest Percentage = Shares Sold Short ÷ Total Outstanding Shares × 100

nodes.name: Short Interest Ratio
nodes.definition: The Short Interest Ratio (SIR), also known as Days to Cover, is calculated as total shares sold short divided by the stock's average daily trading volume. It estimates the number of trading days required for short sellers to cover their positions, and a higher SIR can indicate increased short squeeze risk and lower near-term liquidity.

formulas.source_formula: Short Interest Ratio = Short Interest ÷ Average Daily Trading Volume
supporting_source_formulas: Short Interest Ratio = Short Interest ÷ Average Daily Trading Volume

nodes.name: Short Put
nodes.definition: A short put is an options strategy where the investor writes (sells) a put option, receiving a premium upfront and assuming the obligation to buy the underlying asset at the strike price if exercised. The maximum profit is limited to the premium received, while potential loss increases as the underlying price falls below the strike price, typically scaled by the contract size (commonly 100 shares per contract).

nodes.name: Short Put Break-even Price
aliases: 卖出看跌期权盈亏平衡价
空头看跌期权盈亏平衡点
nodes.definition: The Short Put Break-even Price is the underlying asset price at which a short put position realizes zero profit. It equals the strike price minus the premium received per share. Under a standard equity option contract (100 shares), the premium per share is the total premium divided by 100. This measure excludes transaction costs, taxes, and other fees.

nodes.name: Short Put Maximum Loss
aliases: Maximum Loss of a Short Put
卖出看跌期权最大损失
nodes.definition: Short put maximum loss is the worst-case loss an option writer can incur on a short put position if the underlying asset's price falls to zero. It equals the cost to purchase the underlying at the strike price for the contract size, minus the premium received.

formulas.source_formula: Short Put Maximum Loss = (Strike Price × Contract Size) - Premium Received

nodes.name: Short Put Option Expiration Value
aliases: Short Put Option Value at Maturity
空头看跌期权到期日价值
nodes.definition: The value of a short put option at expiration is equal to the maximum of the difference between the strike price and the stock market price, otherwise zero.

nodes.name: Short Put Option Net Profit/Loss
aliases: Net Profit of Short Put Option
nodes.definition: The net profit/loss of a short put option equals its expiration date value plus the option price.

nodes.name: Short Sale
nodes.definition: A short sale is the sale of borrowed securities with the expectation that their price will decline, allowing the seller to repurchase them at a lower price and return them to the lender. To mitigate credit risk, regulators and brokers require margin to be posted; under common rules (e.g., Regulation T in the U.S.), the initial margin requirement is set at 150% of the market value of the securities sold short.

nodes.name: Short Sale Profit
nodes.definition: Short sale profit represents the gain or loss realized from closing a short position by repurchasing the borrowed shares at a price different from the original short sale price, multiplied by the number of shares involved.

formulas.source_formula: Short Sale Profit = (Short Sale Price − Buy to Cover Price) × Shares Sold
Short Sale Profit = (Short Sale Price - Cover Price) × Shares Borrowed
Short Sale Profit = (Initial Short Sale Price - Repurchase Price) × Number of Shares
Short Sale Rebate Fee = Short Sale Value × Interest Rate

nodes.name: Short Selling
nodes.definition: Short selling is a trading strategy in which an investor borrows and sells securities with the expectation that their price will decline, allowing repurchase at a lower price to realize a gain. Short sale profit equals the difference between the initial selling price and the repurchase (cover) price, multiplied by the number of shares, excluding transaction costs, borrowing fees, and dividends.

nodes.name: Short Selling Profit
nodes.definition: Short selling profit is the gain realized from selling borrowed shares at a higher initial price and repurchasing them at a lower final price, calculated as the price difference multiplied by the number of shares.

formulas.source_formula: Short Selling Profit = (Initial Price - Final Price) × Shares
Short-Term Capital Gains Tax = Net Short-Term Capital Gain × Short-Term Capital Gains Tax Rate
Short-Term Capital Gains Tax = Short-Term Capital Gains × Short-Term Capital Gains Tax Rate

nodes.name: Short-term Borrowings
nodes.definition: Short-term borrowings refer to various loans obtained by an enterprise from banks or other financial institutions with a repayment period of one year or less. They are a significant source of short-term financing for enterprises and are directly recorded as liability items on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Short-term Borrowings Ending Balance
nodes.definition: Short-term borrowings ending balance refers to the total book value of short-term borrowings that have not been repaid by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It reflects the enterprise's short-term liabilities to banks or other financial institutions at a specific point in time.

nodes.name: Short-term Borrowings Opening Balance
aliases: 短期借款期初贷方余额
nodes.definition: Short-term borrowings opening balance refers to the book value of short-term borrowings that have not been repaid at the beginning of an accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). It is typically reflected under the 'Short-term Borrowings' account on the liability side of the balance sheet and serves as important baseline data for calculating changes in borrowings during the period and for cash flow analysis.

nodes.name: Short-term Debt
nodes.definition: Short-term debt refers to financial obligations that are due within one year or one operating cycle (whichever is longer). It includes commercial paper, treasury bills, certificates of deposit, and other money market instruments with an original maturity of one year or less.

formulas.source_formula: Short-term Debt = Commercial Paper + Treasury Bills + Certificates of Deposit + Bankers' Acceptances + Other Short-term Borrowings

nodes.name: Short-term Debt Investments
nodes.definition: Short-term debt investments refer to debt-based investments held by an enterprise that are expected to mature within one year (or one operating cycle) or are intended to be liquidated within one year, such as short-term government bonds and corporate short-term financing bills, with the objective of earning interest income while maintaining liquidity.

nodes.name: Short-term Equity Investment
nodes.definition: Short-term equity investment refers to shares or equity interests in other companies purchased by an enterprise with the intention of obtaining returns through price differences in the short term (typically within one year). Such investments generally do not aim to control or exert significant influence over the investee, and changes in their value are recognized in current period profit or loss.

nodes.name: Short-term Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Short-term growth rate is a percentage metric that measures the growth of a company's core financial indicators (such as revenue or profit) in a specific short-term period (typically one accounting period, e.g., a quarter or year) relative to the previous period. It is a key dynamic indicator for assessing short-term operating performance and market performance.

formulas.source_formula: Short-term Growth Rate = (Current Period Value - Previous Period Value) ÷ Previous Period Value

nodes.name: Short-term Investments
nodes.definition: Short-term investments refer to investments made by an enterprise to utilize temporarily idle funds, purchasing securities that can be readily converted into cash and are not intended to be held for more than one year (including one year), primarily including various marketable securities such as stocks and bonds.

nodes.name: Short-term Treasury Bill Face Value
nodes.definition: Short-term Treasury bill face value refers to the principal amount stated on the bill at issuance (typically for government bonds with maturities of one year or less) and promised by the government to repay to the holder at maturity. It serves as the basis for calculating the issue price, discount rate, and yield of the Treasury bill.

nodes.name: Short-term Treasury Bill Yield
nodes.definition: Short-term Treasury bill yield refers to the annualized return an investor can obtain by holding a short-term Treasury bill until its maturity date. It serves as a key benchmark interest rate in the money market and is generally regarded as the risk-free rate. Its calculation methods vary, including bank discount yield, holding period yield, bond equivalent yield, etc., depending on market conventions and calculation purposes.

nodes.name: Shrinkage
nodes.definition: Shrinkage refers to the loss of inventory that occurs when the recorded (book) inventory exceeds the actual (physical) inventory on hand, typically due to theft, damage, spoilage, miscounts, or administrative errors. It is used in retail and inventory accounting to assess discrepancies and inform internal controls and loss prevention measures.

formulas.source_formula: Shrinkage = Book Inventory - Physical Inventory

nodes.name: Shutdown Point
nodes.definition: The shutdown point is the short-run operating threshold at which a firm should cease production because producing an additional unit does not create economic value. Under this decision rule, the firm shuts down when marginal revenue is less than or equal to marginal cost, ignoring fixed costs, indicating that continuing operations would not increase contribution or reduce losses.

nodes.name: Simple Interest
nodes.definition: Simple interest is the interest calculated solely on the principal for a specified period at a stated annual rate, commonly used for term deposits when compounding is not applied.

formulas.source_formula: Accrued Amount (Simple Interest) = Principal × (1 + Annual Interest Rate × Term in Years)
Simple Interest = Principal × Annual Interest Rate × Time (Years)

nodes.name: Simple Linear Regression (OLS)
nodes.definition: Simple linear regression (OLS) estimates a linear relationship between one independent variable (X) and a dependent variable (Y) by minimizing the sum of squared residuals, yielding the regression slope (a) and intercept (b) for the line Y = aX + b. In finance and accounting, it is used for beta estimation, factor sensitivity, forecasting, and trend analysis.

nodes.name: Simple Moving Average
nodes.definition: A Simple Moving Average (SMA) is the arithmetic mean of a sequence of prices or index values over a specified number of periods. It is used to smooth short-term fluctuations and highlight underlying trends in financial time series for technical analysis and risk monitoring.

formulas.source_formula: Simple Moving Average = Sum of Asset Prices ÷ Window Size
Simple Moving Average (SMA) = Sum of Prices (first Days) ÷ Days

operands.metric: Sum of Data Points in Window

formulas.source_formula: Simple Moving Average (SMA) = Sum of Data Points in Window ÷ Period
Simple Moving Average = Total of Period Data Points ÷ Period

operands.metric: Sum of Closing Prices over N Periods

formulas.source_formula: Simple Moving Average (SMA) = Sum of Closing Prices over N Periods ÷ Number of Periods (N)
Simple Moving Average = Sum of Prices over Period ÷ Period
supporting_source_formulas: Simple Moving Average (SMA) = Sum of Prices over Period ÷ Period
Simple Moving Average = Sum of Prices over Period ÷ Period

formulas.source_formula: Simple Moving Average = Sum of Data in Window ÷ Window Size

nodes.name: Simple Random Sample
nodes.definition: Simple random sampling is a probability sampling method in which each unit in the population has an equal chance of selection. In financial auditing and analytics, SRS is used to select transactions, accounts, or securities without bias for substantive testing, compliance testing, or estimation, ensuring representative evidence and unbiased inference.

nodes.name: Simple Return
nodes.definition: Simple return measures the percentage change in investment value from initial cost to final value without accounting for compounding or time period, reflecting the basic gain or loss on an investment.

formulas.source_formula: Simple Return = (Ending Price - Starting Price) ÷ Starting Price
Simple Return = (Final Value - Initial Cost) ÷ Initial Cost
Simplified Method Deduction = min(Area Used × Simplified Rate × Time Percentage, Gross Income)

nodes.name: Simpson's Rule
nodes.definition: Simpson's Rule is a numerical integration method that approximates the value of a definite integral by approximating the integrand with a quadratic parabola. It is commonly used in financial calculations to approximate complex integrals such as the cumulative distribution function of the standard normal distribution.

operands.metric: Value of Standard Normal Random Variable

formulas.source_formula: Simulated Value = Mean + Standard Deviation × Standard Normal Variate

nodes.name: Single Asset Return
nodes.definition: Single asset return refers to the total return an investor obtains from a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) over a given holding period. It typically consists of two components: interest or dividend income received during the holding period, and capital gains (or losses) resulting from price changes in the asset itself.

nodes.name: Single Asset Return Rate
nodes.definition: Single asset return rate refers to the total rate of return obtained from an asset over a specific holding period (typically one period, such as a year), usually consisting of two components: interest or dividend income received during the period, and capital gains (or losses) resulting from price changes of the asset itself.

nodes.name: Single Investment Return Rate
nodes.definition: The single investment return rate refers to the total rate of return obtained by an investor from an independent investment (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) over a specific period. It typically consists of two components: the return rate from interest or dividend income received during the holding period, and the return rate from asset price changes (capital gains or losses).

nodes.name: Single Order Shortage Quantity
nodes.definition: Single order shortage quantity refers to the quantity of goods that cannot be satisfied within one order cycle due to demand exceeding available inventory in an Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model that allows stockouts. It is a key variable for calculating stockout costs, and its value depends on ordering policies, demand levels, and inventory status, typically calculated through probabilistic models or deterministic formulas.

formulas.source_formula: Single Order Shortage Quantity = Order Cycle Demand × Stockout Probability
Single Order Shortage Quantity = Order Cycle Demand - Order Quantity
Single Order Shortage Quantity = Order Cycle Demand - Current Inventory Level - In-transit Order Quantity

nodes.name: Single-Period Return on Assets
nodes.definition: Single-period return on assets is an indicator that measures the total return of an asset over a specific holding period (such as one year or one month). It consists of two components: the interest or dividend income earned during the period, and the capital gain (or loss) resulting from price changes in the asset itself.

nodes.name: Single-Trial Success Probability
nodes.definition: Single-trial success probability refers to the likelihood of a specific event (typically termed 'success') occurring in a single independent random trial. It is a numerical value between 0 and 1, commonly used to describe the probability of success per trial in Bernoulli trials or the binomial distribution.

nodes.name: Sinking Fund Factor
nodes.definition: The sinking fund factor is a ratio coefficient used to calculate the equal periodic deposit amount required to accumulate a specific future sum (e.g., for debt repayment) by a designated future date. Its value equals the reciprocal of the ordinary annuity future value factor.

formulas.source_formula: Sinking Fund Factor = Equal Periodic Deposit Amount ÷ Target Future Value

nodes.name: Sinking Fund Payment
nodes.definition: A sinking fund payment refers to the equal periodic payment amount that must be deposited into a sinking fund to retire a specific debt at a specified future date, calculated based on the future debt amount, interest rate, and number of periods. It is a key compound metric in debt repayment planning.

operands.metric: Future Value of Ordinary Annuity Factor

formulas.source_formula: Sinking Fund Payment = Future Debt Amount ÷ Future Value of Ordinary Annuity Factor
Sinking Fund Payment = Future Debt Amount × Sinking Fund Factor

nodes.name: Site Preparation and Temporary Facilities Cost
aliases: Temporary Facilities and Site Preparation Expenses
场地平整及临时设施费
nodes.definition: Site preparation and temporary facilities cost refers to the expenses incurred before the commencement of a construction project, including site leveling, removal and clearance of obstacles to make the construction site ready for work, as well as the costs associated with the construction, maintenance, demolition, and restoration of temporary buildings, structures, and other temporary facilities required to meet construction needs.

nodes.name: Skewness
nodes.definition: Pearson's first coefficient of skewness quantifies the asymmetry of a distribution by comparing the mean to the mode and scaling by the standard deviation. Positive values indicate right-skewness (long right tail), while negative values indicate left-skewness (long left tail). In finance, it is used to assess asymmetry in return distributions and risk profiles.

formulas.source_formula: Pearson's Second Coefficient of Skewness = 3 × (Mean - Median) ÷ Standard Deviation

nodes.name: Slope
nodes.definition: Slope is a measure of the inclination of a line (or the tangent of a curve) relative to the horizontal axis. Mathematically, it is typically defined as the ratio of the change in the vertical coordinate to the change in the horizontal coordinate. In financial and economic analysis, it is commonly used in linear regression models to measure the marginal relationship between variables.

formulas.source_formula: Slope = Change in Vertical Coordinate ÷ Change in Horizontal Coordinate

nodes.name: Slope (Rate of Change)
nodes.definition: Slope (rate of change) measures the incremental change in a financial metric per unit change in an independent variable (commonly time), and is used in trend analysis, linear forecasting, and sensitivity assessment across financial and managerial accounting applications.

formulas.source_formula: Slope = (Financial Metric Value 2 - Financial Metric Value 1) ÷ (Time Period 2 - Time Period 1)

nodes.name: Slope of the Demand Curve
aliases: 需求价格曲线的倾斜度
nodes.definition: The slope of the demand curve measures the ratio between the change in price and the change in quantity demanded along the curve. It is typically negative, indicating an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded: as price increases, quantity demanded decreases, and as price decreases, quantity demanded increases.

formulas.source_formula: Smoothed +DM_t = (Smoothed +DM_{t-1} × (Period - 1) + +DM_t) ÷ Period
Smoothed -DM_t = (Smoothed -DM_{t-1} × (Period - 1) + -DM_t) ÷ Period
Smoothing Multiplier = Smoothing Factor ÷ (1 + Days)

nodes.name: Social Security
nodes.definition: Social security is a system established by the state through legislation, funded by mandatory social insurance contributions, which provides material assistance to workers in circumstances such as old age, illness, work-related injury, unemployment, and childbirth. The contribution amount is calculated based on the contribution base and contribution rate, and it serves as a significant source of funds for government transfer payments.

formulas.source_formula: Social Security = Individual Social Security Contribution Amount + Employer Social Security Contribution Amount
Social Security = Pension Insurance + Medical Insurance + Unemployment Insurance + Work-related Injury Insurance + Maternity Insurance

nodes.name: Social Security Contributions Paid by Individuals

formulas.source_formula: Social Security Tax = Social Security Taxable Earnings × Social Security Tax Rate
Social Security Tax = min(Gross Income, Wage Base Limit) × Social Security Rate
Social Security Taxable Earnings = min(Net Earnings, Social Security Wage Base)

nodes.name: Social Security and Housing Fund Contributions
Social Security and Medicare Taxes (Employer + Employee)

operands.metric: Social Security and Medicare Taxes (Single Share)

formulas.source_formula: Social Security and Medicare Taxes (Employer + Employee) = Social Security and Medicare Taxes (Single Share) × 2

nodes.name: Social Security and Medicare Taxes (Single Share)

formulas.source_formula: Social Security and Medicare Taxes (Single Share) = Wages × (Social Security Tax Rate + Medicare Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Solvency Ratio
aliases: Operating Cash Flow to Total Liabilities
nodes.definition: The solvency ratio measures a company's ability to meet its long-term obligations by comparing cash-flow-like earnings (net income plus non-cash charges such as depreciation and amortization) to total liabilities. Higher values indicate greater long-term debt-paying capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Solvency Ratio = (Net Income + Depreciation + Amortization) ÷ Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Solvency Ratios
nodes.definition: Solvency ratios are financial metrics that measure a company's ability to meet its long-term debt obligations and assess its financial stability and leverage.

nodes.name: Sorted Numerical Sequence
nodes.definition: A sorted numerical sequence refers to a new data sequence obtained by rearranging a set of original numerical data according to ascending or descending order rules. It is not a composite indicator calculated through mathematical formulas, but rather a common data processing and presentation method for underlying data, with its results entirely dependent on the values of the original data.

nodes.name: Sortino Ratio
nodes.definition: The Sortino Ratio measures the excess return of an investment over a benchmark per unit of downside risk. Unlike the Sharpe Ratio, it penalizes only harmful volatility by using downside deviation. In this implementation, excess return is measured relative to the risk-free rate.

formulas.source_formula: Sortino Ratio = Excess Return ÷ Downside Deviation

nodes.name: Southbound Stock Connect Market Capitalization
aliases: Market Capitalization of Stock Connect-Hong Kong Stocks
nodes.definition: Southbound Stock Connect market capitalization refers to the total market value of all issued shares of Hong Kong-listed companies eligible for the Southbound Stock Connect program. It is calculated by multiplying the total number of the company's issued shares by the current market trading price of the stock, directly reflecting the overall market valuation size of the company.

nodes.name: Sovereign Default Compensation Amount
nodes.definition: Sovereign default compensation amount refers to the compensation payment required due to a sovereign state or its institutions failing to fulfill contractual obligations (such as debt repayment). It is typically calculated based on the total amount involved in the default, the agreed penalty rate, and the duration of the default, and serves as a key consideration in the assessment of country risk premium.

formulas.source_formula: Sovereign Default Compensation Amount = Total Amount Involved in Default × Penalty Rate × Cumulative Default Duration

nodes.name: Spare Parts and Components Cost
nodes.definition: Spare parts and components cost refers to the procurement cost incurred for replacing and repairing equipment, parts, materials, and components, which is calculated and reserved based on a certain percentage of equipment cost or installation engineering cost to maintain the normal operation of production equipment.

nodes.name: Special Additional Deductions
nodes.definition: Special Additional Deductions refer to specific itemized amounts stipulated by China's Individual Income Tax Law that taxpayers are permitted to subtract from their comprehensive income when calculating taxable income. These items include social insurance premiums such as basic pension insurance, basic medical insurance, unemployment insurance, and housing provident fund contributions. They serve as crucial raw input data for individual income tax calculation, requiring taxpayers to declare based on their actual circumstances, and cannot be derived through formulas.

nodes.name: Special Drawing Rights (SDR)
nodes.definition: Special Drawing Rights (SDR) are an international reserve asset created by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). The SDR’s value is determined by a weighted basket of major currencies and is used as a unit of account and to supplement member countries’ official reserves. The SDR value in USD is computed by multiplying the fixed currency units in the basket by their respective USD exchange rates and summing the results.

nodes.name: Special Payables
nodes.definition: Special payables refer to funds received by an enterprise from the government or other sources, designated for specific or special purposes, typically used for designated engineering projects or capital expenditures, and classified as non-current liabilities of the enterprise.

nodes.name: Specific Consumption Tax
nodes.definition: Specific consumption tax is a method of calculating consumption tax based on the sales quantity of taxable consumer goods (such as weight, volume, number of units, etc.) and a predetermined fixed unit tax amount, rather than on the price or sales revenue of the goods. This method is typically applicable to specific commodities such as beer, yellow wine, and refined oil products.

nodes.name: Specific Financial Metrics
nodes.definition: Specific financial metrics refer to quantitative standards or ratios used to measure and evaluate a company's financial condition, operating results, and cash flows, serving as core tools for financial analysis.

nodes.name: Specific Item Amount
nodes.definition: Specific item amount refers to the monetary value accounted for or recorded for a particular, independent project, account, or cost center in finance, accounting, or project management. It is typically used to reflect specific figures such as investment, cost, revenue, or budget for an individual project, serving as fundamental data for project analysis, budgeting, and financial consolidation.

nodes.name: Specific Overhead Costs
nodes.definition: Specific overhead costs refer to the aggregate of various expense items incurred by an enterprise in its production and operating activities that are not directly associated with the production of specific products or provision of services but are necessary for maintaining overall organizational operations. These costs typically cannot be directly attributed to a particular product or service and must be allocated to different cost objects using certain allocation bases (such as labor hours, machine hours, direct costs, etc.).

nodes.name: Speed of Sound
nodes.definition: The speed of sound refers to the velocity at which sound propagates through a specific medium (such as air, water, or solids), and its magnitude depends on the properties and state of the medium (such as temperature, density, and pressure). In standard atmospheric pressure and air at 15°C, the speed of sound is approximately 340 meters per second.

nodes.name: Spending Amount Threshold
nodes.definition: The spending amount threshold is a composite indicator calculated based on IC card internal parameters, merchant-set transaction limits, and relevant business rules. It is used to control the maximum allowable amount for a single spending transaction and serves as a key parameter in risk management and transaction authorization processes.

formulas.source_formula: Spending Amount Threshold = Card Internal Parameter Value + Merchant-Set Transaction Limit
Spending Amount Threshold = Card Internal Parameter Value × Merchant Risk Coefficient
Spending Amount Threshold = Card Internal Parameter Value + Merchant-Set Transaction Limit - Daily Cumulative Spending Amount

nodes.name: Spending Variance
aliases: 固定制造费用耗费差异
固定制造费用预算差异
nodes.definition: Spending variance is a component of fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance under standard costing. It refers to the difference between the actual fixed manufacturing overhead incurred and the budgeted (or standard) fixed manufacturing overhead, used to measure the budgetary control level of fixed manufacturing overhead.

formulas.source_formula: Spending Variance = Actual Fixed Manufacturing Overhead - Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead

nodes.name: Spot Asset Value
nodes.definition: Spot asset value refers to the value of an asset at the current point in time, calculated by discounting and summing all future expected cash flows generated by the asset using a discount rate that reflects its risk and time value.

nodes.name: Spot Exchange Rate on Balance Sheet Date
aliases: Spot Exchange Rate at Balance Sheet Date
nodes.definition: The spot exchange rate on the balance sheet date refers to the exchange rate used for immediate conversion between two currencies on the day when an enterprise prepares its balance sheet (i.e., the financial reporting cutoff date). In the translation of foreign currency financial statements, it is typically used to translate monetary items in the balance sheet (such as cash and cash equivalents, accounts receivable, accounts payable, etc.) to reflect the true value of these items on the reporting date.

nodes.name: Spot Price
nodes.definition: Spot price refers to the transaction price for the immediate delivery and settlement of an underlying asset (such as stocks, commodities, foreign exchange, etc.) at the current moment in financial or commodity markets. It is directly determined by the immediate market supply and demand and represents raw market data reflecting the current value of the asset.

nodes.name: Spot Price Volatility
nodes.definition: Spot price volatility refers to the phenomenon where the immediate transaction prices of commodities, securities, or financial assets in the spot market fluctuate upward and downward over time. This fluctuation results from the combined effects of various complex factors such as market supply and demand, macroeconomic conditions, policy adjustments, and unexpected events, and serves as fundamental market observation data.

nodes.name: Spot Rate
nodes.definition: The spot rate is the yield to maturity of a zero-coupon security at a given point in time, representing the current market's required annualized yield for a zero-coupon bond of a specific maturity. It is commonly used in bond pricing, cash flow discounting, and the construction of the term structure of interest rates.

nodes.name: Spread Betting Position Value
nodes.definition: Position value in spread betting represents the notional monetary exposure of a position, computed as the stake per point multiplied by the instrument's opening price. It is used to assess leverage, margin requirements, and potential profit or loss sensitivity to price movements.

nodes.name: Spread Betting Profit or Loss
nodes.definition: Spread betting profit or loss is the monetary outcome of a spread bet, calculated by multiplying the stake per point by the difference between the opening price and the closing price of the underlying instrument. It reflects leveraged exposure to price movements, where profits and losses can exceed the initial margin, and a positive value indicates a gain while a negative value indicates a loss.

nodes.name: Spread Commission
nodes.definition: Spread commission represents the monetary impact of a specified point (pip) difference across a given transaction size. It quantifies the commission or cost attributable to the bid–ask spread and point value, commonly used in foreign exchange and other point-based markets.

formulas.source_formula: Spread Cost = Spread × Trade Size

nodes.name: Square Root
nodes.definition: The square root is a mathematical operation function used to calculate the square root of a non-negative value, i.e., a number that, when multiplied by itself, equals the original number. In financial and financial analysis, it is commonly used to calculate derived metrics such as volatility (e.g., standard deviation in Rho value calculations).

formulas.source_formula: Square Root = Radicand ^ (1 ÷ 2)

nodes.name: Stable Growth Rate
nodes.definition: The stable growth rate is the sustainable compound growth rate that a company can maintain over the long term after entering a phase of long-term equilibrium development. It is commonly used to calculate the terminal value (continuing value) in business valuation. In financial analysis, the stable growth rate is typically estimated or assumed based on theoretical models such as the sustainable growth rate model or the potential output growth rate of the macroeconomy.

formulas.source_formula: Stable Growth Rate = (Return on Equity × Retention Ratio) ÷ (1 - Return on Equity × Retention Ratio)
Stable Growth Rate = (Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier × Retention Ratio) ÷ (1 - Net Profit Margin × Total Asset Turnover × Equity Multiplier × Retention Ratio)

nodes.name: Stamp Duty
nodes.definition: Stamp duty is a tax levied on the execution or receipt of legally effective taxable documents (such as contracts, property transfer deeds, business account books, etc.) in economic activities and transactions. The tax amount is directly calculated based on the recorded amount, fees, revenue, or number of documents, according to statutory proportional rates or fixed rates.

nodes.name: Standard Activity Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The Standard Activity Allocation Rate is a predetermined fixed allocation rate calculated based on budgeted or normal activity costs and activity volumes in Activity-Based Costing. It is used to allocate activity costs to cost objects (such as products or services), which can avoid the impact of fluctuations in actual activity costs on product costing and facilitates the provision of stable cost information for decision-making.

nodes.name: Standard Activity Level
nodes.definition: Standard Activity Level refers to the predetermined level of operational activity or output quantity expected to be achieved under normal production conditions, used for establishing cost standards or allocating manufacturing overhead in standard costing or activity-based costing. It serves as a crucial benchmark for measuring efficiency, calculating cost variances, and implementing cost control.

nodes.name: Standard Activity-Based Costing
nodes.definition: Standard Activity-Based Costing is a cost management method that integrates the concepts of standard costing and activity-based costing. It first establishes standard cost consumption rates for various activities (such as standard labor hours, standard material usage, etc.), then calculates the standard cost that should have been incurred based on actual activity volumes (such as actual production batches, actual service instances, etc.). This calculated standard cost is compared with the actual activity costs incurred to analyze cost variances, perform cost control, and evaluate performance.

nodes.name: Standard Allocation Rate
aliases: 固定制造费用标准分配率
nodes.definition: The standard allocation rate is a predetermined rate used under standard costing to allocate manufacturing overhead to products or cost centers. It is typically calculated based on budgeted data and serves as the foundation for cost variance analysis, such as fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance analysis.

operands.metric: Standard Total Labor Hours at Budgeted Production Volume

formulas.source_formula: Standard Allocation Rate = Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Standard Total Labor Hours at Budgeted Production Volume

operands.metric: Total Indirect Costs to be Allocated

formulas.source_formula: Standard Allocation Rate = Total Indirect Costs to be Allocated ÷ Total Allocation Base

nodes.name: Standard Base Freight
nodes.definition: Standard base freight refers to the fundamental freight component in cargo transportation, calculated solely based on core billing parameters such as transportation distance, cargo weight, or volume, excluding surcharges, service fees, or other special charges. It constitutes the core component of the total freight cost.

nodes.name: Standard Base Salary
nodes.definition: Standard base salary refers to the fixed foundational wage standard established by an enterprise according to its internal compensation system or industry practices for a specific position, job grade, or role, before considering factors such as performance, allowances, or overtime. It typically serves as the benchmark for calculating total labor costs, overtime pay, social insurance contribution bases, etc.

nodes.name: Standard Consumption per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard consumption per unit refers to the predetermined quantity standard of resources, such as raw materials, labor hours, or energy, allowed for producing one qualified product under standard production conditions. It is a preset target value, not a calculated figure, primarily used for cost control and efficiency measurement.

nodes.name: Standard Cost
nodes.definition: Standard cost is the total cost calculated based on actual output and standard cost per unit, used for comparison with actual costs.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Cost = Actual Output × Standard Cost per Unit

nodes.name: Standard Cost Driver Rate
nodes.definition: Standard Cost Driver Rate refers to a predetermined allocation rate used in Activity-Based Costing to assign costs from activity centers to cost objects (such as products or services). It is typically based on budgeted or standard costs, calculated by dividing the estimated total cost of an activity center by the estimated total quantity of the cost driver, and is used for cost control and variance analysis.

nodes.name: Standard Cost at Actual Output
aliases: 实际生产量下的标准成本
nodes.definition: Standard cost at actual output refers to the total cost calculated based on the actual quantity of products completed during a specific period, using predetermined standard consumption per unit (e.g., materials, labor hours) and standard prices (e.g., material price per unit, wage rate). It serves as one of the benchmarks for measuring variances between actual costs and standard costs (such as price variances and efficiency variances).

nodes.name: Standard Cost of Fixed Manufacturing Overhead
Standard Cost per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard cost per unit refers to the predetermined cost standard for various production factors (direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead) required to produce one unit of qualified product under normal production efficiency. It is a composite expected cost indicator and serves as a benchmark for cost control, budget preparation, and variance analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Cost per Unit = Standard Direct Materials Cost + Standard Direct Labor Cost + Standard Manufacturing Overhead Cost

nodes.name: Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Standard deviation is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of individual observations from the mean within a dataset, reflecting the volatility or spread of the data. In financial management and finance, standard deviation is commonly used to quantify the risk or stability of investment returns and serves as a core parameter in risk assessment and asset pricing models.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation (Sample)
nodes.definition: Sample standard deviation quantifies the dispersion of prices around their mean, using Bessel's correction (n − 1) to estimate population variance from a sample. It is a core volatility measure and is commonly applied in mean-reversion analytics, including normalization via Z-scores.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Asset A Returns
aliases: Standard Deviation of Asset A's Return
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of Asset A returns is a composite metric calculated through statistical analysis of Asset A's historical return data. It measures the dispersion or volatility of Asset A's returns relative to its average return, serving as a core indicator in risk assessment and portfolio management.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Asset B Returns
aliases: Standard Deviation of Asset B's Return
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of Asset B returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion or volatility of Asset B's returns. It is calculated by measuring the deviation of its historical or expected returns from the average return, serving as a key parameter for assessing asset risk.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Asset Excess Returns
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of asset excess returns is a risk metric that measures the volatility of an asset's or portfolio's returns relative to a benchmark (such as the market portfolio or the risk-free rate). It represents the dispersion of excess returns from their mean and is a key input for calculating risk-adjusted return metrics such as the Sharpe Ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Deviation of Asset Excess Returns = Excess Return ÷ Sharpe Ratio

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Asset Returns
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of asset returns is a statistical metric calculated from other financial data, used to measure the dispersion of returns and reflect the risk level of asset returns.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Benchmark Returns
nodes.definition: Standard deviation of benchmark returns is a statistical measure used to quantify the volatility of benchmark returns, reflecting the dispersion of benchmark return rates relative to their mean. It is commonly used in asset risk analysis and investment decision-making.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Demand During Lead Time
aliases: 订货间隔期需求标准差
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of demand during lead time is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility of customer demand throughout the entire period from order placement to goods receipt. It is typically calculated based on historical daily (or weekly) demand data and the lead time, serving as a key parameter for determining safety stock levels, calculating reorder points, and assessing stockout risk.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Equity Market Returns
Standard Deviation of Expected Daily Cash Balance Changes
aliases: SD of Daily Cash Balance Fluctuations
每日现金余额变化标准差
现金余额日变动标准差
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of expected daily cash balance changes is a statistical measure of the volatility of daily cash balance fluctuations, calculated from historical data or forecasting models. It is used in cash management models (such as the Miller-Orr model) to determine the cash return line and is a non-leaf composite indicator.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Government Bond Market Returns
Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Returns
aliases: Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Return
市场组合收益率标准差
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of market portfolio returns is a statistical measure that quantifies the volatility or risk of the market portfolio's rate of return. It is calculated using historical data or the probability distribution of returns from the assets within the market portfolio. This measure serves as a key parameter for quantifying systematic risk in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Market Returns
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of market returns is a statistical measure calculated from historical market return data, used to quantify the volatility of market returns. It serves as an important tool for measuring market risk, was first introduced by Markowitz in portfolio theory, and plays a key role in the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and beta coefficient calculations.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Random Variable X
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of random variable X is a statistic that measures the dispersion of its values, defined as the positive square root of the variance, reflecting the average deviation of the random variable's values from its mathematical expectation.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Random Variable Y
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of random variable Y is the arithmetic square root of its variance, used to measure the dispersion of the random variable's values from its expected value. It is a core indicator in risk assessment and statistical analysis.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Return on Assets
nodes.definition: Standard Deviation of Return on Assets is a statistical measure that quantifies the dispersion of an asset's (or portfolio's) returns around its expected return (mean return). It reflects the uncertainty or risk level of asset returns; a larger standard deviation indicates more volatile returns and higher risk.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Returns
nodes.definition: Standard deviation of returns is a measure of the volatility of stock returns, estimating its risk level through the dispersion of historical continuously compounded returns.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Returns for Security j
aliases: 第j种资产报酬率标准差
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of returns for Security j is a statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of the investment returns of that security. It reflects the degree to which the actual returns of the security deviate from its average (expected) return. A larger standard deviation indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, which typically corresponds to higher risk.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Returns for Security k
aliases: 第k种证券报酬率标准离差
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of returns for Security k is a statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of the investment returns of that security. It reflects the degree to which the actual returns of the security deviate from its average return (expected return). A larger standard deviation indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, which typically corresponds to higher investment risk.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Returns of Security j
Standard Deviation of Returns of Security k
Standard Deviation of Security A Returns
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of Security A returns is a statistic calculated based on historical return data, used to measure the volatility or risk of Security A returns. It can be derived from periodic return data and serves as a fundamental metric for portfolio risk analysis and the calculation of expected correlation coefficients.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Security A's Returns
Standard Deviation of Security B Returns
aliases: Standard Deviation of Security B Return
证券B报酬率的标准离差
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of Security B returns is a statistic calculated from historical return data, used to measure the volatility or risk of Security B returns, indicating the degree to which returns deviate from the average return. It is not a raw fundamental data item from financial statements but can be decomposed into operations of other metrics.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Security B's Returns
Standard Deviation of Security j
aliases: Standard Deviation of Returns for Security j
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of Security j is a statistical measure of the dispersion of its historical returns relative to its average return, used to quantify the overall risk or volatility of the security. In portfolio theory, it serves as the basis for calculating covariance between securities.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of Stock Returns
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of stock returns is a statistical measure calculated from stock return data, used to gauge the volatility of stock returns and reflect stock investment risk. A larger standard deviation indicates greater return volatility and higher risk; conversely, a smaller standard deviation indicates lower volatility and lower risk.

nodes.name: Standard Deviation of the k-th Security
nodes.definition: The standard deviation of the k-th security is a fundamental statistical measure of the volatility or dispersion of that security's own rate of return. It is calculated based on the security's historical return data. A larger value indicates greater volatility in the security's returns, signifying higher risk. It serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating more complex risk metrics such as portfolio risk and covariance.

nodes.name: Standard Direct Labor Hours per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard direct labor hours per unit refers to the predetermined, necessary working time for direct production workers to produce one qualified product under normal operating conditions in a standard costing system. It includes time for direct processing operations, necessary equipment adjustments, work breaks, and time consumed by normal scrap. It serves as the foundational data for calculating standard direct labor costs and standard variable and fixed manufacturing overhead costs.

nodes.name: Standard Error
nodes.definition: Standard error is an indicator that measures the dispersion between a sample statistic (such as the sample mean) and the population parameter. It reflects the magnitude of sampling error, i.e., the average error that may occur when using a sample to estimate the population.

nodes.name: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead
aliases: Fixed Overhead Standard Cost per Unit
单位产品固定制造费用标准
固定制造费用标准成本
nodes.definition: Standard fixed manufacturing overhead is the predetermined, allocable fixed manufacturing cost (such as factory rent, equipment depreciation, fixed salaries of management personnel, etc.) set for each unit of product in cost management, based on budgeting or standard costing. It is typically calculated by dividing the total budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead by the planned standard capacity (such as standard labor hours or standard output) to derive a standard allocation rate.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead = Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Budgeted Output

nodes.name: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Rate per Hour
aliases: Fixed Overhead Standard Rate per Hour
Standard Fixed Overhead Rate per Hour
固定制造费用标准分配率
固定制造费用标准费率
固定制造费用预定分配率
nodes.definition: The standard fixed manufacturing overhead rate per hour is a predetermined rate used in cost accounting to allocate total fixed manufacturing overhead costs (such as factory rent, equipment depreciation, and other costs that do not vary directly with production volume) to each unit of product based on the budgeted standard labor hours. It is a budgeted figure used to calculate the standard cost of a product, rather than being based on actual incurred costs.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Rate per Hour = Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Budgeted Hours

nodes.name: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Charges
nodes.definition: Standard freight and miscellaneous charges refer to the predetermined standard cost or rate used in financial accounting or cost accounting for calculating and measuring transportation and related miscellaneous expenses associated with material procurement or goods transportation. It is typically based on historical data, industry standards, or contractual agreements, and is used for budgeting, cost control, and variance analysis. It is an essential component of the total standard procurement cost of materials.

nodes.name: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Charges per Unit Material
aliases: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Expenses per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard freight and miscellaneous charges per unit material refer to the predetermined standard rate or unit price set for each unit of material in cost accounting and budgeting, used to calculate its transportation and related miscellaneous expenses. It is typically determined based on historical data, contractual agreements, or market prices, serving as a benchmark input for cost control and budget preparation.

nodes.name: Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Rate Coefficient
nodes.definition: The Standard Freight and Miscellaneous Rate Coefficient is a pre-determined ratio or multiplier used to calculate the total standard freight and miscellaneous charges. It is typically determined by logistics companies based on comprehensive factors such as market conditions, transportation distance, and cargo type, and can be adjusted according to the specific requirements of the shipper. It serves as a key parameter in the freight and miscellaneous charge calculation model.

nodes.name: Standard Freight/Handling Charge per Unit of Material
Standard Hourly Wage Rate
nodes.definition: Standard Hourly Wage Rate refers to the ratio of the total estimated direct labor wages to be paid for producing a unit of product to the standard total labor hours under a standard cost system, serving as the basis for calculating the standard direct labor cost.

operands.metric: Total Estimated Wages for Planned Operating Period

formulas.source_formula: Standard Hourly Wage Rate = Total Estimated Wages for Planned Operating Period ÷ Estimated Operating Days ÷ Estimated Daily Working Hours

operands.metric: Total Estimated Standard Direct Labor Wages

formulas.source_formula: Standard Hourly Wage Rate = Total Estimated Standard Direct Labor Wages ÷ Standard Total Labor Hours × 100%

nodes.name: Standard Hours
nodes.definition: Standard hours refer to the labor time required to complete a specific task or process under standard working conditions, used for cost calculation, production planning, and efficiency evaluation. It is a non-leaf node concept that can be calculated from other time metrics and is often referenced in determining the standard cost per unit.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Hours = Actual Time × (1 + Allowance Rate)

nodes.name: Standard Hours for Completed Products
nodes.definition: Standard hours for completed products refer to the predetermined standard labor time allocated for producing one qualified product in manufacturing cost accounting. It is a standard time consumption benchmark established by enterprises based on production processes, equipment conditions, and historical experience, primarily used for cost calculation and efficiency evaluation.

nodes.name: Standard Hours of Work-in-Process at Month-End
nodes.definition: Standard Hours of Work-in-Process at Month-End refers to the total standard hours calculated at the month-end point for work-in-process, based on the time quota of its respective production stage and its degree of completion (or an agreed conversion coefficient). It is a composite metric used under the standard cost method or the standard proportion method to allocate costs such as direct labor and manufacturing overhead between finished goods and work-in-process at month-end.

nodes.name: Standard Hours per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard hours per unit refer to the direct labor hours that should be consumed to produce one unit of qualified product under standard production conditions. It is a fundamental metric for setting standard costs, preparing production budgets, and conducting efficiency analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Hours per Unit = Workload per Unit ÷ Work Efficiency per Unit

nodes.name: Standard Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Standard inventory cost refers to the predetermined unit cost standard established by an enterprise for internal accounting and control purposes regarding the production or holding of inventory (such as raw materials, work-in-progress, and finished goods) in financial and cost management. It is typically based on reasonable estimates of direct materials, direct labor, and manufacturing overhead, and is used to compare with actual incurred costs for variance analysis and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Standard Labor Cost
nodes.definition: Standard labor cost is a key component of the standard costing system, referring to the predetermined direct labor cost that should be incurred to complete a unit of product or a specific task under standard production conditions. It is typically calculated from basic data such as standard hours and standard wage rates, or aggregated from standard values of sub-items including basic wages, welfare expenses, taxes, and fees. It serves as a critical benchmark for cost control, budget preparation, and labor cost variance analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Labor Cost = Standard Hours × Standard Wage Rate
Standard Labor Cost = Standard Basic Wages + Standard Welfare Expenses + Standard Taxes and Fees + Standard Other Labor Expenses

nodes.name: Standard Labor Hours for Finished Goods
Standard Labor Hours per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard labor hours per unit refers to the predetermined or standardized necessary labor time consumption for producing one unit of qualified product under normal production or construction conditions. It serves as an important basis for production planning, labor cost accounting, and productivity measurement.

nodes.name: Standard Labor Time Allowance
nodes.definition: The Standard Labor Time Allowance is a core component for calculating the standard direct labor cost, referring to the standard direct labor hours required to produce one unit of product under existing production technology conditions. It is typically established through industrial engineering methods such as method study and time study, and is a composite or derived standard rather than raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Labor Time Allowance = Standard Operating Time + Auxiliary Time

nodes.name: Standard Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The standard manufacturing overhead allocation rate is a ratio calculated based on the total budgeted manufacturing overhead and the total budgeted allocation base. It is used to allocate manufacturing overhead to product unit costs in standard costing systems and is a key metric for establishing standard costs per unit of product.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate = Total Budgeted Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Budgeted Labor Hours
Standard Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate = Total Budgeted Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Budgeted Production Worker Wages

nodes.name: Standard Material Consumption for Various Products
nodes.definition: Standard material consumption for various products refers to the established quantity standard of raw materials or auxiliary materials that must be consumed to produce one qualified product under current production and technological conditions. This standard includes the net material usage that constitutes the product itself, as well as reasonable and unavoidable losses during the production process.

nodes.name: Standard Material Consumption per Unit Product
Standard Material Consumption per Unit of Work-in-Process
Standard Material Cost
nodes.definition: Standard material cost refers to the predetermined direct material cost that should be incurred under normal production conditions for producing a unit of product under the standard costing method. It is typically calculated by multiplying the standard quantity of materials by the standard price of materials, and is used for cost control, budgeting, and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Standard Material Cost of Ending Work-in-Process
Standard Material Cost of Finished Products
aliases: Standard Material Cost of Finished Goods
完工产品定额原材料费用
完工产品材料定额成本
nodes.definition: Standard material cost of finished products is the material cost allocated to finished products calculated based on predetermined material consumption standards and planned unit prices. It serves as a foundational metric in cost allocation for determining the material cost allocation rate and the material cost to be allocated to finished products, and is classified as a non-leaf node.

operands.metric: Total Standard Material Consumption of Finished Products

formulas.source_formula: Standard Material Cost of Finished Products = Total Standard Material Consumption of Finished Products × Planned Unit Price of Material

operands.metric: Material Consumption Quota per Unit Product

formulas.source_formula: Standard Material Cost of Finished Products = Quantity of Finished Products × Material Consumption Standard per Unit Product × Planned Unit Price of Material

nodes.name: Standard Material Cost of Work-in-Process at Month-End
Standard Material Cost per Unit
aliases: 单位产品材料标准成本
nodes.definition: Standard material cost per unit refers to the predetermined material cost standard calculated for producing one unit (e.g., one piece, one set) of a specific product, based on pre-established material consumption quotas and planned unit prices of materials, when an enterprise uses the standard costing method to calculate product costs. It serves as the basis for measuring and controlling material consumption in products.

nodes.name: Standard Material Usage
aliases: 单位产品材料消耗定额
nodes.definition: Standard material usage refers to the predetermined quantity of raw materials that should be consumed to produce one unit of product in a manufacturing process. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and cost control, used to calculate the standard cost of direct materials and as a benchmark for comparing actual material consumption to conduct cost variance analysis.

nodes.name: Standard Material Usage Quantity
nodes.definition: Standard Material Usage Quantity refers to the predetermined quantity standard of raw materials that should be consumed to produce a unit of product or complete a specific task under standard costing, based on technical specifications, historical data, and efficiency expectations. It serves as one of the bases for calculating direct material cost variances.

nodes.name: Standard Material Usage per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard material usage per unit refers to the predetermined technical standard or quota for the quantity of direct materials that should be consumed to produce one unit of qualified product under specific production and technological conditions. It is established by the production and technology department based on factors such as product design drawings, process specifications, and material characteristics, and serves as the foundational data for calculating the standard cost of direct materials.

nodes.name: Standard Normal Cumulative Distribution Function
nodes.definition: The Standard Normal Cumulative Distribution Function is a fundamental mathematical and statistical function used to calculate the probability that a random variable in a standard normal distribution (with mean 0 and standard deviation 1) takes a value less than or equal to a specific point. It is the integral of the probability density function from negative infinity to that point, and is commonly used as a calculation tool or model input parameter in fields such as finance and risk management.

nodes.name: Standard Normal Distribution Probability Density Function
nodes.definition: The probability density function of the standard normal distribution (a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1), which describes the relative likelihood (density) of its random variable taking a specific value. This function is even, defined over all real numbers, and is widely used in financial modeling (e.g., in the Black-Scholes model and in calculating price sensitivity parameters for expansion options in real options analysis).

nodes.name: Standard Normal Distribution Quantile Corresponding to Confidence Level
nodes.definition: In statistics and financial econometrics, the standard normal distribution quantile corresponding to a confidence level refers to the critical point value on the standard normal distribution curve associated with a specific confidence level (e.g., 95%, 99%). It represents the probability boundary within which the random variable's value will not exceed that point at a given confidence level, commonly used for constructing confidence intervals or conducting hypothesis testing.

nodes.name: Standard Normal Quantile
nodes.definition: The standard normal quantile refers to the specific value in a standard normal distribution (a normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1) that corresponds to a given cumulative probability (or significance level). It indicates that the probability of a random variable being less than or equal to this value equals the given probability. In financial and statistical applications, it is typically obtained directly by consulting statistical tables or using statistical software functions (e.g., NORM.S.INV) and serves as a fundamental parameter.

nodes.name: Standard Operating Time
nodes.definition: Standard operating time refers to the time required for a worker with average proficiency, under suitable operating conditions and using the most appropriate operating method, to complete a specific task or operation at a normal working pace and with standard operating procedures. It serves as the basis for production planning, cost accounting, efficiency evaluation, and performance management.

nodes.name: Standard Ordering Cost
nodes.definition: Standard ordering cost refers to the estimated costs incurred to complete one standard purchase order under the enterprise's standard cost accounting system, serving as a fundamental component in establishing the total standard material procurement cost.

nodes.name: Standard Other Labor Costs
nodes.definition: Standard Other Labor Costs refer to the predetermined standard costs of various indirect or additional labor-related expenses, excluding basic direct labor wages, for completing specific production or service activities under the standard costing method. These costs typically include benefits, taxes, allowances, and subsidies, and constitute an important component of standard labor costs.

nodes.name: Standard Price
nodes.definition: Standard price is a pre-determined unit price benchmark used for cost accounting and control within the standard costing system. It is typically established based on market conditions, long-term contract prices, or historical data, and serves as the fundamental input for calculating standard costs and conducting cost variance analysis (e.g., material price variance).

nodes.name: Standard Price per Unit of Material
Standard Purchase Price per Unit of Material
nodes.definition: The Standard Purchase Price per Unit of Material is a predetermined base price standard established by an enterprise for implementing a standard cost system, used to account for the unit cost of materials. It is typically determined comprehensively based on market research, supplier quotations, historical purchasing data, and forecasts of future price trends, serving as a key input value for calculating the standard cost of direct materials.

nodes.name: Standard Purchase Quantity
nodes.definition: Standard Purchase Quantity refers to the optimal order quantity calculated using specific models (such as the Economic Order Quantity model) that minimizes total inventory costs (including purchase costs, ordering costs, and holding costs) while meeting production or sales requirements. It serves as a key reference standard for inventory management and procurement decision-making.

nodes.name: Standard Purchase Unit Price of Material
Standard Quantity
nodes.definition: Standard quantity refers to the predetermined benchmark value for the consumption of resources such as materials and labor hours required to produce one unit of product or complete a service under the standard costing method. It is a planning or budgeting figure used for cost control and variance analysis.

nodes.name: Standard Stockout Cost
nodes.definition: Standard stockout cost refers to the expected or standardized loss cost incurred due to inventory supply interruption or insufficient stock that fails to meet customer demand under the standard costing method. It is typically estimated as a component of the total standard material procurement cost and is used for cost control and budget management.

nodes.name: Standard Surcharges
nodes.definition: Standard surcharges refer to additional fees levied beyond the base charges, in accordance with industry practices, contractual stipulations, or specific criteria. These fees typically have clearly defined billing standards or rates and are used to cover specific services, costs, or risks, commonly seen in fields such as transportation, finance, and international trade.

nodes.name: Standard Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The standard tax rate is the basic statutory percentage or scale directly stipulated in tax laws for calculating a taxpayer's tax payable. It does not depend on the calculation of other financial indicators and is one of the core data points in tax policy.

nodes.name: Standard Tax and Fee
nodes.definition: Standard tax and fee refers to a pre-established or commonly applicable benchmark or reference value for calculating taxes and fees for a specific category of economic activities or cost items (such as standard labor cost) under particular regulations, policies, or industry practices. It is typically used in cost accounting, budget preparation, or financial analysis to provide a uniform and standardized basis for estimating taxes and fees.

nodes.name: Standard Total Hours
nodes.definition: Standard total hours refer to the total labor time required to complete a specific work task or produce a unit of product under standard working conditions, serving as the foundation for time management, cost accounting, and production efficiency evaluation.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Total Hours = Actual Time × (1 + Allowance Rate)
Standard Total Hours = Basic Hours + Setup Hours + Rest Hours + Lost Hours

nodes.name: Standard Total Hours at Budgeted Production Level
aliases: Standard Total Hours at Budgeted Production
nodes.definition: Standard total hours at the budgeted production level refers to the total direct labor hour requirement calculated based on the standard hours per unit at the budgeted production volume. It is a foundational composite metric used in cost accounting and budget management for calculating indicators such as the standard fixed overhead allocation rate.

nodes.name: Standard Total Labor Hours at Budgeted Production Volume
Standard Total Purchase Quantity
nodes.definition: Standard Total Purchase Quantity refers to the standard quantity of raw materials or supplies required to be purchased during a budget or planning period to meet production needs and maintain target inventory levels. It is a composite indicator calculated based on fundamental data such as projected production volume, consumption per unit product, and beginning and ending inventory levels. It serves as the core basis for procurement budgeting and cost control.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Total Purchase Quantity = (Consumption per Unit Product × Projected Production Volume) + Projected Ending Material Inventory - Beginning Material Inventory

nodes.name: Standard Total Wages
