nodes.definition: Standard total wages refers to the aggregate sum of all labor remuneration paid to all employees within a specific period, directly calculated based on actual payments. It serves as the foundational data for payroll accounting, encompassing time wages, piece-rate wages, bonuses, allowances and subsidies, overtime pay, etc. The calculation is based on the actual amount disbursed, irrespective of the funding source or payment method.

nodes.name: Standard Unit Fixed Cost
nodes.definition: Standard unit fixed cost is a composite metric calculated by dividing total fixed costs by total output or activity volume. It measures the fixed cost allocated per unit of product, serving as a non-leaf node in cost behavior analysis and is referenced in value-added cost analysis.

nodes.name: Standard Unit Price
nodes.definition: Standard unit price refers to the planned unit price set for direct materials and other items under the standard costing method. It is typically composed of base data such as purchase price and freight/handling charges, or is set as a planned price. It is used to calculate composite metrics such as the standard cost of direct materials.

operands.metric: Standard Purchase Unit Price of Material
Standard Freight/Handling Charge per Unit of Material

formulas.source_formula: Standard Unit Price = Standard Purchase Unit Price of Material + Standard Freight/Handling Charge per Unit of Material

operands.metric: Total Standard Purchase Cost of Material

formulas.source_formula: Standard Unit Price = (Total Standard Purchase Cost of Material + Total Standard Freight/Handling Charges) ÷ Total Standard Purchase Quantity

nodes.name: Standard Variable Cost per Unit
nodes.definition: Standard variable cost per unit refers to the average allocation of variable costs that should be included per unit product under standard costing. It is typically calculated as the ratio of total variable costs to total output, or derived through composite calculations based on indicators such as target profit, unit price, and sales volume. It is a key metric in cost behavior analysis and value-added activity-based costing.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Variable Cost per Unit = Total Variable Costs ÷ Total Output

nodes.name: Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead
aliases: 单位标准变动制造费用
变动制造费用标准分配率
变动制造费用标准成本
标准变动制造费用分配率
nodes.definition: Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead is the predetermined standard cost per unit of product for indirect production expenses that vary with production volume, such as indirect materials and power costs. It serves as a crucial internal benchmark for cost control and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate
Standard Variable Overhead Rate Per Hour
aliases: Standard Variable Overhead Rate per Hour
Variable Manufacturing Overhead Rate per Hour
变动制造费用小时分配率
变动制造费用标准分配率
变动制造费用预定分配率
每小时变动费用标准率
nodes.definition: The standard variable overhead rate per hour refers to the predetermined amount of variable manufacturing overhead allocated for each standard labor hour under standard costing, serving as a core composite indicator for calculating the standard cost of variable manufacturing overhead.

formulas.source_formula: Standard Variable Overhead Rate Per Hour = Total Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead ÷ Total Standard Hours

nodes.name: Standard Wage Rate
nodes.definition: The standard wage rate is the ratio of the total standard wages to the total standard labor hours. It refers to the ratio of the predetermined total wages during the standard usage period to the estimated operating time (effective time), used to represent the wage value per unit of time. It serves as the basis for calculating the standard cost of direct labor and the standard cost per unit of product.

nodes.name: Standard Welfare Expenses
nodes.definition: Standard welfare expenses refer to the costs that an enterprise accrues or calculates in advance for various employee benefits (such as medical expenses, hardship allowances, canteen, childcare facilities, etc.) in accordance with national regulations or internal standards, typically calculated as a fixed percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total payroll.

nodes.name: Standardized Random Variable Value
nodes.definition: Standardized random variable value is a statistical concept referring to the result obtained by standardizing an original random variable through subtracting its mean and dividing by its standard deviation. This process transforms data from any distribution into a standard normal distribution with a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1, facilitating comparison and probability calculations for data with different units or distributions.

nodes.name: Start Date
nodes.definition: Start Date refers to an initial point in time set for time-related calculations or analyses, serving as the basis for calculating subsequent time periods, days, or derived metrics.

nodes.name: Start Time
nodes.definition: Start Time refers to the designated initial moment point of an event, process, time period, or calculation. In the field of finance and accounting, it is often used as a fundamental input value for calculating time intervals, costs, returns, or conducting time value analysis.

nodes.name: Starting Month
nodes.definition: Starting Month refers to the original temporal benchmark point used for calculating other time-related metrics (such as length of service, number of service months, number of financial periods). It typically corresponds to the month of a specific date (e.g., hire date, project start date, contract effective date). It is a fundamental input datum, not a calculated result.

nodes.name: Starting Year
nodes.definition: Starting Year refers to the base raw data used for calculating indicators such as length of service or number of historical periods. It typically denotes the year portion directly extracted from specific dates like an employee's hire date, system activation date, or project launch date. It is a starting point value, not a result derived from calculation.

nodes.name: State Probabilities
nodes.definition: State probabilities describe the distribution of the likelihood of a random variable (e.g., stock returns) occurring under different possible outcomes (states). They form the basis for calculating risk and return metrics such as expected value, variance, and standard deviation. Their sum is 1, and they are typically derived from historical data analysis, model estimation, or subjective judgment.

nodes.name: State Probability
nodes.definition: State probability refers to the probability that a system is in a specific state at the current moment, given the current observation, control input, and the state at the previous moment. It is a core concept in dynamic system analysis, filtering theory, and state estimation (e.g., Bayesian filtering), used to describe the uncertainty of the system state.

nodes.name: State Transition Probability
nodes.definition: State transition probability refers to the likelihood of transitioning from a current state to various other states at the next moment during the development and change of a system or event. It is typically derived from historical data statistics and serves as the core foundational probability data in stochastic process models such as Markov chains.

nodes.name: State-Dependent Return Rate
nodes.definition: State-dependent return rate refers to the rate of return achieved by an asset or investment under specific economic or market conditions. It is commonly used for state-contingent analysis in financial modeling and serves as a basis for calculating metrics such as expected asset returns. It can be derived from financial indicators such as profit and cash flow.

nodes.name: State-Specific Stock Returns
nodes.definition: State-specific stock returns refer to the rate of return on stock investments under specific conditions (such as different market environments or holding periods). They can be calculated as the discount rate that equates the present value of future cash inflows to the stock purchase price, or decomposed into the sum of interest (dividend) yield and capital gains yield.

formulas.source_formula: State-Specific Stock Returns = Interest (Dividend) Yield + Capital Gains Yield

nodes.name: Statutory Appropriation Ratio
aliases: 法定盈余公积提取比例
法定盈余公积金计提比例
nodes.definition: The statutory appropriation ratio refers to the proportion of net profit that a company must appropriate as statutory surplus reserve from its after-tax profit distribution for the year, as stipulated by laws and regulations such as the Company Law. It is typically 10% of the net profit, and the appropriation may cease once the cumulative statutory surplus reserve reaches 50% of the company's registered capital.

nodes.name: Statutory Deduction Items Amount
nodes.definition: Statutory Deduction Items Amount refers to the total sum of costs, expenses, losses, and other allowable deduction items that, according to explicit provisions of national tax laws and regulations, are permitted to be subtracted from the total revenue when calculating taxable income for specific taxes such as Corporate Income Tax, Individual Income Tax, or Land Appreciation Tax. It is a key component in determining the final taxable base (taxable income).

nodes.name: Statutory Deposit Reserve
nodes.definition: Statutory deposit reserve refers to the portion of total deposits that deposit-taking financial institutions, such as commercial banks, are required to deposit with the central bank (e.g., the People's Bank of China) at a specified ratio, as mandated by the central bank's statutory reserve requirement ratio. These funds cannot be used for lending or investment and serve as a key monetary policy tool for the central bank to regulate the money supply.

nodes.name: Statutory Loss Carry-forward Period
nodes.definition: The statutory loss carry-forward period refers to the maximum consecutive number of years, as stipulated by the Enterprise Income Tax Law of the People's Republic of China and related regulations, during which an enterprise's losses incurred in a tax year may be offset against taxable income in subsequent tax years. This period is typically five years, calculated consecutively from the year following the loss year. Regardless of whether the enterprise is profitable or incurs further losses during these five years, they are counted toward the actual loss offset period.

nodes.name: Statutory Ratio
aliases: 法定盈余公积提取比例
nodes.definition: The statutory ratio typically refers to the fixed percentage mandated by laws and regulations, requiring enterprises to allocate a portion of their after-tax profits to statutory surplus reserves (such as statutory surplus reserve). According to relevant regulations under China's Company Law, corporate enterprises must allocate 10% of their after-tax profits to the statutory surplus reserve. When the cumulative allocation reaches 50% of the company's registered capital, further allocation may cease.

nodes.name: Statutory Reserve
nodes.definition: Statutory reserve (statutory surplus reserve) refers to the accumulated funds that an enterprise is legally required to appropriate from its current year's net profit after tax at a specified percentage (typically 10%) in accordance with laws and regulations such as the Company Law. It is used to cover losses, expand production and operations, or convert into capital, and constitutes a component of owners' equity.

nodes.name: Statutory Reserve Appropriation
nodes.definition: Statutory reserve appropriation refers to the mandatory profit distribution action where a company, in accordance with legal provisions, allocates a certain percentage of its after-tax net profit to the surplus reserve account, primarily used to cover losses, expand production and operations, or convert into capital.

formulas.source_formula: Statutory Reserve Appropriation = Current Year Net Profit × 10%

nodes.name: Statutory Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Statutory Surplus Reserve refers to a portion of funds that a company is legally required to appropriate from its after-tax net profit at a fixed rate (typically 10%) in accordance with the Company Law. It is designated for specific purposes such as covering losses, expanding production and operations, or converting into capital, and constitutes a significant component of a company's retained earnings.

nodes.name: Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period
aliases: Accrued Statutory Surplus Reserve for the Period
Statutory Surplus Reserve Extracted in Current Period
当期提取的法定盈余公积
nodes.definition: Statutory surplus reserve appropriated in the current period refers to the portion of retained earnings with specific purposes, which is calculated and appropriated from the after-tax net profit realized in the current accounting period (such as the current year or quarter) at the statutory rate of 10%, in accordance with the Company Law and other relevant regulations.

nodes.name: Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriation
nodes.definition: Statutory surplus reserve appropriation refers to the mandatory allocation of a specified proportion (typically 10%) from net profit after tax, as stipulated by the Company Law, to be set aside as accumulated funds for specific purposes during the distribution of annual after-tax profits. Its purpose is to enhance the company's risk resilience and supplement capital.

nodes.name: Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriation Amount
nodes.definition: The statutory surplus reserve appropriation amount refers to the specific-purpose accumulation fund that an enterprise is legally required to appropriate from its net profit at a specified rate (typically 10%) when distributing after-tax profits for the year, in accordance with the provisions of the Company Law.

nodes.name: Statutory Surplus Reserve Extraction Ratio
aliases: 法定盈余公积计提比例
法定盈余公积金提取比例
nodes.definition: The statutory surplus reserve extraction ratio refers to the proportion that a company must extract from its net profit as statutory surplus reserve when distributing the after-tax profit of the current year, as stipulated by the Company Law of the People's Republic of China. This ratio is typically 10% of the net profit and is used to strengthen the company's capital base and cover future losses.

nodes.name: Statutory Tax Rate
nodes.definition: The statutory tax rate refers to the uniform or standard tax rate explicitly stipulated by laws and regulations such as tax laws and tax ordinances of a country or region, applicable to specific tax types, specific taxpayers, or specific taxable activities. It serves as the basis for calculating the tax payable and is typically directly listed in tax policies, such as the 25% corporate income tax rate or the 13% value-added tax rate. The statutory tax rate is the benchmark for tax collection and administration as well as tax planning, and corresponds to the effective tax rate (the actual burden rate after considering tax incentives and deductions).

nodes.name: Step-Up in Basis
nodes.definition: Step-up in basis is a tax accounting convention under which the cost basis of an inherited asset is adjusted to its fair market value on the decedent’s date of death (or alternate valuation date, where applicable). This adjustment establishes the new cost basis for future gain or loss calculations, typically reducing taxable capital gains upon a subsequent sale. If the fair market value is lower than the original cost basis, the basis is stepped down to the fair market value.

nodes.name: Stochastic Oscillator
nodes.definition: The Stochastic Oscillator is a momentum indicator that compares a security’s closing price to its high–low range over a specified lookback period, scaled from 0 to 100, to help identify overbought and oversold conditions.

nodes.name: Stochastic RSI (StochRSI)
nodes.definition: Stochastic RSI is a momentum oscillator that applies the stochastic calculation to the Relative Strength Index (RSI), measuring the RSI's position relative to its high-low range over a specified lookback period. It oscillates between 0 and 1, helping identify overbought and oversold conditions and potential momentum shifts.

formulas.source_formula: Stochastic RSI = (RSI - Minimum RSI over Lookback Period) ÷ (Maximum RSI over Lookback Period - Minimum RSI over Lookback Period)

nodes.name: Stock Appreciation Right Compensation
nodes.definition: Stock Appreciation Right (SAR) compensation is the payout to a grantee equal to the number of SARs multiplied by the increase in the underlying stock price over the measurement period; it represents the realized value from stock appreciation rights when the stock price exceeds the base or grant price.

formulas.source_formula: SAR Compensation = Number of SARs × Stock Price Increase

nodes.name: Stock Beta Coefficient
nodes.definition: The stock beta coefficient (β coefficient) is an indicator that measures the sensitivity of a stock's (or asset's) return rate relative to changes in the overall market return rate, used to quantify the systematic risk borne by the stock. It originates from the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and is calculated through statistical methods (such as regression analysis), reflecting the co-movement between the price volatility of an individual asset and the overall market volatility.

operands.metric: Covariance of Stock Returns and Market Returns

formulas.source_formula: Stock Beta Coefficient = Covariance of Stock Returns and Market Returns ÷ Variance of Market Returns

operands.metric: Correlation Coefficient between Stock and Market

formulas.source_formula: Stock Beta Coefficient = Correlation Coefficient between Stock and Market × Standard Deviation of Stock Return ÷ Standard Deviation of Market Return

operands.metric: Correlation Coefficient between Stock and Market

formulas.source_formula: Stock Beta Coefficient = Correlation Coefficient between Stock and Market × (Standard Deviation of Stock Returns ÷ Standard Deviation of Market Returns)
Stock Beta Coefficient = (Expected Stock Return - Risk-free Rate) ÷ (Expected Market Return - Risk-free Rate)

nodes.name: Stock Current Price
nodes.definition: Stock current price, also known as the stock's spot price or market price, refers to the actual transaction price in the latest trade executed on a secondary market (such as a stock exchange), matched between buyers and sellers through real-time trading. It is directly determined by immediate market supply and demand, reflecting investors' real-time consensus on the company's value.

nodes.name: Stock Dividend
nodes.definition: Stock dividend refers to a method of profit distribution where a company does not pay cash to shareholders, but instead converts a portion of its retained earnings or capital surplus into company shares, and distributes them to shareholders free of charge in proportion to their existing shareholdings.

nodes.name: Stock Dividend Payout Ratio
nodes.definition: The stock dividend payout ratio is a financial metric that measures the proportion of a company's net profit distributed to shareholders in the form of stock dividends, reflecting the company's profit distribution policy and shareholder return method. It is typically defined as the ratio of total stock dividends to net profit or the ratio of stock dividend per share to earnings per share, used to analyze the extent to which a company distributes profits in the form of stock.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Dividend Payout Ratio = Stock Dividend Per Share ÷ Earnings Per Share × 100%

nodes.name: Stock Downside Price
nodes.definition: Stock downside price is a manifestation of stock price in specific contexts (such as option pricing and risk analysis), specifically referring to the stock price level under expected or actual declining conditions. It is essentially a stock price that can be calculated through various valuation models or theoretical price formulas based on market interest rates, commonly used in financial analyses such as evaluating post-decline option value.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Downside Price = Expected Dividend Per Share ÷ Market Interest Rate
Stock Downside Price = Net Asset Value Per Share × P/B Multiple
Stock Downside Price = Earnings Per Share × Industry Average P/E Ratio

nodes.name: Stock Excess Return
nodes.definition: Stock excess return refers to the portion by which the actual return of a stock exceeds its expected return, calculated through formulas. It reflects the stock's outperformance relative to the market or a benchmark and is commonly used in investment performance evaluation and the calculation of financial metrics such as Beta coefficient.

nodes.name: Stock Exchange Daily Official List (SEDOL)
aliases: 证券交易所每日官方清单
nodes.definition: SEDOL (Stock Exchange Daily Official List) is a seven-character alphanumeric security identifier used primarily in the United Kingdom. Its check digit is validated by computing a weighted sum of the first six characters using weights [1, 3, 1, 7, 3, 9], where digits keep their numeric value and letters A–Z are valued 10–35 (A=10, B=11, …). A SEDOL is valid if the weighted sum plus the check digit is a multiple of 10.

nodes.name: Stock Index
nodes.definition: A stock index is a statistical indicator used to track the performance of a selected group of stocks representing a segment of the stock market, measuring overall market or sector performance and serving as a benchmark for investment.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Index = Sum of Constituent Stock Prices ÷ Divisor

nodes.name: Stock Investment
nodes.definition: Stock investment refers to an investment activity where enterprises or individuals purchase shares issued by listed companies to become shareholders, with the expectation of obtaining dividend income or capital appreciation. In accounting treatment, it is typically recorded under accounts such as trading financial assets, available-for-sale financial assets, or long-term equity investments. Its initial value is measured at cost, with subsequent adjustments potentially made based on fair value or the equity method.

nodes.name: Stock Issuance
nodes.definition: Stock issuance refers to the act by a joint-stock limited company of selling company shares (stocks) to investors in accordance with legal procedures to raise capital. This is the primary method for a company to conduct equity financing. Through issuing shares, a company can increase its share capital and obtain funds for operational development.

nodes.name: Stock Log Return
nodes.definition: Stock log return is a method of measuring stock price changes, calculated as the difference between the natural logarithms of stock prices at two adjacent time points. This calculation assumes continuously compounded returns and is mathematically more convenient than simple returns when computing multi-period returns or volatility.

nodes.name: Stock Market Price
nodes.definition: Stock market price refers to the transaction price of a stock formed through real-time trading between buyers and sellers on secondary markets such as stock exchanges. It reflects the market's immediate assessment of the company's value and is dynamically changing.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Market Price = Earnings Per Share ÷ Price-to-Earnings Ratio
Stock Market Price = Price-to-Earnings Ratio × Earnings Per Share
Stock Market Price = Total Market Capitalization ÷ Total Number of Shares

nodes.name: Stock Market Return Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Stock market return standard deviation is a statistical measure calculated based on historical or expected return series, used to quantify the dispersion of overall market returns around their mean. It is a core parameter for measuring market risk and volatility, and is commonly used in financial models such as calculating country risk premiums.

nodes.name: Stock Price
nodes.definition: Stock price is a general term for the par value, issue price, liquidation price, intrinsic value, and market price of a stock. In a narrow sense, stock price primarily refers to the market trading price, reflecting the consideration paid by investors for purchasing ownership shares in a company, and is one of the core valuation metrics in the capital market.

nodes.name: Stock Price After Rise
nodes.definition: Stock Price After Rise is an expression of stock price in a specific scenario, referring to the per-share price calculated through specific financial models or valuation methods, reflecting the company's value or market expectations. Its essence is a calculable composite indicator and serves as the basis for evaluating the value of up-state options.

nodes.name: Stock Price Change
nodes.definition: Stock price change refers to the upward or downward movement in the price of a stock traded in the market over a period of time, typically expressed in specific points or percentage terms.

nodes.name: Stock Price Decline Percentage
nodes.definition: Stock Price Decline Percentage refers to the relative change in a stock's price from its initial level to its ending level over a specified period, typically expressed as a percentage. This metric is a key parameter for measuring downside risk in stock investments, calculating historical returns, and constructing expected scenarios in financial models (such as the binomial option pricing model).

nodes.name: Stock Price Increase Percentage
nodes.definition: Stock Price Increase Percentage is a composite metric measuring the magnitude of stock price changes, reflecting the degree of price appreciation by calculating the percentage change of the current stock price relative to the original price. In finance, it is commonly used to calculate expected returns, particularly serving as a key input variable under the risk-neutral principle in binomial option pricing models.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Price Increase Percentage = Up Factor - 1

nodes.name: Stock Price Per Share
nodes.definition: Stock price per share refers to the real-time transaction price of each share of a company's stock in the securities market, reflecting the market's immediate assessment of the company's value.

nodes.name: Stock Price Volatility
nodes.definition: Stock price volatility is a statistical measure of the magnitude and uncertainty of stock price movements, typically calculated as the standard deviation or variance of historical return series. It serves as a core parameter in financial asset pricing, risk management, and derivative valuation.

nodes.name: Stock Price in Rising State
nodes.definition: Stock price in a rising state refers to the market price of a stock when it exhibits an upward trend relative to the previous trading day's closing price. It is not a fundamental raw data point but rather a result describing the state of price movement. The magnitude of the rise (return) can be calculated using specific formulas, making it an important reference variable in financial analysis, investment decision-making, and hedging strategies.

nodes.name: Stock Price in a Downtrend
nodes.definition: Stock price in a downtrend refers to the current market price of a stock after it has declined from a certain initial level. Its calculation typically involves the percentage decline based on the initial price and the current price, or in technical analysis, estimation through specific formula combinations incorporating data such as opening price, high price, low price, and closing price. This concept is a fundamental analytical element in financial asset valuation and risk management (e.g., hedging).

formulas.source_formula: Stock Price in a Downtrend = Initial Price × (1 - Percentage Decline ÷ 100)

operands.metric: Exponential Moving Average of the Previous Twelve Periods' Closing Prices

formulas.source_formula: Stock Price in a Downtrend = (2 × Closing Price + High Price + Low Price) ÷ 4 - Exponential Moving Average of the Previous Twelve Periods' Closing Prices

nodes.name: Stock Price on Dividend Distribution Right Transfer Date
aliases: 股利分配权转移日股价
nodes.definition: The stock price on the dividend distribution right transfer date refers to the opening reference price or market trading price of a stock on the first trading day following the record date (i.e., the ex-dividend date) when a listed company distributes dividends. On this day, the stock's trading price is adjusted for the ex-dividend effect to reflect changes in the company's value after the dividend distribution. This price is fundamental data obtained directly from real-time stock market trading and cannot be calculated using other financial indicator formulas.

nodes.name: Stock Purchase Expenditure
nodes.definition: Stock purchase expenditure refers to the total cost of stocks required to establish a hedging portfolio.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Purchase Expenditure = Hedge Ratio × Current Stock Price

nodes.name: Stock Purchase Price
nodes.definition: Stock purchase price refers to the total amount actually paid by an investor to acquire a specific stock in the securities market, typically calculated as the price per share multiplied by the number of shares purchased. It serves as the base cost for calculating investment profit or loss, capital gains tax, and investment returns (such as dividend yield).

formulas.source_formula: Stock Ratio = Advancing Stocks ÷ Declining Stocks

nodes.name: Stock Real Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The stock real rate of return refers to the true rate of return investors obtain from holding stocks after removing the effects of inflation, reflecting the actual growth level of the purchasing power of invested capital.

nodes.name: Stock Repurchase
nodes.definition: Stock repurchase refers to the action of a listed company using its own cash or other means to buy back a certain number of its own shares that have been issued and are outstanding in the open market. The repurchased shares are typically cancelled or held as treasury stock, thereby reducing the number of shares outstanding.

nodes.name: Stock Repurchase Date
nodes.definition: Stock repurchase date refers to the specific date on which a listed company actually buys back its outstanding shares from the open market or specific channels. This is a point-in-time record of the actual execution of the repurchase transaction, classified as basic event data.

nodes.name: Stock Return Standard Deviation
nodes.definition: Stock return standard deviation is a statistical measure of the volatility or risk of an individual stock's returns. It calculates the dispersion of a stock's actual returns relative to its average return. A larger standard deviation indicates more volatile historical returns for the stock, typically implying higher risk; conversely, a smaller standard deviation suggests more stable returns and relatively lower risk.

nodes.name: Stock Selection Alpha
nodes.definition: Stock selection alpha is the portion of a portfolio's excess return (alpha) attributable to security selection decisions, excluding the effects of sector allocation and market timing. It is used in performance attribution to isolate the manager's skill in picking individual securities.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Selection Alpha = Total Alpha - Sector Contribution - Timing Contribution

nodes.name: Stock Split
nodes.definition: A stock split refers to a corporate action in which a publicly traded company divides its existing shares into multiple shares without changing the company's total market capitalization and shareholders' equity. For example, splitting one share into two shares doubles the number of outstanding shares while proportionally reducing the share price to maintain the same total market value. This action is typically intended to lower the per-share price, thereby enhancing the stock's liquidity and attractiveness.

nodes.name: Stock Split Ratio
nodes.definition: The stock split ratio refers to the proportional number of new shares into which one existing share is divided when a company conducts a stock split. For example, a 2-for-1 split has a ratio of 2. It is a parameter directly determined by the company's board of directors to adjust fundamental data such as the number of shares outstanding and the price per share.

nodes.name: Stock Upward Price
nodes.definition: Stock upward price refers to the projected future stock price based on optimistic scenarios (such as high growth, high profitability) under specific valuation models or option pricing frameworks. It is not a raw accounting figure but an expected value derived from financial models, commonly used in option pricing (e.g., binomial tree models) and investment decision analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Upward Price = Expected Dividend ÷ (Discount Rate - Perpetual Growth Rate)

operands.metric: Expected Net Asset Value Per Share

formulas.source_formula: Stock Upward Price = Expected Net Asset Value Per Share × Upward Scenario P/B Ratio
Stock Upward Price = Expected Earnings Per Share × Upward Scenario P/E Ratio

nodes.name: Stock Value
nodes.definition: Stock value refers to the present value sum of all future dividends discounted at the required rate of return by shareholders, reflecting the intrinsic value of a stock and serving as a crucial basis for investment decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Value = Price-to-Earnings Ratio × Earnings Per Share
Stock Value = Par Value + Net Asset Value + Liquidation Price + Issue Price + Market Price

operands.metric: Sum of Present Values of Dividends During Holding Period
Present Value of Estimated Selling Price

formulas.source_formula: Stock Value = Sum of Present Values of Dividends during Holding Period + Present Value of Expected Selling Price

operands.metric: Present Value of Dividends in High-Growth Phase
Present Value of Terminal Value in Stable-Growth Phase

formulas.source_formula: Stock Value = Present Value of Dividends in High-Growth Phase + Present Value of Terminal Value in Stable-Growth Phase
Stock Value at Sale = (Investment + Borrowed Funds) × Stock Appreciation

nodes.name: Stock Yield
nodes.definition: Stock yield is a financial metric that measures the return on stock investment, representing the proportion of income investors receive from dividend income and capital gains relative to the initial investment amount, usually expressed as a percentage. It can be calculated from historical data or used as a discount rate in valuation models.

formulas.source_formula: Stock Yield = Income Amount ÷ Original Investment Amount
Stock Yield = (Dividend + Selling Price - Purchase Price) ÷ Purchase Price

nodes.name: Stock-Market Correlation Coefficient
nodes.definition: The stock-market correlation coefficient is a statistical measure that quantifies the degree of linear relationship between a stock's returns and market returns, calculated using the covariance of stock returns and market returns along with their respective standard deviations.

operands.metric: Covariance of Stock Returns and Market Returns

formulas.source_formula: Stock-Market Correlation Coefficient = Covariance of Stock Returns and Market Returns ÷ (Standard Deviation of Stock Returns × Standard Deviation of Market Returns)

nodes.name: Stockout Cost
nodes.definition: Stockout cost refers to the cost incurred due to lost sales opportunities or customer dissatisfaction resulting from insufficient inventory.

nodes.name: Stockout Probability
nodes.definition: Stockout probability refers to the likelihood or risk that a company's inventory cannot immediately fulfill customer demand when requested during a specific period. It measures the degree of insufficient service level in the inventory system.

nodes.name: Stockout Quantity
nodes.definition: Stockout quantity refers to the volume of goods or raw materials that cannot be supplied to meet customer demand or orders within a specific period, due to actual inventory levels being insufficient.

formulas.source_formula: Stop-Loss = Breakout Price + (Triangle Height × Direction Factor)

nodes.name: Stop-Loss (Ascending Triangle)
nodes.definition: In the context of the ascending triangle chart pattern, the stop-loss level is a predefined price used to limit downside risk after a breakout. It is typically placed at a distance equal to the triangle's height from the breakout price, adjusted by the breakout direction: below the breakout for upside breaks and above the breakout for downside breaks.

formulas.source_formula: Stop-Loss (High Risk) = Cup Bottom
Stop-Loss (Low Risk) = Handle Bottom
Stop-Loss (Medium Risk) = (Cup Bottom + Handle Bottom) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Stop-Loss Exit Price
nodes.definition: The stop-loss exit price is the predefined price level at which a stop-loss order is triggered to automatically close a position, limiting potential losses. In spread betting, for a long position the stop-loss is set below the opening price by a specified number of points, while for a short position it is set above the opening price by the same number of points.

formulas.source_formula: Stop-Loss Exit Price = Opening Price - Position Direction × Stop-Loss Points

nodes.name: Storage Fixed Costs
nodes.definition: Storage fixed costs refer to the fixed expenditures incurred by an enterprise to maintain its warehousing capacity and basic operations over a specific period (typically one year), which do not vary with changes in inventory quantity or value. These expenditures form the foundational component of total storage costs and occur regardless of inventory levels.

nodes.name: Straddle
nodes.definition: A straddle is an options strategy that involves simultaneously buying a call and a put option with the same strike price and expiration date to profit from significant price movements in either direction. The break-even points are the underlying price levels at which the position's payoff equals the total premium paid for both options.

nodes.name: Straddle Breakeven Percentage Movement
aliases: Required Percentage Price Movement for Profit (Straddle)
跨式盈亏平衡所需百分比变动
跨式策略所需价格变动百分比
nodes.definition: Straddle breakeven percentage movement measures the percentage change in the underlying asset's price, up or down from the strike, required for a long straddle to reach breakeven and begin to be profitable. It is calculated as the total premium paid for the call and put divided by the strike price, expressed as a percentage, indicating the volatility hurdle implied by the position.

formulas.source_formula: Straddle Breakeven Percentage Movement = Total Premium ÷ Strike Price × 100

nodes.name: Straight Line Basis
nodes.definition: Straight-line basis is a depreciation method that allocates an asset’s depreciable cost evenly over its estimated useful life. The annual straight-line depreciation expense equals the asset’s cost minus its salvage value, divided by the number of years of useful life.

nodes.name: Straight-Line Amortization
aliases: 债券溢价/折价摊销（直线法）
nodes.definition: Straight-line amortization allocates an amortizable amount (such as a bond premium or discount) evenly across each accounting or interest period, producing a constant amortization expense per period. It simplifies recognition of the premium/discount over the instrument’s life and is commonly used when the difference from the effective interest method is immaterial.

formulas.source_formula: Straight-Line Amortization per Period = Amortizable Amount ÷ Number of Periods

nodes.name: Straight-Line Depreciation
nodes.definition: Straight-line depreciation is a method of allocating the cost of a tangible fixed asset evenly over its useful life, resulting in equal depreciation expense each period.

nodes.name: Straight-Line Depreciation (GDS)
nodes.definition: Straight-line depreciation under the U.S. MACRS General Depreciation System (GDS) allocates an asset’s depreciable base evenly across its useful life, producing a constant annual depreciation expense. The depreciable base equals the asset’s initial cost minus its salvage (residual) value.

nodes.name: Straight-Line Depreciation Expense
nodes.definition: Straight-line depreciation expense is a non-cash charge that allocates an asset's depreciable base (initial cost minus salvage value) evenly over its estimated useful life, recognizing a consistent annual expense in the income statement.

formulas.source_formula: Straight-Line Depreciation Expense = (Initial Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life
Straight-Line Depreciation Expense = (Initial Cost - Salvage Value) ÷ Useful Life (Years)

nodes.name: Strangle
nodes.definition: A strangle is an options strategy involving the simultaneous purchase or sale of a call option and a put option on the same underlying asset and expiration date but with different strike prices. In a long strangle, the trader buys both options, profiting from significant price moves in either direction; the strategy’s breakeven points are determined by offsetting the total premium paid against the respective strike prices.

formulas.source_formula: Stratum Sample Size = Total Sample Size × (Stratum Population ÷ Total Population)

nodes.name: Strike Price
nodes.definition: In finance, the strike price (or exercise price) of an option refers to the fixed price at which the option holder can buy (for a call option) or sell (for a put option) the underlying security or commodity. The strike price is a key variable in derivative contracts, determining the degree of in-the-money status and the payoff at option expiration.

nodes.name: Structure Loss Value
nodes.definition: Structure loss value refers to the direct property loss amount caused by the destruction, damage, smoke contamination, water damage, or demolition of independent buildings or structures such as houses, bridges, and chimneys due to unexpected events like fires or accidents. This value is typically calculated based on factors such as replacement value, degree of depreciation, and burn damage rate, and is a crucial component in assessing actual losses.

nodes.name: Student Loan
nodes.definition: A student loan is a type of loan designed to help students pay for higher education and related expenses, such as tuition, books and supplies, and living costs. These loans typically feature lower interest rates, offer deferred repayment arrangements during the borrower's period of study, and repayments are often linked to post-graduation income levels.

formulas.source_formula: Student Loan = Tuition + Books and Supplies + Living Expenses

nodes.name: Student Loan Interest Deduction
aliases: 可税前扣除的助学贷款利息
nodes.definition: The student loan interest deduction is a U.S. individual income tax deduction that allows eligible taxpayers to deduct up to $2,500 of qualified student loan interest paid during the tax year. The allowable deduction is the lesser of the statutory cap or interest paid and is subject to a modified adjusted gross income (MAGI) phase-out that varies by filing status and tax year; taxpayers filing as married filing separately are ineligible.

nodes.name: Subinterval Count
nodes.definition: Subinterval count refers to the total number of data points whose values fall within a specific numerical range in a given dataset. For example, when analyzing a set of product prices, the number of products priced between 100 and 200 yuan is the subinterval count for that price range.

nodes.name: Subinterval Node
nodes.definition: A subinterval node refers to the key points or boundary points used to partition a large time interval or numerical interval (such as a return calculation period) into several smaller subintervals. For example, when calculating fund returns, the entire calculation period can be divided into multiple subintervals based on the timing of cash flows, where the start and end points of each subinterval are the subinterval nodes.

nodes.name: Submitted Interest Rate Estimate
nodes.definition: Submitted interest rate estimate refers to the proposed expected interest rate level that financial institutions (such as banks) submit to the market or regulatory authorities when issuing bonds, setting loan interest rates, or designing financial products, based on factors such as current market conditions, credit risk, and funding costs. It serves as a preliminary proposal in the pricing process, providing a reference for the final determination of the actual interest rate.

nodes.name: Subscribed Capital
nodes.definition: Subscribed capital refers to the total amount of capital that investors have committed to purchase shares from the company and pay the corresponding consideration. It forms the basis of the company's paid-in capital or share capital and is typically recorded directly in the accounting books.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Capital Reserve
nodes.definition: Subsidiary capital reserve refers to the equity item formed by investors' contributions exceeding the registered capital portion during business combinations or capital changes, or through adjustments of retained earnings, reflecting capital contributions beyond the legal capital.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Current Period Income Tax Expense
aliases: 子公司当期所得税费用
nodes.definition: Subsidiary current period income tax expense refers to the amount of income tax calculated in accordance with tax laws, recognized in the subsidiary's current period income statement as an independent legal entity, and payable. It reflects the income tax liability arising from the subsidiary's current operating activities.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Current Period Surplus Reserve Appropriation
Subsidiary Debt-to-Asset Ratio
nodes.definition: The subsidiary debt-to-asset ratio is a key metric for measuring a subsidiary's financial leverage and long-term solvency, indicating the proportion of the subsidiary's total assets financed by creditors. It is calculated by dividing the subsidiary's total liabilities by its total assets.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Debt-to-Asset Ratio = Subsidiary Total Liabilities ÷ Subsidiary Total Assets

nodes.name: Subsidiary Discretionary Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Subsidiary Discretionary Surplus Reserve refers to the retained earnings that a subsidiary voluntarily appropriates from its after-tax net profit at a self-determined percentage, after setting aside the statutory surplus reserve, based on its actual operational development needs or prudent management strategies.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Earnings
nodes.definition: Subsidiary earnings refer to the final financial results generated by a subsidiary, which is owned or controlled by a parent company, through its operating activities during a specific accounting period, typically represented as net profit. It is a core indicator for measuring the independent operating performance of a subsidiary and serves as the basis for calculating consolidated group financial statements and net profit attributable to the parent company.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Net Profit
nodes.definition: Subsidiary net profit refers to the final operating result generated by a company (subsidiary) from its business activities during a specific accounting period, which is the net amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes from revenue. It is the core data on the subsidiary's individual income statement and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating consolidated indicators such as net profit attributable to the parent company when preparing consolidated financial statements.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Current Year
aliases: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Year
nodes.definition: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Current Year refers to the final operating results generated by a subsidiary through its operating activities, investment activities, and other activities within a complete fiscal year. It serves as a fundamental component for calculating the net profit attributable to the parent company.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Current Year = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense
Subsidiary Net Profit for the Current Year = Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses - Income Tax Expense

operands.metric: Net Gains from Changes in Fair Value

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Current Year = Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Business Taxes and Surcharges - Period Expenses + Net Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Net Investment Income + Other Income - Income Tax Expense

nodes.name: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Period
nodes.definition: Subsidiary Net Profit for the Period refers to the final operating result generated by a subsidiary through its independent business activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year), which is the net amount after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes from revenue. It is the final result on the subsidiary's income statement and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating consolidated indicators such as the parent company's net profit and net profit attributable to the parent company's shareholders.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Owners' Equity
nodes.definition: Subsidiary owners' equity refers to the residual interest in the assets of a subsidiary after deducting its liabilities, which belongs to the owners of the subsidiary (including the parent company and minority shareholders). It follows the fundamental calculation logic of owners' equity and serves as the basis for calculating the value of minority interest.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Owners' Equity = Total Assets of Subsidiary - Total Liabilities of Subsidiary
Subsidiary Owners' Equity = Subsidiary Paid-in Capital + Subsidiary Capital Reserve + Subsidiary Surplus Reserve + Subsidiary Retained Earnings

nodes.name: Subsidiary Paid-in Capital
nodes.definition: Subsidiary paid-in capital refers to the total capital actually received by a subsidiary from its shareholders (the parent company and/or other external investors) as investment contributions. As an investee entity, its paid-in capital is one of the core components constituting its shareholders' equity, reflecting the actual capital investment made by shareholders into the subsidiary.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Paid-in Capital = Subscribed Share Capital + Capital Reserve + Surplus Reserve + Other Capital Reserves - Repaid Share Capital

nodes.name: Subsidiary Statutory Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Subsidiary statutory surplus reserve refers to the retained earnings with specific purposes, which are appropriated by a subsidiary from its current-year after-tax net profit at a statutory rate (typically 10%) in accordance with the Company Law, and constitute part of owners' equity.

nodes.name: Subsidiary Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Subsidiary surplus reserve refers to the accumulated earnings retained within a subsidiary company, derived from its after-tax profits and designated for specific purposes. It includes statutory surplus reserve and discretionary surplus reserve, used to strengthen the company's financial position, cover losses, or expand business operations.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Surplus Reserve = Subsidiary Statutory Surplus Reserve + Subsidiary Discretionary Surplus Reserve
Subsidiary Surplus Reserve = Subsidiary Current Year Net Profit × 10% + Subsidiary Current Year Net Profit × Discretionary Surplus Reserve Withdrawal Ratio

nodes.name: Subsidiary Undistributed Profit
aliases: 子公司未分配利润余额
nodes.definition: Subsidiary undistributed profit refers to the cumulative net profit balance retained by a subsidiary after calculating post-tax profit, deducting surplus reserve appropriations and dividend distributions during a specific accounting period. It reflects the portion of profit not yet distributed to shareholders and constitutes a significant component of the subsidiary's total shareholders' equity, requiring corresponding adjustments in consolidated financial statements.

operands.metric: Subsidiary Current Period Surplus Reserve Appropriation

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Undistributed Profit = Subsidiary Beginning Undistributed Profit + Subsidiary Current Period Net Profit - Subsidiary Current Period Surplus Reserve Appropriation - Subsidiary Current Period Dividend Distribution

operands.metric: Subsidiary Current Period Income Tax Expense
Subsidiary Current Period Surplus Reserve Appropriation

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary Undistributed Profit = Subsidiary Beginning Undistributed Profit + (Subsidiary Current Period Total Profit - Subsidiary Current Period Income Tax Expense) - Subsidiary Current Period Surplus Reserve Appropriation - Subsidiary Current Period Dividend Distribution

nodes.name: Subsidiary's Current Period Appropriation to Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Subsidiary's Current Period Appropriation to Surplus Reserve refers to the amount transferred from after-tax profits to the surplus reserve by a subsidiary, based on its net profit for the current period and according to statutory or articles of association stipulated ratios. This indicator is a key component in calculating changes in the subsidiary's undistributed profits, reflecting the company's internal profit retention and capital accumulation.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary's Current Period Appropriation to Surplus Reserve = Subsidiary's Current Year Net Profit × Discretionary Surplus Reserve Appropriation Ratio

operands.metric: Uncovered Loss at Beginning of Year

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary's Current Period Appropriation to Surplus Reserve = (Subsidiary's Current Year Net Profit - Uncovered Loss at Beginning of Year) × Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriation Ratio

nodes.name: Subsidiary's Current Period Dividend Distribution
nodes.definition: Subsidiary's current period dividend distribution refers to the specific action in which a subsidiary, during the current accounting period, decides to distribute cash dividends or stock dividends to its shareholders (including the parent company and other minority shareholders) according to the profit distribution plan approved by its board of directors or shareholders' meeting. This is an occurred economic transaction in the profit distribution process, directly affecting the subsidiary's retained earnings and liabilities (such as dividends payable).

nodes.name: Subsidiary's Opening Retained Earnings
aliases: 子公司年初未分配利润
子公司未分配利润年初数
nodes.definition: Subsidiary's opening retained earnings refers to the amount of retained earnings directly taken from the subsidiary's individual balance sheet at the end of the previous period when preparing consolidated financial statements. It represents the portion of the subsidiary's accumulated net profit that has not been distributed to shareholders (including the parent company and minority shareholders) at the close of the prior accounting period, and serves as the starting point data for calculating consolidated retained earnings when preparing the current period's consolidated statements.

nodes.name: Subsidiary's Total Profit for the Current Period
nodes.definition: Subsidiary's Total Profit for the Current Period refers to the total profit generated by a subsidiary from both operating and non-operating activities within a specific accounting period, before deducting income tax expenses. It is a key indicator for measuring the subsidiary's overall profitability and serves as the basis for calculating the subsidiary's undistributed profit.

formulas.source_formula: Subsidiary's Total Profit for the Current Period = Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses

nodes.name: Subsidy
nodes.definition: A subsidy refers to funds or benefits directly provided by the government or relevant institutions to support specific industries, enterprises, projects, or individuals, typically without requiring repayment. In accounting treatment, it is often recognized as non-operating income or recorded under specific grant items, serving as a fundamental data point in financial statements.

nodes.name: Subsidy Income
nodes.definition: Subsidy income refers to monetary or non-monetary assets received gratuitously by an enterprise from the government or other institutions, intended to compensate for incurred expenses or losses, or to encourage specific activities.

nodes.name: Substantially Equal Periodic Payment (SEPP)
nodes.definition: Substantially Equal Periodic Payment (SEPP) is a strategy permitted under IRS Rule 72(t) that allows penalty-free early distributions from qualified retirement accounts when withdrawals are structured as substantially equal periodic payments. Under the annuitization method, the annual withdrawal is determined by dividing the retirement account balance by an annuity factor derived from IRS mortality tables, producing fixed annual payments intended to last over the participant’s life expectancy.

nodes.name: Substitute Price
nodes.definition: Substitute price refers to the price of other goods or services in the market that can satisfy similar consumer needs or functions. It is one of the important factors affecting the demand for a specific product.

nodes.name: Subtotal of Cash Inflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period
Subtotal of Cash Outflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period
Subtotal of Cash Outflows from Investing Activities in the Next Period
aliases: Next Period Investing Activities Cash Outflows
Total Cash Outflows from Investing Activities for the Next Period
下期投资活动现金流出合计
下期投资现金流出总额
未来期间投资现金流出小计
nodes.definition: Subtotal of cash outflows from investing activities in the next period refers to the sum of all cash payment items related to investing activities that an enterprise expects to make during a specific future accounting period (such as the next quarter or the next fiscal year). It reflects the total amount of cash the enterprise plans to pay for acquiring long-term assets, making equity or debt investments, and similar activities in the upcoming period.

nodes.name: Sum Insured
nodes.definition: The sum insured is the maximum limit of compensation or benefit payment that the insurance company is liable for, as stipulated in the insurance contract. It serves as the basis for calculating insurance premiums and as the reference for determining the maximum payout limit during claims settlement.

nodes.name: Sum of Actual (Standard, Machine) Hours for All Products
nodes.definition: The sum of actual (standard, machine) hours for all products refers to the total of actual hours, standard hours, or machine hours across all products, used for cost allocation and efficiency analysis, typically aggregated from basic hour data through summation formulas.

nodes.name: Sum of Actual (Standard, Machine) Working Hours for Each Product
Sum of Actual Working Hours for Each Product
Sum of All Data
nodes.definition: Sum of all data refers to the total obtained by adding together all values in a dataset. In accounting and finance, it is commonly used to calculate aggregate amounts for items such as revenue, costs, assets, and liabilities, serving as a fundamental operation for financial analysis and statement preparation.

nodes.name: Sum of All Observations in the Sample
nodes.definition: The sum of all observations in a sample refers to the total obtained by adding all individual observations (data points) from a sample drawn from a population. It serves as the basis for calculating statistical measures such as the sample mean.

nodes.name: Sum of Allocation Bases for All Cost Objects
Sum of Closing Prices over N Periods
Sum of Component Stock Prices
nodes.definition: The sum of component stock prices refers to the simple arithmetic total of the market trading prices (typically closing prices) of all constituent stocks included in a specific stock index or investment portfolio at a given point in time. It serves as the core underlying data for calculating price-weighted stock market indices (such as the Dow Jones Industrial Average) and is classified as a composite indicator.

formulas.source_formula: Sum of Component Stock Prices = Price-Weighted Index × Dow Jones Divisor

nodes.name: Sum of Constituent Stock Prices
nodes.definition: The sum of constituent stock prices refers to the total obtained by directly adding the real-time market prices of all constituent stocks included in a specific stock index (such as the SSE 50, CSI 300, etc.) at a given point in time. It serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating the value of a stock index.

nodes.name: Sum of Data Points
nodes.definition: The sum of data points is a composite metric calculated by summing multiple individual data points. In financial management and analysis, it is used to aggregate data as a basis for calculating central points (such as the average), rather than being a raw, fundamental data item in financial statements.

nodes.name: Sum of Data Points in Window
Sum of Material Quota Sales (or Quota Costs) for Various Products
aliases: Sum of Material Standard Cost for Various Products
产品材料定额销量总和
nodes.definition: The sum of material quota sales (or quota costs) for various products refers to the total material quota cost calculated based on the output of all products, material consumption quotas, and material unit prices. It is commonly used in cost accounting as a basis for allocating common material costs or calculating allocation rates.

nodes.name: Sum of Present Value of Future Period Cash Flows
aliases: Sum of Present Value of Future Cash Flows
Total Present Value of Subsequent Cash Flows
未来现金流量现值总和
资产未来现金流量现值总和
nodes.definition: The sum of the present value of future period cash flows refers to the cumulative value of projected future cash flows from assets in each future period, discounted to the present point in time using a discount rate. It is a composite metric used for asset valuation, investment decision-making, and financial valuation.

nodes.name: Sum of Present Values of Continuing Cash Flows
Sum of Present Values of Dividends During Holding Period
aliases: Present Value of Dividends over Holding Period
nodes.definition: The sum of present values of dividends during the holding period refers to the total value of all expected dividends received during the stock holding period, discounted back to the present point in time using a discount rate. It is a core component of the Dividend Discount Model (DDM) used to assess a stock's intrinsic value. This is a composite metric calculated based on fundamental data (such as periodic dividends and discount rate) through the present value summation formula.

nodes.name: Sum of Present Values of Future Periodic Payments
Sum of Present Values of Periodic Interest Payments
Sum of Squares
nodes.definition: Sum of squares is the aggregate of squared deviations of observations from their arithmetic mean, measuring the total dispersion of a dataset. In finance and accounting analytics, it underpins the calculation of variance and standard deviation, supports ANOVA and regression diagnostics (e.g., R-squared), and is used to quantify volatility and estimation error.

nodes.name: Sum of the Years' Digits
aliases: 使用年数逐年数字之和
nodes.definition: The sum of the years' digits is the cumulative total of the digits representing each year of an asset's estimated useful life. It is a composite value used as the denominator for calculating the depreciation rate under the sum-of-the-years'-digits accelerated depreciation method.

formulas.source_formula: Sum of the Years' Digits = Useful Life × (Useful Life + 1) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Sum of the Years' Digits of Estimated Useful Life
Sum-of-the-Parts Valuation
nodes.definition: Sum-of-the-Parts (SOTP) valuation is a methodology that estimates a company's total value by summing the standalone values of its individual business segments and then adjusting for corporate-level items, including net debt, non-operating liabilities, and non-operating assets. It is commonly used for conglomerates and diversified companies with distinct business units.

nodes.name: Sum-of-the-Years'-Digits Depreciation Expense
nodes.definition: Sum-of-the-Years'-Digits (SYD) depreciation is an accelerated depreciation method that allocates a higher portion of the asset's depreciable base to earlier periods. For a given year, the depreciation expense equals the depreciable base multiplied by the remaining life divided by the sum of the years' digits. This implementation assumes no salvage value, making the initial value equal to the depreciable base.

formulas.source_formula: Sum-of-the-Years'-Digits Depreciation Expense = Initial Value × Remaining Life ÷ Sum of Years' Digits

nodes.name: Sundry Surcharges
nodes.definition: Sundry surcharges refer to additional fees levied beyond principal charges (such as freight or payment for goods) based on specific conditions, regulations, or services. These fees are typically applied to cover extra expenses arising from fuel costs, port operations, exchange rate fluctuations, specific services, etc.

nodes.name: Supplementary Leverage Ratio
nodes.definition: The Supplementary Leverage Ratio (SLR) is a bank capital adequacy regulatory metric introduced under Basel III, used to measure the ratio of a bank's Tier 1 capital to its total leverage exposure, with the aim of limiting excessive leverage.

formulas.source_formula: Supplementary Leverage Ratio = Tier 1 Capital / Total Leverage Exposure

nodes.name: Supply
nodes.definition: Supply (quantity supplied) is the quantity of a good or service that producers are willing and able to offer for sale at a given price over a given period, ceteris paribus. In a linear representation, supply equals a base quantity plus a responsiveness coefficient multiplied by the price per unit.

formulas.source_formula: Supply = Units Supplied + Market Activity × Price per Unit

nodes.name: Supply Function
nodes.definition: The supply function is a mathematical model describing the functional relationship between the quantity supplied of a good and various factors affecting it (such as commodity price, production costs, technological level, prices of related goods, producer expectations, etc.). In simplified analysis, it is typically assumed that other factors remain constant, focusing only on the relationship between supply quantity and the good's own price.

formulas.source_formula: Supply Price per Unit = Supply Price ÷ Quantity Supplied

nodes.name: Support (Support Level)
nodes.definition: Support level is a technical analysis price level at which buying interest is strong enough to halt or reverse a decline, often identified by recent or historical lows within a specified period.

nodes.name: Support and Resistance Levels
nodes.definition: Support and resistance levels are technical analysis thresholds derived from historical price data over a defined rolling period: the support level is the lowest price within the period, and the resistance level is the highest price. Traders use these levels to identify potential entry and exit points, gauge trend strength, and set risk controls such as stop-loss and take-profit orders.

nodes.name: Support and Resistance Touch Count
nodes.definition: Support and resistance refer to price levels where buying or selling pressure tends to slow, halt, or reverse price movements. The touch count quantifies how many observations fall within a tolerance band around a specified level, counting observations at or below the upper tolerance bound as support touches and observations at or above the lower tolerance bound as resistance touches.

nodes.name: Surcharge
nodes.definition: Surcharge is an additional fee added to the base price of a good or service. It may be assessed as a fixed amount or as a percentage of the base price and is commonly used for payment processing fees, fuel surcharges, taxes, or regulatory assessments in pricing and billing.

nodes.name: Surcharge Fee
nodes.definition: A surcharge fee is an additional amount charged by a merchant to customers for using debit or credit cards, typically expressed as a percentage of the transaction amount. It is intended to offset all or part of the Merchant Discount Rate (MDR) and other card acceptance costs.

formulas.source_formula: Surcharge Fee = Transaction Amount × (Surcharge Percentage ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Surcharge Taxes
nodes.definition: Surcharge taxes are additional levies calculated based on the actual amount of turnover taxes paid by taxpayers, such as Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax, at specified rates. They are primarily used to fund specific public expenditures like urban maintenance and construction, and educational development.

formulas.source_formula: Surcharge Taxes = (Value-Added Tax + Consumption Tax) × Applicable Tax Rate

nodes.name: Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Surplus reserve refers to the accumulated funds that an enterprise sets aside from its after-tax profits in accordance with regulations, primarily used to cover losses, expand production and operations, or convert into capital. Among these, the statutory surplus reserve is the portion that must be allocated as required by law.

formulas.source_formula: Surplus Reserve = Statutory Surplus Reserve + Discretionary Surplus Reserve
Surplus Reserve = Current Year Net Profit × Statutory Ratio + Current Year Net Profit × Discretionary Allocation Ratio

nodes.name: Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period
aliases: Current Period Appropriation to Surplus Reserve
nodes.definition: Surplus reserve appropriated in the current period refers to the amount set aside from the net profit realized in the current accounting period according to relevant laws, regulations, or the company's articles of association, and transferred to the surplus reserve account at a specified ratio. It is a crucial step in the profit distribution process and directly affects the amount of retained earnings at the period end.

formulas.source_formula: Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period = Net Profit for Current Period × Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriation Ratio
Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period = Statutory Surplus Reserve Appropriation Amount + Discretionary Surplus Reserve Appropriation Amount
Surplus Reserve Appropriated in Current Period = Net Profit for Current Period × Discretionary Surplus Reserve Appropriation Ratio

nodes.name: Surplus Reserve Transferred Out or Used in Current Period
Surplus Reserve at End of First Quarter
aliases: Surplus Reserve at the End of Q1
nodes.definition: Surplus reserve at the end of the first quarter refers to the portion of retained earnings that a company has appropriated and accumulated from its after-tax profits for specific purposes, as of the financial reporting date of the first quarter (typically January 1 to March 31). It reflects the internal fund accumulation reserved by the enterprise for future development, loss coverage, or capital conversion up to the end of the first quarter.

nodes.name: Surplus Reserve at End of Q2
aliases: 第二季度盈余公积余额
nodes.definition: Surplus reserve at the end of the second quarter refers to the portion of retained earnings accumulated by an enterprise from its after-tax net profit in accordance with national regulations at the close of the second fiscal quarter (typically April 1 to June 30), designated for specific purposes such as covering losses or converting into capital.

nodes.name: Surplus Reserve at the End of the First Quarter

formulas.source_formula: Surrender Charges = Cash Value × Surrender Charge Rate

nodes.name: Surtax
aliases: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax and Education Surcharge
城市维护建设税及教育费附加
nodes.definition: Surtax is a type of tax levied based on the actual amount of Value-Added Tax and Consumption Tax paid by the taxpayer, calculated according to a prescribed tax rate. It is a component in calculating the total cash outflow or cash outflow of an enterprise.

formulas.source_formula: Surtax = (Value-Added Tax + Consumption Tax) × Applicable Tax Rate

nodes.name: Surtax Rate
nodes.definition: The surtax rate refers to the tax rate applied by local governments when levying additional taxes on top of major tax categories (such as Value-Added Tax or Consumption Tax). It is not a single rate, but rather a collective term or aggregate for the specific rates of various surcharges and fees, including Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, Education Surcharge, and Local Education Surcharge. Its specific value is determined by local governments and varies depending on the region (e.g., urban areas, county towns).

nodes.name: Survey and Design Fee
nodes.definition: Survey and Design Fee refers to the payment made to survey and design units for engineering survey and design work required to complete a project during the construction process. It is an important component of other construction costs, typically calculated according to national or industry-published fee standards (such as the 'Engineering Survey and Design Fee Standards').

nodes.name: Surveying and Mapping Fee
nodes.definition: Surveying and mapping fee refers to the payment made to professional surveying institutions or personnel for conducting on-site measurements, mapping, calculations, and producing relevant result reports for land, real estate, engineering projects, etc.

nodes.name: Sustainable Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Sustainable Growth Rate refers to the maximum growth rate in sales that a company can achieve without issuing new shares or repurchasing stock, while maintaining its current operating efficiency (net profit margin and asset turnover) and financial policies (capital structure and earnings retention ratio).

formulas.source_formula: Sustainable Growth Rate = Shareholders' Equity Growth Rate
Sustainable Growth Rate = Retention Ratio × Return on Equity
Sustainable Growth Rate = Retention Ratio × Net Profit Margin × (1 + Debt/Equity) ÷ [Assets/Sales - Retention Ratio × Net Profit Margin × (1 + Debt/Equity)]
Sustainable Growth Rate = Retention Ratio × (Net Income/Sales) × (Assets/Equity) × (Sales/Assets) ÷ [1 - Retention Ratio × (Net Income/Sales) × (Assets/Equity) × (Sales/Assets)]

nodes.name: Swap
nodes.definition: An interest rate swap is a derivative contract in which counterparties exchange fixed and floating interest payments on a specified notional principal without exchanging the principal itself. Periodic gain or loss equals the notional principal multiplied by the difference between the floating rate (here modeled as the SOFR change plus a spread in basis points) and the fixed rate, with total results over the swap term obtained by summing the annual outcomes for each party.

nodes.name: Sweat Equity
nodes.definition: Sweat equity refers to the portion of owners' equity created through founders' or employees' labor, expertise, and operational improvements rather than cash contributions. In a valuation context, it can be approximated as the retained value of the business attributable to effort, net of the initial cash investment.

formulas.source_formula: Sweat Equity = (Selling Price - Purchase Price) - Renovation Expenses
Sweat Equity = Current Valuation × (1 − Ownership Percentage Sold to Investor) − Initial Investment

nodes.name: Symmetrical Distribution
nodes.definition: A symmetrical distribution is a data distribution in which the measures of central tendency—mean, median, and mode—coincide, indicating balanced dispersion around the center with minimal skewness. In financial and accounting analytics, symmetry supports assumptions behind parametric models (e.g., normality), improves comparability across periods, and aids in risk assessment, valuation, and performance analysis by reducing distortions from skewed data.

nodes.name: Synthetic Put Breakeven Price
aliases: Breakeven of Short Stock + Long Call
nodes.definition: Synthetic put breakeven price is the stock price at which a position composed of a short stock and a long call option (a long synthetic put) yields zero profit and zero loss, excluding transaction costs.

nodes.name: Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) - Future Value
nodes.definition: The future value of a Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) represents the accumulated value of equal periodic payments invested at a constant periodic rate of return, assuming payments occur at the end of each period (ordinary annuity). It quantifies the time value of money effect on regular contributions and is widely used in personal finance and investment planning.

formulas.source_formula: Future Value of SIP = Periodic Payment × ( ((1 + Periodic Rate of Return) ^ Number of Periods - 1) ÷ Periodic Rate of Return )

nodes.name: Systematic Risk
nodes.definition: Systematic risk refers to the risk affecting all assets caused by overall economic or market factors, which cannot be eliminated through portfolio diversification. It is typically quantified using metrics such as the beta coefficient and involves multiple elements including policy, macroeconomic, and liquidity factors.

operands.metric: Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Returns

formulas.source_formula: Systematic Risk = Beta Coefficient × Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Return

operands.metric: Covariance of Asset Returns and Market Returns
Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Returns

formulas.source_formula: Systematic Risk = Covariance of Asset Return and Market Return ÷ Variance of Market Portfolio Return × Standard Deviation of Market Portfolio Return

nodes.name: Systematic Risk Coefficient
nodes.definition: The systematic risk coefficient (Beta coefficient) measures the volatility of a single asset's or portfolio's returns relative to the overall market returns, quantifying the systematic risk that cannot be eliminated through diversification. In the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), it is a key parameter for calculating the required rate of return.

nodes.name: Systematic Risk Premium
nodes.definition: Systematic risk premium refers to the additional return required by investors for bearing systematic risk that cannot be diversified away through portfolio construction (such as economic recessions, interest rate changes, wars, and other risks affecting the entire market). It is a core concept in asset pricing models, used to measure the impact of overall market risk on the expected return of assets.

nodes.name: T+1 (T+2, T+3)
nodes.definition: T+X settlement is a market convention whereby a trade settles X business days after the transaction (trade) date, excluding weekends and designated market holidays. Common cycles include T+1, T+2, and T+3, indicating settlement one, two, or three business days after the trade date. The convention standardizes post-trade processing timelines and affects cash, securities delivery, and operational risk.

nodes.name: T-Bill Discount Price
nodes.definition: The T-bill discount price is the present purchase price of a Treasury bill issued at a discount to par, computed by prorating the simple annual yield over a 52-week year for the bill’s maturity and discounting the face value accordingly. It represents the upfront cash outlay required to achieve the specified yield over the T-bill’s term.

formulas.source_formula: T-Bill Discount Price = Face Value ÷ (1 + (Annual Yield ÷ 52 × Maturity Weeks))
Discounted Purchase Price = Purchase Price × (1 - Discount)

nodes.name: T-Bill Effective Yield
nodes.definition: T-Bill effective yield is the annualized holding period return earned by purchasing a Treasury bill at a discount and holding it to maturity. It is calculated using simple interest based on the difference between face value and purchase price, scaled to a 52-week year to reflect the time to maturity.

nodes.name: T-Bill Interest Earned
