nodes.definition: Interest earned from a Treasury bill is the discount realized at maturity, calculated as the difference between the bill's face value and its purchase price. Because T-bills are zero-coupon securities, they do not pay periodic interest; the investor's return is recognized upon redemption at par when held to maturity.

formulas.source_formula: T-Bill Interest Earned = Face Value - Purchase Price

nodes.name: T-Test
nodes.definition: An equal variance independent samples t-test is a hypothesis test that evaluates whether the means of two populations are statistically different, assuming homoscedasticity (equal variances). In financial analytics, it is used to compare average returns, risk-adjusted performance, or other metrics between two strategies, portfolios, or periods.

nodes.name: T-Test (Welch, Unequal Variance)
aliases: Welch 不等方差 t 检验
nodes.definition: Welch's t-test is a two-sample hypothesis test that evaluates whether the means of two independent groups differ when variances and sample sizes may be unequal. In financial analysis, it is commonly used to test differences in average returns, risk metrics, or performance measures across portfolios or time periods without assuming equal variances.

nodes.name: TED Spread
nodes.definition: The TED spread is the difference between the three-month LIBOR and the three-month U.S. Treasury bill yield. It serves as a market-based indicator of perceived credit risk in the banking system and funding stress, widening when interbank lending risk increases and narrowing when conditions stabilize.

formulas.source_formula: TED Spread = 3-Month LIBOR Rate - 3-Month U.S. Treasury Bill Rate

nodes.name: TFSA Contribution Room
aliases: 免税储蓄账户供款额度
免税储蓄账户可供款额度
nodes.definition: TFSA Contribution Room refers to the maximum amount an individual can contribute to a Tax-Free Savings Account in the current year. It is determined by the cumulative TFSA limits established by the Canadian government, reduced by prior contributions and increased by withdrawals from the previous year, reflecting the available capacity to contribute without incurring penalties.

formulas.source_formula: TFSA Contribution Room = (Total Annual Contribution Limits - Total TFSA Contributions) + Previous-Year TFSA Withdrawals + Current-Year Annual Contribution Limit

nodes.name: TIPS Adjusted Principal
aliases: 通货膨胀保值债券调整后本金
nodes.definition: TIPS adjusted principal is the inflation-indexed principal value of a Treasury Inflation-Protected Security, which increases with inflation and decreases with deflation as measured by the CPI. The adjusted principal determines coupon payments and the redemption amount, protecting investors' purchasing power.

formulas.source_formula: TIPS Adjusted Principal = Original Principal × (1 + Inflation Rate)
TTM P/E Ratio = Current Stock Price ÷ Earnings per Share (TTM)

nodes.name: Take-Home Hourly Rate
nodes.definition: Take-home hourly rate is the net pay received per hour after all payroll deductions (such as income tax, social security contributions, and benefit withholdings). It is calculated by dividing net pay by the total hours worked in the pay period and is useful for comparing net compensation to gross hourly wages.

formulas.source_formula: Take-Home Hourly Rate = Net Pay ÷ Hours Worked

nodes.name: Take-Home Pay
nodes.definition: Take-home pay is the net amount an employee receives after all payroll withholdings—such as income taxes, Social Security/Medicare contributions, retirement plan contributions, insurance premiums, and other deductions—are subtracted from gross pay. It reflects the actual cash available to the employee from a pay period.

formulas.source_formula: Take-Home Pay = Gross Pay - Deductions

nodes.name: Take-or-Pay Penalty Fee
nodes.definition: Take-or-pay penalty fee is the amount payable under a take-or-pay provision when the buyer fails to purchase the minimum contractual quantity, typically calculated as the shortfall quantity multiplied by the contract price and the agreed penalty rate.

nodes.name: Tangible Book Value Per Share
aliases: Tangible Net Asset Value Per Share
Tangible Net Book Value per Share
nodes.definition: Tangible Book Value Per Share represents the amount of a company's tangible net assets attributable to each share outstanding, excluding intangible assets such as goodwill and patents. It is used to assess the per-share value backed by physical and financial assets on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Tangible Book Value Per Share = (Total Equity - Preferred Stock - Intangible Assets) ÷ Total Shares Outstanding
Tangible Book Value Per Share = Total Tangible Net Assets ÷ Shares Outstanding
supporting_source_formulas: Tangible Book Value Per Share = Total Tangible Net Assets ÷ Shares Outstanding
Tangible Book Value per Share = Total Tangible Net Assets ÷ Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Tangible Common Equity
nodes.definition: Tangible Common Equity (TCE) represents the portion of equity attributable to common shareholders that is backed by tangible (non-intangible) assets. It is calculated by deducting goodwill, other intangible assets, and preferred equity from the company's book value. TCE is commonly used, especially in financial institutions, to assess loss-absorbing capacity and balance sheet quality.

formulas.source_formula: Tangible Common Equity = Book Value - (Goodwill + Intangible Assets + Preferred Equity)

nodes.name: Tangible Common Equity Ratio
aliases: Tangible Common Equity to Tangible Assets Ratio
Tangible Equity to Tangible Assets Ratio
有形普通股权益对有形资产比率
nodes.definition: The Tangible Common Equity Ratio measures a firm's core equity capital relative to its tangible assets. It is calculated as Tangible Common Equity divided by Tangible Assets and is commonly used in banking to assess capital adequacy and leverage, with higher ratios indicating stronger loss-absorbing capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Tangible Common Equity Ratio = Tangible Common Equity ÷ Tangible Assets

nodes.name: Tangible Net Worth
nodes.definition: Tangible net worth is the portion of net worth backed by physical, financial, and other non-intangible assets, calculated as total assets minus liabilities and intangible assets. It indicates the liquidation value available to creditors and is widely used in credit and solvency assessments.

formulas.source_formula: Tangible Net Worth = Total Assets - Liabilities - Intangible Assets

nodes.name: Tangible Personal Property Tax
nodes.definition: Tangible personal property tax is an ad valorem tax levied on the fair market value of movable, physical assets (excluding real property and intangible assets). The tax due is calculated by applying the applicable tax rate to the property's fair market value; exemptions, thresholds, or assessment adjustments may apply by jurisdiction.

nodes.name: Target
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, a 'target' typically refers to quantitative or qualitative indicators set by an enterprise or investor that are expected to be achieved within a specific future period. It can be a financial indicator (such as target profit, target cost) or a market indicator (such as price target), used to guide planning, budgeting, control, and performance evaluation.

nodes.name: Target Company Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Target Company Earnings Per Share refers to the ratio of the current net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders of the target company to the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding during the period. It is used to measure the profitability and investment value of ordinary shares and serves as a fundamental indicator for calculating the per-share value of the target company.

nodes.name: Target Company Net Asset Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Target Company Net Asset Value Per Share refers to the book value per share attributable to the parent company's common shareholders, reflecting the net asset share corresponding to each share of stock on the balance sheet date. It is a fundamental indicator for assessing a company's intrinsic value and liquidation value.

operands.metric: Shareholders' Equity Attributable to Parent Company Common Shareholders
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End

formulas.source_formula: Target Company Net Asset Value Per Share = Shareholders' Equity Attributable to Parent Company Common Shareholders ÷ Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End

nodes.name: Target Company Net Assets
nodes.definition: Target Company Net Assets refer to the residual equity attributable to the owners of the target company at a specific point in time, after deducting total liabilities from total assets. It is a fundamental financial metric for assessing enterprise value, calculating equity value, and conducting merger and acquisition valuations.

formulas.source_formula: Target Company Net Assets = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

nodes.name: Target Company Net Profit
nodes.definition: Target Company Net Profit refers to the final operating result of a company within a specific accounting period after deducting all costs, expenses, and income taxes. It is a core indicator for measuring a company's profitability and shareholder returns, commonly used in business valuation (e.g., the Modified Average P/E Ratio Method).

formulas.source_formula: Target Company Net Profit = Total Profit - Income Tax Expense

Target Company Net Profit = Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Business Taxes and Surcharges - Selling Expenses - Administrative Expenses - Financial Expenses - Asset Impairment Losses + Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Investment Income - Non-operating Expenses - Income Tax

nodes.name: Target Company Sales Per Share
nodes.definition: Target Company Sales Per Share refers to a financial metric that allocates a company's sales revenue (or total revenue) to each outstanding common share. It measures the sales scale generated per common share and is a commonly used composite indicator for corporate valuation and financial analysis.

nodes.name: Target Company Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Target company value per share is the estimated value per share calculated using the relative valuation method. It is typically derived by multiplying the target company's corresponding per-share financial metric by the average valuation multiple (such as P/E ratio, P/B ratio, etc.) of comparable companies. It is used in scenarios such as mergers and acquisitions and investment decision-making, rather than being an original fundamental data point from financial statements.

operands.metric: Average P/B Ratio of Comparable Companies
Target Company's Book Value Per Share

formulas.source_formula: Target Company Value Per Share = Average P/B Ratio of Comparable Companies × Target Company's Book Value Per Share

operands.metric: Average P/S Ratio of Comparable Companies

formulas.source_formula: Target Company Value Per Share = Average P/S Ratio of Comparable Companies × Target Company's Sales Per Share

operands.metric: Average P/E Ratio of Comparable Companies

formulas.source_formula: Target Company Value Per Share = Average P/E Ratio of Comparable Companies × Target Company's Earnings Per Share

nodes.name: Target Company's Book Value Per Share
Target Company's Earnings Per Share
nodes.definition: Earnings Per Share (EPS) refers to the ratio of net profit attributable to common shareholders to the weighted average number of common shares outstanding. It is a core indicator for measuring corporate profitability, evaluating stock value, and conducting financial analysis.

nodes.name: Target Cost
nodes.definition: Target cost refers to the cost control objective calculated through the deduction method based on competitive market prices, expected revenue, or market analysis, in order to achieve predetermined target profit. It serves as a management tool for profit planning and cost constraint in new product development, budget management, and cost control.

formulas.source_formula: Target Currency Amount = Source Currency Amount × Exchange Rate

nodes.name: Target Date
nodes.definition: Target date refers to a pre-determined specific date in finance, financial management, or project management by which a certain task must be completed, an objective must be achieved, a contractual obligation must be fulfilled, or a financial instrument matures.

nodes.name: Target Dividend Payout Ratio
nodes.definition: The target dividend payout ratio refers to the level of dividend payments that a company's management or board of directors sets and plans to maintain over the long term, typically expressed as the percentage of total dividends relative to net profit. It reflects the company's long-term strategic decision regarding profit distribution versus retained earnings for reinvestment.

nodes.name: Target EBIT
aliases: Planned Earnings Before Interest and Taxes
nodes.definition: Target EBIT refers to the pre-determined, desired level of earnings before interest and taxes that a company aims to achieve within a specific planning period (such as a fiscal year or a project cycle). It is a key financial objective set during financial planning, budgeting, and performance evaluation, used to guide operational decisions and measure management performance.

nodes.name: Target Equity Value
nodes.definition: Target equity value refers to a composite indicator reflecting the fair value of specific equity (the target equity) on the valuation date, calculated through valuation methods such as the asset-based approach, discounted cash flow method, and market multiple method. It is not directly obtained from financial statements but is derived from assessments based on future earnings, comparable market data, or the fair value of assets and liabilities, serving as the basis for evaluating control premiums.

formulas.source_formula: Target Equity Value = Asset Value - Liability Value

nodes.name: Target Future Value
nodes.definition: Target future value refers to the expected value at a specific future point in time, calculated based on present value, interest rate, time period, and other factors through compound or simple interest. It is a core concept in financial planning, investment evaluation, and sinking fund calculations, representing the accumulated result of funds under the effect of time value of money.

nodes.name: Target Inflation Rate
nodes.definition: The target inflation rate is the level of inflation that a central bank or government monetary authority aims to maintain over a future period. It is a forward-looking policy objective used to guide public expectations and direct monetary policy operations, rather than a result calculated from historical data.

nodes.name: Target Investment Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Target Investment Profit Margin is the expected profit level set by an enterprise or project in investment decision-making, typically expressed as the percentage of total annual profit or average annual total profit relative to the total project investment. It is a key indicator for measuring investment efficiency and setting target profits.

nodes.name: Target Net Income
nodes.definition: Target net income is the desired profit level after deducting all fixed and variable costs from total sales revenue, used to evaluate whether a business meets its financial objectives.

formulas.source_formula: Target Net Income = Sales - Fixed Costs - Variable Costs

nodes.name: Target Profit
nodes.definition: Target profit refers to the optimal control objective that an enterprise should achieve through efforts over a future period. It is a core indicator of business strategy, commonly used in budget management, cost-volume-profit analysis, and profit planning.

formulas.source_formula: Target Profit = Total Investment Amount × Target Return on Investment

nodes.name: Target Profit Margin
nodes.definition: Target profit margin is the optimal profit level that a company aims to achieve through efforts over a future period, typically expressed as a percentage of profit to sales revenue or other relevant bases. It is one of the core indicators for strategic planning and budget management in enterprises.

nodes.name: Target Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Target sales revenue refers to the level of sales income a company needs to achieve in order to realize a specific target profit. It is a composite indicator calculated based on metrics such as target profit, fixed costs, and contribution margin ratio, used for target profit analysis and planning.

formulas.source_formula: Target Sales Revenue = (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) ÷ Contribution Margin Ratio

nodes.name: Target Sales Volume
nodes.definition: Target sales volume refers to the quantity of product sales required to achieve a specific target profit under a given unit price, unit variable cost, and fixed cost structure. It is a core calculation metric in cost-volume-profit analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Target Sales Volume = (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) ÷ (Unit Price - Unit Variable Cost)
Target Sales Volume = (Fixed Costs + Target Profit) ÷ Contribution Margin Ratio

nodes.name: Target Security Return Rate
nodes.definition: Target Security Return Rate refers to the expected level of return set by investors or portfolio managers for a specific security or investment portfolio. It is typically calculated based on the investor's risk preference, market conditions, and theories such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM), and is used to evaluate the feasibility of investment decisions.

nodes.name: Target Security's Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The target security's rate of return is a composite metric calculated using financial indicators such as interest (dividend) yield and capital gains yield, used to measure the return on a security investment. It is related to the beta coefficient in the Capital Asset Pricing Model to reflect the risk-adjusted expected return.

formulas.source_formula: Target Security's Rate of Return = Interest (Dividend) Yield + Capital Gains Yield

nodes.name: Target Stock Price
nodes.definition: Target stock price is the price level required to maintain a given price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio after a change in earnings per share (EPS), commonly used to assess valuation impacts of corporate actions like share buybacks.

nodes.name: Target Value
nodes.definition: Target Value is a quantitative metric derived from specific formulas based on current performance status, used to measure the extent of future performance improvement or achievement. It is a core concept in performance management and process control, typically serving as a key reference point in the Plan-Do-Check-Act (PDCA) cycle.

formulas.source_formula: Target Value = Current Status Value - Improvement Value
Target Value = Current Value + (Target - Current Value) ÷ PDCA Cycle

nodes.name: Target Value Benchmark
nodes.definition: In a management by objectives system, the target value benchmark refers to the baseline figure used as a reference for calculating target values. It involves calculable components rather than fundamental raw data, typically derived from parameters such as current performance values, expected target values, and PDCA management cycles, and is used to derive key performance indicators like the target value change percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Target Value Benchmark = Target Value ÷ (1 + Target Value Change Percentage)
Target Value Benchmark = Current Value + PDCA Cycle × (Target Value - Current Value)

nodes.name: Target Value Change Percentage
nodes.definition: Target Value Change Percentage is a metric that measures the relative change of a variable (such as profit or cost) against a benchmark value, expressed as a percentage. It is used to assess the impact of variable changes on the target value and serves as a key component in calculating sensitivity coefficients in sensitivity analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Target Value Change Percentage = Sensitivity Coefficient × Parameter Value Change Percentage

nodes.name: Target Value New Value
nodes.definition: Target Value New Value is a derivative financial metric calculated based on financial indicators such as current value, target value, or improvement value. It reflects the new numerical value of a target after updates or adjustments, commonly used in target management, budget control, and performance evaluation scenarios.

formulas.source_formula: Target Value New Value = Target Value × (1 + Target Value Change Percentage)
Target Value New Value = Current Value + Improvement Value

nodes.name: Targeted Accrual Redemption Note (TARN)
nodes.definition: A Targeted Accrual Redemption Note (TARN) is a structured fixed-income product that accrues periodic coupons until the cumulative coupon amount reaches a predefined target cap, at which point the note is redeemed early. Valuation typically requires modeling coupon accrual dynamics under interest rate uncertainty and discounting expected cash flows to obtain an estimated present value.

nodes.name: Tariff
nodes.definition: Tariff refers to a tax levied by a country's customs authorities on imported and exported goods and items passing through its customs territory in accordance with its legal provisions. It serves as an important policy instrument for regulating import and export trade, protecting domestic industries, and increasing fiscal revenue.

nodes.name: Task Count
nodes.definition: Task count refers to the total number of independent work units or activities that need to be completed or tallied within a specific project, course, workflow, or analytical process. It is commonly used to measure workload, learning progress, or project complexity.

nodes.name: Task Work Time
nodes.definition: Task work time refers to the actual or estimated duration required to complete a specific task or activity, commonly used for workload assessment, efficiency analysis, and project planning.

nodes.name: Tax Adjustment Decrease Amount
nodes.definition: Tax Adjustment Decrease Amount refers to the total sum of amounts that an enterprise needs to deduct from its total accounting profit when calculating taxable income, in accordance with tax regulations. These deductions typically involve tax-exempt, tax-reduced, or loss-offsetting preferential items permitted by tax law, such as government bond interest income, eligible dividends, and allowable carry-forward losses from prior years.

nodes.name: Tax Adjustment Increase Amount
nodes.definition: Tax Adjustment Increase Amount refers to the total sum of amounts added to accounting profit for tax purposes when calculating the taxable income of an enterprise income tax, in accordance with tax regulations. It aggregates various items that require increasing taxable income or reducing pre-tax deductions due to differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations, serving as a key intermediate variable in calculating taxable income.

nodes.name: Tax Adjustment Items Amount
nodes.definition: Tax adjustment items amount refers to the total amount of various items that are added to or deducted from accounting profit according to tax regulations when calculating taxable income. These adjustments aim to align accounting profit with taxable profit as stipulated by tax laws.

nodes.name: Tax Base
nodes.definition: Tax base refers to the basis or standard stipulated by tax laws for calculating the amount of tax payable, serving as a key element in determining the tax liability. It is typically calculated from fundamental data such as cost, profit, and tax rates using specific formulas, rather than being directly taken from the raw data in financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Base = Cost × (1 + Cost Profit Margin) ÷ (1 - Consumption Tax Rate)
Tax Base = Customs Duty-paid Value + Customs Duty + Consumption Tax

nodes.name: Tax Base of Assets
nodes.definition: The tax base of an asset refers to the amount that, according to tax regulations, can be deducted from taxable economic benefits when calculating taxable income during the process of recovering the asset's carrying amount. It represents the value of the asset under tax law and serves as the cost basis allowable for deduction in future tax calculations for the asset.

nodes.name: Tax Base of Liabilities
nodes.definition: The tax base of a liability refers to its carrying amount, less any amount that will be deductible for tax purposes in respect of that liability in future periods when calculating the enterprise's taxable profit. It reflects the value of a liability recognized under tax law and is used to determine whether the liability will give rise to deductible temporary differences in future periods, thereby affecting the calculation of deferred tax assets or liabilities.

nodes.name: Tax Benefit
nodes.definition: Tax benefit refers to the reduction of tax liability achieved by applying tax credits. Refundable tax credits can reduce liability below zero, generating a refund, whereas nonrefundable tax credits reduce liability only to zero.

nodes.name: Tax Benefit of Itemizing Deductions
nodes.definition: The tax benefit of itemizing deductions measures the reduction in income tax liability achieved by claiming itemized deductions instead of the standard deduction. When itemized deductions (including the home mortgage interest deduction) exceed the standard deduction, the excess reduces taxable income, and the associated tax savings equal the excess amount multiplied by the taxpayer's marginal tax rate.

nodes.name: Tax Break
nodes.definition: A tax break is a reduction in tax burden provided through mechanisms such as credits, deductions, or exemptions. A tax credit reduces tax liability on a dollar-for-dollar basis. For a nonrefundable tax credit, the credit cannot reduce the tax liability below zero; any excess credit beyond the liability is not refunded.

nodes.name: Tax Credit Amount
nodes.definition: Tax credit amount refers to the foreign-paid income tax amount that enterprises are permitted to deduct from their payable tax amount when calculating current period tax liability, in accordance with tax regulations. Its core calculation component is the credit limit, which is the tax payable calculated under Chinese tax law on income sourced from a specific country (region), serving as a key indicator for foreign income tax credit.

operands.metric: Total Tax Payable on Domestic and Foreign Income Calculated per Tax Law
Taxable Income from a Specific Country (Region)
Total Taxable Income from Domestic and Foreign Sources

formulas.source_formula: Tax Credit Amount = Total Tax Payable on Domestic and Foreign Income Calculated per Tax Law × Taxable Income from a Specific Country (Region) ÷ Total Taxable Income from Domestic and Foreign Sources

operands.metric: Taxable Income from a Specific Country (Region)
Total Taxable Income from Domestic and Foreign Sources

formulas.source_formula: Tax Credit Amount = Taxable Income × Applicable Tax Rate × Taxable Income from a Specific Country (Region) ÷ Total Taxable Income from Domestic and Foreign Sources

nodes.name: Tax Deduction
nodes.definition: A tax deduction is an allowable reduction from gross income used to compute taxable income. Taxpayers typically choose between itemized deductions and the standard deduction and select the larger amount to maximize the reduction of taxable income.

nodes.name: Tax Deficiency Payable Calculated under Simplified Tax Calculation Method
aliases: Additional Tax Assessed under Simplified Taxation
Tax Payable under Simple Tax Calculation Method from Tax Inspection
nodes.definition: Refers to the value-added tax (VAT) deficiency payable calculated according to the simplified tax calculation method during a tax audit. This method applies to small-scale taxpayers or specific taxable activities of general taxpayers, calculating the tax amount based on sales revenue and the levy rate, with no input tax credit allowed. It is not original data from financial statements.

nodes.name: Tax Deficiency from Audit Calculated under Simplified Tax Method
Tax Expense
nodes.definition: Tax expense is the amount of income tax recognized in the income statement for a reporting period. In this simplified calculation, it equals taxable income multiplied by the effective tax rate.

nodes.name: Tax Incidence
nodes.definition: Tax incidence describes how the economic burden of a tax is divided between producers and consumers. The producer tax burden quantifies the proportion of the tax absorbed by producers, determined by the relative price elasticities of demand and supply: the more inelastic side bears more of the tax.

formulas.source_formula: Producer Tax Burden = Price Elasticity of Demand ÷ (Price Elasticity of Demand + Price Elasticity of Supply)

nodes.name: Tax Liabilities Related to Sale of Used Assets
aliases: Tax Burden on Disposal of Used Assets
Tax Liability from Selling Used Property
Tax on Sale of Old Assets
nodes.definition: Tax liabilities related to the sale of used assets refer to the total amount of various taxes that enterprises or individuals are required to calculate and pay when selling used fixed assets (such as old properties, used equipment, used vehicles, etc.) in accordance with relevant tax laws and regulations. This typically involves the calculation of taxes such as Value-Added Tax (VAT), Land Appreciation Tax (e.g., for selling old properties), etc. The specific tax amount depends on factors such as the nature of the asset, selling price, original cost, appraised value, and applicable tax rates.

nodes.name: Tax Liability
nodes.definition: Tax liability is the total amount of tax owed by an individual or entity to a tax authority, calculated by applying the applicable tax rate to the taxable income.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Liability = Long-Term Capital Gains Tax + Short-Term Capital Gains Tax
Tax Liability = Income × Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax Liability (Tax Credit) on Sale of Old Assets
aliases: Tax Effect from Disposal of Old Asset
Tax on Sale of Old Asset
nodes.definition: Tax liability (or tax credit) on the sale of old assets refers to the cash tax expense or savings arising from the disposal of existing assets in capital budgeting decisions. Its amount depends on the asset's book value, selling price, and applicable tax regulations (such as input tax deduction eligibility, simplified tax calculation applicability, etc.), and is a crucial adjustment item when calculating a project's initial cash outflow.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Liability (Tax Credit) on Sale of Old Assets = (Appreciation Amount × Applicable Tax Rate) - (Deductible Item Amount × Quick Deduction Coefficient)

nodes.name: Tax Liability from Sale of Old Assets
Tax Loss Carryforward
nodes.definition: Tax loss carryforward is a tax accounting mechanism that allows a company to apply net operating losses (NOL) from prior periods against future taxable income, typically subject to statutory limitations (e.g., an 80% of taxable income cap in the U.S.), thereby reducing the taxable base and deferring tax liabilities.

nodes.name: Tax Loss Harvesting
nodes.definition: Tax loss harvesting is an investment tax planning strategy in which realized capital losses are intentionally generated to offset realized capital gains, thereby reducing taxable income and overall capital gains tax liability. Losses are typically applied first against gains of the same holding period (long-term against long-term and short-term against short-term), with any remaining losses used to offset the other category, subject to tax regulations and wash-sale rules.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Owed = Income × Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax Payable
nodes.definition: Tax payable refers to the amount of tax that a taxpayer is required to pay to the tax authority, calculated by applying the applicable tax rate to the taxable income or taxable activity as stipulated by tax laws and regulations.

nodes.name: Tax Payable Calculated under Simplified Tax Method
Tax Payable Calculated under the Simplified Tax Calculation Method
aliases: Tax Payable under Simplified Tax Method
简易计税方法应纳税额
nodes.definition: Tax payable calculated under the simplified tax calculation method refers to the value-added tax (VAT) payable computed based on the sales amount excluding VAT and the applicable levy rate when the taxpayer adopts the simplified tax calculation method. This method is primarily applicable to small-scale taxpayers and specific business scenarios of general taxpayers, with its calculation based on direct multiplication rather than input tax credit deduction.

nodes.name: Tax Payable Reduction Amount
nodes.definition: The Tax Payable Reduction Amount is a composite indicator calculated based on tax preferential policies. It appears as a deduction in the tax payable formula to reduce the amount of tax a company is required to pay. It typically includes components such as tax exemptions and tax credits, and is not an original fundamental data item in financial statements.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Payable Reduction Amount = Taxable Income × Applicable Tax Rate - Actual Tax Payable
Tax Payable Reduction Amount = Taxable Income × (Standard Tax Rate - Preferential Tax Rate)
Tax Payable Reduction Amount = Tax Exemption Amount + Tax Credit Amount

nodes.name: Tax Payable by Tax Type
aliases: Amount of Tax Payable for Each Tax
nodes.definition: Tax payable by tax type refers to the amount of tax that an enterprise or individual is required to pay to the tax authority within a specified tax period, calculated separately for different tax categories (such as Value-Added Tax, Corporate Income Tax, Consumption Tax, etc.) in accordance with national tax laws and regulations.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Payable under Simplified Method = Sales Amount Including VAT ÷ (1 + Levy Rate) × Levy Rate
Tax Payable under Simplified Method = Sales Amount (Excluding VAT) × Levy Rate

nodes.name: Tax Rate
nodes.definition: Tax rate is the statutory ratio or fixed value stipulated by tax law, serving as the fundamental parameter for calculating a taxpayer's tax payable. It is typically expressed as the proportion between the tax payable and the taxable base amount (such as income, sales revenue, etc.).

nodes.name: Tax Reduction and Exemption
nodes.definition: Tax reduction and exemption refers to preferential measures granted by tax authorities in accordance with national tax laws, regulations, and related policies, which partially or fully exempt, reduce, or refund the tax payable by taxpayers.

nodes.name: Tax Reduction and Exemption Amount
nodes.definition: Tax reduction and exemption amount refers to the amount directly deducted from a taxpayer's payable tax according to specific preferential tax policies. Its specific calculation method depends on the taxpayer type (e.g., individual businesses, small and low-profit enterprises) and applicable tax policies, typically based on indicators such as taxable income, tax rates, and other policy reduction amounts.

operands.metric: Portion of Annual Taxable Income Exceeding 1 Million Yuan but Not Exceeding 3 Million Yuan

formulas.source_formula: Tax Reduction and Exemption Amount = Portion of Annual Taxable Income Exceeding 1 Million Yuan But Not Exceeding 3 Million Yuan × (Applicable Tax Rate - 50% × 20%)

operands.metric: Portion of Annual Taxable Income Not Exceeding 1 Million Yuan

formulas.source_formula: Tax Reduction and Exemption Amount = Portion of Annual Taxable Income Not Exceeding 1 Million Yuan × (Applicable Tax Rate - 25% × 20%)

nodes.name: Tax Refunds Received in Year k
Tax Refunds Received in the Next Period
Tax Relief
aliases: Age and Blindness Additional Standard Deduction
nodes.definition: Tax relief refers to the reduction of taxable income or tax liability through deductions, exemptions, and credits. This measure focuses on optimizing the deduction strategy by comparing the sum of itemized deductions with the standard deduction and selecting the larger amount to maximize tax relief for the taxpayer.

nodes.name: Tax Savings
nodes.definition: Tax savings represent the reduction in tax liability achieved by applying deductions against taxable income at the applicable marginal tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Savings = Deduction Amount × Tax Bracket Rate
Tax Savings = Deduction × Marginal Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax Shelter
nodes.definition: A tax shelter is a lawful strategy, structure, or instrument that reduces taxable income or defers tax liabilities through deductions, credits, exclusions, or timing differences. When a tax shelter operates via a deductible expense, the tax savings are calculated by multiplying the deductible amount by the taxpayer's marginal tax rate.

nodes.name: Tax Shield
nodes.definition: Tax shield is the reduction in tax liability resulting from allowable deductions, measured as the deductible amount multiplied by the marginal tax rate. It quantifies the cash tax savings attributable to deductions and is commonly used in valuation, capital budgeting, and tax planning.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Shield = Tax-deductible Expense × Tax Rate
Tax Savings from Deduction = Deductible Amount × Marginal Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax Shield from Lease Payments
nodes.definition: Tax shield from lease payments refers to the tax-saving effect generated by rental expenses in the cash flow analysis of lease decisions. Its amount equals the rental payment multiplied by the income tax rate, and it is a crucial component in calculating the cash flow during the lease period.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Shield from Lease Payments = Rental Payment × Income Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax Shield on Terminal Salvage Value Loss
aliases: Tax Shield from Terminal Value Loss
期末余值变现损失抵税
nodes.definition: Tax shield on terminal salvage value loss refers to the situation where the realized salvage value of an asset is lower than its book value, and the difference can be deducted as a loss to reduce taxable income.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Shield on Terminal Salvage Value Loss = (Salvage Value Realized - Book Salvage Value) × Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax Table
nodes.definition: A tax table is a schedule that maps taxable income ranges to statutory tax liabilities for different filing statuses. It is used to determine an individual's tax liability by selecting the predefined liability corresponding to the taxpayer's filing status within the bracket that contains the taxable income.

nodes.name: Tax Threshold
nodes.definition: The tax threshold refers to the minimum amount stipulated by tax law at which taxation begins on a taxable object. When a taxpayer's taxable income or turnover reaches or exceeds this standard, the entire amount becomes subject to tax; if it falls below this standard, the corresponding tax is exempt. This provision typically applies to individual taxpayers or small-scale taxpayers.

nodes.name: Tax Wedge
nodes.definition: Tax wedge is the difference between gross income and net take-home income after mandatory taxes, representing the effective tax burden on labor income and its impact on disposable earnings.

formulas.source_formula: Tax Wedge = Gross Income - (Gross Income × (1 - Federal Tax Rate) × (1 - State Tax Rate))

nodes.name: Tax and Fee Refunds Receivable in Next Period
aliases: Tax Refunds Received in Next Period
nodes.definition: Tax and fee refunds receivable in the next period refer to various tax refunds, such as value-added tax, consumption tax, and income tax, that a company expects to receive from the government in the next accounting period (e.g., the next reporting period or fiscal year). This is a forecast item for future cash inflows, typically related to operating activities.

nodes.name: Tax and Fee Refunds Received
nodes.definition: Tax and fee refunds received refer to various taxes and fees actually received by an enterprise that are refunded by the government according to preferential tax policies such as 'collect first, refund later' or 'immediate refund upon collection', including value-added tax, consumption tax, income tax, education surcharge, etc. In the cash flow statement, this item is a component of cash inflows from operating activities, and its amount must be calculated and reported by analyzing the occurrence amounts of relevant accounting accounts.

nodes.name: Tax and Fee Refunds Received in Year k
nodes.definition: Tax and fee refunds received in year k refer to the total cash amount actually received by an enterprise from the government during the k-th fiscal year for various tax and fee refunds. This typically constitutes a form of government subsidy granted to enterprises in accordance with national preferential tax policies (such as 'collect first, refund later' or 'refund upon collection'), with common refundable taxes and fees including Value-Added Tax (VAT), Consumption Tax, Income Tax, and Education Surcharge.

nodes.name: Tax per Unit
nodes.definition: Tax per unit refers to the tax payable per unit of product, typically involving indirect taxes such as consumption tax, value-added tax, and business tax. It is a composite indicator rather than a basic raw data point, which can be calculated by dividing total tax by product quantity or based on tax rate and product price. It plays an important role in target cost management and product pricing.

formulas.source_formula: Tax per Unit = Total Tax ÷ Product Quantity
Tax per Unit = Unit Product Price × Consumption Tax Rate

nodes.name: Tax-Adjusted Total Debt Service
nodes.definition: Tax-Adjusted Total Debt Service represents the period's cash outflow required to service debt, computed as principal repayment plus interest expense adjusted for tax deductibility. It is commonly used in credit and solvency analysis and as the denominator in the Debt-Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR).

formulas.source_formula: Total Debt Service = Interest × (1 - Tax Rate) + Principal
Tax-Deductible Amount = min(Donation Amount, Maximum Deductible Amount)

nodes.name: Tax-Equivalent Yield
nodes.definition: Tax-equivalent yield is the yield on a taxable investment required to match the after-tax return of a tax-exempt investment, typically used to compare municipal bond yields with taxable bond yields at a given marginal tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Tax-Exempt Yield ÷ (1 - Marginal Tax Rate)
supporting_source_formulas: Tax-Equivalent Yield = Tax-Exempt Yield ÷ (1 - Marginal Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Tax-Exempt Income
nodes.definition: Tax-exempt income refers to revenue items that are not subject to personal income tax or corporate income tax according to national tax laws. These items can be directly deducted from total income when calculating taxable income, such as government bond interest, eligible dividends, and portions of personal wages like social security and housing fund contributions.

nodes.name: Tax-Exempt Purchased Raw Material Price
nodes.definition: Tax-exempt purchased raw material price refers to the actual cost of raw materials paid by an enterprise according to purchase contracts or relevant documents for producing export products in specific businesses such as processing with imported materials. This cost enjoys tax-exempt treatment in tax processing and serves as the fundamental original data for calculating relevant deductions in export tax rebates.

nodes.name: Tax-Exempt Yield Equivalence
nodes.definition: Tax-exempt yield equivalence is the yield that a tax-exempt investment must offer to produce the same after-tax return as a taxable investment, calculated by adjusting the taxable yield for the investor's tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Tax-Exempt Yield Equivalence = Taxable Yield × (1 - Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Tax-Free Savings Account (TFSA) Over-Contribution Tax
aliases: 免税储蓄账户超额供款税
nodes.definition: The TFSA over-contribution tax is a penalty imposed by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) on excess TFSA contributions, calculated at 1% per month on the excess amount until it is withdrawn or sufficient contribution room is created. The implementation here annualizes the monthly tax (12 months) and aggregates penalties across years based on the total contributions relative to the annual TFSA limit.

nodes.name: Tax-exclusive Sales Amount
nodes.definition: Tax-exclusive sales amount refers to the portion of the total price and extra charges collected from the buyer when selling goods or providing services that does not include Value-Added Tax (VAT) or other taxes. It serves as the basis for calculating the output VAT amount.

nodes.name: Tax-inclusive Purchase Cost
nodes.definition: Tax-inclusive purchase cost refers to the total cost of purchasing materials or goods by an enterprise, which includes relevant taxes and fees (such as value-added tax). It serves as one of the fundamental data points for calculating actual procurement expenditures and conducting cost accounting.

nodes.name: Tax-inclusive Purchase Price
nodes.definition: Tax-inclusive purchase price refers to the total price paid by an enterprise to suppliers for purchasing goods or services, which includes value-added tax and other turnover taxes. It serves as the basis for calculating tax-exclusive costs, input VAT, and final profits.

nodes.name: Tax-inclusive Sales Revenue
nodes.definition: Tax-inclusive sales revenue refers to the total amount collected by the taxpayer from the buyer for the sale of goods, provision of taxable services, or labor, including all payments and extra charges, which contains the value-added tax (VAT) payable. It serves as the basis for calculating VAT output tax or tax payable under the simplified tax calculation method.

formulas.source_formula: Tax-inclusive Sales Revenue = Tax-exclusive Sales Revenue × (1 + VAT Rate)

nodes.name: Tax-to-GDP Ratio
nodes.definition: The tax-to-GDP ratio measures the proportion of a nation's gross domestic product collected as tax revenue, indicating the overall tax burden and the government's capacity to finance public services. It is commonly used for international comparisons and fiscal policy analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Tax-to-GDP Ratio = (Tax Revenue ÷ Gross Domestic Product) × 100%

nodes.name: Taxable Amount of Products
nodes.definition: Taxable amount of products refers to the monetary base used for taxation on product sales as stipulated by tax laws. It is typically the portion of sales revenue or adjusted amount that is multiplied by the tax rate when calculating product tax, value-added tax, and other levies.

nodes.name: Taxable Area
nodes.definition: Taxable area refers to the floor area or land area of real estate (such as buildings or land) that must be included in the tax base for calculating property taxes, such as real estate tax, in accordance with relevant tax laws and regulations.

nodes.name: Taxable Capital Gain
nodes.definition: Taxable capital gain is the portion of capital gain on property disposal that exceeds allowable exclusions and is subject to capital gains tax, calculated as the excess of net selling price over adjusted cost basis minus any applicable capital gains exclusion.

nodes.name: Taxable Document Tax Calculation Amount
nodes.definition: Taxable Document Tax Calculation Amount refers to the monetary amount involved in economic transactions that serves as the basis for calculating the stamp tax payable according to tax laws. It is the specific amount recorded on taxable documents (such as contracts, property transfer deeds, etc.) that is subject to stamp tax.

nodes.name: Taxable Estate Amount
aliases: 超过免税额的应税遗产金额
nodes.definition: Taxable estate amount refers to the portion of a decedent’s estate that exceeds the applicable estate tax exclusion limit and is potentially subject to estate tax. It is computed as the excess of the estate’s fair market value over the exclusion limit, floored at zero. This measure identifies the taxable base but does not calculate the actual tax owed.

nodes.name: Taxable Foreign Earned Income
aliases: Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE) – Taxable Income
外国劳动所得免税额（FEIE）后应税所得
nodes.definition: Taxable Foreign Earned Income is the portion of a U.S. taxpayer’s foreign earned income that remains subject to U.S. federal income tax after applying the Foreign Earned Income Exclusion (FEIE). The FEIE allows eligible expats to exclude up to a statutory, inflation-indexed limit of foreign earned income; any excess over this limit is taxable. The exclusion applies to earned income (wages and self-employment) and not to passive income such as interest, dividends, or rental income.

nodes.name: Taxable Gift
nodes.definition: Taxable gift refers to the portion of a donor's transfer that exceeds both the annual exclusion per recipient and any remaining lifetime exclusion, forming the basis for potential gift tax liability under estate and gift tax rules.

nodes.name: Taxable Gift Amount
nodes.definition: Taxable Gift Amount refers to the portion of a gift that exceeds the annual gift tax exclusion and is therefore reportable for gift tax purposes, potentially applying against the donor's lifetime unified credit/exemption.

nodes.name: Taxable Income
nodes.definition: Taxable income refers to the income base subject to taxation when calculating corporate income tax according to tax laws. It is typically calculated using either the direct method (adjusting total revenue) or the indirect method (adjusting accounting profit) and is a core concept in corporate income tax computation.

formulas.source_formula: Taxable Income = Gross Income - Itemized Deductions
Taxable Income = Total Revenue × Taxable Income Rate
Taxable Income = Interest Income + Dividends + Capital Gains - Fees - Exemptions
Taxable Income = min(Gross Income, State Taxable Wage Base)
Taxable Income = Gross Income - Total Deductions
Taxable Income = Gross Income - Deductions

operands.metric: Social Security and Housing Fund Contributions

formulas.source_formula: Taxable Income = Pre-tax Income - Social Security and Housing Fund Contributions - Tax Threshold

operands.metric: Allowable Loss Carryforwards from Prior Years

formulas.source_formula: Taxable Income = Total Revenue - Non-taxable Revenue - Tax-exempt Revenue - Various Deductions - Allowable Loss Carryforwards from Prior Years

operands.metric: Allowable Losses Carried Forward from Previous Years

formulas.source_formula: Taxable Income = Total Revenue - Non-taxable Revenue - Tax-exempt Revenue - Various Deductions - Allowable Losses Carried Forward from Previous Years
Taxable Income = Total Revenue - Non-taxable Revenue - Tax-exempt Revenue - Various Deductions - Allowable Loss Carryforwards

nodes.name: Taxable Income Derived from a Country (Region)
aliases: Taxable Income from a Foreign Country (Region)
境外所得应纳税所得额
来源于境外的应税所得
nodes.definition: Taxable income derived from a country (region) refers to the portion of income earned by a Chinese resident enterprise or individual from sources outside China, in a specific foreign country or region, which must be included in the taxable income when calculating enterprise income tax or individual income tax according to Chinese tax laws. This income may have been subject to income tax in the foreign jurisdiction and may be eligible for foreign tax credit upon repatriation to China in accordance with relevant regulations.

nodes.name: Taxable Income Derived from a Specific Country (Region)
aliases: Taxable Income from a Foreign Country (Region)
nodes.definition: Refers to the income derived by a Chinese resident enterprise or non-resident enterprise from a specific country or region outside China, which is subject to calculation and payment of enterprise income tax according to the provisions of the Chinese Enterprise Income Tax Law. This portion of income must be considered separately when calculating the enterprise's total global taxable income and may involve the credit for foreign taxes already paid.

nodes.name: Taxable Income Rate
nodes.definition: The taxable income rate is a pre-determined percentage set by tax authorities for specific industries or taxpayers when it is difficult to accurately calculate their taxable income. It is commonly used in the assessed collection method, whereby the taxpayer's total revenue or cost expenses are multiplied by this rate to estimate their taxable income, which is then used to calculate the payable corporate income tax.

nodes.name: Taxable Income Sourced from a Specific Country (Region)
Taxable Income for the Current Year
nodes.definition: Taxable income for the current year refers to the income amount calculated according to tax laws on which an enterprise is liable to pay corporate income tax within a tax year. It is derived from the enterprise's total revenue, minus non-taxable income, tax-exempt income, various statutory deductions, and allowable losses carried forward from previous years.

nodes.name: Taxable Income from Business Operations
aliases: 经营所得应纳税额基数
nodes.definition: Taxable income from business operations refers to the balance, used as the tax base for calculating and paying individual income tax (on business income), derived by individual industrial and commercial households, investors in sole proprietorships, individual partners in partnerships, and contracted or leased operators from their total revenue generated from production and business activities within a tax year, after deducting costs, expenses, losses, and allowable carryover losses from prior years.

nodes.name: Taxable Income from a Specific Country (Region)
Taxable Sales
nodes.definition: Taxable sales refer to the sales amount on which value-added tax (VAT) should be calculated and paid by taxpayers according to tax laws when taxable sales activities occur. It serves as the basis for calculating VAT output tax or tax payable.

nodes.name: Taxable Temporary Differences
nodes.definition: Taxable temporary differences refer to differences arising between the carrying amount of an asset or liability and its tax base, which will result in an increase in taxable income in future periods, thereby giving rise to deferred tax liabilities. In simple terms, these are expenses or losses recognized in accounting currently but not deductible for tax purposes until future periods, leading to lower current tax payments and higher future tax payments.

nodes.name: Taxable Turnover
nodes.definition: Taxable turnover refers to the amount of business revenue used as the tax base for calculating turnover taxes (such as Value-Added Tax, Business Tax, etc.) payable by taxpayers in accordance with tax regulations. It typically comprises the total consideration and additional charges received by an enterprise within a specified period for providing taxable services, transferring intangible assets, or selling immovable property, but may be subject to deductions or adjustments based on specific tax policies.

nodes.name: Taxable Wage Base
aliases: 州失业保险应税工资基数
nodes.definition: The taxable wage base is the maximum amount of an employee's earnings subject to Social Security payroll tax for a given year. Social Security tax is applied only up to this limit; any earnings above the limit are not subject to the Social Security portion of FICA.

nodes.name: Taxable Yield Equivalence
nodes.definition: Taxable yield equivalence is the pre-tax yield that a taxable investment must offer to equal the after-tax return of a tax-exempt investment, calculated by dividing the tax-exempt yield by one minus the investor’s marginal tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Taxable Yield Equivalence = Tax-Exempt Yield ÷ (1 - Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Taxation
nodes.definition: Taxation is a form of fiscal revenue obtained by the state to meet public needs, whereby it compulsorily and gratuitously participates in the distribution of social products based on public power, in accordance with legally established standards and procedures. For enterprises, taxation constitutes a statutory obligation calculated and paid to the government according to tax laws, directly impacting their profits and cash flow.

nodes.name: Taxes
nodes.definition: Taxes refer to various taxes and surcharges incurred by an enterprise, excluding corporate income tax and deductible value-added tax. They typically include consumption tax, business tax, urban maintenance and construction tax, etc., and can be calculated using financial indicators such as direct costs, indirect costs, profit, sales revenue, and tax rates.

formulas.source_formula: Taxes = Product Sales Revenue × Tax Rate
Taxes = Tax Rate × Tax Base
Taxes = (Direct Costs + Indirect Costs + Profit) × Tax Rate

nodes.name: Taxes Credited
nodes.definition: Taxes credited refers to the amount of tax that a taxpayer, in accordance with tax laws and regulations, deducts from the current period's tax payable, having completed the statutory crediting procedures or calculations. It is a composite indicator calculated based on the creditable tax base and the applicable tax rate, commonly seen in scenarios such as Value-Added Tax (VAT) input tax credit, Corporate Income Tax pre-tax deductions, and international tax credits.

formulas.source_formula: Taxes Credited = Purchase Price × Applicable Tax Rate
Taxes Credited = Taxable Income × Credit Ratio
Taxes Due = Gross Interest × Tax Rate

nodes.name: Taxes Payable
nodes.definition: Taxes Payable (Taxes and Fees Payable) refers to various taxes and fees that an enterprise is obligated to pay according to tax laws within a specific accounting period but has not yet paid, classified as current liabilities. The amount is typically calculated based on the taxable amount and the applicable tax rate, with specific formulas varying by tax type.

formulas.source_formula: Taxes Payable = Taxable Income × Income Tax Rate
Taxes Payable = Taxable Amount × Applicable Tax Rate
supporting_source_formulas: Taxes Payable = Taxable Amount × Applicable Tax Rate

nodes.name: Taxes Payable from Previous Period
nodes.definition: Taxes Payable from Previous Period refers to the total amount of various taxes and fees that an enterprise has accrued according to tax laws but has not yet actually paid by the end of the last accounting period (such as the previous month, quarter, or year). It reflects the enterprise's tax obligations to the state at the end of the previous period and is an important component of current liabilities.

nodes.name: Taxes and Related Charges Paid
nodes.definition: Taxes and related charges paid refers to the total amount of various taxes and fees actually paid in cash during the period, as presented in the cash flows from operating activities section of the cash flow statement. It is an important composite indicator reflecting the actual cash outflow of a company's tax burden.

formulas.source_formula: Taxes and Related Charges Paid = Income Tax Expense + Business Tax and Surcharges + Value-added Tax Payable (Tax Paid)

nodes.name: Taxes and Surcharges
nodes.definition: Taxes and surcharges refer to various taxes and fees that an enterprise is obligated to bear in accordance with tax laws and regulations during its daily business operations, which are directly related to operating revenue. These mainly include Consumption Tax, Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax, Education Surcharge, Resource Tax, Property Tax, Land Use Tax, Vehicle and Vessel Tax, Stamp Duty, etc. This account records taxes and fees recognized in current period profit or loss and is a significant deduction item in calculating operating profit.

formulas.source_formula: Taxes and Surcharges = Consumption Tax + Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax + Education Surcharge + Local Education Surcharge + Resource Tax + Property Tax + Land Use Tax + Vehicle and Vessel Tax + Stamp Duty

operands.metric: Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate

formulas.source_formula: Taxes and Surcharges = (Consumption Tax + Value-added Tax + Business Tax) × (Urban Maintenance and Construction Tax Rate + Education Surcharge Levy Rate + Local Education Surcharge Levy Rate) + Resource Tax + Property Tax + Land Use Tax + Vehicle and Vessel Tax + Stamp Duty

nodes.name: Taxes and Surcharges Paid
nodes.definition: Taxes and Surcharges Paid is a composite indicator in the cash flow statement that reflects the actual cash payments made by an enterprise for various taxes and surcharges during a specific accounting period. Its value is calculated by aggregating the debit turnover of relevant tax and surcharge accounts for the current period, excluding any tax refunds received during the period.

formulas.source_formula: Taxes and Surcharges Paid = Income Tax + Business Tax and Surcharges + Value-added Tax Payable (Tax Paid)

nodes.name: Taxes and Surcharges Payable in Next Period
aliases: Taxes and Surcharges for Next Period
nodes.definition: Taxes and Surcharges Payable in Next Period refers to the total sum of various taxes and fees related to business operations that an enterprise expects to pay in the next accounting period (such as the next month, next quarter, or next year). It typically includes consumption tax, urban maintenance and construction tax, education surcharge, resource tax, property tax, urban land use tax, vehicle and vessel tax, stamp duty, etc. It is an important cash outflow or expense item that must be considered when forecasting future net operating income.

nodes.name: Taxes and Surcharges on Project Settlement
Taxes in Administrative Expenses
nodes.definition: Taxes in administrative expenses refer to various tax expenditures incurred and recorded under the current profit and loss account 'Administrative Expenses' in accordance with tax laws during the daily organization and management of production and business operations, such as property tax, vehicle and vessel tax, land use tax, and stamp duty.

nodes.name: Taylor Rule
nodes.definition: The Taylor Rule is a monetary policy targeting rule proposed by economist John B. Taylor in 1992. It suggests that central banks should set short-term interest rates based on the deviation of the inflation rate from its target and the output gap between actual GDP and potential GDP, in order to stabilize economic activity.

nodes.name: Taylor's Rule
nodes.definition: Taylor's Rule is a monetary policy guideline that prescribes how a central bank should set the nominal policy interest rate (e.g., the federal funds rate) in response to deviations of inflation from its target and the output gap, around an equilibrium real interest rate. The rule typically assigns weights (commonly 0.5) to the inflation gap and the output gap.

nodes.name: Technology Level Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Technology Level Growth Rate is an indicator measuring the compound growth rate of a company's technological capabilities or inputs. It is typically calculated using core technology-related metrics such as R&D expenditure, number of technical personnel, or patent counts. It reflects the dynamic changes in a company's technological advancement and serves as a key component in assessing long-term growth potential and sustainable growth rate.

nodes.name: Temporal Method
nodes.definition: The temporal method is a foreign currency translation approach that remeasures a subsidiary's financial statements into the parent company's functional currency. Monetary items are remeasured at the current (closing) exchange rate, while non-monetary items are remeasured at their historical transaction rates. Remeasurement gains or losses are recognized in profit or loss, ensuring that measurement bases are preserved for non-monetary items.

nodes.name: Tenkan-Sen (Conversion Line)
nodes.definition: The Tenkan-Sen (Conversion Line) is a component of the Ichimoku Cloud that equals the midpoint between the highest high and the lowest low over a specified lookback period, providing insight into short-term trend direction and momentum.

formulas.source_formula: Tenkan-Sen = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Tenkan-sen
nodes.definition: Tenkan-sen is a component of the Ichimoku Kinko Hyo indicator that represents a short-term support and resistance level and serves as a signal line for potential price reversals.

formulas.source_formula: Tenkan-sen = (Highest High + Lowest Low) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Tenor of Bill
nodes.definition: Tenor of bill refers to the length of time from the date of issue to the maturity date specified on the bill, which is a key element in determining when the bill needs to be paid.

nodes.name: Tentative Minimum Tax
aliases: 替代性最低税的暂定税额
nodes.definition: Tentative Minimum Tax (TMT) is the Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) liability computed by applying AMT rates to Alternative Minimum Taxable Income (AMTI) after the AMT exemption. The TMT is compared to the regular tax liability; if TMT exceeds regular tax, the difference is paid as AMT.

nodes.name: Term
nodes.definition: Term refers to the length of a time period, typically expressed in units such as years, months, or days. In the field of finance and accounting, it is a fundamental time parameter required for calculating the time value of money, evaluating bonds, computing interest rates, and numerous other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Term (Years)
nodes.definition: Term (Years) refers to the length of time from the deposit (or investment) date to the maturity (or withdrawal) date, typically calculated and expressed in years. It is one of the key factors determining the interest amount in interest calculations.

formulas.source_formula: Term Months = Term Years × 12

nodes.name: Term Risk Premium
nodes.definition: Term risk premium refers to the additional rate of return required by investors for holding long-term bonds or assets, due to the risk of price fluctuations caused by future interest rate changes. It constitutes a component of the nominal interest rate or required rate of return, compensating for the increased uncertainty associated with longer investment horizons.

nodes.name: Term to Maturity
nodes.definition: Term to Maturity refers to the number of remaining complete interest accrual or payment cycles from the current status or a specified date until the final maturity date of a contract, loan, bond, or other financial instrument with a fixed term. These cycles are typically measured in months, quarters, or years. It is a fundamental data point describing a temporal state, not a composite indicator derived through calculation.

nodes.name: Terminal Asset After-Tax Cash Flow
aliases: After-Tax Cash Flow from Terminal Asset
nodes.definition: Terminal Asset After-Tax Cash Flow refers to the net cash inflow or outflow generated from the disposal or operation of an asset at the end of its project or useful life, after considering the impact of income taxes. It is a key metric for evaluating terminal value in project investment decisions (such as Net Present Value calculations), typically calculated based on factors including terminal asset disposal proceeds, book value, and tax rate.

formulas.source_formula: Terminal Asset After-Tax Cash Flow = Terminal Asset Disposal Proceeds - Gain on Asset Disposal × Income Tax Rate

nodes.name: Terminal Asset Disposal Proceeds
nodes.definition: Terminal asset disposal proceeds refer to the cash or cash equivalent income obtained by an enterprise at the end of an accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year) through the sale, transfer, retirement, or other disposal of its long-term assets (such as fixed assets, intangible assets).

nodes.name: Terminal Capitalization Rate
nodes.definition: The terminal capitalization rate is the expected market cap rate applied to a property's stabilized net operating income at the end of the holding period to estimate its resale (terminal) value, reflecting prevailing yield requirements for comparable assets at exit.

nodes.name: Terminal Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Terminal Growth Rate refers to the constant, long-term growth rate used in business valuation (such as the Discounted Cash Flow model) to forecast the perpetual growth of a company's free cash flow or related financial metrics (e.g., net income, net operating assets) after it enters a stable development phase. It is typically a low and sustainable rate used to calculate the terminal value beyond the explicit forecast period.

nodes.name: Terminal Investment Value
nodes.definition: Terminal Investment Value refers to the total value of a current sum of money (present value) invested at a specific interest rate (simple or compound) for a certain period, at a future point in time (the terminal date). It reflects the time value of money, serves as a fundamental metric for assessing the future value of a single cash flow, and forms the basis for calculating holding period returns.

nodes.name: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow
aliases: Final Forecast Period Free Cash Flow
nodes.definition: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow refers to the cash flow generated from operating activities in the final period of a detailed forecast of a company's future operations, after meeting necessary capital expenditures and additional working capital requirements, which is freely available to all capital providers (including creditors and shareholders). It is a key input variable for calculating the terminal value in business valuation.

operands.metric: Terminal Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
Terminal Period Increase in Working Capital

formulas.source_formula: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow = Terminal Period Net Operating Profit After Tax + Terminal Period Depreciation and Amortization - Terminal Period Capital Expenditures - Terminal Period Increase in Working Capital

operands.metric: EBIT in the Final Forecast Period
Terminal Period Increase in Working Capital

formulas.source_formula: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow = Terminal Period EBIT × (1 - Income Tax Rate) + Terminal Period Depreciation and Amortization - Terminal Period Capital Expenditures - Terminal Period Increase in Working Capital

nodes.name: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow to Firm
aliases: Transition Period Free Cash Flow to Firm
转换阶段实体现金流量
nodes.definition: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow to Firm is a composite cash flow metric used in business valuation to bridge the forecast period and the perpetuity period. It is typically calculated based on forecast period cash flows and perpetuity period cash flows using specific formulas, serving as a key input for entity value assessment.

operands.metric: Final Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to Firm

formulas.source_formula: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow to Firm = Final Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to Firm × (1 + Perpetual Growth Rate)

operands.metric: Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to Firm
Perpetuity Period Free Cash Flow to Firm

formulas.source_formula: Terminal Period Free Cash Flow to Firm = (Forecast Period Free Cash Flow to Firm + Perpetuity Period Free Cash Flow to Firm) ÷ 2

nodes.name: Terminal Period Increase in Working Capital
Terminal Period Net Operating Profit After Tax
Terminal Point of Initial Cash Flow
nodes.definition: The terminal point of initial cash flow refers to the specific time point (e.g., the end of year 0 or year N) in project investment evaluation when the project's construction period ends and the operating period begins. It marks the transition point where the project shifts from the capital-investment construction phase to the cash-inflow generating operating phase, serving as the starting time benchmark for constructing the project's cash flow sequence.

nodes.name: Terminal Value
nodes.definition: Terminal value is the present value sum of all future cash flows beyond the forecast period, extending into perpetuity.

nodes.name: Terminal Value (Exit Multiple Method)
nodes.definition: Terminal value (TV) using the exit multiple method estimates the business's value at the end of the projection period by applying an industry-derived exit multiple to a relevant financial metric (e.g., EBITDA or revenue), reflecting market-based valuation of comparable transactions.

formulas.source_formula: Terminal Value = Financial Metric × Exit Multiple

nodes.name: Terminal Value Per Share
nodes.definition: Terminal value per share refers to the market value of equity or intrinsic value corresponding to each common share of a company at a specific valuation point in time (typically at the end of a forecast period or reporting period). It is not an account directly presented in financial statements but is a core valuation metric derived either by dividing the total equity value of the company by the total number of shares outstanding at the period end, or through valuation models (such as the Dividend Discount Model or Free Cash Flow Discount Model). It is commonly used to assess a stock's reasonable price and calculate growth rates.

nodes.name: Terminal Value in Up Scenario
aliases: 股价上涨时的期末价值
nodes.definition: Terminal value in the up scenario refers to the expected value of an asset or related derivative at a specific future point in time (terminal date) when the underlying asset price is in an upward state (up state), as used in financial option pricing or binomial tree models. It is typically employed to calculate the possible value of an option at expiration or a valuation date under optimistic market conditions.

nodes.name: Terms of Trade
nodes.definition: Terms of Trade (TOT) measures the relative price of a country's exports in terms of its imports. It is calculated as the export price index divided by the import price index, multiplied by 100, indicating the purchasing power of exports. A higher TOT suggests more favorable trade conditions, where a unit of exports can buy more imports.

formulas.source_formula: Terms of Trade = (Export Price Index ÷ Import Price Index) × 100

nodes.name: Tertiary Industry Consumption of Fixed Capital
Tertiary Industry Intermediate Input
nodes.definition: Tertiary industry intermediate input refers to the cost of externally purchased goods and services consumed once during the production activities of tertiary industry enterprises within the reporting period. It is a key component in calculating the value added of the tertiary industry and is reflected as total intermediate consumption in input-output accounting.

formulas.source_formula: Tertiary Industry Intermediate Input = Total Output of Tertiary Industry - Value Added of Tertiary Industry

operands.metric: Intermediate Input in Other Operating Expenses

formulas.source_formula: Tertiary Industry Intermediate Input = Cost of Externally Purchased Goods + Cost of Externally Purchased Services + Intermediate Input in Administrative Expenses + Intermediate Input in Selling Expenses + Net Interest Expense + Intermediate Input in Other Operating Expenses

nodes.name: Tertiary Industry Production Subsidies
nodes.definition: Tertiary industry production subsidies refer to non-repayable payments made directly by the government to production units (such as enterprises or institutions) within the tertiary industry (service sector) to support or promote their production activities. It is one of the key original components in macroeconomic accounting for calculating net taxes on production and value added.

nodes.name: Tertiary Industry Production Taxes
nodes.definition: Tertiary industry production taxes refer to various taxes, fees, and surcharges paid to the government in national economic accounting for the production, sale, transfer of goods and services, or use of production factors (such as labor, land, and assets) in the tertiary industry (service sector). They are a component of net production taxes in calculating the value added of the tertiary industry using the income approach.

formulas.source_formula: Tertiary Industry Production Taxes = Tertiary Industry Net Production Taxes + Tertiary Industry Production Subsidies

operands.metric: Value Added of the Tertiary Industry
Tertiary Industry Consumption of Fixed Capital
Operating Surplus of the Tertiary Industry

formulas.source_formula: Tertiary Industry Production Taxes = Tertiary Industry Value Added - Tertiary Industry Compensation of Employees - Tertiary Industry Consumption of Fixed Capital - Tertiary Industry Operating Surplus + Tertiary Industry Production Subsidies

nodes.name: Testing Expenses
nodes.definition: Testing expenses refer to various costs incurred by an enterprise to inspect and verify the performance, safety, and compliance of products, technologies, systems, or services with established standards.

nodes.name: Texas Ratio
nodes.definition: The Texas Ratio assesses a bank's financial stability by comparing non-performing assets to the sum of tangible common equity and loan loss reserves. A higher ratio indicates heightened risk of financial distress.

formulas.source_formula: Texas Ratio (%) = Non-performing Assets ÷ (Tangible Common Equity + Loan Loss Reserves) × 100

nodes.name: The Most Likely Cash Flows to Be Generated by the Asset in the Future Period
Theoretical Ex-Rights Price (TERP)
nodes.definition: The theoretical ex-rights price is the implied share price after a rights issue, calculated by adding the pre-rights market value and the cash proceeds raised, then dividing by the total shares outstanding post-issue; it benchmarks the expected dilution and pricing following the offering.

formulas.source_formula: Theoretical Ex-Rights Price (TERP) = (Pre-rights Market Value + Funds Raised) ÷ Total Shares Post-issue

nodes.name: Theoretical Futures Price (Cost of Carry Model)
aliases: 期货价格（持有成本模型）
理论期货价格（持有成本模型）
nodes.definition: The theoretical futures price under the cost of carry model equals the spot price plus carrying costs, including storage, insurance, and the financing cost of holding the asset over the contract term, assuming no arbitrage and constant rates.

formulas.source_formula: Theoretical Gain = Index Change × Multiplier

nodes.name: Theoretical Value (Of a Right)
nodes.definition: The theoretical value of a subscription right during the ex-rights period represents the fair value of the detachable right to purchase shares at the subscription price. It is calculated as the difference between the ex-rights market price and the subscription price, scaled by the number of rights required to acquire one share, and typically excludes transaction costs and taxes.

formulas.source_formula: Theoretical Nil-Paid Price = Cum-Rights Price - Theoretical Ex-Rights Price

nodes.name: Theoretical Value of a Right (Cum Rights Period)
aliases: 含权期认股权理论价值
含权期配股权理论价值
nodes.definition: The theoretical value of a subscription right during the cum rights period represents the fair value per right when the shares still trade with rights attached. It is calculated by allocating the difference between the market price (including rights) and the subscription price across the total number of shares represented by the rights bundle (existing shares plus the new share to be purchased), reflecting the economic benefit of exercising the right before the stock trades ex-rights.

nodes.name: Theta
nodes.definition: Theta is one of the option Greeks, used to measure the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in time to expiration. It represents the change in the option's price for a one-unit decrease in time to expiration, all else being equal, and is typically negative to reflect time decay.

operands.metric: Option Price Change (due to Interest Rate Change)

formulas.source_formula: Theta = Change in Option Price ÷ Change in Time to Expiration

nodes.name: Theta (Time Decay)
nodes.definition: Theta measures the sensitivity of an option's price to the passage of time, defined as the partial derivative of the option value with respect to time (∂V/∂t).
