Holding other inputs constant, the expected change in the option's price over a small interval is approximated by theta multiplied by the change in time to expiration; theta is typically negative for long options, reflecting time decay.

nodes.name: Theta Decay
nodes.definition: Theta decay is the cumulative reduction in an option's time value as time passes, assuming other pricing inputs remain constant. It is computed as the option's per-day theta multiplied by the number of elapsed days.

nodes.name: Three-Sigma Limits
nodes.definition: Three-sigma limits are statistical process control thresholds set at three standard deviations above and below the process mean, used to establish the upper control limit (UCL) and lower control limit (LCL) for monitoring process stability and identifying special-cause variation.

nodes.name: Throughput
nodes.definition: Throughput is the production rate, representing the number of units completed per unit of time. It is used in managerial and cost accounting to evaluate process capacity, flow efficiency, and operational performance.

formulas.source_formula: Throughput = Inventory ÷ Production Time

nodes.name: Throughput Time
nodes.definition: Throughput time is the total elapsed time required for a unit to pass through the entire production process, including value-added processing time and non-value-added delays such as inspection, movement, and queue (waiting). It is used to assess flow efficiency, identify bottlenecks, and guide operational improvements.

formulas.source_formula: Throughput Time = Processing Time + Inspection Time + Move Time + Queue Time

nodes.name: Tick
nodes.definition: A tick is the minimum price increment at which a security can trade. A tick movement adjusts the quoted price by one tick size. The calculation provided yields the new price after an upward tick by adding the tick size to the current price, and is used to model minimum-increment price changes in order books, quote updates, and trade executions.

nodes.name: Tick Value
nodes.definition: Tick value is the monetary amount represented by a single minimum price movement (tick) of a trading instrument, typically calculated as the instrument's tick size multiplied by its contract multiplier. It is used in futures and other derivatives to quantify the profit or loss impact per tick.

formulas.source_formula: Tick Value = Tick Size × Contract Multiplier

nodes.name: Tier 1 Capital
aliases: 核心一级资本与其他一级资本之和
nodes.definition: Tier 1 Capital is a composite indicator for measuring a bank's capital adequacy, consisting of Common Equity Tier 1 Capital and Additional Tier 1 Capital. It is used to absorb losses and serves as the basis for calculating regulatory metrics such as the Capital Adequacy Ratio and the Supplementary Leverage Ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Tier 1 Capital = Common Equity Tier 1 Capital + Additional Tier 1 Capital

nodes.name: Tier 1 Capital Ratio
nodes.definition: Tier 1 Capital Ratio is a key regulatory metric that measures a bank's core capital adequacy by comparing its Tier 1 capital to its total risk-weighted assets, indicating the bank's ability to absorb losses and maintain financial stability under the Basel III framework.

formulas.source_formula: Tier 1 Capital Ratio = Tier 1 Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets × 100
supporting_source_formulas: Tier 1 Capital Ratio (%) = Tier 1 Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets × 100
Tier 1 Capital Ratio = Tier 1 Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets × 100

nodes.name: Tier 1 Common Capital Ratio
aliases: 普通股一级资本充足率
nodes.definition: The Tier 1 Common Capital Ratio measures a bank’s Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital relative to its risk-weighted assets, expressed as a percentage. It evaluates the quality and adequacy of core equity capital to absorb losses under regulatory frameworks such as Basel III.

formulas.source_formula: Tier 1 Common Capital Ratio = (Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) Capital ÷ Risk-Weighted Assets) × 100
Tier 1 Common Capital Ratio = ((Tier 1 Capital - Preferred Stock - Noncontrolling Interests) ÷ Total Risk-Weighted Assets) × 100

nodes.name: Tier 1 Leverage Ratio
nodes.definition: The Tier 1 Leverage Ratio measures a bank's core capital (Tier 1 Capital) relative to its average total assets, indicating the institution's ability to absorb losses and comply with regulatory capital adequacy requirements. It is commonly presented as a percentage and used in supervisory assessments of leverage risk.

formulas.source_formula: Tier 1 Leverage Ratio = (Tier 1 Capital ÷ Total Assets) × 100
supporting_source_formulas: Tier 1 Leverage Ratio = (Tier 1 Capital ÷ Total Assets) × 100
Tier 1 Leverage Ratio = (Tier 1 Capital ÷ Total Assets) × 100%

formulas.source_formula: Tier 1 Leverage Ratio (%) = (Tier 1 Capital ÷ Average Total Assets) × 100

nodes.name: Time
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, time refers to the dimension over which the value of money changes, with its core being the time value of money, meaning that a unit of currency today is worth more than the same unit in the future. It serves as a fundamental input parameter for calculating discounting, valuation, risk management, and numerous other financial metrics.

nodes.name: Time (Years)
nodes.definition: Time (Years) is the most fundamental unit of time in financial calculations, typically referring to the duration length for which a sum of money is invested, borrowed, or an asset is utilized. It is an essential raw input parameter for calculating financial metrics such as future value, present value, interest, depreciation, etc., and has no calculation formula itself, belonging to basic data.

nodes.name: Time Adjustment Factor
nodes.definition: The time adjustment factor is a multiplier used in asset valuation to adjust the transaction price or value of a comparable reference asset, reflecting differences arising from changes in market conditions, price levels, or the time value of money between its transaction date and the valuation base date.

nodes.name: Time Change
nodes.definition: Time change refers to the length of the time period from the start time to the end time, typically expressed in units of years, months, days, hours, minutes, or seconds. In financial management and finance, it is a fundamental metric for calculating holding period returns, discount factors, option time value decay, etc.

formulas.source_formula: Time Change = End Time - Start Time

nodes.name: Time Decay
nodes.definition: Time decay (Theta) is an option Greek that measures the rate at which an option's extrinsic value (premium) declines solely due to the passage of time, holding other factors constant. Theta is typically expressed per day and is negative for long options positions, reflecting the erosion of time value as expiration approaches.

nodes.name: Time Horizon
nodes.definition: Time horizon refers to the fundamental unit or concept used to measure the length or span of time, such as year, month, or day. In the field of finance and accounting, it typically serves as a given input parameter in analysis or calculations, used to describe the maturity period of bonds, the cycle of investment projects, the repayment period of loans, etc. It is a fundamental element for assessing the time value of money and risk-return trade-offs.

nodes.name: Time Outstanding
nodes.definition: Time outstanding refers to the actual length of time that newly issued common shares have been in circulation from the date of issuance to the end of the reporting period (or calculation cutoff date), typically expressed in days or months. It is a fundamental time parameter used in calculating the weighted average number of common shares outstanding.

nodes.name: Time Outstanding in the Prior Period
Time Premium
nodes.definition: Time premium is the difference between the market price of an option and its intrinsic value, reflecting the time value of the option due to its remaining term to expiration, representing the portion of the option's value that exceeds its intrinsic value.

formulas.source_formula: Time Premium = Option Value - Intrinsic Value

nodes.name: Time Quota
nodes.definition: Time quota refers to the working time required for a worker group or individual of a specific trade or technical grade to complete one qualified product under given production technology and organizational conditions. It is typically measured in 'man-days' and serves as a crucial foundation for production planning and cost accounting.

nodes.name: Time Repurchased in the Prior Period
Time Since Repurchase
nodes.definition: Time Since Repurchase refers to the time difference between the date a stock repurchase occurs and the reporting date. It is used as a time-weighting factor for calculating the weighted average number of common shares outstanding and the weighted average diluted common shares outstanding. It is a derivative concept in financial analysis used to adjust share count calculations.

formulas.source_formula: Time Since Repurchase = Reporting Date - Stock Repurchase Date

nodes.name: Time Standard
nodes.definition: Time standard refers to the standard time required to complete a specific process or work unit, serving as an important basis for production planning, cost accounting, and determining staffing and equipment requirements.

nodes.name: Time Step
nodes.definition: Time step is a key parameter in numerical simulation (e.g., Computational Fluid Dynamics, CFD) for discretizing the time dimension, referring to the time interval from one computational moment to the next. Its magnitude is typically determined based on stability conditions (e.g., the CFL criterion) to ensure the convergence and stability of the numerical solution.

formulas.source_formula: Time Step ≈ Grid Size ÷ (Maximum Velocity + Speed of Sound)

nodes.name: Time Value
nodes.definition: Time value is the portion of an option's price that exceeds its intrinsic value, reflecting the value attributed to time remaining until expiration, expected volatility, interest rates, and demand. It represents the market's assessment of the option's potential for future profitability beyond its current intrinsic worth.

formulas.source_formula: Time Value = Option Premium - Intrinsic Value

nodes.name: Time Value After Down Then Up Movement
Time Value of Money
nodes.definition: Time value of money is a core concept in financial management, referring to the principle that a given amount of money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. Its calculation relies on parameters such as present value, interest rate, and time period, quantified through simple or compound interest formulas, and serves as the foundation for evaluating investments, financing, and option pricing.

formulas.source_formula: Time Value of Money = Future Value - Present Value

nodes.name: Time Value of an Option
nodes.definition: Time value of an option, also called extrinsic value, is the portion of an option's premium attributable to time to expiration, implied volatility, interest rates, and expected dividends. It is calculated as the option's market price minus its intrinsic value and generally decays as expiration approaches (theta decay).

formulas.source_formula: Time Value of an Option = Current Option Price - Intrinsic Value

nodes.name: Time Value with Downward then Upward Movement
aliases: Time Value with Decrease then Increase
先降后升货币时间价值
nodes.definition: Time value with downward then upward movement is a composite measure of the time value of money, describing the process where time value first decreases and then increases under the influence of variables such as interest rates, time, or volatility. It is commonly used in the valuation of complex financial instruments, such as option pricing or discounted cash flow analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Time Value with Downward then Upward Movement = (Upward Probability × Upward Option Intrinsic Value + Downward Probability × Downward Option Intrinsic Value) ÷ (1 + Risk-free Rate) - Current Option Intrinsic Value

nodes.name: Time Weighted Period for Previously Issued Shares
aliases: Time Weighting Factor of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Time weighted period for previously issued shares refers to the length of time used to calculate the weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding in the prior period, specifically for time-weighting newly issued or repurchased ordinary shares during the current period. It typically denotes the duration from the transaction date of new issuances or repurchases to the end of the prior period (or reporting period end), reflecting the proportional time these shares were actually outstanding during the prior period.

nodes.name: Time Weighting
nodes.definition: Time weighting is a calculation parameter or method used in weighted average calculations (such as calculating the weighted average number of shares outstanding) to assign corresponding weights to different time periods, reflecting their relative importance within the total duration of the reporting period. It is not an independent primary accounting item itself, but rather a component within the calculation process.

operands.metric: Number of Days in the Period
Total Number of Days in the Reporting Period

formulas.source_formula: Time Weight = Number of Days in the Period ÷ Total Number of Days in the Reporting Period

operands.metric: Number of Months in the Period
Total Number of Months in the Reporting Period

formulas.source_formula: Time Weight = Number of Months in the Period ÷ Total Number of Months in the Reporting Period
Time to Clear Market = Homes Available ÷ Homes Sold

nodes.name: Time to Maturity
nodes.definition: Time to Maturity refers to the remaining length of time from the current date to the maturity date of a financial instrument (such as bonds, options), typically expressed in days or years. It is a key factor in calculating financial variables such as option prices and bond values, conforming to the definition of a non-leaf node.

formulas.source_formula: Time to Maturity = Maturity Date - Current Date
Time to Maturity = (Maturity Date - Current Date) ÷ Day Count Basis

nodes.name: Time to Maturity / Remaining Time
nodes.definition: Time to maturity refers to the time interval from the current point in time to a future target point (such as the maturity date or exercise date), and is a key derived time variable in financial valuation, option pricing, and project management.

formulas.source_formula: Remaining Time = Total Time - Elapsed Time
Remaining Time = Target Date - Current Date

nodes.name: Time-Weighted Rate of Return
nodes.definition: The Time-Weighted Rate of Return is a method for measuring portfolio performance. It divides the entire investment period into several sub-periods, calculates the return for each sub-period separately, and then geometrically averages these sub-period returns to obtain a compound return that is unaffected by cash inflows and outflows during the period. This method more purely reflects the investment management skill of the fund manager or the investment strategy itself.

nodes.name: Time-Weighting Factor
nodes.definition: The time-weighting factor is a calculated metric used in financial data adjustments (such as calculating the weighted average diluted number of common shares) to reflect the proportion of the time shares are outstanding relative to the total reporting period. It is typically derived as the ratio of the outstanding period to the total period, rather than being a raw underlying accounting figure.

operands.metric: Number of Days Shares are Outstanding
Total Number of Days in Reporting Period

formulas.source_formula: Time-Weighting Factor = Number of Days Shares are Outstanding ÷ Total Number of Days in Reporting Period

operands.metric: Number of Months Shares are Outstanding
Total Number of Months in Reporting Period

formulas.source_formula: Time-Weighting Factor = Number of Months Shares are Outstanding ÷ Total Number of Months in Reporting Period
Time-Weighting Factor = Shares Outstanding Period ÷ Total Reporting Period
Time-Weighting Factor = Outstanding Period ÷ Total Period

nodes.name: Times Interest Earned
nodes.definition: Times Interest Earned (TIE) measures how many times a company's earnings before interest and taxes can cover its interest obligations. It is calculated as EBIT divided by total interest expense and indicates the firm's debt service capacity and the safety margin for interest payments.

formulas.source_formula: Times Interest Earned (TIE) = EBIT ÷ Total Interest Payable
Times Interest Earned = Earnings Before Interest and Taxes (EBIT) ÷ Total Interest Expense

nodes.name: Times Revenue Valuation
nodes.definition: Times revenue valuation is a method that estimates a company’s value by multiplying its revenue by an industry-specific multiplier, commonly used when revenue growth is prioritized over profitability.

nodes.name: Times-Revenue Method
nodes.definition: The times-revenue method is a valuation approach that estimates a company's value by multiplying its revenue by an industry- or market-derived revenue multiple. It is commonly applied to early-stage or high-growth businesses with volatile or negative earnings, though it does not directly account for profitability or cost structure.

nodes.name: Tobin's Q Ratio
nodes.definition: Tobin's Q Ratio is a valuation metric that compares a firm's total asset value to its market value to assess how the market prices the company's assets relative to their replacement or book value. It is used in corporate finance and investment analysis to gauge valuation signals and potential investment opportunities.

formulas.source_formula: Tobin's Q Ratio = Total Asset Value ÷ Market Value

nodes.name: Tolerable Misstatement
nodes.definition: Tolerable misstatement is the maximum amount of misstatement in an account balance or class of transactions that an auditor is willing to accept without considering audit risk when planning and performing audit work. It is a key parameter in audit sampling used to determine sample size and evaluate audit results.

formulas.source_formula: Tolerable Misstatement = Tolerable Misstatement Rate × Assumed Average Misstatement Rate × Population Recorded Amount
Tolerable Misstatement = (Population Book Value × Risk Coefficient) ÷ Sample Size + (Expected Population Misstatement × Expansion Factor)

nodes.name: Tolerable Misstatement Rate
nodes.definition: Tolerable misstatement rate is a key concept in auditing, referring to the maximum ratio of misstatement amount to total book value that an auditor considers acceptable without affecting the overall opinion on the financial statements during audit sampling. It is commonly used to determine sample size in audit sampling and serves as a critical parameter for assessing audit risk and the acceptability of control testing.

nodes.name: Ton-Trip Fee
nodes.definition: The ton-trip fee is an additional charge levied based on cargo weight when calculating freight for full-load road cargo transportation. It primarily compensates for loading, unloading, and handling costs incurred at origin and destination during short-haul transportation, constituting a component of road freight rates.

nodes.name: Tooling Cost
nodes.definition: Tooling cost refers to the expenses incurred by an enterprise for the purchase, use, and maintenance of various tools and implements during production, operations, or project construction. Depending on the value and useful life of the tools, these costs may be capitalized as fixed assets, recorded as low-value consumables, or expensed as current period administrative costs.

nodes.name: Total Accumulated Losses from Prior Years
nodes.definition: Total accumulated losses from prior years refer to the cumulative sum of net losses reported on the financial statements over multiple past accounting periods, resulting from annual revenues being insufficient to cover costs and expenses. These losses are carried forward to subsequent years, affecting the company's distributable profits and income tax calculations.

formulas.source_formula: Total Acquisition Cost = Base Purchase Price + Earnout Payment

nodes.name: Total Acquisition Cost (Including Earnout)
aliases: 交易总对价（含或有对价）
nodes.definition: Total Acquisition Cost (including earnout) represents the full purchase consideration in a business combination, combining the upfront base purchase price with contingent consideration (earnout) that becomes payable if post-closing performance targets are achieved. This metric is used in deal structuring and transaction modeling to reflect the potential total outlay for an acquirer when earnout arrangements are present.

nodes.name: Total Activity Cost
aliases: 作业成本库归集总成本
nodes.definition: Total Activity Cost refers to the aggregate cost formed by allocating various resource expenses to activity cost pools through resource drivers under Activity-Based Costing. It serves as the basis for calculating activity cost allocation rates and reflects the total value of resources consumed in performing specific activities.

operands.metric: Actual Activity Costs Incurred in the Current Period

formulas.source_formula: Total Activity Cost = Actual Activity Costs Incurred in the Current Period

nodes.name: Total Activity Volume
nodes.definition: Total Activity Volume refers to the sum of resources consumed or outputs produced by all activities driven by a specific cost driver in an Activity-Based Costing (ABC) system. It is typically calculated by aggregating the workload of individual tasks that constitute the total activity, and serves as the basis for calculating the activity cost allocation rate.

nodes.name: Total Actual Working Hours of All Products
nodes.definition: Total actual working hours of all products refers to a composite indicator obtained by summing the actual working hours of each product. It is commonly used in cost accounting processes such as manufacturing overhead allocation rate calculation and serves as fundamental data for cost allocation.

nodes.name: Total Adjustment Items
nodes.definition: Total Adjustment Items is the aggregate item in the detailed schedule of tax adjustment items, reflecting the sum of all adjustment amounts made to accounting profit according to tax regulations when calculating taxable income. It is a key intermediate indicator for determining taxable income.

formulas.source_formula: Total Adjustment Items = Total Income Adjustment Items + Total Deduction Adjustment Items + Total Asset Adjustment Items + Total Special Item Adjustments + Total Other Adjustment Items

nodes.name: Total Administrative Expenses
nodes.definition: Total administrative expenses refer to the sum of all expenses incurred by an enterprise for organizing and managing production and operational activities during a specific accounting period. It is typically calculated as the product of a calculation base and an administrative expense rate, constitutes a significant component of total cost expenses, and is used to assess the enterprise's management efficiency and financial health.

nodes.name: Total Admitted Value of On-balance-sheet Assets
nodes.definition: Total Admitted Value of On-balance-sheet Assets refers to the net admitted value of assets obtained by aggregating all on-balance-sheet assets of an insurance company after risk adjustment and admission processing according to solvency regulatory rules under the insurance regulatory framework. It reflects the actual asset value recognized by the regulatory authority that can be used to cover the insurer's liabilities and risks, serving as a crucial foundational data point for calculating regulatory metrics such as the solvency adequacy ratio.

nodes.name: Total Allocation Base
nodes.definition: Total Allocation Base is the denominator used to calculate the allocation rate in cost accounting, representing the sum of all allocation base amounts (such as labor hours, machine hours, etc.) for cost objects. It is a composite metric that can be derived through summation.

nodes.name: Total Allocation Base for All Cost Objects
aliases: 各产品分配标准的合计
nodes.definition: Total Allocation Base for All Cost Objects is an intermediate metric used in the cost allocation process to calculate the allocation rate. It is derived by summing the allocation bases (such as weight, labor hours, raw material consumption, etc.) for each cost object and is a calculable composite metric.

nodes.name: Total Amount Allocated
nodes.definition: Total Amount Allocated refers to the aggregate sum of resources such as costs, expenses, or profits that serves as the dividend in allocation calculations. Its value is typically derived by aggregating other fundamental allocation items (e.g., profits, costs) rather than being sourced directly from original accounting records, and it is a key element in calculating the allocation rate.

nodes.name: Total Amount Involved in Default
nodes.definition: Total Amount Involved in Default refers to the full sum of money implicated in a contract or debt relationship due to one party's failure to fulfill agreed terms (such as non-payment at maturity), which serves as the basis for calculating default penalties or compensation. It typically refers to the overdue principal or the contractual principal amount.

nodes.name: Total Amount Payable to Depositors
nodes.definition: Total Amount Payable to Depositors is a core liability on a bank's balance sheet, referring to the aggregate sum of all deposits absorbed by the bank from various clients, including individuals and enterprises, representing the total debt the bank owes and must repay to its depositors.

nodes.name: Total Amount of Asset Adjustment Items
nodes.definition: Total Amount of Asset Adjustment Items refers to the aggregated value of all tax adjustments or accounting adjustments related to assets when preparing financial statements (such as the Annual Corporate Income Tax Return). It is typically used to reflect the overall scale of adjustments made to the carrying value of assets or related profits and losses due to differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations.

nodes.name: Total Amount of Deduction Adjustment Items
aliases: 扣除类纳税调整项目合计
nodes.definition: The total amount of deduction adjustment items refers to the aggregate sum of all deduction items requiring upward or downward tax adjustments during the enterprise income tax final settlement, based on tax law provisions regarding various costs, expenses, losses, and other deductible items calculated from the accounting profit. It reflects the total difference between accounting treatment and tax law provisions concerning deductible items.

nodes.name: Total Amount of Income Adjustment Items
aliases: 收入类纳税调整项目合计
收入调整项目汇总金额
nodes.definition: Total Amount of Income Adjustment Items refers to the aggregate amount of all income-related adjustment items after reconciling the differences between accounting income recognized under accounting standards and income deductible before tax as permitted by tax laws, during an enterprise's annual corporate income tax filing. It is typically reflected in the 'Detailed Schedule of Tax Adjustment Items' (A105000) and represents the total net increase or decrease in taxable income from income adjustments when calculating taxable income.

nodes.name: Total Amount of Other Adjustment Items
nodes.definition: Refers to the aggregate amount of various income, deduction, or asset items requiring tax adjustments during corporate income tax final settlement, arising from differences between accounting treatment and tax regulations, excluding specifically listed adjustment items. This total amount reflects the net adjustment impact of all discrepancy items not individually detailed in the tax adjustment item schedule.

nodes.name: Total Amount of Special Item Adjustments
aliases: Total Amount of Special Adjustment Items
nodes.definition: The total amount of special item adjustments refers to the aggregate sum of amounts for individual items that require adjustment according to tax laws or accounting standards for specific, non-recurring, or specially characterized transactions or events in corporate tax filing or accounting treatment. These adjustments are typically not included in regular revenue, cost, or expense adjustments but are specific adjustments made for particular circumstances (such as deemed sales, non-taxable income, special asset depreciation, etc.).

nodes.name: Total Amount of Taxable Income Adjustment Items
aliases: Amount of Taxable Income Adjustments Increase
nodes.definition: Total Amount of Taxable Income Adjustment Items refers to the aggregate amount of specific items that require an increase in taxable income when calculating corporate income tax payable, based on tax regulations that adjust accounting profit for tax purposes. These items typically include adjustments related to revenue, deductions, assets, and special transactions, with the summarized result reported in the 'Adjustment Increase Amount' column of the tax return.

nodes.name: Total Amount to be Allocated
nodes.definition: The Total Amount to be Allocated refers to the aggregate sum of indirect costs, expenses, or other resources that need to be apportioned to various cost objects (such as products, departments, or projects) according to specific allocation criteria during the cost or expense allocation process. It is an intermediate concept derived from the aggregation or calculation of base data and serves as a key component in determining the allocation rate.

formulas.source_formula: Total Amount to be Allocated = Total Service Volume × Allocation Rate
Total Amount to be Allocated = Allocation Rate × Total Allocation Base

operands.metric: Total Indirect Costs to be Allocated

formulas.source_formula: Total Amount to be Allocated = Total Indirect Costs to be Allocated

nodes.name: Total Annual Profit
nodes.definition: Total annual profit refers to the sum of pre-tax profit generated by an enterprise in a specific accounting year through operating activities, investment activities, and non-operating activities (non-operating income and expenses). It is a key indicator for measuring the comprehensive profitability of an enterprise on an annual basis.

formulas.source_formula: Total Annual Profit = Operating Profit + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses

Total Annual Profit = Operating Revenue - Operating Costs - Taxes and Surcharges - Selling Expenses - Administrative Expenses - R&D Expenses - Financial Expenses - Credit Impairment Losses - Asset Impairment Losses + Gains from Changes in Fair Value + Investment Income + Other Income + Non-operating Income - Non-operating Expenses

nodes.name: Total Assessment Base
nodes.definition: Total Assessment Base refers to the aggregate sum of various amounts that serve as the basis or benchmark for calculating certain expenses (such as indirect costs). It typically constitutes a portion of direct costs or contract value, used to accrue related expenses according to a specified percentage.

nodes.name: Total Asset Turnover
nodes.definition: Total Asset Turnover reflects the ability of a company's total assets to support operating revenue over a certain period, measuring the utilization efficiency of the company's overall assets.

formulas.source_formula: Total Asset Turnover = Sales Revenue ÷ Total Assets
Total Asset Turnover = Total Sales ÷ Total Assets

nodes.name: Total Asset Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: In finance, the total asset turnover ratio is a financial ratio used to measure the efficiency with which a company utilizes its assets to generate sales revenue or operating income. This ratio falls under profitability and operating efficiency metrics and is commonly used in DuPont analysis to calculate Return on Equity (ROE). Typically, companies with lower profit margins have higher asset turnover ratios, while those with higher profit margins have lower asset turnover ratios.

formulas.source_formula: Total Asset Turnover Ratio = Sales Revenue ÷ Total Assets
Total Asset Turnover Ratio = Net Operating Income ÷ Average Total Assets

nodes.name: Total Assets
nodes.definition: Total assets refer to all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise, including current assets and non-current assets. It is a fundamental financial metric for measuring a company's scale, financial position, and value, widely used in financial ratio analysis and capital structure assessment.

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets = Liabilities + Owners' Equity
Total Assets = Current Assets + Non-current Assets
supporting_source_formulas: Total Assets = Current Assets + Non-current Assets

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets = Current Assets + Fixed Assets + Intangible Assets
Total Assets = Current Assets + Long-term Investments + Fixed Assets + Intangible Assets + Other Assets
Total Assets = Current Assets + Long-term Investments + Fixed Assets + Intangible Assets and Other Assets
Total Assets = Liabilities + Contributed Capital + Beginning Retained Earnings + Revenue - Expenses - Dividends

nodes.name: Total Assets at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Total assets at the beginning of a period refers to the aggregate value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It is typically carried forward directly from the total assets at the end of the preceding accounting period. As a fundamental point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, it is used for subsequent financial analysis and calculations (e.g., calculating average assets).

nodes.name: Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter
aliases: Total Assets at the Beginning of Q2
nodes.definition: Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter refers to the total book value of assets on the first day of the second quarter (typically April 1), which is a direct line-item figure on the balance sheet, reflecting the overall asset scale of the enterprise at the start of the second quarter.

nodes.name: Total Assets at Beginning of Year
aliases: Total Assets at the Beginning of the Year
nodes.definition: Total assets at the beginning of the year refer to the sum of the book values of all asset items presented on the balance sheet at the start of an accounting year (typically January 1st). It is a point-in-time figure directly taken from the opening balances in the company's books, reflecting the financial position and resource scale at the commencement of the fiscal year.

nodes.name: Total Assets at End of First Quarter
aliases: Total Assets at the End of the First Quarter
nodes.definition: Total assets at the end of the first quarter refer to the sum of a company's assets at the conclusion of the first quarter, reflecting its financial position at that point in time. It can be derived from the total assets line item on the balance sheet or calculated using the accounting equation 'Assets = Liabilities + Owners' Equity'.

operands.metric: Total Liabilities at End of First Quarter
Total Owners' Equity at End of First Quarter

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets at End of First Quarter = Total Liabilities at End of First Quarter + Total Owners' Equity at End of First Quarter

nodes.name: Total Assets at End of Q1
Total Assets at End of Q2
aliases: Total Assets at the End of Q2
第二季度期末资产总额
nodes.definition: Total assets at the end of the second quarter refer to the aggregate value of all assets owned or controlled by an enterprise at the specific point in time when the second fiscal quarter concludes (typically June 30), including both current assets and non-current assets.

nodes.name: Total Assets at End of Q3
Total Assets at End of Second Quarter
aliases: Total Assets at the End of the Second Quarter
nodes.definition: Total Assets at End of Second Quarter refers to the total value of all resources owned or controlled by an enterprise as of the last balance sheet date of the second quarter (typically June 30), from which future economic benefits are expected to flow. As a point-in-time indicator, it reflects the scale and structure of the enterprise's financial resources at a specific moment and serves as the basis for calculating financial ratios such as average total assets and asset turnover ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets at End of Second Quarter = Total Current Assets + Total Non-current Assets

operands.metric: Average Total Assets for Second Quarter
Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets at End of Second Quarter = Average Total Assets for Second Quarter × 2 - Total Assets at Beginning of Second Quarter

nodes.name: Total Assets at End of Third Quarter
aliases: Total Assets at the End of the Third Quarter
nodes.definition: Total Assets at End of Third Quarter refers to the aggregate book value of all economic resources owned or controlled by an enterprise at the specific point in time marking the conclusion of the third fiscal quarter (typically September 30). It is a critical point-in-time figure on the balance sheet, directly reflecting the scale of the enterprise's assets at quarter-end.

nodes.name: Total Assets at Period End
aliases: Total Assets at End of Period
nodes.definition: Total Assets at Period End is a composite indicator on the balance sheet, representing the total value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the reporting period end (e.g., fiscal year-end). It is calculated through formulas, reflecting the enterprise's operating results, changes in financial position, and asset allocation over a specific period, and is commonly used as the basis for calculating other financial metrics.

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets at Period End = Total Liabilities + Owners' Equity
Total Assets at Period End = Current Assets at Period End + Non-current Assets at Period End

operands.metric: Increase in Assets during the Period
Decrease in Assets during the Period

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets at Period End = Total Assets at Period Beginning + Increase in Assets during the Period - Decrease in Assets during the Period

nodes.name: Total Assets at Year-End
nodes.definition: Total Assets at Year-End refers to the sum of the book values of all asset items listed on a company's balance sheet at the end of each fiscal year (typically December 31st). It directly reflects the total economic resources owned or controlled by the enterprise at a specific point in time and serves as fundamental raw data for assessing the company's scale, financial structure, and solvency.

nodes.name: Total Assets at the End of Base Period
aliases: Total Assets at Base Period End
nodes.definition: Total assets at the end of the base period refer to the total value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the conclusion of a specific reference period (the base period) used for comparative purposes. It is typically derived from the balance sheet at the end of the base period and serves as the foundational raw data for calculating dynamic indicators such as asset growth rate.

nodes.name: Total Assets for the Period
nodes.definition: Total assets for the period refer to the aggregate value of all economic resources owned or controlled by an enterprise at the end of a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a fiscal year). It is the most critical summary figure on the balance sheet, directly reflecting the scale of the enterprise.

nodes.name: Total Assets in Base Period
nodes.definition: Total assets in the base period refer to the aggregate value of all assets owned by an enterprise at the end of a specific period designated as the benchmark for comparison. It serves as the reference basis for calculating subsequent changes in assets or related financial indicators, such as projected total assets.

nodes.name: Total Assets of Previous Period
nodes.definition: Total assets of the previous period refer to the aggregate amount of all asset items presented on the balance sheet at the end of the preceding accounting period (e.g., previous quarter, previous fiscal year), reflecting the total value of economic resources owned or controlled by the enterprise at the end of the prior period.

nodes.name: Total Assets of Subsidiary
nodes.definition: Total assets of a subsidiary refer to the aggregate value of all resources owned or controlled by the subsidiary as of the balance sheet date that are expected to generate economic benefits. It represents the sum of the book values of all asset items (such as current assets, fixed assets, intangible assets, etc.) and serves as the fundamental raw data for calculating financial metrics like return on assets.

nodes.name: Total Assets to Revenue Ratio
nodes.definition: The Total Assets to Revenue Ratio reflects the proportion of a company's total assets relative to its sales revenue, indicating the extent to which assets support business operations.

formulas.source_formula: Total Assets to Revenue Ratio = Total Assets ÷ Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Total Auxiliary Production Cost
nodes.definition: Total auxiliary production cost refers to the aggregate amount of all expenses incurred by a company's internal auxiliary production departments (such as power supply, water supply, machinery maintenance, transportation, etc.) within a specific period for providing products or services to basic production departments, administrative management departments, and others. It serves as fundamental data for cost accounting and is typically accumulated based on actual direct costs such as material costs, labor costs, and manufacturing overhead.

nodes.name: Total Auxiliary Production Costs
nodes.definition: Total auxiliary production costs refer to the aggregate of all production expenses incurred by an enterprise's auxiliary production workshops (such as power supply, water supply, machinery maintenance, etc.) within a specific period for providing products or services. In accounting, these costs are accumulated on the debit side of the 'Auxiliary Production Cost' account and serve as the basis for calculating the unit cost of auxiliary production products or services.

formulas.source_formula: Total BOE/D = Oil Production (bbl/d) + BOE from Gas

nodes.name: Total Base Amount
nodes.definition: The Total Base Amount typically refers to the total wage base used for calculating social insurance premiums, housing provident fund contributions, or other fees (such as general price measure fees) within a specific reporting period (e.g., a calendar year). In contexts such as annual business reports, it often refers to the cumulative sum of the declared contribution wage bases for all employees of an entity during the reporting period.

nodes.name: Total Beginning Net Assets
nodes.definition: Total beginning net assets refers to the total economic interests of owners (or shareholders) in the enterprise's assets at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or a quarter). Its amount equals total beginning assets minus total beginning liabilities, reflecting the enterprise's financial net worth at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Total Beginning Owner's Equity
nodes.definition: Total beginning owner's equity refers to the total amount of owner's equity at the start of the current accounting period. It is directly taken from the ending balance of the previous accounting period's (e.g., the prior year) financial statements and reflects the residual value of equity attributable to owners at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Total Bond Financing Proceeds
nodes.definition: Total bond financing proceeds refer to the total amount of funds a company actually raises from the capital market by issuing bonds. It is typically equal to the total face value of the bonds issued; however, after accounting for issuance costs (such as underwriting fees, legal fees, etc.), the net proceeds available to the company are less than this total amount. This metric is an important figure for measuring the scale of a company's debt financing.

nodes.name: Total Bond Interest
nodes.definition: Total bond interest refers to the cumulative sum of all interest payments made by the issuer to bondholders over the entire life of the bond, based on the bond's coupon rate and face value.

nodes.name: Total Bond Value
nodes.definition: Total bond value refers to the sum of the present values of all future cash flows from the bond (including periodic interest payments and the principal repayment at maturity), discounted to the present time using an appropriate discount rate (typically the market interest rate or the investor's required rate of return). It represents the theoretical price or fair value of the bond in the market.

nodes.name: Total Book Assets
nodes.definition: Total book assets refer to the sum of the book values of all asset items presented on the financial statements at a specific point in time (typically the balance sheet date), in accordance with accounting standards and the historical cost principle. It reflects all resources owned or controlled by the enterprise that are expected to generate economic benefits.

nodes.name: Total Book Value
nodes.definition: Total book value refers to the net value of all assets or individual assets of an enterprise measured according to accounting principles and methods, typically calculated as the original asset value minus accumulated depreciation (or amortization) and impairment provisions, reflecting the carrying value of assets on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Total Book Value = Carrying Amount of Assets - Asset Depreciation or Amortization - Asset Impairment Provisions

nodes.name: Total Borrowings at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Total borrowings at the beginning of a period refers to the aggregate book balance of all borrowing accounts (such as short-term borrowings, long-term borrowings, etc.) at the start of a specific accounting period (e.g., a fiscal year, quarter, or month). It is a point-in-time figure that reflects the total principal amount of borrowings undertaken by the enterprise at the beginning of the period.

nodes.name: Total Borrowings at Period End
aliases: 期末负债总额（借款部分）
nodes.definition: Total borrowings at period end refers to the aggregate sum of all outstanding principal amounts of borrowings at the conclusion of a specific accounting period (such as month-end, quarter-end, or year-end). It is directly sourced from the company's accounting records or loan agreements, reflecting the scale of the company's borrowing liabilities at that point in time. This figure serves as fundamental data for analyzing the company's debt position and calculating related financial metrics.

nodes.name: Total Budget Allocation Standard
nodes.definition: Total Budget Allocation Standard refers to the benchmark or aggregate indicator used during the budget preparation and management process to determine the total amount of allocable resources for various budget items or cost centers. It typically serves as the foundation and ceiling for subsequent specific allocations (such as calculating allocation standard values).

nodes.name: Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead
aliases: 固定制造费用预算总额
nodes.definition: Total Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead refers to the total amount of manufacturing overhead costs that are expected to be incurred during the budget period to support production activities and do not vary with changes in production volume or business activity. It is directly determined during the budget preparation phase based on historical data, contractual agreements, or management decisions, and serves as a fundamental data point for cost control and variance analysis.

nodes.name: Total Budgeted Hours
nodes.definition: Total Budgeted Hours refers to the pre-estimated total number of labor hours required to complete the production plan or work tasks for a specific period (such as a budget cycle) during the budgeting process. It serves as fundamental input data for developing financial budgets such as labor cost budgets and manufacturing overhead allocation rates.

nodes.name: Total Budgeted Manufacturing Overhead
nodes.definition: Total Budgeted Manufacturing Overhead refers to the total estimated manufacturing overhead costs expected to be incurred during the budget period to complete the budgeted activity level. It consists of two parts: the fixed manufacturing overhead budget and the variable manufacturing overhead budget, and serves as the basis for calculating the standard manufacturing overhead allocation rate.

operands.metric: Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead per Unit

formulas.source_formula: Total Budgeted Manufacturing Overhead = Fixed Manufacturing Overhead Budget + (Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead per Unit × Budgeted Activity Level)

nodes.name: Total Budgeted Overhead
nodes.definition: Total budgeted overhead refers to the sum of all planned expenses during the budget period that support overall operations and production activities but cannot be directly attributed to specific products or services. These expenses typically include administrative costs, rent, utilities, depreciation, and certain research and development support costs, serving as a crucial basis for comprehensive budgeting and cost control.

nodes.name: Total Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead
aliases: Flexible Budget for Variable Manufacturing Overhead
变动制造费用预算总额
弹性预算下变动制造费用
nodes.definition: Total Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead refers to the pre-calculated total amount of variable manufacturing overhead based on a specific activity level (such as direct labor hours or machine hours) and a standard allocation rate under the flexible budgeting method. It is a key component of the manufacturing overhead budget.

operands.metric: Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate

formulas.source_formula: Total Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead = Budgeted Activity Level (Direct Labor Hours) × Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate

operands.metric: Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate

formulas.source_formula: Total Budgeted Variable Manufacturing Overhead = Budgeted Activity Level (Machine Hours) × Standard Variable Manufacturing Overhead Allocation Rate

nodes.name: Total Business Volume
nodes.definition: Total business volume refers to the aggregate quantity or total scale of all business activities completed by an organization, department, or business unit within a specific period (such as monthly, quarterly, or annually). It is a comprehensive metric that can be represented as the number of transactions processed, sales completed, services provided, or total workload accounted for, used to measure operational scale, efficiency, and outcomes.

formulas.source_formula: Total Buydown Savings = Loan Amount × (Reduction Rate (Year 1) + Reduction Rate (Year 2) + Reduction Rate (Year 3))

nodes.name: Total Capital
nodes.definition: Total capital refers to the overall capital of a company, including debt capital and equity capital, serving as a fundamental component in the calculation of Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC), and is classified as a non-leaf node.

formulas.source_formula: Total Capital = Total Debt + Total Equity
supporting_source_formulas: Total Capital = Total Debt + Total Equity

formulas.source_formula: Total Capital = Total Assets - Operating Current Liabilities
Total Capital = Working Capital + Long-term Investments + Fixed Assets + Intangible Assets and Deferred Assets + Other Long-term Assets

nodes.name: Total Capital After Capital Increase
aliases: Total Registered Capital After Capital Injection
nodes.definition: Total capital after capital increase refers to the total amount of a company's registered capital after it has been increased through methods such as introducing new shareholders or existing shareholders making additional investments. It reflects the total capital subscribed by the company's shareholders in the articles of association after the capital increase transaction is completed.

nodes.name: Total Capital Contributed by Partners
nodes.definition: Total capital contributed by partners refers to the aggregate sum of capital actually invested into a partnership (such as a general partnership, limited partnership, or private fund) by all partners in accordance with the partnership agreement. It is directly sourced from accounting records or the partnership agreement, representing the simple summation of the actual capital contributions made by each partner, and reflects the actual capital base received by the enterprise for operations and liability assumption.

nodes.name: Total Capital Cost
nodes.definition: Total capital cost, also known as the cost of capital, refers to the expense or opportunity cost incurred by a company to raise and utilize all capital (including debt capital and equity capital). It is typically calculated using the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) model, reflecting the comprehensive financing cost of the company's overall capital structure. It serves as a key parameter for evaluating investment projects, calculating economic profit, and other decision-making processes.

formulas.source_formula: Total Capital Cost = Annual Capital Usage Cost ÷ [Total Financing × (1 - Financing Fee Rate)]

Total Capital Cost = [Debt Capital Interest × (1 - Income Tax Rate)] ÷ [Total Debt Financing × (1 - Debt Financing Fee Rate)] × (Debt Capital ÷ Total Capital) + Cost of Equity × (Equity Capital ÷ Total Capital)

nodes.name: Total Capital Market Value
nodes.definition: Total capital market value refers to the sum of the market values of a company's equity capital and debt capital. It is an important metric for measuring the overall valuation of a company in the capital market, commonly used in capital structure analysis and weighted average cost of capital (WACC) calculations.

nodes.name: Total Carrying Cost
nodes.definition: Total carrying cost refers to the sum of all related expenses incurred by an enterprise for holding and maintaining inventory. These costs include not only directly visible expenditures such as warehouse rent, labor, and insurance, but also opportunity costs (such as interest) arising from capital occupation, as well as potential inventory obsolescence and deterioration.

nodes.name: Total Cascading Tax
nodes.definition: Total Cascading Tax is the aggregate amount of indirect taxes imposed cumulatively at successive production and sales stages when input tax credits are unavailable, capturing the tax-on-tax burden prevalent in non-credit or pre-GST regimes.

nodes.name: Total Cash
nodes.definition: Total cash refers to the sum of all cash and cash equivalents held by an enterprise or individual at a specific point in time, reflecting the entity's immediate payment capability and liquidity position.

nodes.name: Total Cash Dividends
nodes.definition: Total cash dividends refer to the aggregate amount of cash dividends actually paid to all shareholders during a specific accounting period, as resolved by the board of directors or shareholders' meeting. It reflects the cash outflow from the company for profit distribution to shareholders.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cash Flows = (Coupon Payment × Average Life Years) + Face Value

nodes.name: Total Cash Holdings
nodes.definition: Total Cash Holdings refers to the aggregate amount of cash a company holds to meet transactional, precautionary, and speculative needs under cash management models in financial management. It is typically calculated by minimizing total costs (the sum of transaction costs and opportunity costs) to determine the optimal value and serves as a core indicator of cash management strategy.

nodes.name: Total Cash Inflow
nodes.definition: Total cash inflow refers to the aggregate amount of all cash and cash equivalents flowing into an enterprise during a specific period. It is typically calculated using net cash flow and cash outflow, serving as a key indicator in cash flow statements and analysis to assess the enterprise's cash generation capacity.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cash Inflow = Net Cash Flow - Cash Outflow

nodes.name: Total Cash Inflow for the Period
nodes.definition: Total cash inflow for the period refers to the aggregate sum of all cash received by an enterprise through operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities during a specific accounting period (such as a quarter or a year). It is a direct summary item in the cash flow statement, reflecting the enterprise's ability to generate cash during that period.

nodes.name: Total Cash Inflow from Operating Activities
aliases: Total Cash Inflows from Operating Activities
经营活动现金流入合计
经营活动现金流入总量
nodes.definition: Total Cash Inflow from Operating Activities refers to the aggregate sum of all cash received by an enterprise during the reporting period through its routine operating activities, including cash from sales of goods or services, tax refunds received, and other cash receipts related to operating activities. This metric is a core component of the cash flow statement, classified as a composite indicator. It is calculated by summing its sub-items and is used to assess the cash-generating capacity of an enterprise's core business operations.

operands.metric: Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities
Total Cash Outflow from Operating Activities

formulas.source_formula: Total Cash Inflow from Operating Activities = Net Cash Flow from Operating Activities + Total Cash Outflow from Operating Activities

operands.metric: Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Services
Other Cash Receipts Related to Operating Activities

formulas.source_formula: Total Cash Inflow from Operating Activities = Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Services + Tax Refunds Received + Other Cash Receipts Related to Operating Activities

operands.metric: Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Rendering of Services
Cash Received from Other Operating Activities

formulas.source_formula: Total Cash Inflow from Operating Activities = Cash Received from Sales of Goods and Rendering of Services + Tax Refunds Received + Cash Received from Other Operating Activities

nodes.name: Total Cash Inflows for the Period
Total Cash Inflows from Investing Activities in Next Period
aliases: Next Period Investing Activities Cash Inflows Subtotal
Total Cash Inflows from Investing Activities for Next Period
下期投资现金流入合计
下期投资现金流入总额
未来投资活动现金流入小计
nodes.definition: Refers to the aggregate amount of all cash inflows that an enterprise expects to receive from investing activities in the next accounting period (such as the next quarter or the following fiscal year). These cash inflows typically arise from the recovery of investments, receipt of investment returns, disposal of fixed assets, intangible assets, and other long-term assets.

nodes.name: Total Cash Outflow
nodes.definition: Total Cash Outflow refers to the sum of all cash expenditures related to investment, financing, and operating activities within a specific period (typically a financial analysis cycle or project period). In project investment financial evaluation, particularly when preparing the total investment cash flow statement, it is a key calculation step used to ultimately determine net cash flow and various evaluation metrics.

nodes.name: Total Cash Outflow for the Period
nodes.definition: Total cash outflow for the period refers to the total amount of cash actually paid by an enterprise during a specific period due to investment activities, operating activities, etc. It is a key indicator for preparing cash flow statements, making project investment decisions, and conducting financial analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cash Outflow for the Period = Construction Investment + Working Capital + Operating Costs + Value-Added Tax Payable + Input Tax + Surtax + Sustaining Capital Investment

nodes.name: Total Cash Outflow from Operating Activities
nodes.definition: Total cash outflow from operating activities refers to the aggregate sum of all cash actually disbursed by an enterprise in its daily business operations to maintain normal functioning. This includes cash expenditures directly related to core business activities, such as purchasing raw materials, paying employee salaries, remitting various taxes and fees, and covering rent, utilities, and similar expenses.

nodes.name: Total Cash Outflows for the Period
Total Cash Outflows from Operating Activities
nodes.definition: Total cash outflows from operating activities refers to the aggregate sum of all cash actually disbursed by an enterprise in its daily business operations to maintain normal functioning. It is a fundamental data point in the cash flow statement, derived directly from accounting records, and reflects the enterprise's cash expenditures in routine business activities such as procurement, salary payments, and tax payments.

nodes.name: Total Cash Receipts
nodes.definition: Total cash receipts refer to the aggregate sum of all cash actually received by an enterprise during a specific accounting period through all operating activities, investing activities, and financing activities. It reflects the enterprise's ability to generate cash and serves as a fundamental data point for analyzing its cash flow position.

nodes.name: Total Cash Received from Issuing Shares
aliases: 发行股票实际收到股款净额
吸收投资所收到的现金
吸收权益性投资所收到的现金
nodes.definition: Total cash received from issuing shares refers to the net cash amount actually flowing into the enterprise after deducting issuance expenses such as commissions and fees paid to underwriters and brokers, raised through the issuance of shares (including common shares, preferred shares, etc.). This amount reflects the net cash inflow obtained by the enterprise through equity financing activities.

nodes.name: Total Cash Received from Share Issuance
Total Cash Return During Holding Period
aliases: Total Cash Income During Holding Period
nodes.definition: Total cash return during holding period refers to the sum of all cash-form returns actually received by an investor throughout the entire period of holding a specific asset (such as stocks or bonds), including, for example, stock dividends and bond interest. These returns are cash directly flowing into the investor's account, which can be directly traced from transaction records or financial statements without requiring complex calculations.

nodes.name: Total Common Shares Outstanding at Period End
aliases: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Period End
报告期末普通股总股数
nodes.definition: Total common shares outstanding at period end refers to the total number of shares issued and held by common shareholders at the conclusion of a specific accounting period (such as quarter-end or year-end). It serves as a crucial base figure for calculating key financial metrics such as earnings per share and dividends per share.

formulas.source_formula: Total Compounding Periods = Compounding Frequency × Years

nodes.name: Total Comprehensive Income
nodes.definition: Total Comprehensive Income refers to the total change in owners' equity during a specific accounting period resulting from all transactions and events other than those with owners in their capacity as owners. It reflects the entity's total performance achieved during the reporting period, including realized and recognized net profit, as well as other comprehensive income that is unrealized but recognized in accordance with accounting standards.

nodes.name: Total Consumption
nodes.definition: Total consumption refers to the aggregate monetary expenditure by individuals, households, or the entire economy on goods and services within a specified period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It reflects the overall scale and level of consumption activity and serves as a key indicator for measuring economic demand.

nodes.name: Total Consumption Amount
nodes.definition: Total Consumption Amount refers to the total monetary sum paid by individuals, households, enterprises, or specific groups for purchasing goods and services within a defined period (such as a day, month, or year). It serves as the fundamental raw data for measuring consumption levels.

nodes.name: Total Consumption During Delivery Period
nodes.definition: Total consumption during delivery period refers to the total quantity of parts or materials consumed by an enterprise during the time required for goods to be delivered from the supplier.

formulas.source_formula: Total Consumption During Delivery Period = Order Quantity per Batch ÷ Daily Delivery Quantity × Daily Consumption Quantity

nodes.name: Total Contract Amount
nodes.definition: Total Contract Amount refers to the original gross sum explicitly agreed upon by both parties in a contract, which is required to be paid or received for fulfilling all obligations or transactions under the contract. It is typically the aggregate of various fees, prices, or remunerations, serving as the most fundamental and core financial data of the contract. This amount is directly derived from the contractual terms and is not calculated through other financial indicators.

nodes.name: Total Contribution Limit
nodes.definition: The total contribution limit is the statutory cap on aggregate annual additions to a qualified retirement plan from all sources (employee elective-deferrals, employer contributions, and catch-up contributions where applicable). It is applied as the lesser of 100% of compensation or the preset maximum for the plan year, with higher limits permitted for participants age 50 and over under catch-up rules.

nodes.name: Total Contribution Margin
nodes.definition: Total contribution margin is the balance remaining after subtracting total variable costs from sales revenue. It measures the extent to which product sales revenue contributes to covering fixed costs and generating profit after covering variable costs, and is an important composite indicator for analyzing operating leverage effects.

formulas.source_formula: Total Contribution Margin = Unit Contribution Margin × Sales Volume
Total Contribution Margin = Sales Revenue - Total Variable Costs
Total Contribution Margin = Sales Revenue × Contribution Margin Ratio

nodes.name: Total Contribution Margin of All Products
nodes.definition: Total Contribution Margin of All Products refers to the difference between the total sales revenue from all products sold by an enterprise within a certain period and the corresponding total variable costs. It reflects the total contribution made by all product sales revenue towards covering fixed costs and generating profit after compensating for variable costs.

nodes.name: Total Cost
nodes.definition: Total cost refers to all expenses incurred by a company in various business activities, including opportunity costs and transaction costs in cash management, ordering costs, purchasing costs, and holding costs in inventory management, as well as variable costs and fixed costs in general cost management.

nodes.name: Total Cost (High-Low Method)
nodes.definition: Total Cost (High-Low Method) represents the linear cost estimate derived from the high-low method, calculated as the fixed cost plus the variable cost per unit multiplied by the activity units. It is used to estimate mixed costs at a specific activity level under the assumption of linear cost behavior.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost = Fixed Cost + (Variable Cost per Unit × Units of Activity)

nodes.name: Total Cost (Including Stockout and Safety Stock)
aliases: Total Inventory Cost including Stockout and Safety Stock
nodes.definition: Total cost (including stockout and safety stock) refers to the sum of stockout costs, safety stock costs, and other relevant inventory costs (such as ordering costs and holding costs) in inventory management.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost (Including Stockout and Safety Stock) = Stockout Cost + Safety Stock Cost
Total Cost (Including Stockout and Safety Stock) = Ordering Cost + Holding Cost + Stockout Cost
Total Cost Allocated = Cost per Unit × Units Produced

nodes.name: Total Cost Object Allocation Base
nodes.definition: Total Cost Object Allocation Base refers to the sum of the numerical values of all allocation bases (such as weight, labor hours, raw material consumption, etc.) adopted by all cost objects (e.g., different products) used to allocate common costs during the cost allocation process. It serves as the key denominator for calculating the cost allocation rate, used to reasonably apportion total costs to various cost objects.

nodes.name: Total Cost Related to Batch Size
nodes.definition: Total cost related to batch size (continuous supply) refers to the sum of ordering costs and holding costs under the condition of goods being supplied and consumed simultaneously.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost Related to Batch Size = (Annual Demand ÷ Order Quantity per Batch) × Ordering Cost per Batch + 1/2 × Order Quantity per Batch × (1 - Daily Consumption Rate ÷ Daily Delivery Rate) × Unit Holding Cost

nodes.name: Total Cost and Expense
nodes.definition: Total cost and expense refers to all expenditures incurred by an enterprise in the production and operation process for producing and selling all products or providing services, typically calculated on an annual basis. It is a composite indicator that can be calculated through two approaches: cost composition or cost behavior.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost and Expense = Total Fixed Cost + Total Variable Cost
Total Cost and Expense = Cost of Goods Sold + Selling Expenses + Administrative Expenses + Financial Expenses
Total Cost and Expense = Total Direct Cost and Expense + Total Indirect Cost and Expense
Total Cost and Expense = Operating Cost + Depreciation + Amortization + Interest Expense + Sustaining Capital Investment

nodes.name: Total Cost and Expense Amount
nodes.definition: Total cost and expense amount refers to the sum of all costs and expenses incurred by an enterprise during a specific period (typically an accounting period) for conducting production and operating activities. It encompasses expenditures from product manufacturing to sales, management, financing, and other operational stages.

nodes.name: Total Cost at Highest Activity Level
nodes.definition: Total cost at the highest activity level refers to the total cost corresponding to the highest observed activity level in historical data under the high-low method. It is an intermediate data point used for decomposing mixed costs and calculating the variable cost per unit and total fixed costs, rather than an independent accounting item.

operands.metric: Total Cost at Lowest Activity Level

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost at Highest Activity Level = Total Cost at Lowest Activity Level + Variable Cost per Unit × (Highest Activity Level - Lowest Activity Level)

nodes.name: Total Cost at Highest Production Level
Total Cost at Lowest Activity Level
nodes.definition: Total cost at the lowest activity level refers to the actual total cost incurred when the activity level (such as production volume, sales volume, or labor hours) is at its minimum in the company's historical operational data. It serves as fundamental raw data for cost behavior analysis (e.g., the high-low method) and is used to separate fixed and variable components of costs.

nodes.name: Total Cost at Lowest Production Level
Total Cost at Maximum Production
aliases: Total Cost at Highest Production Period
nodes.definition: Total cost at maximum production refers to the total cost incurred by an enterprise during the period when output reaches its highest level. It is calculated by adding fixed costs to the product of unit variable cost and maximum output. This is a key composite indicator in cost management and forecasting, relying on fundamental concepts such as unit variable cost and fixed costs.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost at Maximum Production = Fixed Costs + Unit Variable Cost × Maximum Output
Total Cost at Maximum Production = Average Fixed Cost + Unit Variable Cost × Maximum Output

nodes.name: Total Cost at Minimum Production Level
nodes.definition: Total cost at minimum production level refers to the total cost incurred by an enterprise during its period of lowest output. According to cost behavior, it can be decomposed into the sum of fixed costs and variable costs, where variable costs are the product of unit variable cost and minimum production volume. This indicator is a composite metric in cost estimation and analysis, commonly used as a key data point in cost behavior analysis methods such as the high-low method.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost at Minimum Production Level = Fixed Costs + Unit Variable Cost × Minimum Production Volume

nodes.name: Total Cost for Next Period
nodes.definition: Total cost for the next period refers to the aggregate amount of all costs that an enterprise is expected to incur during the next accounting period (such as the next month, next quarter, or next year). It is commonly used for budgeting, cost forecasting, and financial planning, serving as a crucial basis for evaluating future operational efficiency and formulating pricing strategies.

nodes.name: Total Cost of Finished Goods
nodes.definition: Total cost of finished goods refers to the aggregate cost of all products completed during the current month, calculated by adding the beginning work-in-process inventory cost to the expenses incurred during the month, and then subtracting the ending work-in-process inventory cost.

operands.metric: Ending Work in Process Inventory Cost

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost of Finished Goods = (Beginning Work-in-Process Inventory Cost + Current Month Incurred Expenses) - Ending Work-in-Process Inventory Cost

nodes.name: Total Cost of Goods Purchased or Produced
Total Cost of Inventory with Gradual Replenishment and Usage
aliases: Total Cost under Gradual Replenishment in EOQ Model
nodes.definition: In the Economic Order Quantity (EOQ) model with gradual replenishment and usage, total cost refers to the minimum sum of ordering costs and holding costs under the optimal order quantity, taking into account the difference between the supply rate and the demand rate.

nodes.name: Total Cost of New Project
nodes.definition: Total Cost of New Project refers to the sum of all costs expected or actually incurred by an enterprise during a specific period (usually one year) for implementing a new technical solution, investment project, or operational plan. It includes all fixed and variable costs directly related to the project, serving as a key financial indicator for evaluating the economic feasibility of new projects and making investment decisions.

nodes.name: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO)
nodes.definition: Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) represents the aggregate cost of acquiring and operating an asset over its useful life, including the initial purchase price and ongoing operating costs incurred during the lifespan.

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost of Ownership = Purchase Price + (Annual Operating Costs × Lifespan)

nodes.name: Total Cost of a Basket of Goods and Services
nodes.definition: The total cost of a basket of goods and services refers to the sum of all costs incurred to produce or provide a specific set of goods and services within a given period. In cost behavior analysis, it is typically composed of total fixed costs and total variable costs; in cost accounting, it can also be calculated through the relationship between the cost of work-in-progress at the beginning and end of the period and the production expenses incurred during the current period. This concept is the core foundation for constructing price indices, such as the Consumer Price Index (CPI).

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost of a Basket of Goods and Services = Total Fixed Costs + Total Variable Costs
Total Cost of a Basket of Goods and Services = Total Fixed Costs + Variable Cost per Unit × Total Product Quantity

operands.metric: Cost of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Goods at Beginning of Period
Production Expenses Incurred in Current Period
Cost of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Goods at End of Period

formulas.source_formula: Total Cost of a Basket of Goods and Services = Cost of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Goods at Beginning of Period + Production Expenses Incurred in Current Period - Cost of Work-in-Progress and Semi-finished Goods at End of Period

nodes.name: Total Costs and Expenses
nodes.definition: Total costs and expenses represent the monetary expression of all expenditures incurred by an enterprise within a specific accounting period for producing goods, providing services, and maintaining daily operations. It typically includes cost of sales, taxes and surcharges, and various period expenses, serving as a crucial indicator for measuring the total consumption of enterprise resources.

nodes.name: Total Credit Balance of Other Payables Subsidiary Accounts
aliases: Aggregate Credit Balance of Other Payables Subsidiary Accounts
Total Credit Balance of Other Payables Details
其他应付款贷方余额汇总
其他应付款贷方明细合计
nodes.definition: Refers to the sum of the credit balances of all subsidiary accounts under the 'Other Payables' account (such as payable rent, payable deposits, temporary receipts payable, etc.) at the end of an accounting period. It reflects the total amount of various miscellaneous debts that the enterprise needs to pay or repay, excluding major payable items.

nodes.name: Total Credit Balance of Other Payables Subsidiary Ledger Accounts
Total Credit Balance of Other Receivables Subsidiary Accounts
aliases: Aggregate Credit Balance of Other Receivables Subsidiary Accounts
Total Credit Balance of Other Receivables Details
其他应收款贷方余额合计
其他应收款贷方明细余额
nodes.definition: The total credit balance of other receivables subsidiary accounts refers to the sum of the credit balances of all subsidiary accounts under the 'Other Receivables' account in the enterprise's accounting books. It typically appears during balance sheet reclassification adjustments and is used to calculate the amount of the 'Other Payables' item.

nodes.name: Total Credit Balance of Other Receivables Subsidiary Ledger Accounts
Total Current Assets
nodes.definition: Total current assets refer to the sum of all current assets that can be converted into cash or utilized within one year or one operating cycle exceeding one year. It is a core indicator for assessing a company's short-term solvency and working capital management efficiency.

operands.metric: Non-current Assets Due within One Year

formulas.source_formula: Total Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Trading Financial Assets + Notes Receivable + Accounts Receivable + Prepayments + Interest Receivable + Dividends Receivable + Other Receivables + Inventory + Non-current Assets Due Within One Year + Other Current Assets
Total Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Net Accounts Receivable + Inventory
Total Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Accounts Receivable + Inventory + Other Receivables

operands.metric: Non-current Assets Due within One Year

formulas.source_formula: Total Current Assets = Cash and Cash Equivalents + Notes Receivable + Accounts Receivable + Other Receivables + Inventory + Prepaid Expenses + Non-current Assets Due Within One Year

nodes.name: Total Current Assets at Beginning of Period
nodes.definition: Total current assets at the beginning of the period refers to the aggregate book value of all current asset items on the balance sheet at the start of a specific accounting period (such as a fiscal year or quarter).
