nodes.definition: Trading financial liabilities refer to financial liabilities that an enterprise actively undertakes for short-term profit, measured at fair value with changes in value directly recorded in current period profit or loss, such as short-term bonds issued or short-term borrowings assumed for trading purposes.

nodes.name: Trading Revenue
nodes.definition: Trading revenue refers to the total inflow of economic benefits realized by an enterprise through trading activities in its daily operations, such as sales of goods, provision of services, or transfer of asset use rights. It is a core item on the income statement. In accounting practice, its recognition follows the accrual basis principle and is typically calculated by summing core operating revenue and other operating revenue, or by multiplying sales volume by unit selling price.

formulas.source_formula: Trading Revenue = Core Operating Revenue + Other Operating Revenue + Deemed Sales Revenue

nodes.name: Trading Unit
nodes.definition: A trading unit refers to the standardized quantity or value of the underlying asset represented by each contract lot or each transaction in financial markets such as futures and securities. It is the minimum trading quantity unit established by the market to standardize transactions, improve efficiency, and facilitate calculation.

nodes.name: Traditional IRA Deduction Status
aliases: IRA Deduction Status for Traditional IRA
传统个人退休账户扣除状态
nodes.definition: Traditional IRA deduction status classifies whether a taxpayer may claim a full, partial, or no deduction for contributions to a Traditional Individual Retirement Arrangement (IRA) based on Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI), tax filing status, and the IRS phase-out thresholds for the specified tax year when covered by a workplace retirement plan.

nodes.name: Traditional IRA Early Withdrawal Penalty
aliases: 传统个人退休账户提前提取罚金
nodes.definition: The Traditional IRA early withdrawal penalty is a 10% additional tax assessed on distributions taken before age 59.5, unless IRS-qualified exceptions apply. This penalty is separate from ordinary income tax on the distribution and is intended to discourage premature withdrawals from retirement savings.

nodes.name: Trailing 12 Months Price/Earnings Ratio
nodes.definition: The trailing twelve months price-to-earnings (TTM P/E) ratio measures the current market price per share relative to earnings per share generated over the most recent twelve months. It evaluates equity valuation by indicating how much investors are willing to pay for each dollar of recent earnings.

nodes.name: Trailing 12 Months Revenue
nodes.definition: Trailing 12 Months (TTM) revenue is the total revenue generated over the most recent 12 months, commonly calculated by summing the revenue from the latest four fiscal quarters. It provides a timely view of a company's current run-rate, smooths seasonal fluctuations, and supports performance benchmarking and valuation analysis.

formulas.source_formula: TTM Revenue = Revenue (Quarter 1) + Revenue (Quarter 2) + Revenue (Quarter 3) + Revenue (Quarter 4)

nodes.name: Trailing Price-to-Earnings Ratio
nodes.definition: The trailing price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio measures a stock's valuation by dividing the current market share price by the trailing twelve months (TTM) earnings per share (EPS). It indicates how many times investors are paying for each dollar of the company’s actual past earnings.

formulas.source_formula: Trailing Price-to-Earnings Ratio = Current Share Price ÷ Trailing Earnings per Share (EPS)

nodes.name: Trailing Stop
nodes.definition: A trailing stop is a dynamic stop-loss order for a long position set at a fixed percentage below the highest price reached since entry. It adjusts upward as the price makes new highs to help lock in profits while limiting downside risk.

nodes.name: Trailing Stop Loss
nodes.definition: A trailing stop loss is a dynamic risk control order that adjusts upward with rising prices, set at a fixed percentage below the highest price reached since entry. It helps protect unrealized gains during uptrends while limiting downside risk by triggering an exit if the price falls by the specified trailing percentage from its peak.

formulas.source_formula: Trailing Stop Loss = Highest Price × (1 - Trailing Percentage ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Trailing Twelve Months (TTM)
nodes.definition: Trailing Twelve Months (TTM) is a rolling financial measure that presents the most recent 12-month total for a metric by adding the current year-to-date amount to the previous fiscal year's full amount and subtracting the prior-year year-to-date for the equivalent period. It provides an up-to-date view of annual performance, smoothing seasonality and capturing the latest trend.

formulas.source_formula: TTM = Current Year-to-Date (YTD) + Prior Fiscal Year Data - Prior-Year Year-to-Date (YTD)

nodes.name: Trailing Twelve Months (TTM) Dividend Yield
aliases: 滚动十二个月股息收益率
过去十二个月股息收益率
nodes.definition: Trailing Twelve Months (TTM) Dividend Yield measures the percentage return from dividends over the most recent twelve months relative to the current share price. It is calculated by summing dividends from the last four quarters and dividing by the current share price, then expressing the result as a percentage.

formulas.source_formula: TTM Dividend Yield (%) = Total Dividends (TTM) ÷ Current Share Price × 100

nodes.name: Transaction Amount
nodes.definition: Transaction amount refers to the total sum of money agreed upon by buyers and sellers in a financial or commercial transaction for the exchange of goods, services, or financial assets. It serves as the basis for calculating related fees (such as handling charges) and assessing the scale of the transaction.

nodes.name: Transaction Condition Adjustment Factor
nodes.definition: The Transaction Condition Adjustment Factor is a multiplier used in asset valuation (particularly real estate appraisal) to adjust the transaction price of comparable properties. It aims to eliminate the impact of deviations from normal market levels caused by special transaction conditions (such as related-party transactions, distress sales, auctions, etc.), thereby adjusting the price of comparable properties to reflect normal market transaction conditions.

nodes.name: Transaction Cost
nodes.definition: Transaction cost refers to the total expenses incurred by a company for buying and selling securities, typically including the fixed cost per transaction.

formulas.source_formula: Transaction Cost = (Total Number of Transactions ÷ Transaction Volume per Trade) × Fixed Cost per Transaction

nodes.name: Transaction Cost per Sale of Marketable Securities to Replenish Cash
nodes.definition: In financial management, this refers to the fixed costs incurred by a company each time it sells its holdings of marketable securities (such as bonds, stocks, etc.) to convert them into cash. These costs typically include broker commissions, handling fees, taxes, and are a key input parameter for calculating the optimal cash balance under the inventory model.

nodes.name: Transaction Costs
nodes.definition: Transaction costs refer to all expenses associated with purchasing or selling financial assets, commodities, or services, typically consisting of fixed fees and variable fees calculated as a percentage of the transaction amount, directly impacting the calculation of net investment returns and total investment amount.

nodes.name: Transaction Costs on Disposal
aliases: 交易性金融资产出售费用
nodes.definition: Transaction costs on disposal refer to various fees directly paid to complete the transaction during the sale or disposal of assets (such as trading financial assets, stocks, bonds, etc.). These costs typically include commissions, handling fees, transfer fees, stamp duties paid to brokers or trading platforms. They directly reduce the net cash inflow obtained from the sale of assets, thereby affecting the final investment return.

nodes.name: Transaction Exposure
nodes.definition: Transaction exposure is the potential gain or loss in the value of a foreign-currency-denominated cash flow caused by exchange rate movements between the date a transaction is contracted and the date it is settled.

formulas.source_formula: Transaction Exposure = Original Foreign Currency Amount × (Exchange Rate at End ÷ Exchange Rate at Start - 1)

nodes.name: Transaction Fee
nodes.definition: Transaction fee is a service charge levied by financial institutions or service providers on clients for financial transactions (such as securities, futures, or foreign exchange trading), calculated according to predetermined rules based on transaction amount or contract size. It typically consists of a fixed fee and/or a variable fee calculated as a percentage of the transaction amount, and is a key factor affecting transaction costs.

formulas.source_formula: Transaction Fee = Opening Fee + Closing Fee
Transaction Fee = Transfer Fee + Securities Trading Fee + Brokerage Commission
Transaction Fee Revenue = Gross Merchandise Value × Fee Percentage

nodes.name: Transaction Fees
nodes.definition: Transaction fees are charges assessed per electronic payment transaction, typically comprising a variable percentage of the transaction amount and a fixed fee component. They represent the cost merchants incur to process payments and are relevant for pricing, margin analysis, and cost control.

nodes.name: Transfer Fee
nodes.definition: Transfer fee refers to the collective term for a series of taxes, levies, and administrative charges incurred during the process of registering the change of ownership or usage rights of an asset (such as real estate, securities, vehicles, etc.). These fees are borne by the buyer, seller, or both parties jointly. Its specific composition and calculation rules vary depending on the asset type, nature of the transaction, local policies, and the specific circumstances of the transacting parties.

operands.metric: Securities Registration and Clearing Institution Transfer Fee

formulas.source_formula: Transfer Fee = Securities Trading Handling Fee + Securities Trading Supervision Fee + Securities Registration and Clearing Institution Transfer Fee

nodes.name: Transfer Income
nodes.definition: Transfer income refers to various regular transfer payments made by the state, work units, and social organizations to resident households, as well as regular income transfers between households. It does not originate from current production or service activities but rather from the redistribution of income, constituting a significant component of total household income.

nodes.name: Transfer Payments
nodes.definition: In macroeconomics and finance, transfer payments refer to the redistribution of income and wealth by the government without receiving corresponding goods or services. Such payments are unilateral and non-exhaustive (not consuming resources or generating output), and are excluded from the expenditure approach to calculating Gross Domestic Product (GDP) because they represent a reallocation of resources rather than expenditure on newly produced goods and services.

formulas.source_formula: Transfer Payments = Welfare + Fiscal Aid + Social Security + Government Subsidies

nodes.name: Transfer Tax
nodes.definition: Transfer tax is a levy imposed by a governmental authority on the transfer of title or ownership of real property. It is commonly assessed as a percentage of the property's value or as a fixed dollar amount per specified value unit (e.g., per $1,000 of property value), and forms part of real estate transaction costs.

formulas.source_formula: Transfer Tax = (Property Value ÷ Threshold) × Tax Rate
Transfer Tax = Property Value × (Tax Rate ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Transfer-out Ratio
aliases: 不可抵扣进项税分摊比例
nodes.definition: The transfer-out ratio refers to the calculation ratio used to allocate the total input VAT for the current period to the portion of non-deductible sales when calculating the non-deductible input VAT. This ratio is typically determined based on the proportion of sales from non-deductible output VAT items (such as tax-exempt sales and sales under simplified tax calculation methods) to total sales for the period. It is a key parameter in the calculation of input VAT transfer-out under the value-added tax system.

operands.metric: Deductible Sales for the Current Period
Total Sales Revenue for the Period

formulas.source_formula: Transfer-out Ratio = 1 - (Deductible Sales for the Current Period ÷ Total Sales for the Current Period)

nodes.name: Transition Period Cash Outflow
nodes.definition: Transition period cash outflow refers to the total amount of all cash payments incurred to sustain and achieve operations during the period when a project or enterprise transitions from the construction phase or a specific stage to normal operations. It is a key component of transition period cash flow.

formulas.source_formula: Transition Period Cash Outflow = Construction Investment + Working Capital + Operating Costs + Value-Added Tax Payable + Input Tax + Surtax + Sustaining Capital Investment

nodes.name: Translation Exposure
nodes.definition: Translation exposure is the potential gain or loss recognized when translating foreign currency–denominated assets and liabilities into the home currency due to changes in exchange rates. It affects reported financial statements (e.g., through cumulative translation adjustments) but does not directly alter cash flows.

formulas.source_formula: Translation Exposure = Asset Value × (Exchange Rate Final - Exchange Rate Initial)

nodes.name: Transport Volume
nodes.definition: Transport volume refers to the quantity of transportation work completed by a transportation enterprise within a specific reporting period (such as a month, quarter, or year). It is a fundamental operational metric for measuring the scale of production and operations. It is typically measured in physical units, such as freight turnover (ton-kilometers), passenger turnover (passenger-kilometers), or simple freight volume (tons) and passenger volume (passenger trips).

nodes.name: Transportation Cost
nodes.definition: Transportation cost refers to the fee paid by an enterprise to carriers for moving goods or merchandise from one location to another. In accounting treatment, it is typically recorded as a basic original expense and directly allocated to relevant cost or expense accounts based on supporting documents such as contracts and invoices.

nodes.name: Transportation Costs
nodes.definition: Transportation costs refer to the fees paid by an enterprise to carriers for moving goods or merchandise from one location to another, constituting a significant component of procurement costs or cost of sales.

nodes.name: Transportation Distance
nodes.definition: Transportation distance refers to the actual path length traveled by goods or services from the point of origin to the destination, typically measured in kilometers or miles. It is a fundamental raw data point in logistics and transportation activities, directly sourced from business operations or measurements, and serves as a critical input value for calculating composite indicators such as freight charges, logistics costs, and carbon emissions.

nodes.name: Transportation Loss Rate
nodes.definition: Transportation Loss Rate is an indicator used to measure the extent of loss or damage to products or goods during transportation, typically expressed as a percentage, reflecting the quantity loss from shipment to receipt.

nodes.name: Transposition Error
nodes.definition: A transposition error is a data entry mistake in which two adjacent digits are reversed (e.g., 64 recorded as 46). In accounting, such errors often cause a discrepancy whose absolute difference is divisible by 9, enabling a quick diagnostic test in reconciliations and audit procedures.

nodes.name: Treasury Bill Investment Yield
nodes.definition: Treasury Bill Investment Yield is the annualized return on a Treasury bill calculated as the discount from face value divided by the purchase price, scaled by the ratio of days in the year to days remaining to maturity. It expresses yield as a percentage of the amount invested using a 365/366-day money market convention, enabling comparison with coupon-bearing securities of the same maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Treasury Bill Investment Yield = ((Face Value - Purchase Price) ÷ Purchase Price) × (Days in Year ÷ Days to Maturity)

nodes.name: Treasury Bill Purchase Price
nodes.definition: Treasury bill purchase price refers to the actual consideration amount paid by investors when buying treasury bills (typically referring to government bonds with maturities of one year or less) in the market. This price is usually lower than the face value of the bond (i.e., issued at a discount), and the difference between the price and the face value represents the interest income investors can obtain by holding the bond until maturity.

nodes.name: Treasury Bills
nodes.definition: Treasury Bills (T-bills) are zero-coupon government debt instruments issued by the Ministry of Finance with maturities of one year or less. T-bills are issued at a discount to face value and redeemed at face value upon maturity, paying no periodic interest, thereby generating a positive yield to maturity.

nodes.name: Treasury Bond Market Average Yield
nodes.definition: The Treasury Bond Market Average Yield refers to the average yield of all or a representative group of treasury bonds (e.g., bonds with different maturities) in the market over a specific period (such as a day, week, month, or year). It reflects the overall return level of the treasury bond market during that period and serves as a key indicator for gauging market interest rate trends and investors' average return requirements for treasury bonds.

nodes.name: Treasury Bond Yields by Maturity
nodes.definition: Treasury bond yields by maturity refer to the annualized return rates investors can obtain by holding bonds with different remaining maturities (e.g., 1-year, 5-year, 10-year, etc.) to maturity when traded in the market. They reflect the market's assessment of the time value of money and risk premiums over different time horizons, serving as fundamental data for constructing the treasury yield curve and acting as crucial benchmark rates in financial markets.

nodes.name: Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS) Interest Payment
aliases: 通胀保值债券利息支付
nodes.definition: The TIPS interest payment is the coupon cash flow paid to holders of Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, calculated by applying the coupon rate to the inflation-adjusted principal. The coupon rate should be expressed per payment period (e.g., semi-annual) to align with the payment frequency.

nodes.name: Treasury STRIPS
aliases: Separate Trading of Registered Interest and Principal of Securities
分离交易的注册利息和本金证券
nodes.definition: Treasury STRIPS are U.S. Treasury securities whose coupon and principal cash flows are separated and traded individually as zero-coupon bonds. STRIPS are issued at a discount and accrete to face value at maturity, providing a single payment at maturity. Their yield to maturity is derived from the discount between purchase price and face value over the remaining time to maturity.

nodes.name: Treasury STRIPS Taxable Interest
nodes.definition: Treasury STRIPS taxable interest represents the total original issue discount (OID) accrued on a zero-coupon U.S. Treasury STRIPS investment over the holding period. Although STRIPS do not pay periodic coupons, OID accrues through compounding and is generally taxable annually. The total taxable interest equals the difference between the investment’s future value at the stated annual interest rate and the initial investment amount.

formulas.source_formula: Treasury STRIPS Taxable Interest = Investment Amount × ((1 + Annual Interest Rate) ^ Years) - Investment Amount

nodes.name: Treasury Stock
nodes.definition: Treasury stock refers to shares that a company has repurchased from the open market, thereby reducing the number of shares outstanding. These shares are held in the company's treasury, do not carry voting rights, are not entitled to dividends, and are presented as a contra-equity account on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Treasury Stock = Cost of Repurchased Shares

nodes.name: Treasury Stock (Treasury Shares)
nodes.definition: Treasury stock (treasury shares) refers to a company's own shares that have been repurchased and held by the company. Repurchasing shares reduces shareholders' equity. Under the cost method, the reduction equals the total repurchase cost. Under the par value method, the reduction is allocated between common stock at par value and the reduction of additional paid-in capital, but the total reduction equals the repurchase price per share times the number of shares repurchased.

nodes.name: Treasury Stock - Current Period
nodes.definition: Treasury stock - current period refers to a company's own issued shares that have been repurchased and held during the current accounting period through the open market or other means. After being reacquired by the company, these shares are no longer considered outstanding and are presented as a deduction within the shareholders' equity section of the balance sheet, reflecting the company's reacquisition of its own ownership.

nodes.name: Treasury Stock Method
nodes.definition: The Treasury Stock Method estimates the incremental shares from in-the-money options and warrants for diluted earnings per share (EPS). It assumes all such instruments are exercised, the proceeds are used to repurchase shares at the average market price, and the net increase in shares is added to basic shares to compute diluted shares.

formulas.source_formula: Diluted EPS (Treasury Stock Method) = Net Income ÷ Diluted Weighted-Average Shares Outstanding

nodes.name: Treasury Stock Shares
nodes.definition: Treasury stock shares refer to the number of a company's own shares that have been repurchased from the open market or shareholders and have not yet been canceled or reissued. It reflects the actual quantity of the company's own shares held and is a specific item on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Treasury Yield
nodes.definition: Treasury yield quoted on the bank discount basis for Treasury bills measures the annualized return relative to face value using a 360-day year. It is computed as the discount from par divided by face value, scaled by 360 divided by the days to maturity, and is commonly used for quoting T-bill yields in money markets.

nodes.name: Trend Analysis
nodes.definition: Trend analysis is a financial analytical technique that applies ordinary least squares (OLS) linear regression to historical financial variables (e.g., revenue, expenses, EPS, cash flows) to quantify the direction and magnitude of change over time and to support forecasting. The slope of the trend line measures the average rate of change per period, while the intercept represents the baseline value when the independent variable equals zero.

formulas.source_formula: Trend Component = Time Series - Cyclical Component
Trend Line Intercept = (Σ(Y) - Trend Line Slope × Σ(X)) ÷ n

nodes.name: Trend Real GDP
nodes.definition: Trend Real GDP refers to the level of real output that an economy can sustain over the long term under the assumption of full employment and full utilization of resources. It excludes the effects of short-term economic fluctuations (such as business cycles) and reflects the economy's fundamental growth potential.

nodes.name: Trendline
nodes.definition: A trendline is a straight line plotted on a price chart by connecting at least two pivot highs (for a descending trendline) or pivot lows (for an ascending trendline). It helps technical analysts visualize the prevailing direction of price movement and identify dynamic support or resistance. A linear trendline can be represented in slope–intercept form and applied across different time frames to assess trend strength and direction.

formulas.source_formula: Trendline Price = Slope × Time + Intercept

nodes.name: Treynor Ratio
nodes.definition: The Treynor ratio measures a portfolio’s excess return over the risk-free rate per unit of systematic risk, as captured by the portfolio’s beta. It evaluates how effectively a portfolio compensates investors for bearing market-related risk and is most appropriate for well-diversified portfolios where unsystematic risk is minimized.

formulas.source_formula: Treynor Ratio = (Portfolio Return - Risk-free Rate) ÷ Portfolio Beta

nodes.name: Triangular Arbitrage Profit
nodes.definition: Triangular arbitrage profit is the gain realized by exploiting pricing discrepancies among three currency exchange rates by sequentially converting one currency into two others and back to the original, assuming no transaction costs or bid–ask spreads. It measures the difference between the final amount after the currency cycle and the initial amount.

formulas.source_formula: Triangular Arbitrage Profit = Initial Amount (USD) × USD to EUR Exchange Rate × EUR to GBP Exchange Rate × GBP to USD Exchange Rate − Initial Amount (USD)
Triangular Arbitrage Profit = ( ( ( Initial Amount (USD) ÷ USD/EUR Exchange Rate ) ÷ EUR/GBP Exchange Rate ) × USD/GBP Exchange Rate ) - Initial Amount (USD)

nodes.name: Trimmed Mean
nodes.definition: Trimmed mean is a robust average that removes an equal percentage of the smallest and largest observations before averaging, reducing the influence of outliers in financial and economic data series and providing a more stable central tendency for analysis and reporting.

formulas.source_formula: Trimmed Mean = Sum of Trimmed Data ÷ Number of Trimmed Data

nodes.name: Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA)
nodes.definition: The Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA) is a trend-following technical indicator designed to reduce lag by combining three Exponential Moving Averages (EMAs) of the same period: the EMA of price (EMA1), the EMA of EMA1 (EMA2), and the EMA of EMA2 (EMA3). TEMA provides a smoother and more responsive measure of trend direction compared with a single EMA, making it useful for identifying trend changes while mitigating delays inherent in moving averages.

formulas.source_formula: TEMA = 3 × EMA1 - 3 × EMA2 + EMA3

nodes.name: Triple Net Lease
nodes.definition: In U.S. commercial real estate, a triple net lease (NNN lease) is a form of net lease where, in addition to base rent, the tenant is responsible for three major property expenses: real estate taxes, building insurance, and maintenance costs. Because the landlord passes these operating expenses to the tenant, the base rent for such leases is typically lower compared to gross leases.

nodes.name: Triple Net Lease Total Payment
nodes.definition: Triple Net Lease Total Payment refers to the tenant's annual total cash outflow under a triple net (NNN) lease, comprising base rent plus tenant-borne property taxes, property insurance, and operating expenses (e.g., maintenance and repairs). It represents the full occupancy cost under NNN terms in commercial real estate.

formulas.source_formula: Triple Net Lease Total Payment = Base Rent + Property Taxes + Insurance + Operating Expenses

nodes.name: Trough Price
nodes.definition: Trough price typically refers to the lowest point or bottom price level reached by a commodity or asset price fluctuation within a specific time period. In contexts such as agricultural product cost-benefit analysis, it may refer to fundamental raw price data, such as purchase price or unit price, serving as a critical starting point for cost-benefit calculations and market analysis.

nodes.name: Troy Ounce to Grain Conversion
nodes.definition: Troy Ounce to Grain Conversion specifies the standardized relationship used in precious metals and commodities markets, where 1 troy ounce equals 480 grains. This conversion facilitates accurate weight reporting, pricing, and settlement for bullion and historical metrology.

nodes.name: Troy Ounce to Grams Conversion
nodes.definition: The troy ounce to grams conversion expresses the metric weight equivalent for precious metals. One troy ounce equals 31.103 grams. This conversion is widely used in bullion markets for pricing, inventory measurement, and financial reporting of precious-metal holdings.

nodes.name: Troy Ounce to Kilogram Conversion
nodes.definition: Troy ounce to kilogram conversion expresses the transformation of precious metal weights from troy ounces to kilograms using a fixed conversion factor, commonly applied in bullion markets, commodities trading, and inventory valuation for accurate metric reporting.

nodes.name: Troy Ounce to Pennyweight Conversion
nodes.definition: The troy ounce to pennyweight conversion expresses the equivalence between two mass units in the troy system used for precious metals, where 1 troy ounce equals 20 pennyweight. This conversion supports accurate metals pricing, assay reporting, and inventory valuation in accounting and trading workflows.

nodes.name: Troy Ounce to Pound Conversion
nodes.definition: Troy ounce to pound conversion expresses the weight measured in troy ounces—commonly used for precious metals—into standard pounds using a fixed conversion factor. This conversion supports inventory measurement, valuation, reporting, and logistics in commodities and precious metals accounting.

nodes.name: Troy Ounce to Standard Ounce Conversion
aliases: 金衡盎司与常衡盎司换算
nodes.definition: Troy Ounce to Standard Ounce Conversion translates weight measured in troy ounces—commonly used for precious metals—into standard (avoirdupois) ounces, facilitating consistent valuation, pricing, inventory management, and financial reporting in commodities and bullion markets.

nodes.name: True Range
nodes.definition: True Range is a volatility measure defined as the maximum of the intraday range and the absolute price gaps relative to the previous close: max(High − Low, |High − Previous Close|, |Low − Previous Close|). It captures gap risk and serves as the base input for computing the Average True Range (ATR).

nodes.name: True Strength Index
nodes.definition: The True Strength Index (TSI) is a momentum-based technical analysis oscillator that measures trend direction and strength by double-smoothing price changes with exponential moving averages. It oscillates around zero, helping identify trend confirmations, potential reversals, and overbought/oversold conditions.

nodes.name: Tuition
nodes.definition: Tuition refers to the basic fee charged by schools or educational institutions to students to compensate for the provision of educational services (such as teaching, facility usage, etc.). It is typically determined directly based on the program of study, academic year, credits, or specific policies, and constitutes a core component of a student's educational expenses.

nodes.name: Turnover Materials
nodes.definition: Turnover materials refer to materials that can be used multiple times in the production and operation process, essentially retaining their original physical form, but whose value gradually transfers to product costs. They are classified as enterprise inventory but do not constitute the physical part of the product, such as formwork and baffles in the construction industry, as well as general packaging materials and low-value consumables.

nodes.name: Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: Turnover ratio measures the percentage of a mutual fund or portfolio's holdings that are replaced within a year, calculated as the lesser of purchases or sales of securities relative to the fund's average net assets, indicating trading activity, cost implications, and investment strategy aggressiveness.

formulas.source_formula: Turnover Ratio (%) = (New Assets Value ÷ Average Net Assets) × 100

nodes.name: Twenty Eight Thirty Six Rule (28/36 Rule)
nodes.definition: The 28/36 rule is a mortgage underwriting guideline stating that a borrower's Housing Expense-to-Income Ratio (front-end debt-to-income) should not exceed 28% of gross monthly income, and the Total Debt-to-Income Ratio (back-end DTI) should not exceed 36%. The housing expense-to-income ratio measures monthly housing costs (e.g., mortgage payment, property taxes, homeowners insurance, HOA dues) relative to gross monthly income and is used to assess affordability and credit risk.

nodes.name: Two and Twenty
nodes.definition: Two and Twenty is a common hedge fund fee structure consisting of a fixed management fee (typically 2% of Assets Under Management) and a performance fee (typically 20% of profits). The management fee compensates the manager for operating the fund and is calculated as a percentage of AUM, often based on period-end or average AUM. The performance fee rewards investment returns above a benchmark or hurdle, sometimes subject to a high-water mark. The provided function computes the management fee component on end-of-year AUM.

nodes.name: Two-Tailed Tests
nodes.definition: A two-tailed test evaluates whether a sample statistic differs from a population parameter in either direction (higher or lower). The Z-score (test statistic) quantifies how many standard deviations the sample mean is from the population mean under the assumption of normality. In finance and accounting analytics, two-tailed Z-tests are used to assess whether observed means (e.g., transaction values, returns, costs) significantly deviate from expected benchmarks.

formulas.source_formula: Two-and-Twenty Total Fees = Management Fee + Performance Fee

nodes.name: Typical Price
nodes.definition: Typical Price is the average of an asset's high, low, and close prices for a given period. It serves as a representative price level and is commonly used as an input in technical indicators such as the Money Flow Index (MFI).

formulas.source_formula: Typical Price = (High + Low + Close) ÷ 3
supporting_source_formulas: Typical Price = (High + Low + Close) ÷ 3
Typical Price = (High Price + Low Price + Closing Price) ÷ 3

nodes.name: U-1 Unemployment Rate
nodes.definition: The U-1 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the civilian labor force that has been unemployed for 15 weeks or more, highlighting long-term unemployment within the labor market.

formulas.source_formula: U-1 Unemployment Rate = (Unemployed 15 Weeks or More ÷ Civilian Labor Force) × 100

nodes.name: U-2 Unemployment Rate
aliases: Job Losers and Completed Temporary Jobs Unemployment Rate
工作丢失及临时工作完成者失业率
nodes.definition: The U-2 unemployment rate measures the share of the civilian labor force composed of job losers and persons who completed temporary jobs, expressed as a percentage. It highlights short-term job loss dynamics and turnover within the labor market.

formulas.source_formula: U-2 Unemployment Rate (%) = (Job Losers + Completed Temporary Jobs) ÷ Civilian Labor Force × 100

nodes.name: U-3 Unemployment Rate
nodes.definition: The U-3 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the civilian labor force that is unemployed and actively seeking work. It is the official unemployment rate reported by statistical agencies and reflects individuals without jobs who have looked for work within the reference period.

formulas.source_formula: U-3 Unemployment Rate = Total Unemployed ÷ Labor Force × 100

nodes.name: U-4 Unemployment Rate
aliases: 包含气馁劳动者的失业率
nodes.definition: The U-4 unemployment rate is a broader measure of labor underutilization that includes discouraged workers in addition to the unemployed. It is calculated as the share of the total labor force including discouraged workers that is either unemployed or discouraged, expressed as a percentage.

formulas.source_formula: U-4 Unemployment Rate (%) = (Unemployed + Discouraged Workers) ÷ (Labor Force excluding Discouraged Workers + Discouraged Workers) × 100
U-4 Unemployment Rate = (Unemployed + Discouraged Workers) ÷ (Labor Force + Discouraged Workers) × 100

nodes.name: U-6 (Unemployment) Rate
nodes.definition: The U-6 unemployment rate is a broad measure of labor underutilization reported by the Bureau of Labor Statistics. It includes unemployed persons actively seeking work, individuals marginally attached to the labor force, and those working part-time for economic reasons (underemployed). It is calculated as the sum of unemployed, marginally attached, and underemployed persons divided by the labor force plus marginally attached persons, expressed as a percentage.

formulas.source_formula: U-6 Unemployment Rate = (Total Unemployed + Marginally Attached Workers + Underemployed Workers) ÷ (Labor Force + Marginally Attached Workers) × 100

nodes.name: U-6 Unemployment Rate
nodes.definition: The U-6 unemployment rate is the broadest measure of labor underutilization. It includes the unemployed, individuals marginally attached to the labor force, and those employed part-time for economic reasons, expressed as a percentage of the expanded labor force (civilian labor force plus marginally attached).

formulas.source_formula: U-6 Unemployment Rate = (Unemployed + Marginally Attached Workers + Employed Part-time for Economic Reasons) ÷ (Labor Force + Marginally Attached Workers) × 100

nodes.name: U.S. Dollar Index (USDX)
nodes.definition: The U.S. Dollar Index (USDX) is a geometrically weighted index that measures the value of the U.S. dollar against a basket of six major foreign currencies (EUR, JPY, GBP, CAD, SEK, CHF). It is calculated by multiplying an indexing factor by the currency pair exchange rates raised to fixed weights, reflecting the relative importance of each currency in the basket. The index is normalized using an indexing factor so that the base period aligns with historical reference levels.

formulas.source_formula: UFMI Premium = Loan Amount × UFMI Rate

nodes.name: USD to KYD Conversion
nodes.definition: Converts an amount in U.S. dollars (USD) to Cayman Islands dollars (KYD) using a fixed exchange rate.

nodes.name: Ulcer Index
nodes.definition: The Ulcer Index is a technical analysis downside risk indicator that measures the depth and duration of price declines from recent highs. It is computed as the square root of the average of squared percentage drawdowns over a specified look-back period, emphasizing downside volatility only. In this implementation, the average is obtained by dividing the sum of squared percentage drawdowns by the look-back period.

formulas.source_formula: Ultimate Loss = Reported Claims × Loss Development Factor
Ultimate Losses = Earned Premiums × Expected Loss Ratio

nodes.name: Ultimate Net Loss
nodes.definition: Ultimate net loss is the final amount of loss borne by the insurer after reducing the gross loss by the deductible, salvage value, and other recoveries, and capping the result at the policy limit. It represents the insurer’s net liability for a claim and is commonly used in claims settlement and excess-of-loss reinsurance.

formulas.source_formula: Ultimate Net Loss = min(Adjusted Loss, Policy Maximum)

nodes.name: Ultimate Oscillator
nodes.definition: The Ultimate Oscillator is a weighted momentum oscillator that combines three timeframes (7, 14, and 28 periods) of buying pressure relative to true range to reduce false signals from typical oscillators. It scales between 0 and 100, with higher values indicating stronger upward momentum and lower values indicating stronger downward momentum, and is often used to identify divergences and potential overbought/oversold conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Ultimate Oscillator = 100 × (4 × Average7 + 2 × Average14 + 1 × Average28) ÷ (4 + 2 + 1)

nodes.name: Unadjusted Basis
nodes.definition: Unadjusted basis is the initial cost basis of an asset at acquisition, equal to the cash consideration paid plus liabilities assumed and capitalizable property-related taxes and closing costs, prior to any subsequent adjustments such as improvements, depreciation, amortization, or impairments.

formulas.source_formula: Unadjusted Basis = Cash Payment + Mortgage + Property Taxes + Closing Costs

nodes.name: Unamortized Bond Discount
nodes.definition: Unamortized bond discount refers to the remaining portion of the difference between a bond's face value and its lower issuance price that has not yet been allocated to interest expense through amortization (i.e., periodic recognition) over the bond's life. It is a contra account to the carrying value of bonds payable.

nodes.name: Unamortized Bond Issuance Costs
nodes.definition: Unamortized bond issuance costs refer to the expenses incurred by an enterprise when issuing bonds that have not yet been allocated to the profit or loss of each period over the bond's term. These costs are initially recognized as part of the bond's carrying amount, as an adjustment to an asset or liability, and are subsequently amortized using the effective interest method to reflect the true cost of financing of the bond.

nodes.name: Unamortized Bond Premium
nodes.definition: Unamortized bond premium refers to the portion of the premium arising from issuing bonds at a price above their face value that has not yet been amortized into interest expense over the bond's life. This remaining premium must be amortized in each accounting period until maturity to adjust the actual interest expense.

nodes.name: Unappropriated Retained Earnings
nodes.definition: Unappropriated retained earnings represent the portion of retained earnings not restricted or set aside for specific purposes (such as legal reserves or capital commitments), and therefore available for dividends or other discretionary uses. They are reported within shareholders' equity on the balance sheet or the statement of changes in equity.

formulas.source_formula: Unappropriated Retained Earnings = Total Retained Earnings - Appropriated Retained Earnings

nodes.name: Unbiased Predictor
nodes.definition: Under the Unbiased Expectations Hypothesis (Expectations Theory), the forward rate implied by current spot rates is an unbiased predictor of future short-term interest rates. This measure estimates the future one-year spot rate from the current one-year and two-year spot rates, assuming rates are expressed in decimals and there is no term premium.

formulas.source_formula: Implied Forward Rate = ((1 + Spot Rate (Period 2))^(Period 2) ÷ (1 + Spot Rate (Period 1))^(Period 1))^(1 ÷ (Period 2 - Period 1)) - 1

nodes.name: Uncovered Interest Arbitrage
nodes.definition: Uncovered interest arbitrage is a strategy that involves investing in a foreign currency money market instrument without hedging the foreign exchange exposure. The total return is determined by the foreign interest rate differential combined with the subsequent change in the foreign exchange rate relative to the domestic currency.

formulas.source_formula: Uncovered Interest Arbitrage Return = Foreign Interest Rate Differential + Foreign Exchange Rate Change

nodes.name: Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP)
nodes.definition: Uncovered Interest Rate Parity (UIP) posits that, without hedging exchange rate risk, the expected return on domestic deposits equals the expected return on foreign deposits after accounting for expected exchange rate movements. Under UIP, the expected future spot (or the UIP-implied forward rate) is the current spot exchange rate scaled by the ratio of the two countries' gross interest factors.

nodes.name: Uncovered Loss at Beginning of Year
Undated Issue
nodes.definition: An undated issue (perpetual bond) is a fixed-income security with no maturity date. Its present value equals the constant periodic coupon divided by the investor's required rate of return (discount rate), assuming coupons continue indefinitely and the discount rate remains positive.

formulas.source_formula: Perpetual Bond Value = Coupon Payment ÷ Discount Rate

nodes.name: Underapplied Overhead
nodes.definition: Underapplied overhead is the condition where actual manufacturing overhead exceeds budgeted or applied overhead, yielding a positive overhead variance. It indicates that overhead costs were underestimated or insufficiently applied to production and typically requires period-end adjustment to cost of goods sold or inventory. In this context, a positive Overhead Variance (Actual Overhead − Budgeted Overhead) signals underapplied overhead, while a negative variance signals overapplied overhead.

nodes.name: Undercast
nodes.definition: Undercast refers to the amount by which an estimate or recorded figure is lower than the actual realized amount. In budgeting and forecasting, it quantifies conservative estimates or understatements relative to actual outcomes, helping evaluate forecast accuracy and variance against actual performance.

formulas.source_formula: Undercast = Actual Value - Estimated Value

nodes.name: Underemployment Rate
nodes.definition: Underemployment rate measures the percentage of the labor force that is employed below their capacity in terms of hours, skills, or experience. It indicates the extent to which available labor resources are underutilized within an economy.

formulas.source_formula: Underemployment Rate = (Underemployed ÷ Total Labor Force) × 100

nodes.name: Underfunded Pension Plan
nodes.definition: An underfunded pension plan, often referred to as an at-risk plan, is a defined benefit pension plan whose funding target attainment percentage falls below prescribed regulatory thresholds, indicating insufficient assets relative to the funding target. Under common standards (e.g., U.S. PPA/ERISA guidance), a plan is considered at risk when the current year funding target attainment percentage is below 80% and the previous year percentage is below 70%, which may trigger higher minimum required contributions and additional compliance measures.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Current Price
aliases: Spot Price of the Underlying Asset
nodes.definition: Underlying asset current price refers to the real-time trading price or observable market quotation of an asset (such as stocks, commodities, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis for derivative contracts (e.g., options, futures) in financial markets at a specific point in time. It is the fundamental data for financial product pricing and trading decisions.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Downside Price
nodes.definition: The Underlying Asset Downside Price is a derivative concept referring to the estimated or calculated future price of an underlying asset under a specific downside scenario assumption, derived through probabilistic models or valuation methods. It is not an original accounting data point but a scenario analysis value computed based on parameters such as the underlying asset price, volatility, and downside threshold, commonly used to evaluate the value of derivative instruments like downside options.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Market Price
aliases: Market Price of the Underlying Asset
nodes.definition: Underlying asset market price refers to the immediate transaction price agreed upon for a specific asset (such as stocks, bonds, commodities, etc.) in an open, active trading market where buyers and sellers engage in voluntary and fair transactions. It is raw price data directly observed and obtained from the market, serving as fundamental input information for asset valuation, financial derivative pricing, and investment decision-making.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price
nodes.definition: Underlying asset price refers to the value representation of a specific asset at the current or a future point in time. In financial derivatives trading, the underlying asset typically refers to tradable assets such as stocks, bonds, commodities, currencies, and indices.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price Appreciation Rate
nodes.definition: The underlying asset price appreciation rate refers to the percentage increase in the value of the underlying asset from the beginning to the end of a period, used to measure the degree of change in asset price. It is a key composite indicator for calculating investment returns, evaluating investment performance, and option pricing.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price Change
aliases: Price Movement of the Underlying Asset
nodes.definition: Underlying Asset Price Change refers to the difference in the price of the underlying asset, upon which financial derivatives (such as options, futures) depend, between two distinct observation points. This metric is a key intermediate variable for calculating the value of financial derivatives, risk exposure (e.g., Delta), and profit and loss, and is classified as a composite indicator derived from underlying market prices.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price During Stock Price Decline
aliases: Underlying Asset Price in a Down Market
股价下跌时标的资产价格
nodes.definition: Refers to the market price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, indices, etc.) that serves as the basis for financial derivative contracts (e.g., options) during specific periods or scenarios when stock market prices are falling.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price Volatility
nodes.definition: Underlying asset price volatility is an indicator used to measure the uncertainty or degree of risk of future price movements of an underlying asset (such as stocks, commodities, etc.), typically expressed as a percentage. Higher volatility indicates that the asset price may experience larger upward or downward movements over a future period, implying greater uncertainty.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price at Expiration
nodes.definition: The underlying asset price at expiration refers to the actual market trading price of the underlying asset (such as stocks, indices, etc.) specified in the option contract on its expiration date. It is the key market data determining the option's value at expiration, which cannot be calculated through models and must be obtained directly from real-time market quotes.

nodes.name: Underlying Asset Price in Downward Scenario
Underlying Asset Volatility
nodes.definition: Underlying asset volatility is a quantitative measure of the uncertainty or risk associated with future price movements of the underlying asset, typically expressed as the standard deviation of asset returns. It can be calculated from historical price data and holds significant reference value in option pricing, risk management, and investment decision-making.

formulas.source_formula: Underlying Asset Volatility = Standard Deviation of Asset Returns

nodes.name: Underlying Profit
nodes.definition: Underlying profit is a non-GAAP profitability measure that adjusts accounting profit to exclude non-recurring or unusual items, aiming to reflect the core, recurring performance of a company's standard operations.

formulas.source_formula: Underlying Profit = Revenue - Total Regular Expenses - Total Non-recurring Items

nodes.name: Underpayment Penalty
nodes.definition: Underpayment penalty is a tax penalty assessed for failing to pay the full amount of tax due on time. It is typically calculated monthly as a percentage of the underpaid tax amount for each month or partial month the balance remains unpaid, and may be subject to a statutory cap.

formulas.source_formula: Underpayment Penalty = Underpayment Amount × Monthly Penalty Rate × Months Overdue

nodes.name: Underpayment Penalty Safe Harbor Threshold
aliases: Minimum Tax Payment to Avoid Underpayment Penalty
少缴税罚金安全港阈值
nodes.definition: The Underpayment Penalty Safe Harbor Threshold is the minimum tax payment amount required under IRS safe harbor rules to avoid an underpayment penalty. Taxpayers can avoid penalties by paying the lesser of 90% of the current year's tax or a specified percentage of the prior year's tax, with the percentage depending on Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).

nodes.name: Underpricing
nodes.definition: Underpricing refers to the phenomenon where a stock's first-day closing price exceeds its IPO offer price, indicating the issuer priced the shares below the level set by market demand. The underpricing amount measures the absolute price difference between the first-day closing price and the IPO offer price; a positive amount indicates underpricing.

formulas.source_formula: Underpricing Amount = First-day Closing Price - IPO Offer Price

nodes.name: Underwater
nodes.definition: Underwater refers to a condition where the outstanding loan balance on an asset exceeds its current market value, resulting in negative equity for the asset holder and potentially constraining financial flexibility.

nodes.name: Underwater Mortgage
nodes.definition: An underwater mortgage refers to a situation where the current market value of a property is less than the outstanding mortgage principal, resulting in negative home equity and potentially constraining refinancing or sale options.

nodes.name: Underweight
nodes.definition: Underweight refers to holding a smaller portfolio weight in a security relative to its benchmark. Underweight percentage quantifies the extent to which the portfolio weight is below the benchmark weight, calculated as the benchmark weight minus the portfolio weight. A positive result indicates an underweight position, while a negative result indicates an overweight position.

formulas.source_formula: Underweight Percentage = Benchmark Weight - Portfolio Weight

nodes.name: Underwriting Expense Ratio
nodes.definition: The underwriting expense ratio measures the proportion of insurance premiums consumed by underwriting-related operating expenses over a period, indicating an insurer's cost efficiency in writing and servicing policies. A lower ratio generally signifies better operating efficiency and stronger underwriting performance.

formulas.source_formula: Underwriting Expense Ratio = Underwriting Expenses ÷ Premiums

nodes.name: Underwriting Fee
nodes.definition: Underwriting fee is the compensation charged by investment banks or securities firms for providing underwriting services to companies issuing securities (such as stocks or bonds). This fee represents a core cost paid by the issuer to obtain the underwriter's professional services in areas such as securities pricing, sales, and distribution.

nodes.name: Underwriting Income
nodes.definition: Underwriting income is the profit (or loss) generated from an insurer's core underwriting operations, calculated as premiums from insurance policies minus claims and underwriting-related expenses. It excludes investment income and reflects the insurer's operating performance in pricing risk, managing claims, and controlling expenses.

formulas.source_formula: Underwriting Income = Premiums Collected - (Claims Paid + Expenses Incurred)

nodes.name: Underwriting Spread
nodes.definition: Underwriting spread is the per-share difference between the public offering price and the price paid by underwriters to the issuer, representing the gross compensation to underwriters for distribution, pricing, and risk-bearing services in primary market offerings such as IPOs and follow-on offerings.

formulas.source_formula: Underwriting Spread per Share = Public Offering Price per Share - Underwriters' Purchase Price per Share

nodes.name: Undistributed Profit at End of Q2
aliases: Retained Earnings as of Q2 End
第二季度未分配利润余额
nodes.definition: Undistributed profit at the end of the second quarter refers to the cumulative balance of net profit retained by the enterprise and not yet distributed after one quarter of operations (typically from April 1 to June 30), following the allocation of statutory surplus reserves, discretionary surplus reserves, and profit distributions to investors.

nodes.name: Unearned Discount
nodes.definition: Unearned discount refers to the unrecognized portion of the precomputed finance charge on a loan. Under the Rule of 78 (sum-of-the-digits method), the remaining finance charge that has not yet been earned by the lender is determined based on the number of payments remaining relative to the total payment schedule.

formulas.source_formula: Unearned Discount = Total Finance Charge × (Remaining Payments × (Remaining Payments + 1)) ÷ (Total Payments × (Total Payments + 1))

nodes.name: Unearned Interest
nodes.definition: Unearned interest refers to the portion of the precomputed finance charge that has not yet been earned by the lender at the time of early repayment. Under the Rule of 78 (Sum-of-the-Digits method), the unearned interest rebate is calculated based on the sum of the digits weighting of remaining payments relative to the original payment schedule, providing a standardized approach for consumer loans with precomputed finance charges.

formulas.source_formula: Unearned Interest (Rule of 78) = Total Finance Charge × (Remaining Payments × (Remaining Payments + 1)) ÷ (Original Payments × (Original Payments + 1))

nodes.name: Unearned Premium
nodes.definition: Unearned premium is the portion of written premium received by an insurer that has not yet been recognized as revenue because the corresponding coverage period has not elapsed. It is recorded as a liability and amortized into earned premium over the policy term, typically on a time-proportion (pro rata) basis.

formulas.source_formula: Unearned Premium = Total Premium × (1 - Time Elapsed ÷ Policy Duration)
Unearned Premium = Total Premium ÷ Policy Period Days × (Policy Period Days - Elapsed Days)

nodes.name: Unearned Revenue
nodes.definition: Unearned revenue (deferred revenue) is a liability representing cash received for goods or services not yet delivered. As performance obligations are satisfied over time, a portion of the liability is recognized as revenue and the remaining balance is adjusted downward accordingly.

formulas.source_formula: Unearned Revenue (Adjusted) = Initial Unearned Revenue - Revenue Recognized per Period

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance
nodes.definition: Unemployment insurance is a social insurance system mandated by national legislation, funded through collective social contributions, which provides material assistance to workers who have temporarily lost their livelihood due to unemployment, ensuring their basic living standards and promoting their re-employment.

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance Contribution Base
aliases: 失业保险缴费工资基数
nodes.definition: The unemployment insurance contribution base refers to the wage income benchmark used to calculate the amount of unemployment insurance premiums payable by employers and individuals. Typically, the employer's contribution base is the total wages of the unit in the previous year, while the individual's contribution base is the individual's total wages in the previous year. Specific upper and lower limits are determined by local governments based on factors such as the average social wage.

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance Contribution Rate
nodes.definition: The unemployment insurance contribution rate refers to the percentage rate determined by national regulations, under which employers and individual employees respectively contribute unemployment insurance premiums based on a specified percentage of the employer's total payroll or the employee's individual wage. Typically, employers contribute 2% of their total employee payroll, while individual employees contribute 1% of their own wages, though specific rates may be adjusted according to local policies.

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Amount
aliases: 失业保险个人缴纳金额
nodes.definition: The Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Amount refers to the unemployment insurance premium calculated and paid by individual workers participating in the urban employee unemployment insurance scheme, based on a specified percentage of their monthly wages as stipulated by national regulations. It constitutes a component of individual social security expenditures and is used to provide basic living security and employment assistance during periods of unemployment.

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance Individual Contribution Rate
aliases: 个人失业保险缴费比例
nodes.definition: The unemployment insurance individual contribution rate refers to the percentage of an employee's monthly wage that must be contributed to unemployment insurance. According to current regulations, this rate is typically 1% of the employee's monthly wage and is withheld by the employer from the employee's salary.

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance Premium
nodes.definition: Unemployment insurance premium refers to the fee paid by employers and individual employees according to state regulations, calculated as a certain percentage of the employee's wage income, used to establish the unemployment insurance fund. It is one of the prerequisites for employees to claim unemployment insurance benefits after becoming unemployed.

formulas.source_formula: Unemployment Insurance Tax = Taxable Income × State Unemployment Tax Rate

nodes.name: Unemployment Insurance and Taxes in Management Expenses
Unemployment Rate
nodes.definition: The unemployment rate measures the percentage of the labor force that is unemployed and actively seeking work. It is calculated by dividing the number of unemployed persons by the total labor force and expressing the result as a percentage.

formulas.source_formula: Unemployment Rate (%) = (Unemployed ÷ Labor Force) × 100

nodes.name: Unemployment Rate (U-5)
nodes.definition: The U-5 unemployment rate measures the percentage of the expanded labor force—defined as the civilian labor force plus marginally attached workers—that is not employed. It includes unemployed persons and marginally attached workers (including discouraged workers) relative to the expanded labor force.

formulas.source_formula: Unemployment Rate (U-5) = (Unemployed Persons + Marginally Attached Workers) ÷ (Civilian Labor Force + Marginally Attached Workers) × 100

nodes.name: Unfavorable Variance
nodes.definition: Unfavorable variance is the positive difference by which actual costs or values exceed budgeted, standard, or projected amounts. It signals cost overruns, revenue shortfalls, or performance inefficiencies relative to plan and is central to budgeting and variance analysis in management accounting.

formulas.source_formula: Unfavorable Variance = Actual Value - Budgeted Value
Unhedged Amount = Contract Amount × Spot Rate

nodes.name: Unified Tax Credit
nodes.definition: The Unified Tax Credit is a nonrefundable federal transfer tax credit that offsets gift and estate tax liabilities up to the applicable credit amount, which is derived from the basic exclusion amount. It reduces or eliminates estate tax payable after exemptions and prior taxable gifts are considered, and may be affected by portability and lifetime gift use.

nodes.name: Unissued Shares
nodes.definition: Unissued shares are authorized by a company’s charter but have not yet been issued. They represent the difference between total authorized shares and total issued shares (the sum of outstanding shares and treasury stock), indicating the potential shares available for future issuance.

formulas.source_formula: Unissued Shares = Total Authorized Shares - (Total Outstanding Shares + Treasury Stock Shares)

nodes.name: Unit Benefit Formula
nodes.definition: The unit benefit formula is a defined benefit pension plan accrual method that calculates an employee’s annual retirement benefit as the product of credited years of service, an accrual rate expressed as a percentage of salary, and the employee’s career average salary, linking benefit accruals to both service and pay under plan provisions.

nodes.name: Unit Consumption
nodes.definition: Unit consumption refers to the fixed quantity of a specific resource (such as raw materials, energy, or labor hours) required to complete one unit of work (e.g., producing one product, delivering one service) in production, manufacturing, or the execution of a specific task. It serves as a fundamental input data point for cost accounting, budget preparation, and resource requirement planning.

nodes.name: Unit Consumption Price Change
nodes.definition: Unit consumption price change is a derivative indicator that represents the change in unit price, typically calculated by comparing unit consumption prices across different periods, such as the change amount or change rate, used to analyze consumption price fluctuations or cost change trends.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Consumption Price Change = (Current Period Unit Consumption Price - Prior Period Unit Consumption Price) ÷ Prior Period Unit Consumption Price
Unit Consumption Price Change = Current Period Unit Consumption Price - Prior Period Unit Consumption Price

nodes.name: Unit Contribution Margin
nodes.definition: Unit Contribution Margin refers to the balance of the selling price per unit minus its variable cost per unit. It is used to measure the contribution of each unit of product to fixed costs and profit, and is a core indicator in management accounting for analyzing cost behavior and profitability.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Contribution Margin = Unit Sales Price - Unit Variable Cost
Unit Contribution Margin = Unit Price - Unit Variable Cost

nodes.name: Unit Contribution Margin by Product
nodes.definition: Unit Contribution Margin by Product refers to the amount remaining when the selling price per unit of a specific product is subtracted by the corresponding variable cost per unit. This amount is used to cover the company's fixed costs and ultimately forms profit, serving as a key indicator for measuring the profitability of individual products.

nodes.name: Unit Cost
nodes.definition: Unit cost refers to the total cost incurred to produce each unit of product, typically calculated by dividing the sum of the beginning work-in-process inventory cost and the production costs incurred during the current month by the total output.

nodes.name: Unit Cost of Auxiliary Production
nodes.definition: Unit cost of auxiliary production refers to the average cost per unit of product or service, calculated by allocating the total expenses incurred by auxiliary production departments (such as maintenance, power supply, and water supply workshops) for providing services to primary production and other departments, averaged over the total quantity of products or services provided.

operands.metric: Total Quantity of Auxiliary Products or Services

formulas.source_formula: Unit Cost of Auxiliary Production = Total Auxiliary Production Expenses ÷ Total Quantity of Auxiliary Products or Services

nodes.name: Unit Cost of Finished Goods
nodes.definition: Unit cost of finished goods refers to the average cost allocated per unit of finished product, used to measure production efficiency and profitability.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Cost of Finished Goods = Total Cost of Finished Goods ÷ Finished Goods Output

nodes.name: Unit Cost of Inventory
nodes.definition: Unit cost of inventory refers to the average cost value corresponding to each unit of inventory held by an enterprise (such as one piece, one kilogram, or one carton), used to measure the cost level of stock goods or materials.

nodes.name: Unit Cost of Inventory Prior to Current Shipment
aliases: Unit Cost of Inventory Prior to Shipment
nodes.definition: Unit cost of inventory prior to current shipment refers to the average cost per unit (e.g., per piece, per kilogram) of a specific batch of inventory calculated before the enterprise dispatches (sells or withdraws) that batch. This cost is typically determined based on the inventory valuation method chosen by the enterprise (such as FIFO, weighted average method, etc.) and is used to ascertain the cost of goods issued and to carry forward the cost of sales.

nodes.name: Unit Cost of Inventory Prior to This Shipment
Unit Count
nodes.definition: Unit count is a measurement unit, typically used to quantify the specific number of equipment, machinery, vehicles, or particular products. In financial and operational management, it is commonly employed to measure the physical scale of production, sales, or inventory.

nodes.name: Unit Direct Labor Cost
nodes.definition: Unit direct labor cost refers to the direct labor expenses incurred in producing a single unit of product. It serves as a crucial foundation for calculating product variable costs, cost control, and budget preparation. It reflects the efficiency and cost level of direct labor input in the production process.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Direct Labor Cost = Total Direct Labor Cost ÷ Product Output
Unit Direct Labor Cost = Standard Labor Hours per Unit × Wage Rate per Labor Hour

nodes.name: Unit Direct Material Cost
aliases: 单位产品直接材料成本
nodes.definition: Unit direct material cost refers to the total cost of raw materials, primary materials, auxiliary materials, spare parts and components, purchased semi-finished goods, packaging materials, and low-value consumables consumed in producing one unit of a product, which constitute the physical substance of the product. Under standard costing, it is a predetermined cost target based on material price standards and standard material usage per unit of product.

nodes.name: Unit Fixed Cost
nodes.definition: Unit fixed cost refers to the fixed cost allocated to each unit of product produced or service provided within a certain period. Fixed costs are those that do not vary with changes in production volume or business activity within a relevant range, such as rent, equipment depreciation, administrative salaries, and insurance premiums. Unit fixed cost decreases as production volume increases and is a fundamental composite indicator in cost behavior analysis and management accounting.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Fixed Cost = Total Fixed Cost ÷ Production Volume

nodes.name: Unit Holding Cost
nodes.definition: Unit holding cost refers to the total of various expenses incurred by an enterprise to maintain one unit of inventory (such as one item of goods or one ton of raw materials) over a specific period (typically one year). These expenses primarily include warehouse rental or depreciation, labor costs for warehouse management, insurance premiums for inventory, interest losses or opportunity costs from capital tied up, and risk costs such as potential damage, obsolescence, or depreciation of inventory.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Holding Cost = Total Storage Cost ÷ Storage Quantity

nodes.name: Unit Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Unit inventory cost refers to the average cost incurred by an enterprise to acquire and hold each unit of inventory over a specific period. It is a core indicator for inventory cost management and accounting, with calculation methods including the weighted average method at month-end and the moving weighted average method.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Inventory Cost = (Actual Cost of Existing Inventory + Actual Cost of Current Purchase) ÷ (Quantity of Existing Inventory + Quantity of Current Purchase)
Unit Inventory Cost = (Beginning Inventory Cost + Current Period Purchase Cost) ÷ (Beginning Inventory Quantity + Current Period Purchase Quantity)

nodes.name: Unit Manufacturing Cost
aliases: Cost of Goods Manufactured per Unit
nodes.definition: Unit manufacturing cost refers to the total production cost required to manufacture one unit of product, typically calculated by dividing the total manufacturing cost over a specific period by the total production volume during that period. It is a core metric for cost accounting, product pricing, and profitability analysis.

nodes.name: Unit Market Value
nodes.definition: Unit market value refers to the trading price or fair value of a single financial asset (such as per share of stock, per fund unit) in the open market, which is the result of the equilibrium of market supply and demand. In financial analysis, it serves as fundamental data directly used to calculate valuation metrics such as total market capitalization, price-to-earnings ratio, and price-to-book ratio, and is not itself derived from specific financial formulas.

nodes.name: Unit Material Quota
nodes.definition: Unit material quota refers to the predetermined standard quantity of material consumption for producing one unit of qualified product (or completing one unit of workload) under specific production technology and management conditions. It serves as essential foundational data for material cost accounting, cost control, and production planning in enterprises.

nodes.name: Unit Opportunity Cost
nodes.definition: Unit opportunity cost refers to the potential maximum benefit foregone for each additional or reduced unit of activity (such as production, transaction, or investment) in a specific decision. It measures the value of the alternative that must be sacrificed to obtain one unit of current benefit.

nodes.name: Unit Period Cost
nodes.definition: Unit period cost refers to the average period cost borne by an enterprise per unit of product produced or service provided during a specific accounting period. Period costs include administrative expenses, selling expenses, and financial expenses. This metric is used to measure the level of period costs consumed per unit of output.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Period Cost = Period Costs ÷ Product Output
Unit Period Cost = (Administrative Expenses + Selling Expenses + Financial Expenses) ÷ Product Output

nodes.name: Unit Price
nodes.definition: Unit price is the selling price per unit of a good or service, used in financial management for pricing decisions, cost analysis, and profit planning. It can be calculated using financial metrics such as total price, quantity, cost, and profit.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Price = Total Price ÷ Quantity
Unit Price = Unit Cost ÷ (1 - Gross Profit Margin)

nodes.name: Unit Price per Product
nodes.definition: Unit price per product refers to the selling price of each individual product. In cost-volume-profit analysis, it can be calculated using financial metrics such as profit, fixed costs, sales volume, and unit variable cost, and is a key variable for calculating contribution margin and assessing profitability.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Price per Product = Unit Variable Cost + Unit Contribution Margin

nodes.name: Unit Product Consumption
aliases: 单位产品材料消耗定额
nodes.definition: Unit product consumption refers to the average quantity of a specific raw material, energy, or other resource consumed in the production process to manufacture one unit (e.g., one piece, one set) of a particular product. It serves as a fundamental data point in cost accounting, material management, and production planning.

nodes.name: Unit Product Cost
nodes.definition: Unit product cost refers to the average cost incurred to produce a single unit of product, reflecting the expense level of similar products. It is the cost allocated to each unit by distributing the total cost based on different consumption levels, typically calculated by dividing total cost by total output. It is a key metric in cost accounting and pricing decisions.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Product Cost = Total Product Cost ÷ Product Quantity
Unit Product Cost = (Production Cost + Period Expenses) ÷ Product Quantity
Unit Product Cost = (Direct Materials + Direct Labor + Manufacturing Overhead) ÷ Product Quantity

nodes.name: Unit Product Price
nodes.definition: Unit product price refers to the amount charged to customers per unit of product, forming the basis of sales revenue. Its determination methods vary, commonly including cost-plus pricing based on costs, as well as pricing strategies that consider target profit, market competition, and customer value perception.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Product Price = (Unit Fixed Cost + Unit Variable Cost) × (1 + Cost-Plus Rate)

nodes.name: Unit Product Required Equipment Setup Time
aliases: 单位产品设备准备时间
单台设备必要调整时间
nodes.definition: Unit Product Required Equipment Setup Time refers to the average preparation and adjustment time necessary for equipment to switch from one product or state to another for the production of each unit of product during the manufacturing process. It is one of the factors to be considered when establishing labor time standards and calculating manufacturing overhead.

nodes.name: Unit Product Rest Time
nodes.definition: Unit Product Rest Time refers to the non-working time reserved or accounted for in the production process for operators to rest per unit of product produced. It is one of the components constituting the total standard direct labor hours and reflects the humanization factors and reasonable intervals for labor efficiency considered in standard time setting.

nodes.name: Unit Product Selling Price
nodes.definition: Unit product selling price refers to the amount charged to customers for the sale of a single product. It is typically determined by market supply and demand, competitive conditions, corporate pricing strategy, or negotiation with customers, and serves as the fundamental data for calculating sales revenue.

nodes.name: Unit Product Work Efficiency
nodes.definition: Unit product work efficiency is an efficiency metric that measures the relationship between the workload required to complete a unit product and the standard time consumed during the production process, used to evaluate the utilization efficiency of production resources.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Product Work Efficiency = Unit Product Workload ÷ Unit Product Standard Time

nodes.name: Unit Product Workload
nodes.definition: Unit product workload refers to the total amount of work required to produce one qualified product, serving as a fundamental component for calculating productivity metrics such as standard hours per unit.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Product Workload = Standard Hours per Unit × Work Efficiency per Unit

nodes.name: Unit Profit
nodes.definition: Unit profit refers to the amount remaining after deducting all related costs (including direct costs and allocated indirect expenses) from the revenue generated by selling a single product or providing a single service. It is a core metric for measuring the profitability efficiency of a company's products or services.

nodes.name: Unit Quantity Cost
nodes.definition: Unit quantity cost refers to the cost amount allocated to each unit of product, typically calculated by dividing total cost by total quantity, commonly used in cost calculation for joint products or by-products.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Quantity Cost = Joint Cost ÷ Total Quantity of Joint Products

nodes.name: Unit Selling Price
nodes.definition: Unit selling price refers to the price charged by an enterprise for selling a single product, typically calculated through financial methods such as cost-plus pricing and sales profit margin pricing. It is a key indicator for formulating sales strategies, conducting profitability analysis, and managing target costs.

formulas.source_formula: Unit Selling Price = (Unit Fixed Cost + Unit Variable Cost) × (1 + Cost-plus Rate)
Unit Selling Price = (Unit Manufacturing Cost + Unit Period Expenses) ÷ (1 - Sales Profit Margin - Consumption Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Unit Selling Price of the Product
nodes.definition: The unit selling price of the product refers to the price charged to customers for each unit of a specific product sold by the enterprise in the market. It serves as the basis for calculating sales revenue, profit, and conducting market pricing analysis.

nodes.name: Unit Stockout Cost
nodes.definition: Unit stockout cost refers to the average economic loss incurred per unit of inventory shortage (e.g., one piece, one kilogram) due to supply interruption. It is a key intermediate variable for calculating total stockout cost, determining economic order quantity, and setting safety stock levels, typically encompassing potential costs such as lost profit from missed sales opportunities, additional expenses for emergency procurement, and loss of goodwill.
