It can typically be broken down into specific cost items such as direct materials, direct labor, manufacturing overhead, selling expenses, and administrative expenses. It serves as the basis for calculating weighted average cost and for cost analysis and decision-making.

nodes.name: Various Deductions
nodes.definition: Various Deductions refer to the total sum of costs, expenses, taxes, losses, and other expenditures that are permitted to be subtracted from total revenue according to tax laws when calculating taxable income. In both Individual Income Tax and Corporate Income Tax, it is a collective concept composed of multiple specific deduction items, and its amount needs to be derived by aggregating other specific deduction items.

formulas.source_formula: Various Deductions = Standard Deduction of 60,000 yuan + Special Deductions + Special Additional Deductions + Other Deductions Determined by Law

nodes.name: Various Expenses
nodes.definition: Various expenses refer to the consumption of various economic resources incurred by an enterprise in its daily operations to generate revenue, excluding cost of sales, such as selling, administrative, and research and development expenses, which directly reduce the current period's profit.

nodes.name: Various Other Expense Items
nodes.definition: Various other expense items refer to the aggregate of miscellaneous, secondary, or difficult-to-classify expense outlays in an enterprise's total costs and expenses, excluding major cost items (such as direct materials, direct labor, depreciation, amortization, interest expense, etc.). These items are typically consolidated as 'Total Other Expenses' in business operating costs, income statements, or specific expense calculations (e.g., super-deduction).

nodes.name: Vasicek Interest Rate Model
nodes.definition: The Vasicek Interest Rate Model is a stochastic differential equation that describes the evolution of interest rates over time, incorporating mean reversion to a long-term equilibrium level and volatility-driven random shocks.

nodes.name: Vega
nodes.definition: Vega is a sensitivity metric calculated through mathematical models (such as the Black-Scholes option pricing model), measuring the sensitivity of an option's price to changes in volatility. It is not a raw data item from financial statements.

nodes.name: Vega-Based Option Price Change
aliases: Option Price Change due to Volatility
期权价格变动（波动率敏感度）
维加影响下的期权价格变动
nodes.definition: Vega-based option price change quantifies the expected change in an option's price resulting from a specified change in implied volatility. It is calculated as the product of the option's vega (the sensitivity of the option price to volatility) and the change in implied volatility, assuming other factors remain constant.

nodes.name: Vehicle and Vessel Tax
nodes.definition: Vehicle and Vessel Tax is a property tax levied by the government on the owners or managers of vehicles and vessels that are legally required to be registered within China, primarily used to compensate for public expenditures in transportation infrastructure construction, maintenance, and improvement.

nodes.name: Vehicle and Vessel Usage Tax
nodes.definition: Vehicle and Vessel Usage Tax is a property tax levied by the state on entities and individuals who own and use vehicles and vessels within China. The tax paid by enterprises is typically recorded under the 'Business Taxes and Surcharges' account.

nodes.name: Velocity of Money
nodes.definition: Velocity of money measures the rate at which money is exchanged in an economy, calculated by dividing gross domestic product (GDP) by the money supply, indicating how many times a unit of currency circulates within a given time period.

nodes.name: Vertical Analysis
nodes.definition: Vertical analysis expresses each financial statement line item as a percentage of a base figure, enabling comparison of relative proportions within a single period.

formulas.source_formula: Vertical Analysis Percentage = (Financial Metric ÷ Total Sales) × 100
Vertical Analysis Percentage = (Item Value ÷ Total Value) × 100

nodes.name: Vested
nodes.definition: In legal and financial contexts, 'vested' refers to an individual's immediate and secured right to an asset or benefit (such as employer contributions in a retirement plan), which cannot be forfeited by any third party, even if actual possession or receipt is deferred to the future.

formulas.source_formula: Vested = Total Employer Contributions × Vesting Percentage
Vested Amount = Total Employer Contributions × Vesting Percentage

nodes.name: Vested Benefit Percentage
nodes.definition: Vested benefit percentage represents the proportion of employer-provided benefits (such as pension or stock options) that an employee has earned the irrevocable right to receive, determined by the years of service and the company’s vesting schedule.

nodes.name: Vested Shares per Year
nodes.definition: Vested shares per year represent the number of equity awards that become exercisable or owned by the employee in each year under a linear vesting schedule, calculated as the product of total granted shares and the annual vesting rate.

formulas.source_formula: Vested Shares per Year = Total Shares × Vesting Rate per Year

nodes.name: Vesting
nodes.definition: In legal and financial contexts, vesting refers to the point in time when an individual gains an irrevocable right to a specific asset or benefit, such as employer contributions in a retirement plan or stock options. Once vested, this right cannot be forfeited by any third party, even if actual possession or distribution occurs in the future.

nodes.name: Vesting Period
nodes.definition: The vesting period refers to a predetermined, fixed duration in agreements such as insurance or share-based payments, starting from the grant date and lasting until the beneficiary (e.g., an employee or policyholder) becomes eligible to exercise the right (e.g., to exercise options or receive insurance benefits). During this period, the beneficiary must continue to provide services or meet other conditions for the right to ultimately vest.

nodes.name: Viager Occupied Value
nodes.definition: Viager occupied value is the present value of a property in a viager (life annuity) transaction, adjusted downward based on the seller’s age to reflect the buyer’s obligation to pay a life annuity and the uncertainty of occupancy duration.

formulas.source_formula: Viager Occupied Value = Market Value × (1 − Age × Age Reduction Factor)

nodes.name: Viager Total Value Paid
nodes.definition: Viager Total Value Paid represents the aggregate amount a buyer commits to pay under a viager real-estate contract, comprising the initial down payment plus all scheduled cash installments expected over the seller’s statistical remaining lifetime.

formulas.source_formula: Viager Total Value Paid = Down Payment + Total Installments

nodes.name: Volatility
nodes.definition: Volatility is a statistical measure of the magnitude of price fluctuations and risk of an asset (such as stocks, bonds), typically expressed as the standard deviation of price returns. It reflects the intensity of price movements; higher volatility indicates greater price instability and higher risk.

formulas.source_formula: Volatility = (Current Period Value - Previous Period Value) ÷ Previous Period Value × 100%

nodes.name: Volatility Change
nodes.definition: Volatility change refers to the absolute change or percentage change in volatility metrics across different periods, reflecting variations in the volatility of financial data or asset prices. It is a composite indicator calculated based on volatility, not a leaf node, and is commonly used in financial analyses such as option value changes.

formulas.source_formula: Volatility Change = Current Period Volatility - Previous Period Volatility
Volatility Change = (Current Period Volatility - Previous Period Volatility) ÷ Previous Period Volatility × 100%

nodes.name: Volatility Ratio
nodes.definition: Volatility Ratio is a technical analysis measure that compares the current day's true range to the average true range (ATR), indicating how current price volatility relates to historical volatility and helping identify potential breakouts or patterns.

formulas.source_formula: Volatility Ratio = True Range ÷ Average True Range
supporting_source_formulas: Volatility Ratio = True Range ÷ Average True Range
Volatility Ratio = True Range ÷ Average True Range (ATR)

formulas.source_formula: Volatility Ratio = True Range ÷ EMA of True Range

nodes.name: Volatility Smile
nodes.definition: Volatility smile is the U-shaped pattern formed by plotting implied volatilities of options with the same expiration and underlying asset against their strike prices, indicating higher implied volatility for deep in-the-money and out-of-the-money options relative to at-the-money options.

nodes.name: Volatility Swap Payoff
nodes.definition: Volatility swap payoff is the monetary amount received or paid at settlement of a volatility swap contract, calculated as the notional value multiplied by the difference between realized volatility and the pre-agreed volatility strike.

formulas.source_formula: Volatility Swap Payoff = Notional Value × (Realized Volatility - Volatility Strike)

nodes.name: Volume Discount
nodes.definition: Volume discount is a pricing strategy where the unit price decreases as the purchase quantity increases, typically structured in tiers to incentivize larger orders.

formulas.source_formula: Volume Force = Volume × (2 × ((DM ÷ CM) - 1)) × Trend × 100

nodes.name: Volume Index
nodes.definition: A volume index is a relative number that measures the change in the quantity or physical volume of a group of goods or services between two different periods (e.g., the reporting period and the base period) after eliminating the effects of price changes. It reflects changes in the actual output of economic activities and is commonly used in constant price accounting, such as calculating the gross fixed capital formation at constant prices.

nodes.name: Volume Price Trend Indicator
nodes.definition: Volume Price Trend (VPT) is a cumulative technical indicator that combines price movement and volume to assess the strength of price trends and confirm price direction.

formulas.source_formula: Volume Ratio = Advancing Volume ÷ Declining Volume

nodes.name: Volume Variance
aliases: 固定制造费用能量差异
nodes.definition: Volume variance is a component of fixed manufacturing overhead cost variance, reflecting the impact of the difference between actual output and budgeted output on the allocation of fixed manufacturing overhead. It is calculated by subtracting the standard cost of fixed manufacturing overhead from the budgeted fixed manufacturing overhead, and is classified as a composite indicator.

operands.metric: Standard Cost of Fixed Manufacturing Overhead

formulas.source_formula: Volume Variance = Budgeted Fixed Manufacturing Overhead - Standard Cost of Fixed Manufacturing Overhead

nodes.name: Volume Weighted Average Price
nodes.definition: Volume Weighted Average Price (VWAP) is a technical indicator that measures the average price a security has traded at throughout the day, weighted by volume. It reflects both price and volume activity, providing a benchmark for traders to assess price trends and execution quality within a single trading session.

formulas.source_formula: VWAP = Total Value Traded ÷ Total Volume Traded

nodes.name: Voluntary Reserve
nodes.definition: Voluntary reserve refers to the amount of cash or assets that an insurance company chooses to hold beyond the minimum regulatory reserve requirements, typically expressed as a percentage of total revenue, to enhance financial stability and risk management.

formulas.source_formula: Voluntary Reserve = Total Revenue × (Reserve Percentage ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Vomma
nodes.definition: Vomma is the second-order partial derivative of an option's value with respect to the volatility of the underlying asset, measuring the rate of change of vega as volatility changes. It captures the convexity of vega and is crucial for understanding how an option's sensitivity to volatility itself shifts when implied volatility moves.

nodes.name: Vortex Indicator
nodes.definition: The Vortex Indicator (VI) is a technical analysis tool used to identify trend reversals by comparing the current period’s high and low to the previous period’s high and low, producing two oscillating lines: VI+ and VI-.

nodes.name: Wage Allocation Rate
nodes.definition: The wage (expense) allocation rate is a proportional coefficient used to allocate labor costs between finished goods and work-in-process at month-end, calculated based on standard labor hours.

operands.metric: Actual Wages Incurred in the Current Month

formulas.source_formula: Wage Allocation Rate = (Actual Wages for Beginning Work-in-Process + Actual Wages Incurred in Current Month) ÷ (Standard Hours for Finished Goods + Standard Hours for Ending Work-in-Process)

nodes.name: Wage Cost Allocated to a Specific Product
nodes.definition: Wage cost allocated to a specific product is the result of multiplying the actual labor hours used for that product by the wage allocation rate for production workers.

nodes.name: Wage Expense
nodes.definition: Wage expense represents the total compensation incurred by an entity for hourly labor within a reporting period. It typically includes regular pay for standard hours and additional overtime pay for hours worked beyond the standard workweek, measured on a gross basis before payroll taxes, deductions, and benefits.

nodes.name: Wage Income
nodes.definition: Wage income refers to the basic monetary compensation received by an individual for providing labor services through employment or engagement with a specific entity or organization. It typically includes wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increments, labor dividends, allowances, subsidies, and other earnings related to employment or engagement, constituting a significant component of an individual's disposable income.

nodes.name: Wage Indexing Factor
nodes.definition: The wage indexing factor is the ratio used by the Social Security Administration to adjust an individual's past earnings to the wage level of the year they turn age 60. It is calculated as the National Average Wage Index (NAWI) in the age-60 year divided by the NAWI in the specific prior year being indexed, and is applied when computing Average Indexed Monthly Earnings (AIME).

formulas.source_formula: Wage Indexing Factor = National Average Wage Index (Age 60 Year) ÷ National Average Wage Index (Specific Year)

nodes.name: Wage and Salary Income Amount
nodes.definition: Wage and salary income amount refers to the total sum of all monetary income received by an individual due to employment or appointment, including wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increases, labor dividends, allowances, subsidies, and other income related to employment or appointment. It serves as the original starting point data for calculating the taxable income for individual income tax.

nodes.name: Wages
nodes.definition: Wages refer to the labor compensation directly paid by an employer to an employee based on the employment contract, considering factors such as attendance records and performance results. It serves as the fundamental raw data for payroll accounting and is typically recorded as an expense account in accounting treatment.

nodes.name: Wages Allocable to Finished Goods
aliases: Labor Cost Allocated to Finished Products
分摊至完工产品的人工成本
完工产品应分配的工资
nodes.definition: Wages allocable to finished goods refers to the portion of total labor costs allocated to completed products based on the wage allocation rate (typically based on standard labor hours), used for accurate product costing in cost accounting.

operands.metric: Standard Labor Hours for Finished Goods

formulas.source_formula: Wages Allocable to Finished Goods = Standard Labor Hours for Finished Goods × Wage Allocation Rate

nodes.name: Wages Allocable to Work-in-Process at Month-End
aliases: Labor Cost Allocated to Work-in-Process Inventory at Month-End
月末在产品应分配的工资
nodes.definition: Wages allocable to work-in-process at month-end refer to the portion of total labor costs allocated to unfinished products based on the wage allocation rate.

operands.metric: Standard Hours of Work-in-Process at Month-End

formulas.source_formula: Wages Allocable to Work-in-Process at Month-End = Standard Hours of Work-in-Process at Month-End × Wage Allocation Rate

nodes.name: Wages Payable
nodes.definition: Wages payable refers to the total amount of wages, including various salaries, bonuses, and allowances, that an enterprise owes to its employees based on wage rates, attendance, performance, and other fundamental data but has not yet actually paid. It constitutes a current liability of the enterprise.

nodes.name: Wages and Benefits Charged Against Profits
aliases: Compensation and Benefits Charged Against Profits
利润分配中的工资福利
nodes.definition: Refers to expense items in enterprise accounting where a portion of profits is directly used to pay employees or provide employee benefits. It is typically not directly included in operating costs or period expenses, but rather treated as a profit distribution or expense under specific management decisions, directly affecting the enterprise's final distributable profits or retained earnings.

nodes.name: Wages and Benefits Paid from Profits
Wages and Salaries Income
nodes.definition: Wages and salaries income refers to all forms of labor remuneration received by an individual due to holding an office or being employed by a specific unit or organization. This typically includes basic wages, salaries, bonuses, year-end salary increases, labor dividends, various allowances, subsidies, and all other income related to the office held or employment. It is one of the taxable items stipulated under China's Individual Income Tax Law, and the tax payable is usually calculated based on monthly income.

nodes.name: Wages and Welfare Expenses
nodes.definition: Wages and welfare expenses refer to various welfare expenditures provided by an enterprise to its employees beyond direct compensation such as wages, bonuses, and allowances. They are typically accrued at a certain percentage (e.g., 14%) of the total payroll and are used to cover employee medical expenses, living hardship subsidies, expenditures for collective welfare facilities (such as canteens and bathrooms) and related personnel salaries, aiming to improve employees' living and working conditions.

nodes.name: Wages and Welfare Paid from Profits
Warrant Premium
nodes.definition: Warrant premium is the amount by which a warrant's market price exceeds its intrinsic value (the in-the-money component). It reflects time value, implied volatility, and other market factors affecting the warrant's pricing.

formulas.source_formula: Warrant Premium (%) = ((Warrant Price + Exercise Price - Current Share Price) ÷ Current Share Price) × 100

nodes.name: Wastage
nodes.definition: Wastage refers to the quantity of raw materials, products, or goods that is reduced due to unavoidable scrap, defects, evaporation, breakage, or other causes during production, storage, or transportation. It is typically calculated as the original total quantity minus the final usable or remaining quantity.

nodes.name: Wastage Rate
nodes.definition: Wastage rate is a key performance indicator that measures the extent of material loss during production, warehousing, or construction processes. It is typically expressed as a percentage and is used for cost control, budgeting, and material consumption quota management.

formulas.source_formula: Wastage Rate = (Wastage Quantity ÷ Net Usage Quantity) × 100%
Wastage Rate = (Raw Material Application Quantity - Actual Raw Material Usage) ÷ Raw Material Application Quantity × 100%

nodes.name: Waste Rate
nodes.definition: Waste rate is a ratio that measures the actual consumption of materials or resources exceeding the planned or theoretical net usage in production or operational processes. It is a key indicator for cost control and efficiency analysis, commonly used in variance analysis under standard costing.

formulas.source_formula: Waste Rate = (Wastage Quantity ÷ Net Usage) × 100%

nodes.name: Waterfall Payment
nodes.definition: Waterfall payment refers to the priority-based allocation of available cash to creditors, where interest obligations are satisfied before principal and higher-priority claims are paid before lower-priority claims. It is commonly used in structured finance to govern the order of cash distribution among tranches or creditors.

nodes.name: Wealth Added Index
nodes.definition: The Wealth Added Index measures shareholder value creation by comparing total equity returns (share price gains plus dividends) against the company's cost of equity. A positive WAI indicates value creation for shareholders, while a negative WAI indicates value destruction.

formulas.source_formula: Wealth Added Index = (Share Price Gains + Dividends) - Cost of Equity

nodes.name: Wealth Tax
nodes.definition: Wealth tax is a levy imposed on an individual's net worth (total assets minus liabilities). The wealth tax liability is calculated by applying a tax rate to net worth and may be adjusted by a residency factor to reflect jurisdictional rules on taxable assets. This measure is typically used in systems employing a flat rate on net wealth.

formulas.source_formula: Wealth Tax Liability = Net Worth × Tax Rate × Residency Factor

nodes.name: Weather Futures Payout
nodes.definition: Weather futures payout is the monetary amount owed under a weather derivative or futures contract, calculated by multiplying the deviation of the observed temperature from a preset benchmark by a contractual multiplier. It is commonly applied in heating degree day (HDD) or cooling degree day (CDD) structures to hedge temperature-related revenue and cost exposures.

formulas.source_formula: Weather Futures Payout = (Average Temperature - Benchmark Temperature) × Multiplier
Weekly EI Benefit Amount = Average Weekly Insurable Earnings × Benefit Rate

nodes.name: Wei
nodes.definition: Wei is the smallest denomination of Ether (ETH), equal to 10^(-18) ETH. It is used to express precise monetary amounts in Ethereum-based transactions, smart contracts, and on-chain accounting. The conversion expresses Wei as Ether multiplied by 10^18.

nodes.name: Wei (Gwei to Ether Conversion)
nodes.definition: Wei is the smallest denomination of Ether (ETH) on the Ethereum blockchain. Gwei equals 10^9 Wei and is commonly used to quote gas prices. This entry specifies the conversion from Gwei to Ether using the fixed conversion factor where 1 Ether = 10^9 Gwei.

formulas.source_formula: Wei Value = Ether Amount × Wei per Ether

nodes.name: Wei to Ether Conversion
nodes.definition: Wei to Ether Conversion refers to converting an amount denominated in Wei, the smallest denomination of Ether (ETH), into Ether by dividing by the conversion factor of 10^18. This unit conversion is used for valuation, pricing gas, and precise accounting of Ethereum transactions and balances.

nodes.name: Weight
nodes.definition: Weight is a relative concept for a specific indicator, representing its relative importance in overall evaluation or calculation. In statistics and finance, weight is commonly used to calculate weighted averages, where its value depends not only on the values of individual units but also on their frequency of occurrence or assigned importance proportion.

nodes.name: Weight of Asset A
nodes.definition: The weight of Asset A refers to a predetermined proportion or coefficient assigned to a specific Asset A when calculating portfolio risk (e.g., standard deviation) or regulatory capital requirements (e.g., credit risk-weighted assets). It reflects the relative importance of that asset within the overall portfolio or risk exposure, typically set directly based on regulatory provisions, internal policies, or investment strategies, rather than derived from a formula.

nodes.name: Weight of Asset in Market Portfolio
nodes.definition: The weight of an asset in the market portfolio refers to the proportion or share of a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) in the total value of the entire market portfolio (typically a theoretical portfolio comprising all tradable risky assets). It measures the importance of that asset relative to the entire market and serves as the basis for calculating metrics such as the expected return of the market portfolio.

nodes.name: Weight of Each Asset in the Market Portfolio
nodes.definition: The weight of each asset in the market portfolio refers to the proportion of an individual asset's market value (e.g., stocks, bonds) to the total market value of all assets within the market portfolio, which represents the entire market. This proportion directly reflects the relative size and importance of that asset in the overall market and serves as a fundamental input parameter for financial models such as the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM).

nodes.name: Weight of Individual Asset in Portfolio
nodes.definition: The weight of an individual asset in a portfolio refers to the proportion of the market value of a specific asset (such as a stock or bond) to the total value of the entire investment portfolio composed of multiple assets. It reflects the relative importance and capital allocation of that asset within the portfolio.

nodes.name: Weight of Individual Assets in a Portfolio
nodes.definition: The weight of individual assets in a portfolio refers to the proportion or percentage of the market value of each asset (such as stocks, bonds, etc.) relative to the total value of the entire portfolio. It measures the degree to which that asset influences the overall performance and risk of the portfolio, serving as key foundational data for asset allocation and risk management.

nodes.name: Weight of Security j
nodes.definition: The weight of security j refers to the proportion of the total portfolio value allocated to security j (such as a specific stock or bond) when constructing an investment portfolio. It reflects the relative importance and investment share of that security within the portfolio.

nodes.name: Weight of the k-th Security
nodes.definition: The weight of the k-th security refers to the proportion of its value within an investment portfolio, typically determined by its market value relative to the total market value of the portfolio, or derived through mathematical models such as mean-variance optimization. It serves as a fundamental parameter for calculating portfolio risk and return.

operands.metric: Market Value of the k-th Security
Total Market Value of the Portfolio

formulas.source_formula: Weight of the k-th Security = Market Value of the k-th Security ÷ Total Market Value of the Portfolio

nodes.name: Weighted Alpha
nodes.definition: Weighted Alpha is a time-weighted measure of a security's benchmark-relative performance (alpha) over a defined period, typically one year. It emphasizes recent returns by assigning higher weights to more recent observations and summarizes the weighted excess returns per day over the period.

nodes.name: Weighted Average
nodes.definition: Weighted average is an average calculated by summing the products of each value multiplied by its corresponding weight, then dividing by the total weight. Its magnitude depends not only on the values themselves but also on their respective weights. In finance, it serves as a fundamental mathematical tool for calculating metrics such as Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) and inventory costs.

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average = Weighted Sum ÷ Total Weight

nodes.name: Weighted Average Contribution Margin Ratio
nodes.definition: The weighted average contribution margin ratio is a composite ratio calculated by weighting the contribution margin ratios of individual products by their respective sales proportions in a multi-product enterprise. It reflects the contribution level of the product mix to overall profitability and is commonly used in cost-volume-profit analysis and break-even point calculations.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Correlation
aliases: 组合加权平均相关系数
nodes.definition: Weighted average correlation is the portfolio-level correlation measure computed as the weighted mean of each asset's average correlation with the rest of the portfolio, using the assets' portfolio weights as weights. It is used to assess diversification and overall co-movement risk.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Cost
nodes.definition: Weighted average cost refers to the average cost calculated based on the weight of each cost item in the total cost.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Cost of Capital
aliases: After-Tax Weighted Average Cost of Capital
After-tax Weighted Average Cost of Capital
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) refers to the composite cost of capital calculated by weighting the cost of each capital source (such as common stock, preferred stock, bonds, and long-term debt) by its proportion in the total capital structure. It serves as a crucial discount rate for evaluating investment projects and calculating Economic Value Added (EVA).

nodes.name: Weighted Average Cost of Equity
aliases: 加权平均权益资本成本
加权平均股权资本成本
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Cost of Equity represents the overall required rate of return on a company's equity, calculated as the sum of each equity component's cost multiplied by its proportion of total equity. It consolidates the costs of different equity sources (e.g., common equity, preferred equity, retained earnings) according to their weights in the equity structure and is expressed as a decimal rate.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Cost per Share
nodes.definition: Weighted average cost per share represents the average purchase cost allocated to each share when multiple acquisitions occur at different prices. It is calculated by dividing the total cost of all purchase batches by the total number of shares acquired, and is commonly used to determine the cost basis for capital gains taxation and to assess investment performance.

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Cost per Share = Total Cost of Purchases ÷ Total Number of Shares Purchased

nodes.name: Weighted Average Coupon
nodes.definition: Weighted average coupon (WAC) is the principal-weighted average of the coupon rates in a mortgage pool or fixed-income portfolio. It is calculated by weighting each loan's coupon rate by its outstanding principal balance, indicating the pool's average nominal interest rate.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Credit Rating
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Credit Rating (WACR) measures a portfolio’s average credit quality by assigning numeric values to credit ratings and computing the weighted average using each holding’s portfolio weight. It facilitates comparison of overall credit risk across bond funds and fixed-income portfolios.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Diluted Common Shares Outstanding
aliases: 稀释普通股加权平均数
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Diluted Common Shares Outstanding is a composite metric used in calculating diluted earnings per share. It is derived by adding the weighted average number of common shares outstanding used in calculating basic earnings per share to the weighted average number of additional common shares that would be issued assuming the conversion of all dilutive potential common shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, stock options, etc.). This metric reflects the comprehensive impact of potentially dilutive securities on the number of common shares.

operands.metric: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Basic EPS
Weighted Average Number of Additional Common Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Common Shares

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Diluted Common Shares Outstanding = Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Basic EPS + Weighted Average Number of Additional Common Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Common Shares

nodes.name: Weighted Average Increment from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Common Shares
Weighted Average Life
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Life (WAL) measures the average time to receive principal repayments on an amortizing security, weighting each period by the proportion of principal returned. It reflects principal timing and is commonly used for bonds, loans, and mortgage-backed securities.

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Life = Total Weighted Principal ÷ Total Principal Payments

nodes.name: Weighted Average Loan Age
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Loan Age (WALA) measures the average age of loans in a mortgage-backed securities pool, weighted by each loan’s initial nominal principal, typically expressed in months since origination. It indicates the pool’s seasoning and is used in prepayment and cash flow analysis.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Market Capitalization
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Market Capitalization describes the market-cap-weighted structure of an index, where each constituent's weight is proportional to its market capitalization relative to the index's total market capitalization. The constituent weights, often expressed as percentages, indicate each security's contribution to the index based on size.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Maturity
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Maturity (WAM) refers to the weighted average of the time to maturity for each security in a mortgage-backed security (MBS) portfolio, with the weight being the outstanding principal balance of each security. It is used to estimate the average remaining term of the underlying mortgages.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Additional Common Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Common Shares
Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Assumed Conversion
aliases: Incremental Shares from Dilutive Potential Ordinary Shares
假定转换增加的普通股加权平均数
稀释性潜在普通股转换增加的普通股加权平均数
nodes.definition: This concept is an intermediate adjustment item in calculating diluted earnings per share. It refers to the weighted average number of additional ordinary shares that would be outstanding if all dilutive potential ordinary shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, share options, etc.) were converted into ordinary shares at the beginning of the period or the date of issuance, weighted for the period they were outstanding during the reporting period. Its value is derived through assumption and weighted calculation, rather than being raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Ordinary Shares
aliases: Weighted average number of additional ordinary shares from conversion of dilutive potential ordinary shares
增加的普通股股数的加权平均数（稀释）
稀释性潜在普通股转换增加的股数加权平均
nodes.definition: The weighted average number of additional ordinary shares from conversion of dilutive potential ordinary shares is a composite metric used in calculating diluted earnings per share. It represents the weighted average (by time) of the increased number of shares assuming all dilutive potential ordinary shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, stock options, etc.) are converted into ordinary shares. This metric is derived based on the quantity of potential ordinary shares, conversion ratios, issuance dates, etc., following accounting standards (e.g., assuming conversion at the beginning of the period for those issued in prior periods, and at the issuance date for those issued during the current period). It is used to adjust the denominator of basic earnings per share to reflect the potential dilution effect.

operands.metric: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in Diluted EPS Calculation
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in Basic EPS Calculation

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Ordinary Shares = Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in Diluted EPS Calculation - Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding in Basic EPS Calculation

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Additional Ordinary Shares from Dilutive Potential Ordinary Shares Conversion
aliases: Additional Weighted Average Shares from Dilutive Securities
Weighted Average Increase in Common Shares from Conversion of Dilutive Potential Common Shares
潜在普通股转换增加加权股数
稀释性股数增加加权平均
nodes.definition: The weighted average number of additional ordinary shares from dilutive potential ordinary shares conversion refers to the weighted average, calculated for the purpose of determining diluted earnings per share, of the increased number of shares assuming the conversion of dilutive potential ordinary shares (such as convertible bonds, warrants, and share options) into ordinary shares. This average is computed by applying time-weighting factors from the assumed conversion date to the end of the reporting period for each dilutive instrument. This metric is a composite adjustment to the denominator of diluted earnings per share and is not directly derived from raw financial statement data.

aliases: 加权平均流通普通股股数

nodes.definition: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding is a composite metric calculated using the weighted average method to determine the average number of common shares during the reporting period. It incorporates the time-weighting of factors such as share issuance and repurchase, serving as the key denominator for calculating basic earnings per share.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding Expected at Period End
aliases: Expected Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding
预期加权平均普通股股数
nodes.definition: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding expected at period end refers to the average number of common shares calculated on a time-weighted basis, after considering potential changes in the number of common shares during the reporting period (such as new issuances, repurchases, etc.), used to forecast metrics like earnings per share for future periods (e.g., the next reporting period). It is a forward-looking composite indicator.

operands.metric: Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period
Expected New Common Shares Issued During the Period
Expected Common Shares Repurchased During the Period

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding Expected at Period End = Number of Common Shares Outstanding at Beginning of Period + Expected New Common Shares Issued During the Period × Expected Time Outstanding ÷ Expected Reporting Period Duration - Expected Common Shares Repurchased During the Period × Expected Time After Repurchase ÷ Expected Reporting Period Duration

aliases: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding

nodes.definition: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding at period end refers to the number of shares calculated by weighting the shares issued at different points in time according to their proportion of the reporting period in circulation. This calculation is performed to more accurately reflect the actual number of common shares available throughout the period when computing metrics such as earnings per share for a financial reporting period (e.g., quarter or year), considering that the number of common shares may change due to new share issuances or share repurchases during the period.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Basic EPS
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for Current Period
Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding for the Next Period
aliases: Next Period's Weighted Average Shares Outstanding
下期加权平均普通股股数
下期发行在外普通股加权平均股数
下期普通股加权平均数
nodes.definition: The weighted average number of common shares outstanding for the next period refers to an average share count calculated based on the time-weighting of common share issuances and repurchases during the next period (typically the next financial reporting period), used for metrics such as earnings per share for the next period. It reflects the average level of common equity actually available to shareholders throughout the entire upcoming reporting period.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding (Pre-change)
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding (Previous Period)
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding Before Changes
aliases: 变动前普通股加权平均数
期初发行在外普通股加权平均数
调整前普通股加权平均数
nodes.definition: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding before changes refers to the number of ordinary shares issued at the beginning of the period, weighted by the time they were outstanding during the reporting period, calculated before considering changes such as new issuances or repurchases of ordinary shares during the current period. This figure is used to reflect the time-weighting effect of the number of ordinary shares when calculating earnings per share. It serves as one of the base data points for determining the number of ordinary shares corresponding to the net profit attributable to ordinary shareholders when calculating both basic and diluted earnings per share.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding During the Period
aliases: Weighted Average Number of Common Shares Outstanding
Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding

nodes.definition: Refers to the average number of shares outstanding during the reporting period, weighted by the time they were outstanding. It is the key denominator for calculating basic earnings per share. The calculation is based on the number of shares at the beginning of the period, with subsequent issuances or repurchases of ordinary shares weighted by the portion of the reporting period they were outstanding.

operands.metric: Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of the Period
Number of New Ordinary Shares Issued During the Period
Number of Ordinary Shares Repurchased During the Period

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding During the Period = Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of the Period + Number of New Ordinary Shares Issued During the Period × Time Outstanding ÷ Reporting Period Time - Number of Ordinary Shares Repurchased During the Period × Time Repurchased ÷ Reporting Period Time

nodes.definition: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding expected refers to the average number of shares calculated by weighting the ordinary shares outstanding during the reporting period based on the time they were outstanding. It serves as the basis for calculating key per-share metrics such as expected earnings per share and expected other comprehensive income per share.

operands.metric: Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of the Period
Number of New Ordinary Shares Issued During the Period
Number of Ordinary Shares Repurchased During the Period

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding Expected = Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding at the Beginning of the Period + Number of New Ordinary Shares Issued During the Period × (Days Outstanding ÷ Days in the Reporting Period) - Number of Ordinary Shares Repurchased During the Period × (Days Since Repurchase ÷ Days in the Reporting Period)

Number of New Ordinary Shares Issued During the Period
Number of Days New Ordinary Shares are Outstanding
Number of Days in the Reporting Period

It reflects the impact of changes in the number of ordinary shares during the reporting period on earnings per share using the weighted average method, considering the number of shares at the beginning of the period, newly issued shares, repurchased shares, and their respective time-weighting, typically calculated based on the number of days.

nodes.definition: The weighted average number of ordinary shares outstanding is the denominator used in calculating basic earnings per share. It is weighted based on the period the ordinary shares are outstanding during the reporting period, reflecting the impact of changes in the capital structure on earnings per share during the period.

nodes.definition: According to the Application Guidance of Accounting Standards for Business Enterprises No. 34 - Earnings Per Share, the 'Weighted Average Number of Ordinary Shares Outstanding' is a fundamental metric for calculating both basic and diluted earnings per share. It reflects the average number of ordinary shares calculated during the reporting period, taking into account changes in the number of ordinary shares due to events such as new share issuances, share repurchases, stock dividends, stock splits, or reverse stock splits, and their respective time weights. This metric is a composite indicator calculated using the weighted average method, rather than raw data directly obtained from accounting records.

It is calculated based on the time-weighted number of shares at the beginning of the period, newly issued shares, and repurchased shares, reflecting the average number of shares after considering the timing of share changes.

nodes.definition: The weighted average number of shares outstanding refers to the average number of shares calculated by weighting the time period each share was outstanding during the reporting period, used in metrics such as earnings per share to reflect potential changes in the number of common shares due to issuances, repurchases, or other reasons.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Price of Market Basket in Base Period
aliases: 基期市场篮子加权平均价格
nodes.definition: The weighted average price of the market basket in the base period is a key benchmark indicator in the compilation of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). It refers to the composite average price calculated by weighting the prices of each good or service in the base period market basket according to their respective shares in the total base period expenditure. It serves as the denominator or base value for calculating the fixed-base price index.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Price of Market Basket in Current Period
Weighted Average Rating Factor (WARF)
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Rating Factor (WARF) is a credit risk metric that measures the notional-weighted average of numerical credit rating factors across a portfolio, commonly used in structured finance to assess overall portfolio credit quality.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Remaining Term (WART)
nodes.definition: Weighted Average Remaining Term (WART) measures the average time to maturity of a portfolio by weighting each instrument's remaining term by its outstanding principal. It is commonly used in fixed-income and asset-backed securities to assess the portfolio’s principal-weighted time to maturity.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Shares Outstanding
nodes.definition: Weighted average shares outstanding represents the average number of common shares in circulation during a reporting period, adjusted for any shares issued or repurchased, used primarily in earnings per share (EPS) calculations.

nodes.name: Weighted Average Unit Cost
aliases: 全月一次加权平均单价
nodes.definition: Weighted average unit cost is an inventory costing method, calculated by dividing the sum of beginning inventory cost and current period purchase cost by the sum of beginning inventory quantity and current period purchase quantity, primarily used to determine the unit cost of goods issued during the period and ending inventory.

formulas.source_formula: Weighted Average Unit Cost = (Beginning Inventory Cost + Current Period Purchase Cost) ÷ (Beginning Inventory Quantity + Current Period Purchase Quantity)

nodes.name: Weighted Average of Current Prices in Market Basket
aliases: Weighted Average Price of Market Basket
市场篮子加权平均价格
篮子商品加权平均价格
nodes.definition: The weighted average of current prices in a market basket is a composite indicator calculated by taking the weighted average of the prices of multiple goods or services within the basket. It relies on the current prices of each good or service and their corresponding weights (typically reflecting market importance or expenditure share). Calculated via a weighted average formula, it is used to measure the average price level of basket goods and is a core computational step in compiling price indices such as the Consumer Price Index.

nodes.name: Weighted Harmonic Mean
nodes.definition: The weighted harmonic mean is a statistical measure used in finance to average ratios (e.g., price-to-earnings) by incorporating relative importance through weights. It gives greater influence to smaller values and is appropriate when averaging rates or multiples across entities, portfolios, or periods, especially when weights represent investment size, market capitalization, or relevance.

nodes.name: Weighted Moving Average
nodes.definition: Weighted Moving Average (WMA) is a price smoothing technique that assigns greater weights to more recent observations within a fixed window, enhancing responsiveness to new information. It is commonly used in technical analysis to highlight trend direction while reducing short-term noise.

nodes.name: Weighted Portfolio Return
nodes.definition: Weighted portfolio return is the overall return of an investment portfolio computed as the sum of each asset's return multiplied by its portfolio weight, reflecting the contribution of each holding to total performance. Under an equal-weighted approach, all assets have identical weights (1/n).

nodes.name: Welfare Expenses
nodes.definition: Welfare expenses refer to costs incurred by an enterprise for providing various benefits to employees beyond salaries, bonuses, and allowances, primarily aimed at improving employees' living standards and safeguarding their health.

nodes.name: Welfare Fund
nodes.definition: A welfare fund is a portion of retained earnings that a company allocates from its after-tax net profit according to regulations, specifically designated for improving collective employee welfare facilities (such as constructing staff dormitories, canteens, nurseries, etc.).

nodes.name: Welfare Fund Appropriated from After-tax Profit
nodes.definition: The welfare fund refers to funds specifically allocated from after-tax profit according to statutory or corporate charter provisions (typically 5% to 10%) for the construction of collective welfare facilities for employees, classified as an owners' equity item.

nodes.name: Whole Life Annuity
nodes.definition: A whole life annuity is an insurance-linked annuity that provides payments for the lifetime of the annuitant. In accumulation analysis, its after-tax future value can be modeled by compounding the principal at the net annual return (gross return less annual charges) over the investment horizon and applying income tax upon withdrawal.

nodes.name: Whole Life Annuity Due
nodes.definition: A whole life annuity due is a level stream of identical payments made at the beginning of each period that continues indefinitely (in perpetuity). Its present value discounts the perpetual series of beginning-of-period cash flows at the effective interest rate per period.

formulas.source_formula: Whole Life Annuity Future Value = Principal × [(1 + Annual Rate) × (1 - Annual Charge)]^Years × (1 - Tax Rate)

nodes.name: Whole-Life Cost
nodes.definition: Whole-life cost (life-cycle cost) is the comprehensive sum of all costs associated with acquiring, owning, operating, maintaining, financing, depreciating, and disposing of an asset over its entire lifespan, including environmental and social impact costs. It supports capital budgeting, procurement, and asset management decisions by revealing the asset’s true total cost.

formulas.source_formula: Whole-Life Cost = Purchase Cost + Installation Cost + Design Cost + Operating Cost + Maintenance Cost + Financing Cost + Depreciation Cost + Disposal Cost + Environmental Cost + Social Impact Cost

nodes.name: Wholesale Price
nodes.definition: Wholesale price refers to the price applied when goods or services are sold by producers or large wholesalers to retailers, other wholesalers, or corporate clients during the wholesale stage. It is typically lower than the retail price due to large purchase volumes and the absence of direct sales to end consumers.

nodes.name: Wholesale Price Index (WPI)
nodes.definition: The Wholesale Price Index (WPI) measures the average change over time in the prices of a representative basket of goods at the wholesale or producer level relative to a base period, and is commonly used to assess producer price inflation.

formulas.source_formula: Wide-Ranging Day Signal = Volatility Ratio - Threshold

nodes.name: Wide-Ranging Days
nodes.definition: Wide-ranging days are trading sessions in which the volatility ratio exceeds a predefined threshold, indicating unusually large intraday price movement. This signal is commonly used in technical analysis to screen for potential reversals or significant momentum shifts.

nodes.name: Wiener Process
nodes.definition: The Wiener process is an important continuous-time stochastic process in mathematical finance and probability theory, used as a mathematical model to describe the irregular motion (i.e., Brownian motion) of particles subjected to numerous tiny random collisions in a fluid. In finance, it is commonly used as the foundation for modeling the stochastic fluctuations of asset prices.

nodes.name: Wilder's DMI (ADX)
nodes.definition: Wilder's Directional Movement Index (DMI) is a technical analysis framework that quantifies trend direction and strength using the Positive Directional Indicator (+DI), Negative Directional Indicator (-DI), and the Average Directional Index (ADX). +DI and -DI compare directional movement relative to the True Range (TR), while ADX smooths the Directional Movement relationship (DX) to measure the strength of the prevailing trend irrespective of direction.

nodes.name: Williams %R
nodes.definition: Williams %R is a momentum oscillator that measures the closing price's position relative to the highest high and lowest low over a specified lookback period, typically ranging from -100 to 0. It is used to identify overbought (near -20) and oversold (near -80) conditions and potential reversal points in financial markets.

formulas.source_formula: Williams %R = −100 × (Highest High − Closing Price) ÷ (Highest High − Lowest Low)

nodes.name: Win Rate
nodes.definition: Win rate is a trading performance metric that measures the proportion of profitable trades to total trades executed, indicating the frequency with which a strategy achieves gains. It is expressed as a decimal or percentage between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%).

formulas.source_formula: Win Rate = Number of Winning Trades ÷ Total Trades

nodes.name: Win/Loss Ratio
nodes.definition: The win/loss ratio is the ratio of the number of winning trades to the number of losing trades, indicating how often a trading strategy wins relative to how often it loses. It does not reflect the magnitude of gains or losses.

formulas.source_formula: Win/Loss Ratio = Number of Winning Trades ÷ Number of Losing Trades

nodes.name: Winsorized Mean
nodes.definition: Winsorized mean is a robust measure of central tendency computed after replacing a specified percentage of the lowest and highest observations with the nearest remaining values, reducing the influence of outliers. It is commonly used in financial data analysis to mitigate the impact of extreme values when estimating averages for performance metrics, risk assessments, or benchmarking.

formulas.source_formula: Winsorized Mean = Sum of Winsorized Values ÷ Number of Observations

nodes.name: Withdrawal Penalty
aliases: Certificate of Deposit Early Withdrawal Penalty
nodes.definition: Withdrawal penalty refers to the additional cost incurred when funds are withdrawn from tax-advantaged retirement accounts before eligible age, typically comprising a statutory penalty on the withdrawn amount plus income taxes owed on the distribution. It is used to estimate the total cost impact of early distributions from accounts such as IRAs and 401(k)s.

formulas.source_formula: Early Withdrawal Penalty = Withdrawal Amount × Early Withdrawal Penalty Rate

nodes.name: Withholding Tax
nodes.definition: Withholding tax is the portion of an employee's wages withheld by an employer and remitted to the tax authority as a prepayment of the employee’s income tax. It is calculated on taxable income after standard deductions and withholding allowances, using progressive tax brackets based on filing status, and may include any additional withholding requested by the taxpayer.

nodes.name: Worden Stochastics
nodes.definition: Worden Stochastics is a technical analysis oscillator that expresses the percentile rank of the most recent closing price relative to the closing prices over a specified lookback period, scaled from 0 to 100, to help identify potential overbought or oversold conditions.

formulas.source_formula: Worden Stochastics = (100 ÷ (Lookback Period - 1)) × (Rank - 1)

nodes.name: Work Completed
nodes.definition: Work completed refers to the total volume or value of work that has been actually finished for a project or task at a specific point in time. It is commonly used to measure project progress and serves as a key component in calculating the project completion percentage.

nodes.name: Work Efficiency
nodes.definition: Work efficiency refers to the ratio between work output completed within a specific period and the resources invested (such as time, manpower, and material resources), used to measure the effectiveness and economy of work processes.

nodes.name: Work Injury Insurance
nodes.definition: Work Injury Insurance is a social insurance system designed to provide workers or their dependents with medical treatment, financial compensation, and vocational rehabilitation assistance from the state and society in the event of accidental injury, occupational disease, temporary or permanent loss of working capacity, or even death arising from work or work-related causes.

nodes.name: Work Loss Value
nodes.definition: Work Loss Value refers to the monetary measurement of economic losses caused by the inability to work normally due to casualties in enterprise occupational injury and fatality accidents. It is typically calculated based on data such as the total lost workdays resulting from the accident, the enterprise's pre-tax profits of the previous year, and the total number of employees, and is used to assess the indirect impact of the accident on the enterprise's production and operations.

nodes.name: Work in Process
nodes.definition: Work in Process refers to items that are currently in the production process, have not completed all processing stages, and cannot be sold as finished goods. It is a significant component of a company's inventory, and its cost primarily includes direct materials already consumed, direct labor, and allocated manufacturing overhead.

nodes.name: Work-in-Process (WIP) Ending-Beginning Balance Difference
nodes.definition: The Work-in-Process (WIP) Ending-Beginning Balance Difference is the variance between the ending work-in-process inventory cost and the beginning work-in-process inventory cost. It reflects the net change in the cost of goods in process during the reporting period and serves as a crucial intermediate indicator for calculating the total output of the current period.

operands.metric: Ending Work in Process Inventory Cost

formulas.source_formula: Work-in-Process Ending-Beginning Balance Difference = Ending Work-in-Process Inventory Cost - Beginning Work-in-Process Inventory Cost

nodes.name: Work-in-Process Quantity
nodes.definition: Work-in-process quantity refers to the physical count of products that have not completed all processing stages and cannot be sold as finished goods at a specific point in time (e.g., month-end). It serves as the foundational data for calculating work-in-process costs and is typically obtained through direct methods such as physical inventory counts, physical enumeration, weighing, or measurement.

nodes.name: Work-in-Progress (WIP) Inventory Cost
nodes.definition: Work-in-Progress (WIP) inventory cost represents the accumulated production costs assigned to partially completed goods at a specific date, including raw materials consumed, direct labor incurred, and manufacturing overhead applied. It is reported within inventory on the balance sheet and supports inventory valuation and cost of goods manufactured calculations.

nodes.name: Workers' Compensation Cost
nodes.definition: Workers' compensation cost is the employer's insurance expense calculated based on payroll and an applicable rate per $100 of payroll, reflecting the cost to insure employees against work-related injuries and illnesses.

nodes.name: Workforce Headcount
nodes.definition: Workforce headcount refers to the number of personnel who actually participate in and perform specific work tasks in particular production, service, or management activities. It is one of the fundamental metrics for measuring labor input, conducting production planning, and calculating labor hour costs.

nodes.name: Working Capital
nodes.definition: Working capital refers to the balance of current assets minus current liabilities used for daily business operations, reflecting a company's short-term solvency and operational efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Working Capital = Current Assets - Current Liabilities

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital = Long-term Capital - Long-term Assets
Working Capital Changes = Changes in Accounts Receivable + Changes in Liabilities + Changes in Inventories + Changes in Other Operating Activities

nodes.name: Working Capital Configuration Ratio
aliases: Working Capital to Current Assets Ratio
nodes.definition: The Working Capital Configuration Ratio is the ratio of working capital to current assets, used to measure the proportion of a company's current assets supported by long-term capital (non-current liabilities and owners' equity). It reflects the adequacy of a company's working capital and its short-term financial security.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Configuration Ratio = (Current Assets - Current Liabilities) ÷ Current Assets
Working Capital Configuration Ratio = Working Capital ÷ Current Assets

nodes.name: Working Capital Increment in the Final Forecast Period
aliases: Change in Working Capital for the Terminal Period
Working Capital Increase in the Final Forecast Period
预测期最后一期营运资金变动
预测期末营运资金增加额
nodes.definition: The working capital increment in the final forecast period refers to the net increase or decrease in working capital in the last period of the forecast timeframe (typically the detailed forecast period) relative to the preceding period, within the context of business valuation or financial forecasting. It reflects the change in short-term net working capital that the enterprise needs to invest or release to maintain normal operations at the end of the forecast period, serving as a critical adjustment item when calculating Free Cash Flow to the Firm (FCFF) or Free Cash Flow to Equity (FCFE).

nodes.name: Working Capital Investment
nodes.definition: Working capital investment is the difference between a company's current assets and current liabilities, used to measure the net funds available for operations in the short term and short-term solvency, and is often a key component of the initial invested capital.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Investment = Working Capital to Current Assets Ratio × Current Assets
Working Capital Investment = Current Assets - Current Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Working Capital Investment = Current Assets - Current Liabilities

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Investment = Annual Operating Revenue × Operating Revenue to Capital Ratio

nodes.name: Working Capital Management
nodes.definition: Working capital management is the process by which a company comprehensively manages its current assets and current liabilities, aiming to support daily operations and maximize corporate value by optimizing the efficiency and risk of components such as accounts receivable, inventory, and cash. It encompasses fund utilization, turnover, and strategy formulation.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Management = Sales Revenue ÷ Average Working Capital

nodes.name: Working Capital Provided Through Other Channels
Working Capital Provided by Other Sources
nodes.definition: Working capital provided by other sources refers to funds obtained by an enterprise through liability methods other than working capital loans from financial institutions such as banks, which can be used for the enterprise's operational turnover in its daily business activities. These funds typically originate from short-term liabilities naturally formed during the business operation process, such as accounts payable to suppliers, notes payable issued, advance payments received from customers, and various other payables. This portion of funds plays a significant role in the enterprise's working capital management and constitutes a component of its short-term financing.

nodes.name: Working Capital Ratio
nodes.definition: Working capital ratio measures a company's ability to cover its current liabilities with its current assets, indicating short-term liquidity and financial health.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities
supporting_source_formulas: Working Capital Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities

nodes.name: Working Capital Reduction in the Final Forecast Period
aliases: Decrease in Working Capital at the End of Forecast Period
末期营运资本变动减少额
预测期末营运资本减少额
预测期营运资本净减少
nodes.definition: Working capital reduction in the final forecast period refers to the amount by which working capital decreases in the last year (or period) of the forecast horizon relative to the preceding period, within a corporate financial forecasting model. Working capital typically refers to the difference between operating current assets (such as accounts receivable and inventory) and operating current liabilities (such as accounts payable). This reduction indicates a decrease in the net working capital employed by the business at the end of the forecast period and is typically treated as a cash inflow, incorporated into the calculation of operating cash flow for the final forecast period.

nodes.name: Working Capital Requirement
nodes.definition: Working capital requirement refers to the total amount of liquid funds that an enterprise needs to occupy to maintain its daily production and operating activities (such as purchasing raw materials, paying wages, selling products, etc.). It reflects the scale of an enterprise's short-term funding needs during its operating cycle and is a key indicator for assessing its short-term solvency and operational efficiency.

nodes.name: Working Capital Turnover
nodes.definition: Working capital turnover is an activity (efficiency) ratio that measures how effectively a company utilizes its working capital to generate sales. It is calculated by dividing net sales by average working capital; higher values indicate more efficient use of short-term assets and liabilities.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Turnover = Net Sales ÷ Average Working Capital

nodes.name: Working Capital Turnover Ratio
nodes.definition: The Working Capital Turnover Ratio is a financial ratio used to measure a company's efficiency in utilizing working capital to generate sales revenue. This ratio is calculated by dividing net sales by average working capital, reflecting the amount of sales generated per dollar of working capital invested.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Turnover Ratio = Net Sales ÷ Average Working Capital

nodes.name: Working Capital Turnover Times
nodes.definition: Working Capital Turnover Times refers to the number of times working capital is cycled within a specific period (usually one year), used to measure the efficiency of working capital utilization and the management level of liquidity. A higher value of this indicator typically indicates faster working capital turnover and higher utilization efficiency.

formulas.source_formula: Working Capital Turnover Times = 365 ÷ (Days Inventory Outstanding + Days Sales Outstanding - Days Payable Outstanding + Prepaid Expenses Turnover Days - Deferred Revenue Turnover Days)

nodes.name: Working Ratio
aliases: Operating Expense Ratio (excluding Depreciation and Debt Expenses)
nodes.definition: Working ratio measures the proportion of cash-operating expenses to annual gross income. It excludes depreciation and debt-related expenses from total annual expenses. A value below 1 indicates that operating revenues cover operating costs; a value above 1 indicates they do not.

formulas.source_formula: Working Ratio = (Total Annual Expenses - (Depreciation + Debt Expenses)) ÷ Annual Gross Income

nodes.name: Workload
nodes.definition: Workload refers to the total amount of resources required to complete a specific task or project. It is a composite metric that can be calculated using basic indicators such as task quantity, working time per task, resource requirements, work efficiency, manpower input, and project duration. It is commonly used for project estimation, cost accounting, and resource allocation.

formulas.source_formula: Workload = Workload Coefficient × Manpower Input × Project Duration

nodes.name: Workload Coefficient
nodes.definition: The workload coefficient is an adjustment parameter used to quantify factors such as task complexity, technical difficulty, and risk level. In project management, cost estimation, and financial accounting, it typically serves as a multiplier, combined with baseline data such as labor input and project duration, to more accurately calculate or assess total workload, resource requirements, or project costs.

nodes.name: Workload of Individual Subtasks
nodes.definition: Workload of individual subtasks refers to the quantitative assessment of resources, time, or effort consumed by each smaller, more specific sub-task after decomposing an overall task or project. It constitutes the fundamental unit of the total workload.

nodes.name: Wraparound Mortgage Payment
nodes.definition: A wraparound mortgage payment is the single monthly payment on a wraparound (all-inclusive) loan that encompasses the remaining balance of the original mortgage and the additional financing needed to complete a property purchase. It is computed by amortizing the original mortgage balance at its original rate and the incremental loan amount at the new wraparound rate over a common term, then summing the two payments.

formulas.source_formula: Wraparound Payment = Original Monthly Payment + New Monthly Payment

nodes.name: Write-Down
nodes.definition: A write-down is the reduction of an asset's carrying amount to its fair market value when that value falls below the carrying amount, with the difference recognized as a loss in profit or loss and the asset's book value reduced on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Write-Down = Carrying Value - Fair Market Value

nodes.name: Write-Up
nodes.definition: Write-up refers to the upward adjustment of an asset’s carrying amount to reflect its fair market value when fair market value exceeds book value. The write-up amount equals the excess of fair market value over book value and is commonly recognized in purchase price allocation during mergers and acquisitions to align acquired assets with their fair values for financial reporting.

formulas.source_formula: Write-Up = Fair Market Value - Book Value

nodes.name: Write-offs and Recoveries for the Period
aliases: Write-off and Reversal Amount for the Period
nodes.definition: Write-offs and recoveries for the period refer to the total or net amount of bad debt actually written off (i.e., confirmed as uncollectible and charged off) by an enterprise during the current accounting period, plus the amount recovered (i.e., reversed) due to the partial or full collection of previously written-off bad debts in the current period. It reflects the actual change in the allowance for doubtful accounts during the period and is a key component in calculating the ending balance of the allowance for doubtful accounts.

nodes.name: Written Premium
nodes.definition: Written premium is the total contractual premium on insurance policies issued during a specified period, reflecting production rather than earned revenue. It represents the amount policyholders agreed to pay for policies written, commonly presented on a gross or net basis depending on reinsurance, and may be approximated as the number of policies sold multiplied by the premium per policy when pricing is uniform.

formulas.source_formula: Written Premium = Number of Policies Sold × Premium per Policy

nodes.name: Written-Down Value
nodes.definition: Written-down value is the carrying amount of an asset on the balance sheet after deducting accumulated depreciation or amortization from its original cost. It represents the asset’s current net book value used for financial reporting and analysis.

formulas.source_formula: Written-Down Value = Original Cost - Accumulated Depreciation
YTD Growth Factor = Current Value ÷ Initial Value

nodes.name: Year 1 EBIT of Continuing Period
aliases: EBIT of First Year in Terminal Period
永续期首年息税前利润
nodes.definition: Year 1 EBIT of the continuing period refers to a company's earnings before interest and taxes in the first year after the forecast period ends, when the company enters a stable growth phase (i.e., the continuing or terminal period) in business valuation. It reflects the company's core operating profitability under a long-term steady state and serves as the key starting point for calculating the continuing period's free cash flow to the firm and net operating profit after tax.

formulas.source_formula: Year n Withdrawal = Year (n-1) Withdrawal × (1 + Inflation Rate)

nodes.name: Year to Date Return
nodes.definition: Year to Date (YTD) return measures the percentage change in the value of an investment from the beginning of the current calendar year to the present date, indicating its performance over that period.

formulas.source_formula: YTD Return = ((Current Value ÷ Initial Value) - 1) × 100

nodes.name: Year-End Bonus
nodes.definition: Year-end bonus is a lump-sum payment made to employees at the end of the fiscal or calendar year, calculated as a percentage of the employee’s annual base salary.

formulas.source_formula: Year-End Bonus = Annual Salary × (Bonus Percentage ÷ 100)
Year-End Gain = End-of-Year Value - Purchase Value

nodes.name: Year-Over-Year Growth
nodes.definition: Year-over-year growth measures the percentage change in a financial metric by comparing the current period's value to the same period in the previous year, providing insight into long-term performance trends.

formulas.source_formula: YOY Growth = ((Current Value ÷ Previous Value) - 1) × 100

nodes.name: Year-end Balance of Asset Impairment Provisions
aliases: Year-end Balance of Asset Impairment Provision
资产减值准备期末余额
nodes.definition: The year-end balance of asset impairment provisions refers to the cumulative remaining amount in the impairment provision accounts for various assets (such as accounts receivable, inventory, fixed assets, etc.) accrued by an enterprise in accordance with accounting standards at the end of the fiscal year. It reflects the anticipated potential value losses of assets and is presented as a contra account to the corresponding assets on the balance sheet.

nodes.name: Year-end Loan Balance
nodes.definition: Year-end loan balance refers to the total principal amount of all loans extended by financial institutions (such as banks) to borrowers that remain outstanding at the end of a fiscal year (typically December 31). It reflects the scale and stock of credit assets held by financial institutions at that point in time.

nodes.name: Year-end Net Asset Value
nodes.definition: Year-end net asset value refers to the residual equity value attributable to owners (shareholders) after deducting total liabilities from total assets at the end of a specific fiscal year. It is a core static indicator for measuring a company's financial position and shareholder wealth.

formulas.source_formula: Year-end Net Asset Value = Total Assets - Total Liabilities

operands.metric: Net Asset Value from Two Years Prior

formulas.source_formula: Year-end Net Asset Value = (Current Year-end Net Asset Value + Previous Year-end Net Asset Value + Net Asset Value from Two Years Prior) ÷ 3

nodes.name: Year-end Owners' Equity
nodes.definition: Year-end owners' equity refers to the residual interest in the assets of an entity after deducting its liabilities at the end of an accounting year, reflecting the net asset position of the enterprise at a specific point in time and serving as a core item on the balance sheet.

formulas.source_formula: Year-end Owners' Equity = Total Year-end Assets - Total Year-end Liabilities
Year-end Owners' Equity = Beginning Owners' Equity + Current Year Net Profit

nodes.name: Year-end Retained Earnings
nodes.definition: Year-end retained earnings refer to the cumulative balance of profits remaining after profit distribution (such as allocation to surplus reserves, distribution of dividends to shareholders, etc.) at the end of each fiscal year, which is to be allocated or carried forward for future periods. It is a significant component of shareholders' equity.

Year-on-Year Secondary Industry Value-Added Rate
aliases: Previous Year Secondary Industry Value Added Ratio
Value Added Rate of Secondary Industry in Same Period Last Year
