上年第二产业增加值率
上年第二产业附加价值率
nodes.definition: The Year-on-Year Secondary Industry Value-Added Rate refers to the ratio of the value added created by the secondary industry (typically including industry and construction) to its total output during the same period (e.g., the same quarter or month) of the previous year. It reflects the capacity and efficiency of the secondary industry in generating new value during the production process in the same period of the previous year, serving as an important indicator for measuring industrial economic efficiency.

nodes.name: Year-over-Year Data
nodes.definition: Year-over-year data refers to the value of a specific financial metric (such as operating revenue, net profit, etc.) during the same accounting period (e.g., month, quarter, year) in the previous year. It is not a raw data item but rather historical data derived through time-dimension data queries or calculations, serving as a fundamental component for calculating derived financial metrics such as year-over-year growth rates.

formulas.source_formula: Year-over-Year Data = Current Period Data ÷ (1 + Year-over-Year Growth Rate)

nodes.name: Year-over-Year Growth Rate
nodes.definition: Year-over-Year Growth Rate is a key financial and economic indicator used to measure the growth magnitude of a specific economic metric (such as sales revenue or profit) in a given period (e.g., current month or quarter) compared to the same period in the previous year. It is primarily employed to eliminate the effects of seasonal fluctuations and reflect the true development pace of the indicator across years.

nodes.name: Year-over-Year Growth Rate of Accounts Receivable
nodes.definition: The Year-over-Year Growth Rate of Accounts Receivable is a financial metric that measures the growth rate of the ending balance of accounts receivable in a given period (usually one year) compared to the ending balance of the previous comparable period. It is used to analyze a company's credit policy, sales collection efficiency, and potential bad debt risk.

operands.metric: Accounts Receivable at End of Current Period
Accounts Receivable at End of Previous Period

formulas.source_formula: Year-over-Year Growth Rate of Accounts Receivable = (Accounts Receivable at End of Current Period - Accounts Receivable at End of Previous Period) ÷ Accounts Receivable at End of Previous Period × 100%

nodes.name: Year-over-Year Statistical Period Data
nodes.definition: Year-over-Year Statistical Period Data refers to the original numerical values obtained from the statistical recording of specific fundamental financial or operational metrics (such as operating revenue, costs, profits, total assets, etc.) during the same corresponding period in the previous year (e.g., the same quarter, month, or week). It is primarily used for comparison with current period data to analyze trends in business or financial performance.

nodes.name: Year-to-Date Annualized Yield
nodes.definition: Year-to-Date Annualized Yield projects the percentage return observed from the beginning of the year up to the current date into an equivalent annual rate, assuming the same growth pace continues for the remainder of the year.

nodes.name: Yearly Probability of Dying
nodes.definition: The yearly probability of dying represents the likelihood that an individual within a specified population will die during a one-year period, calculated as the ratio of deaths to the initial population exposed to risk.

formulas.source_formula: Yearly Probability of Dying = Deaths ÷ Population at Start

nodes.name: Yearly Probability of Living
nodes.definition: The yearly probability of living represents the likelihood that an individual will survive for one year, calculated as the complement of the yearly probability of dying. It is a fundamental metric in actuarial science and insurance for pricing life insurance and annuity products.

formulas.source_formula: Yearly Probability of Living = 1 - Yearly Probability of Dying
Yearly Probability of Living = Survivors ÷ Initial Population

nodes.name: Yearly Rate of Return
nodes.definition: Yearly rate of return, also known as compound annual growth rate (CAGR), measures the mean annual growth rate of an investment over a specified time period longer than one year, accounting for compounding.

formulas.source_formula: Annual Return = (Ending Value ÷ Beginning Value)^(1 ÷ Holding Period Years) - 1

nodes.name: Yearly Renewable Term Reinsurance Premium
aliases: 年度可续保再保险保费
nodes.definition: Yearly Renewable Term (YRT) reinsurance premium refers to the annual premium payable under a reinsurance agreement where the coverage is renewed each year based on the net amount at risk, adjusted for the policyholder's age and a base premium rate.

formulas.source_formula: YRT Premium = Net Amount at Risk × Base Rate × (1 + Age ÷ 100)

nodes.name: Years Certain Annuity Payout
nodes.definition: Years certain annuity payout is the fixed periodic payment amount received from an annuity that guarantees payments for a specified number of periods, regardless of the annuitant's survival.

formulas.source_formula: Years to Double (Rule of 72) = 72 ÷ Annual Rate of Return

nodes.name: Years to Double Investment (Rule of 72)
nodes.definition: The Rule of 72 is a heuristic that estimates the number of years required for an investment to double given a constant annual rate of return. The doubling time is approximated by dividing 72 by the annual rate of return (expressed as a percentage), making it useful for quick mental calculations and preliminary financial planning.

formulas.source_formula: Years to Double Investment = 72 ÷ Annual Rate of Return

nodes.name: Years to Maturity
nodes.definition: Years to Maturity refers to the remaining time length from the current date (or a specified start date) to the maturity date of a financial instrument (such as a bond), typically expressed in years. It is a crucial input variable for calculating key metrics like yield to maturity and belongs to the category of date-dependent composite indicators.

formulas.source_formula: Years to Maturity = (Maturity Date - Current Date) ÷ 365
Years to Maturity = (Maturity Date - Start Date) ÷ 365

nodes.name: Yield Basis
nodes.definition: Yield basis is the annual coupon payment of a fixed-income security divided by its purchase price, expressed as a percentage. It standardizes bond pricing into a yield metric for easy comparison across bonds with different prices and characteristics.

formulas.source_formula: Yield Basis = Coupon Amount ÷ Purchase Price

nodes.name: Yield Curve Spread
nodes.definition: Yield curve spread refers to the difference between longer-term and shorter-term Treasury yields, commonly the 10-year minus the 2-year yield. It gauges the slope of the yield curve and is widely used to assess interest rate term structure, financial conditions, and recession risk when inverted.

formulas.source_formula: Yield Curve Spread = 10-Year Treasury Yield - 2-Year Treasury Yield
Yield Factor = 1 + Net Investment Income ÷ (Average Shares Outstanding × Maximum Price per Share)

nodes.name: Yield Maintenance Premium
nodes.definition: Yield maintenance premium is a prepayment penalty on fixed-rate loans that compensates the lender for the lost interest income when a borrower repays the loan early, ensuring the lender receives the same yield as if all scheduled payments were made to maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Yield Maintenance Premium = Present Value × (Loan Interest Rate − Treasury Yield)

nodes.name: Yield Pickup
nodes.definition: Yield pickup is the additional interest rate gained when an investor sells a lower-yielding bond and purchases a higher-yielding bond, representing the incremental return from switching bonds in a portfolio.

formulas.source_formula: Yield Pickup = New Bond Yield - Current Bond Yield

nodes.name: Yield Spread
nodes.definition: Yield spread is the difference between the yield on a long-term bond and a short-term bond, typically expressed in basis points, used to assess the shape of the yield curve and economic outlook.

formulas.source_formula: Yield Spread = Yield1 - Yield2

operands.metric: Long-term Government Bond Yield to Maturity

formulas.source_formula: Yield Spread = Long-Term Treasury Yield - Short-Term Treasury Yield
Yield Spread = Yield of Security 2 - Yield of Security 1
Yield Spread (Basis Points) = (Yield1 - Yield2) × 100

nodes.name: Yield on Cost
nodes.definition: Yield on Cost (YOC) measures the annual return on an investment relative to its original cost, expressed as a percentage. It combines capital appreciation and dividend income to assess the profitability of a stock investment based on the purchase price.

formulas.source_formula: Yield on Cost = (Current Dividend ÷ Initial Price) × 100
Yield on Cost = (Price Increase + Dividends Paid) ÷ Purchase Price × 100

nodes.name: Yield on Earning Assets
nodes.definition: Yield on Earning Assets is a financial solvency ratio that measures the efficiency with which a financial institution uses its interest-generating assets to produce interest income, expressed as a percentage or ratio.

formulas.source_formula: Yield on Earning Assets = Interest Income ÷ Earning Assets

nodes.name: Yield to Average Life
nodes.definition: Yield to Average Life is the internal rate of return of a bond calculated using the bond's average life instead of its stated maturity, reflecting the yield based on the weighted average time to principal repayment.

formulas.source_formula: Yield to Average Life = (Total Cash Flows ÷ Market Price)^(1 ÷ Average Life Years) - 1

nodes.name: Yield to Call
nodes.definition: Yield to Call (YTC) is the internal rate of return earned by an investor if a callable bond is held until the call date, calculated as the discount rate that equates the bond’s current market price to the present value of its future coupon payments and call price.

formulas.source_formula: YTC = (Coupon Payment + (Call Price - Market Value) ÷ Years Until Call) ÷ ((Call Price + Market Value) ÷ 2)

nodes.name: Yield to Maturity
aliases: Internal Rate of Return on Bond
nodes.definition: Yield to Maturity (YTM) is the discount rate that equates the present value of a bond's future cash flows to its current purchase price. It represents the bond's internal rate of return, reflecting the expected annualized return if held until maturity, and is commonly used to estimate the pre-tax cost of debt capital.

formulas.source_formula: Yield to Maturity = (Face Value / Present Value)^(1 / Period) - 1
Yield to Maturity = ((Face Value × Coupon Rate) + (Face Value - Market Price) ÷ Years to Maturity) ÷ ((Face Value + Market Price) ÷ 2)
Yield to Maturity (Treasury STRIPS) = (Face Value ÷ Purchase Price)^(1 ÷ Years to Maturity) - 1

nodes.name: Yield to Maturity of Comparable Company Long-term Bonds
nodes.definition: The yield to maturity of comparable company long-term bonds refers to the internal rate of return that investors can obtain by holding the bond until its maturity date. It reflects the expected return of the bond and is an important indicator for estimating a company's pre-tax cost of debt capital. It is calculated based on fundamental data such as bond price, coupon interest, face value, and time to maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Yield to Maturity of Comparable Company Long-term Bonds = [Bond Face Value × (1 + Coupon Rate × Bond Effective Term) - Bond Purchase Price] ÷ (Bond Purchase Price × Remaining Term to Maturity) × 100%

nodes.name: Yield to Maturity of Comparable Company's Long-term Bond
Z-Score
nodes.definition: Z-score measures how many standard deviations a price is from its mean, commonly used in quantitative and technical analysis to identify deviations that may signal mean reversion opportunities.

formulas.source_formula: Z-Score = (Observed Value - Population Mean) ÷ Population Standard Deviation
Z-Score = (Value - Mean) ÷ Standard Deviation
Z-Score = (Price - Mean) ÷ Standard Deviation

nodes.name: Z-Test
nodes.definition: A z-test is a statistical hypothesis test used to determine whether a sample mean significantly differs from a known population mean when the population standard deviation is known and the sample size is large. In financial analysis, it is applied to evaluate differences in average returns, transaction amounts, or other financial metrics under normality assumptions.

nodes.name: Z-value Corresponding to Confidence Level
nodes.definition: The Z-value corresponding to a confidence level refers to the critical value in a standard normal distribution that corresponds to a specific confidence level (e.g., 90%, 95%, 99%). It represents the distance from the mean to that point on the normal distribution curve, where the area (probability) covered equals half of the confidence level (for a two-tailed test). This value is typically obtained by consulting a standard normal distribution table or using statistical software and serves as a key foundational parameter for constructing confidence intervals and conducting hypothesis testing.

nodes.name: Z-value for Confidence Level
nodes.definition: The Z-value for a confidence level is a critical point value on the standard normal distribution corresponding to a specific confidence level (e.g., 90%, 95%, 99%) in statistics. It represents the quantile point under the standard normal distribution curve where the central area equals that confidence level. For example, the Z-value for a 95% confidence level is approximately 1.96, meaning that 95% of the data in a standard normal distribution falls within the range of the mean ± 1.96 standard deviations. This value is typically obtained by consulting a standard normal distribution table or using statistical software, and is used for constructing confidence intervals or conducting hypothesis testing.

nodes.name: ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment
nodes.definition: The ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment is a survey-based macroeconomic indicator that measures the net balance between the percentage of optimistic and pessimistic expert expectations about the economy, commonly reported for Germany. It reflects forward-looking sentiment by financial analysts and economists and is computed as the difference between the share of optimists and pessimists.

formulas.source_formula: ZEW Indicator of Economic Sentiment = Optimistic Percentage - Pessimistic Percentage

nodes.name: Zakat
nodes.definition: Zakat is an obligatory charitable levy in Islamic finance, assessed at 2.5% of an individual's net wealth (total wealth minus liabilities) when that net wealth meets or exceeds the nisab threshold. The nisab is determined by the market value of either 87.48 grams of gold or 612.36 grams of silver. If net wealth is below the nisab, no zakat is due.

nodes.name: Zero
nodes.definition: In the field of finance and accounting, 'Zero' typically refers to the specific numerical value zero or a zero-value state. It can indicate a cash balance of zero, the integer result after rounding down amounts, items counted as zero, or change given in cash transactions. It is a fundamental raw data point, not a financial metric derived from complex calculations.

nodes.name: Zero Cost Collar
nodes.definition: A zero cost collar is an options hedging strategy that combines purchasing a protective put and selling a covered call on an existing stock position, typically structured so the net option premium is approximately zero. It limits downside risk to the put strike while capping upside potential at the call strike, with minimal or no net cash outlay.

nodes.name: Zero Coupon Inflation Swap
nodes.definition: A Zero-Coupon Inflation Swap (ZCIS) is an inflation derivative in which counterparties exchange, at maturity, a single payment based on the cumulative inflation over the period versus a fixed rate payment. The fixed leg payment under annual compounding is determined by applying the agreed fixed rate to the notional over the life of the swap. ZCIS is commonly used for hedging inflation exposure and inferring breakeven inflation rates.

nodes.name: Zero Coupon Swap
nodes.definition: A Zero Coupon Swap is an interest rate swap in which one leg (typically the fixed leg) accrues over the life of the contract and is settled as a single payment at maturity, rather than via periodic coupons. The floating leg is often compounded over the same horizon. Zero coupon swaps are used to hedge or take views on the term structure of interest rates, and their valuation relies on discount factors and implied forward rates derived from spot rates.

nodes.name: Zero-Beta Portfolio
nodes.definition: A zero-beta portfolio is constructed so that its beta relative to the market is zero, implying no systematic (market) risk exposure. Its expected returns should be independent of market movements, and it is often used in CAPM applications, market-neutral strategies, and as a benchmark for isolating idiosyncratic performance.

nodes.name: Zero-Coupon Bond Price
aliases: Present Value of a Zero-Coupon Bond
nodes.definition: Zero-coupon bond price refers to the present value of a bond that pays no periodic interest and is repaid at face value only at maturity. Its calculation is based on the time value of money principle, obtained by discounting the face value to the present point in time using the market discount rate.

formulas.source_formula: Zero-Coupon Bond Price = Maturity Value ÷ (1 + Interest Rate) ^ Years to Maturity
Zero-Coupon Bond Price = Face Value ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Periods

nodes.name: Zero-Coupon Bond Value
nodes.definition: The present value of a zero-coupon bond, calculated by discounting its face value back to today using the appropriate discount rate over the time to maturity.

formulas.source_formula: Zero-Coupon Bond Value = Face Value ÷ (1 + Discount Rate) ^ Time to Maturity

nodes.name: Zero-Coupon CD Annual Yield
aliases: 零息定期存单年收益率
nodes.definition: Zero-Coupon CD Annual Yield is the effective annual rate, expressed as a percentage, that equates the present purchase price to the face value received at maturity over a specified number of years. It reflects the compounded return assuming the CD is held to maturity and excludes tax and interim cash flows.

formulas.source_formula: Zero-Coupon CD Annual Yield (%) = ((Face Value ÷ Purchase Price)^(1 ÷ Years) - 1) × 100

nodes.name: Zero-Coupon Mortgage Maturity Value
aliases: 零息抵押贷款到期价值
nodes.definition: Zero-coupon mortgage maturity value is the total payoff due at the end of the loan term when no periodic interest payments are made; interest accrues and compounds on the principal, and both principal and accumulated interest are paid at maturity.

nodes.name: Zero-Coupon Rate
nodes.definition: The zero-coupon rate (spot rate) is the annualized yield applicable to a single cash flow at a specific maturity that discounts that cash flow to its present value. It is typically derived by solving the bond pricing equation so that the present value of coupon payments and principal equals the observed market price, often under semiannual compounding conventions. Zero-coupon rates are foundational inputs for constructing the par yield curve and the broader term structure of interest rates.

nodes.name: Zero-Proof Bookkeeping
nodes.definition: Zero-proof bookkeeping is a reconciliation technique that verifies the equality of total debits and total credits. A zero difference between the sum of debits and the sum of credits confirms that entries are balanced, serving as a simple control for manual bookkeeping and small sets of transactions.

nodes.name: Zero-Volatility Spread (Z-spread)
nodes.definition: The zero-volatility spread (Z-spread) is the constant spread added to each point on the Treasury spot rate curve such that the present value of a bond’s cash flows, discounted using the adjusted spot rates, equals the bond’s current market price. It represents the bond’s compensation for credit and liquidity risk over the risk-free yield curve, assuming no volatility and a parallel shift across maturities.

nodes.name: Zig Zag Indicator
nodes.definition: The Zig Zag indicator is a technical analysis tool that filters out minor price fluctuations by plotting points only when price moves by at least a specified percentage from the last extreme, thereby highlighting significant swings and trend reversals.

nodes.name: Zomma
aliases: Zomma（伽玛对波动率的变化率）
伽玛对隐含波动率的敏感度
nodes.definition: Zomma is a higher-order options Greek representing the rate of change of Gamma with respect to Implied Volatility (∂Gamma/∂σ). It quantifies how shifts in implied volatility impact Gamma and, indirectly, Delta, assisting in advanced options risk management and hedging.

formulas.source_formula: Zomma = (Gamma Final - Gamma Initial) ÷ (Implied Volatility Final - Implied Volatility Initial)

nodes.name: e (Base of Natural Logarithm)
nodes.definition: e is a mathematical constant, the base of the natural logarithm, with an approximate value of 2.71828. In financial mathematics, e is the core foundation for models such as continuous compound interest calculation and the standard normal distribution probability density function.

nodes.name: t-Statistic
nodes.definition: The t-Statistic (t-Score) quantifies the standardized difference between a sample mean and a hypothesized population mean when the population standard deviation is unknown, using the sample standard deviation and sample size. It supports inference via the Student's t-distribution for hypothesis testing and confidence intervals in small-sample contexts common in financial and accounting analyses.

nodes.name: π (Pi)
nodes.definition: Pi (π) is a universal mathematical constant in mathematics and physics, defined as the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter, which is also equal to the ratio of a circle's area to the square of its radius. It is an infinite non-repeating decimal, commonly approximated as 3.14159.
